Upāsana means: in the arthavāda of the upāsya, just as the deity's svarūpa is taught by the śruti, so, having approached it by the mind, āsana — meditative dwelling — without the interruption of laukika-pratyayas, until the manifestation of the abhimāna of one's Ātman as that deity's svarūpa, in the manner of the laukika ātmābhimāna — as in "devo bhūtvā devān apyeti" (Bṛ. Up. 4.1.2), "kindevato'syāṃ prācyāṃ diśy asi" (Bṛ. Up. 3.9.20), and other śruti.
BR_C01_S03_V10: Verily this deity, having struck off mṛtyu, the pāpman of these deities, sent him to where the end of these directions is, and there she deposited their pāpmans. Therefore one should not approach a (foreign/border) people, nor go to that frontier, lest one be overtaken by mṛtyu, the pāpman.
BR_C01_S03_V10::block-0: It has been said: "sā vā eṣā devatā ... dūraṃ ha vā asmān mṛtyur bhavati." But how does mṛtyu become far for the knower? It is said: by virtue of being incompatible with such knowership. The pāpman born of saṅga from the contact of indriyas with viṣayas is in opposition to one whose abhimāna is of the prāṇa-Ātman; for it is the cause of the abhimāna of the particular ātmans of vāk and the rest, and the cause of natural ajñāna; whereas the abhimāna of the prāṇa-Ātman is born of śāstra. Therefore from the knower thus described, the pāpman becomes far — this is right, by virtue of contradiction. The śruti now displays this:
BR_C01_S03_V10::block-1:
"Sā vā eṣā devatā" — the meaning is as before. Of these deities of vāk and the rest, the "pāpman, mṛtyu" — for everyone dies through the pāpman generated by the saṅga of the contact of indriya with viṣaya, prompted by natural ajñāna; that is mṛtyu — that mṛtyu, from the deities who are themselves of the form of prāṇa-ātma-abhimāna, "apahatya" — having struck off, having severed.

Properly, prāṇa is called "apahantṛ" only in the sense of the mere abhimāna of the prāṇa as Ātman; it is by mere contradiction that the pāpman becomes far for the knower. But what then did the prāṇa do, having struck off the pāpman, mṛtyu, of the deities? It is said: "yatra" — wherever, "āsām" — of these directions beginning with the eastern, "antaḥ" — the end, "tat" — there, "gamayāṃ cakāra" — caused them to go.

Objection: there is no end of the directions; how then could she lead them to the end? Reply: since the directions are conceptually ascertained (kalpita) by means of the limits set by the people endowed with śrauta-vijñāna, the region inhabited by the people opposed to them is itself the "end of directions," just as "the end of the country" is the wilderness — hence no fault. Having taken them there, of these deities, "pāpmanaḥ" (genitive — but here in dvitīyā-bahuvacana sense, accusative plural), "vinyadadhāt" — the prāṇa-deity deposited variously, with subordination, established. By implication, this is among those low-born people who are devoid of the abhimāna of the prāṇa-Ātman; for the pāpman is born of indriya-saṃsarga, hence its dependence on prāṇis is understood.

Therefore one should not approach (na iyāt) such a foreign people; one should not commune with them by conversation, sight, and so on. By such contact, contact with pāpman is established, for that is the seat of pāpman. And the place where they dwell, denoted by the term "end of directions," one should not approach — even if devoid of people, even people separate from that region — this is the intention. "Net" is a particle in the sense of fear. "Pāpmānaṃ mṛtyum anvavāyāni" — "may I not follow after, may I not undergo" — being thus afraid, one should not approach either the people or the end (of the directions): this connects with the previous clause.
BR_C01_S03_V11: Verily this deity, having struck off mṛtyu, the pāpman of these deities, then carried these (deities) beyond mṛtyu.
BR_C01_S03_V11::block-0: "Sā vā eṣā devatā" — this is the fruit of the knowledge and karma of the prāṇa-Ātman: the becoming of vāk and the rest as the deva-svarūpas of agni and the rest is now stated. "Athainā mṛtyum atyavahat" — since the pāpman, mṛtyu, the cause of adhyātmika-pariccheda (the limitation of one to the body), is struck off by prāṇātma-vijñāna, therefore that prāṇa is the apahantṛ of mṛtyu, the pāpman. Therefore this very prāṇa carried these vāk-and-other deities, beyond the pāpman, mṛtyu in question — "atītya avahat" — caused them to attain their own apariccinna (unlimited) form of agni-and-other-deva-svarūpa.
BR_C01_S03_V12: He carried vāk first; when she was released from mṛtyu, she became Agni; this Agni, having transcended mṛtyu, blazes beyond it.
BR_C01_S03_V12::block-0: "Sa vai vācam eva prathamām atyavahat" — that prāṇa carried vāk first, that is, foremost — for in the udgītha-karman, in comparison with the other karaṇas, vāk is sādhakatama (the most efficient instrument), hence her prādhānya (primacy); that very prathamā he carried, performed the carrying. When carried beyond mṛtyu, what is her form? It is said — that vāk, "yadā" — at which time, was "atyamucyata" — released, freed of herself from the pāpman, mṛtyu, then she —
BR_C01_S03_V12::block-1: "agnir abhavat" — that vāk, even before being agni, on separation from mṛtyu, became agni indeed. The distinction in being separated from mṛtyu is only this: "so'yam atikrāntaḥ agniḥ" — this very agni, transcended (mṛtyu), "pareṇa mṛtyum," beyond mṛtyu, dīpyate — blazes. Before mokṣa, while bound by mṛtyu, in the form of adhyātma-vāk, he was not luminous as he is now; now, on separation from mṛtyu, beyond mṛtyu, he blazes by virtue of mṛtyu-viyoga.
BR_C01_S03_V13: Then he carried prāṇa (the sense of smell); when it was released from mṛtyu, it became Vāyu; this Vāyu, having transcended mṛtyu, blows beyond it.
BR_C01_S03_V13::block-0: Likewise — "prāṇaḥ" here means ghrāṇa (the sense of smell) — "vāyur abhavat" — became Vāyu; and it "pavate" — blows, having transcended mṛtyu, beyond it. The rest is as already explained.
BR_C01_S03_V14: Then it carried the eye beyond death; when that was released from death, it became the sun. That sun, having transcended death, glows with surpassing splendour.
BR_C01_S03_V14::block-0: Likewise the eye became the sun; and that sun shines forth radiantly. The same pattern that obtained for speech-becoming-fire is here re-stated: the organ, freed from the taint of death by the action of mukhya-prāṇa, abides as a luminous deity transcending mortality.
BR_C01_S03_V15: Then it carried hearing beyond death; when that was released from death, it became the directions; these directions which we now perceive have transcended death.
BR_C01_S03_V15::block-0: Likewise the ear became the directions; the directions stand established by the partition into east and so on. As speech and the eye, having shed the asura-blemish through prāṇa, became the deities of fire and sun, so the ear, similarly purified, abides as the quarters distinguished as east, south, west, and north — and these very quarters, fixed in their respective stations, are the immortal residue of the organ that the ear was.
BR_C01_S03_V16: Then it carried the mind beyond death; when that was released from death, it became the moon; that moon, having transcended death, shines. So this deity carries beyond death anyone who knows thus.
BR_C01_S03_V16::block-0:
The mind became the moon, and it shines. Just as it carried the former sacrificer beyond death by transforming him into speech-and-fire and the rest, so does this prāṇa-deity, ha vai (verily, indeed), carry beyond death the present sacrificer also, by re-establishing him as speech-and-fire and so on — that is, anyone who thus knows the prāṇa as endowed with the fivefold ensemble of speech and the rest. The śruti corroborates this: ‘In whichever way they meditate upon him, that very thing he becomes’ (Śat. Br. X.5.2.20). The fruit, therefore, accrues precisely in the form of the upāsanā undertaken; the karaṇa-s, purified of the asura-taint, abide as devatā-s and constitute the very body of the knower's release from mortality.

Here the pravṛtti-mārga of vāg-ādi entangled in puṇya-pāpa is contrasted with the nivṛtti-aspect of prāṇa, which is by nature free of such contamination; meditation on prāṇa therefore amounts to meditation on the unstained Self present as the principle of life in all the karaṇa-s.
BR_C01_S03_V17: Then he sang for himself the food to be eaten; for whatever food is eaten is eaten by him alone, and he is established here.
BR_C01_S03_V17::block-0:
Now ‘for himself.’ Just as the speech and the rest performed the singing for the sake of the Self, so the mukhya-prāṇa too, having first sung for the common Prājāpatya fruit shared by all the prāṇa-s during the three pavamāna-stotra-s, now, in the remaining nine stotra-s, sang for himself, ātmane — that is, for his own sake — annādya, namely food and what is eaten, food-and-edible (anna-ādya as karmadhāraya samāsa: anna ca tat ādya ca). It has already been stated that the connection of the kartṛ with his desire is established by the express word of the text (vācanika).

An objection may be raised: how is it ascertained that the food was sung-up by prāṇa for his own sake? To this the Bhagavān answers — yat kiñca, ‘whatever soever.’ This phrase is meant to comprehend food in general without restriction; hi denotes the reason. Whatever food at all is eaten in the world by living beings, it is eaten anena eva — by this very prāṇa. The word ana (अन) is a well-known designation of prāṇa: the form ending in s (anas) signifies a cart, while the other, ending in a vowel, is a synonym of prāṇa; so the meaning is ‘by prāṇa alone is it eaten.’

Furthermore, not only is the food eaten by prāṇa, but in that very food — when it has been transformed into the configuration of the body — iha pratitiṣṭhati, here he, prāṇa, comes to be established. Hence it was for his own pratiṣṭhā that the prāṇa sang up the food. And even the eating of food by prāṇa is itself only for his pratiṣṭhā; therefore, unlike vāg-ādi, in prāṇa there obtains no association either with kalyāṇa (auspicious) or with pāpman (the asura-taint of evil). The siddhānta thus stands: prāṇa, the seat of nivṛtti, remains pure of the dvandva of merit and demerit which inheres in the karaṇa-s entangled in pravṛtti.
BR_C01_S03_V18: Those gods said: ‘This much indeed is all — namely food — that thou hast sung up for thyself; allot us a share in this food of thine.’ ‘Then enter into me from all sides,’ he said. ‘So be it,’ they replied, and sat down enclosing him on every side. Therefore whatever food he eats by means of this prāṇa, by that they are satisfied. Even so do his own kin take refuge in him who knows thus; he becomes the supporter of his kin, the foremost, the leader, the eater of food, the lord. And whoever among his kin should wish to rival one who knows thus is unable to support his dependents; but whoever follows him, or whoever wishing to support his own dependents follows this knower, is alone able to support his dependents.
BR_C01_S03_V18::block-0:
‘Those gods.’ Pūrvapakṣa: the avadhāraṇa ‘by him alone is it eaten’ is unwarranted, since vāg-ādi too are seen to receive benefit on account of food. Siddhānta: this is no fault, for that benefit is mediated through prāṇa. To exhibit precisely how the food-given benefit accrues to vāg-ādi by way of prāṇa, the text proceeds.

Te — those vāg-ādi devatā-s, called devatā-s because they illumine their respective spheres — abruvan, said to the mukhya-prāṇa: ‘idam etāvat, this much, no more than this; vai is for recollection; this is the whole of it; what then? — yat annam, that food which sustains the prāṇa is eaten in the world; tat sarvam ātmane āgāsīḥ, all that thou hast sung up for thyself, that is, hast appropriated to thyself by the singing. We for our part cannot subsist without food. Therefore anu, afterwards; naḥ, us; asmin anne, in this food which is now thine and intended for thyself; ābhajasva, cause us to share — the absence of the ṇic suffix is chāndasa — make us partakers of food too.’

The other answers: ‘If you indeed are seekers of food, mā, me; abhisaṃviśata, sit down all about me, abhimukhyena, facing me, on every side.’ When prāṇa had thus spoken, ‘so be it,’ tatheti, they said, and they pari-samantāt nyaviśanta, settled down with full resolve all around him, that is, having encompassed prāṇa they took up their seats. To those thus settled, by the consent of prāṇa, the food being eaten by prāṇa himself — food which sustains prāṇa — becomes a source of satisfaction. There is no independent connection of vāg-ādi with food. Hence the avadhāraṇa ‘anenaiva tad adyate’ is fully justified.

This very point the text states: tasmāt — because the vāg-ādi devatā-s are settled around him only as dependants on prāṇa and by his consent, therefore yat annam anena prāṇena atti loka, whatever food the world eats by this prāṇa, tena annena etāḥ vāg-ādyāḥ tṛpyanti, by that food are these vāg-ādi-s satisfied. Whoever knows the prāṇa as the support of vāg-ādi — ‘speech and the rest, the five, are dependent on prāṇa’ — him too, evam ha vai, his own kindred, jñātayaḥ, abhisaṃviśanti, sit down around as the vāg-ādi sat round prāṇa; the import being that he becomes one to whom his kindred resort.

For him whose kindred have settled around in this manner, just as for prāṇa with respect to vāg-ādi, the knower becomes bhartā by his own food; likewise śreṣṭhaḥ; puraḥ etā, going in front, as prāṇa goes before vāg-ādi; annādaḥ, anāmayāvī (free from disease) is the meaning; adhipatiḥ, the lord who, taking his stand, protects, the independent master, just as prāṇa is to vāg-ādi. To one who thus knows prāṇa accrues this stated phala. Further, ya u ha eva-vidam — whoever, in the midst of his own kindred, against this knower of prāṇa, pratiḥ pratikūlaḥ bubhūṣati, wishes to be a rival, he, like the asura-s rivalling prāṇa, na ha eva alam, is not competent, bhāryebhyaḥ, for those who are to be supported, that is, to support them. But, on the contrary, ya eva — whoever among the kindred follows after this knower, like the vāg-ādi after prāṇa; or whoever, anu-vartayan, by following him, wishes to support his own dependants, just as the vāg-ādi were eager to subsist by following prāṇa — sa ha eva alam, he indeed is competent, bhāryebhyo bhartum, to support his dependants, not the other, the self-willed one. All this has been declared as the fruit of the knowledge of prāṇa's qualities.

For the establishment of prāṇa's being the Self of kārya and karaṇa, the text introduces his āṅgirasatva — ‘so'yāsya āṅgirasaḥ.’ The reason for the appellation āṅgirasa, ‘from this cause is he āṅgirasa,’ has not yet been stated; the next mantra is begun for the very purpose of supplying that reason. For the kārya-karaṇa-ātmatva of prāṇa hinges upon establishing that hetu.
BR_C01_S03_V19: He is Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, for he is the rasa (essence) of the limbs (aṅga-s); prāṇa indeed is the essence of the limbs — prāṇa surely is the essence of the limbs; therefore from whichever limb prāṇa departs, that very limb withers, for he indeed is the essence of the limbs.
BR_C01_S03_V19::block-0: Just before, the dependence of vāg-ādi on prāṇa was stated; how that is to be vindicated is now shown.
BR_C01_S03_V19::block-1:
‘So'yāsya āṅgirasaḥ’ and the rest is taken up afresh just as it stood, for the sake of what follows. The clause ‘prāṇo vā aṅgānāṃ rasaḥ’ recalls only what was already explained. How? — prāṇo vā aṅgānāṃ rasaḥ. Prāṇa indeed; the word hi indicates prasiddhi, ‘what is well known’; aṅgānāṃ rasaḥ; well known is this aṅga-rasatva of prāṇa, not of vāg-ādi; hence ‘prāṇo vai’ as a recalling utterance is appropriate. How is this prasiddhi established? In answer the word tasmāt is connected as the upasaṃhāra-particle: yasmāt — from whichever, kasmāt — without specification of any particular, ‘from any aṅga at all,’ aṅgāt śarīrāvayavāt aviśeṣitāt prāṇa utkrāmati apasarpati, that very aṅga, tat eva, śuṣyati, becomes nīrasa, dries up, comes to dryness. Hence the conclusion: tasmāt eṣa hi vai aṅgānāṃ rasaḥ, ‘therefore he indeed is the rasa of the limbs.’

Thereby it is established that prāṇa is the Self of kārya and karaṇa. For only on the going forth of the ātman would the limb come to dryness — that is, to maraṇa. Therefore by him, prāṇa, all prāṇī-s live. Hence, setting aside vāg-ādi, prāṇa alone is to be meditated upon — such is the comprehensive purport (samudāya-artha).
BR_C01_S03_V20: He alone, indeed, is Bṛhaspati: speech truly is Bṛhatī (the Ṛk), and he is its lord; therefore he is Bṛhaspati.
BR_C01_S03_V20::block-0: ‘Eṣa u.’ Not only is prāṇa the Self of kārya and karaṇa, that is, of rūpa and karman; but also of the names which are Ṛc, Yajus, and Sāman. Thus, glorifying prāṇa as sarvātmaka in order to commend his upāsyatva, the text continues —
BR_C01_S03_V20::block-1:
Eṣa u eva, this very already-introduced Āṅgirasa, is Bṛhaspati. How Bṛhaspati? — it is now told: vāg vai bṛhatī; Bṛhatī is the metre of thirty-six syllables. Anuṣṭubh too is Speech; how? — by the śruti ‘vāg vā anuṣṭup’ (Tai. Saṃ. I.3.5); and that anuṣṭubh-Speech is comprehended within the Bṛhatī-metre; therefore it is justified to say ‘vāg vai bṛhatī’ as an established truth.

Within Bṛhatī, all ṛc-mantras are comprehended, since they are all hymned along with prāṇa: ‘prāṇo bṛhatī’ (Ait. Ār. II.1.6) and ‘prāṇa ṛca ity eva vidyāt’ (Ait. Ār. II.2.2) are other śruti-vacanas to that effect. Speech being the very nature of ṛc, the inclusion of ṛc within prāṇa stands. How so? — tasyāḥ — of that vāc, of bṛhatī, of ṛc, eṣaḥ — this prāṇa, patiḥ — the lord, because he is its producer; for the ṛk is brought forth by the air propelled by the kauṣṭhya-fire (the digestive fire of the body); or pati in the sense of pālana, the protector of speech; for vāc is preserved by prāṇa, since one who has no prāṇa has no power to articulate words. Therefore Bṛhaspati — that is, prāṇa is the Ātman of the ṛc-s — such is the meaning.
BR_C01_S03_V21: He alone is also Brahmaṇaspati: speech truly is brahman, and he is its lord; therefore he is Brahmaṇaspati.
BR_C01_S03_V21::block-0: Thus also of the Yajus-mantras. How? — Eṣa u eva Brahmaṇaspatiḥ. Vāg vai brahma — brahman here is yajus; and that is itself a particular form of speech (vāg-viśeṣa). Of that vāc, of yajus, of brahman, eṣaḥ patiḥ; therefore Brahmaṇaspatiḥ, just as before.
BR_C01_S03_V21::block-1: Pūrvapakṣa: how is it ascertained that Bṛhatī and brahman here mean Ṛc and Yajus respectively, and not something else? Siddhānta: it is established (i) by the sāmānādhikaraṇya-nirdeśa with sāman immediately following — ‘vāg vai sāma’; and similarly ‘vāg vai bṛhatī’ and ‘vāg vai brahma’: when speech and bṛhatī, and speech and brahman, stand in apposition, their being respectively Ṛc and Yajus is fitting. (ii) Pariśeṣāt — by the residue: when sāman has been spoken of, only Ṛc and Yajus remain to be intended. (iii) Vāg-viśeṣa-tvāc ca — because Ṛc and Yajus are particular forms of speech, the apposition with speech is appropriate to them. (iv) Aviśeṣa-prasaṅgāt — for ‘sāma’ and ‘udgītha’ explicitly designate particulars; so for the words bṛhatī and brahman also it is fitting that they too designate particulars; otherwise, if no particular were determined, the statement would be useless, and if the particular meant were merely vāc in general, there would be paunaruktya in both passages. Moreover, the words ṛc, yajus, sāman, udgītha are seen to occur in this very order in the śruti-passages — hence the determination.
BR_C01_S03_V22: This very (prāṇa) is sāman. Speech indeed is sā, this (prāṇa) is ama; this is the sāman-ness of sāman, because it is sā and ama. Or rather, because it is equal (sama) to a tiny insect, equal to a mosquito, equal to an elephant, equal to these three worlds, equal to this entire universe—therefore indeed it is sāman. He who knows this sāman thus attains union with sāman, attains the same world as sāman.
BR_C01_S03_V22::block-0: "This very prāṇa indeed is sāman." How so? The text answers: "vāk verily is sā"—whatever is denoted by the feminine pronoun is speech (vāk); for the pronoun "sā" has as its sphere every object denoted by a feminine word. Likewise, "this prāṇa is ama"; the word "ama" has as its sphere every object denoted by a masculine word. Another śruti confirms this: "By what do you obtain my masculine names? He should answer: by prāṇa. By what my feminine names? By speech" (Kau. Up. 1.7). Hence the word "sāman" denotes the pair speech-and-prāṇa. Likewise the term sāman denotes merely the aggregate of notes etc. effected by prāṇa, that is, the chant; therefore there is no entity called sāman apart from speech and prāṇa, since the notes, syllables, and so on are produced by prāṇa and depend on prāṇa. "This very prāṇa is sāman." Because the sāman, in the form sā-and-ama, has speech-and-prāṇa as its self—since it is sā and ama—therefore this is the sāman-ness of sāman, that is, of the chant which is the aggregate of notes; and so it is celebrated upon earth.
BR_C01_S03_V22::block-1: "Or rather, because it is sama, equal," by the manner about to be stated, equal to all—thus the connection with "therefore sāman" is to be made. The particle "vā" (or) is to be understood as introducing an alternative ground for deriving the word sāman. By what manner, then, is prāṇa equal? It is said: equal to a puttikā—to the body of a tiny ant; equal to a mosquito—to the body of a mosquito; equal to nāga—to the body of an elephant; equal to these three worlds—to the cosmic body of Prajāpati; equal to this entire universe—to Hiraṇyagarbha in the form of the world. The equality of prāṇa lies in its being entirely present in the bodies of ants and the rest, just as cow-ness pervades each cow; not in being merely of the size of those bodies, since prāṇa is formless and all-pervading. Nor is the equality of the kind seen in a lamp inside a pot or palace, contracting and expanding to the dimensions of its container; for śruti declares: "All these are indeed equal, all are infinite" (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.13). Yet for what is all-pervading there is no contradiction in its assuming, in bodies, a mode of activity coextensive with the body. Thus, of one who knows prāṇa, called sāman because of this equality—prāṇa whose greatness has been disclosed by śruti—this is the fruit: he attains, that is, reaches, sāyujya with sāman, that is, with prāṇa—union, the state of self-identification with the same body and senses; or sālokya, residence in the same world, according to the particular form of meditation. "He who thus knows this" sāman as prāṇa as described—the meaning is, he meditates upon it until the realization "I am prāṇa" becomes manifest.
BR_C01_S03_V23: This very (prāṇa) is udgītha. Prāṇa indeed is "ut," for by prāṇa is all this upheld; speech alone is "gīthā"—"ut" and "gīthā"—that is udgītha.
BR_C01_S03_V23::block-0: "This very prāṇa is udgītha." Now, udgītha is a particular bhakti, a portion of the sāman, not the act of singing aloud (udgāna); for the topic is sāman. How is prāṇa udgītha? "Prāṇa indeed is ut"—because by prāṇa all this world is uttabdha—is held aloft, propped up, sustained—this is the meaning. The word "ut" indicates the property of upholding, and so denotes a quality of prāṇa; therefore prāṇa is "ut." "Speech alone is gīthā," because the udgītha-bhakti is a particular kind of word; since the root "gai" denotes "sound," gīthā is just speech. No form of the udgītha-bhakti is conceivable apart from word; hence the restriction "speech alone is gīthā" is justified. "Ut" is prāṇa, and "gīthā" is speech that depends on prāṇa; the two are designated by one word—"that is udgītha."
BR_C01_S03_V24: Concerning this there is also this story: while drinking soma, Brahmadatta Caikitāneya said, "May this king strike off my head if Ayāsya Āṅgirasa chanted the udgītha by means of any other than this!"—for it was indeed by speech and by prāṇa that he chanted.
BR_C01_S03_V24::block-0: To strengthen the doctrine just stated, a story is begun—
BR_C01_S03_V24::block-1: "Concerning this there is also (a story)." "That"—on this matter just stated—"there is also"—a story too is heard. Brahmadatta by name; Caikitāna means the descendant of Cikitāna, and Caikitāneya the youthful descendant of his lineage. While "drinking the king"—the soma at a sacrifice—he said: what? "May this king, in the cup, being drunk by me, strike off the head of me, the speaker of falsehood"—the form "vipātayatāt" is the tāṅ-substitute (loṭ in benediction): let it strike off, plainly, if I be a speaker of falsehood, that is the sense. How does the possibility of being a speaker of falsehood arise? It is said: "if from this prāṇa here, joined with speech, Ayāsya"—Ayāsya Āṅgirasa here denotes the chief prāṇa, since the udgātṛ at the sattra of the primordial Viśvasṛj-ṛṣis was so designated—"chanted the udgītha by some other deity, distinct from speech-and-prāṇa, then I should be a speaker of falsehood; let the deity strike off the head of me who hold a contrary view." Thus he uttered an oath, displaying the firmness with which one should hold to this knowledge. The śruti itself sums up the very meaning settled by the story in its own words: "by speech"—principally identified with prāṇa—"and by prāṇa"—which is one's own self—"that Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, the udgātṛ, chanted"—this meaning is settled by the oath.
BR_C01_S03_V25: Of this sāman, he who knows its wealth comes to possess wealth. Its wealth is the very tone (svara). Therefore one about to perform priestly office should desire (a good) tone in his speech; with that speech endowed with tone he should perform the priest's office. Hence in a sacrifice people wish to see one possessed of (a fine) tone, just as one possessed of wealth. He who knows thus the wealth of sāman comes to possess wealth.
BR_C01_S03_V25::block-0: "Of this very (sāman)." "This" connects with the prāṇa under discussion; "this" with the gesture indicates the chief (prāṇa). Of the sāman—of the prāṇa denoted by the word sāman—he who knows the "svam," the wealth: what becomes of him? "Wealth indeed comes to him." Having allured the eager listener by mention of fruit, the text proceeds: "its wealth is svara alone." Svara is the sweetness in the throat; that alone is its wealth, its ornament; for adorned by it the udgāna is seen as opulent. Since this is so, "one about to perform ārtvijya"—the priest's act of chanting—"should desire svara in speech"—svara residing in speech; he who would secure for sāman the quality of being rich through tone. This rule is laid down here in passing: when the quality of having tone is to be produced in sāman by sweetness of voice, mere wishing does not yield sweet tone; therefore one should employ tooth-cleaning, oil-drinking and the like according to capacity—this is the meaning. With speech thus refined and endowed with tone, one should perform the priestly office. "Therefore"—because the svara that is sāman's own wealth adorns it—"in a sacrifice they desire to see" the udgātṛ possessed of svara, just as worldly folk desire to see a wealthy man. Indeed it is well known in the world; "so too"—he whose wealth there is, that wealthy man people wish to see. The connection of the established knowledge of the quality with its fruit is now concluded: "wealth indeed comes to him who knows thus this wealth of sāman."
BR_C01_S03_V26: Of this sāman, he who knows its gold (suvarṇa) comes to possess gold. Its gold is the tone alone. He who knows thus this gold of sāman comes to possess gold.
BR_C01_S03_V26::block-0: Now another quality, of the form of "possession of gold," is enjoined. This too is just sweetness of tone. The difference is only this: the former is the sweetness in the throat; this is figurative, denoted by the word "suvarṇa." "Of this very sāman, he who knows the suvarṇa, gold comes to him"—because of the common element "suvarṇa" between tone (su-svara) and gold (suvarṇa). The sense is: ordinary gold is the fruit of the knowledge of this quality. "Its gold is the tone alone. Gold comes to him who thus knows this gold of sāman"—everything as before.
BR_C01_S03_V27: Of this sāman, he who knows its support (pratiṣṭhā) becomes well-established. Speech alone is its support; for established in speech this prāṇa is sung. Some, however, say it is established in food.
BR_C01_S03_V27::block-0: Now, intending to enjoin the quality of pratiṣṭhā (support), the text says: "Of this very sāman, he who knows the pratiṣṭhā"—pratiṣṭhā is that in which one stands firmly, namely speech. He who knows that pratiṣṭhā as a quality of sāman becomes firmly established. Per śruti, "Whatever quality one meditates on, even so does one become" (Śat. Br. 10.5.2.20)—so this characterization as a quality is appropriate. To one allured by fruit as before and asking eagerly "what is the pratiṣṭhā?" the text says: "Of this sāman, speech alone (is the support)." "Vāk" is the designation of the seats such as the root of the tongue, etc.; that very thing is its pratiṣṭhā. The text adds: "In speech"—in the seats such as the root of the tongue—"resting there, this prāṇa is sung," attains the state of song; therefore the support of sāman is speech. "Some others say it is sung as resting in food"—it is fitting that here it gains stability. Since neither side of the alternative is reproachable, one may meditate on the pratiṣṭhā-quality alternatively—"the support is speech, or food."
BR_C01_S03_V28: Now, then, the abhyāroha (ascent) consisting of the pavamāna verses. The prastotṛ priest indeed performs the prastāva of the sāman; while he begins, the sacrificer should mutter these (mantras): "From the unreal lead me to the real; from darkness lead me to light; from death lead me to immortality." When he says, "From the unreal lead me to the real"—"unreal" is death, "real" is immortality; "from death lead me to immortality, make me immortal"—this is the meaning. "From darkness lead me to light"—death is darkness, light is immortality; "from death lead me to immortality, make me immortal." "From death lead me to immortality"—here there is nothing hidden. Then in the other stotras let him sing for himself food. Therefore in those let him choose a boon, whatever desire he wishes for. The udgātṛ who knows thus, whatever desire he desires, for himself or for the sacrificer, that he obtains by chanting. This is itself world-conquering: there is no fear of being unfit for any world for him who knows thus this sāman.
BR_C01_S03_V28::block-0: Now the rite of japa for one possessed of the knowledge of prāṇa is to be enjoined. The knowledge possessed of which one is qualified for the japa-rite has been stated. "Now," thereafter—because the japa-rite when employed by such a knower yields, as its fruit, ascent (abhyāroha) into divine state—therefore it is enjoined here. Since by the connection with udgītha (japa) would be applicable everywhere, the words "of the pavamānas" restrict it; and when its performance in all three pavamānas is obtained, again a temporal restriction is made: "that prastotṛ indeed performs the prastāva of the sāman." When that prastotṛ begins the prastāva of the sāman, at that moment one should mutter these. The name of this japa-rite is "abhyāroha"—because by this very japa-rite the knower ascends, with face turned, into the divine state, hence "abhyāroha." By the plural "these," three Yajus formulas are intended. From the accusative form, and because the formulas have arisen in the brāhmaṇa portion, the accent is to be employed as it is read—not the mantra-accent. This is a sacrificer's japa-rite.
BR_C01_S03_V28::block-1: These are the formulas: "From the unreal lead me to the real," "From darkness lead me to light," "From death lead me to immortality." Since the meaning of the mantras is veiled, the brāhmaṇa itself explains their meaning: that mantra—what did it state? What is its meaning? It is said: "from the unreal lead me to the real." "Death indeed is the unreal"—natural (i.e., non-scriptural) action and knowledge are called death; and "unreal" because they are the cause of utter downward course. "Real is immortality"—the action and knowledge taught in scripture is the real, since it causes non-dying it is amṛta. Therefore, "from the unreal"—from action that is unreal and from ignorance—"me, to the real"—to scriptural action and knowledge—"lead"—make me attain the state of being a means to the divine state, this is the meaning. The text states the import of the sentence: "Make me immortal—this is what it says." Likewise: "From darkness lead me to light." "Death is darkness"—for all ignorance, being of the nature of concealment, is darkness; that itself, being the cause of dying, is death. "Light is immortality," the divine form opposed to the foregoing. Since knowledge is of the nature of light it is jyotis; that itself, being indestructible, is amṛta; hence "from darkness lead me to light." As before, "from death lead me to immortality" and so on; "make me immortal—this is what it says"—the meaning is, make me attain the divine fruit of the state of Prajāpati. The first mantra (asks) to be brought from the state of being a non-means to the state of a means; the second (asks) to be brought from the state of means—still of the nature of ignorance—to the goal-state. "From death lead me to immortality"—since the combined meaning of the two earlier mantras is here stated by the third, its meaning is straightforward. "Here"—in this third mantra—"there is nothing veiled, no concealed import as in the previous two mantras"; the meaning is just as heard.
BR_C01_S03_V28::block-2: Having performed the sacrificer's chant in the three pavamānas, "thereafter, in the remaining stotras, let him sing for himself food"—the udgātṛ who knows prāṇa, being prāṇa-natured, behaves like prāṇa. Since this udgātṛ knows prāṇa as described, he is, like prāṇa, capable of accomplishing the desire; therefore the sacrificer should ask for a boon when these stotras are being employed; whatever desire he wishes for, that boon let him solicit. The phrase "the udgātṛ who knows thus" is to be construed before the word "therefore." "Whatever desire the udgātṛ desires—for himself or for the sacrificer—that he obtains by chanting."
BR_C01_S03_V28::block-3: Thus, attainment of the prāṇa-self by the combination of knowledge and action has been declared; there is no occasion for doubt there. But one might doubt whether, in the absence of action, attainment of prāṇa occurs or not; to remove that doubt the text says: "This itself is world-conquering." "This"—even the bare prāṇa-vision, separated from action—"is itself world-conquering," itself a means to (winning) worlds. "There is no āśā—aspiration, prayer—for being unfit for any world" indeed. For one in whom the conviction "I am the prāṇa-self" has arisen, aspiration for the attainment of that is impossible. One who is in his village does not aspire "when shall I reach my village" as one in the forest does. Aspiration is for an unattained object, an anātman; not for what is one's own self. Therefore there is no "āśā"—"may I sometime fail to attain the prāṇa-self."
BR_C01_S03_V28::block-4: Of whom (is this true)? "Of him who knows thus this sāman"—prāṇa as described, with its greatness duly determined: "I am prāṇa, unassailable by the demoniac sins consisting of attachment to sense-objects, pure; the pentad of speech and the rest, having me as their basis, take the form of the selves of fire and so on, free from the demoniac sins of sense-attachment born of natural (non-scriptural) cognition; the bond of the use of food in all beings rests on me; I am the Self of all beings on account of being Āṅgirasa; I am the Self of speech which is the form of Ṛk, Yajus, Sāman, and Udgītha, by pervading and by effecting it; the outer wealth, ornament, of me as sāman attaining song-form is sweet tone; more inward than that is the figurative goldenness which is sweet tone; my support, when I attain song-form, are the seats of throat and the rest; thus qualified, I am completely present in the bodies of ants and the rest, on account of being formless and all-pervading"—up to the manifestation of this conviction he meditates—this is the meaning.
BR_C01_S04_V01: In the beginning, this (universe) was the Self alone, in the form of a Person. He, looking around, saw nothing else than himself. He first said, "I am." Hence the name "I" arose. Therefore even now, when one is addressed, he first says, "It is I," and then declares whatever other name he has. Because he, before all this, burned up (auṣat) all sins, therefore he is called puruṣa. He who knows thus indeed burns up him who would precede him.
BR_C01_S04_V01::block-0: "In the beginning, this was the Self alone." The attainment of Prajāpatihood by means of the combined knowledge and action has been explained; and by the bare vision of prāṇa (also)—through "This itself is world-conquering" and the rest. Now, by describing the supremacy etc., in respect of creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the world, of (Hiraṇyagarbha) Prajāpati, who is the fruit (of those means), the excellence of the fruit of Vedic knowledge and action is to be described—this is the purpose for which (the present passage) is begun. By that, an indirect praise of the knowledge and action enjoined in the karma-kāṇḍa is also accomplished. But what is really intended is this: all this fruit of knowledge and action is just saṃsāra, since śruti speaks of it as conjoined with fear, dispassion, and the like, since it has the character of effect and instrument, and since it has gross, manifest, impermanent things as its sphere; whereas the Brahman-knowledge alone, about to be set forth, is the cause of mokṣa—this for the sake of what follows. For one who is not indifferent to the saṃsāric domain, with its distinctions of means and end, has no qualification for the knowledge of the Self's oneness, just as one who is not thirsty has none for drinking. Therefore the description of the surpassing nature of the fruit of knowledge and action serves what follows. So it will be said: "This is the goal of all" (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.7), "This is dearer than a son" (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.8), and so on.
BR_C01_S04_V01::block-1: "The Self alone"—"Self" here means Prajāpati, the first born of the egg, the embodied one. He, the very fruit of Vedic knowledge and action—what? "This"—the multiplicity of bodies, undivided from his Prajāpati-body—"was alone the Self" "in the beginning," before the production of other bodies. He was "of human form" (puruṣa-vidha)—of the shape of a person, characterized by head, hands, etc.—the Virāj. He, the first emerged, having looked around—having reflected, "who am I, of what nature?"—did not see anything else, any other entity, apart from his Self, which is of the nature of prāṇa-and-aggregate, of the form of effect and instrument; he saw only the Self, the Self of all. So, refined by Vedic knowledge of past births, he uttered first, "I am that Prajāpati, I am the Self of all." Hence ("tatas")—because, due to the impression of prior knowledge, he first declared the Self with "I," therefore—the name "I" arose; the upaniṣad will state the name "aham" disclosed by śruti. Therefore—because such was the conduct in the cause, Prajāpati—therefore in his effects, the creatures, even at this present time, when one is addressed "who are you?", saying first "It is I"—designating himself first by the appellation of the causal Self—and then, to the questioner desiring to know the particular name, declaring afterwards the particular individual designation, "Devadatta," or "Yajñadatta"—he tells the name given to that particular embodied one by his parents. And that Prajāpati, in past births, in the state of aspirant, by the proper performance of action, knowledge, and meditation, was prior, foremost, among all those wishing to attain Prajāpatihood through the performance of action, knowledge, and meditation; from that aggregate of would-be-Prajāpatis, he, at the outset, "burned up" (auṣat)—what?—all sins consisting of attachment and ignorance, the obstructing causes of Prajāpatihood. Since this is so, he is "puruṣa"—because he formerly burned (pūrvam auṣat). Just as this Prajāpati, having burned up all the obstructing sins, became puruṣa Prajāpati, so another also, by the fire of the performance of action, knowledge, and meditation, or merely by the strength of knowledge alone, "burns up," reduces to ashes—whom?—him who would precede him, the present knower, who would wish to become Prajāpati first; that one, indeed. The text shows him: "He who knows thus," who, by virtue of the very capacity, has eminence in knowledge and meditation. (Objection:) Then the very wish for Prajāpatihood is for one's harm, since by such a knower he gets burned. (Reply:) No fault; the burning is just the absence of attaining Prajāpatihood first, due to absence of preeminence in knowledge and meditation. The one with surpassing means attains Prajāpatihood first; the one with inferior means does not attain it; thus he is said to burn the latter. He is not perceived as actually scorched by the other with surpassing means—as in the world, when many race together, he who reaches the goal first leaves the others as if scorched, with their strength taken away; just so.
BR_C01_S04_V02: He was afraid; therefore one who is alone fears. He thought, "Since there is nothing other than myself, of what should I be afraid?" From that very thought his fear departed. For of what should he have been afraid? Fear arises only from a second.
BR_C01_S04_V02::block-0: What was just praised — the Prājāpatya rank that is the fruit of the knowledge-and-action prescribed by the karma-kāṇḍa — has not in fact transcended the domain of saṃsāra. To exhibit this very purport, the śruti now says —
BR_C01_S04_V02::block-1:
"He was afraid." "He" — that Prajāpati, the first embodied being of human shape who has been described — "was afraid," became frightened, just like ourselves: this is what is asserted. Since this puruṣa-shaped one, possessed of body and organs, was afraid because he was endowed with the inverted vision (viparīta-darśana) regarding the destruction of the Self (ātman), therefore even today, due to that very common feature, one who is alone (ekākī) fears.

Further, exactly as with us, the cause that dispels the fear-producing inverted vision is the vision of the Self as it actually is (yathābhūta-ātma-darśana). This Prajāpati performed īkṣā — reflection. How? "Since there exists nothing other than me, no second thing standing as a counter-entity apart from the Self, then in the absence of any cause for the destruction of the Self, of what indeed should I be afraid?"

From that vision of the Self as it really is, this Prajāpati's fear departed (vīyāya) — clearly went away. The fear of that Prajāpati was caused solely by avidyā; in the vision of the supreme reality (paramārtha-darśana) it does not stand. Hence — "For of what should he have been afraid?" Why was he afraid at all? In the determination of the supreme reality, fear is simply not possible: this is the import.

Because fear arises from a second, from another thing (dvitīya). And the "second thing" is in fact set up only by avidyā. For a second that is not seen cannot be the cause of the birth of fear, as is taught in the mantra-text "There, what delusion, what grief, for one who sees the Oneness?" (Īśā 7). And it is fitting that he removed fear by the vision of Oneness; for fear is from a second, and through the vision of Oneness the vision of a second is removed — there remains no second from which fear could arise.
BR_C01_S04_V02::block-2: Here objectors raise this question (pūrvapakṣa): Whence did the vision of Oneness arise in Prajāpati? Or who instructed it to him? If it sprang up without any instruction, the same possibility would apply to people like ourselves. If, on the other hand, it had as its cause the impressions (saṃskāra) created in another birth, then the vision of Oneness becomes futile. For just as Prajāpati's vision of Oneness — though present from the previous birth — did not remove the binding cause that is avidyā (since being yet conjoined with avidyā he was born and was afraid), the same futility of the vision of Oneness would result for everyone. If it be said that the last vision alone is what releases — no; for the same recurrence may again take place as before, hence non-conclusiveness (anaikāntya). Therefore the vision of Oneness is altogether futile.
BR_C01_S04_V02::block-3:
This is no fault — for it arises from a superior cause, just as in the world. Just as, when the body and organs are pure, born of meritorious karma and free from defects, sharpness of intellect, memory and learning is observed, so for Prajāpati, who has the most excellent birth conjoined with body and organs purified by the burning up of every cause contrary to dharma, knowledge, dispassion and lordship — for him the vision of Oneness, springing up without instruction, is fitting. So says the smṛti also: "Knowledge unobstructed, dispassion, lordship and dharma — these four are co-arisen with Prajāpati."

If it be said that, given their co-arising, fear should not be possible — "darkness does not rise along with the sun" — no, because the saying about co-arising is meant to refute another (pūrvapakṣa), not to deny fear here. If it be objected that, on this view, śraddhā, devotion, prostration and the like cease to be causes — that one might suppose: the causes of knowledge enjoined in śruti and smṛti, such as "The man of faith, devoted to it, restrained in senses, attains knowledge" (Gītā 4.39) and "Know that by prostration" (Gītā 4.34), would lose their causal status, since, like Prajāpati, knowledge would be caused by dharma practised in another birth — no; for there obtains a difference between alternative causes (vikalpa), conjoint causes (samuccaya), and the qualification or non-qualification of causes.

In the world, the various causes of effects that depend on causes are alternated in many ways; or they conjoin. And among these alternatives and conjunctions there arises further a distinction by way of the cause being qualified or unqualified. For instance: in the dependent effect that is the cognition of form, even without daylight in darkness the contact of eye with form is the cause of cognition of form for night-creatures; for yogins, mind alone is the cause; for us, contact and daylight, conjoined with the various lights of sun, moon, etc., are the joined causes; and these differ as qualified by particular kinds of light or not.

Just so, in the knowledge of the Self's Oneness as well, in some cases the karma performed in another birth is the cause — as in Prajāpati. In some cases tapas is the cause: "By tapas seek to know Brahman" (Tait. Up. 3.2.1). In some cases, on the strength of "The person who has a teacher knows" (Chānd. Up. 6.14.2), "The man of faith attains knowledge" (Gītā 4.39), "Know that by prostration" (Gītā 4.34), "From the teacher alone" (Chānd. Up. 4.9.3), "It is to be known, to be seen, to be heard" (Bṛ. Up. 2.4.5; 4.5.6), the causes of attaining one-pointed knowledge are śraddhā and the rest, since they are causes of removing the obstructive adharma, etc. And the hearing, reflection and meditation upon the Vedānta texts have the to-be-known as their direct object; and on the destruction of obstructions like sin etc., the inherent capacity of the Self and the mind to give rise to the cognition of the actual entity manifests. Therefore knowledge is never without cause, and śraddhā, prostration and the like are never without efficacy.
BR_C01_S04_V03: He took no delight; therefore one who is alone takes no delight. He desired a second. He became as large as a man and woman closely embracing. He caused this very Self to fall into two parts; thence arose husband and wife. Therefore, said Yājñavalkya, this body is, as it were, half of oneself, like one of the two halves of a split pea. Therefore this space is filled by woman. He united with her; thence human beings were born.
BR_C01_S04_V03::block-0:
Hence too the Prājāpatya state belongs only to the saṃsāra-sphere — for that Prajāpati "took no delight," did not experience joy; he was filled with discontent (arati), just like ourselves. Even now, due to the same property of being alone, "one who is alone does not delight," does not experience joy. "Delight" (rati) is the play arising from union with the desired object. The disturbance of mind that arises in one engaged with desire when the desired is not obtained is called arati.

For the dispelling of that arati, he desired a "second" — a wife-substance capable of removing arati; he made grasping (gṛddhi) for it. And to him thus longing for a woman, there came about a state as though embraced by a woman. He, by that desire-fulfilling-power (satya-eṣitva), "became this much" — became of this magnitude. Of what magnitude? Just as in the world a man and woman closely embracing for the dispelling of arati would be of a certain extent, of that very extent he became.

He split this very Self of just that magnitude into two — into two forms. The emphatic "this very" (imam eva) is to qualify it from the original cause-Virāj: it is not that Virāj, like milk turning utterly into curd, with total transformation became this much; rather, while remaining established as Self, by the satya-saṅkalpa-power of Virāj there came to be a separate body of the size of a man-and-woman embracing, distinct from the Self. And the same Virāj is also that — by the co-reference in "He became this much."

"From that" — from that splitting — "husband and wife came to be": this is the etymology of the worldly couple. Hence, since one half of one's very Self stood apart as woman, this body is the half-piece (ardha-bṛgala) of oneself — "half" and "piece" both, that is, like a half-split pea. Before the woman is taken, half-piece of whom? Of one's own Self. Thus indeed said Yājñavalkya — son of Yajñavalka ("reciter of yajña"), the Daivarāti; or else son of Brahman.

Since this puruṣa-half is hollow (ākāśa), empty by the woman-half, by re-marriage it is filled with the woman-half — like joining the half-piece back. He, that Prajāpati known as Manu, united with her — Śatarūpā by name, his own daughter conceived as wife — went to maithuna. "From that" — from that union — "human beings were born," came forth.
BR_C01_S04_V04: She thought, "How does he unite with me, having begotten me from himself? Well, let me hide myself!" She became a cow, the other became a bull; he united with her, and from that cattle were born. She became a mare, the other a stallion; she became a she-ass, the other a he-ass; he united with her, and from that one-hoofed animals were born. She became a she-goat, the other a he-goat; she a ewe, the other a ram; he united with her, and from that goats and sheep were born. Thus indeed he created all this, whatever pairs there are, even down to the ants.
BR_C01_S04_V04::block-0:
"She," Śatarūpā, "this one," reflecting on the smṛti-prohibition against intercourse with the daughter, thought: "How is this not-to-be-done deed — that he, having begotten me from himself, unites with me? Even if he is shameless, let me now hide myself, become disguised by another species." Reflecting thus, she became a cow.

When he had begotten her, the same intent, urged again and again by the karma of beings, came upon Śatarūpā and Manu. Thereupon "the other became a bull." "He united with her," and so on, as before. "From that, cattle were born." Likewise "she became a mare, the other a stallion"; "she became a she-ass, the other a he-ass." Now from the union of mare-and-stallion, of he-ass-and-she-ass, the one-hoofed (eka-śapha) — namely the three: horse, mule, donkey — were born. Then "she became a she-goat, the other a he-goat (basta)"; "she a ewe, the other a ram". "He united with her" — the repetition "with her, with her" denotes vīpsā, intensification: he united with the she-goat and the ewe. "From that, goats and sheep (ajāvayaḥ) were born."

"Thus indeed," by this very rule, "whatever pair (mithuna) there is here, in the form of male-and-female pair, down to the ants — all that he created" — he created the entire world.
BR_C01_S04_V05: He knew: "I am verily the creation, for I have created all this." Thence he became Creation. One who knows this becomes a creator, like Prajāpati, in this his creation.
BR_C01_S04_V05::block-0:
"That Prajāpati," having created this entire world, knew. How? "I am verily — I myself — sṛṣṭi, the creation" — for what is created (sṛjyate) is called sṛṣṭi, the world. The world that was created by me, being non-different from me, is myself; it is not separate from me. Why so? Because I — "hi" — "created (asṛkṣi) all this world," I am the one who has created it: that is the sense.

Since Prajāpati indicated himself by the word "sṛṣṭi," "thence" — therefore — "he became sṛṣṭi," came to be called by the name "Sṛṣṭi." "In this his creation" — in this world that is the creation of Prajāpati — he, like Prajāpati, becomes a creator of the world that is non-separate from his own Self. Who? "He who knows thus," who like Prajāpati knows the world non-separate from his own Self in the manner described — "I am the world with respect to the body, the elements, and the deities."
BR_C01_S04_V06: Then he churned thus, and from his mouth as the womb and from his hands he created Agni. Therefore both these — mouth and hands — are without hair on the inside, for the womb is hairless inside. When they say, "Sacrifice to that one, sacrifice to that one," naming each god — these are but his manifold projection, for he is all the gods. Then whatever was moist he created from his semen, and that is Soma. This whole world is just this much — food and the eater of food. Soma is food, Agni the eater. This is Brahman's surpassing creation; for he created the gods who are higher than himself, and he, being mortal, created immortals — therefore the surpassing creation. He who knows this becomes a creator in this his surpassing creation.
BR_C01_S04_V06::block-0:
Thus, having created this mithuna-natured world, that Prajāpati, intending to create the deities that govern the brāhmaṇa and other varṇas, first — "atha" and "iti" being twin words used to indicate gesture — by this manner thrust his hands into his mouth and "churned" (abhyamanthat), made the churning facing forward.

Having churned the mouth with the hands, from the mouth and yoni and from the hands as yoni, he created Agni — the sustainer of the brāhmaṇa class. Since for the burning Agni this pair — mouth and hands — is the womb, both these are alomaka, devoid of hair. Entirely so? No: "on the inside" (antarataḥ). For there is a similarity here with the yoni. What? "For the yoni of women is hairless inside." Likewise the brāhmaṇa too was born from Prajāpati's very mouth. Therefore, by the kinship of birth, the elder favours the younger — Agni favours the brāhmaṇa. Hence it is established by śruti and smṛti that the brāhmaṇa has Agni as his deity and the mouth as his strength.

Likewise, by the arms which are the seat of strength, he created Indra ("vala-bhid") and the other deities that govern the kṣatriya class, and the kṣatriya himself. Therefore the kṣatra is Aindra and has its strength in the arms — known from śruti and smṛti. Likewise from the thighs, since effort (īhā) is rooted there, he created Vasus and other deities that govern the vaiśya class, and the vaiśyas. Hence the vaiśya is engaged in agriculture etc. and has Vasus as deities. Likewise from the feet he created Pūṣan, whose deity is the earth, and the śūdra capable of service.

Here, the creation of the kṣatra-deities and the rest, though not directly stated in this passage and to be stated later, is summed up as if stated, for the completeness of the account of creation. As the śruti is settled, the determined sense is: Prajāpati alone is all the gods — for what is created is non-separate from the creator, and the gods were created by Prajāpati alone.

This being the established import of the section, what follows is, by way of praising it, the citation of an inferior view fit to be censured — censure of the other for the sake of praising the one. "Thence," in the karma-section, those who are merely ritualists, at the time of yāga, say this — "Sacrifice to that Agni, sacrifice to that Indra," and the like — taking each deity Agni etc. as different, since the names, mantras, hymns, rites etc. differ. So they hold; but one should not know it thus. Why? Because all that diversity of gods is the very projection (visṛṣṭi) of this Prajāpati; for indeed "this very prāṇa, Prajāpati, is all the gods."
BR_C01_S04_V06::block-1:
Here some objectors raise a divergent view (vipratipatti). Some say Hiraṇyagarbha is the supreme alone; others say he is bound to saṃsāra. He is the supreme — by the mantra-text "They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni" (Ṛg 1.164.46), and the śruti "This is Brahman, this Indra, this Prajāpati, all these gods" (Ait. Up. 3.1.3); and by the smṛti "Some call him Agni, others Manu, Prajāpati" (Manu 12.123), and "That which is beyond the senses, ungraspable, subtle, unmanifest, eternal, all-being, inconceivable — He himself shone forth" (Manu 1.7).

Or he may be a saṃsārin: by the śruti "He burnt up all sins" (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.1) — for one not bound to saṃsāra, the question of burning sins does not arise; from the mention of his being conjoined with fear and discontent; and "Then, being mortal, he created the immortals" (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.6); and "Behold Hiraṇyagarbha as he is born" (Śvet. 4.12); and from the smṛti in the section on the maturation of karma — "Brahmā, the world-creators, Dharma, Mahat, and the Unmanifest — these the wise call the highest sāttvika course" (Manu 12.50). If, then, on this view two contradictory meanings cannot both stand, the authoritative status of śruti would be jeopardised — so it is objected.
BR_C01_S04_V06::block-2:
No (this is the siddhānta) — there is no contradiction, since another mode of explanation is possible. Through connection with a particular upādhi, an alternative qualified description is intelligible. By such śrutis as "Seated, he travels far; lying, he goes everywhere. Who other than I can know that god of joy and sorrow?" (Kaṭha 1.2.21), saṃsāritva belongs only by way of upādhi, not in reality (paramārtha). Of itself he is not a saṃsārin.

Thus the oneness and the manyness of Hiraṇyagarbha. Likewise of all jīvas, by the śruti "That thou art" (Chānd. 6.8.7). Hiraṇyagarbha, with reference to the surpassing purity of his upādhi, is mostly described as the supreme by śruti and smṛti vāda; saṃsāritva they show in only some places. Of jīvas, due to the abundance of impurities in their upādhi, saṃsāritva is mostly spoken of; but with reference to the dissolution of the entire upādhi-distinction, all are spoken of as the supreme by the śruti-smṛti texts.
BR_C01_S04_V06::block-3: But by tārkikas (logicians), having abandoned the strength of āgama and reasoning out many contradictory positions — "there is, there is not, an agent, a non-agent" — the meaning of the śāstra is rendered confused. By them ascertainment of meaning is hard to attain. But for those who follow śāstra alone, with their pride quelled, the meaning of śāstra concerning deities and the like is as well-determined as a directly perceived object.
BR_C01_S04_V06::block-4: Here the distinction by way of eater (attṛ) and food (ādya) within the one Prajāpati-deity is intended. There Agni was spoken of as the eater; now the food, Soma, is spoken of. "Then whatever in the world is moist, of the nature of liquid, that he created from his semen," from his own seed — by the śruti "From semen, the waters" (Ait. Up. 1.1.4). Soma is of the nature of liquid. Therefore whatever moist Prajāpati created from semen is Soma. "This much is this whole world" — only this much, no more. What? Food and eater. Soma is food, since being liquid he nourishes; Agni is the eater, by his heat and dryness.
BR_C01_S04_V06::block-5:
There it is settled thus: Soma is food, that which is eaten is just Soma; he who is the eater is Agni — the determination is by the strength of meaning. Even Agni, when offered up, belongs to the Soma-side; even Soma, when sacrificing, is Agni, by being the eater. Thus seeing the world, of the nature of Agni-and-Soma, as the very Self, one is not tainted by any defect; and one becomes Prajāpati.

This is "Brahman's," Prajāpati's, "surpassing creation" — surpassing even himself. Which? Because he created from himself the gods who are more excellent (śreyas), more praiseworthy than himself, the creation of gods is the surpassing creation. How is creation surpassing the Self? Because, being mortal (martya), of the nature of dying, by the fire of karma-and-jñāna having burnt up all sins from himself, he created the immortals (amṛta) — gods of the nature of not-dying. Hence this surpassing creation is the fruit of excellent knowledge — that is the meaning. Therefore he who knows this surpassing creation as one's own Self of Prajāpati becomes, in this surpassing creation, like Prajāpati — that is, becomes a creator like Prajāpati.
BR_C01_S04_V06::block-6: "That, this then was the unmanifest (avyākṛta)." The whole Vedic means, of the nature of knowledge and karma, depending on agent and other accessory factors, terminating in the fruit of Prajāpati-rank, has just this much sādhya-domain — namely this manifest world that is saṃsāra. Now, the seed-state prior to the manifestation of this very manifest world (consisting of sādhya and sādhana), inferred like the seed of a tree from the sprout and other effects, the śruti wishes to indicate. For this saṃsāra-tree, with karma as its seed and avidyā as its field, must be uprooted with its root. Only when uprooted is the puruṣārtha completed — as said in Kaṭhaka, "Roots above, branches below" (Kaṭha 2.3.1), in the Gītā, "Roots above, branches below" (Gītā 15.1), and in the Purāṇa, "The eternal Brahma-tree."
BR_C01_S04_V07: That, this then, was unmanifest. It became distinguished by name and form: "He has this name, he has this form." So even now this world is distinguished by name and form: "He has this name, he has this form." He has entered here, even up to the tips of the nails — as a razor lies hidden in its case, or as fire dwells in its source. They do not see him, for he is incomplete. When breathing he is called prāṇa; when speaking, speech; when seeing, the eye; when hearing, the ear; when thinking, mind. These are mere names of his functions. He who worships him as one or another of these does not know, for he is incomplete in any one of them. One should worship him as the Self, for therein all these become one. The Self is the trace by which one finds all this; and just as one finds a lost animal by tracking its footprints, so one who knows thus finds glory and praise.
BR_C01_S04_V07::block-0:
"That, this here." "That" — the world in seed-state prior to manifestation, at "that time" (tarhi); since it is not directly perceptible, it is referred to by a pronoun expressing what is not in direct view. Because it has connection with past time, the world being then about-to-be-manifested. The particle "ha" is for the sake of easy apprehension, indicating tradition (aitihya). When it is said "thus indeed it then was," one easily grasps even that hidden seed-state — as in "Yudhiṣṭhira, ha, was a king," the indirect mode is easily understood.

"This" — refers to the manifest world, possessed of name-and-form, of the form of sādhya-and-sādhana, as already described. From the co-reference of "that" and "this" — pointing to the world in its hidden and perceptible states — only the oneness of the world in both states is understood: "That very thing is this; and this very thing was that unmanifest."
BR_C01_S04_V07::block-1:
On this view, it is settled that there is neither origination of the non-existent nor destruction of the existent — that is, of the effect. Such a world, being unmanifest, was differentiated by name and form alone — through name and through form. Since "vyākriyata" is used both as object and as agent, it itself, as the very Self, was differentiated — "vi-ā-akriyata," attained the manifestation determined by particular name and form, by virtue implying a controller, agent, instrument, action, and cause.

"He has this name" — by the indeterminate term "asau" ("such-and-such") it indicates the name in general: he has the name Devadatta or Yajñadatta. Likewise "this form" indicates form in general — white, black, etc. This very thing that was unmanifest is now also being differentiated by name and form: "He has this name, he has this form."

That for whose sake the entire śāstra is undertaken, in whom by natural avidyā the superimposition of agency, action, and fruit has been made; who is the cause of the whole world; in whom name and form, like foam in clear water, lie unmanifest and become manifest; and who, distinct from these name-and-form, is by his own nature eternally pure, conscious, and free — He, while differentiating name-and-form which are unmanifest as his very Self, has "entered here" into all the bodies, from Brahmā down to a clump of grass, that are receptacles of karma-fruits, possessed of hunger, thirst, and so on.
BR_C01_S04_V07::block-2:
But objection: it has been said that the unmanifest itself was differentiated; how then is it now stated, "The supreme Self alone, while differentiating the unmanifest, has entered here"? No fault — for the supreme Self too is intended as having the very form of the unmanifest world. We have said that the world, with its implied controller, agent, action, and cause, was differentiated as the unmanifest. And the word "unmanifest" stands in co-reference with "this" (idam). Just as this manifest world is qualified by various particularities like a controller and many other accessory factors and causes, so the unmanifest is also possessed of these very particularities — without abandoning them. The difference is only that one is manifest, the other unmanifest.

In the world we see usage according to the speaker's intention — "The village has come," "The village is empty." Sometimes, when only the dwellings are intended by the word "village," we say "the village is empty"; sometimes, when the inhabitants are intended, "the village has come"; and sometimes both are intended, as in "one should not enter the village." So here too, when non-difference between Self and not-Self is intended, the world is spoken of as both manifest and unmanifest. When the world alone is intended, we say it is born and dies. When the Self alone is intended, we have "The great unborn Self," "Not gross, not subtle," "That is this — neti, neti," and the like.
BR_C01_S04_V07::block-3:
But further objection: this whole world has been differentiated by the supreme differentiator and is everywhere pervaded by Him at all times; how is He then conceived as having entered here? For only an unentered region can be entered by a limited entity, as a man enters a village — but not by space, since it is always already entered. By a different property, like a stone or a serpent? Granting then that the supreme Self did not enter in his own form, but, while remaining there, came to be by means of another property, and so figuratively is said to have entered — like a serpent within a stone, or water in a coconut. No: by the śruti "Having created that, he entered into that very thing" (Tait. Up. 2.6.6). It is heard that the Creator, without taking on a different state, having created the effect, afterwards entered. Just as in "Having eaten, he goes," the eating and going are sequenced and the agent remains the same, so here too. But the rise of a different state in one who already abides cannot account for this. And entry by way of separating from one place and joining another is not seen for the partless and unlimited.

If entry is heard, He must have parts — no; by śrutis like "The puruṣa is divine, formless" (Muṇḍ. 2.1.2), "Without parts, without action" (Śvet. 6.19), and śrutis denying every distinguishing property. Like a reflection's entry? No, since separation by another substance is not possible. Like the entry of qualities into substance? No, because the Self is not dependent. The dependent quality, eternally subordinate, is figuratively said to enter the substance; not so for Brahman, since His independence is heard, and entry of that kind cannot be made out. Like the seed in the fruit? No: it would entail being possessed of parts, of growth and decay, of origin and destruction. And Brahman is not so qualified, by the śruti and reasoning of "unborn, undecaying" (Bṛ. 4.4.25).

Is it that a different saṃsārin, limited, has entered here? No: by the śruti "That deity reflected" beginning, leading to "Let me differentiate name and form" (Chānd. 6.3.2), it is the same deity who is the agent of entry and differentiation. So too "Having created that, he entered into that very thing" (Tait. 2.6.6); "He, splitting that very tip, entered through this door" (Ait. 1.3.12); "Having determined all forms, the wise one, having made names, sits speaking them" (Tait. Ār. 3.12.7); "Thou art the boy and also the girl; thou, when aged, walkest with a staff" (Śvet. 4.3); "He who first made the bipeds" (Bṛ. 2.5.18); "Form after form" (Bṛ. 2.5.19) — by all these mantra-texts there is no entry of any other than the supreme.

From the difference among those entered, supremes are many? No: by "One god, manifoldly entered" (Tait. Ār. 3.14.1), "One being, manifold he becomes" (Tait. Ār. 3.11.1), "Thou art one, having entered into many" (Tait. Ār. 3.14.13), "One god, hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings" (Śvet. 6.11), and the like.
BR_C01_S04_V07::block-4:
Let the question whether the entry is fitting or not stand aside for a moment. If it be said: those who have entered are saṃsārins, and since the supreme is non-different from them, the supreme also is a saṃsārin — no; by the śruti "He has transcended hunger and the rest" (Bṛ. 3.5.1). From observed happiness and suffering — no; by the śruti "He, being external, is not affected by the world's suffering" (Kaṭha 1.3.11). Contradicted by perception etc. and so unjustified — no; perception etc. concerns particularities arising from the upādhi and its substrate.

By śrutis like "You cannot see the seer of seeing" (Bṛ. 3.4.2), "By what should one know the knower?" (Bṛ. 2.4.14; 4.5.1), "The unknown knower" (Bṛ. 3.8.11), there is no perception with the Self as object. What then? Perception of the form "I am happy," "I am suffering," has for its object only the reflection of the Self in the upādhi of intellect etc. — for the figurative co-reference of the subject and the object is in the form "this — I," and by "There is no other seer than this" (Bṛ. 3.8.11) any other Self is denied.

And happiness and suffering, having body-parts as their qualified substrate, are properties of the object. If it be said that by the śruti "For the love of the Self" (Bṛ. 2.4.5; 4.5.6) they have the Self as their purpose — no; by "Where there is, as it were, another" (Bṛ. 4.3.31), where Self-purpose belongs to the avidyā-domain, and by "There, by what should one see whom?" (Bṛ. 2.4.14; 4.5.15), "Here there is no plurality whatsoever" (Bṛ. 4.4.19; Kaṭha 2.1.11), "There, what delusion, what grief, for one who sees the Oneness?" (Īśā 7) — the negation in the domain of vidyā shows that they are not properties of the Self.

If it be said: contrary to logician's tenets, this is unfitting — no; by reasoning too, suffering of the Self is not possible. The Self is not qualified by suffering as an object of perception, since the Self is not an object of perception. Like the quality of sound in space, suffering is in the Self? No: the contradiction in being object of one and the same cognition cannot be made out. The Self, eternally to be inferred, cannot be made the object of a perceptual cognition that grasps happiness. And if it were made the object, since the Self is one, there would be no subject. If it be said the same thing is both subject and object, like a lamp — no, since simultaneity is impossible and parts cannot be predicated of the Self. By this the same is rejected for cognition's being both grasper and grasped.

And suffering and Self being objects of perception and inference respectively, the relation of quality and substance does not give rise to a sound inference. Suffering is always object of perception; it has co-reference with form etc. Even if suffering were a quality of the Self produced by mind-conjunction, it would entail the Self's being possessed of parts, undergoing change, and being non-eternal. For no quality is observed coming or going to a substance with which it is conjoined without modifying that substance. And nothing partless is seen undergoing modification, nor anything supporting non-eternal qualities is seen as eternal — and space is not held eternal by the āgamavādins, and there is no other example. If it be said that the modified is yet eternal because the cognition of it does not cease — no; for modification is not made out except by substance's parts becoming otherwise. If parts and eternity together — no; for what is parted has its parts presupposing prior conjunction, and so separation can occur. "It is not seen in diamond" — no; for prior conjunction is to be inferred there too.
BR_C01_S04_V07::block-5:
Like the reflection of the sun in water, the entry of the Self is in the manifest effect, observed as a reflection. The Self, unobserved before origination, is, after the effect's creation and manifestation, observed within the intellect — like the reflection of sun in water — and is referred to as having created the effect and entered, as if entered, by such texts as "He has entered here," "Having created that, he entered into that very thing" (Tait. 2.6.6), "He, splitting that very tip, entered through this door" (Ait. 1.3.12), "That deity reflected — Let me enter into these three deities through this living Self" (Chānd. 6.3.2).

But for the all-pervading and partless, an entry of the form of leaving one place and reaching another in space-time is never possible. And there is no seer other than the supreme Self — "There is no other seer than this," "There is no other hearer than this" (Bṛ. 3.8.1) — as we have said. The texts about creation, entry, sustenance, and dissolution are for the sake of upalabdhi (realization), since the realization is heard to be the puruṣārtha — "He knew only the Self; therefore all that became him" (Bṛ. 1.4.10), "The knower of Brahman attains the supreme" (Tait. 2.1.1), "He who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍ. 3.2.9), "The man with a teacher knows; for him there is delay only that long" (Chānd. 6.14.2); and from smṛti "Knowing me thus in truth, then he enters into Me" (Gītā 18.55), "Of all knowledges that is foremost; from it indeed the immortal is attained" (Manu 12.85).

From censure of the perception of difference, the texts of creation etc. can have purport in conveying the Self's oneness. Therefore, what is figuratively called "entry" is just the realisability of what abides in the effect.
BR_C01_S04_V07::block-6:
"Up to the tips of the nails" — the consciousness of the Self is observed up to the tips of the nails. How has He entered? In the world, in a razor-case (kṣura-dhāna) — that in which a razor is put — namely the barber's instrument-case, the razor is observed to be inside, deposited there. Or, as the all-supporting Agni — viśvam-bharaḥ, since he supports all — in his nest (kulāya), namely in the wood and the like, is deposited; for there, when churned, he is observed.

Just as a razor abides in one part of its case, and as Agni abides pervading the wood entirely, so the Self abides pervading the body both generally and particularly. There alone is He observed as endowed with the actions of breathing, etc., and seeing, etc.

Therefore, that Self that has thus entered, qualified by breathing and the rest, "they do not see" — they do not realise. "But isn't this a denial of what is not the topic — the term 'sight' has not been introduced?" — no fault: since the texts of creation etc. have for their main purport the realisation of the Self's oneness, sight is indeed the topic, by the mantra "He became conformable to every form; that form of his is for showing forth" (Bṛ. 2.5.19).

The reason for the Self's being seen as qualified by breathing etc. He states: "For he is incomplete (akṛtsna)" — yes: he, as qualified by the action of breathing etc. Why incomplete? "While breathing," only doing the breathing-action, he is called prāṇa, by the name prāṇa; for since he performs the breathing-action he is called "prāṇa" — "prāṇiti." While doing one action, he is not also doing another action — like a quail-cooker, a cook. Hence, since the other actions are not included, he is incomplete.

Likewise, while speaking, doing the speaking-action — vāk; while seeing, eye ("caṣṭe" — sees); while hearing — ear. By "While breathing, prāṇa; while speaking, vāk" — the rise of action-power is shown. By "while seeing, eye; while hearing, ear" — the rise of cognition-power is shown, since the cognition-power has name-and-form for its object. Ear and eye are instruments of cognition; and cognition has name-and-form as its instrument; for there is nothing knowable other than name-and-form, and ear and eye are the instruments of their grasping. Action belongs to name-and-form, inheres in prāṇa; for its expression with prāṇa as its substrate, vāk is the instrument; so are the hand, foot, anus, and reproductive-organ — vāk standing for them all. For all this is the differentiated: "This is threefold — name, form, and action" (Bṛ. 1.6.1) will be said.

"While thinking, mind" — "manute," thinks; the common instrument of all manifestations of cognition-power is the mind, with which one thinks. The Self, as the agent thinking, is called "manas." These prāṇa and the rest are this Self's "karma-names" — names born of action — and not designating the substance simply; therefore they do not declare the entire Self-substance. Thus is the Self differentiated, manifested by the actions of breathing etc., by the names-and-forms born of those very actions. He who, thence, worships any one of these — prāṇa, eye etc. — as a separate one, without conjoining the rest, does not know the whole.
BR_C01_S04_V07::block-7: How then does one knowing him know? "As the Self alone" — He who is, who pervades, all those qualifications spoken of — prāṇa etc. — is called "Self." One who thus comprehends all the qualifications becomes complete. For in the form of the bare substance, He pervades all the qualifications produced by the upādhi-distinct actions of prāṇa and the rest. So it will be said: "He thinks, as it were; he moves, as it were" (Bṛ. 4.3.7). Therefore one should worship Him as the Self alone. Thus the whole is grasped in his own substance-form. Why complete? Because in this Self, which is without upādhi, all the differences caused by the upādhi-of-prāṇa and the rest — designated by names born of the actions of prāṇa etc. — like the various reflections of the sun in water in the one sun, become one, attain non-difference.
BR_C01_S04_V07::block-8: The text "One should worship as the Self alone" (Bṛ. 1.4.7) is not a fresh injunction (apūrva-vidhi), since it is already obtained alternately. By texts directed at conveying the Self — "That which is direct and immediate, the Brahman" (Bṛ. 3.4.1; 3.5.1), "What is the Self? — He who is the cognitive" (Bṛ. 4.3.7) — knowledge of the Self has been produced.
