Therein, by the very knowledge of the Self's nature, the avidyā-of-the-form-of-superimposing-agency-and-fruit on the not-Self, having that as object, is removed. When that is removed, the impossibility of defects like desire, etc., entails the impossibility of contemplation of the not-Self; hence by what remains, only contemplation of the Self obtains. Therefore, on this view, that worship is not to be enjoined — being already obtained.
BR_C01_S04_V07::block-9:
Let the alternative obtainment of Self-worship stand aside as a question whether necessary or fresh. It would be a fresh injunction (apūrva-vidhi), since, given the unity of knowledge and worship, it is unobtained. From the words "He does not know" introducing knowledge, and "One should worship as the Self alone" (Bṛ. 1.4.7), the unity of meaning of "vid" and "upās" is understood. By śrutis like "For by it one knows all this" and "He knew only the Self" (Bṛ. 1.4.10), knowledge is upāsana. And being unobtained, it is fit for an injunction. In a mere description of the Self's own nature, no human pravṛtti can be made out. Hence this is a fresh injunction.

By similarity to action-injunctions: just as injunctions like "yajeta" (one should sacrifice), "juhuyāt" (one should offer) are action-injunctions, by them no distinction is shown of this Self-worship-injunction "One should worship as the Self alone" (Bṛ. 1.4.7), "The Self is to be seen" (Bṛ. 2.4.5; 4.5.6), and the like. By cognition's being a mental action: as a mental action is enjoined in "One should mentally meditate on the deity for whom the oblation is taken when about to perform the vaṣaṭkāra" (Ait. Br. 3.8.1), so an action of the form of cognition is enjoined in "One should worship as the Self alone" (Bṛ. 1.4.7), "He should be heard, reflected on, meditated upon" (Bṛ. 2.4.5; 4.5.6).

Thus we have said the unity of "vid" and "upās." By the obtainment of the three components of the bhāvanā: just as in the bhāvanā "yajeta," the three components — what? by what? how? — are understood as removing the expectation about the bhāvya etc., so in the bhāvanā "upāsīta," being enjoined — "What should one worship? By what? How?" — the expectation is satisfied by the same śāstra: "One should worship the Self by mind, accompanied by renunciation, brahmacarya, śama, dama, restraint, fortitude, and the rest, with their auxiliary actions." The three components are thus established. And just as the entire darśa-pūrṇamāsa section serves the darśa-pūrṇamāsa injunction by way of presenting the injunction-topic, so the upaniṣad's Self-worship section serves only by way of presenting the Self-worship injunction. "Neti, neti" (Bṛ. 2.3.6), "Not gross" (Bṛ. 3.8.8), "One only, without a second" (Chānd. 6.2.1), "Transcending hunger" (Bṛ. 3.5.1), and the like — these texts serve by communicating the particular nature of the Self to be worshipped. The fruit is mokṣa or the cessation of avidyā.
BR_C01_S04_V07::block-10: Others explain thus: by upāsana, one should bring about another particular cognition having the Self as object; by that the Self is known; and that alone is the dispeller of avidyā, not the cognition produced by the Vedānta-text concerning the Self. In this sense are the texts: "Having known, let one practise prajñā" (Bṛ. 4.4.21), "He should be seen, heard, reflected on, meditated upon" (Bṛ. 2.4.5; 4.5.6), "He is to be sought, to be inquired into" (Chānd. 8.7.1), and others.
BR_C01_S04_V07::block-11:
No: there is no separate meaning. "One should worship as the Self alone" (Bṛ. 1.4.7) is not an apūrva-vidhi. Why? Because, apart from the cognition arising from the texts that state the Self's nature and deny the not-Self, there is no other thing to be done — mental or external. There injunction has efficacy where, beyond the cognition produced by the mere hearing of the injunction-text, a human pravṛtti is recognized — as in "By darśa-pūrṇamāsa one desirous of heaven should sacrifice" and the like. For the cognition produced by the darśa-pūrṇamāsa-injunction-text is not itself the performance of darśa-pūrṇamāsa; that depends on adhikāra etc. and is its sequel.

But beyond the cognition produced by texts that convey the Self — "neti, neti" (Bṛ. 2.3.6) and the rest — no human activity like darśa-pūrṇamāsa is possible, because the cognition produced by such texts causes the cessation of all activity. For an indifferent cognition does not produce activity; and being the dispeller of the cognition of the not-Self and not-Brahman by texts like "One only, without a second" (Chānd. 6.2.1) and "That thou art" (Chānd. 6.8.7), it cannot give rise to activity, since pravṛtti would be inconsistent with the cessation of avidyā.

If it be said: from the mere text-produced cognition, the cognition of not-Brahman and not-Self does not cease — no; by texts like "That thou art" (Chānd. 6.8.7), "neti, neti" (Bṛ. 2.3.6), "All this is the Self" (Chānd. 7.25.2), "One only, without a second" (Chānd. 6.2.1), "Brahman alone is this immortal" (Muṇḍ. 2.2.11), "There is no other seer than this" (Bṛ. 3.8.11), "That very Brahman, know thou" (Kena 1.5), since they teach that.

If it be said these communicate the object for the seeing-injunction — no; the answer is what we said: there is no separate meaning. By the very texts that convey the Self-substance like "That thou art" (Chānd. 6.8.7), since at the very time of hearing, sight of that is accomplished, no other practice, like the seeing-injunction, need be performed. "Even from the description of the Self's nature there is no entrance into Self-cognition without an injunction" — no, for from hearing the Self-affirming text, Self-cognition has already arisen — what need to do what is done? "Even at that hearing, one does not engage" — no, for there is the fault of regress: just as one does not engage in hearing the meaning of the Self-affirming text without an injunction, neither would one engage in hearing the meaning of the injunction-text without another injunction; thus an endless regress.

If it be said the continuous remembrance, born of the text-produced Self-cognition, is something other than the bare hearing-cognition — no, since it is obtained by implication. As soon as the cognition of the Self arises from the Self-conveying text, it arises while removing the false cognition of that very Self; and on the cessation of the false cognition concerning the Self, the natural remembrances having difference from the Self as their object, born from that, no longer arise — for when the Self is grasped, every other thing is grasped as anartha (non-good), being possessed of many defects like impermanence, suffering, and impurity, and the Self being opposite to them. Therefore, on the apprehension of the Self, the absence of the not-Self-cognitions and their remembrances is implied. By way of the residual, the continuity of the cognition-and-remembrance of the Self's oneness exists by implication, and so is not to be enjoined.
BR_C01_S04_V07::block-12: Both Self and not-Self stand alike as not yet known; why then is effort applied to Self-worship alone — "One should worship as the Self alone" (Bṛ. 1.4.7) — and not to the cognition of the rest? It is answered: "That very thing" — that very Self-tattva is the topic — "is the trace," the path, of "all this" — the genitive expressing determination: in this whole. "That this Self is" — that this very Self-tattva. Is nothing else to be known? Even granting that they are to be known, they require no separate cognition apart from the knowledge of the Self. Why? Because by knowing this Self, all this — all not-Self things, whatever is other — is known. "But by knowing one thing, another is not known" — the answer to that is given in the dundubhi-passage. How is this called the "trace"? It is said: just as in the world by a footprint — a place marked by the hooves of cattle is called "footprint" — by that footprint one searching for a lost beast finds it — so by attaining the Self, one attains all that is.
BR_C01_S04_V07::block-13:
But: when the topic is knowing the Self and thereby knowing all else, how is finding (lābha), which is not the topic, spoken of? No: it is the very intent that knowledge and finding are co-meaning. For non-finding of the Self is itself non-knowing; therefore knowing alone is the finding of the Self. Not as in finding of the not-Self, where there is the un-attained-being-attained nature; here the finder and the to-be-found are not different.

Where the not-Self is to be found by the Self, there the Self is the finder, the not-Self the to-be-found. And that, being unattained, separated by the actions of producing etc., is to be obtained by employing particular instruments and producing a particular action. That, of the form of the un-attained-being-attained, is non-eternal, springing from desire-and-action born of false knowledge — like obtaining a son in dream. But this Self is the opposite of that. Just by being the Self, He is not separated by actions of producing etc. Even though He is by nature eternally attained, the bare avidyā is the obstruction. Just as, when shell is being grasped wrongly as silver, the non-grasping is mere obstruction by inverted cognition, so the grasping is mere cognition: cognition serves only to remove the obstruction of inverted cognition. Just so here too, the Self's non-finding is mere obstruction by avidyā; therefore by vidyā the mere removal of that is finding — no other is ever possible. Therefore, in attaining the Self, the futility of any means apart from knowledge will be shown. Therefore, with confidence intending the unity of meaning of knowledge and finding, the text says — having begun with knowledge — "anuvindet," since "vindati" has the sense of finding.
BR_C01_S04_V07::block-14: The fruit of the qualified-knowledge is now stated: "Just as this Self has reached fame (kīrti) by entry into name and form, by such names and forms as 'Self' etc., and praise (śloka) — the aggregation with prāṇa and the rest — so he who knows finds praise and fame, finds glory and the aggregation along with desired things." Or: he who knows the entity as described — what the seekers of mokṣa long for, the kīrti named knowledge of unity, attains the praise (śloka) — its fruit, mokṣa — that is the principal fruit.
BR_C01_S04_V08: This Self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than anything else, since it is innermost. If one were to say to a man who calls something other than the Self dear, "What is dear to you will perish," he is indeed authoritative — it would be so. One should worship the Self alone as dear. He who worships the Self alone as dear — what is dear to him does not perish.
BR_C01_S04_V08::block-0:
Why again is the Self-tattva alone to be known, ignoring everything else? It is said: "This," the Self-tattva, is "dearer" — more dear — "than a son." In the world a son is renowned as dear; "dearer than him" — thus showing unsurpassed dearness. Likewise dearer than wealth — gold, jewels, etc.; likewise "than anything else" — than whatever is in the world renowned as dear. Why is the Self-tattva dearer, and not prāṇa, etc.? It is answered: "It is innermost (antaratara)." The combination of prāṇa and the body, more inward than the external like sons and wealth, is closer to the Self; "than that, more inward," "this Self."

In the world, what is unsurpassedly dear is to be obtained by every effort; so this Self is dearer than all worldly dear ones; therefore in attaining it the greatest effort is to be applied — that is the meaning. The duty-bound effort for obtaining other dear things is to be relinquished.

Why, when one of two — Self-dear or not-Self-dear — is to be relinquished and the other accepted, is it the Self-dear that is to be accepted with the relinquishment of the other, and not the contrary? It is said: "He who, to one calling something not-Self — a son or the like — dearer than himself, would say, 'What is dear to you will be obstructed (rotsyati), will encounter obstruction of prāṇa, will perish' — that one" who speaks for the Self as dear — why does he so say? Because he is "īśvara" — competent, qualified to so speak. Hence "so it would be": "his prāṇa will be obstructed," what he said. Since he speaks the truth (yathābhūta-vādī), he is competent to say. Some explain "īśvara" as meaning "swift"; let it be so if there is such usage.

Therefore, abandoning other-dear, one should worship the Self alone as dear. He who thus worships the Self alone as dear — having ascertained that the Self alone is dear, no other, and that other worldly dear is itself non-dear — he contemplates. "To him" — to such a knower — "the dear does not perish (na pramāyukam)," of the nature of dying. This is a mere restatement (nityānuvāda) of an established fact, since for the Self-knower there is no other dear or undear; or it is for the praise of the Self-grasping; or it is for the prescription of the fruit-and-quality of dearness for the dull-minded who see the Self imperfectly, since the suffix of habit is used.
BR_C01_S04_V09: On this they say: people think that by knowledge of Brahman they will become all. What did Brahman know, that it became all?
BR_C01_S04_V09::block-0:
The Brahma-vidyā has been laid down in sūtra-form: "One should worship as the Self alone" (Bṛ. 1.4.7). The whole Upaniṣad is for that very purpose. Wishing to expound this sūtra, intent on stating its purpose, the text begins.

"On this" — referring to what is to be said in the next sentence, the entity-to-be-illumined. "They say" — brāhmaṇas, those desirous of knowing Brahman, having approached a guru, having become the boat for crossing the boundless great ocean of suffering caused by the wheel of birth, old age, death, fatigue, and grief, wishing to cross to its further shore, having become disenchanted with the form of sādhya-and-sādhana of the means and fruit of dharma and adharma, wishing to attain the eternal, unsurpassed welfare distinct from that.

What do they say? "By Brahma-vidyā," by the knowledge by which Brahman, the supreme Self, is known — by that Brahma-vidyā, "the whole, without remainder, will we become" — "we shall become" — thus "people think." The word "manuṣyāḥ" is used to make the qualification specific: it is humans who are particularly qualified for the means of prosperity and supreme good — that is the purport. Just as in the karma-section they think the attainment of the fruit from karma is certain, so they think the attainment of the fruit of being-all-Self from Brahma-vidyā is certain — for the authoritativeness of the Veda is alike in both.

Here a contradicted reality is hinted at; therefore we ask: What is that Brahman, by knowing which people think they will become all? What did it know, by knowing which the Brahman became all? Now, Brahman is heard to be all (sarvam). If, without knowing anything, it became all, let it be so for others too — what is the use of Brahma-vidyā? If by knowing it became all, then since the fruit of being-all is accomplished by knowledge, it would be on a level with karma-fruits, and so the impermanence of the fruit of Brahma-vidyā would result. And there would be the fault of regress: that too became all by knowing another; and again, even before that, by knowing yet another; and so on.

Without knowing it did not become all — for then the meaning of the śāstra would be deformed (śāstrārtha-vairūpya). Then the fault of impermanence of the fruit? Not even one fault, since a particular meaning is intelligible (artha-viśeṣa-upapatti).
BR_C01_S04_V10: Brahman, verily, was this in the beginning. It knew only itself, "I am Brahman." Therefore it became all. Whoever among the gods awoke to this, he indeed became that; and so among the seers, and so among men. Seeing this, the seer Vāmadeva realised, "I was Manu and I was the sun." Even now, whoever knows thus, "I am Brahman," becomes this all. Even the gods cannot prevent his becoming so, for he is their very Self. But he who worships another deity, thinking, "He is one and I am another," does not know. He is like an animal to the gods. As many animals serve a man, so each man serves the gods. Even when one animal is taken away it is unpleasant; how much more when many. Therefore the gods do not like that men should know this.
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-0: If, having known something, that Brahman became all, we ask: what was that Brahman known, on knowing which it became all? When this is asked, the śruti gives an answer untainted by every fault.
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-1:
Apara-Brahman is meant here, since the becoming-all is something to be accomplished; for the Para-Brahman has no becoming-all to be accomplished by knowledge. The becoming-all that is accomplished by knowledge is declared in "therefore it became all." Hence in "Brahman, verily, was this in the beginning," it is the Apara-Brahman that ought to be intended.

Or, by reason of the qualification of men, the meaning may be the man-who-shall-become-Brahman; for "all men, expecting to become all, deem so" — men are the topic. They alone have specific qualification for the means of prosperity and the highest good, not the Para-Brahman, nor even Prajāpati the Apara. Therefore — by the knowledge of the Apara-Brahman as duality and unity, joined with action — having attained the state of Apara-Brahman, withdrawn from the enjoyable, his bondage of desire and karma cut off through attaining all, becoming about to be Para-Brahman because of the cause that is brahma-vidyā, he is called "Brahman." Such usage in reference to a coming condition is seen in the world ("he is cooking the rice") and in śāstra ("the wandering ascetic gives the gift of fearlessness to all beings"); so here too — thus some explain that "Brahman" means the man who is going to become Brahman.
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-2: That is not so, owing to the fault of impermanence in the becoming-all. There is nothing in the world, in truth, that becomes another thing under some condition and yet remains eternal. So if the becoming-all is brought about by the cause of the knowledge of Brahman, and is also eternal — that is contradictory. And if impermanent, the fault stated is its parity with the fruit of action. If you hold that the becoming-all which is the fruit of brahma-vidyā is the removal of the not-allness made by avidyā, then the postulation of "the man who shall become Brahman" is futile. For even before the knowledge of Brahman every creature, being Brahman, is in truth eternally the all; only by avidyā has not-being-Brahman and not-being-all been superimposed — as silver upon mother-of-pearl, or surface and dirt upon space. So here too what is superimposed by avidyā upon Brahman, namely not-being-Brahman and not-being-all, is dispelled by brahma-vidyā. If you accept this, then it is right to say that what existed in truth, the Para-Brahman, the primary referent of the word "Brahman," is what is spoken of in the sentence "Brahman, verily, was this in the beginning," since the Veda speaks of things as they are. But not the supposition that "Brahman" denotes a man-becoming-Brahman, contrary to the meaning of the word — that is improper, being abandonment of what is heard and supposition of what is unheard. And if it be said that besides what is wrought by avidyā there really is non-Brahman-ness and non-all-ness — no; for that cannot be removed by brahma-vidyā. Brahma-vidyā has nowhere been seen to be the remover or producer of any real attribute of a thing; it is seen everywhere only as the dispeller of avidyā. So here too let only the avidyā-wrought non-Brahman-ness and non-all-ness be dispelled by brahma-vidyā; brahma-vidyā can neither create nor destroy a real entity. Therefore the abandonment of the heard and the postulation of the unheard is utterly futile.
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-3: If you say avidyā is impossible in Brahman — no; for vidyā is enjoined with respect to Brahman. If there were no superimposition of silver upon mother-of-pearl, mother-of-pearl, when before the eyes, would not be made known by saying "this is mother-of-pearl, not silver." In the same way, the knowledge of unity in Brahman would not need to be enjoined — "All this verily is Sat," "All this is Brahman," "All this is the Self," "There is no duality here apart from Brahman" — if there were no superimposition of avidyā upon Brahman. We do not say there is no superimposition of non-Self attributes upon Brahman, as upon mother-of-pearl. What then? We say Brahman in itself is not the cause of superimposition of non-Self attributes, nor the agent of avidyā. So Brahman is not avidyā's agent nor deluded. Nor is some other non-Brahman, conscious, deluded agent of avidyā admitted; for the śrutis say, "There is no other knower than this," "There is no other knower than this," "That thou art," "It knew its own Self alone, 'I am Brahman,'" "He thinks 'this is one and I am another'; he does not know"; and from the smṛtis, "The same in all beings," "I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa," "In a dog and in an outcast equally," and the mantra-utterance "He who in all beings," "In whom all beings." If you say the teaching of śāstra would then be purposeless — yes indeed, once realised it has no further purpose; but if you object that even the realisation is purposeless — no, since the cessation of non-realisation is observed. If you object that even that cessation is impossible in unity — no, contradicting what is seen; for the cessation of non-realisation is in fact seen to occur from the very knowledge of unity. To say of what is observed that it is impossible is contradiction of perception, and no one accepts contradiction of perception. Nor is anything observed itself "impossible," simply because it is observed. If you say the very seeing is impossible, the same reasoning applies there too.
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-4: From śruti, smṛti, and reasoning such as "a man becomes pure by pure action," "vidyā and karma take hold of him," "the thinker, the cogniser, the agent, the knowledge-self, the puruṣa" — a saṃsārī is known as different from the Para; and from such śrutis as "This is that, neti neti," "He transcends hunger," "the Self free from sin, decay, and death," "in the rule of this Imperishable" — the Para is known as different from the saṃsārī. In the tarka-śāstras of Kaṇāda, Akṣapāda and others, an Īśvara distinct from the saṃsārī is established by inference; and from the seen activity of seeking removal of saṃsāric pain, the saṃsārī is plainly known as other than Īśvara. From the śruti and smṛti "speechless, unheeding," "to me, O Pārtha, there is nothing," and from "He is to be sought, He is to be enquired into," "knowing him, one is not soiled," "the knower of Brahman attains the highest," "this is to be seen as one only," "he who, O Gārgya, departs without knowing this Imperishable," "having known him, the wise one," "praṇava is the bow, the arrow is the Self, Brahman is called the target," the indication of action and agent is also given. And on account of the teaching of a special path and place for the seeker of liberation: if there were no difference, whose journey would be from where? In the absence of difference, the southern and northern paths and the place to be reached would all be impossible; only on a saṃsārī differing from the Para does all this fit. Also from the teaching of action and knowledge as means: if the saṃsārī were different from Brahman, the teaching of karma and jñāna for prosperity and the highest good would be apt for him, but not for Īśvara, who is fully content. Therefore it is fit to say that "Brahman" denotes the man-going-to-be-Brahman — so it is held. No: for the teaching about Brahman would then be purposeless. If a saṃsārī, being non-Brahman, by knowing his own self alone as "I am Brahman," became all, then the fruit of becoming all-Self would be accomplished by the knowledge of the saṃsārī-self alone, and the teaching of Para-Brahman would surely be purposeless. If you say that since such knowledge of the saṃsārī-self does not lead to any human end, the teaching is meant to bring about Brahman-hood by the device of saṃpat, "I am Brahman" — well, when the very nature of Brahman is unknown, what should one bring into saṃpat as "I am Brahman"? Saṃpat can be made only when the lakṣaṇa of Brahman is known. From "This Self is Brahman," "that which is direct and immediate, Brahman," "the Self," "that is real, that is the Self," "the knower of Brahman attains the highest" — taking up the topic — and from "hence verily from this Self," the thousandfold sāmānādhikaraṇya of "Brahman" and "Self" is understood as oneness of meaning. Saṃpat is performed of the different upon the different, never in unity. "This whole, what is this Self," so saying, the very Self that is to be seen is shown as one. Therefore the saṃpat of Brahman-hood upon the Self does not stand.
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-5: If you say: the supposition of being a sādhaka in Brahman, as in the case of ourselves — that is unbecoming, since the text says "It knew its own Self alone, therefore it became all" — no; this would amount to censure of the śāstra. This is not our supposition; it is the śāstra-maker's. Therefore your censure falls upon the śāstra. He who wishes to do what is dear to Brahman should not, by supposition contrary to the meaning of śāstra, abandon his own purpose. Nor is your impatience justified even in this much. All multiplicity is merely imagined in Brahman, by hundreds of texts: "this is to be seen only as one," "there is no multiplicity here at all," "where there appears to be duality," "one only without a second," and so on. All worldly transaction is imagined in Brahman; it is not real. So this little we say: this very supposition is your own "becoming."
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-6: Therefore — that Brahman, the creator, which entered, that Brahman, vai (used for emphasis), this body-resident which is grasped, agre — even before awakening — was Brahman alone, and was all this; only by non-awakening, by superimposition upon the Self that "I am non-Brahman, not-all," and superimposing further "I am the doer, possessed of activity, enjoyer of fruits, happy, sorrowful, saṃsārī." In truth it is Brahman alone, and yet all that is distinct from it. Then somehow, by a compassionate teacher awakened — "You are not a saṃsārī" — it knew its own Self, the natural Self, free of the particularities superimposed by avidyā: this is the meaning of the word eva.
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-7: Tell us, who is this natural Self, knowing whom Brahman became the knower? "Surely you remember the Self; it has been shown — the one which, having entered here, breathes as prāṇa, breathes out as apāna, fills as vyāna, ascends as udāna, equalises as samāna." But this is your indicating it like "that ox," "that horse"; you do not show the Self directly. "Then the seer, hearer, thinker, cogniser is the Self." But here too you do not show directly the very nature of the agent of seeing and the rest; for going is not the very nature of the goer, nor splitting of the splitter. "Then the seer of seeing, the hearer of hearing, the thinker of thinking, the cogniser of cognising is the Self." What special difference is there here in the seer? Whether it is the seer of seeing or of a pot, in any case it is just a seer. You speak only of the special character of the seen — "seer of seeing." Whether the seer is of seeing or of a pot, the seer is just a seer. No, there is a particularity here. He who is the seer of seeing — if he were seeing itself, he would always see seeing; for the seeing is never not seen by the seer, since the seer must have eternal seeing. If the seer's seeing were impermanent, then any visible seeing might at some time not be seen — as a pot is, by impermanent seeing. But it is not so that the seer of seeing ever fails to see seeing. "Are there then two seeings of the seer — eternal and unseen, and another impermanent and seen?" Yes. The impermanent seeing is well known, by observing the blind and the unblind; if seeing were eternal, all would be unblind. But the seer's seeing is eternal, by śruti, "there is no destruction of the seer's seeing"; and by inference — even in the blind, there is, in dream, a seeing whose objects are reflections of pots and so on; that is not destroyed when the other seeing is destroyed. That is the seer's seeing. By that unbroken eternal seeing, the very nature, called self-luminous, the seer always sees the other impermanent seeing — that arising in dream and waking, in the form of vāsanā-cognitions — and so is the seer of seeing. Thus seeing is His very nature, like heat in fire; not as the Kāṇādas hold, that there is some other conscious seer apart from seeing.
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-8: That Brahman knew the Self alone, of the form of eternal seeing, free from the superimposed impermanent seeings: it knew. "But this is contradicted by the śruti 'one cannot know the knower of knowing,' which forbids cognition of the cogniser." Not so; cognition in this manner is not contradictory: this much is cognised — "the seer of seeing." And the cognition is not dependent upon another cognition. Once one knows that the seer's seeing is eternal, one does not desire some further seeing whose object is the seer; for the desire for a seeing whose object is the seer ceases at the very impossibility of such. No one desires of a non-existent object. Nor can any seen seeing dare to make the seer its object, that one might desire it. Nor does one desire one's own self as an object. Therefore "it knew its own Self" means only the cessation of the superimposition of ignorance, not the objectifying of the Self.
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-9: How then did it know? "I am the seer of seeing, the Self, Brahman, I am." "Brahman" — that which is direct and immediate, the inmost Self of all, beyond hunger and so on, the neti-neti, neither gross nor subtle, marked by such characteristics — that very thing am I, not another, a saṃsārī, as you say. Therefore from such knowledge, that Brahman became all — by removal of the superimposition of non-Brahman, by cessation of its effect, the not-being-all, it became all. Therefore it is rightly said by men, "by brahma-vidyā we shall become all." The asked question — what was that Brahman, on knowing which it became all? — has been settled: "Brahman, verily, was this in the beginning. It knew its own Self, 'I am Brahman.' Therefore it became all."
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-10: There — whoever among the gods awoke, awakened to the Self by the said procedure, he, the awakened Self, became that Brahman; so among the seers, so among men. "Of the gods," and so on, is from the standpoint of the worldly view, not on the supposition of their being Brahman. We have said that the Puruṣa entered all forms; everywhere only Brahman has entered. Hence "of the gods" and the rest is said in conformity with the worldly view caused by the upādhis of body and the rest. In truth, in each, only Brahman was, agre — before awakening — being differently conceived in the bodies of gods and others; it knew its own Self alone, and so became all.
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-11: To strengthen this meaning that the becoming-all is the fruit of brahma-vidyā, the śruti cites mantras. How? Seeing this Brahman, "I am that Self," from this very seeing of Brahman the seer named Vāmadeva attained — pratipede ha, indeed attained. Established in this seeing of Brahman as Self, he saw these mantras: "I was Manu, I was the Sun," and so on. "Seeing this Brahman" indicates brahma-vidyā; "I was Manu, I was the Sun" indicates the becoming-all that is its fruit. The very phrase "seeing, attained the all-Self-becoming as fruit" shows liberation as accomplished by means joined to brahma-vidyā — like "eating, one is satisfied." "That becoming-all by brahma-vidyā belonged to the great gods and the rest by abundance of vīrya, but not now to men of the present age — particularly because of their lesser vīrya": such a notion may arise in someone. To dispel it, the śruti says — this Brahman now under topic, which has entered all beings, marked by the action of seeing and so on, even now, in this present time, whoever, with outward eagerness withdrawn, knows the Self thus, "I am Brahman" — having dispelled the particular features superimposed by upādhi-born error, free from saṃsāric attributes, immediate, not external, "I alone am Brahman" — by the cessation of the avidyā-made not-being-all, by brahma-vijñāna, becomes this all. There is no difference, between the great-vīrya Vāmadeva and the like and the lesser-vīrya present-day men, in Brahman or in its knowledge. As to whether for present-day men the fruit of brahma-vidyā is uncertain, the śruti says: of him, the brahma-knower by the said procedure, the great-vīrya gods cannot — even cannot — prevent his becoming-Brahman-all; how much less others.
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-12: What doubt is there that gods and the like can hinder the attainment of the fruit of brahma-vidyā? — It is said: by mortals' indebtedness to gods and the like; "by brahmacarya to the seers, by sacrifice to the gods, by progeny to the fathers" — the śruti shows the man indebted from the very moment of birth. From the simile of the animal and from the śruti "now this is verily," gods, like creditors guarding their own livelihood, would obstruct men dependent upon them in the attainment of immortality — this doubt is reasonable. Gods protect men as their own animals and bodies; for it will be shown that gods have larger livelihood, dependent on action, with each man being like many animals. "Therefore the gods do not like that men should know this" — this will be said. And "as one wishes safety for his own world, so all beings wish safety for one who knows thus." When one becomes a knower of Brahman, by the cessation of being-for-another, he is no longer their world or animal — this purport is gathered from the words "unpleasant" and "safety." Therefore the gods do indeed obstruct the brahma-knower in attaining the fruit of brahma-vidyā. And they have power.
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-13: If so, then in the attainment of fruits of other actions too, the gods' obstruction would be like quaffing a drink; alas, then there would be no trust in the performance of the means of prosperity and highest good. Likewise Īśvara's lordship in obstructing, by reason of his inconceivable power; likewise time, action, mantra, herb, austerity. For these are well known in śāstra and the world as the causes of attainment or failure of fruit; hence too there would be no confidence in the performance of the meaning of śāstra. Not so. From the variegation of the world, every entity is undertaken by some specific cause; on the position of "natural," both these would not stand. The doctrine that karma is the cause of fruits like pleasure and pain — accepted by Veda, smṛti, reasoning and the world — is settled. Then gods, Īśvara, and time are not subverters of the fruit of karma, since they are subordinate to karma's requirement; karma, śubha or aśubha, of men cannot have its own being without depending on the kārakas of god, time, Īśvara, and so on, nor can it bestow fruit even when it has come into being, for activity essentially needs many causes such as kārakas. Hence gods, Īśvara, and the like are conformable to action, and so there is no want of trust in the attainment of the fruit of action. Of these too there is sometimes subordination to action, since their power is not to be set aside. The relation of principal and subordinate among karma, time, daiva, dravya, and svabhāva is not fixed and is hard to know; thence the world is deluded — some say only karma is the kāraka, not anything else, in attaining fruit; others, only daiva; some, time; some, dravya-svabhāva; others, all these together. There among them, accepting the principality of karma, are the Veda-smṛti utterances such as "a man becomes pure by pure action, and impure by impure." Though one of these is principal and the others are restrained at that time, still there is no uncertainty about karma's relation to fruit, since the principality of karma is established by śāstra and reasoning.
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-14: No: for the fruit of attaining Brahman is the mere removal of avidyā. Where it has been said gods would obstruct the fruit of attaining Brahman, in that gods have no capacity to obstruct. Why? Because the fruit of attaining Brahman is not separated in time from vidyā. How? As in the world, the eye's contact with light is the time at which form is manifest, so the cognition concerning the Self and the disappearance of ignorance about it are simultaneous; therefore when brahma-vidyā has arisen, no effect of avidyā can stand, like darkness's effect when a lamp is present. By whom and to whom should gods cause obstruction, when the very Self of the gods is the brahma-knower? This very point is stated: the Self, the very nature, the object of meditation, that which is to be known by all śāstras, namely Brahman, is the very nature of the gods; the brahma-knower becomes their Self at the very time of brahma-vidyā — by the removal of the mere veil of avidyā — as the silver-appearance of mother-of-pearl becomes mother-of-pearl, as we have said. Therefore gods cannot make effort against the Self. Effort directed at obstruction by gods is fruitful where the fruit is non-Self, mediated by space, time, and other causes; not here, where the fruit is in the Self, simultaneous with vidyā, not mediated by space, time, or cause — there is no occasion.
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-15: If so, then by absence of continuity of vidyā-cognition, and from the seen presence of contrary cognitions and their effects, only the last cognition of the Self removes avidyā, not the earlier — Not so; for the first cognition would be uncertain too: if the first Self-directed cognition does not remove avidyā, neither does the last, since the object is the same. "Then continuity of cognition removes avidyā, not interrupted" — Not so; in the presence of life-cognitions and the like, continuity is impossible, since they are contradictory. "Then by setting aside life-cognitions and the like, vidyā-continuity to the very moment of death" — Not so; since the number and continuity of cognitions cannot be settled, the meaning of śāstra is not ascertained — "by such-and-such number of cognitions in continuity is avidyā removed" — and that is unwelcome. "It is settled that mere continuity is enough" — Not so; from the indistinctness of beginning and end, since whether the first or up-to-death continuity is meant, both faults of beginning and end will arise. "Then it does not remove" — Not so; from the śruti "therefore it became all," and from "the knot of the heart is rent," "there what delusion?" and so on.
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-16: If you say it is arthavāda — Not so; that would render all Upaniṣads of every śākhā mere arthavāda, since all Upaniṣads conclude only with this much purport. "It is established as object of direct cognition" — Not so; the answer has been given: "by the directness of the removal of avidyā, sorrow, delusion, fear, and like faults, this is direct" — so the answer was made. Hence whether first, last, continuous, non-continuous — this is no objection, since the fruit-bearing of vidyā ends with the removal of avidyā and the like; whichever cognition produces the fruit of removing the faults of avidyā etc. — first, last, continuous, or non-continuous — that itself is vidyā, by acceptance; the objection has not even a whiff of relevance. As to what was said about the perception of contrary cognitions and their effects — Not so; that is the cause of the persistence of the residue. The action by which the body was begun was caused by the fault of contrary cognition; that very action, joined with the fault of contrary cognition, has the capacity to bestow fruit. Until the fall of the body, as a means to fruit-enjoyment, it draws contrary cognition and rāga and the like to that extent — like a released arrow, fruit-bearing already begun. Therefore vidyā does not remove that, since there is no contradiction; rather, vidyā arrests, in its own seat, the avidyā-effect that is contrary to its own self and is about to arise — being as yet unborn; the past is otherwise. Moreover, contrary cognition does not arise in the vidyā-possessor, since it has no object — contrary cognition arises taking some general thing whose particular nature is unascertained, like silver upon mother-of-pearl. For one in whom the particular has been ascertained, since the entire abode of contrary cognition has been crushed, contrary cognition does not arise as before, as is seen in the absence of further such cognition once mother-of-pearl is rightly cognised. Sometimes, even after vidyā, by impressions left from previous contrary cognitions, recollections that appear like contrary cognitions arise and produce the delusion of contrary cognition without cause — like one who, knowing the directions, suddenly is bewildered as to direction. If contrary cognition arose in the right-knower as before, there would be no trust in right knowledge, and the activity in śāstra-meaning would be improper, and every pramāṇa would become non-pramāṇa, since pramāṇa and non-pramāṇa would be undistinguishable. By this, the question why right knowledge is not immediately followed by the fall of the body is answered. As to actions, gathered before the rise of knowledge or after, whose fruit has not yet begun to operate, their destruction is established by the very śruti negating the obstruction in fruit-attainment: "and his actions are exhausted," "his only as long as," "all sins burn away," "knowing him one is not soiled by sinful action," "these two do not cross him," "the done and undone do not torment him," "this verily does not torment him," "he fears nothing whatever"; and from smṛtis like "the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes."
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-17: As to being bound by debts — that is in the sphere of the avidyā-possessor; for the indebted is the avidyā-possessor, since agency and so on are possible for him. "Where there were as another" — it will be said: when the non-different real, called Self, by avidyā becomes as it were another — like a second moon by an eye-disorder — then śruti shows the action of seeing and so on, dependent on the many kārakas made by avidyā, and its fruit, in "there one would see another." When, by vidyā, the avidyā-made delusion of multiplicity is removed, "there what would one see by what?" — śruti shows the impossibility of action. Therefore indebtedness applies only to the sphere of the avidyā-possessor, since action is possible there, not elsewhere. We shall show this in detail by the very sentences that we shall begin to explain hereafter.
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-18: Now, here itself: any non-knower of Brahman, on his part, worships some other deity — separate from his Self — by stuti, namaskāra, yāga, bali, upahāra, praṇidhāna, dhyāna, and so on; he upāsate, sits down, having gone into subordination to that deity, with the cognition "that anātman is other, separate from me; I am another, qualified; I, like an indebted one, must do return service to him" — he does not know, does not understand, the truth. He is not merely a non-knower with the fault of avidyā; rather, like a cow being employed for carrying, milking, and other services, he is to be enjoyed by the various services, sacrifice and the like, by each god and the like. So he is qualified, like an animal, in all artha-actions — that is the meaning. For of this non-knower, qualified by varṇa-āśrama distinction, the fruit of action joined with vidyā or alone, prescribed by śāstra, is the rise from man-hood up to Brahmā's status; the fruit of contrary, natural action is decline from man-hood down to immobile beings. We shall explain how this is in the rest of the chapter, beginning "now there are three worlds." The fruit of vidyā is the becoming-all-Self — this has been shown briefly. This entire Upaniṣad ends with showing the distinction of vidyā and avidyā. We shall show that this is the meaning of the entire śāstra.
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-19: Since this is so, the gods do indeed have power to obstruct or favour the avidyā-possessor — this is shown: as in the world many animals, cows, horses, and the like, support a man, their owner, their adhiṣṭhātṛ — so each non-knowing man, being like many animals, supports the gods ("gods" implies fathers and the like), supports them, with the disposition: "these — Indra and the rest — are other than I, my rulers; I, like a servant, by stuti, namaskāra, ijyā and the like, doing worship, shall obtain prosperity and the highest good as their gift." Just as in the world, when the owner of many animals has even one animal taken away, robbed by a tiger or the like, much grief arises, so when a man like many animals turns away from animal-hood, what wonder if it is unpleasant to the gods — like the householder when many animals are robbed. Therefore that is not pleasant to them — what? — that men should somehow know this, the Brahman-Self truth. Such is the smṛti of Vyāsa in the Anugītā: "by the action-doers, O son of Kuntī, the deva-loka is filled. The gods do not desire that mortals rise above." Hence gods, like animals threatened by tigers, wish to obstruct brahma-vijñāna — "may they not, who are our enjoyables, rise." Whom they wish to liberate they will join with śraddhā and the rest; the contrary they will join with aśraddhā and the rest. Therefore the seeker of liberation should be intent on serving the gods, intent on śraddhā and bhakti, gentle, undeluded; this is what the words "unpleasant to the gods" suggestively show, regarding the attainment of vidyā or vidyā itself.
BR_C01_S04_V10::block-20: The śāstra-meaning has been outlined as "let one worship as Self alone"; in the explication, by the arthavāda "thus they say, what by brahma-vidyā" and so on, the connection and purpose were stated; and the cause of avidyā in saṃsāra-qualification was stated by "now he who worships another deity" and so on. There it has been said that the non-knower, like an indebted animal, is dependent on the duty of doing actions toward the gods and the rest. Now what is the cause of doing actions to the gods and the rest? Varṇas and āśramas. What then are the varṇas? Hence this is begun. Bound to actions whose cause is this distinction, this dependent one transmigrates as qualified. To show this very meaning, the creation of Indra and the rest was not stated immediately after the creation of Agni; the creation of Agni was shown for completing Prajāpati's creation. The creation of Indra and the rest is to be seen there itself, since it is part of that. Here it is stated to show the cause of the non-knower's qualification for action.
BR_C01_S04_V11: Brahman, verily, was this in the beginning, one only. Being one, it did not flourish. It superiorly created the kṣatra, the noble form, those kṣatras among the gods: Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, Rudra, Parjanya, Yama, Mṛtyu, Īśāna. Therefore there is nothing higher than the kṣatra. Hence at the rājasūya the brāhmaṇa worships the kṣatriya from below; he places his fame, namely Brahman, in the kṣatra alone. The womb of the kṣatra is verily Brahman. Therefore even when the king attains supremacy, in the end he takes refuge in Brahman, his own womb. Whoever injures him injures his own womb; he becomes more sinful, like one who has injured a superior.
BR_C01_S04_V11::block-0: "Brahman verily was this in the beginning" — that Brahman, having created Agni and assumed the form of Agni, called "Brahman" because of the brāhmaṇa-jāti-abhimāna, vai, this kṣatra and the rest, was Brahman alone, undivided, ekam eva — there was no distinction of kṣatra and the rest. That one Brahman, lacking a kṣatra-protector and the rest, did not flourish, na vyabhavat — was not adequate for action, the meaning is. Then that Brahman — desiring action whose cause is brāhmaṇa-jāti, thinking "I am a brāhmaṇa, this is my duty," for its own karma-doership-flourishing — superiorly created kṣatra in praiseworthy form, ati asṛjata, with abundance. What is created? Kṣatra, the kṣatriya class. He shows it through individual instances: "those well-known in the world," devatrā among the gods — kṣatrāṇi: in jāti-designation the plural is by smṛti's option, or by individual multiplicity, by figurative use of bhedopacāra. What are they? Those specifically anointed are pointed out: Indra is king of the gods; Varuṇa of the waters; Soma of brāhmaṇas; Rudra of animals; Parjanya of lightning and the like; Yama of the fathers; Mṛtyu of diseases and the like; Īśāna of the lights — such are the kṣatras among the gods. Then, presided over by these god-kṣatras, the man-kṣatras of the Soma and Sūrya lines, Purūravas and the rest, are also to be regarded as created; for that very purpose the creation of the god-kṣatras was undertaken. Since by Brahman the kṣatra is created with such excellence, there is nothing higher than the kṣatra; not even the brāhmaṇa-jāti is its restrainer. Therefore the brāhmaṇa, though the cause, of the kṣatriya, being placed below the kṣatriya who stands above, worships him — where? At the rājasūya. He places that ātmīya yaśas, the form of fame called "Brahman," in the kṣatra alone — he places it. When the king anointed at the rājasūya, seated on the throne, addresses "O Brahman," the ṛtvik replies, "You, O King, are Brahman." This is what is meant by "he places his fame in the kṣatra alone." That is the kṣatra's very womb, namely Brahman. Therefore though the king attains supremacy, the perfection of rājasūya consecration, in the end, at the close of the action, he takes refuge in Brahman alone, the brāhmaṇa-jāti, his own womb — places the purohita in front, the meaning is. He who, by pride of strength, injures his own womb the brāhmaṇa-jāti, the brāhmaṇa, looks down upon him with disrespect — he reaches his own womb, that is, severs and destroys his own source. Doing this he becomes pāpīyān, more sinful: previously the kṣatriya is sinful by cruelty; by injury to his own source, much more so. As in the world, having injured a praiseworthy superior, looking him down, one becomes more sinful — like that.
BR_C01_S04_V12: He still did not flourish. He created the viś, those classes of gods named in groups: Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Viśvedevas, Maruts.
BR_C01_S04_V12::block-0: Even when the kṣatra was created, he did not flourish, sa naiva vyabhavat. Brahman did not flourish for action, by the lack of a procurer of wealth. He created the viś for procuring the wealth that is the means of action. Who is this viś? "Those god-classes" — niṣṭhā in svārtha; those distinct god-jātis is the meaning — "are spoken of group by group, gaṇaśaḥ" — for the viś is generally a group; for those acting together are capable in earning wealth, not one by one. Vasus is a class of eight; the Rudras eleven; the Ādityas twelve; Viśvedevas, thirteen offspring of Viśvā — or all the gods; the Maruts seven groups of seven.
BR_C01_S04_V13: He still did not flourish. He created the śūdra varṇa, Pūṣan. This earth is verily Pūṣan, for she nourishes all this, whatever there is.
BR_C01_S04_V13::block-0: He still did not flourish, by the absence of a servitor; he created the śūdra varṇa — śūdra eva śaudra, vṛddhi being in svārtha aṇ. Who is this śūdra-varṇa that was created? Pūṣan — "that which nourishes is Pūṣan." Who again is this Pūṣan? It is specifically pointed out: this earth is Pūṣan. The śruti itself gives the etymology — for she nourishes all this, whatever there is.
BR_C01_S04_V14: He still did not flourish. He superiorly created that praiseworthy form, dharma. That is the kṣatra of the kṣatra, namely dharma. Therefore there is nothing higher than dharma. The weaker hopes to overcome the stronger by dharma, as if by a king. That which is dharma is verily satya. Therefore they say of one speaking the truth, "he speaks dharma," and of one speaking dharma, "he speaks satya" — for both are this.
BR_C01_S04_V14::block-0: Even after creating four varṇas, he did not flourish, since by the kṣatra's fierceness there was apprehension of unrestraint. He superiorly created that of praiseworthy form — what? — dharma. This praiseworthy form created is the kṣatra of the kṣatra, the restrainer even of the kṣatra, fiercer than the fierce — yad dharmaḥ. Therefore, since it restrains even the kṣatra, there is nothing higher than dharma; for by it all are restrained. How so? It is said: even abalīyān, weaker, hopes to conquer the balīyān, stronger, by dharma, as means of strength — as in the world the householder hopes to conquer even the all-strongest king. Therefore it is established that dharma is universally restraining since strongest of all. That which is dharma, the practical mark, undertaken by worldly men, is satya; satya means accordance with śāstra-meaning. The same, when actually performed, is named dharma; when known by the meaning of śāstra, it becomes satya. Hence at the time of conduct, those nearby who know the difference of both say of one speaking satya, that is, speaking according to śāstra, "he speaks dharma," speaks the well-known worldly nyāya. Conversely, of one speaking dharma, the worldly conduct, they say, "he speaks satya," speaks what is not contrary to śāstra. What was said — both, when known and performed, this is dharma alone. Therefore that dharma, marked by jñāna and anuṣṭhāna, restrains śāstra-knower and the rest. Therefore it is the kṣatra even of the kṣatra. Hence the non-knower, having abhimāna in it, has abhimāna in particular niceties of brahma-kṣatra-viṭ-śūdra causes for performing its specific anuṣṭhāna. These are by nature the very causes of qualification for action.
BR_C01_S04_V15: This same: brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya, śūdra. By Agni alone among the gods Brahman became, and as brāhmaṇa among men; as kṣatriya through the kṣatriya, as vaiśya through the vaiśya, as śūdra through the śūdra. Therefore in Agni alone among the gods do they seek the world, and in the brāhmaṇa among men. By these two forms verily Brahman became. Now whoever departs from this world without seeing his own world, like the unstudied Veda or any unperformed action, that, being unknown, does not nourish him. And even if one not knowing thus performs much puṇya-karma, in the end it perishes. Let one worship the Self alone as the world. Of him who worships the Self alone as the world, his action does not perish. Whatever he desires, that he creates from this very Self.
BR_C01_S04_V15::block-0: This created cāturvarṇya — brāhmaṇa, kṣatra, viṭ, śūdra; this is upasaṃhāra for the next purpose. That creator-Brahman, by Agni alone, not by any other form, among the gods became Brahman, the brāhmaṇa-jāti; as the brāhmaṇa, in his proper form, became Brahman among men. Among the other varṇas, attaining further modification: as kṣatriya — became kṣatriya, presided over by Indra and the rest; as vaiśya, vaiśya; as śūdra, śūdra. Since the creator-Brahman remained unmodified in Agni and in the brāhmaṇa, while modified in the kṣatra and the rest, therefore in Agni alone, among the gods, do they seek the loka, the karma-fruit — meaning, having performed the action linked to Agni; for that very purpose that Brahman is established as Agni, the seat of action. Hence having performed action in that Agni, they pray for its fruit — this is fitting. "In the brāhmaṇa among men" — among men, in seeking the karma-fruit, there is no expectation of Agni-mediated kriyā; rather, by the mere attainment of the form of jāti, the puruṣārtha is accomplished. Where the puruṣārtha is dependent on devas, there alone is expectation of Agni-related kriyā. Smṛti too: "by japa alone the brāhmaṇa is perfected, no doubt; whether he does anything else or not, the friendly-to-all is called brāhmaṇa." From the seeing of the way of the wandering ascetic too. Hence in brāhmaṇa-hood alone among men do they seek the karma-fruit. Since by these two forms — brāhmaṇa-Agni — the karma-doer-and-seat forms — the creator-Brahman directly became.
BR_C01_S04_V15::block-1: Here some say that the param-ātma-loka is sought in Agni and in the brāhmaṇa. That is wrong, since varṇa-distinction is here introduced, in the topic of avidyā-qualification, for karma-qualification, and since it is qualified by what follows. If by the word loka the Para-ātman is meant, the qualification by what follows — "without seeing his own loka" — would be useless. If the prakṛta loka being sought through Agni-dependence is other than one's own loka, then "sva" is a fitting qualification, intended to exclude the prakṛta-para-loka. Since svatva of the param-ātma-loka does not vary, while svatva of avidyā-made things varies — and the śruti speaks of the variability of karma-made things, "it perishes" — the qualification fits.
BR_C01_S04_V15::block-2: Varṇas are created by Brahman for action; that action, named dharma, is restrainer of all by way of duty, and is the means of puruṣārtha. Therefore even if without action one's own loka, called param-ātmā, is attained though unseen, what use is its being made the goal? Hence: atha — for the rejection of the pūrvapakṣa. Whoever, ha vai, from this saṃsāric pinda-grasping caused by avidyā-kāma-karma, by abhimāna in Agni-dependent karma or in mere brāhmaṇa-jāti karma, from the āgantuka, asvabhūta loka, does not, before death, see his own loka, called Self, sva by non-deviation, as "I am Brahman," and praiti, dies — though it is one's own loka, being avidyā-veiled, like an unknown stranger, like a number-filling stranger in the world, the Self does not nourish him, does not protect him by removing sorrow, delusion, fear and the like; just as in the world the unstudied Veda does not nourish him by awakening of action and the like; or any other worldly action, like agriculture, unperformed, undisplayed by oneself, does not nourish by giving its own fruit; thus the Self, one's own loka, by its own eternal Self-nature unmanifested, by non-removal of avidyā and the like, does not nourish. "What use of this protection by sight of one's loka? Action's fruit-attainment is fixed, and good-fruit-causing actions are abundant; protection by them will be inexhaustible." Not so; what is done has decay. This is said: yat iha vai, in saṃsāra, like a wonder, even some great soul, anevaṃvit, not knowing his own loka by the said procedure, ignorant, mahat bahu, much aśvamedha and the like, puṇya karma whose iṣṭa-fruit is desired, performs continuously — "by this alone shall I have endlessness" — that karma of the avidyā-possessor, since it is caused by avidyā-born desire, like a manifestation arisen from the delusion of dream-vision, antataḥ at the end of fruit-enjoyment, kṣīyate eva, perishes. Since its causes, avidyā and kāma, are unsteady, the cessation of what is done is fixed. Hence there is no hope of endlessness in puṇya-karma's fruit-protection. Therefore, the Self alone as one's loka — "ātmānam" in the sense of "sva-loka," since sva-loka is in the topic and "sva" is not used here — let him worship. He who worships the Self alone as loka — "his karma does not perish"; from the very absence of karma — this is nityānuvāda; the meaning is, that for the non-knower the saṃsāra-suffering of karma-decay is continuous, but not so for him — like "when Mithilā burns nothing of mine burns."
BR_C01_S04_V15::block-3: Some others explain: by the connection with vidyā in the worshipper of Self as own-loka, karma itself does not perish. They postulate two senses for loka, the karma-samavāyī, namely: one in vyakta state, the seat of karma, named Hairaṇyagarbha; he who worships that limited karma-samavāyī loka in vyakta form has limited karma-Self vision, hence his karma perishes; he who worships that very karma-samavāyī loka in avyakta state, the cause-form, has unlimited-karma-Self vision, hence his karma does not perish. This is a fine supposition but not śrauta. By the prakṛta sva-loka word, the param-ātman is denoted; having broached "sva-loka," abandoning "sva" and inserting "ātman" again as a re-designation of the same — "let him worship the Self alone as loka" — there is no occasion for postulating a karma-samavāyī loka. The qualification by what follows, with the topic of pure vidyā — "what shall we do with progeny, we whose this Self, this loka" — also confirms; from the lokas made of son, action, apara-vidyā, it distinguishes — "this Self is our loka," "his loka is not exhausted by any karma; this is his highest loka." One-sentencehood with these qualified statements is fitting; here too "sva-loka" is the qualification. "From this he creates whatever he desires" — wrong? Not so. Here sva-loka is the param-ātman; from worship of him, he indeed becomes him; once this is established, "whatever he desires, that he creates from this Self" —
BR_C01_S04_V15::block-4: If you say it is wrong to mention fruit other than the attainment of the Self, no — it is sva-loka-upāsana-praise. From sva-loka itself everything desired is fulfilled, and nothing else is to be sought, by āpta-kāmatva — "from the Self prāṇa, from the Self hope," as in another śruti. Or for showing the becoming-all-Self, as before. If indeed it is the Para-Self that is attained, then the use of the word "ātman" — "asmād hyevātmanaḥ" — is fitting: "from this very prakṛta Self, namely the loka." Otherwise, "from the avyakta-state karma" should have been said with qualification, to exclude the prakṛta param-ātma-loka and the vyakta state; for, in the prakṛta and qualified, it is impossible to grasp an unheard intermediate state.
BR_C01_S04_V16: Now this Self is the world of all beings. By what he sacrifices and offers, he becomes the world of the gods. By what he recites, the world of the seers. By what he offers oblations and seeks progeny for the fathers, the world of the fathers. By what he houses men and gives them food, the world of men. By what he gets grass and water for cattle, the world of cattle. By what beasts and birds and ants live in his house, of these their world. As one wishes safety for his own world, so all beings wish safety for the knower thus. This indeed has been known and inquired into.
BR_C01_S04_V16::block-0: "Now this Self." Here it has been said that the avidyā-possessor with abhimāna in varṇa-āśrama, restrained by dharma, is dependent like an animal on the duty of doing actions to gods and the rest. What are those actions, by the duty of which he becomes dependent like an animal? Who are the gods and others to whom, by his actions like an animal, he renders service? Both are now elaborated:
BR_C01_S04_V16::block-1: "Atho" is for sentence-introduction. This — the prakṛta householder, qualified for action, the non-knower, the body-organ-aggregate-conditioned piṇḍa called Self — is the loka, the enjoyable Self, of all beings, gods down to ants, since he serves all by varṇa-āśrama-prescribed actions. By which specific actions does he serve which specific beings, and become whose loka? It is told. "What he sacrifices and offers": yāga, intended for a deity, the abandoning of svatva; the same with abundance of pouring is homa — by such homa-yāga-marked karma, by way of indispensable duty, dependent on the gods like an animal, he is bound, hence loka of the gods. By what he recites, his daily svādhyāya, the loka of the seers. By what he gives the fathers, piṇḍa-water and the like, and what he undertakes for progeny — "desire" implies also begetting, that is, he begets progeny — by such karma, by way of indispensable duty, the fathers' loka, dependent on them as enjoyers. By what he houses men by gift of land, water and the like in his house, and feeds those dwelling or visitors who come asking, by that, the loka of men. By what he gets grass and water for cattle, by that, the loka of cattle. By what in his house wild animals and birds, along with ants, live on grain-balls, scrap-pots, washings of vessels and the like, by that, the loka of these. Since by performing these actions he serves the gods and others, therefore — as in the world one wishes ariṣṭi, freedom from harm and non-deviation from svatva, for one's own loka, one's own deha, and through fear of svatva-deviation guards by nourishment, protection and so on; even so, in the case of one knowing thus — "I am the enjoyable of all beings; in this manner I am to make return-service like an indebted one" — having so determined himself, all beings — gods and others as said — wish ariṣṭi, freedom from destruction, and protect on every side from the deviation of svatva, like householders their cattle. "Therefore that is unpleasant to them." That is this — the indispensable duty, like a debt, of the said actions, has been known in the topic of the five mahā-yajñas, and inquired into in the topic of avadāna.
BR_C01_S04_V16::block-2: "This Self alone was this in the beginning." If, knowing Brahman, he is freed from this animal-state of duty-bondage, by whom is he caused to be engaged in karma-bondage-qualification, helpless as it were, but not in the means of liberation, the qualification for vidyā? It was said: gods protect. Yes; they protect those who have ascended their own qualification-territory; otherwise akṛtābhyāgama and kṛta-nāśa would result. They do not protect a general puruṣa not ascended to specific qualification. Therefore there must be that by which, urged, he, helpless, becomes outward-faced from his own loka. Surely it is avidyā; for the non-knower, becoming outward-faced, engages. Even she does not engage; she is of the nature of veiling the very nature of the thing. She becomes the bīja of the engager, like blindness which is the cause of activity falling into a pit. Then say what it is that is the cause of activity. It is here said — eṣaṇā kāma. While avidyā is natural, in the Kāṭhaka śruti "the foolish chase outward objects of desire" speaks of it; and in smṛti, "this is desire, this is anger," and in Manu, "all activity has desire as its cause." This very meaning is shown in detail up to the end of the chapter.
BR_C01_S04_V17: The Self alone was this in the beginning, one only. He desired: "may I have a wife, may I beget offspring, may I have wealth, may I perform action." This much indeed is desire; even desiring more, one would not find more. Therefore even now one alone desires: "may I have a wife, may I beget offspring, may I have wealth, may I perform action." So long as he does not get any one of these, he thinks himself incomplete. His completeness is this: the mind is his self, speech his wife, breath his offspring, eye his human wealth (for by the eye he obtains it), ear his divine (for by the ear he hears it), the body itself his action (for by the body he acts). This is the fivefold sacrifice; fivefold the animal, fivefold the man, fivefold this all, whatever there is. He who knows thus obtains this all.
BR_C01_S04_V17::block-0: "The Self alone was this in the beginning." Self alone — the natural non-knower, the varṇī marked by the body-organ aggregate, before connection with a wife, is called Self. Hence what was distinct from Self, the desired wife and the rest, was not; he was alone — possessing avidyā which is the seed of the eṣaṇā for wife and the rest, alone he was. Tinged by the natural avidyā-vāsanā which is the superimposition of agency, kāraka, kriyā, fruit upon the very Self, he akāmayata, desired. How? "Wife, the cause of qualification for action, may I, the doer, have; without her I am unqualified for action; hence for the attainment of karma-qualification let there be a wife. Then may I be born — let me, in the form of progeny, be born; then may I have wealth, the means of action, in form of cattle and the like; then may I perform action — the means of prosperity and the highest good — by which, becoming free from debt, I may obtain the lokas of the gods and the rest; let me perform that action and the kāmya means like son, wealth, heaven, and the rest." "This much indeed is desire" — limited to this much, that is. Only so much is to be desired as object: namely, the eṣaṇā marked by the means — wife, son, wealth, action — and the three lokas — manuṣya, pitṛ, deva — as the fruit of this means-eṣaṇā; for that purpose is the means-eṣaṇā marked by wife, son, wealth, action. Therefore there is one and only one eṣaṇā, namely loka-eṣaṇā; this same one, eṣaṇā, with reference to the means is twofold; hence it will be settled, "both these are eṣaṇās only." Since all undertaking is for the sake of fruit, loka-eṣaṇā being implied, has been stated; hence "this much verily is desire" is settled. When meal is mentioned, satisfaction is not to be mentioned separately, since the meal is for it. These two eṣaṇās, marked by sādhya and sādhana, are kāma; impelled by which the non-knower, helpless, like a silkworm, wraps himself: settling himself in the path of action, becoming outward-faced, he does not know his own loka. So in the Taittirīyaka, "smitten by the smoke of fire, he does not know his own loka." How is this much-ness settled for kāmas, since they are infinite? — for kāmas are infinite. Anticipating this, the cause is given: since na-icchan-cana — even desiring more, ataḥ, beyond this means-fruit-marked, bhūyaḥ, more, na vindet — would not find. There is nothing in the world, dṛṣṭa or adṛṣṭa, to be obtained beyond this means-and-fruit; for kāma's object is what is to be obtained; and apart from this such an object does not exist; hence it is fitting to say: "this much indeed is kāma." The meaning is: the dṛṣṭārtha or adṛṣṭārtha eṣaṇā-pair marked by sādhya-sādhana in the sphere of avidyā-possessor's qualification is kāma; therefore, the knower should rise above this. Since thus the non-knower, the previous non-Self-desirer, desired, so the still earlier; this is the loka-condition. Of Prajāpati too, this was the sarga: he, by avidyā, was afraid; then, impelled by kāma, alone, not enjoying, for relief from arati, desired a woman, united with her; thence this sarga arose, as said. Hence in his creation, even now in this present time, before the wife-action, alone, one desires: "May I have a wife, may I be born, may I have wealth, may I perform action," the meaning of the sentence is as said. He, so desiring, [continued in next verse] —
BR_C01_S05_V01: These verses speak of the seven foods that the father generated by intelligence (medhā) and austerity (tapas). One is common to all; two he allotted to the gods; three he made for himself; one he gave to the animals. In this rest all that breathes and all that does not. Why are they not exhausted though they are eaten always? He who knows this imperishability eats food with the face — he goes to the gods and lives on vigour: such are the verses.
BR_C01_S05_V01::block-0:
"Yat saptānnāni medhayā" — avidyā has been the topic at hand. Therein the unenlightened one worships another devatā with the notion "that one is other, I am other." That one, identifying with the orders of varṇa and āśrama, regulated by the obligation of works, performing the rites beginning with juhoti and impelled by desire, while serving the gods and the rest, is — as has been said — "the world of all beings." 

Just as that world is created by each one of his own works, by all beings as that which is to be enjoyed by him, so too he, by the fivefold (pāṅkta) works beginning with juhoti, has emitted all beings and the entire jagat as that which is to be enjoyed by himself. Thus, in proportion to his own karma and vidyā, each one is enjoyer and enjoyed, agent and act of all towards all. This very point we shall expound in the prakaraṇa on knowledge, in the Madhuvidyā: "All is the effect of all, the madhu" — for the sake of cognising the unity of the Self.

Whatever jagat he has emitted as his own food by the fivefold pāṅkta kāmya rite beginning with juhoti, and by vijñāna, that entire jagat, when distributed sevenfold by way of effect and cause, is termed "seven foods," because it is bhojya. By that, he is the father of those foods. These mantras, being summary sūtras illuminating these foods together with their viniyoga, are now set forth.
BR_C01_S05_V02: "That the father generated the seven foods by intelligence and austerity" — indeed by intelligence, by austerity, the father generated. "One is common to him" — this very food which is eaten now is that common food. He who worships this is not freed from sin, for it is mixed. "Two he allotted to the gods" — the offered (huta) and the offered-after (prahuta); therefore men make oblations and after-oblations to the gods. Yet others say these are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa; therefore one should not be a performer of the iṣṭi (kāmya) sacrifices. "One he gave to the animals" — that is milk; for in the beginning men and animals subsist on milk. Therefore they make a new-born child first lick ghee or suckle at the breast; and of a calf they say "it is not yet a grass-eater." "In that all rests, what breathes and what does not" — in milk indeed all that is, breathing and non-breathing, rests. As to what is said, that one offering oblations of milk for a year conquers death — one should not so know; the very day he offers, that day he wins over recurrent death; thus the knower offers all food to the gods. "Why are they not exhausted, being always eaten?" — the puruṣa is the imperishable, for he again and again generates this food. "He who knows this imperishable" — the puruṣa is the imperishable, for he generates this food by thought after thought, by works; were he not to do this, it would be exhausted. "He eats food by the face" — the face is the principal part. "He goes to the gods, he lives on vigour" — this is praise.
BR_C01_S05_V02::block-0:
"Yat saptānnāni" — "yat" is an adverb qualifying "ajanayat." By medhā, that is, by prajñā, by vijñāna; and by tapas, that is, by karma. For knowledge and works alone are denoted by the words medhā and tapas, since they are the topic at hand; not the other meanings of medhā and tapas, since that is not the present prakaraṇa. The pāṅkta karma is indeed the means consisting of wife and the rest. And just before, in "ya evaṁ veda," jñāna has been the topic. Therefore one should not entertain a doubt taking medhā and tapas in their ordinary acceptations.

Thus the supplementary sense is: those seven foods which the father generated by jñāna and karma — these we shall now illumine. There the meaning of the mantras, being veiled, is generally hard to grasp; hence the brāhmaṇa proceeds to expound that meaning. What then is the meaning of "yat saptānnāni medhayā tapasā ajanayat pitā"? It is replied — by the very particle "hi," indicating well-known import, the brāhmaṇa expounds: this mantra has a well-established sense. And by the mantra cited as a recapitulation, "yad ajanayat," its well-known purport is set forth. Therefore the brāhmaṇa speaks without hesitation: "medhayā hi tapasā ajanayat pitā."
BR_C01_S05_V02::block-1:
Pūrvapakṣa: How is this sense well-known? Siddhānta: It is so because the fatherhood of the works ending with progeny — the means of worldly fruits — is a matter of direct experience; and it has been declared by passages such as "jāyā te syāt." There it has been stated that the divine wealth, vidyā, karma, and son are the means with respect to creating the worlds that are fruits. What is to be stated further is itself well-known. Therefore it is fitting to say "medhayā" and so on.

For the eṣaṇā regarding fruits is well-known in the world; and the eṣaṇās have been declared as wife and the rest in "etāvān vai kāmaḥ." In the sphere of brahmavidyā, since all is one, kāma cannot obtain. By this very statement, the world-creatorship by means of the natural, non-scriptural prajñā and tapas has indeed been admitted; for the unwished-for fruit, ending in the immobile creatures, has karma and vijñāna for its cause. But what is intended is the scriptural relation of sādhya and sādhana, since vairāgya towards that is intended in view of the prescription of brahmavidyā: this entire saṁsāra, characterised by the manifest and unmanifest, impure, non-eternal, of the form of sādhya and sādhana, sorrowful, and a domain of avidyā — for one who has become detached from this, brahmavidyā is to be entered upon.
BR_C01_S05_V02::block-2:
Now the distribution of the foods by division is set forth — the mantra-pada "ekam asya sādhāraṇam." Its exposition: "This is that common food of his" — of the assembly of enjoyers. What is it? "Yad idam adyate" — what is eaten, enjoyed, day by day by all living beings, that the father, having created, allotted as common food for the sake of all enjoyers.

"He who worships this" — the food that supports the life of all beings, that is being eaten — that is, becomes intent upon it; for upāsana means devotedness, as is seen in usage like "he attends upon the guru," "he attends upon the king." Therefore the meaning is: one whose chief aim is the enjoyment of food for the body's maintenance, not one whose chief aim is the unseen-purposed karma. Such a one "is not freed from pāpman," from adharma — is not released. So the mantra-line: "moghaṁ annaṁ vindate" (Ṛg-veda 10.97.6) and the rest. So too the smṛti: "One should not cook food for one's own sake"; "He who eats without offering to these is verily a thief" (Bhagavad-gītā 3.13); "In one who eats food, the slayer of an embryo is purged" (Manu 8.137), and so on.

But why is he not freed from pāpman? "For it is mixed" — what is enjoyed by living beings is the common, undivided portion of all; precisely because it is meant for all, even a morsel placed into one's own mouth is seen to cause pain to another — for the hope "may this be mine" is bound up in all. Hence one cannot even swallow without causing pain to another. So too the smaraṇa, "For men, an evil deed (is committed in eating)."
BR_C01_S05_V02::block-3:
Pūrvapakṣa: Some say it is the food called Vaiśvadeva that the householder offers daily.

Siddhānta: Not so. The being-common-to-all-eaters of the food called Vaiśvadeva is not, like the food eaten by all living beings, a matter of direct experience. Nor is the statement "yad idam adyate" appropriate to it. And since the Vaiśvadeva is itself included within the food eaten by all living beings, it is fitting to take in food eaten by dogs, caṇḍālas, and the like — for, apart from the Vaiśvadeva also, food eaten by dogs, caṇḍālas, and the like is observed; there "yad idam adyate" is appropriate.

If such food were not included, by the word "sādhāraṇa" it would follow that it is not generated by the father and not assigned by him — but it is desired that all kinds of food are created and assigned by him. Nor is non-cessation of pāpman fitting for one performing the scripturally ordained Vaiśvadeva karma, since there is no prohibition of it; nor is it like the natural-aversion-causing acts such as fishing, since it is performed by the cultured, and there is the hearing of penalty in its omission; and there is the fitness of penalty in the other case too, by the mantra-line "I am food, I am food, I eat the eater of food" (Taittirīya-upaniṣad 3.10.6).
BR_C01_S05_V02::block-4:
"Dve devān abhājayat" — the mantra-pada. The two foods which, having created, he allotted to the gods — what are these two? It is told: "huta" and "prahuta." Huta is offering in the fire; prahuta, after offering, is the carrying out of the bali. Since the father allotted these two foods, huta and prahuta, to the gods, therefore even now, at the proper time, householders make oblation to the gods, thinking, "this food is being given by us to the gods," and after offering they perform the bali — this is the meaning.
