"Now others say" — the two foods given by the father to the gods are not huta and prahuta, but rather Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa. Since the indication of duality is alike in both, and on account of being well-known, huta-prahuta is the prima-facie view (pūrvapakṣa). Although duality may obtain in huta-prahuta, yet it is the very Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa, taught by śruti, whose being food-of-the-gods is more well-known, since they are revealed by mantras; and where there is the obtaining of the principal and the subordinate, the cognition is more readily of the principal; and Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa are principal in comparison with huta-prahuta. Therefore it is fitting to take these alone — "two he allotted to the gods."

Since these two foods called Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa were established by the father for the sake of the gods, in order to avoid obstruction to their being for the gods, "one should not be an iṣṭi-yājuka," that is, habituated to the iṣṭi-sacrifice; for by the word iṣṭi the kāmya iṣṭis are meant — this is the well-known Śatapatha usage; the meaning is, owing to the use of the suffix denoting habit, one should not be principally engaged in offering kāmya iṣṭis.
BR_C01_S05_V02::block-5:
"Paśubhya ekaṁ prāyacchat" — what is that food which the father gave to the animals? "That is payaḥ," milk. How then is it understood that the animals are owners of this food? It is replied: "For first, in the beginning," since men and animals live on milk alone — for that food is fitting for them; otherwise how could they alone, from the start, regularly subsist on it?

How do they live on it from the start? It is told: since men and animals subsist by that very food even today, just as the assignment was originally made by the father — therefore, when a child is just born, the men of the three varṇas, in the jāta-karma rite, make him lick ghee mixed with gold; or thereafter they suckle him at the breast as may be possible; among others, they apply the breast first — among animals other than men. Then, of a new-born calf, when asked, "How big is the calf?" they answer, "a non-grass-eater" — meaning, it does not yet eat grass; it is so very young that it still subsists on milk alone.

And what they live on at first, in the jāta-karma and so on, namely ghee, and what others live on, namely milk itself — in every way it is on milk alone that they live; for ghee, being a transformation of milk, is itself of the nature of milk.

But why, though seventh, is the animals' food expounded as fourth? Because of being the means of karma; for karma — agnihotra and the like — depends on milk as its means; and that karma, accomplished by means of wealth, is the sādhana of the threefold sādhya food yet to be expounded, just as the previously stated foods Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa are. Hence, since it belongs to the karma-side, it is taught conjoined with karma; the equality of being-a-means, the connection of purpose, and that mere temporal succession is not a cause; also, ease of comprehension in the exposition — for foods can easily be expounded continuously, and being so expounded are easily understood.

"In that all is established, what breathes and what does not" — what is its sense? It is told: in that animal-food, milk, the entire jagat, characterised as adhyātma, adhibhūta, and adhidaiva, is established — "yat prāṇiti," what has prāṇic activity, and "yat na," the immobile, like rock and the rest. There by the very particle "hi," indicating what is well-known, it has been expounded.

How is the substance milk the substratum of all? By the obtaining of causality; and causality means inhering in the karmas like agnihotra — for the entire jagat is of the nature of the transformations of the oblations of agnihotra and the like; the śruti-smṛti utterances on this stand established by hundreds. Hence the explanation by means of "hi" is fitting.

As to what other brāhmaṇas say in this connection: "Offering oblations of milk for a year, one conquers recurrent death" — for, in a year, three hundred and sixty oblations and seven hundred and twenty (such), the bricks of the yājuṣmatī, become equal to the days and nights of the year, and one obtains the year, Agni, and Prajāpati. Doing thus, offering oblations for a year, one conquers recurrent death — having departed hence, having become one with the gods, one does not die again — thus speak the brāhmaṇa-utterances. "One should not so know" — one should not so view it. The very day he offers, that day he conquers recurrent death; he does not require the repetition of a year. Thus the knower — by virtue of what was said, that all this is established in milk because all is of the nature of the transformation of milk-oblations — attains identity with the jagat by a single day. This is what is told: he conquers recurrent death.
BR_C01_S05_V02::block-6:
"Why are they not exhausted, eaten as they are always?" When the father, having created the seven foods, distributed them severally to the various enjoyers, then on, since the existence of those enjoyers depends upon them, they are eaten always, ceaselessly. By the obtaining of exhaustion through use, exhaustion of those foods is fitting; yet they are not seen exhausted, since the world is observed to abide without falling away from its form. There must be some cause of inexhaustibility. Hence the question, "Why are they not exhausted?"

Its reply: "The puruṣa indeed is the imperishable." Just as he previously was, as the father generating foods by medhā and as the enjoyer by the pāṅkta karma connected with wife and the rest — even so those to whom the foods were given, themselves being enjoyers of those foods, are also fathers, since by medhā and tapas they too generate those foods.

This is what is being declared: the puruṣa, who is the enjoyer of foods, is the akṣiti, the cause of inexhaustibility. How is he the imperishable? It is told: because he generates again and again this seven-fold food enjoyed, characterised as karya and karaṇa, of the nature of action and fruit — "by thought after thought," by the prajñā arising at each successive moment, and "by works," by the activities of speech, mind, and body. "If he were not to do this seven-fold food declared, even for a moment, by prajñā and works, then it would be cut off, since it is being eaten ceaselessly, it would be exhausted."

Therefore, just as this puruṣa, the enjoyer of foods, ceaselessly performs in accord with his prajñā and karma, by that very fact the puruṣa is the akṣiti, since his agency is unceasing; therefore foods, even though eaten, are not exhausted — this is the meaning.

Hence this entire world, mounted on the continuum characterised by prajñā and kriyā, of the form of sādhya and sādhana, of the nature of action and fruit, supported by the unbroken series of the karmas and vāsanās of compounded multiple living beings — momentary, impure, without essence, like the current of a river or the succession of a lamp's flames, like the plantain stalk without core, similar to foam, māyā, mirage, water, dream and the like — yet, to the eyes of those whose vision is fixed thereon, it appears as if eternal and substantial. To produce vairāgya, this is told: "by thought after thought he generates by works; if he were not to do this, it would be exhausted." For brahmavidyā is to be entered upon by those who have become detached from this — by the fourth (the renunciate) chiefly.

"He who knows this akṣiti" — the three foods yet to be expounded have, on this very occasion, been already expounded; hence the fruit of knowing their true nature is summed up: he who knows this akṣiti, the cause of inexhaustibility, as stated — "the puruṣa indeed is the imperishable, for he generates this food by thought after thought, by works; were he not to do this, it would be exhausted" — that one "eats food by the face" (pratīka).

Its meaning is told: "the face" is mukhyatva, principal status; that is, in the principal capacity. He who knows that the puruṣa, the father, is the inexhaustibility of foods — he eats food, not as a subordinate to food. Unlike the ignorant, the knower, being the very Self of foods, becomes the enjoyer alone, not entering the state of being-enjoyed.

"He goes to the gods, he lives on vigour" — "goes to the gods" means he attains the state of being a god; "lives on ūrj," on amṛta — this is the praśaṁsā; there is no further new sense.
BR_C01_S05_V03: "Three he made for himself" — mind, speech, prāṇa: these he made for himself. "I was elsewhere-minded, I did not see; I was elsewhere-minded, I did not hear" — for one sees with the mind, hears with the mind. Desire, resolve, doubt, faith and unfaith, firmness and unfirmness, modesty, intelligence, fear — all this is mind alone. Therefore even one touched from behind discerns by the mind. Whatever sound there is, that is speech alone, for she is determined by the end (of her object). She herself is not. Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna, ana — all this is prāṇa alone. Of this is constituted this Self — speech-formed, mind-formed, prāṇa-formed.
BR_C01_S05_V03::block-0:
Of the pāṅkta karma, the three foods set forth as fruits, owing to their being effects and on account of their wide scope, are distinguished and elevated above the previous foods. For their exposition, the subsequent text proceeds up to the end of the brāhmaṇa.

"Trīṇy ātmane akuruta" — what is its sense? It is told: mind, speech, prāṇa — these three are the foods. The father, having first created mind, speech, and prāṇa, made them for himself, that is, for his own sake.

Regarding the mind, there might be a doubt as to its existence and form; therefore it is said: there does indeed exist a mind, distinct from the external organs such as the ear, on account of what is well-known: even when there is connection between the external organ and the object, when one is turned-toward, one does not grasp the object. When asked, "Did you see this form?" one says: "My mind was elsewhere — being elsewhere-minded, I did not see"; and when asked, "Did you hear this word of mine?" — "I was elsewhere-minded, I did not hear it."

Therefore, in whose absence — though there is connection between the eye and the like, though they are competent to grasp form and the rest, with their respective objects — there does not arise the cognition of form, sound, and the rest, and in whose presence it does arise: that other thing, called manas, the inner instrument, conjoined with the objects of all organs, is recognised. Hence everyone in the world "sees indeed by the mind, hears by the mind"; for, when the mind is occupied elsewhere, seeing and the rest are absent.
BR_C01_S05_V03::block-1:
Once the existence of the mind is established, this is said for the sake of its svarūpa: kāma — desire for woman-association and the like; saṅkalpa — the determining of an object presented to one in the form of "white," "blue" and the like; vicikitsā — knowledge of the form of doubt; śraddhā — āstika-buddhi in regard to unseen-purposed karmas, and in respect of devatās and the rest; aśraddhā — the contrary buddhi; dhṛti — the holding-up which sustains at the close of the body and the like; adhṛti — its opposite; hrī — modesty; dhī — prajñā; bhī — fear: all such states are mind alone; these are the forms of the mind, the inner instrument.

Another ground is given for the existence of the mind: there does exist an inner instrument called manas because, of what is not within the eye's range, even one touched from behind by someone else, discerns with discrimination, "This is the touch of a hand," "This is of the knee." If there were no instrument of discrimination called manas, by what mere skin alone could the cognition of discrimination arise? That which is the cause of the cognition of discrimination is the manas.
BR_C01_S05_V03::block-2:
There exists indeed a manas, and its svarūpa has been ascertained. The three foods of karmas, called manas, vāk, prāṇa, fruits as they are, the adhyātma, adhibhūta, and adhidaiva — were intended to be expounded. Of these, the adhyātmika vāk, manas, prāṇa — the manas has been expounded.

Now comes the start: vāk is to be expounded. Whatever sound there is in the world — a noise expressible by the palate and the like, of the nature of phonemes, by living beings, or any other caused by musical instruments, clouds and the like — every dhvani is verily that vāk. Thus far the svarūpa of vāk has been told.

Now its function is told: this vāk, indeed, is determined by the end — the conclusion of the meaning, the determination of the meaning. She herself is not, however, like the meant, to be illumined; she is solely the illuminator of the meaning, since she is of the nature of light, like a lamp and the like; for the light of a lamp and the like is not illumined by another light. So vāk is solely illuminator, not herself to be illumined — thus śruti wards off infinite regress (anavasthā): "she is not to be illumined; the vāk's function is illumining alone" — this is the sense.
BR_C01_S05_V03::block-3:
Now prāṇa is told: prāṇa is the function in the heart, moving in mouth and nose, called prāṇa from "praṇayanāt" (carrying forward). Apāna is the downward function up to the navel-region, owing to its carrying away of urine, faeces and the like. Vyāna, of vigorous activity, is the junction of prāṇa and apāna, and is the cause of vigorous works. Udāna is the upward function with locus from the soles of the feet to the head, the cause of upward motion and the like. Samāna, located in the region of the abdomen, the digester of food and drink, so called from "samaṁ nayanāt" — its bringing equally what has been eaten and drunk. Ana — the function which is the common ground of these particular functions, related to the general activity of the body.

Thus all this multitude of prāṇic functions stated is prāṇa alone. By "prāṇa," the function-bearing adhyātmika ana has been declared; and its function has been expounded by the very showing of the variety of its functions. Thus the adhyātmika foods called manas, vāk, prāṇa have been expounded.

"Etan-mayaḥ" — modified out of these. Begun by these, the prājāpatya — vāk, manas, prāṇa. What is this Self that is the conglomeration of body and organs? The piṇḍa (gross body), held by the unwise to be of the form of the Self. By saying "etan-maya" generally, then specifically "vāṅmaya, manomaya, prāṇamaya," this is made clear.
BR_C01_S05_V04: These three are the three worlds. Speech is this world; mind is the antarikṣa-world; prāṇa is the yonder world.
BR_C01_S05_V04::block-0: Now the ādhibhautika expansion of those very prājāpatya foods is told —
BR_C01_S05_V04::block-1: The three worlds, called bhūr, bhuvar, svar — these very ones are vāk, manas, prāṇa. There the particularisation: vāk is this world; manas, the antarikṣa world; prāṇa, the yonder world.
BR_C01_S05_V05: These three are the three Vedas. Speech is the Ṛg-veda; mind is the Yajur-veda; prāṇa is the Sāma-veda.
BR_C01_S05_V06: Gods, fathers, men — these very ones. Speech is the gods; mind is the fathers; prāṇa is men.
BR_C01_S05_V07: Father, mother, offspring — these very ones. Mind is the father; speech is the mother; prāṇa is the offspring.
BR_C01_S05_V07::block-0: So, too, the sentences "the three Vedas" and the rest are of straightforward sense.
BR_C01_S05_V08: The known, the to-be-known, the unknown — these very ones. Whatever is known, that is a form of speech; for speech indeed is the known. Speech, having become that, protects him.
BR_C01_S05_V08::block-0:
The known, the to-be-known, the unknown — these very ones. Among them, the particular: "yatkiñca vijñātam," whatever is clearly known is the form of vāk. There the cause is given by the text itself — "vāk hi vijñātā," because vāk is of the nature of light. How could she be unknown, who makes others known? "By vāk alone, your majesty, kinship is known" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka-upaniṣad 4.1.2) — so will be told.

The fruit for the knower of the particular form of vāk is told: vāk herself, having become "that," the known, protects him — the knower of the vibhūti of vāk as stated; that is, food, in the form of the known, becomes his bhojya — this is the meaning.
BR_C01_S05_V09: Whatever is to be cognized clearly is the form of mind, for mind itself is what is to be cognized; one becomes that very thing-to-be-cognized through the mind, and so partakes of it. (9)
BR_C01_S05_V09::block-0:
Likewise, whatever is vijijñāsya — that is, whatever one desires to know with full clarity, the object that stands before cognition as something yet to be ascertained — all that is the form of the mind. The reason is given by the particle hi: "manaḥ hi vijijñāsyam" — because the mind itself, by virtue of being of a doubt-bearing character (sandihyamānākāratva), is the very thing-to-be-cognized. The mind is that wherein the alternatives of doubt arise; hence whatever stands as a candidate for resolved cognition is essentially of the same nature as the mind that frames it.

The fruit obtained by one who knows this manifestation of mind is then stated, parallel to what was said before regarding speech: "mana enaṃ tat bhūtvāvati" — having become that thing-to-be-cognized, the mind protects him, and he attains the state of being food (annatva) in the very form of vijijñāsya. The teaching is that just as before annatva accrued through the form of vāc, here it accrues through the form of vijijñāsya which is the mind. The aspirant, by upāsanā, is absorbed into the form he meditates upon and becomes nourishment to that very deity, no longer separate from it.
BR_C01_S05_V10: Whatever is uncognized is the form of prāṇa, for prāṇa itself is uncognized; one becomes that very uncognized thing through prāṇa, and so partakes of it. (10)
BR_C01_S05_V10::block-0:
Likewise, whatever is avijñāta — what lies altogether outside the range of cognition (vijñānāgocara) and is not even an object of doubt — that is the form of prāṇa. The reason is again given by hi: "prāṇo hi avijñātaḥ" — for prāṇa is of avijñāta-rūpa, since the śruti speaks of it as anirukta ("undefined"). Thus the threefold division — vāc, manas, prāṇa — corresponds exactly to the threefold object: vijñāta (the cognized), vijijñāsya (the to-be-cognized), and avijñāta (the uncognized).

Given this established triple distinction, statements such as "trayo lokāḥ" and the rest are merely vācanika — they are warranted by the words of śruti alone and not by independent inference. The rule is to be remembered as resting on the text itself (vacanād eva niyamaḥ), since everywhere we observe forms that fall under vijñāta and the rest, and only śruti can fix the particular allotment.

"Prāṇa enaṃ tad bhūtvāvati" — prāṇa, having become that, protects him; that is, prāṇa becomes food for him precisely in its uncognized form (avijñātarūpa). It is observed in the world that even when the help rendered by ācārya, father and the like is not clearly cognized, sons and pupils are nevertheless benefited by them; in just the same way, even though manas and prāṇa are sandihyamāna and avijñāta respectively, the relation of being annatva — of becoming food, that is, of being the sustaining substratum that nourishes the upāsaka — is fully intelligible in their case.
BR_C01_S05_V11: Of that speech, the earth is the body and this fire is the luminous form. As far as speech extends, so far does the earth extend, and so far does this fire. (11)
BR_C01_S05_V11::block-0: The expansion of speech, mind and prāṇa with respect to the elemental order (ādhibhautika) has been explained. Now begins the exposition with respect to the divine order (ādhidaivika).
BR_C01_S05_V11::block-1:
"Tasyai" — of that speech of Prajāpati which has been introduced as annatva, food. The earth (pṛthivī) is its śarīra, that is, the external substrate (bāhya ādhāra); and the jyotīrūpa, the luminous instrument (karaṇa), is this terrestrial fire (pārthivo'gniḥ), which is held in the earth as its supported (ādheya). For Prajāpati's vāc is twofold by nature: as kārya (effect) and as ādhāra it is unilluminated, and as karaṇa and as ādheya it is illuminated. Both together — pṛthivī and agni — constitute Prajāpati's very vāc, nothing else.

Therefore, in whatever measure speech becomes manifest as differentiated into adhyātma and adhibhūta, in just that measure does the earth stand as ādhāra throughout — being just so much in extent as effect (kāryabhūtā). And in just that same measure is this fire — the ādheya, the karaṇa-rūpa, that has entered into the earth in the form of light — extent for extent, and no more. The ensuing mantras follow the same logic (samānam uttaram); each member's measure determines the measure of its own ādhāra and ādheya pair.
BR_C01_S05_V12: Now of this mind, the heaven is the body and yonder sun is the luminous form. As far as the mind extends, so far does the heaven extend, and so far does yonder sun. These two were paired and from them prāṇa was born; he is Indra. He is without rival; for verily a second one is a rival, and he who knows thus has no rival. (12)
BR_C01_S05_V12::block-0:
"Atha" — now, of this very mind that has just been spoken of as Prajāpati's food: the heaven (dyauḥ), that is, the dyu-loka, is the body, the kārya, the ādhāra; and the luminous form (jyotīrūpa) — the karaṇa, the ādheya — is yonder sun (asāv ādityaḥ). In whatever measure the mind extends adhyātmically and adhibhautically, the heaven, as the substrate of the mind that is of the nature of light-instrument, stands disposed in just so much extent; and yonder sun, the karaṇa as ādheya, is just so much, and no more.

Now these two — fire and sun — being the ādhidaivika mātāpitarau, the divine mother and father of speech and mind, paired together (mithunaṃ samaitām, samagacchetām) in mutual conjugation. As if to say: "Begotten by the mind that is the father, that is the sun, and illumined by speech that is the mother, that is fire, I shall do action" — thus they came together antarā rodasyoḥ, in the space between heaven and earth. From their conjunction prāṇa, that is, vāyu, was born — for the sake of action, which is parispanda, motion. He who was thus born is Indra, the Supreme Lord (parameśvara).

Not merely is he Indra; he is asapatna — "he for whom no rival exists." Then what is meant by "rival"? "Dvitīyo vai sapatnaḥ" — that which presents itself as standing opposite, as a counterpart (pratipakṣatvenopagataḥ), is what is called "second," and that is termed sapatna. Although speech and mind, being two, are the dvitīya in number, they do not partake of the relation of being rivals to prāṇa, since with respect to prāṇa they have approached only as subordinates (guṇabhāva), just as in the adhyātma sphere they are subordinated to prāṇa. 

Here comes the prāsaṅgika fruit of the knowledge of being rivalless: "Nāsya sapatnaḥ pratipakṣo bhavati" — for the knower as described, no rival, no opponent, comes to be — for him who knows prāṇa thus, as asapatna, in the manner taught.
BR_C01_S05_V13: Now of this prāṇa, the waters are the body and yonder moon is the luminous form. As far as prāṇa extends, so far do the waters extend, and so far does yonder moon. These all are equal, all are infinite. He who worships them as finite wins a finite world; but he who worships them as infinite wins an infinite world. (13)
BR_C01_S05_V13::block-0:
"Atha" — of this prāṇa now under consideration, namely the prāṇa that is Prajāpati's anna — and not the prajā-prāṇa just immediately mentioned (in V12, where prāṇa was called the offspring) — the waters are the body, the kārya, the substrate of the karaṇa; and as before, the luminous form is yonder moon. There, in whatever measure prāṇa extends among the divisions of adhyātma and the rest, in just that pervasive measure are the waters, and in just that measure is yonder moon — the ādheya entered into those waters, the karaṇa-bhūta — pervading both adhyātma and adhibhūta in equal extent.

These are the three foods produced by the father through the fivefold (pāṅkta) action — vāc, manas and prāṇa. The whole jagat, both adhyātma and adhibhūta, is pervaded by these three; nothing remains over and beyond them, neither of the nature of effect (kārya) nor of instrument (karaṇa). All these together are Prajāpati. Therefore "ta ete" — these vāk, manas, prāṇa — are all sama, equal, all of equal pervasion, established as pervading the entire range of living beings together with adhyātma and adhibhūta. For this very reason they are anantāḥ, infinite, since they exist as long as saṃsāra exists; for saṃsāra is not understood by the dismissal of kārya and karaṇa — saṃsāra has been said to be of the very nature of kārya-karaṇa.

He who worships these — the very selves of Prajāpati — as antavataḥ, finite, partitioned, either under the form of adhyātma or of adhibhūta, attains a fruit conformable to that very upāsanā: he wins an antavān loka, becomes himself partitioned, and does not become the very self of these. But he who worships these as anantān — sarvātmaka, the selves of all beings, unpartitioned (aparicchinna) — he wins the very anantam loka. Thus the contrast turns wholly on whether the upāsaka apprehends them as parikalpita-bheda or as sarvātmaka — and the fruit faithfully follows the form of contemplation.
BR_C01_S05_V14: He, this Prajāpati, is the year of sixteen parts. Of him, the nights are fifteen parts, and his sixteenth part is the constant one. By the nights alone he is filled and by them again he wanes. On the new-moon night, having entered with this sixteenth part into all that breathes, he is born forth in the morning. Therefore on that night one should not cut off the prāṇa of any breathing creature — not even of a chameleon — out of reverence for this very deity. (14)
BR_C01_S05_V14::block-0: It was said that the father, by the pāṅkta action, having created the seven foods, made three of them for himself; these three, as the fruit of the pāṅkta action, have been explained. But how, then, are these the fruit of the pāṅkta karman? It is now answered: because in these three foods themselves the pāṅkta-character (pāṅktatā) is recognized, since vitta and karman too are possible there. There, as has been explained, pṛthivī and agni are the mother, dyauḥ and āditya are the father, and prāṇa, which lies between them, is the offspring. There it remains to bring vitta and karman within compass; to that end this section commences.
BR_C01_S05_V14::block-1:
"Sa eṣa saṃvatsaraḥ" — this Prajāpati who is of the form of the three foods, who has been the topic, is here particularly designated as Saṃvatsara, the year. Ṣoḍaśakalaḥ — sixteen kalās, sixteen members, are his; thus he is the sixteen-membered Saṃvatsara, of the form of time. Of this Prajāpati, who is of the nature of time, the rātrayaḥ — that is, the day-and-night cycles, in other words the tithis — are the fifteen kalās. Dhruvā, the constant, ever-fixed one, is his sixteenth kalā, the completer of the sixteen.

He is filled and emptied by these very nights, the spoken-of tithis. From pratipad onward, in the bright fortnight, the moon Prajāpati is filled with the increasing kalās, and grows until on full-moon night his disc is complete; by those very kalās diminishing in the dark fortnight he wanes, until at the new moon only the one constant kalā remains. That Prajāpati of the form of time, on the new-moon (amāvāsyā) night, having entered with this sixteenth, the dhruvā kalā, into all that breathes — the prāṇabhṛt — through whatever water it drinks and whatever herbs it eats, all that as oṣadhi-ātman becomes pervaded — abides on the new-moon night and is then born next morning, joined with the second kalā.

Thus this Prajāpati is pāṅkta in form: heaven and the sun are mind, the father; earth and fire are speech, wife and mother; their offspring is prāṇa; the tithis of the moon are vitta, since they share the dharma of upacaya and apacaya like wealth; and the kāla-portions in the form of those kalās being the cause of the world's transformation — that is karman. Thus this entire Prajāpati became, in conformity with the eṣaṇās — "may I have a wife, and beget offspring, and have wealth, and perform action" — the fruit of the pāṅkta karman; for in worldly life too the rule holds that the kārya conforms to its kāraṇa.

Since this moon, having entered all living beings with the dhruvā kalā, abides through this night, therefore on this amāvāsyā night one should not cut off the prāṇa of any prāṇabhṛt — should not slay any creature — not even of a kṛkalāsa, the chameleon. The kṛkalāsa is by nature a pāpātman, who by his very disposition is killed by other beings; for even seeing him is reckoned amaṅgala, inauspicious. 

Objection (pūrvapakṣa): But the killing of any creature has already been altogether prohibited by "ahiṃsan sarvabhūtāny anyatra tīrthebhyaḥ." Reply (siddhānta): Granted, it has been prohibited; nevertheless this verse is not for the sake of an exception (pratiprasava) permitting hiṃsā on days other than amāvāsyā, nor for permitting it specifically on the chameleon; what then? It is for the apaciti — for the worship — of this very deity, the Soma-devatā.
BR_C01_S05_V15: That sixteen-membered year, Prajāpati, is verily this — this very man who knows thus. His fifteen kalās are his wealth alone, and his sixteenth kalā is his ātman itself. By wealth alone he is filled and by it he wanes. This — what this ātman is — is the nave; wealth is the felly. Therefore even if one suffers utter loss, yet if he lives in his self, men say, "He has only lost the felly." (15)
BR_C01_S05_V15::block-0:
He of whom indirectly (parokṣābhihitaḥ) it was said "saṃvatsaraḥ Prajāpatiḥ ṣoḍaśakalaḥ" must not be regarded as utterly remote (atyantaṃ parokṣaḥ); for the very same is now perceived directly (pratyakṣa upalabhyate). Who is this? — "yo'yam evaṃvit-puruṣaḥ" — that man who knows the Prajāpati of the form of the three foods as his very self; he is the evaṃvit-puruṣa. By what common feature is he Prajāpati? That is now stated. 

Of this evaṃvit-puruṣa the cattle and other forms of vitta alone are the fifteen kalās, since they share the dharma of upacaya and apacaya, increase and decrease — and karman is also accomplished through wealth. For the completion of the whole, his ātmā — the body itself (piṇḍa eva) — is for this knower the sixteenth kalā, occupying the place of the dhruvā. He, like the moon, is filled with wealth and wanes through the loss of wealth — this is well-known in the world.

This is nabhya — what is hita, beneficial, to the nave (nābhi); or, that which deserves the nave (nābhiṃ vā arhati). What is that? "yad ayam ātmā" — what this ātman is, the piṇḍa, the body. The pradhi — the wealth — is in the position of the surrounding parts, the external — like the felly and the rim of a wheel surrounding the spokes and the nave (cakrasyevāra-nemy-ādi).

Therefore even if he suffers sarva-jyāni — the carrying away of all that he has, total deprivation — should he yet live in himself, that is, in the position of the wheel's nave, men say of him: "pradhinā agāt" — "he has wasted only as regards the felly, the external retinue" — just as a wheel might be without its felly and rim. The intent is that, since he is alive, he can again be replenished through wealth that occupies the position of the felly and rim. This vindicates the dignity of the ātman as the dhruvā kalā, the unfailing center, while wealth occupies the variable circumference.
BR_C01_S05_V16: Now there are verily three worlds: the world of men, the world of the fathers, and the world of the gods. The world of men is to be won by son alone, not by any other action; the world of the fathers by karman; the world of the gods by vidyā. The world of the gods is the most excellent of worlds — therefore men extol vidyā. (16)
BR_C01_S05_V16::block-0: It has thus been explained that by the pāṅkta karman, joined with deva, vitta and vidyā, one becomes the Prajāpati of the form of the three foods; and immediately afterwards it has been said that wife and the rest, that is, vitta, occupy the place of the surrounding entourage. Now, in regard to the means — putra, karman and aparā vidyā — only the bare general fact has been gathered: that they are means for attaining the lokas; the specific connection (viśeṣa-sambandha-niyama) of putra and the rest with their respective fruit, the loka-prāpti, has not been settled. That specific connection between the means — putra etc. — and the corresponding fruit must now be stated; with that purpose this next kaṇḍikā is composed.
BR_C01_S05_V16::block-1:
"Atha" is for vākya-upanyāsa, the introduction of a new statement. "Trayaḥ" — and "vāva" is for emphatic restriction (avadhāraṇārtha) — there are just three lokas worthy of the means taught in the śāstra; not less, not more. Which are they? — they are stated: the world of men (manuṣya-loka), the world of the fathers (pitṛ-loka), and the world of the gods (deva-loka). Of these, this very manuṣya-loka is to be conquered, that is, attained, by the means putra alone — putreṇaiva jayyaḥ — and by no other karman; how, by means of putra, it is to be conquered will be stated later in the text; "vidyayā vā" — "or by vidyā" — is also to be supplied as the negated alternative.

By karman alone, of the form of agnihotra and the rest, the pitṛ-loka is to be conquered — neither by putra nor by vidyā. By vidyā the deva-loka is to be conquered — neither by putra nor by karman. The deva-loka is verily the most excellent — praśastatamaḥ — among the three lokas. Therefore, because vidyā is the means to that, men praise vidyā (vidyāṃ praśaṃsanti). Thus the doctrine of pravṛtti-mārga (the way of putra and karman) is acknowledged within its scope, and yet the supremacy of vidyā, which inclines toward nivṛtti, is established by the very fact that the deva-loka, won by vidyā alone, is supreme.
BR_C01_S05_V17: Now therefore the sampratti (handing-over). When a father thinks he is about to depart, he calls his son and says: "You are Brahman, you are the yajña, you are the world." The son replies: "I am Brahman, I am the yajña, I am the world." Whatever has been studied has its unity in the word "Brahman"; whatever yajñas there are have their unity in the word "yajña"; whatever worlds there are have their unity in the word "world" — this much, indeed, is all this. May he, being all this, sustain me from this world (so I may be released). Therefore they call a son who has been thus instructed loka-ya (one who secures the world for the father), and therefore they instruct him. When one who knows thus departs from this world, he enters his son together with these very prāṇas. If anything has been done amiss by him, the son frees him from all of it; therefore he is called putra (son). Through the son alone he stands firm in this world; thereupon these divine, immortal prāṇas enter into him.
BR_C01_S05_V17::block-0:
Thus the three sādhanas — putra (son), karman, and vidyā — have been distributed according to the threefold fruit, namely the three worlds. The wife is not enumerated as a separate sādhana, since she serves merely as the means for begetting the son and for performing karman; wealth too is no separate sādhana, being subordinate to karman. It is well known that vidyā and karman bring about the conquest of the worlds through the very acquisition of one's own self. But since the son is not of the nature of a kriyā (action), the manner in which he becomes the cause of conquering the world is not understood; hence this must be told. Therefore now this is begun.

Sampratti is sampradāna (handing over); sampratti is the name of the karman about to be expounded. For the father transfers his own activity into the son in this manner; hence this karman is called sampratti. At what time is it to be performed? He says: when that father thinks "I am about to depart" — that is, "I shall die" — through perceiving inauspicious portents, then he summons the son and says: "You are Brahman, you are the yajña, you are the world." Thus addressed, the son replies — for he, having been previously instructed, knows "this is to be done by me" — he says these three sentences: "I am Brahman, I am the yajña, I am the world."

Thinking the import of these to be hidden, the śruti proceeds to expound: whatever has been studied or remains unstudied — all of that has its unity, its oneness, in this single word "Brahman." The meaning is: whatever activity of study, concerned with the Veda, was my duty up till this time, henceforth let that be yours — "You are Brahman" means "let it have you as its agent." Likewise, whatever yajñas were to be performed, performed and unperformed by me, of all of those there is unity in this word "yajña"; the yajñas of which I was the agent — henceforth "You are the yajña," they shall have you as their agent. Whatever worlds were to be won by me, won and unwon, of all of those there is unity in this word "world"; henceforth "You are the world," they are to be won by you. From this point on, the kratu — comprising the duties of study, yajña, and conquest of worlds — is consigned to you by me, while I am released from the kratu which is the bondage of duties to be performed. And the son receives all that just so, since he has been instructed.

There, perceiving this intention of the father, the śruti declares: this much indeed is all this — that which is to be done by a householder, namely the Vedas to be studied, the yajñas to be performed, and the worlds to be conquered. "Let him sustain me from this world" — having severed this whole burden, dependent on me, from me, and placed it on himself — let him preserve me from this world; the lṛṭ-sense is here in laṅ, since in the Veda there is no rigid restriction of tense. Because the son thus accomplished will release the father from the bondage of duties to be done in this world, therefore the brāhmaṇas call the son thus instructed loka-ya (world-securing) for the father — beneficial as regards the world. For this very reason fathers instruct him: "may he be world-securing for us."

When that father, thus knowing, having transferred to his son the kratu of duties, departs from this world — that is, dies — then he enters his son with these very vāk, manas, and prāṇa under discussion, that is, pervades the son. Since the cause of the ādhyātmika delimitation has fallen away, the father's vāk, manas, and prāṇa take on their own ādhidaivika form as earth, fire, etc. — like the light of a broken pot-lamp.
BR_C01_S05_V18: Divine speech, from the earth and from fire, enters him; and that indeed is the divine speech by which whatever he says comes to pass.
BR_C01_S05_V18::block-0: How this happens will be told: "From the earth and from fire," etc. Thus the śruti has herself shown that putra, karman, and aparā-vidyā have as their respective ends the human world, the world of the fathers, and the world of the gods. Here certain disputants, ignorant of the specific purport declared by the śruti, claim that putra and the rest are means to mokṣa. The śruti has shut their mouths by this very passage — beginning with "may a wife be mine" and the rest, characterising it as the fivefold kāmya-karman, and concluding by allotting to putra and the rest their specific instrumental functions. Therefore it is established that the śruti about the three debts pertains to one who is avidvas, not to the knower of the supreme Self. And it will be said: "What shall we do with offspring, we whose Self is this very world" (BU 4.4.22).
BR_C01_S05_V18::block-1: But others say: even the conquest of the world of fathers and the world of gods is just the turning-back from those worlds; therefore, by putra, karman, and aparā-vidyā practised conjointly (samuccita), one withdrawn from these three worlds attains mokṣa through the knowledge of the supreme Self — thus they would have putra and the rest to be means of mokṣa indirectly (paramparayā). To shut their mouths too, this following śruti is set forth, undertaking to display the fruit, for the karmin householder who has accomplished sampratti and who knows the threefold-anna ātma-vidyā. Nor can it be said that this very fruit is the fruit of mokṣa, because of its connection with the three annas; because it is shown that anna is the effect of medhā and tapas and is begotten again and again; because perishing is heard of in "if he should not do this, it would perish" (BU 1.5.2); because the body has the fitness of effect-and-instrument as having the form of jyotis; and because the conclusion is given as "this is verily the triad" (BU 1.6.1) — namely, of the nature of nāma-rūpa-karman. Nor is it possible to gather from this very passage that this same triad of sādhanas, when combined, yields mokṣa for one and the threefold-anna fruit for another, since the passage is exhausted in showing only the threefold-anna fruit as the result of putra and the rest.
BR_C01_S05_V18::block-2: From the earth and from fire, the divine vāk — that vāk which is of the nature of the ādhidaivika — enters him, the one who has accomplished sampratti. For all speech has the divine vāk, characterised by earth and fire, as its upādāna; that vāk is, in others, obstructed by ādhyātmika defects such as attachment. When in the knower these defects fall away, like water when an obstruction is broken or like the light of a lamp, it pervades. This is what is being said: the divine vāk from earth and fire enters him. And that divine vāk is pure, free from the defects of falsehood and the rest, by which divine vāk whatever he speaks for himself or for another, that comes to pass — meaning his speech becomes infallible and unobstructed.
BR_C01_S05_V19: From the heaven and from the sun, the divine manas enters him; and that indeed is the divine manas by which he becomes blissful, and moreover does not grieve.
BR_C01_S05_V19::block-0: Likewise, from the heaven and from the sun, the divine manas enters him — and that divine manas is by its very nature unsullied; by that manas this man becomes ānandin, that is, sukhin (happy). And further he does not grieve, since the conjunction with the causes of grief and the rest does not occur.
BR_C01_S05_V20: From the waters and from the moon, the divine prāṇa enters him; and that indeed is the divine prāṇa, which, whether moving or not moving, is not pained, and moreover is not destroyed. He who knows thus becomes the Self of all beings; as is this deity, so is he. As all beings cherish this deity, even so do all beings cherish him who knows thus. Whatever sorrows these creatures undergo — that remains with them; only what is meritorious goes to him, for evil does not approach the gods.
BR_C01_S05_V20::block-0: Likewise, from the waters and from the moon, the divine prāṇa enters him. Of what character is that divine prāṇa? — He says: that prāṇa, which moves among the variety of living beings and does not move (in its samaṣṭi-vyaṣṭi forms — or moving in the mobile and not moving in the immobile), is not pained, that is, is not joined with fear arising from any cause of suffering; and moreover does not perish, is not destroyed, suffers no injury. He, who knows thus the threefold-anna-ātma-darśana as has been stated — he becomes the Self of all beings, the prāṇa of all beings, the manas of all beings, the vāk of all beings; thus, by being the Self of all beings, he becomes omniscient and omnipotent. Just as that already-established deity Hiraṇyagarbha — even so there is no obstruction anywhere to his omniscience or omnipotence; "saḥ" indicates the dārṣṭāntika reference. Further, just as all beings cherish this Hiraṇyagarbha-deity through ijyā (worship) and the rest, even so all beings cherish the one who knows thus — they continually offer him pūjā characterised by ijyā and the rest.
BR_C01_S05_V20::block-1: Now this is doubted: it has been said, "He becomes the Self of all beings"; but if he is the Self of the bodies and organs of all living beings, he would be conjoined with the sukha and duḥkha of all beings — this is not so. Because he has an unbounded buddhi (apariccinna-buddhi) — for it is observed that those of bounded ātma-buddhi have the conjunction with duḥkha at insult and the like, in the form "I have been insulted by him"; but for him whose Self is sarvātman, the bounded ātma-buddhi distinguishing the insulter and the insulted being absent, the duḥkha caused by that does not arise. As with the duḥkha of death — by the absence of the cause: just as when someone dies, duḥkha arises in another due to the cause of "this is my son or brother," but in the absence of that cause, even one who sees that death has no duḥkha; so for the Īśvara, who is apariccinna-ātman, duḥkha does not arise in the absence of the defects such as the mithyā-jñāna of "mineness" which are the causes of duḥkha. This is what is being said: whatever these creatures grieve, the duḥkha caused by that grief etc. is conjoined precisely along with the creatures themselves, since it is born of bounded buddhi; but for the sarvātman, with whom would what be conjoined or disjoined? — Only the puṇya, the auspicious — the fruit referred to is puṇya — goes to him who is established in the position of Prajāpati; for puṇya unsurpassed has been done by him, hence only its fruit goes to him; and pāpa does not approach the gods, since there is no scope for the fruit of pāpa — the meaning is, the duḥkha which is the fruit of pāpa does not reach him.
BR_C01_S05_V21: Now therefore the inquiry into the vrata. Prajāpati indeed produced the karmas (organs); created, they contended with one another. Speech resolved: "I shall surely speak"; the eye: "I shall see"; the ear: "I shall hear"; and so the other karmas, each according to its function. Mṛtyu, becoming weariness, took possession of them; having reached and seized them, he confined them. Therefore speech grows weary; the eye grows weary; the ear grows weary. But him he did not reach — this prāṇa in the middle. They resolved to know him: "This is the best among us, who, whether moving or not moving, is not pained and is not destroyed. Come, let us all assume his form." They all became his form; therefore they are designated by his name as "prāṇas." By him alone they call the family in which one is born who knows thus. And whoever contends with one who knows thus dries up; having dried up, he in the end dies. So far, with reference to the body.
BR_C01_S05_V21::block-0: It has been said indifferently, "All these are equal, all infinite" (BU 1.5.13), regarding the upāsana of vāk, manas, and prāṇa, and no specific distinction lying in any one of them was stated. Should it be accepted just thus, or, on examination, can some particular distinction be ascertained as regards the vrata-upāsana? — Hence what follows.
BR_C01_S05_V21::block-1:
"Now next" — that is, hereafter, the vrata-mīmāṃsā, the inquiry into the upāsana-karman; the inquiry proceeds: among these prāṇas, whose karman is to be held as a vrata? Therein, Prajāpati ha — the word "ha" is in the sense of "kila" ("so the tradition has it") — Prajāpati, having produced the prajās, produced the karmas — namely the indriyas, vāk and the rest — they are called "karmas" because they are for the sake of karman; he created the karaṇas vāk and the rest. Those, when produced, contended with one another, set up rivalry. How? Speech resolved: "I shall surely speak — through my own activity of vadana I shall not desist"; "if there is anyone equal to me, capable of not desisting from his own activity, let him too show his vīrya." Likewise the eye: "I shall see"; the ear: "I shall hear"; and so the other karmas (karaṇas) according to their function — "yat yat yasya karma yathā-karma" — those karaṇas Mṛtyu, the slayer, becoming Śrama, the form of weariness, seized; how? Those karaṇas, engaged in their own activity, he reached, showing himself in the form of Śrama; and having reached, he confined them, that is, dislodged them from their own karmas.

Therefore even today, vāk engaged in its own karman of vadana grows weary, joined to Mṛtyu in the form of Śrama, and slips from its own karman; likewise the eye grows weary; the ear grows weary. But this very prāṇa, the chief — "this in the middle" — Mṛtyu in the form of Śrama did not reach. By that, even today the prāṇa proceeds in its own karman unwearied. Those other karaṇas resolved (held in mind) to know him: "This among us is the best, the most praiseworthy, the foremost, since he, while moving and not moving, is not pained and moreover is not destroyed — come, now let us all become his form, take the prāṇa as our Self" — having thus determined, they all became his form, accepted the prāṇa-form alone as their Self, and adopted the prāṇa-vrata, thinking, "our vratas do not suffice for warding off Mṛtyu." Since the other karaṇas have being-with-form by the prāṇa-form, by their own self of motion and self of light — for activity of motion is not possible apart from prāṇa, and they are always seen, in their own activities, to be preceded by the activity of motion — therefore these vāk and the rest are designated, that is named, by this very prāṇa-name as "prāṇas."

He who thus knows the prāṇa-Self of all karaṇas and the appellation by the word prāṇa — for that very knower laymen designate that family, that family in which the knower is born — that family becomes celebrated by the knower's name itself — "this is so-and-so's family" — like "the Tāpatyas." For one who knows thus, namely the prāṇa-form of vāk and the rest and their being called by the prāṇa-name, this is the fruit. Further, whoever contends with one who knows thus, becoming his pratipakṣa, in this very body dries up, undergoes desiccation; having dried up, in the end he dies, not suddenly without affliction. Thus this prāṇa-Self vision has been stated as ādhyātmika; the upasaṃhāra of what was said is for the purpose of introducing the ādhidaivata exposition.
BR_C01_S05_V22: Now with reference to the deities. "I shall surely blaze" — so Agni resolved; "I shall surely heat" — so Āditya; "I shall surely shine" — so Candramas; thus other deities, each according to its own deva-function. Just as among these prāṇas the middle prāṇa is, so among these deities is Vāyu; for the other deities set (m-loch), but Vāyu does not. Vāyu is the deity that does not set.
BR_C01_S05_V22::block-0: "Now next" — hereafter the ādhidaivata, the deity-related darśana, is being expounded. Of which deity-particular is the holding of the vrata superior — that is the inquiry. All as in the ādhyātmika. "I shall surely blaze" — Agni resolved; "I shall surely heat" — Āditya; "I shall surely shine" — Candramas; thus the other deities, each according to its own deva-function. Just as among these prāṇas vāk and the rest, the middle prāṇa is unattained by Mṛtyu, not dislodged from its own karman, his prāṇa-vrata unbroken — even so, among these deities Agni and the rest, is Vāyu. The others set (m-lochanti), reach their setting, desist from their own karmas — just as ādhyātmika vāk and the rest are other deities, Agni and the rest. But Vāyu does not set — like the middle prāṇa; therefore that deity is asta-mitā (un-set), namely this Vāyu. Thus, having inquired ādhyātma and adhi-daivam, it is determined: the vrata of prāṇa and Vāyu, those two ātmans, alone is unbroken.
BR_C01_S05_V23: Now this verse occurs: "Whence the sun rises and where he sets" — that is, from prāṇa indeed he rises, and into prāṇa he sets. The devas made that the dharma — the same today, the same tomorrow. For whatever vrata they then upheld, that they perform even today. Therefore one should keep just one vrata: let one inhale and exhale, fearing "may not the evil one, Mṛtyu, reach me." If one undertakes it, let him fulfill it; thereby he conquers union with that deity, and dwelling in the same world.
BR_C01_S05_V23::block-0:
Now this verse, the prakāśaka of the very same matter, becomes the mantra. "Whence" — from which Vāyu — the sun rises, and ādhyātmically, in the form of the eye, from prāṇa; and where it sets, in which Vāyu and prāṇa it goes — at the time of evening twilight and at the time of sleep for the puruṣa — that dharma the devas made it; vāk and the rest, Agni and the rest, having previously deliberated, took up the prāṇa-vrata and the Vāyu-vrata. "That itself today, that very same tomorrow" — that is, even today and in the future time it is followed and shall be followed by the devas — this is the intent.

There this verse is briefly explained by the brāhmaṇa: this sun rises from prāṇa, sets into prāṇa. "The devas made it the dharma — the same today, the same tomorrow" — what is its meaning? It is said: whatever vrata these — vāk and the rest, Agni and the rest — held in that time, namely the prāṇa-vrata and the Vāyu-vrata, that they perform even today, follow it and shall follow it; their vrata is unbroken indeed. But the vāk-vrata and the rest, the Agni-vrata and the rest — those are broken; for they are seen as merging into Vāyu and prāṇa at setting-time and at sleeping-time. And this is said elsewhere: "When indeed a man sleeps, then vāk merges into prāṇa, manas into prāṇa, the eye into prāṇa, the ear into prāṇa; when he awakens, they are reborn from prāṇa — thus ādhyātmically. Now ādhidaivatically: when Agni follows the wind, then it goes out — therefore they say, 'it has been put out by him'; for it follows the wind. When the sun sets, it enters the wind; the moon enters the wind; the directions are established in the wind; from the wind alone they are reborn" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.3.3.6, 8).

Since this very vrata is what runs through vāk and the rest and Agni and the rest, namely this — the parispanda-ātmaka nature of Vāyu and prāṇa — the vrata followed by all the devas, therefore another also should keep just this one vrata. Which? Let him perform prāṇana-activity and apānana-activity (let him breathe in and out); for the parispanda-activity of prāṇa-apāna, of the form of prāṇana-apānana, has no cessation; therefore let him keep this very one vrata, abandoning the activities of the other indriyas. "Lest the evil Mṛtyu in the form of Śrama reach me" — the word "net" expresses fear — "if I should slip from this vrata, I am wholly seized by Mṛtyu"; thus, frightened, let him hold the prāṇa-vrata.

If at any time he should undertake, that is, begin the prāṇa-vrata, let him desire to fulfill it; for if he were to desist from this vrata, prāṇa and the devas would be defeated; therefore let him fulfill it. By that — by this vrata, by the prāṇa-Self-realisation in all beings ("vāk and the rest, Agni and the rest, are of my Self; I am the prāṇa-ātman, the cause of all parispanda") — by such holding of the vrata, he conquers, that is, attains the sāyujya — sa-yug-bhāva, oneness of Self — with that very prāṇa-deity, or sa-loka-tā, the state of being in the same loka — this is in regard to weakness of vijñāna.
BR_C01_S06_V01: This is indeed a triad — nāma, rūpa, karman. Of names, vāk (speech) is the uktha; for from it all names arise. It is their sāman, for it is equal to all names. It is their Brahman, for it bears all names.
BR_C01_S06_V01::block-0: What was begun, in the avidyā-domain, as the vyākṛta jagat, characterised by sādhya and sādhana, possessing as fruit even the highest excellence — namely the attainment of the prāṇa-Self — and what is the prior state of this jagat before its vyākaraṇa, denoted by the term avyākṛta — like the seed of a tree — all this is the triad. What is that triad? — nāma, rūpa, karman; that is anātman alone, not the Self, that which is the immediate, non-mediate Brahman; therefore one should turn back from this — for this purpose the passage "trayaṃ vā idaṃ" and the rest is begun. For one whose mind is not turned away from this anātman, the buddhi to upāsate, "I am Brahman," the Self alone as the loka, does not arise, because of the contradiction between the externally-directed and inwardly-directed pravṛtti. As in the Kāṭhaka: "The self-existent pierced the openings outward, hence one looks outward, not inward; some wise one, desiring immortality, turned the eye inward and beheld the inner Self" (Kaṭha 2.1.1).
BR_C01_S06_V01::block-1: But how can it be conceived that this saṃsāra — vyākṛta and avyākṛta, of the nature of kriyā, kāraka, and phala — is just nāma-rūpa-karman-ātmaka and not Ātman? Here it is said: of those names as set forth — "vāk" denotes śabda-sāmānya, since it is said "whatever sound is, that very speech" (BU 1.5.3); the meaning of the word "vāk" is the mere śabda-sāmānya — that is the uktha (cause, upādāna) of these particular names, just as the sea-salt mountain is for the sea-salt grains. Therefore he says: "From this" — from this nāma-sāmānya — all names like "Yajñadatta," "Devadatta," with all their distinctions, arise, that is, are produced and differentiated, like the salt-grains from the salt-mountain; and the effect is non-different from the cause. Likewise, by the inclusion of the particulars in the sāmānya — but how is the relation of sāmānya and viśeṣa? — this śabda-sāmānya is the sāman of these particular names — sāman because of samatva, that is, sāmānya. For this is, since by all names — its own ātma-particulars — equal. Further, by the non-difference of ātma-attainment of the particular names: that from which something acquires its ātman, that is seen as undivided from it, like pots from clay. How is the ātma-attainment of the particular names from vāk? — He says: this thing denoted by the word "vāk" is their Brahman, their Self; from that comes the ātma-attainment of the names, since a śabda-distinct svarūpa is not possible for them. He shows this: this śabda-sāmānya, indeed, bears, that is, sustains by the giving of svarūpa, all names — particular śabdas. Thus by the establishment of the relation of effect-cause, of sāmānya-viśeṣa, and of the giving of ātman, the mere śabda-tā of the particular names is established. Likewise, in the next two also, all should be applied as has been said.
BR_C01_S06_V02: Now, of forms (rūpas), the eye (cakṣus) is their uktha; for from this all forms arise. This is their sāman, for this is equal to all forms. This is their Brahman, for this sustains all forms.
BR_C01_S06_V02::block-0: Now, at this point, of forms — those distinguished as white, non-white, and the rest — "the eye" (cakṣus) is mentioned. By the word cakṣus is denoted the generic object of the eye, namely the universal of form, that is, the mere capacity to be illumined. Hence from this all particular forms arise. This is their sāman; this is equal to all forms; this is their Brahman; for this sustains all forms — the explanation here parallels the preceding sections.
BR_C01_S06_V03: Now, of actions (karmas), the body/self (ātman) is their uktha; for from this all actions arise. This is their sāman, for this is equal to all actions. This is their Brahman, for this sustains all actions. This triad is one — it is this self (ayam ātmā); and the self, though one, is this triad. This is the immortal veiled by the real (satya): prāṇa indeed is the immortal; name and form are the real; by these two this prāṇa is veiled.
BR_C01_S06_V03::block-0:
Now at this point is stated how all the particular actions — those of cognition and perception, and those of motion — are subsumed in the mere generic notion of action. How? Of all the particular actions, ātman, the body, is the common locus; the action of the ātman (body) is itself called "ātman" — for it has been said that one performs action by means of this body, the ātman; and in the body all action becomes manifest. Hence, by reason of being located in it (tātsthya), the word ātman denotes action — the bare generic of action — as their uktha and the rest, just as before.

This triad as described — name, form, and action — being mutually dependent, mutually causing each other's manifestation, mutually dissolving into one another, conjoined like three staves leaned together (tridaṇḍa-viṣṭambha-vat), is one. By what does the oneness obtain? It is said: "this Self" (ayam ātmā) — this aggregate, the body which is the complex of effect-and-instrument (kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta), as expounded in the section on the three foods by "This self verily consists of that" (Bṛ.U. 1.5.3) and the rest. For this whole — the differentiated and the undifferentiated — is just this much: name, form, and action. The Self, however, being one, this very triad of name, form, and action stands established as the aggregate of effect-and-instrument under the threefold division of adhyātma, adhibhūta, and adhidaiva.

This very thing the text now states; and explaining the import of "the immortal veiled by the real" (amṛtaṃ satyena cchannam), it says: prāṇa indeed is the immortal — that which has the nature of an instrument, the inner support, of the nature of self, immortal, indestructible. Name and form are satya — they consist of effect, the bodily condition. Prāṇa, of the nature of activity, is their support; it is veiled — kept unmanifest — by the two outer ones, mortal, body-shaped, subject to origination and decay. This very thing has been displayed as the essential nature of saṃsāra, the domain of avidyā. Hence onward, in the fourth (chapter), the Self as the domain of vidyā (true knowledge) is to be ascertained — that section is now begun.
BR_C02_S01_INTRO1::block-0:
"One should meditate on the Self alone" (ātmety eva upāsīta); "by seeking that, all becomes sought"; and that very Self-reality, being dearest of all, is to be sought — "Verily, I knew the Self alone — I am Brahman" — the Self-reality, the one, is the domain of vidyā (true knowledge). But that which is the domain of difference-perception — "the other is yonder, I am other" — "such a one does not know," and is the domain of avidyā. By such statements as "It is to be seen as one alone" (Bṛ.U. 4.4.20) and "From death to death he goes who sees here as if there were many" (Bṛ.U. 4.4.19), the domains of vidyā and avidyā are distinctly separated throughout all the Upaniṣads.

There, the entire domain of avidyā has been expounded — through the distinctions of means and ends, and the rest — up to the close of the third chapter. And that whole expounded avidyā-domain is twofold: the inner prāṇa, the supporter — like the central pillar of a house — manifesting, immortal; and the outer, of the nature of effect, non-illuminating, subject to origination and decay, comparable to the grass, kuśa, and clay of a house, denoted by the word satya, mortal. By that, prāṇa, denoted by the word amṛta, is veiled — so it has been concluded.

That very prāṇa is variously extended through the differentiations of outer supports. "Prāṇa, the one, knows" — so it is said. Of that very prāṇa, the outer body is one common (form), declared by such body-emphasizing words as Virāṭ, Vaiśvānara, the Self of the form of puruṣa, Prajāpati, Ka, Hiraṇyagarbha — its instruments distributed among the sun and the rest. "Brahman is one and many; only this much, nothing beyond this; and present in each separate body as a sentient agent and enjoyer" — thus is presented Gārgya the brāhmaṇa, the speaker, who has approached avidyā's domain itself as the Self. The hearer is Ajātaśatru, of the contrary view of the Self.

In this way, when the meaning is conveyed in the form of a narrative dialogue (ākhyāyikā) with pūrvapakṣa and siddhānta, it comes under the sway of the hearer's mind. In the contrary case — when conveyed by sentences merely following the subject in the manner of logic (tarka-śāstra) — the matter would be hard to comprehend, owing to the extreme subtlety of the reality. So in the Kāṭhaka: "He whom many do not obtain even for the hearing" (Ka.U. 1.2.7) and the like — by such passages it is shown elaborately that this is to be grasped only by an intellect well refined and divine, and is not to be apprehended by the intellect of the average. "He who has a teacher knows" (Ch.U. 6.14.2); "From the teacher alone is knowledge" (Ch.U. 4.4.3) — so in the Chāndogya. "The knowers, the seers of reality, will instruct you in knowledge" (Bh.G. 4.34) — so in the Gītā. And here too, by the dialogue between Śākalya and Yājñavalkya, the extreme depth of Brahman will be set forth with great solemnity. Therefore, since this is fitting, the discourse begins by employing the form of pūrvapakṣa and siddhānta through narrative for the purpose of conveying the reality.

The purpose is also instruction in the rule of conduct (ācāra-vidhi); for from such a narrative the meaning concerning the proper conduct of speaker and hearer is grasped. The narrative is also intended to ward off the bare logical intellect — "This understanding is not to be reached by mere reasoning" (Ka.U. 1.2.9), "Not to one consumed by tarka-śāstra" (Mokṣa-dharma 247.18) — by śruti and smṛti. Faith (śraddhā) is the supreme means in Brahman-cognition — this too is the purport of the narrative; for in the dialogue extreme faithfulness is seen in both Gārgya and Ajātaśatru. "The man of faith obtains knowledge" (Bh.G. 4.39) — so the smṛti.
BR_C02_S01_V01: Oṃ. There was Dṛpta-Bālāki, of the Gārgya lineage, learned and eloquent. He said to Ajātaśatru of Kāśi: "Let me tell you of Brahman." Ajātaśatru said: "For these very words we give a thousand (cows). The people indeed run, crying 'Janaka, Janaka!'"
BR_C02_S01_V01::block-0:
There, the proponent of the pūrvapakṣa, the knower of Brahman as the avidyā-domain, is Dṛpta-Bālāki — "dṛpta" meaning "proud," puffed up precisely because his Brahman-knowledge is not complete; "bālāki" meaning the offspring of Balākā; "dṛpta" plus "bālāki" = Dṛpta-Bālāki. The word "ha" carries the sense of tradition (aitihya) in narrative. "Anūcāna" — capable in recitation, a speaker, eloquent. "Gārgya" — by gotra. "Āsa" = was, at some particular time. He, having approached Ajātaśatru — Ajātaśatru by name — "the Kāśya," the king of Kāśi — said: "Let me tell you of Brahman" — that is, "Let me declare Brahman to you."

Thus addressed, Ajātaśatru replied: "We give a thousand cows for this very speech" — namely the speech "Let me tell you of Brahman" by which you addressed me. The intent is: just that much is the cause for giving a thousand cows. To the question — "Why is not the actual telling of Brahman expected as the cause for the thousand-gift, and only this speech 'Let me tell you of Brahman' is expected as cause?" — the answer: because the śruti itself states the king's intention — "Janaka the giver, Janaka the hearer" — in this twofold statement "Janaka, Janaka" is repeated; the word "vai" indicates well-known fact. "Janaka eager to give, Janaka eager to hear" — those eager to hear, to expound, to receive Brahman, run, that is, approach (such a king); hence "you have presumed all that in me too."
BR_C02_S01_V02: Gārgya said: "That puruṣa who is in the sun — him I meditate upon as Brahman." Ajātaśatru said: "Do not, do not converse with me about this. As surpassing all beings, head, king, do I meditate on him." Whoever meditates thus becomes surpassing all beings, head, king.
BR_C02_S01_V02::block-0:
To the king thus eager to listen and turned toward him, Gārgya said: "That very one which dwells in the sun, and in the eye, the single self-identifier — having entered through the eye into the heart here, abiding as the enjoyer and agent — that very one I see as Brahman; this I meditate upon in this aggregate of effect-and-instrument. Therefore I tell you of him, the puruṣa, as Brahman; meditate (thus)."

Thus addressed, Ajātaśatru replied, warding him off with his hand — "Mā, mā" — "Do not converse with me about this Brahman as if it were yet to be cognized." The doubling "mā mā" is for the sake of (firmly) negating. The sense: "In this matter, when our cognition's object is identical, we should be put down by your showing us as not knowing; therefore do not converse, do not initiate dialogue with me about this Brahman. If you know something other (than this), that Brahman you may speak of; not that which I already know. If, however, you think — 'You know Brahman in general, but not the particular fruits of meditation' — that should not be supposed; for I know all that you say. How? 'Surpassing' (atiṣṭhāḥ): that which transcends and stands above (all) beings — "atiṣṭhāḥ". "Head of all beings": the chief. "King": as endowed with the quality of effulgence — by these qualifying epithets, this Brahman, distinguished thus, in this aggregate of effect-and-instrument as agent and enjoyer, is what 'I meditate upon' — so I do. The fruit also for the meditator thus distinguished: he who meditates on this thus becomes surpassing all beings, head, king. For the fruit is precisely according to the qualified meditation — by śruti: 'As one meditates upon Him, so one becomes' (Śat.Brā. 10.5.2.20).
BR_C02_S01_V03: Gārgya said: "That puruṣa who is in the moon — him I meditate upon as Brahman." Ajātaśatru said: "Do not, do not converse with me about this. As the great one, white-clad Soma the king, do I meditate on him." Whoever meditates thus has Soma pressed and well-pressed for him daily; for him food does not fail.
BR_C02_S01_V03::block-0:
When Brahman as the sun was rejected by Ajātaśatru through dialogue, Gārgya proposed another Brahman in the moon. "That very one which dwells in the moon and in the mind, the single puruṣa, enjoyer and agent" — the qualifying clause is as before. "Bṛhat" — great; "pāṇḍara-vāsāḥ" — having white garment; because the prāṇa identifying with the moon is of watery body. "Soma the king" — the moon, and that which is the food, the creeper-bodied (soma plant) pressed in the yajña — having unified these, "this very one I meditate as Brahman."

For him who meditates upon (Brahman) as endowed with the qualities stated, Soma is pressed (suta) day by day in the yajña; "prasuta" — pressed thoroughly, abundantly, in the modification — meaning, he gains capacity for the performance of yajña of both kinds. And for him who meditates upon (Brahman) as the embodiment of food, food does not fail.
BR_C02_S01_V04: Gārgya said: "That puruṣa who is in lightning — him I meditate upon as Brahman." Ajātaśatru said: "Do not, do not converse with me about this. As the brilliant one (tejasvī) do I meditate on him." Whoever meditates thus indeed becomes brilliant; brilliant becomes his offspring.
BR_C02_S01_V04::block-0: Likewise, in lightning, in the skin, and in the heart — one deity. "Tejasvī" — the qualifying epithet. From that, its fruit: he becomes brilliant (tejasvī); his offspring also becomes brilliant — because of acceptance of the manyness of lightnings, the abundance of fruit accrues both in oneself and in offspring.
BR_C02_S01_V05: Gārgya said: "That puruṣa who is in space (ākāśa) — him I meditate upon as Brahman." Ajātaśatru said: "Do not, do not converse with me about this. As the full and unmoving (pūrṇam apravarti) do I meditate on him." Whoever meditates thus is filled with offspring and cattle; his progeny does not depart from this world.
BR_C02_S01_V05::block-0: Likewise, in space — that is, the space of the heart — and in the heart, one deity. "Pūrṇam" (full) and "apravarti" (unmoving) — two qualifying epithets. The fruit of the qualification "full" is this: "he is filled with offspring and cattle." The fruit of the qualification "unmoving" is: "his progeny does not depart from this world" — that is, the unbroken continuance of progeny.
BR_C02_S01_V06: Gārgya said: "Verily, that Person who is in the wind (vāyu) — Him alone do I worship as Brahman." Ajātaśatru replied: "Pray, do not converse with me about Him! Verily, I worship Him as Indra Vaikuṇṭha, the unconquered army." He who worships Him thus becomes ever victorious, never conquered, and a vanquisher of his foes from the other side.
BR_C02_S01_V06::block-0:
Likewise, in the wind (vāyu), in the prāṇa, and in the heart, there is one and the same deity; her distinguishing descriptions are these — Indra, the supreme Lord; Vaikuṇṭha, that is, one who cannot be subdued; and "the army never before vanquished by foes" — apparājitā senā — since the troop of the Maruts is well known as her host.

The fruit of the upāsanā is also stated correspondingly: jiṣṇuḥ — of victorious nature; aparājiṣṇuḥ — never overcome by others by his very disposition; and anyatastyajāyī — one who triumphs over rival adversaries from any side. Thus the contemplator partakes of the very qualities he meditates upon, since the deity worshipped and the worshipper come to share one nature.
BR_C02_S01_V07: Gārgya said: "Verily, that Person who is in fire (agni) — Him alone do I worship as Brahman." Ajātaśatru replied: "Pray, do not converse with me about Him! Verily, I worship Him as the all-enduring (viṣāsahi)." He who worships Him thus becomes all-enduring, and his progeny too becomes all-enduring.
BR_C02_S01_V07::block-0:
In fire (agni), in speech (vāc), and in the heart, there is one and the same deity; her distinguishing description here is — viṣāsahiḥ, the one who endures and forbears the assaults of others. By reason of the abundance of fire, the abundance of fruit follows, just as in the previous case.

Thus the contemplator who has identified the deity in agni, in vāc, and in the hṛd as one comes to gain endurance both in himself and in his offspring, since the upāsana of viṣāsahi yields the very capacity of viṣāsahitva.
BR_C02_S01_V08: Gārgya said: "Verily, that Person who is in the waters — Him alone do I worship as Brahman." Ajātaśatru replied: "Pray, do not converse with me about Him! Verily, I worship Him as the conformable (pratirūpa)." He who worships Him thus has only what is conformable coming to him, never what is non-conformable, and there is born from him a son who is likewise conformable.
BR_C02_S01_V08::block-0:
In the waters, in the seed (retas), and in the heart, there is one and the same deity; her distinguishing description is — pratirūpaḥ, that is, anurūpaḥ — "the one who conforms," not contrary to śruti and smṛti — this is the import.

The fruit accordingly is this — what conforms to the injunctions of śruti and smṛti alone reaches him, and never the reverse; and further, from him is born offspring of just such a conforming nature. Hence by upāsanā of the pratirūpa-deity the worshipper attains conformity in his own life and in his progeny.
BR_C02_S01_V09: Gārgya said: "Verily, that Person who is in the mirror — Him alone do I worship as Brahman." Ajātaśatru replied: "Pray, do not converse with me about Him! Verily, I worship Him as the lustrous (rociṣṇu)." He who worships Him thus becomes lustrous, his progeny also becomes lustrous, and over all those whom he meets he shines surpassingly.
BR_C02_S01_V09::block-0:
In the mirror — that is, in any object of clear, transparent nature, and elsewhere in such things as a sword (khaḍga) — and inwardly (hārde) in the natural purity of sattva, there is one and the same deity; her distinguishing description is — rociṣṇuḥ, of luminous nature.

And the fruit too is just that — by reason of the abundance of substrates of luminosity (rocanādhāra-bāhulya), the abundance of fruit follows. Thus the upāsaka, contemplating the deity through her quality of self-shining, comes to outshine all whom he encounters.
BR_C02_S01_V10: Gārgya said: "Verily, that sound which follows behind one as he goes — Him alone do I worship as Brahman." Ajātaśatru replied: "Pray, do not converse with me about Him! Verily, I worship Him as the life-breath (asu)." He who worships Him thus attains in this world his full span of life; the prāṇa does not depart from him before the appointed time.
BR_C02_S01_V10::block-0:
"Yantam" — going; the sound which here "paścāt" — from behind — "anūdeti" — follows after; and within the body (adhyātman) the prāṇa which is the cause of life — having unified the two, he speaks: asuḥ, that is, the prāṇa which is the cause of life, is the quality (guṇa) of that deity.

The fruit is — "sarvam āyur asmin loka eti" — that is, the full life-span as appropriated by karman comes to him; before the time fixed by the fruition of karman (karmaphala-paricchinna-kāla), even though he be afflicted by maladies and the like, the prāṇa does not abandon him. Thus the upāsanā of the deity as asu yields the unbroken span of life.
BR_C02_S01_V11: Gārgya said: "Verily, that Person who is in the quarters of space — Him alone do I worship as Brahman." Ajātaśatru replied: "Pray, do not converse with me about Him! Verily, I worship Him as the second-possessing (dvitīya), the inseparable (anapaga)." He who worships Him thus becomes one possessed of a companion; his retinue is never severed from him.
BR_C02_S01_V11::block-0:
In the quarters (dikṣu), in the two ears (karṇayoḥ), and in the heart, there is one and the same deity — namely, the two Aśvins, those gods whose nature is to be ever inseparable. The quality of that deity is dvitīyavattvam, that is, anapagatvam — non-separation, mutual inseparability — for among the directions and among the Aśvins both, just such a dharma ("this and another together") obtains; both possess this property of pairedness.

And that very same is the fruit for the worshipper too — namely, gaṇa-vicchedaḥ — non-severance of his attendant retinue — and dvitīyavattva — possession of a companion. Thus by the upāsana of the deity as the inseparable pair, the worshipper himself remains never alone and never bereft of his troop.
BR_C02_S01_V12: Gārgya said: "Verily, that Person who consists of shadow — Him alone do I worship as Brahman." Ajātaśatru replied: "Pray, do not converse with me about Him! Verily, I worship Him as Death (mṛtyu)." He who worships Him thus attains in this world his full span of life; death does not come upon him before the appointed time.
BR_C02_S01_V12::block-0:
In the shadow — that is, in the outer darkness (bāhya tamas), and inwardly in the obscuring ignorance (āvaraṇātmaka ajñāna) which is of the nature of veiling — and in the heart, there is one and the same deity; her distinguishing description is — mṛtyuḥ, Death.

The fruit is the same as before in respect of full life-span; what is distinctive here is the absence of affliction by maladies and the like, by reason of death's not approaching him before the time. Thus the upāsanā of the deity under the aspect of mṛtyu yields freedom from untimely demise and from the calamities that herald it.
BR_C02_S01_V13: Gārgya said: "Verily, that Person who is in the self (ātman) — Him alone do I worship as Brahman." Ajātaśatru replied: "Pray, do not converse with me about Him! Verily, I worship Him as the self-possessing (ātmanvī)." He who worships Him thus becomes self-possessing, his progeny also becomes self-possessing. Then Gārgya fell silent.
BR_C02_S01_V13::block-0:
In the self — that is, in Prajāpati and in the buddhi (intellect) — and in the heart, there is one and the same deity; her distinguishing description is ātmanvī, that is, ātmavān, "possessed of self."

The fruit is — ātmanvī ha bhavati — he becomes "possessed of self" (ātmavān); ātmanvinī ha asya prajā bhavati — his progeny also becomes "possessed of self". The peculiarity here is that, by reason of abundance of intellect (buddhi-bahulatva), this attainment is realised especially in the offspring (prajāyāṁ sampādanam).

Now, since these so-called "brahmans" — those Brahman-conceptions advanced by Gārgya — were known beforehand by Ajātaśatru himself and have thus been refuted in due succession, that Gārgya, his stock of Brahman-knowledge being exhausted (kṣīṇa-brahmavijñānaḥ), with no further reply manifesting itself (apratibhāsamāna-uttaraḥ), sat silent with his head bent down (tūṣṇīm avākśirā āsa). This śravaṇa thus exhibits the limit of upāsanā-grounded brahma-knowledge, and points beyond to the supreme Ātman to be unfolded by Ajātaśatru.
