BR_C02_S01_V14: He, Ajātaśatru, said: "Is it just so much?" "Yes, just so much." "By so much it is not (truly) known." Then Gārgya said: "Let me approach you (as a pupil)." || 14 ||
BR_C02_S01_V14::block-0:
Observing Gārgya in that posture, Ajātaśatru said — "Is it just so much?" — meaning: Has Brahman been determined only to this extent, or is there yet something further? The other replied — "Just so much, indeed." Ajātaśatru then said — "By so much that has been (thus) known, Brahman is not (truly) known" — implying: Why are you puffed up, asking me to expound Brahman to you?

Pūrvapakṣa: Is it then said that what was known thus far is no knowledge at all? Siddhānta: No; for these expositions are heard along with their fruits, and the sentences of the Upaniṣad cannot be construed as mere arthavāda (eulogy). Sentences expressive of an apūrva injunction govern each upāsanā taught — such as "You stood pre-eminent over all beings" (Bṛ.U. 2.1.2) and the like; and corresponding fruits are everywhere heard, severally distributed. If they were arthavāda, this would be incongruous.

How then is it said "By so much it is not (truly) known"? There is no fault here, since the statement looks to the qualified hearer (adhikārin). For the sake of teaching Brahman, Gārgya, who is a knower of non-principal Brahman (amukhya-brahmavit), came forward to instruct the eager Ajātaśatru; it is therefore quite fitting that Ajātaśatru, the knower of the principal Brahman (mukhya-brahmavit), should tell Gārgya the knower of non-principal Brahman: "That principal Brahman which you have undertaken to expound — that you do not know."

Were even the knowledge of the non-principal Brahman to be wholly rejected, he would not have said "by so much" — he would have said "nothing at all has been known by you." Therefore there are these many (forms of) Brahman within the sphere of avidyā; and since the knowledge of the supreme Brahman comes through the door of just such (preliminary) knowledge, it is quite proper to say "by so much it is not (truly) known."

That these (lower Brahmans) are objects of knowledge within the sphere of avidyā, and that they are constituted of name, form, and karman, has been shown in the third adhyāya. Therefore by saying "it is not known by so much," the speaker has shown that there is a further Brahman yet to be known. Gārgya, knowing the rule of conduct that this should not be told to one who has not formally approached, himself says: "Let me approach you" — i.e., "Let me come to you," as another disciple would approach his guru.
BR_C02_S01_V15: Ajātaśatru said: "It is contrary to the order that a brāhmaṇa should approach a kṣatriya, thinking 'He will teach me Brahman.' Yet I will indeed make you know." Taking him by the hand, he rose. The two came upon a man who was asleep. He addressed him by these names: "Great one, clad in white raiment, Soma, king!" He did not rise. Then (Ajātaśatru) awoke him by rubbing him with the hand, and he rose. || 15 ||
BR_C02_S01_V15::block-0:
Ajātaśatru said — "This is pratiloma (against the order), against the rule"; what is that? — "that a brāhmaṇa, the highest varṇa, who is qualified for the office of teacher, should approach a kṣatriya — not naturally a teacher — in the manner of a disciple, thinking 'He will teach me Brahman'"; this is forbidden in the śāstras of conduct. Therefore stand fast as a teacher; I myself will instruct you — about that knowing which Brahman is known, that principal Brahman which is to be known.

Observing Gārgya somewhat abashed, in order to inspire confidence Ajātaśatru took him by the hand and rose. The two — Gārgya and Ajātaśatru — came upon a sleeping man at some place in the royal palace. Reaching that sleeping man, he addressed him by these names — "Great one, clad in white raiment, Soma, king!"

Though thus addressed, the sleeper did not rise. Not awakening, he then woke him up by rubbing him with the hand again and again, and he rose. Hence (it is shown that) he whom Gārgya intended (as Brahman) is not, in this body, the agent and enjoyer Brahman.
BR_C02_S01_V15::block-1:
How is this understood — that by the going to the sleeping man, the addressing, and the non-rising, the non-Brahman-ness of the (Brahman) intended by Gārgya has been demonstrated?

In the waking state, just as the puruṣa intended by Gārgya is the agent and enjoyer Brahman present amid the sense-organs, so too the (Self) intended by Ajātaśatru — its master — is also present, as a king is among his servants; but the cause of distinguishing master and servant — i.e., what Gārgya and Ajātaśatru respectively meant — is, on account of their being mixed together, undetermined as to its specific character. The fact that the enjoyer is solely the seer (draṣṭṛ) and not the seen, and that the non-enjoyer is solely the seen and not the seer — both of these, here being mixed, cannot be shown discretely; hence the going to the sleeping man.

Pūrvapakṣa: But even when the man is asleep, if he is addressed by particular names, only the enjoyer would respond, not the non-enjoyer; so determination is impossible. Reply: No; for the (Brahman) intended by Gārgya has been distinguished by specific marks. He who, hidden by satya, is the immortal prāṇa-Self, undimmed when speech and the rest are setting; whose body is the waters (and so) clad in white raiment; who is great (bṛhan) on account of having no rival; who is the sixteen-phased Soma the king — such a one, established in his own activity, even when not (specifically) recognised, abides as one whose nature does not set; and Gārgya does not intend any other activity contradictory to his at that time. Therefore he ought to be awakened when called by his own names; and he was not awakened. Hence by the residue (pāriśeṣya), the (Brahman) intended by Gārgya is shown to be a non-enjoyer.

If he were of the nature of an enjoyer, he would necessarily enjoy his proper object when present; for fire, being of the nature of burning and illuminating, does not fail to burn straw or kindling that is in contact with it, nor to illuminate what is to be illumined; if it does not burn or illumine its own object when reached, it cannot be ascertained that it is fire — burner or illuminator. Likewise, if Gārgya's prāṇa were of the nature of one apprehending sound and the rest when present, it would have apprehended the words "Bṛhan, Pāṇḍaravāsas" and so on as its own object — just as fire would burn or illumine straw and kindling that come into contact, without exception. Therefore, since the sounds present were not apprehended, it is determined that he is of the nature of a non-enjoyer; for that whose nature is settled does not deviate from it ever; hence is established the non-enjoyership of the prāṇa.

Pūrvapakṣa: Non-awakening is due to non-grasping the relation of those particular vocative names — just as, in a gathering of many seated people, one being addressed, hearing yet not grasping that "this man is calling me" by his particular name, does not specifically respond; in the same way, the prāṇa, having no grasp of "these — Bṛhan and the like — are my names," does not pick up the call-words, not from sheer non-cognition.

Reply: No; for if a presiding deity is admitted, non-grasping is unintelligible. For one who admits that the prāṇa, whose adhidaiva form is the moon, is the enjoyer in the body — for him, the relation by particular name must necessarily be grasped for transactional usage with that deity; otherwise transaction in calling, etc., would not be possible.

Even on the view of a separate (Self), this is unfit on account of non-cognition (sambodhana failing). For one who holds an enjoyer distinct from prāṇa — even for him, on being called by names like "Bṛhan," since the names of greatness etc. are at that time applicable to that (Self)…
BR_C02_S01_V16: Ajātaśatru said: "Where, while this one was thus asleep — this puruṣa consisting of vijñāna — was he then? Whence has this one come back?" That Gārgya did not know. || 16 ||
BR_C02_S01_V16::block-0:
Thus, having established the existence of a Self distinct (from the prāṇa etc.), Ajātaśatru said to Gārgya: "Where — at what time — was this puruṣa consisting of vijñāna asleep — i.e., before being awakened by the rubbing of the hand? Vijñāna — that by which one cognises — denotes the antaḥkaraṇa, the buddhi; consisting of that, partaking of that nature, is vijñānamaya. What is meant by 'partaking of that nature'? Apprehensibility in it, apprehensibility through it, and (its being) the apprehender.

How, when the suffix mayaṭ has many senses, is precisely the sense of 'mainly that' here grasped? Because in passages like "This very Self is Brahman, consisting of vijñāna, of mind" (Bṛ.U. 4.4.5) the usage seen is precisely in the sense of 'mainly that'; because being a modification of supreme Vijñāna is unestablished; because in "y eṣa vijñānamayaḥ" the construction is one of accepted reference (anuvāda); and because the senses of 'limb' and 'comparison' are impossible here — by elimination, only the sense 'mainly' (prāya) remains. Therefore the antaḥkaraṇa, of the nature of saṅkalpa-vikalpa, is meant; "consisting of that" is its sense. Puruṣa — because of lying in the city (puri śayanāt).

"Where was this one then?" — the question is for revealing his (true) nature. Before the awakening, the Ātman is of a nature contrary to action, agent, and fruit — which is intended to be shown by the absence of effects; for prior to awakening no effect such as karma — happiness etc. — is grasped. Hence on account of this not being prompted by karma, that very svābhāvya (innate state) of the Ātman is understood — that state in which he was, from which having fallen he becomes a saṃsārin contrary to (his own) nature. With this in view (Ajātaśatru) asks Gārgya, who lacks insight, in order to develop his understanding.

"Where was he? Whence did this one come back?" — both these should have been asked by Gārgya himself; yet since Gārgya did not ask, Ajātaśatru does not remain idle; he proceeds, thinking "He must indeed be enlightened," since he had pledged "I will indeed make (you) know." Even thus being prompted, Gārgya did not understand either to ask or to state where this Ātman was before awakening, or whence this returning had come — Gārgya did not know.
BR_C02_S01_V17: Ajātaśatru said: "Where this one — this puruṣa consisting of vijñāna — was thus asleep: then, having taken into himself, by means of the (inner) vijñāna, the vijñāna of these prāṇas (organs), he lies in this ether within the heart. When he takes them in, then this puruṣa is said 'svapiti' (he sleeps); then prāṇa is taken in, speech is taken in, the eye is taken in, the ear is taken in, the mind is taken in." || 17 ||
BR_C02_S01_V17::block-0:
Ajātaśatru said this in order to deliver the intended meaning. "Where this one — this puruṣa consisting of vijñāna — was thus asleep: where (and whence) we asked, hear the explanation. Where this one was thus asleep — then, at that time, having taken in by vijñāna — the specific cognition manifested in the antaḥkaraṇa, born of the nature of the upādhi — the vijñāna (i.e., the operative power) of these speech and other prāṇas in their respective objects, taking up their special faculties — he lies in this ether within the heart" — that which is called ākāśa is the supreme Self himself; in that ether of his own Self, he sleeps, in his innate, non-saṃsāric (state). Not the ether alone, but on the strength of another śruti — "Then, dear one, he becomes united with sat" (Ch.U. 6.8.1) — he leaves aside the specific Self-form due to the relation with the liṅga-upādhi, and rests in the unspecific, innate, mere Self alone — this is the meaning.

How is it understood that, when he gives up the lordship of the body and senses, he is then established in his own Self? By the prevalence of the term (its name). What is that prevalent name? — He says: When at the time he takes — i.e., draws in — those vijñānas of speech and the rest, then this puruṣa's name 'svapiti' becomes well-known about him; this name is figurative; svayam ātmānam api gacchati — he goes to his own Self — hence svapiti.

True, by the prevalence of the name svapiti the form of the Self distinct from the saṃsāric attributes is grasped, but is there yet a reasoning here? Anticipating this doubt, he says: At that time, in sleep, prāṇa is taken in. "Prāṇa" here means the organ of smell (ghrāṇendriya), since the context is of speech etc.; for the saṃsāric attribute of the Self is marked through the upādhi being connected with speech etc. They are thus all withdrawn by him — How? — Speech is taken in, the eye is taken in, the ear is taken in, the mind is taken in. Therefore, when speech and the rest are withdrawn, the Self is recognised as resting in his own Self alone, due to the absence of the action–agent–fruit identity.
BR_C02_S01_V18: When he wanders by means of the dream-experience, those are his worlds; then he becomes, as it were, a great king; or, as it were, a great brāhmaṇa; or, as it were, he goes to high or low (states). Just as a great king, taking with him his subjects, moves about as he pleases in his own country, so this one, taking with him these prāṇas, moves about as he pleases in his own body. || 18 ||
BR_C02_S01_V18::block-0:
Pūrvapakṣa: Even in the dream-state characterised by perception, though disjoined from effects (kārya) and instruments (karaṇa), saṃsāric characteristics are seen in him — just as in waking, he, being happy, sad, separated from kindred, grieves and is deluded; therefore this (Self) is endowed with grief and delusion as attributes; these grief, delusion, joy, sorrow etc. of his are not superimposed (adhyāropita) by the delusion born of the conjunction of effect and instrument.

Siddhānta: No, on account of (their) being false (mṛṣā). The Self under discussion — when by the dream-mode characterised by perception (svapna-vṛtti) he wanders — at that time these are indeed his worlds, the fruits of his karma. What are they? At that time, on the one hand, he becomes, as it were, a great king; this great-kingship is, as it were, his world — not great-kingship in reality, as in waking; likewise, as it were, a great brāhmaṇa; or, as it were, he goes to high — divinity etc. — and to low — animality etc.; these high and low states.

False (mṛṣā) indeed are these worlds of great-kingship and the rest, on account of the use of the word "as it were" (iva), and on account of the deviation seen. Therefore he is not connected, in dream, with grief and delusion etc. born of separation from kindred and the rest.
BR_C02_S01_V18::block-1:
Pūrvapakṣa: Just as in waking the worlds are unfailing throughout the waking time, so too in dream these worlds of his — great-kingship etc. — that arise during the dream-time and are unfailing throughout the dream-time, are simply Self-constituted, not superimposed by avidyā.

Siddhānta: But that the waking identity with cause-and-effect (body and senses) and with the deity (devatā-ātmatva) is superimposed by avidyā and not real, has been demonstrated by showing the Self distinct as vijñānamaya. How then will the dream-world, like a corpse coming back to life, be brought forward as an example?

True; that in the distinct vijñānamaya the showing of cause-effect-and-deity-Self is superimposed by avidyā — like the cognition of silver in shell — this is established only by the very logic of demonstrating a distinct Self, and not by any reasoning of its purification (viśuddhi); thus is this asserted. (Pūrvapakṣa:) But the example, even if absent, is being raised again — viz., the dream-perception of cause-effect-and-deity-Self of waking. (Reply:) Every reasoning, looking to some specific feature, becomes non-redundant.

First, the great-kingship etc. experienced in dream are not Self-constituted (i.e., his very Self), since the world seen is other than the Self — a reflection of waking. The great king himself, lying in the closed inner chambers on the bed, with senses withdrawn, seeing dreams, sees as it were his Self again endowed with retinue (and royal apparel), as in waking — going on a procession, enjoying enjoyments, as it were. There is no second great king, equipped with retinue, wandering abroad in the world by day, well-known, whom the sleeping one sees; nor is sight of objects with form possible for one with senses withdrawn; nor in the body is there room for another body equal to it; for it is the bodily one alone who has dream-vision.

Pūrvapakṣa: He on the bed sees himself proceeding on the road — he is not seeing dreams outside.

Reply: That is just what is said: "That great king, having taken his subjects — those serving as means of royal estate, retinue, and others — moves about as he pleases in his own country, acquired by his prowess." Likewise, this vijñānamaya — "etat" being an adverb of action — "having taken these prāṇas" — having withdrawn from the waking stations — moves about as he pleases in his own body, not outside; he experiences vāsanās similar to the things previously experienced, illumined by desire and karma — this is the meaning.

Therefore, in dream, the worlds, falsely superimposed as Self-constituted, are non-existent in fact; so too in waking — this is to be recognised. Therefore is established this much: that the vijñānamaya is pure, free from action-agent-fruit. Since worlds — the seen — are seen as objects of the seer (draṣṭṛ), of the nature of action-agent-fruit, marked by cause-and-instrument; and so too in dream — therefore that vijñānamaya, the seer, is other than the seen waking-and-dream-worlds, and is pure.
BR_C02_S01_V19: Now when he is in deep sleep (suṣupta), and knows nothing whatever, the seventy-two thousand nāḍīs called hitā, going forth from the heart to the puritat (pericardium), are spread; through them he creeps back and lies in the puritat. Just as a youth, or a great king, or a great brāhmaṇa, having reached the supreme state of bliss, would lie down — even so this one then lies. || 19 ||
BR_C02_S01_V19::block-0: In the dream-perception-mode (svapna), since the heap of vāsanās is the seen, it is grasped that the Self has the purity of not having those attributes. There it was said "he wanders as he pleases," stating that the wandering is by the force of desire (kāma); but a connection of seer with seen as natural to him might be suspected as impurity. Hence, to declare his purification, (the Upaniṣad) says —
BR_C02_S01_V19::block-1:
"Now when he is in deep sleep" — when he wanders by dream, then too he is pure indeed; but again, when, having abandoned the dream-mode of vision, he is at the time deeply asleep — i.e., well asleep, gone to saṃprasāda, his innate state — he is calmed in his innate nature, like water that has shed the turbidity of its connection with another. When does he become deeply asleep? When at that time he knows no thing whatever — the meaning is, he does not know any object whatever (such as sound) connected with another thing — "any" being supplied; the previous sense is more apt: in deep sleep the absence of specific cognition (viśeṣa-vijñāna-abhāva) is what is intended.

Thus the deep-sleep state has been declared as the absence of specific cognition. By what process does he become deeply asleep? — The nāḍīs by name hitā — i.e., having that name — vessels arising from the digested essence of food, of the body, two and seventy thousand — that is, two thousand more than seventy thousand — these seventy-two thousand, from the heart — the heart, namely the lump of flesh shaped like a lotus — from that flesh-lump, they spread to the puritat (the pericardium that envelops the heart, as is described); the body, marked by that, is here intended by the word puritat. "Spread to the puritat" — they pervade the whole body, like the network of fig-leaves, going forth outwardly.

There the heart is the seat of the buddhi, the antaḥkaraṇa; the other external instruments are dependent on that buddhi placed there. Therefore the buddhi, by force of karma, projects the ear and the rest through these nāḍīs from their stations of the conch of the ear etc., as a fish-net is cast; having projected, in the waking state it presides over them. The vijñānamaya pervades that buddhi by way of the radiance of his own self-consciousness manifested. At the time of withdrawal it contracts together with it; that is the sleep of this vijñānamaya; the experience of the waking expansion is enjoyment. He follows the nature of the buddhi-upādhi, like the moon's reflection following the water and the rest.

Therefore, after the buddhi pertaining to waking objects creeps back through those nāḍīs, having creept back, he lies (rests) in the puritat (i.e., the body) — pervading the body indistinctly like a heated iron-ball, and like fire pervading throughout — this is the meaning. Although in fact he is innately abiding in his own Self, on account of his following the buddhi enmeshed in karma, he is said to lie in the puritat. There is no body-connection in deep sleep. "For he has crossed all sorrows of the heart" (Bṛ.U. 4.3.22), as will be said. This is the state freed from all saṃsāric pain.

Here the example: "Just as a youth — i.e., a very small boy — or a great king — i.e., one of fully obedient subjects, doer of the prescribed — or a great brāhmaṇa — i.e., one perfectly mature in vidyā and discipline — having reached the atighnī — the state that overwhelmingly slays sorrow, the supreme blissful state — would lie." The natural happiness of these — youth and the rest — being in their innate state, is well-known in the world as unsurpassed; their misery, when modified, is not natural; so their innate state is taken as the example, being well-known. Their sleep itself is not intended (as the example), since sleep is the very thing exemplified, and there would be no distinction between example and exemplified — for distinction requires some specific feature.
BR_C02_S01_V19::block-2:
The reply to the question "Where was he then?" has been given. By this determination of the question, the natural purity (viśuddhi) and non-saṃsāra-hood of the vijñānamaya have been declared. Now begins the disposing of the second question, "Whence has he come?"

Pūrvapakṣa: Whoever is in some village or city, and goes elsewhere, goes from that very village or city, not from another; this being so, the question "Where was he?" should suffice; for the place from which he came would be the very place where he was, not another. Hence the question "Whence has he come?" is purposeless. Are you finding fault with the śruti?

Reply: No; rather, I wish to hear another sense of the second question; therefore I urge its purposelessness.

Then this: the sense of "whence" as apādāna (point of departure) cannot be retained — for in the sense of apādāna there would be redundancy, but not in another sense. Then let the question's sense be "on what occasion?" — "Whence has this one come?" meaning "on what occasion is this coming here?"

(Reply:) Not even the sense of occasion (nimitta), since the answer is incongruous with that. The śruti gives the origination of the entire universe from the Self, on the example of fire-and-sparks; for fire is not the occasion of the sparks' rushing forth, but is rather their apādāna; in the same way, the supreme Self is heard as the apādāna of the vijñānamaya — in the passage "From this Self." Therefore, by the contrariness of the answer, the sense of "whence" as occasion cannot be expounded.

Pūrvapakṣa: But on the apādāna view too, the fault of redundancy stands as before.
BR_C02_S01_V19::block-3:
(Reply:) That is no fault — for by the two questions, the deletion of action-agent-fruit-Self-hood from the Ātman is intended. Here the spheres of vidyā and avidyā have been laid down: "One should worship It as the Self" (Bṛ.U. 1.4.7), "He realised the Self alone" (Bṛ.U. 1.4.10), "One should worship the Self alone as the world" (Bṛ.U. 1.4.15) — this is the sphere of vidyā; and the avidyā-sphere — the fivefold karma and its fruit, the threefold food, of the nature of name-form-action.

Of these, all that needed saying about the avidyā-sphere has been said. But the Ātman, the object of vidyā, was merely set forth, not determined. For its determination, it was begun "Let me tell you Brahman" (Bṛ.U. 2.1.1), and "I will indeed make you know" (Bṛ.U. 2.1.15). Hence that Brahman, the object of vidyā, must be made known in its true nature; and its true nature is empty of the distinction of action-agent-fruit, supremely pure and non-dual — this is what is intended.

Hence the śruti raises two questions corresponding to that — "Where was he? Whence did he come?" Therein, where (one) is, that is the locus (adhikaraṇa); what is, that is the loci-occupier (adhikartavya); and the distinction between locus and locus-occupier is seen in the world. Likewise, that from which one comes is the apādāna; one who comes is the agent (kartṛ); they are seen as distinct. Thus, world-fashion, there arises the notion that the Ātman was as one in another, came from another as different, by some other distinct sādhana — this notion has to be removed by the answer.

This Ātman did not exist as one (different) in another, nor did one (different) come from another, nor is there any other sādhana in the Ātman. What then? — He existed in his very Self alone. Hence "He goes to his own Self" (Ch.U. 6.8.1), "He becomes united with sat then, dear one" (Ch.U. 6.8.1), "Embraced by the Prājña Self" (Bṛ.U. 4.3.21), "He is established in the supreme Self" (Pr.U. 4.9), and similar śrutis testify. Hence, no other (Self) comes from another. This is shown by the śruti itself: "From this Self," since there is no other thing apart from the Self.

Pūrvapakṣa: But there is some other thing, distinct from the Self, such as prāṇa. (Reply:) No; for prāṇa and the rest are themselves produced from That alone.
BR_C02_S01_V20: Just as a spider goes forth by means of its thread, just as small sparks fly forth from a fire — even so, from this Self all prāṇas, all worlds, all gods, all beings issue forth. Its upaniṣad (secret doctrine) is: "the Truth of truth" (satyasya satyam). The prāṇas are indeed truth (satya); of them, this is the truth. || 20 ||
BR_C02_S01_V20::block-0: How is that? It is said —
BR_C02_S01_V20::block-1:
There the example: "Just as in the world the spider — the lūtā insect — being one well-known, would go forth (uccaret) by a thread undivided from its own self." There is in its going forth no other instrumental cause apart from itself. "And just as from one homogeneous fire, small sparks — particles, parts of the fire — go forth (vyuccaranti), variously or severally." Just as these two examples show activity even in the absence of any difference of operative cause, and (further show) prior to activity, the unity by nature — even so, from this Ātman, the vijñānamaya — i.e., from the form which is its own prior to awakening — "all prāṇas" — speech and the rest, "all worlds" — earth and the rest, "all karma-fruits, all gods" — Agni and the rest, presiding over the prāṇas and the worlds, "all beings" — from Brahmā down to a tuft of grass — "all (selves)" — in this reading, the specific selves awakening through the contact with the upādhi — issue forth.

From which Ātman this immovable-and-movable universe, like sparks from fire, ceaselessly issues forth, in which alone it dissolves like a bubble in water, and constituted of which it remains during the time of subsistence — of that Ātman, of that Brahman, the upaniṣat — "the term that brings (the meaning) close (upa-nigamayati)" is called upaniṣat; on the strength of śāstra, the special sense of "that which conveys (the truth) closely" (upa-nigamayitṛtva) is established for this word.

What is that upaniṣad? — "satyasya satyam." That is everywhere a secret teaching, since the meaning is supramundane and hard to grasp; therefore he himself states the meaning — "The prāṇas are indeed satya; of them, this is the satya." The two following brāhmaṇas will be the explanation of this very sentence.
BR_C02_S01_V20::block-2:
Granted; let the next two brāhmaṇas be for the explanation of the upaniṣad. The upaniṣad of "this" has been spoken of. Yet we do not know — is this upaniṣad of the vijñānamaya Ātman under discussion, the saṃsārin who arose by the rubbing of the hand, the enjoyer of sound and the rest, or of some non-saṃsārin?

What follows from each? If of the saṃsārin: then the saṃsārin alone is to be known; from his knowledge alone is the attainment of all (puruṣārthas); he alone is denoted by the word Brahman; his vidyā alone is brahmavidyā. But on this view, the śrutis declaring the unity of the supreme Brahman — "One should worship It as the Self" (Bṛ.U. 1.4.7), "He realised the Self alone — 'I am Brahman'" (Bṛ.U. 1.4.10) — would be violated; and in the absence of any other saṃsārin, the teaching would be purposeless.

If of the non-saṃsārin: then vidyā regarding him is brahmavidyā, and from the knowledge of that Brahman comes the attainment of all-being-ness; all this would be on the strength of śāstra. But on this side, where is the saṃsārin? Hence, since this is a great occasion of confusion even for the learned, an unanswered point of question, we shall therefore investigate, to the best of our ability, the sentences expounding brahmavidyā, in order to instruct the inquirers after Brahman.
BR_C02_S01_V20::block-3:
First, the supreme is not a saṃsārin — for the śruti of origination from one distinguished by an additional state, namely the enjoyer of sound and the rest, awakened by rubbing of the hand. Nor is the supreme — the prashāstā devoid of hunger etc. — non-existent. Why? Because, having pledged "I will declare Brahman" (Bṛ.U. 2.1.15), having awakened the sleeping man by rubbing the hand, having shown him as the enjoyer of sound and the rest, having through him led to that further state called suṣupti through dream, the śruti shows from that very Self distinguished by the suṣupti-state the origination, by the analogies of fire-sparks and spider — "Even so from this" — and no other cause of the origination of the world is heard in between; for the context is precisely of the vijñānamaya.

And in another śruti of like context, that of the Kauṣītakins — having begun with the puruṣas of the sun and others — "He said: O Bālāki, he who is the maker of these puruṣas, whose work this is — he indeed is to be known" (Kau.U. 4.19) — shows that it is precisely the awakened vijñānamaya that is to be known, not any other thing. Likewise, having said "All things become dear for the sake of the Ātman" (Bṛ.U. 2.4.5), it shows that he who is the well-known dear Ātman is alone to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon.

Likewise, in the laying down of vidyā: "One should worship It as the Self" (Bṛ.U. 1.4.7), "He, this, is dearer than the son, dearer than wealth" (Bṛ.U. 1.4.8), "He realised the Self alone — 'I am Brahman'" (Bṛ.U. 1.4.10) and so on — these statements would have congruity (only) on the absence of a (different) supreme. He will say: "If a man knows the Self as 'I am he'" (Bṛ.U. 4.4.12). And in all the Vedāntas, the inwardness of the Ātman as object of cognition is shown — as "I," not the externality of being known like sound and the rest, presented as "this Brahman."

So too of the Kauṣītakins — "One should not seek to know speech, one should know the speaker" (Kau.U. 3.8) and so on — they show that the agent, distinguished from speech and the other instruments, alone is to be known.

Pūrvapakṣa: He is non-saṃsārin only when distinguished by another state. (Reply:) Then it might be: "He who in waking is the enjoyer of sound etc., the vijñānamaya, having gone to the further state called suṣupti, becomes another, the non-saṃsārin supreme prashāstā" — No; for it is unseen. Such a substance is nowhere observed except in the system of the Vaināśikas. In the world a cow standing or going does not become a cow, while one lying becomes another species like a horse. Logically too: a substance ascertained by pramāṇa as having such-and-such attributes remains so endowed in another place, time, or state; if it deviates therefrom, all transactions of pramāṇa would collapse.

And so, the men learned in nyāya — Sāṃkhyas, Mīmāṃsakas, and the rest — establish, by hundreds of arguments, the absence of any non-saṃsārin.

Pūrvapakṣa: But the saṃsārin too lacks the power to know the activities of creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the universe; therefore (your view) is unfit. (Reply:) That which has been set up by you with great elaboration — that the enjoyer of sound and the rest, the very saṃsārin distinguished by another state, is here the maker of the world — that is unsound; for the lack of capability to know the activities of creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the world is plainly seen in every saṃsārin. How can the saṃsārin like ourselves construct the world distinguished by the disposition of earth and the rest, which cannot be conceived of even mentally? Hence (the view) is unfit.
BR_C02_S01_V20::block-4:
From a hundred such śruti-passages — "He who is all-knowing, all-wise" (Mu.U. 1.1.9; 2.2.7), "He who transcends hunger and thirst" (Bṛ.U. 3.5.1), "Unattached, he does not get attached" (Bṛ.U. 3.9.26), "At the rule of this Imperishable" (Bṛ.U. 3.8.9), "He who, dwelling in all beings — the inner controller, the immortal" (Bṛ.U. 3.7.15), "He who having drawn forth those puruṣas, transcended (them)" (Bṛ.U. 3.9.26), "This is indeed the great unborn Self" (Bṛ.U. 4.4.22), "This is the bridge that holds all asunder" (Bṛ.U. 4.4.22), "The lord of all, ruler of all" (Bṛ.U. 4.4.22), "The Self that is free from sin, undecaying, undying" (Ch.U. 8.7.1, 8.7.3), "That created tejas" (Ch.U. 6.2.3), "In the beginning the Self alone, indeed, was this" (Ai.U. 1.1.1), "He, being external, is not stained by world-grief" (Ka.U. 2.2.11) — and from smṛti — "I am the source of all; from me all proceeds" (Bh.G. 10.8) — there is the supreme, the non-saṃsārin, by śruti, smṛti, and reasoning; and he is the cause of the universe.

Pūrvapakṣa: But it has been said that "Even so from this Self" shows the origination from the saṃsārin himself. Reply: No; since it is the supreme that is the topic, by "This ether within the heart" (Bṛ.U. 2.1.17), the reference "From this Self" is fitting only of the supreme. As the answer to the question "Where was he?" (Bṛ.U. 2.1.16), the supreme Self denoted by ākāśa was spoken — "He lies in this ether within the heart" (Bṛ.U. 2.1.16). From śrutis like "He becomes united with sat then, dear one" (Ch.U. 6.8.1), "They go each day to that Brahmaloka but do not find it" (Ch.U. 8.3.2), "Embraced by the Prājña Self" (Bṛ.U. 4.3.21), "He is established in the supreme Self" (Pr.U. 4.7), it is determined that the word ākāśa denotes the supreme Self; also, in "There is a small space within" (Ch.U. 8.1.1), the use of the word ātman is upon that very (ākāśa). It is just the supreme Self that is the topic. Therefore it is fitting (that) "Even so from this Self" denotes the supreme Self alone as the source; and we have already shown the saṃsārin's lack of capacity for the activity-knowledge of creation, sustenance, and dissolution.

Here too brahmavidyā has been begun: "One should worship It as the Self" (Bṛ.U. 1.4.7), "He realised the Self alone — 'I am Brahman'" (Bṛ.U. 1.4.10); and "Brahmavijñāna" is the knowledge whose object is Brahman. "Let me tell you Brahman" (Bṛ.U. 2.2.1) and "I will make you know Brahman" (Bṛ.U. 2.1.15) was begun. There now: the non-saṃsārin Brahman is the cause of the universe, free from hunger and the rest, of the very nature of eternal-pure-conscious-free; opposite is the saṃsārin. Hence one should not grasp "I am Brahman." To meditate on the supreme deity, the supreme Lord, as identical with the lowly saṃsārin — how would that not bring fault? Therefore "I am Brahman" is unfit. One should rather seek to propitiate (Brahman) by flowers, water-offering, eulogy, namaskāra, oblations, svādhyāya, dhyāna, yoga, and the like; through propitiation, having known Brahman the All-Ruler, one becomes (it). One should not contemplate the non-saṃsārin Brahman as identical with the saṃsārin Self — like fire as cold, like ākāśa as having form. The pas­sages teaching the identity of Brahman with Ātman…
BR_C02_S01_V20::block-5:
(Reply:) No; from the mantra-and-brāhmaṇa statements, the very entry of that one (i.e., the supreme) is heard. Beginning with "He made cities" (Bṛ.U. 2.5.10), and in "As puruṣa, he entered the cities" (Bṛ.U. 2.5.18); "He became corresponding to every form, that form being for his being seen" (Bṛ.U. 2.5.19); "Having arranged all forms, the wise one, having made names, sat reciting them" (Tai.Ā. 3.12.7) — in all the recensions, in thousands of mantra-passages, the entry of the very Creator, the non-saṃsārin, into bodies is shown.

Likewise the brāhmaṇa-passages: "Having created that, he entered into that very thing" (Tai.U. 2.6.6); "He, splitting that very crown, entered through that door" (Ai.U. 1.3.12); "That deity — having entered these three deities by this jīva-Self" (Ch.U. 6.2.3); "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth" (Ka.U. 1.3.12), and the like.

And in all śrutis the word ātman is used for Brahman; and the word ātman denotes the inner Self; and from the śruti "This is the inner Self of all beings" (Mu.U. 2.1.4); and from the absence of any saṃsārin distinct from the supreme — by śrutis like "One only, without a second" (Ch.U. 6.2.1), "This is verily Brahman" (Mu.U. 2.2.11), "All this is the Self alone" (Ch.U. 7.25.2) — it is quite proper to determine "I am Brahman."
BR_C02_S01_V20::block-6:
When the meaning of the śāstra stands thus, then comes the saṃsāra-hood of the supreme Self; and being so, the purposelessness of the śāstra (in one alternative), and on non-saṃsāra-hood the purposelessness of teaching — both faults plainly accrue. If the supreme Self, the inner Self of all beings, experiences the pains arising from contact with all bodies, the saṃsāra-hood of the supreme is plainly entailed; and so the śrutis declaring the non-saṃsāra-hood of the supreme would be in conflict, as also the smṛtis and all reasonings.

If somehow it can be propounded that he is not connected with the pains arising from prāṇa-and-body relation, the absence of anything to be accomplished or avoided in the supreme Self renders the fault of purposelessness of teaching unavoidable.

Here, some offer a remedy: the supreme Self has not entered the beings directly in his own form; rather, he has come into a state of modification (vikāra) and assumed the status of vijñānātman; and that vijñānātman is, vis-à-vis the supreme, both other and not-other — in respect of being other, it has connection with saṃsāra-hood; in respect of being not-other, it is fit for the determination "I am Brahman." Thus everything will be unopposed.
BR_C02_S01_V20::block-7:
On the modification (vikāra) view of the vijñānātman, these alternatives present themselves: of the supreme Self, like an earthen substance composed of many substances, partite, the vijñānātman would be a partial transformation, like a pot — or, of the supreme remaining in his prior configuration, one part transforms, like hair and salty soil — or, the entire supreme transforms, like milk.

(i) When some particular substance among an aggregate of like-natured many substances becomes the vijñānātman, then on account of homogeneity oneness is figurative only, not real; that violates the siddhānta. (ii) Or if the supreme Self is an avayavin pervading parts that are eternally compactly co-existent, of him in that state, the vijñānātman is one part, the saṃsārin — even then, since the avayavin pervades all the avayavas, faults or qualities found in the part are of the avayavin (whole); thus the saṃsāra-fault of the vijñānātman would attach to the supreme Self himself; this also is undesirable. (iii) On the all-transformation view, like milk, all śruti-smṛtis are violated, and that is undesirable.

All these views conflict with śruti-smṛti and reason, e.g., "Indivisible, actionless, peaceful" (Śve.U. 6.19), "Divine, formless puruṣa, with outer and inner, unborn" (Mu.U. 2.1.2), "All-pervading like ākāśa, and eternal" (Śat.Br. 10.6.3.2), "This is the great unborn Self, undecaying, undying, immortal" (Bṛ.U. 4.4.25), "Never is he born, nor does he die" (Bh.G. 2.20), "This is unmanifest" (Bh.G. 2.25), and so on.

On the eka-deśa view, of the unmoving supreme Self, the vijñānātman cannot wander to various karma-fruit-regions, or else the supreme too becomes saṃsārin — as said. "As a spark, having broken off from the supreme, the vijñānātman wanders" — even so, by the breaking-off of a part there is injury (kṣati) of the supreme; and on its wandering, in the supreme there comes a hole through the rearrangement of the other parts, conflicting with the avraṇa-vāda; and on the wandering of the vijñānātman, which is a part of the supreme, since there is no place void of the supreme, by the pushing and rearrangement of other parts the supreme would suffer pain like a heart-spear.

Pūrvapakṣa: There is no fault, since (this is) the śruti of the example of fire-and-sparks. Reply: No; for the śruti is jñāpaka (informative), not maker (kāraka). The śāstra does not undertake to alter the realities of things, but to make known things as they are, that were unknown. Therefore? Hear what follows. The well-known attributes of the world's substances — gross, subtle, and so on — are taken as examples; the śāstra, in undertaking to declare another substance not in conflict with them, does not, by adopting that worldly example, declare the violation of the worldly fact; and the example, even if invoked, would be useless if the example does not fit the exemplified.

For "fire is cold" or "the sun does not burn" cannot be established by hundreds of examples, since the substance has been ascertained otherwise by another pramāṇa; and one pramāṇa does not contradict another; for one pramāṇa makes known precisely that which is not the object of another pramāṇa.

Without resorting to the words and meanings well-established in the world, an unknown substance cannot be made known by the āgama. Therefore, by following the established mode of reasoning, the assumption of the supreme Self as having parts, as part-and-whole, cannot be expounded as the ultimate reality.

Pūrvapakṣa: But "small sparks" (Bṛ.U. 2.1.20), "a portion of myself" (Bh.G. 15.7) is heard and remembered. Reply: No; for these are for the firmness of (the doctrine of) unity…
BR_C02_S01_V20::block-8:
Here the knowers of the tradition relate a story: A certain prince, abandoned by his parents the moment he was born, was reared in a hunter's house. He, ignorant of his lineage, having only a hunter-conviction, follows only hunter-caste-acts; he does not say "I am a king" and follow royal-acts. Then a most compassionate person, knowing the prince's fitness for attaining the regal fortune, makes him aware of his sonship: "You are not a hunter; you are the son of such-and-such a king; somehow you have entered a hunter's house." He, thus made aware, abandons the conviction and acts of hunter-caste, and follows the path of his fathers and grandfathers — "I am the king."

Likewise, this one, distinguished from the supreme like a spark of fire, of that very class, has entered this dense forest of body, sense and the rest; being non-saṃsārin, he yet follows the saṃsāric attributes of body and senses — "I am the body-sense-aggregate; lean, fat, happy, sad" — not knowing his supreme-Self-hood. "You, of this nature, are the supreme Brahman alone, the non-saṃsārin" — thus instructed by the teacher, abandoning the pursuit of the three eṣaṇās, he attains "I am Brahman alone."

Here, like the prince's regal-conviction, the Brahman-conviction is firmly fixed; for, when it is said "You are like a spark, dropped from the supreme Brahman," the spark's fall from fire (still) is in view of the unity of fire (with itself before falling). Therefore for the firmness of unity-conviction the examples of gold-and-jewel-and-iron-fire-spark are given; not for the establishment of differences such as origination etc.

Like a saline lump (sea-salt block) — by the determination of the unbroken homogeneity of awareness — "It is to be regarded as one only" (Bṛ.U. 4.4.20). And if the variegation of Brahman, like a painting or like a tree-and-sea, with origination etc., were intended, he would not have summed up "like a saline lump, one taste, without inner or outer"; nor would he have used "It is to be regarded as one only" (Bṛ.U. 4.4.20); and "He who sees as if many here" (Bṛ.U. 4.4.19) — the censuring statement.

Therefore, in all the Vedāntas, the imagining of origination, sustenance, dissolution and the like is solely for the firmness of one-form-unity-conviction, not to produce the conviction of those (differences themselves).
BR_C02_S01_V20::block-9:
And the imagining of a saṃsāric portion of the partless, non-saṃsāric supreme Self is not reasonable, on account of the supreme Self's intrinsic placelessness. The imagination of a partial saṃsāra-hood in the place-less supreme would amount to the imagining of the very supreme as saṃsārin.

Or — like the ākāśa in pots and water-jars — the part is due to extrinsic upādhis. Even then, in the discerning, no notion arises of "the supreme-Self-portion is engaged in separate transaction." If the figurative notion is found in the undiscerning and discerning alike — No; for in the undiscerning it is a false cognition, and in the discerning it serves merely as a basis of practical transaction — just as "the sky is black, red," even in the discerning, the blackness or redness of the ākāśa serves only the purpose of practical transaction; it is not that the sky truly is black or red.

Therefore, the wise should not imagine, in regard to the apprehension of Brahman's true nature, the conceptualisation of Brahman's parts-and-whole, locus-and-loci, modification-and-modifying, etc., since the import of all the upaniṣads is the removing of all imagining. Hence, abandoning all imaginings, like the ākāśa, the (Self) is to be apprehended as featureless — from a hundred śrutis like "All-pervading like ākāśa, eternal" (Śat.Br. 10.6.3.2), "Unstained by world-pain, external" (Ka.U. 2.2.11). One should not imagine the Self as different from Brahman — like a cold portion in fire, or a portion of darkness in the luminous sun — since the import of all the upaniṣads is the removal of all imagining.

Therefore, all transactions in the non-saṃsāric Self are caused by the upādhis of name and form (nāma-rūpa) — from the mantra-words "He became corresponding to every form" (Bṛ.U. 2.5.19), "Having arranged all forms, the wise one having made names sat reciting them" (Tai.Ā. 3.12.7), and the like — there is no intrinsic saṃsāra-hood of the Self; like the cognition of a red crystal etc., born of the contact of the upādhi of red lac etc., it is illusory only, not in fact.

From śruti-smṛti-reasonings — "He as it were meditates, as it were trembles" (Bṛ.U. 4.3.7), "He neither increases by deed nor diminishes" (Bṛ.U. 4.4.23), "He is not stained by sinful action" (Bṛ.U. 4.4.23), "Equal in all beings" (Bh.G. 13.27), "In a dog and in a śva-pāka" (Bh.G. 5.10) and the like — the supreme Self's non-saṃsāra-hood alone (is established).

Hence, the alternative "vijñānātman is part, modification, śakti, or other" cannot be specifically maintained on the admission of partlessness. The aṃśa etc. śruti-and-smṛti statements aim at oneness, not at the propounding of difference, since the connection (with) the intended sense is in a single-statement (eka-vākyatā) — as we have said.
BR_C02_S01_V20::block-10:
Pūrvapakṣa: When all upaniṣads aim at the knowledge of the supreme Self's unity, why then is a sense contrary to it — the difference of the vijñānātman — imagined? Some say: For removing the conflict with the validity of the karmakāṇḍa. The sentences propounding karman rest on the multiple of action-instrument-fruit-enjoyer-agent; in the absence of vijñānātman-difference, when there is the unity of the non-saṃsārin supreme Self, how should they engage in actions for desired fruits, or restrain from actions of undesired fruits? Or for whose liberation, being bound, would the upaniṣad be undertaken? Moreover, on the supreme-Self-unity-vādin's side, how is the teaching of supreme-Self-unity? Or how is the fruit of the apprehension of that teaching? For teaching is for the destruction of the bondage of the bound; in its absence, the upaniṣad-śāstra is without object.

(Reply:) Then on the upaniṣad-vādin side, the path of objections-and-replies with the karmakāṇḍa-vādin would be parallel — by the same (logic) by which, in the absence of difference, the karmakāṇḍa cannot find its support and pramāṇya, so too the upaniṣad. (Reply to that:) Then let only that whose pramāṇya does not bring its own destruction be valid — the karmakāṇḍa; but on supposing the validity of the upaniṣads, the destruction of their own meaning would follow, so let there be no validity. For the karmakāṇḍa, being a pramāṇa, cannot become a non-pramāṇa; nor does a lamp illumine and not illumine the same illuminable.

And from conflict with pratyakṣa and other pramāṇas — not only do the upaniṣads, in propounding Brahman-unity, bring about the destruction of their own meaning and of the validity of the karmakāṇḍa; they also conflict with the pramāṇas — pratyakṣa and the rest — that ascertain difference. Therefore the upaniṣads have no pramāṇya at all; or let there be another sense; in any case, never the sense of the apprehension of Brahman-unity.
BR_C02_S01_V20::block-11:
(Siddhānta:) No, on account of (this objection) being already answered. The pramāṇa-hood or non-pramāṇa-hood of a pramāṇa is occasioned by its causing or not causing pramā (right cognition); else there would be the contingency of pramāṇa-hood for posts and the like with regard to sound and other objects of pramā.

Therefore? If the upaniṣads cause the pramā of apprehension of Brahman-unity, how can they be non-pramāṇa? "They do not cause it indeed — like 'fire is cold'" — if you say so, you yourself, in saying that, must be told: Does your sentence, intended to negate the validity of the upaniṣads, do its negating of the upaniṣad's validity at all, or does fire not show form-illumination? If it does — if it does, then let your sentence be a pramāṇa for the negating of, say, but then fire too becomes an illuminator of form. (And) on the validity of the negating sentence, the validity of the upaniṣads holds anyway.

Now you tell what removal there is of this. "But pratyakṣa, in my sentence, is the apprehension of the negation of the upaniṣad's validity; and in fire, the apprehension of form-illumination, is pramā." Then what is your hostility to the upaniṣads, which produce, as direct (pratyakṣa) experience, the pramā in the apprehension of Brahman-unity, when (they) are in fact heard? Negation is not possible.

And the cessation of grief and delusion etc. is the directly seen fruit, born by tradition of the apprehension of Brahman-unity — as we have said. Hence, on account of the answer already given, there is no doubt of non-pramāṇa-hood of the upaniṣad.
BR_C02_S01_V20::block-12:
What was said — that there is non-pramāṇa-hood because of self-meaning destruction — that too is not (so), since there is no obstruction to the apprehension of that meaning. There is not, from the upaniṣads, the apprehension "Brahman is one without a second, and indeed not so" — as from the sentence "Fire is hot and cold" the apprehension of two contrary meanings.

And we have said this even in concession; this is not the rule with respect to the validity of a sentence — that one sentence has many meanings; and on its having many meanings, that there should be the self-meaning, and an opposite meaning that destroys it. This is not the rule among the votaries of sentence-pramāṇa: that one sentence, contrary or non-contrary, propounds many meanings; for one-sentence-hood is on account of singleness of meaning.

And no upaniṣad-sentence does the negating of Brahman-unity. The popular sentence "Fire is hot and cold" — there is no eka-vākyatā; the part is anuvāda, repeating what is the object of another pramāṇa. "Fire is cold" is one sentence; "Fire is hot" is the reminder of another pramāṇa-experience, not by itself disclosing a meaning. Hence with "Fire is cold" it has no eka-vākyatā, since it is exhausted in reminding of another pramāṇa-experience.

What is taken to be a sentence propounding contrary meanings is the confusion arising from the use of co-referentiality of the words śīta-and-uṣṇa with the word agni; never the multi-meaning-hood of one sentence, popular or vedic.
BR_C02_S01_V20::block-13:
What was said — that the upaniṣad-sentence destroys the pramāṇya of the karmakāṇḍa — that is not (so), on account of (its) other purport. The upaniṣads are devoted to the propounding of Brahman-unity; they do not bar the teaching of means in the attainment of desired aims, or the assignment of the puruṣa-niyoga in those (means), since the multi-meaning-hood is itself untenable. And the karmakāṇḍa-sentences do not fail to produce pramā in their own meaning. If a sentence produces pramā in its own non-overlapping meaning, whence would there be a conflict with another?

Pūrvapakṣa: Since on Brahman-unity (everything) is without object, no pramā arises. Reply: No, since pramā is direct (pratyakṣa). From sentences like "By dārśa-pūrṇamāsa let the seeker of svarga sacrifice" (?), "A brāhmaṇa is not to be slain" (?), and the like, pramā arises directly; that will not arise (only) on the inference "the upaniṣads will declare Brahman-unity"; and inference cannot, in conflict with pratyakṣa, attain pramāṇya. Hence what was sung (by you) — "pramā does not arise at all" — is unsound.

Moreover, having taken up just the action-instrument-fruit appearing through avidyā, when one engages in the general means of attaining the desirable and avoiding the undesirable, the śruti, in declaring particularities to one ignorant, neither asserts the truth nor falsehood of the worldly fact of action-instrument-fruit-difference, nor blocks it — being intent on enjoining the means of attaining-and-avoiding desirable-undesirable fruits.

Just as the śruti, engaged in the optional rites (kāmya), though desires are products of false cognition, takes up the desires as they come and prescribes only their means; it does not refuse, on the ground that desires are products of false cognition and hence of the form of evil. Likewise the śāstra of the eternal agnihotra etc., taking just as they come the action-instrument-difference produced by false cognition, and seeing some result — desired-fruit-attainment or undesired-fruit-avoidance — prescribes the agnihotra and the rest as actions, not as having for object an unreal thing in the sphere of avidyā; — like (the rule) in kāmya rites.

Nor do the avidyā-bound puruṣas fail to engage, since (such engaging is) seen — like one with desires.

Pūrvapakṣa: Only the wise have adhikāra in karman. (Reply:) No; for in the brahma-aikya-vidyā, conflict with karma-adhikāra has been declared. By this, the answer to the imagined fault, namely the absence of fruit by apprehension of the teaching since (Brahman-unity) is without object, is to be known.

And from the variety of human desires-passions etc. — many are the desires of men; and rāga and other dosas are varied. Hence the śāstra cannot turn away the mind taken away by attachment to external objects; nor can it engage in objects the mind naturally averse to external objects. Rather, only this much is from the śāstra: the manifestation of the relation of means-end specific — "this is the means to the desirable, this to the undesirable" — like, in darkness, knowledge of form etc. by lamp; the śāstra does not, like servants by force, turn (anyone) away or engage (anyone). For we see men, on account of their being heavy with passion etc., transgressing even the śāstra. Therefore, looking to the variety of human dispositions, it teaches in many ways the relation of means-end specific. There the men, of themselves according to taste, engage in particular means; the śāstra, like the sun and the lamp, simply remains indifferent.

Likewise, even the supreme puruṣārtha appears to some as if not the puruṣārtha; whoever has whatever apparition, sees the puruṣārtha in that form; and intends to take up means corresponding to it…
BR_C02_S01_V20::block-14:
Some who think themselves learned, by force of their own minds, hold all pramāṇas to be mutually contradictory; they thus also raise pratyakṣa and other oppositions to Brahman-unity. Sound and so on are taken as objects of ear and the rest, distinct, by direct (pratyakṣa) experience; for those declaring Brahman-unity there would be conflict with pratyakṣa. Likewise, by ear and the rest, the apprehenders of sound and so on, the agents of dharma-and-adharma, distinct in each body, the saṃsārins, are inferred; there for those declaring Brahman-unity, there is conflict with anumāna; likewise they speak of conflict with āgama — "The seeker of village let him sacrifice" (Tai.Ā. 17.10.4), "The seeker of cattle let him sacrifice" (Tai.Ā. 16.12.8), "The seeker of svarga let him sacrifice" (Tai.Ā. 16.3.3), and the like — from these one knows the desires for village, cattle, svarga and the rest, and the performers of their means as different.

Here it is replied: those of corrupted minds by faulty reasoning, the lowest among brāhmaṇas and the like, are pitiable, having lost the tradition of the meaning of the āgama in their understanding. How? Those who say "From sound and the rest, perceived directly through ear and the rest, Brahman-unity is contradicted" must be questioned: Is the unity of ākāśa contradicted by the difference of sounds and the rest? If not, then there is no conflict with pratyakṣa.

And what was said — that, in each body, apprehenders of sound and the rest and agents of dharma-and-adharma are inferred as different, and so there is conflict with anumāna for those declaring Brahman-unity — they should be asked: By whom are the different (selves) inferred? If they say "by all of us, skilled in inference" — when asked "Who are you, skilled in inference?" — what is the answer? If, denying the inference-skill of body, sense, mind, individually, they say "We are Selves having body-sense-mind as instruments, skilled in inference, since actions are accomplished by many factors" — then on the inference-skill, your having multiplicity is entailed; for actions accomplished by many factors is admitted by you. There, inference is an action; that, by the factors of body-sense-mind-Self, having Self as agent, is brought about — this you have premised; in saying "we are skilled in inference," you have admitted that the Selves having body-sense-mind as instruments are individually multiple.

Aho, the inference-skill displayed by the tail-and-horn-less tārkika-bullocks! He who does not even know the Self himself — how, the deluded one, would he know the difference or non-difference pertaining to it? What does he infer? By what mark? There is no mark intrinsic to the Self that proves its difference, by which mark one could establish difference of Self. The marks bearing names-and-forms cited as proving Self-difference belong to nāma-rūpa — they are upādhis of the Self — like the cavities of pot, water-jar, store-room, ground-pit for the ākāśa. When one sees a difference-mark of ākāśa, then one would obtain a difference-mark of the Self also.

Even with hundreds of tārkikas, accepting Self-features as extrinsic, the difference-mark of the Self cannot be shown; intrinsic — that is far removed, since the Self is not an object. Whatever (the opponent) takes as Self-attribute, that is admitted to be of the nature of nāma-rūpa, and from the admission that nāma-rūpa is other than the Self — from the śruti "Ākāśa, by name, is the producer of name and form; that within which they are, that is Brahman" (Ch.U. 8.14.1), "I will produce names and forms" (?)…
BR_C02_S02_INTRO1::block-0:
"I will declare Brahman" (Bṛ.U. 2.1.15) was begun. There it has been declared that whence the universe is born, of which it consists, and into which it dissolves — that is the one Brahman.

Of what nature, however, is that universe that is born and dissolves? Of the nature of the five elements (pañca-bhūtas); and the elements are of the nature of nāma-rūpa; and nāma-rūpa has been said to be satya. Of that satya, of the nature of the five elements, the satya is Brahman.

How are the elements satya? — by the (forthcoming) Brāhmaṇa of the murta-amurta (formed and formless). Since the elements are of the nature of formed and formless, the elements as kārya-karaṇa (effect-and-instrument), and the prāṇas as well, are satya.

With the wish to determine the satyatā of those elements as kārya-karaṇa, the two (next) brāhmaṇas are begun — that very (set) is the explanation of the upaniṣad. For only by way of determining the satyatā of effect-and-instrument is the satya of satya, Brahman, determined. Here it has been said: "The prāṇas indeed are satya; of them, this is the satya" (Bṛ.U. 2.1.20). What are the prāṇas, what is the extent of the upaniṣads of the prāṇas, what are they — on the occasion of the brahma-upaniṣad, the form of the karaṇas, the prāṇas, is being determined; like the determining of well, garden, etc., on a road taken.
BR_C02_S02_V01: He who knows the infant together with its abode (ādhāna), its supporting frame (pratyādhāna), its post (sthūṇā), and its tether (dāma), wards off the seven hostile foes that hate him. This infant indeed is the middle prāṇa; this verily is its abode, this its supporting frame, prāṇa is its post, and food its tether.
BR_C02_S02_V01::block-0:
"He who knows the infant together with the ādhāna (abode), pratyādhāna (supporting frame), sthūṇā (post) and dāma (tether)" — this is the result for him. What is that result? "He wards off the seven hate-bearing brothers" — for brothers are of two kinds, those who hate and those who do not. Among them, those brothers who hate are called dviṣato bhrātṛvyān, and these he wards off. The seven prāṇas situated in the head are the gateways to the apprehension of objects; the attachments to objects which spring from them are, by very nativity (sahajatva), "brothers" (bhrātṛvya). They indeed turn this person's gaze, which is naturally seated in the Self, outward toward objects; on this account they are hating brothers, since they obstruct the vision of the inner Ātman. So too it is said in the Kāṭhaka: "The Self-existent pierced the openings outward; therefore one looks outward, not at the inner Self" (Ka.U. 2.1.1) and so forth. Therefore, he who knows the infant and the rest, that is, who ascertains their true nature (yāthātmya), "wards off these brothers" — apāvṛṇoti, destroys them.

Now, to the listener whose face has been turned toward the teaching by the hearing of the fruit, He says: "This indeed is the infant." Who is that? "He who is this middle prāṇa" — the prāṇa within the body, the subtle body (liṅgātman), which has entered the body in fivefold form, and which has been spoken of as "the great one clad in white, O Soma the king" (BU 4.3.20-style passage), into which the organs beginning with speech and mind are bound — by analogy with the picket and the peg — that very one is like an infant, since with regard to objects he is, like the other organs, unskilled.

"The infant together with its ādhāna" — has been mentioned. What then is the ādhāna of this infant who stands in the place of a calf, that is, of the organic self (karaṇātman)? "This very body is its ādhāna," the effect-aggregate; ādhānam means that wherein something is established (ādhīyate'sminniti). For this body is the ground (adhiṣṭhāna) of that infant prāṇa; in this body alone are the organs established and made effective and become gateways of cognition; they are not bound merely to prāṇa as such. So indeed Ajātaśatru showed: when the organs are withdrawn, the cognizing one (vijñānamaya) is not perceived, but when the organs are dispersed throughout the body's regions, the cognizing one is perceived as one cognizing — and this was demonstrated by waking the man with the rubbing of the hand.

"This is the pratyādhāna" — the head. Pratyādhāna is so called because it is established in particular regions, prati-ādhīyate.

"Prāṇa is the sthūṇā" — the strength produced from food and drink; "prāṇa" and "strength" are synonyms. Prāṇa is indeed the prop of strength in this body — as is shown by "when this Self enters into weakness, as if into delusion" (BU 4.4.1) — just as the calf is propped by the post. Some hold that the wind which sides with the body is the sthūṇā called prāṇa.

"Food is the dāma" — for food when eaten is transformed in three ways. The gross transformation, becoming these two — urine and faeces — passes back to this very earth. The middle juice (rasa), through the sequence of blood and the rest, builds up its own product, the body composed of the seven dhātus; for when its own kind of food arrives the body grows, since it is made of food, and in the contrary case it wastes and falls. But the subtlest essence — called amṛta, ūrk, energy (prabhāva) — coming up from the navel to the region of the heart, and entering the seventy-two thousand nāḍīs that branch out from the heart, becomes the cause of the stay in the body of that aggregate of organs called the subtle body (liṅga), known as the infant, generating the strength called sthūṇā. Thereby food on both sides, like the rope between collar and calf and stake (paśu-vatsa-dāma-vat), becomes the binding link between prāṇa and the body.
BR_C02_S02_V02: These seven inexhaustibles attend on him. Those red lines in the eye — by them Rudra is attached to him; the waters in the eye — by them Parjanya; the pupil — by it Āditya; what is black — by it Agni; what is white — by it Indra; by the lower lash the earth is attached to him, by the upper, the heaven. His food never wastes who knows this.
BR_C02_S02_V02::block-0: Now certain upaniṣads (secret teachings) are stated regarding that very infant when he is borne in the eye, his supporting frame (pratyādhāna).
BR_C02_S02_V03: Concerning that, this verse occurs: "There is a bowl with mouth below and bottom above; in it is placed every kind of glory. On its rim sit seven seers; speech, the eighth, is in colloquy with Brahman." "The bowl with mouth below and bottom above" — this is that head; for indeed it is the bowl with mouth below and bottom above. "In it is placed every kind of glory" — the prāṇas verily are the manifold glory; this is what is said of the prāṇas. "On its rim sit seven seers" — the prāṇas verily are the seers; this is what is said of the prāṇas. "Speech, the eighth, is in colloquy with Brahman" — for speech, the eighth, is in colloquy with Brahman.
BR_C02_S02_V03::block-0:
"Concerning that" — that is, in this matter — "this śloka, this mantra, occurs" — "the bowl with mouth below" etc. There the śruti itself expounds the meaning of the mantra: "the bowl with mouth below, bottom above." What is that bowl with mouth below and bottom above? "This indeed" — the head; for it has the form of a bowl. How? Since the mouth (bila) is below — for the mouth has the form of an opening (bila) — and the bottom is above (ūrdhva-budhna), for the head has the form of a bowl's bottom.

"In it is placed every kind of glory" — just as soma is in the bowl, so in this head is placed, that is, established, the manifold (viśvarūpa, of every form), namely glory. What then is that? "The prāṇas verily are the manifold glory" — the prāṇas, hearing and the rest, and the maruts, the airs, sevenfold spread out among them, are glory: this is what the mantra says, since they are the cause of the cognition of sound and other objects.

"On its rim sit seven seers" — the prāṇas, of the nature of pulsation (parispanda), they alone are the seers; this is what the mantra says of the prāṇas.

"Speech, the eighth, is in colloquy with Brahman" — speech, when conversing with Brahman, is the eighth. He gives the reason for that: "For speech is the eighth, since it converses with Brahman."
BR_C02_S02_V04: These two are Gotama and Bharadvāja: this is Gotama, this is Bharadvāja. These two are Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni: this is Viśvāmitra, this is Jamadagni. These two are Vasiṣṭha and Kaśyapa: this is Vasiṣṭha, this is Kaśyapa. Speech is Atri, for by speech is food eaten (atti). Atri is verily the name of "eater" (attṛ). He becomes the eater of all, and all becomes his food, who knows this.
BR_C02_S02_V04::block-0:
Who, then, are the seers seated on the rim of that bowl? "These two are Gotama and Bharadvāja" — the two ears: this is Gotama, this is Bharadvāja, the right and the left, or in the reverse order. So too pointing to the eyes, He says: "These two are Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni" — the right is Viśvāmitra, the left is Jamadagni, or in the reverse order. "These two are Vasiṣṭha and Kaśyapa" — pointing to the nostrils, He said: the right nostril is Vasiṣṭha, the left is Kaśyapa, as before.

"Speech itself is Atri" — the seventh, on account of its connection with the act of eating; for by speech is food eaten. Therefore atti is indeed the well-known name — meaning "eater," because of being the eater (attṛtvāt); being himself "atti," he is by indirection (parokṣa) called "atri."

By this knowledge of the etymology (nirvacana) "atri," he becomes the eater of all this aggregate of food, the prāṇa. The meaning is: he becomes the eater alone; in that highest state he is not eaten back by any other — "and all becomes his food." He who thus knows the true nature (yāthātmya) of prāṇa, having become the middle prāṇa standing in ādhāna and pratyādhāna, becomes the enjoyer alone, not the enjoyed; that is, he turns away from being the food.
BR_C02_S03_V01: Two indeed are the forms of Brahman: the gross (mūrta) and the subtle (amūrta), the mortal and the immortal, the stationary and the moving, the sat and the tyat.
BR_C02_S03_V01::block-0:
"The prāṇas verily are truth (satya)" — so it has been said. The upaniṣads (secret teachings) concerning the prāṇas have been expounded incidentally to the upaniṣad of Brahman, and "these are those prāṇas" too. But what is the nature of those prāṇas, and how is their truth (satyatva) to be understood? — that needs to be stated. So this brāhmaṇa is begun in order to ascertain the nature (svarūpa) of the five elements which are the satyas (true ones), and which constitute body and organs, with a view to determining, by the removal of the particular adjuncts (upādhi-viśeṣa-apanaya), through "neti neti" (BU 2.3.6), the true nature of Brahman.

There, Brahman is twofold: connected with the body and organs produced by the five elements, designated mūrta and amūrta, of mortal and immortal nature; and the form of the impressions (vāsanā) generated by these — omniscient, almighty, sopākhya (with name and feature), the locus of all transactions whose nature is action, agent, and fruit. That same Brahman, when freed from all particular adjuncts (vigata-sarva-upādhi-viśeṣa), is the object of perfect realization (samyag-darśana-viṣaya), unaging, immortal, fearless, beyond the reach of speech and mind because of non-duality (advaitatva), and is indicated by "neti neti" (BU 2.3.6).

There, the Brahman that is indicated through the method of negation (apoha-dvāra) by "neti neti" — "these two indeed" — the word vāva is used for emphatic restriction, meaning "these two alone" — "are the rūpas of Brahman, the supreme Self," rūpe being so called because by them alone the formless supreme Brahman is rendered conceivable, when they are superimposed by avidyā (avidyādhyāropyamāna). What are those two? "The gross and only the gross," and "the subtle and only the subtle" — that is the meaning. With self-qualifications implied (antarṇīta), the two — gross and subtle — are restricted to be only two.

Now, what are those qualifications of the gross and the subtle? "Mortal" — having the property of dying — "and immortal," its opposite; "and stationary" (sthita) — limited (paricchinna), staying after going (gati-pūrvaka), enduring; "and yat" — "that which goes" — pervasive (vyāpi), unlimited, opposed to the stationary; "and sat" — having a particular non-common attribute by which it is distinguished from others; "and tyat" — its opposite, ever fit to be designated only as "that" (tyat), as remote (parokṣa).
BR_C02_S03_V02: Now that which is gross is whatever is other than air and space; this is mortal, this is stationary, this is sat. Of this gross, mortal, stationary, sat, the essence (rasa) is yon one that gives heat (the sun), for he is the essence of sat.
BR_C02_S03_V02::block-0:
There the gross is qualified by four qualifications; so too the subtle. Now He divides which are the qualifications of the gross and which the others. "That, this, is the gross" — that whose parts are coalesced (mūrchitāvayava), whose parts have entered into one another, dense, compact — that is the meaning. What is that? "Whatever is other." Other than what? "Other than air and space" — than the two elements; what remains is the three elements beginning with earth. "This is mortal" — this aggregate of three elements called gross is mortal, having the property of dying. Why? Because "this is stationary"; for the limited (paricchinna), being conjoined with another thing, comes into conflict — as a pot with a pillar, wall and so on. So the gross, being stationary, limited, related to other things, becomes mortal due to the conflict with other things. "This is sat," possessed of a particular non-common attribute that distinguishes it; therefore it is limited; from being limited it is mortal; therefore gross. Or, from being gross, it is mortal; from being mortal, stationary; from being stationary, sat. Hence, on account of the non-deviation (avyabhicāra) of the four properties from one another, one may freely show the relation of qualifier and qualified, and of cause and effect, among them as one wishes. In all cases, however, the three elements qualified by the four qualifications constitute the gross form (mūrta-rūpa) of Brahman.

When one of the four qualifications is grasped, the others are eo ipso grasped. Therefore He says: "Of this gross, of this mortal, of this stationary, of this sat" — of the three elements qualified by the four qualifications — "this is the rasa," the essence. For of the three elements the most quintessential is the sun; the three elements have this for their sap, since their distinguished forms are produced by the activity of this. This is the form of the adhidaivika (cosmic) effect — that the sun, this orb that gives heat. The reason "for of sat this is the rasa" is given because the sun is gross and is the essence of these three elements. The sun himself is gross, and tapping; he is the most quintessential. The adhidaivika organ within the orb shall be spoken of later.
BR_C02_S03_V03: Now the subtle: air and space — this is the immortal, this is the moving (yat), this is the tyat. Of this subtle, of this immortal, of this moving, of this tyat, the essence is yonder Person who is in the orb (of the sun); for of tyat this is the essence. — Thus with regard to the gods.
BR_C02_S03_V03::block-0: "Now the subtle" — now the subtle is being spoken of. "Air and space" — what remains, the two elements. "This is amṛta" — because of being non-gross, of being non-stationary, hence not opposed to anything, immortal, having no property of dying. "This is yat" — opposed to the stationary, pervasive, unlimited; and since it is undivided in its specific nature from the others (anyebhyo'pravibhajyamāna-viśeṣam), "this is tyat" — fit to be designated only as "tyat," remote, as before. "Of this subtle, of this immortal, of this yat, of this tyat" — the four-qualification-bearing subtle — "this is the rasa." Who is that? "He who is yonder Person within the orb" — he who is called Hiraṇyagarbha, the prāṇa of organic nature — he is the essence of the two subtle elements as before, the most quintessential. The two subtle elements are quintessenced by this Person, for the manifestation of those two elements out of the unmanifest (avyākṛta) is for the production of the body of Hiraṇyagarbha; therefore, on account of that purpose, the two elements are essenced by him. "For of tyat this is the rasa" — since this Person, who is in the orb, is not grasped like the orb itself, and is the essence of the two elements, therefore there is similarity (sādharmya) between the Person seated in the orb and the two elements. Hence the well-known reason-construction is appropriate — "for of tyat this is the rasa."
BR_C02_S03_V03::block-1:
Some hold: the rasa is the cause; he is the conscious (cetana) Hiraṇyagarbha cognitive Self; and there it is the karman of this cognitive Self of Hiraṇyagarbha that becomes the prompter (prayoktṛ) of air and space; that karman, having air and space as its support (ādhāra), becomes the prompter of the other elements; thus by his own karman he is the prompter of air and space, and so he is called their rasa, that is, cause. — That is not so, on account of dissimilarity with the rasa of the gross; for of the three gross elements the rasa is seen to be the gross orb itself, of the same class (samānajātīya) as the three elements, not a conscious entity. So too of the two subtle elements, it is fitting that the rasa be of the same class with them, namely subtle, since the run of the passage is uniform; for as the gross and the subtle are divided as having the four properties, so the dividing of rasa and rasavat in respect of the gross and the subtle is appropriate by the same parallel reasoning, and not by half-mutilation (na tu ardha-vaiśasam).

If it be said: even with respect to the gross rasa, the conscious one with the orb as upādhi is intended — this is too little to say (atyalpam), because everywhere the gross and the subtle are intended only in the form of Brahman. If it be said: the word puruṣa is unsuitable in the case of the inert — no; for the word puruṣa is seen used for the very subtle body (liṅga) marked with wings, tail and the rest, in such passages as "Verily, being like this we shall not be able to procreate offspring; let us make these seven puruṣas one puruṣa; and they made these seven puruṣas one puruṣa" (Śata. Br. 6.1.1.3) and so on, and in another śruti the word puruṣa is applied to the annarasamaya and the rest. "Thus with regard to the gods" — this concluding statement of what has been said is for the sake of stating the division concerning the Self (adhyātma).
BR_C02_S03_V04: Now with regard to the Self (adhyātmam): this very gross is whatever is other than prāṇa and the space within the Self; this is mortal, this is stationary, this is sat. Of this gross, of this mortal, of this stationary, of this sat, the essence is the eye, for of sat this is the essence.
BR_C02_S03_V04::block-0:
Now the division of the gross and the subtle is being stated with regard to the Self (adhyātma). What is that gross? "This very thing." What is this? "Whatever is other than prāṇa" (i.e., than the air, vāyu), "and that which is the inner space within the Self" — within, in the Self, the space (ākāśa); and the prāṇa which is in the body — leaving aside these two, whatever is other, namely the three elements that build up the body. "This is mortal" and the rest is the same as before.

"Of this sat, this is the rasa" — "namely the eye."
