Of the bodily effect of the Self-aggregate, this is the essence; for by this essence, this whole body is essenced — as the orb of the sun was the rasa with regard to the gods. Also by primacy (prāthamya), since the eyes alone come into being first — "the rasa of light became fire" (BU 1.2.2) is the indication; for the eye is of the nature of light (taijasa). The three elements pertaining to the Self have this for their essence. "For of sat this is the rasa" — this is given as the reason for both grossness and being-essence.
BR_C02_S03_V05: Now the formless: prāṇa, and that which is the space within the self—this is immortal, this is moving (yat), this is reality (tyat). Of this very formless, immortal, moving (yat), real (tyat), the essence is this puruṣa who is in the right eye; for he is indeed the essence of that real (tyat). (5)
BR_C02_S03_V05::block-0: Now (atha), at present, the formless (amūrta) is being expounded. That pair of bhūtas which remained over from the previous classification, namely prāṇa (vāyu) and that ākāśa which dwells within the self, constitutes the formless. The remaining wording is to be construed as before. The essence (rasa, sāra) of this formless real (tyat) is the puruṣa in the right eye. The specification "in the right eye" is given because the seat is directly attested by śāstra; for śāstra directly attests that the liṅga (subtle body) presides especially in the right eye, since this is observed to be the consistent usage in all śrutis. The phrase "of that real (tyat) this is the essence" is to be construed as before; since no further special qualifier is taken, the purport of the reason here is precisely the formless-essence character itself.
BR_C02_S03_V06: Of this very puruṣa the form (is described): like a saffron-dyed garment, like white wool, like the indragopa insect, like a flame of fire, like a white lotus, like a sudden flash of lightning. Indeed, like a sudden flash of lightning, becomes his glory who knows thus. Now therefore the teaching: "not so, not so" (neti neti); for there is nothing higher than this "not so." Now its name: "the Reality of the real" (satyasya satyam); the prāṇas are indeed the real, and this is their Real. (6)
BR_C02_S03_V06::block-0: The division of Brahman's two upādhis—the formed (mūrta) and the formless (amūrta)—as cause and effect (kārya-karaṇa), as adhyātma and adhidaiva, both denoted by the word "satya," has now been expounded. Now we shall expound the form of this puruṣa, the liṅga (subtle body) which is the aggregate of the instruments. It consists of vāsanā—a wondrous configuration produced by the conjunction of vāsanā arising from formed and formless objects with vijñāna (cognition)—like the painted figures on a canvas, comparable to māyā, indrajāla, and the mirage, the seat of all delusion. Here the Vijñānavāda Vaināśikas, deluded, hold that just this much—a stream of cognitions—is the Self. The Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas concur in holding that this very vāsanā-form is, like the form of cloth, a guṇa of the Ātman regarded as a substance. The Sāṅkhyas hold that this triguṇa, autonomous, resting on pradhāna, exists for the sake of the Self and engages on account of puruṣārtha as cause.
BR_C02_S03_V06::block-1: Even certain ones who deem themselves Aupaniṣadas construct the following scheme. There is one heap consisting of the formed and formless (mūrtāmūrta-rāśi); a supreme heap, the Paramātman; and distinct from these a third, the middle heap—an aggregate of vidyā, karma, and prior cognition together with the agent, the experiencer, the vijñānamaya which Ajātaśatru awakened. The employer is the karma-heap; the employed instrument is the aforementioned mūrtāmūrta-bhūta-heap. In this they make a compromise with the Tārkikas. Having said that this karma-heap rests on the liṅga, then, fearing thereafter that they would fall into Sāṅkhya, they say: the entire karma-heap—just as fragrance, while resting on the flower, comes also to rest on flower-distilled oil even after separation from the flower—similarly, even when separated from the liṅga, takes recourse to a portion of the Paramātman. That portion of Paramātman, though by nature nirguṇa, becomes saguṇa by guṇa-karma that comes from elsewhere; and the vijñānātman, as agent and experiencer, is bound and liberated. Thus they also follow the Vaiśeṣika view. And this karma-heap is adventitious to the bhūta-heap, of itself nirguṇa, since it is part of Paramātman; while avidyā, arisen of itself, though non-adventitious, is, like saline soil, a non-Self property. By this construction they follow the Sāṅkhya view as well.
BR_C02_S03_V06::block-2: All of this they consider charming as a harmonization with the Tārkikas; but they do not perceive the Upaniṣadic siddhānta nor the contradiction with all reasoning. How? The defects already stated have been pointed out: if the Paramātman has parts, then saṃsāritva, woundability, and the inconsistency of traversing the locus of karma-fruit follow; if the vijñānātman is eternally distinct, oneness with the Supreme is impossible. If it be said that only the liṅga is so postulated as a metaphorical locality of the Paramātman—like the ākāśa enclosed in a pot, jar, or hollow of earth—and that even after the liṅga's dissolution, vāsanā has recourse to the Paramātman's locus, and that avidyā arises of itself like saline soil—such postulations are simply untenable. Nor can the migration of vāsanā to a substance other than its substrate be conceived even in thought. The śrutis do not admit this: "Desire, resolve, doubt" (Br. Up. 1.5.3), "In the heart alone are the forms" (Br. Up. 3.9.20), "It seems to think, it seems to move" (Br. Up. 4.3.7), "The desires that rest in his heart" (Br. Up. 4.4.7), "He has then crossed all the heart's sorrows" (Br. Up. 4.3.22), and the like. Nor is it valid to construe these śrutis as having a sense different from what is heard, since their purport is the establishment of the Self's nature as Para-Brahman, and since the entire purpose of all Upaniṣads exhausts itself in this much. Therefore those who are clever in fabricating the meanings of śruti distort the Upaniṣadic meaning. Even so, if it accorded with the Veda, let it be—I have no quarrel. But the trinity-heap (rāśitraya) view is incompatible even with "There are two forms indeed of Brahman" (Br. Up. 2.3.1). When mūrta and amūrta are forms, and the vāsanās produced thereby are the formed-formless forms, and Brahman is the third "having form," with no fourth in between—then the determination "there are only two forms of Brahman" suits. Otherwise one must postulate that they are forms of the vijñānātman, a portion of Brahman, or of the Paramātman through the medium of vijñānātman; in which case the dual-number expression "two forms only" is incongruous, and "forms" in the plural together with the vāsanās would be more apt—two as mūrta-amūrta and the vāsanās as third. If, again, it is said that mūrta and amūrta alone are the Paramātman's forms while the vāsanās belong to vijñānātman, then the formula "of the Paramātman undergoing modification through the medium of vijñānātman" becomes useless, since the vāsanā too is undifferentiated in being via the medium of the vijñānātman; and that one substance modifies another via another substance cannot be postulated in the primary sense. Nor is the vijñānātman a substance other than the Paramātman; postulating so destroys the siddhānta. Therefore, for those bewildered about the Vedic meaning, such postulations born of their own minds are extraneous to the akṣara; for the Vedic meaning is not extraneous to the akṣara, nor is anything extraneous useful for the Vedic meaning, the Veda being independent in its authority. Hence the rāśitraya postulation is incongruous.
BR_C02_S03_V06::block-3: The phrase "the puruṣa who is in the right eye" (Br. Up. 2.3.5) refers to the liṅgātman introduced in the adhyātma context, and in the adhidaiva to "that puruṣa who is in this orb" (Br. Up. 2.3.3). By the word "of him" (tasya), since the topic is taken up, that very same is taken up—he who is the essence of that formless, not the vijñānamaya. Objection: Why are these forms not those of the vijñānamaya alone, since the vijñānamaya is also the topic, and "of him" may invoke the topic? Answer: Not so, since the vijñānamaya is to be made known as formless. If these forms—saffron-dyed and the rest—belonged to the vijñānamaya, then the teaching of the vijñānamaya as inexpressible-in-form by "neti neti" (Br. Up. 2.3.6) could not stand. Objection: Perhaps the ādeśa is of a different one, not the vijñānamaya. Answer: No; for in the conclusion at the end of the sixth (chapter) the same is summed up: having introduced the vijñānamaya by "By what should one know the Knower?" (Br. Up. 4.5.15), it says "That is this: not so, not so" (Br. Up. 4.5.15). Also the pledge "I shall make known" (Br. Up. 2.1.15) thereby has its purpose. If indeed it be intended to make known the trans-empirical svarūpa of the vijñānamaya itself, with all upādhi-distinctions destroyed, then this pledge becomes meaningful: the one to whom this is made known knows the very Self as "I am Brahman," attains śāstra-niṣṭhā, and fears nothing from anywhere. But if, on the other hand, the vijñānamaya is one and "neti neti" (Br. Up. 2.3.6) refers to another, then the contrary view—"That Brahman is one, I am another"—would be apprehended; not "I have known the Self alone as 'I am Brahman'" (Br. Up. 1.4.10). Therefore these forms belong only to the puruṣa-as-liṅga referred to by "of this very (one)." And when the Real of the real, the Paramātman's svarūpa, is to be expounded, the real (satya) must first be exhaustively expounded; the vāsanās are the special forms of the satya; their forms are now stated.
BR_C02_S03_V06::block-4: These are the forms of this puruṣa, the liṅgātman under discussion. What are they? They are stated. Just as in the world, mahā-rajana means turmeric, and a garment dyed by it is māhārajana—just like such a garment in the world, so in conjunction with woman and other objects there arises in the citta a vāsanā-form of that hue, by which the puruṣa is said to be "colored," like a garment. Just as in the world there is white wool—pāṇḍu-āvika, what comes from the avi (sheep), wool and the like, and as it is whitish—so is another vāsanā-form. Just as in the world the indragopa (cochineal-like insect) is intensely red, so is its vāsanā-form. The gradation of redness depends in some cases on the particular object and in others on the cittavṛtti of the puruṣa. Just as in the world the flame of fire is luminous, so in some person at some time the vāsanā-form is. As white as a puṇḍarīka lotus, so too in someone the vāsanā-form is. As a single flash of lightning illuminates everything all around in the world, so the vāsanā-form arises in some person according to the increase of jñāna's illumination. Of these vāsanā-forms there is no determination of beginning, end, middle, number, place, time, or cause—because the vāsanās are innumerable and the causes of vāsanā are infinite. Thus he will say in the sixth: "made of this, made of that" (Br. Up. 4.4.5) and so on. Therefore the illustrations "like the saffron-dyed garment" and the rest are not for determining the form or number, but for showing the manner—of such kinds are the vāsanā-forms. As to the vāsanā-form mentioned at the end—"like a sudden flash of lightning"—it is said that of Hiraṇyagarbha emerging from the unmanifest, the manifestation occurs all at once, like a flash of lightning. That vāsanā-form belonging to him (Hiraṇyagarbha)—he who knows it has glory "like a sudden flash of lightning," "ha vai" being the words of emphasis: just so does his glory, his fame, become—as Hiraṇyagarbha's. Thus, he who knows that final vāsanā-form as stated.
BR_C02_S03_V06::block-5: Having thus exhaustively stated the svarūpa of the satya, now, for determining the very svarūpa of that which we earlier said is "the Real of the real," this teaching of Brahman is begun. Thus (atha)—after, that is, immediately after the determination of the satya's svarūpa; what is left over is the very Real of the real; therefore (ataḥ), for that reason, we shall expound the svarūpa of the Real of the real. Ādeśa means determination, of Brahman. What then is this determination? It is now stated: "Not so, not so (neti neti)"—such is the determination.
BR_C02_S03_V06::block-6: Objection: How is it that by these two words "neti neti" (Br. Up. 2.3.6) the Real of the real is sought to be determined? Answer: by the negation of all upādhi-distinctions. In that wherein no distinction exists—neither name, nor form, nor action, nor difference, nor jāti, nor guṇa—through which alone the activity of words occurs; and none of these exists in Brahman; therefore it cannot be determined as "this is that," the way one says in the world "that is a bull, it moves, it is white, it has horns." Brahman is determined through superimposed name, form, and action by such words as "Brahman is vijñāna and ānanda" (Br. Up. 3.9.28), "Brahman, the Self, is verily a mass of vijñāna" (Br. Up. 2.4.12). But when its very svarūpa, void of all upādhi-distinctions, is to be determined, then it cannot be determined in any way. Then this alone is the means: determination through the negation of any determination that may have been obtained—"neti neti" (Br. Up. 2.3.6).
BR_C02_S03_V06::block-7: And this pair of negations is for vīpsā (repetition) and vyāpti (pervasion); whatever is obtained, that is negated. When this is so, the doubt regarding Brahman's being undetermined is removed. Otherwise, by the two negations only the two topics in hand are negated; what other Brahman remains beyond the two negated topics has not been determined—"What kind is it then?"—the doubt would not cease. So the determination would be useless, since it would not remove the puruṣa's desire to know; and the sentence "I shall make Brahman known" would remain incomplete in purport. But when the desire to know along all directions, times, etc., is removed by the negation of all upādhis, then like a solid lump of salt, of one taste, a mass of prajñāna, with nothing within or without, the Real of the real—"I am Brahman"—the desire to know ceases on all sides; the prajñā stands established in the Self alone. Hence the two negations "neti neti" are for vīpsā. Objection: Having made such elaborate preparation, is it proper to determine Brahman thus? Indeed it is. Why? Because—"this not, this not"—"iti" indicates the modes of what is to be pervaded as the object of the two negations, as in "each village is delightful"—there is no other determination beyond. Hence this alone is the determination of Brahman. As stated, "its upaniṣad is the Real of the real" (Br. Up. 2.1.20)—in this manner that supreme Brahman is the Real of the real. Hence appropriately is stated the name (nāmadheya) of Brahman; nāmadheya is just nāma. What is this Real of the real? "The prāṇas are the real, and of them this is the Real."
BR_C02_S04_INTRO1::block-0: "One should worship the Self alone"; that very Ātman is the Self-truth (ātmatattva) to be sought after in all this, since dearer than son and the rest—such was the sentence advanced and its connection and purpose stated by "Knowing that very Self as 'I am Brahman,' he became all this" (Br. Up. 1.4.10). Thus the inner Self has been advanced as the subject of brahmavidyā. The subject of avidyā has likewise been set forth: beginning with "He does not know, thinking 'That is one and I am another'" (Br. Up. 1.4.10), the saṃsāra characterized by the fivefold karma based on the division of the four varṇas, with means and ends, the seed-sprout-like saṃsāra whose nature is manifest and unmanifest, consisting of name, form, and karma, summed up by "Indeed this is threefold: name, form, karma" (Br. Up. 1.6.1)—the śāstric kind characterized by elevation up to Brahmaloka, and the descent ending in the immobile, non-śāstric—was already shown by "There are two indeed" (Br. Up. 1.3.1) and so on. How, then, may one detached from this avidyā-domain qualify for the brahmavidyā concerning the inner Self?—the entire avidyā-domain has been concluded in the third (chapter). In the fourth, having introduced the inner Self as the subject of brahmavidyā by "Let me declare Brahman to you" (Br. Up. 2.1.1) and "I shall make Brahman known" (Br. Up. 2.1.1), that Brahman, one without a second, void of all distinctions, has been made known by "neti neti" (Br. Up. 2.3.6) through the negation of all bhūta-properties denoted by the word "satya" of the nature of action, agent, and fruit. As an aṅga to this brahmavidyā, sannyāsa is intended to be enjoined, since the fivefold karma characterized by wife, son, wealth, and the like, belonging to the avidyā-domain, is not the means of attaining the Self. For one means employed for another result becomes contrary; running or going is not the means of removing hunger and thirst. The śruti enjoins son and the other means as means of attaining manuṣya-loka, pitṛ-loka, and deva-loka, not as means of attaining the Self—and that with specification. Nor are they enjoined for the brahmavid, since they are heard as kāmya: "This much indeed is desire" (Br. Up. 1.4.17); the brahmavid is one of fulfilled desires, and for one of fulfilled desires, desire is impossible; and from the śruti "For us whose Self is this, this world" (Br. Up. 4.4.22).
BR_C02_S04_INTRO1::block-1: Some, however, describe even the brahmavid as connected with the eṣaṇās; but they have not heard the Bṛhadāraṇyaka. The eṣaṇās for sons and the rest belong to the non-knower's domain; in the vidyā-domain, by "For us whose Self is this, this world" (Br. Up. 4.4.22), "What shall we do with progeny?"—this division has not been heard by them as made by the śruti. Moreover, when the vidyā—whose svarūpa is the destruction of all action, agent, and fruit—is present, the contradiction characterized by the inconsistency of avidyā together with its effects has not been understood by them; nor have they heard the words of Vyāsa. The contradiction is the contrary functioning of karma and vidyā in nature, of avidyā- and vidyā-character. "There is this Vedic word: 'Perform karma, abandon karma.' What goal do they reach by vidyā? What goal by karma?" (Mokṣa-dharma 241.1.2). "This indeed I wish to hear; let your honor expound it to me. They function thus mutually opposed, contrary." To this question, the answer—"By karma the creature is bound, by vidyā he is liberated…"…
BR_C02_S04_V01: "Maitreyī!" said Yājñavalkya. "Verily, I am about to depart from this stage, dear one. Come, let me make a final settlement with you and Kātyāyanī." (1)
BR_C02_S04_V01::block-0: "Maitreyī!" said Yājñavalkya. The ṛṣi named Yājñavalkya addressed his own wife Maitreyī. "I am udyāsyan—about to go upward, to another āśrama known as pārivrājya (renunciation); 'are' is a vocative; from this gārhasthya (householder) sthāna (āśrama) I am, indeed, desirous of going upward." Therefore: "hanta"—"I seek your te (your) permission." Further: "With this second wife of yours, Kātyāyanī, let me make a final settlement (anta), an end—dividing the property; the relation that arose between you two through me as husband, that relation I would now sever by performing a division of substance; having shared the wealth between you, I shall depart."
BR_C02_S04_V02: She, Maitreyī, said: "My lord, if indeed this whole earth filled with wealth were mine, would I become immortal by it?" "No," said Yājñavalkya, "as the life of the well-equipped is, so would your life be; but of immortality there is no hope through wealth." (2)
BR_C02_S04_V02::block-0: Thus addressed, she said: "Yat"—if; "nu" indicates conjecture; "me"—mine; "this earth, bhagoḥ—lord, sarvā—the whole, encircled by the ocean, were filled with wealth—dhana—how?" "How" carries the sense of either remonstrance—"by no means"—or of inquiry. "By that karma achievable through wealth-filled-earth, the agnihotra and the like, would I become immortal?"—the connection is at a distance. Yājñavalkya replied: if "how" is taken as remonstrance, the response is concurrence: "No," said Yājñavalkya. If as inquiry, then it is the answer: "You will not at all become immortal; rather, just as in the world the life of the well-equipped (sādhana-vat) is endowed with the means and enjoyments of pleasure, so will your life be. But of immortality there is no hope, even mentally, through wealth, that is, through karma achievable by wealth."
BR_C02_S04_V03: She, Maitreyī, said: "What shall I do with that by which I do not become immortal? What the venerable one (bhagavān) knows—that alone tell me." (3)
BR_C02_S04_V03::block-0: Maitreyī said: thus addressed, Maitreyī replied: if so, then by that wealth through which I do not become immortal, what shall I do? What the venerable (bhagavān) knows alone as the means of immortality (amṛtatvasādhana), that alone, the means of immortality, tell me—me, for myself.
BR_C02_S04_V04: Yājñavalkya said: "Dear, indeed, were you to me, dear one, even before; and now you speak what is dear. Come, sit down, I shall expound (it) to you; while I expound, do you meditate (upon it)." (4)
BR_C02_S04_V04::block-0: Yājñavalkya said. Thus, when the means of immortality through wealth had been rejected, Yājñavalkya, contented at the fulfillment of his own intention, said: "Dear—iṣṭā—bata"—he said with affection—"are, Maitreyī, having previously also been dear to us, you now speak what is dear, that is, agreeable to my mind. Therefore come, āssva—sit down—I shall expound—I shall now narrate to you that ātmajñāna which is the means of immortality desired by you. While I, expounding, am narrating, do you meditate (nidididhyāsasva)—desire to fix the words by certainty as to their sense."
BR_C02_S04_V05: He said: "Verily, not for the sake of the husband is the husband dear, but for the sake of the Self is the husband dear. Verily, not for the sake of the wife is the wife dear, but for the sake of the Self is the wife dear. Verily, not for the sake of sons are sons dear, but for the sake of the Self are sons dear. Verily, not for the sake of wealth is wealth dear, but for the sake of the Self is wealth dear. Verily, not for the sake of brāhmaṇa-hood is brāhmaṇa-hood dear, but for the sake of the Self. Verily, not for the sake of kṣatra-hood is kṣatra-hood dear, but for the sake of the Self. Verily, not for the sake of the worlds are the worlds dear, but for the sake of the Self. Verily, not for the sake of the gods are the gods dear, but for the sake of the Self. Verily, not for the sake of beings are beings dear, but for the sake of the Self. Verily, not for the sake of all is all dear, but for the sake of the Self is all dear. The Self, indeed, Maitreyī, is to be seen, to be heard, to be reflected upon, to be meditated upon. Through the seeing, hearing, reflection, and knowledge of the Self, indeed, all this is known." (5)
BR_C02_S04_V06: Brahman (the brāhmaṇa class) repudiates him who knows that brāhmaṇa-class as other than the Self; the kṣatra repudiates him who knows that kṣatra as other than the Self; the worlds repudiate him who knows the worlds as other than the Self; the gods repudiate him who knows the gods as other than the Self; beings repudiate him who knows beings as other than the Self; everything repudiates him who knows the all as other than the Self. This Brahman, this kṣatra, these worlds, these gods, these beings — this all is the Self.
BR_C02_S04_V06::block-0:
Now an objection: how can one thing become known when another is known? This is no fault, replies the bhāṣya, for there is nothing whatever apart from the Self; were anything other to exist, that would not be comprehended in this knowing — but no other does exist; the Self alone is everything; therefore, when the Self is known, everything stands known.

How then is the Self itself the all? The śruti makes this heard: ब्रह्म — the brāhmaṇa-class — परादात् (would cast away, repudiate, render foreign) तं that man; whom? — yo'nyatrātmanaḥ, one who knows the brāhmaṇa-class otherwise than as the very nature of the Self, namely, who knows: "this brāhmaṇa-class is not the Self." Him that brāhmaṇa-class repudiates, as if saying: "this man views me as something whose essence is not the Self," for the Paramātman is verily the Self of all.

Likewise क्षत्रम् — the kṣatriya-class; likewise the worlds, the gods, the beings, the all. इदं ब्रह्म, idam — "this Brahman," and so on through what has just been enumerated — all of it is the Self alone, यदयमात्मा, this very Ātman that was set forth as "to be seen, to be heard" (BU 2.4.5). For from the Self all is born, into the Self alone all dissolves, and during the time of subsistence all is constituted of the Self, since nothing is apprehended apart from the Self; therefore the Self alone is all.
BR_C02_S04_V07: As, when a drum is being struck, one cannot grasp the external sounds (in isolation), but by grasping the drum, or the beating of the drum, the sound is grasped.
BR_C02_S04_V07::block-0:
How then can it now be grasped that all this is verily the Self? Since pure cit pervades everywhere, the very nature of cit is understood to be the all. To this end an illustration is offered: in the world it is observed that whatever has no separate apprehension apart from the nature of something — that thereby has the very being of that thing.

स यथा — "as" introduces the dṛṣṭānta. As in the world, of a drum or kettle (दुन्दुभेः) being struck (हन्यमानस्य) with a stick or the like, one cannot grasp (न शक्नुयात् ग्रहणाय) the bāhya śabdas — the particular sounds isolated apart from the general drum-sound — for those particulars do not exist apart from that general drum-sound. But by grasping the drum (दुन्दुभेस्तु ग्रहणेन), as the universal-cum-particular "these are drum-sounds," the particular sounds become grasped. Or, by grasping the drum-stroke (दुन्दुभ्याघातस्य) — that is, the universal sound qualified by the striking of the drum — the particulars contained in it become grasped; they cannot be apprehended on their own by any cleavage, since they have no being as separate particulars.

In the same way, in dream and waking, no object whatever is grasped apart from prajñāna; therefore it is fitting that, apart from prajñāna, those objects have no separate being.
BR_C02_S04_V08: As, when a conch is being blown, one cannot grasp the external sounds (in isolation), but by grasping the conch, or the blowing of the conch, the sound is grasped.
BR_C02_S04_V08::block-0: Likewise, स यथा शङ्खस्य ध्मायमानस्य — of a conch being blown, that is, being supplied with breath and filled, one is not able to grasp the external (isolated) sounds — and so on, all of it as before.
BR_C02_S04_V09: As, when a vīṇā is being played, one cannot grasp the external sounds (in isolation), but by grasping the vīṇā, or the playing of the vīṇā, the sound is grasped.
BR_C02_S04_V09::block-0:
Likewise, वीणायै वाद्यमानायै — "of the vīṇā being played" (vīṇāyāḥ vādyamānāyāḥ in standard form). The taking up of multiple illustrations here is to indicate the manifoldness of the universals; for there are many universals and particulars distinct in kind, both sentient and insentient.

The purpose is to show how, by a graded sequence, all are subsumed in one supreme universal, the prajñāna-ghana. Just as the universals and particulars of drum-sound, conch-sound and vīṇā-sound are subsumed in śabdatva (sound-ness), so too — at least in the time of subsistence — since the particulars are not other than the universals, the oneness of Brahman is capable of being apprehended.
BR_C02_S04_V10: As, from a fire kindled with damp fuel, manifold smokes (and sparks) issue forth, even so, O dear, of this great Being, this is the breathing forth — namely the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvāṅgirasa, the Itihāsa, the Purāṇa, the Vidyās, the Upaniṣads, the verses, the sūtras, the anuvyākhyānas, the vyākhyānas — all these are His very breathings forth.
BR_C02_S04_V10::block-0:
Thus, even at the time of utpatti (origination), prior to origination, the world is verily Brahman alone — this is comprehensible. As fire alone is the unity of fire prior to the differentiation of sparks, smoke, embers and flames, so too the world, modified into name and form, prior to its arising, is fittingly grasped as the prajñāna-ghana itself. This is what is now stated.

स यथा आर्द्रैधाग्नेः — आर्द्रैरेधोभिरिद्धोऽग्निः, the fire kindled with damp fuel; अभ्याहितात् — placed (as a sacrificial fire); पृथक् धूमाः, manifold smokes; the mention of smoke implies sparks etc. as well — smokes, sparks and the like विनिश्चरन्ति, issue forth. एवं — "so it is" — as is this dṛṣṭānta. अरे, O Maitreyī, of this Paramātman, the great Being now under discussion, this is निश्वसितम् — like an exhalation; just as a man's exhalation occurs without effort, evaṃ vai are.

What is this exhalation-like effortless production? — "the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, Atharvāṅgirasa" — the four-fold mantra-collection; इतिहास — such as the Urvaśī-Purūravas dialogue "उर्वशी हाप्सराः" (Śat. Br. 11.5.1.1) — itself a Brāhmaṇa passage; पुराणम् — "असद्वा इदमग्र आसीत्" (Tai. Up. 2.7.1) etc.; विद्या — devajana-vidyā, "vedaḥ so'yam" etc.; उपनिषदः — "प्रियमित्येतदुपासीत" (BU 4.1.3) etc.; श्लोकाः — mantras arising from Brāhmaṇa, "तदेते श्लोकाः" (BU 4.4.8) etc.; सूत्राणि — vastu-saṅgraha sentences in the Veda such as "आत्मेत्येवोपासीत" (BU 1.4.7); अनुव्याख्यानानि — explanations of mantras; व्याख्यानानि — arthavādas; or alternatively, anuvyākhyānāni are explanations of the saṅgraha-vākyas — as in the fourth adhyāya the rest of the chapter is the anuvyākhyāna of "आत्मेत्येवोपासीत" or "अन्योऽसावन्योऽहमस्मीति न स वेद यथा पशुरेवं" (BU 1.4.10); vyākhyānas are explanations of mantras. Thus the Brāhmaṇa is eight-fold.

Thus only mantra and brāhmaṇa are taken up. The Veda already exists with its fixed arrangement; its manifestation is like the breath of a man, not preceded by puruṣa-buddhi-prayatna; therefore it is independent pramāṇa in its own object. Hence what is uttered there must be received exactly as so, by those desiring the highest good of the Self — whether jñāna or karma. For the modification (vikriyāvasthā) of rūpa is in dependence on the manifestation of nāma; both nāma and rūpa, the upādhis of the Paramātman, when being differentiated, are like foam on water, indeterminable as either identical or different, and in all states constitute saṃsāra; therefore only "name" was spoken of as the niḥśvasita, since by stating that, the niḥśvasita-status of the rest is established.

Or else: it has been said that all duality is the domain of avidyā ("ब्रह्म तं परादात् … इदं सर्वं यदयमात्मा," BU 2.4.6); thereby the Veda's authority might be doubted. To dispel that very śaṅkā, this is said: like the breath of a man, since it arises without effort, the Veda is pramāṇa — not like any other treatise.
BR_C02_S04_V11: As the ocean is the one converging-place of all waters, so the skin is the one converging-place of all touches; the nostrils, of all smells; the tongue, of all tastes; the eye, of all forms; the ear, of all sounds; the mind, of all volitions (saṅkalpas); the heart, of all knowledges; the hands, of all actions; the generative organ, of all delights; the anus, of all evacuations; the feet, of all paths; speech, of all the Vedas.
BR_C02_S04_V11::block-0:
Furthermore: not only at the times of subsistence and origination is there abhāva of the world apart from prajñāna and hence its Brahman-nature; the same holds at the time of pralaya. Just as bubbles, foam and the like have no being apart from water, so all effects — name, form and action — when dissolving back into prajñāna, have no being apart from it. Therefore the one Brahman, prajñāna-ghana, of homogeneous taste, is to be apprehended.

The illustration is for showing pralaya. स यथा — "as," introducing the dṛṣṭānta. As the ocean is the one converging-place (एकायनम् = ekagamanam, ekapralayaḥ, attainment to non-distinction) of all waters in rivers, ponds and reservoirs — so त्वक् is the eka-ayana of all touches: soft, harsh, hard, slimy and the like, which are constitutive of vāyu. "त्वक्" here means the touch-object-universal, into which the particular touches enter — like waters into the ocean — and become void of being apart from it; for those particulars were only configurations of that universal.

That very general touch, denoted by the word "त्वक्," enters the saṅkalpa of mind — that is, the universal of mind's objects — like particular touches into the universal touch-object, and becomes void apart from it. Likewise, the mind-object enters the buddhi's universal-object and becomes void apart from it. Becoming mere vijñāna, it dissolves in the supreme Brahman, the prajñāna-ghana, like waters in the ocean.

Thus, by this graded sequence, when sound and the rest, together with their grasping organ (karaṇa), have dissolved in the prajñāna-ghana, then, on account of the absence of upādhi, like a saindhava-ghana (lump of salt), the prajñāna-ghana stands as one-rasa, infinite, shoreless, undivided Brahman. Therefore the Self alone is one without a second; thus is it to be known.

Likewise the nostrils are the universal-object of all gandhas (specifications of pṛthivī); the tongue, of all rasas (specifications of ap); the eye, of all rūpas (specifications of tejas); the ear, of all śabdas, as before. So all the universal-objects of ear, etc., enter the universal-object of mind, the saṅkalpa; and that, in turn, the universal-object of buddhi, mere vijñāna; and becoming mere vijñāna, that dissolves in the supreme prajñāna-ghana.

Likewise the objects of the karmendriyas — the particulars of speaking, taking, going, evacuating and delighting — enter their respective kriyā-universals and are no longer apt for differentiation, like the particular-waters in the ocean. Those universals are mere prāṇa; and prāṇa is mere prajñāna — as the Kauṣītakins recite: "yo vai prāṇaḥ sā prajñā, yā vai prajñā sa prāṇaḥ" (Kau. Up. 3.3).

Objection: throughout, only the pralaya of the viṣaya is mentioned, not of the karaṇa; what is the import? Reply: well said. But śruti regards the karaṇa as belonging to the same class as the viṣaya, not to a separate class. The karaṇa is but another configuration of the viṣaya itself, serving as its self-grasper — as a lamp is a configuration of rūpa-particulars, used as karaṇa to illumine all rūpas. So all karaṇas are alternate configurations of the very viṣaya-particulars, used to illumine those particulars themselves, like a lamp. Therefore no separate effort need be made for the pralaya of the karaṇas; since they are of the same essence as the viṣayas, by the pralaya of the viṣayas the pralaya of the karaṇas stands established.
BR_C02_S04_V12: As a lump of salt cast into water dissolves into the very water and one cannot grasp it back as before — yet from wherever one takes it up, it is verily salt — so indeed, O dear, is this great Being, infinite, shoreless, mere vijñāna-ghana. Arising from these elements, it perishes along with them; after departing there is no separate cognition (saṃjñā) — so I declare, O dear — thus indeed spoke Yājñavalkya.
BR_C02_S04_V12::block-0:
Here it had been declared: "this all is the Self" (BU 2.4.6); for that the hetus were stated — being of the nature of the Self, being born from the Self, and dissolving into the Self. Thereby, since at origination, subsistence and pralaya there is abhāva apart from prajñāna, the propositions "prajñānaṃ brahma" and "ātmaivedaṃ sarvam" have been established by reasoning.

This pralaya, the Paurāṇikas say, is svābhāvika (natural). But the buddhi-pūrvaka pralaya — the one occasioned by Brahmavidyā for the brahmavidās — that, they declare, is ātyantika (final), occurring through the cessation of avidyā; for the sake of that, this special undertaking is begun.
BR_C02_S04_V12::block-1:
Here the dṛṣṭānta is taken up: स यथा etc. सैन्धवखिल्यः — sindhoḥ vikāraḥ saindhavaḥ; the word sindhu denotes water, sindhuḥ being water from "syandanāt" ("flowing"). Saindhava is its modification or what arises in it; saindhava-cum-khilya, where khila itself is khilya (the suffix -ya in svārtha sense). Cast (प्रास्तः, prakṣiptaḥ) into water — its very source, sindhu — it dissolves along with (अनुविलीयते) the dissolving water. The hardness which the lump had acquired through contact with earth and fire departs upon contact with its own source; that departure is the udaka's vilayana, and along with that the saindhava-khilya is said to dissolve. So it is stated: "उदकमेवानुविलीयेत."

नो ह — "never" — of this khilya, उद्ग्रहणाय — for picking it up and grasping it as before — would there be the capacity, even in a most skilful person; the iva-word here is anarthaka (without separate sense) — "there is no capacity for grasping." Why? यतो यतः — from whichever region one takes up that water and tasting it (आदाय आस्वादयेत्), it is the salt-taste (lavaṇāsvāda) alone that is in the water, not the khilya-state.

As is this dṛṣṭānta, evameva vai are Maitreyī — this great Being, named Paramātman: "from this great Being, partitioned by avidyā through connection with the kāryakaraṇa-upādhi, you have come to a khilya-state, mortal, endowed with saṃsāra-dharmas of birth, death, hunger, thirst and the rest, of nāma-rūpa-kārya nature, thinking 'I belong to such-and-such lineage'; that khilya-state of yours, born of the bhrānti caused by contact with the kāryakaraṇa-upādhi, is to be cast into the great Being — your own source, like a great ocean — the Paramātman, ageless, deathless, fearless, pure, of one rasa like a saindhava-lump, prajñāna-ghana, infinite, shoreless, undivided, free from avidyā-wrought illusory bheda. Once it is so cast in, the khilya-state — swallowed by its source, the bheda-bhāva wrought by avidyā — being destroyed, this great Being remains one, non-dual."

महत् च तत् भूतं च = mahad-bhūtam, since it is greater than all (sarva-mahattaratvāt) and the cause of ākāśa and the rest; भूतम् — perfectly accomplished in all three times, since its svarūpa is unchanging — hence the niṣṭhā-suffix is taikāliko (covering all three times). Or else, the bhūta-śabda is in the sense paramārthavācī: "great-and-pāramārthika." Worldly things, though great — like the Himavān etc. produced like dream and māyā — are not paramārtha-vastu; therefore it is qualified: "this is mahat-and-bhūta."

अनन्तम् — "having no end." Lest this be construed as merely āpekṣika (relative), it is qualified: अपारम् — "shoreless." Vijñapti is vijñāna; vijñāna-cum-ghana is vijñāna-ghana; the word ghana is for the negation of any other class — like "suvarṇa-ghana" or "ayoghana"; the eva-word is for avadhāraṇa: no other class exists in the interval. If this is one, non-dual, paramārthatas pure, untainted by saṃsāra-duḥkha, what is the cause of the Self's khilya-state — "born, dead, happy, sorrowful, I, mine" and the rest, oppressed by manifold saṃsāra-dharmas? It is replied: एतेभ्यो भूतेभ्यः — these elements which have transformed into the kāryakaraṇa-viṣaya-ākāra, of nāma-rūpa nature, comparable to foam and bubbles in clean water of the Paramātman; whose dissolution into prajñāna-ghana Brahman, by the paramārtha-viveka-jñāna, has been spoken of, like rivers in the ocean. From these elements as causes, denoted by the word "satya," it arises (समुत्थाय) like a saindhava-khilya — as "sūrya-candra" arises from waters [text truncated].
BR_C02_S04_V13: She, Maitreyī, said: "Right here the venerable one has bewildered me — that there is no separate cognition after departing." He said: "Truly, O dear, I do not utter bewilderment; sufficient indeed, O dear, is this for vijñāna (true knowing)."
BR_C02_S04_V13::block-0:
Thus admonished, she — Maitreyī — said: "Right here, in this single vastu Brahman, by speaking of contradictory dharmas, the bhagavān has caused bewilderment in me" — so she states: "atraiva mā bhagavān (worship-worthy) amūmuhat (made bewildered)." How were contradictory dharmas declared by him? He first proposed "vijñānaghana eva" and then "na pretya saṃjñāsti." How can it be vijñānaghana? And how can there be no saṃjñā after departing? Fire is not at once hot and cold; therefore I am bewildered here.

स होवाच — Yājñavalkya replied: na vā are maitreyi ahaṃ mohaṃ bravīmi — "I do not utter a bewildering statement." Then how did you state contradictory dharmas — vijñānaghana, and absence of saṃjñā? Reply: I have not posited these as belonging to one and the same dharmin. You yourself, by bhrānti, have construed one vastu as endowed with contradictory dharmas; I did not say so. What I said was this: the khilya-state of the Self, which is the kāryakaraṇa-related state set forth by avidyā — when that is destroyed by vidyā, then the viśeṣa-saṃjñā occasioned by it (pertaining to the body and the rest, of the nature of seeing-as-other), being dissolved together with the kāryakaraṇa-saṅghāta-upādhi, perishes for want of cause — like the moon's reflection (and its lights) ceasing when its supports such as water are destroyed. Not that there is destruction of the paramārtha-candrāditya-svarūpa; in the same way, the asaṃsāri Brahman-svarūpa, the vijñāna-ghana, is not destroyed; that was meant by "vijñānaghana eva." That is the Self of all the world; in pāramārthika terms there is no destruction by the destruction of bhūtas; what is vināśin is only the avidyā-kṛta khilya-state, since śruti elsewhere says: "vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyam" (Chā. Up. 6.1.4).

The pāramārthika reality is this: avināśī vā are'yam ātmā. Therefore alaṃ — sufficient — vai are, this great Being, infinite, shoreless, as expounded, is for vijñātum, for full knowing; for it will be said: "na hi vijñātur vijñāter viparilopo vidyate'vināśitvāt" (BU 4.5.30 [in some recensions BU 4.3.30 / 4.5]).
BR_C02_S04_V14: For where there is duality, as it were, there one smells another, there one sees another, there one hears another, there one speaks to another, there one thinks of another, there one knows another. But where everything has become the very Self, then by what and whom should one smell, by what and whom should one see, by what and whom should one hear, by what and whom should one speak, by what and whom should one think, by what and whom should one know? By what should one know that by which all this is known—by what, O Maitreyī, should one know the Knower?
BR_C02_S04_V14::block-0:
How then is it said that after death there is no consciousness? Listen. The phrase 'where (yatra) there is duality, as it were' refers to that limited individual self which is fashioned by avidyā—a self generated through the upādhi of the aggregate of body and organs (kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta), a fragmentary form (khilya-bhāva). 'For (hi)' indicates the cause: because in Brahman, which is in truth non-dual (advaita), duality is perceived 'as it were' (iva)—as if there were another thing apart from the Self.

Objection (pūrvapakṣa): Since duality is being used in comparison, must not duality itself be real? Reply: No; for another śruti declares, 'All modification is mere name, an effort of speech' (Chā. Up. 6.1.4), and again 'One only, without a second' (Chā. Up. 6.2.1) and 'All this is just the Self' (Chā. Up. 7.25.2). Therefore, precisely because duality there appears 'as it were', the 'other' (itara) self—which is a fragment cut off, as it were, from the supreme Self—is not real, like the reflected moon in water with respect to the actual moon.

The construction 'one smells another by another' (itaro itareṇa itaraṁ jighrati) is meant to display all the kārakas: 'one' (the agent), 'by means of another' (the instrument), 'another' (the object). The verb 'jighrati' (smells) denotes both the action and its fruit, just as 'cuts' (chinatti) denotes lifting the axe, striking, and the splitting of the cleavable—all conveyed by one word, since the action terminates in its fruit and the fruit is not apprehended apart from the action. Thus 'another smeller, by another organ of smell, smells another smellable thing'—and so for the rest, ending with 'knows'. This is the state pertaining to him who is in avidyā.

But where (yatra), through brahmavidyā, avidyā has been brought to destruction, there is no other apart from the Self. 'Where verily for him' (the knower of Brahman) all name-and-form has been dissolved into the Self alone and has become the very Self—where thus everything has become the very Self—there by what instrument should one smell what smellable, who should smell? Likewise should one see, should one know? Everywhere action is accomplished only through the kārakas; hence in the absence of kārakas the action is impossible, and in the absence of action there is no fruit.

Therefore, the empirical transaction of action, factors, and fruit obtains only while avidyā exists, not for the knower of Brahman; for since all is the Self, there exists no kāraka, action or fruit apart from the Self. Nor does that which is non-Self ever become the Self for anyone. Hence non-Selfhood is fabricated by avidyā alone; in truth (paramārthatas) nothing exists apart from the Self. Therefore, when the conviction of the supreme oneness of the Self arises, the conviction of action, factors and fruit cannot stand. From this contradiction, for the knower of Brahman there is the absolute cessation (atyanta-nivṛtti) of actions and their means—the decisive turn from pravṛtti to nivṛtti.

The expression 'by what (kena) whom (kam)' is a phrase of dismissal, used to show the impossibility in every other manner: by no means whatsoever, of any kind, by anyone, of anyone, can there be smelling—this is the import. Even in the state of avidyā where another perceives another, still 'that by which all this is known—by what should one know Him?' For the instrument by which one knows is engaged with respect to the knowable; the knower's desire-to-know is directed only to the knowable, never to himself. Just as fire is not its own object, the Self cannot be its own object; and where there is no object, the knowing of the knower cannot occur. Therefore, that Knower (vijñātṛ) by whom all this is known—by what instrument and by what other could He be known? When in fact, for the knower of Brahman who has discriminated the supreme reality, the Knower alone abides, solitary and non-dual, 'that Knower, O Maitreyī, by what indeed should one know?'
BR_C02_S05_INTRO1::block-0:
What was to be expounded—namely, that means of immortality which is wholly independent of karma—was begun in the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa. That means is the knowledge of the Self, distinguished by the renunciation of all (sarva-sannyāsa) as its accessory. When the Self is known, all this becomes known; the Self is the dearest of all; therefore the Self is to be seen (draṣṭavyaḥ); and the modes of vision—'is to be heard, to be reflected upon, to be meditated upon' (śrotavyaḥ, mantavyaḥ, nididhyāsitavyaḥ)—were stated. There 'is to be heard' is by means of the teacher and scripture (āgama); 'is to be reflected upon' is by reasoning (tarka).

There too the reasoning was given: as the supporting cause for the proposition 'All this is the Self alone' (Chā. Up. 7.25.2), namely that the Self is the one common ground (eka-sāmānya), the one source of arising (eka-udbhava), and the one place of dissolution (eka-pralaya). Now an objection may be raised that this hetu—which is the Self's being the one common ground, source of origination, and place of dissolution—is unestablished (asiddha). To remove that doubt this brāhmaṇa is begun.

Since the entire world of earth and the rest, mutually serving as helper and helped, and whatever in worldly experience exists thus mutually helping is seen to be preceded by a single cause, of one common essence, with a single dissolution—therefore this world too, characterised by earth and the rest, by reason of being mutually helping and helped, deserves to be of like nature. This indeed is the meaning that is brought to light in this brāhmaṇa.

Or else, having stated as the hetu the Self's being the origin, sustenance and dissolution of the proposition 'All this is the Self' (Chā. Up. 7.25.2), the conclusion (nigamana) of the matter proposed is now drawn through the madhu-brāhmaṇa, in which scripture is principal. So indeed do the Naiyāyikas declare: 'Nigamana is the restatement of the proposition by reason of the citation of the hetu.'

Others have explained: from the section beginning with the dundubhi-illustration up to here, scripture is given for the sake of 'is to be heard'; before the madhu-brāhmaṇa, the matter of 'is to be reflected upon' is shown by demonstration of grounds; and by the madhu-brāhmaṇa the injunction of nididhyāsana itself is taught. In every way, however, just as it is settled by scripture, so it is to be reflected upon by reasoning; and just as it is judged by reasoning, that very thing, ascertained by reasoning and scripture together, is to be made the object of nididhyāsana. Hence a separate injunction of nididhyāsana would be without purpose; and therefore the separate division of contexts for śravaṇa, manana and nididhyāsana is without purpose—this is our view. In every way, the meaning of the two adhyāyas is here brought to its consummation in this brāhmaṇa.
BR_C02_S05_V01: This earth is honey (madhu) for all beings, and all beings are honey for this earth. The shining, immortal Person who is in this earth, and, with reference to the self, the shining, immortal Person who is bodily—he is just this Self, this Immortal, this Brahman, this All.
BR_C02_S05_V01::block-0:
'This earth' is the well-known earth. It is 'madhu' for all beings—for all living beings from Brahmā down to a tuft of grass: that is, it is their effect (kārya) and is like honey to them. As one cake of honey is fashioned by many bees, so this earth is fashioned by all beings. Likewise, 'all beings are madhu for this earth (pṛthivyai)'—they are the effect of this earth.

Further, the Person in this earth—'tejomaya', made of the radiance which is pure consciousness alone (cinmātra-prakāśamaya), 'amṛtamaya', of the nature of the deathless—and that adhyātma Person 'in the body' (śārīra), abiding in the body, similarly tejomaya and amṛtamaya, who is the abhimānin of the liṅga-śarīra: he too is madhu for all beings inasmuch as he serves them, and all beings are madhu for him—this is implied by the force of the connective 'ca' (and).

Thus this set of four—earth, beings, the cosmic Person in earth, the bodily Person—is one effect (eka-kārya) for all beings, and all beings are its effect; hence it has a single causal antecedent (eka-kāraṇa-pūrvakatā). Since from one cause this has come forth, that one alone is paramārthatas Brahman; the rest, being effect, is mere name—'an effort of speech, a modification, a mere name' (vāc-ārambhaṇaṁ vikāro nāmadheyam). This in brief is the meaning of all the madhu-paryāyas.

'He is just this'—the very one announced as 'all this is what this Self is' (Bṛ. Up. 2.4.6). 'This is the Immortal'—the means of immortality of which the knowledge of the Self was declared to Maitreyī, that very deathless. 'This is Brahman'—that which was introduced at the beginning of the adhyāya as 'I shall declare Brahman to thee' (Bṛ. Up. 2.1.1), 'I shall make thee know' (Bṛ. Up. 2.1.15), and the vidyā concerning which is called brahmavidyā. 'This is all'—because from the knowledge of this Brahman everything becomes (known).
BR_C02_S05_V02: These waters are honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for these waters. The shining, immortal Person who is in these waters, and, with reference to the self, the shining, immortal Person who is made of seed—he is just this Self, this Immortal, this Brahman, this All.
BR_C02_S05_V02::block-0: Likewise the waters. With reference to the self (adhyātmam), the waters have their special seat in the seed (retas).
BR_C02_S05_V03: This fire is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this fire. The shining, immortal Person who is in this fire, and, with reference to the self, the shining, immortal Person who is made of speech—he is just this Self, this Immortal, this Brahman, this All.
BR_C02_S05_V03::block-0: Likewise the fire. The fire has its special seat in speech.
BR_C02_S05_V04: This wind is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this wind. The shining, immortal Person who is in this wind, and, with reference to the self, the shining, immortal Person who is the prāṇa—he is just this Self, this Immortal, this Brahman, this All.
BR_C02_S05_V04::block-0: Likewise the wind, and adhyātmam the prāṇa. The honey-nature (madhutva) of the beings is from their being helpers as the begetters of the body; the honey-nature of those within them—the tejomaya and the rest—is from their being helpers as the instruments. Thus also it has been said: 'Of that speech, the body is the earth, the form of light is this fire' (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.11).
BR_C02_S05_V05: This sun is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this sun. The shining, immortal Person who is in this sun, and, with reference to the self, the shining, immortal Person who pertains to the eye—he is just this Self, this Immortal, this Brahman, this All.
BR_C02_S05_V05::block-0: Likewise the sun is madhu, and adhyātmam, the cākṣuṣa (the one pertaining to the eye).
BR_C02_S05_V06: These quarters are honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for these quarters. The shining, immortal Person who is in these quarters, and, with reference to the self, the shining, immortal Person who pertains to hearing and is the echo—he is just this Self, this Immortal, this Brahman, this All.
BR_C02_S05_V06::block-0: Likewise the quarters are madhu. Although hearing is the adhyātma counterpart of the quarters in general, at the moment of the answering of sound (śabda-pratiśravaṇa) it is specially present; hence adhyātmam 'prātiśrutka'—prātiśrutka means that which arises in the prati-śrutkā, namely, in the moment of the answering echo.
BR_C02_S05_V07: This Moon is the honey of all beings; of this Moon all beings are the honey. He who is this shining, immortal Person in this Moon, and, with reference to the body, he who is this shining, immortal Person identified with the mind — this very one is that which is this Self, this is the Immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
BR_C02_S05_V07::block-0: In like manner the Moon is to be construed; with reference to the body (adhyātmam), the Person identified with the mind (mānasaḥ) is intended.
BR_C02_S05_V08: This Lightning is the honey of all beings; of this Lightning all beings are the honey. He who is this shining, immortal Person in this Lightning, and, with reference to the body, he who is this shining, immortal Person identified with the lustre of the skin — this very one is that which is this Self, this is the Immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
BR_C02_S05_V08::block-0: Likewise the Lightning is to be construed; the term taijasaḥ means "that which subsists in the lustre of the skin (tvak-tejas)" — this is what is intended adhyātmam, with reference to the body.
BR_C02_S05_V09: This Thunder is the honey of all beings; of this Thunder all beings are the honey. He who is this shining, immortal Person in this Thunder, and, with reference to the body, he who is this shining, immortal Person made of sound and especially of voice — this very one is that which is this Self, this is the Immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
BR_C02_S05_V09::block-0: Likewise the Thunder. Although "that which subsists in sound" (śabde bhavaḥ śābdaḥ) is, in itself, equally adhyātmam, yet because it manifests itself in a special manner in voice (svara), it is here designated as sauvaraḥ — "that which subsists in voice" — and this is what is intended adhyātmam.
BR_C02_S05_V10: This Ākāśa is the honey of all beings; of this Ākāśa all beings are the honey. He who is this shining, immortal Person in this Ākāśa, and, with reference to the body, he who is this shining, immortal Person identified with the ākāśa within the heart — this very one is that which is this Self, this is the Immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
BR_C02_S05_V10::block-0: Likewise the Ākāśa is to be construed; with reference to the body, the ākāśa within the heart (hṛdyākāśaḥ) is intended.
BR_C02_S05_V11: This Dharma is the honey of all beings; of this Dharma all beings are the honey. He who is this shining, immortal Person in this Dharma, and, with reference to the body, he who is this shining, immortal Person identified with dharma — this very one is that which is this Self, this is the Immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
BR_C02_S05_V11::block-0:
It has been said that the host of beings beginning with earth and ending with ākāśa, together with the host of deities — being themselves the aggregate of the body and the organs (kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta-ātmānaḥ) — render service to each individual embodied being, and thereby become honey for him. But that by which they are impelled, and connected with the embodied beings, so as to render service in the form of honey — this remains to be told; and so the present passage is begun.

The text now turns to declare the cause that engages the elements and organs in their mutual ministrations: dharma (along with satya, jāti, and the inner Self), under whose impulsion alone the aggregate of body and organs operates.
BR_C02_S05_V11::block-1:
"Ayaṁ dharmaḥ" — although dharma is itself imperceptible (apratyakṣaḥ), yet, because of its perceptible effect produced by it, it is referred to by the demonstrative "this" (ayam), as though it were perceptible — "this dharma" — just like a perceptible object. Dharma has already been expounded as that which is characterised by śruti and smṛti (śruti-smṛti-lakṣaṇaḥ), as the regulator even of the kṣatriya class and others (kṣattrādīnām api niyantā), as the producer of the variety of the world (jagato vaicitryakṛt), since it is the cause of the transformations of earth and the rest (pṛthivyādīnāṁ pariṇāma-hetutvāt), and as that whose form is the observances performed by living beings (prāṇibhir anuṣṭhīyamāna-rūpaḥ); on this account it is referred to demonstratively as "this dharma."

In the section dealing with śāstra and ācāra, satya and dharma were indicated without distinction (abhedena nirdeśaḥ), as being respectively characterised by śāstra and by ācāra; but here, even though there is essential oneness, they are designated separately (bhedena vyapadeśaḥ), because, in the form of seen and unseen (dṛṣṭa-adṛṣṭa-bheda-rūpeṇa), they initiate effects of different kinds.

That dharma which is unseen (adṛṣṭaḥ), called apūrva, initiates its effect under an unseen form, in two aspects — general and particular (sāmānya-viśeṣa-ātmanā). In its general form (sāmānya-rūpeṇa) it is the impeller of earth and the rest; in its particular form (viśeṣa-rūpeṇa) it is the impeller of the aggregate of body and organs adhyātmam. There, in dharma considered as the impeller of earth and the rest, dwells "the shining, immortal Person in this dharma"; and likewise, in the dharma which is the agent producing the aggregate of body and organs adhyātmam, dwells the dhārmaḥ — "that which subsists in dharma."
BR_C02_S05_V12: This Satya (Truth) is the honey of all beings; of this Satya all beings are the honey. He who is this shining, immortal Person in this Satya, and, with reference to the body, he who is this shining, immortal Person identified with truth — this very one is that which is this Self, this is the Immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
BR_C02_S05_V12::block-0:
Likewise that same dharma, when, in its seen aspect, it is being performed in the form of conduct (dṛṣṭena anuṣṭhīyamānena ācāra-rūpeṇa), comes to be called satya; thus it is dharma itself in another mode. This too is of two kinds, in the form of general and particular (sāmānya-viśeṣa-ātma-rūpeṇa) — the general inhering in earth and the rest (pṛthivyādi-samaveta), the particular inhering in the aggregate of body and organs (kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta-samaveta).

There, that which subsists in the satya inhering in earth and the rest as the form of present action (vartamāna-kriyā-rūpe satye), and likewise that which subsists adhyātmam in the satya inhering in the aggregate of body and organs, is the sātyaḥ — "that which subsists in satya"; as another śruti declares, "By satya the wind blows" (Tai. Nā. 2.1: satyena vāyur āvāti).
BR_C02_S05_V13: This Mānuṣa (the human kind) is the honey of all beings; of this Mānuṣa all beings are the honey. He who is this shining, immortal Person in this Mānuṣa, and, with reference to the body, he who is this shining, immortal Person identified with humanity — this very one is that which is this Self, this is the Immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
BR_C02_S05_V13::block-0: This particular aggregate of body and organs (kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta-viśeṣaḥ), set in motion by dharma and satya, becomes joined to a particular generic class (jāti-viśeṣa); that generic class is the human and the rest (mānuṣa-ādiḥ). All hosts of living beings are seen acting as mutual benefactors and beneficiaries (parasparopakāryopakāraka-bhāvena) only as qualified by the generic class "man" and so on. Hence the generic class "man" and the rest is also the honey of all beings. There too, this generic class — "man" and the rest — is fit to be designated in both modes: as outward (bāhyā) and as pertaining to the body (ādhyātmikī).
BR_C02_S05_V14: This Self is the honey of all beings; of this Self all beings are the honey. He who is this shining, immortal Person in this Self, and he who is this Self that is shining and immortal — this very one is that which is this Self, this is the Immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
BR_C02_S05_V14::block-0:
That aggregate of body and organs which is qualified by the generic class "man" and the rest — that itself, here called "this Self" (ayam ātmā), is the honey of all beings.

Objection (pūrvapakṣa): Is this not simply the same as that which was previously denoted by the word "the embodied one" (śārīra-śabdena nirdiṣṭaḥ), under the head of earth (pṛthivī-paryāyaḥ)?

Reply (siddhānta): No; for there only the earthen portion (pārthiva-aṁśasya eva) was taken into account. Here, on the contrary, the aggregate of body and organs that is meant is one which has the nature of all (sarvātmā), in which all particular distinctions of adhyātma, adhibhūta, adhidaiva and the rest have ceased (pratyastamita-adhyātma-adhibhūta-adhidaiva-ādi-sarva-viśeṣaḥ), and which is qualified by the entire host of beings and deities (sarva-bhūta-devatā-gaṇa-viśiṣṭaḥ) — this is what is called "this Self."

In this Self, then, is set forth the shining, immortal Person, the formless essence (amūrta-rasaḥ) which is the Self of all (sarvātmakaḥ); whereas in the case of earth and the rest he was set forth only partially (ekadeśena), since there no specific adhyātma was at issue, and hence he was not set forth in this comprehensive sense. And that which now remains over — the one made of vijñāna (vijñānamayaḥ), for whose sake alone this aggregate of body and subtle marks exists — that is the one designated in the words "He who is this Self."

Thus, by this final summing up, the Self is shown to be Brahman alone — the goal in which the entire honey-doctrine (madhu-vidyā) culminates.
BR_C02_S05_V15: Verily this Self is the sovereign of all beings, the king of all beings. Just as in the hub and the felly of a chariot all the spokes are fixed, so in this Self are fixed all beings, all gods, all worlds, all prāṇas and all these selves.
BR_C02_S05_V15::block-0:
The Self into whom, in the closing portion as that which remains over and is of the nature of pure cognition (vijñānamaya), the seeker was made to enter — this is that very Self. When that which is conditioned by the body-and-organ aggregate fashioned by avidyā has been led, by Brahman-knowledge, into the Paramātman, then that very same Self, spoken of as without an interior or an exterior, the entire mass of cognition (prajñāna-ghana), the very ātman just indicated in the previous portion as "luminous" and the rest, the knowing Self (vijñānātmā), the knower — this is the Self of all beings, to be worshipped by all, the over-lord (adhipati) of all beings, the independent ruler of all, not in the manner of a prince or a minister; rather, he is the king of all beings. The qualifier of kingship is "adhipati": some person becomes a king by adopting a king-befitting conduct yet is not the supreme lord, hence Śaṅkara distinguishes him by "adhipati." Thus the knower of Brahman, the Self of all beings, becomes liberated.

What was said earlier — "By Brahman-knowledge men hope to become the All; what then did that Brahman know by which it became all this?" (Bṛ. U. 1.4.9) — that very thing has now been expounded thus: having heard, through the teacher and the scripture, that the Self alone is verily the Self of all, having reflected upon it through reasoning, and having directly realised it as the Madhu-brāhmaṇa has set forth — therefore, even prior to such Brahman-realisation, what was Brahman alone had become non-Brahman through avidyā, and what was the All alone had become non-all. But that very avidyā being dispelled by this realisation, the knower of Brahman, being Brahman alone, became Brahman; being all, he became all.

The purport of the śāstra, for which the discourse was undertaken, is now complete. To the effect that in this Self of all, in the all-Self knower of Brahman, the entire universe is fixed, an illustration is offered: "Just as in the hub and felly of a chariot all the spokes are fixed" — the meaning is well known. Even so, in this Self that has become the supreme Self, in the knower of Brahman, are fixed all beings from Brahmā down to the tuft of grass, all gods such as Agni and the rest, all worlds such as bhūḥ and the rest, all prāṇas such as speech and the rest, and all these selves which, like the moon reflected in waters, enter into each separate body — all these are fashioned by avidyā; the entire universe is fixed in him.

What was said before, that the knower of Brahman Vāmadeva realised "I was Manu, I was the Sun" (Bṛ. U. 1.4.10) — this very state of being the Self of all has now been explained. The knowing Brahman-knower, having all upādhis as his, becomes the Self of all and becomes everything; bereft of upādhis and of all designations, without an interior or an exterior, the entire mass of cognition, unborn, undecaying, immortal, fearless, motionless, of the form indicated by neti-neti, neither gross nor minute — such are his attributes. Not knowing this very purport, certain logicians and others who deem themselves learned, even āgama-knowers, fancying the meaning of the śāstra to be self-contradictory and giving rise to alternatives, fall into bottomless delusion. This very purport these two mantras restate: "Unmoving, one, swifter than the mind" (Īś. U. 4), "It moves, it does not move" (Īś. U. 5). So too in the Taittirīyaka, "Than which there is nothing higher and nothing other" (Tai. Nā. 10.4), "Singing this sāman he sits: I am food, I am food, I am food" (Tai. U. 3.10.6) and the like. So also in the Chāndogya: "Eating, sporting, taking delight" (Chā. U. 8.12.3), "If he desires the world of the fathers" (Chā. U. 8.2.1), "Of all odours, of all tastes" (Chā. U. 3.14.2), "Omniscient, all-knowing" (Mu. U. 1.1.9) and so on.
BR_C02_S05_V15::block-1:
The Brahman-knowledge, which is the means of immortality and which Maitreyī sought from her husband saying "That alone, sir, by which the venerable one knows the means of immortality, that please tell to me" (Bṛ. U. 2.4.3), is now brought to completion. To extol this very Brahman-knowledge the present narrative has been introduced. To exhibit the purport of that narrative in brief, these two mantras occur. For thus, being praised by the mantra and the brāhmaṇa together, the standing of Brahman-knowledge as the means of immortality and of the attainment of all is laid bare and brought upon the royal road — like the rising sun dispelling the darkness of night.

Moreover, Brahman-knowledge is praised in this manner: that which is guarded by Indra is hard to obtain even for the gods; for even by the two Aśvins, the physicians of the gods, this Indra-guarded knowledge was obtained only with vast effort — by severing the Brāhmaṇa's head, fixing on him a horse's head, and when that was severed by Indra, again restoring his own head, and through that restored head the entire Brahman-knowledge was heard from the Brāhmaṇa himself; since beyond it no means of human end has been, will be, or is now, there can be no praise higher than this. Further, Brahman-knowledge is extolled thus: in the world it is well known that action is the means to all human ends, and that action is to be accomplished by wealth, so by it there is not even hope of immortality; but that very immortality is attained by Self-knowledge alone, independent of action. For although fitting to be spoken of in the action-section, it has been declared in the pravargya-section, having been lifted out of the action-section because of being opposed to action, accompanied solely by renunciation, for the sake of immortality — therefore there is no means of human end higher than this.

Further, Brahman-knowledge is praised thus: the whole world delights in pairs of opposites, as the śruti says, "Verily he did not delight; therefore one who is alone does not delight" (Bṛ. U. 1.4.3); but Yājñavalkya, common though he was with the world, by the strength of Self-knowledge abandoned the saṃsāra-relish in wife, sons, wealth and the rest, and became one satisfied with knowledge, delighting in the Self alone. Further, Brahman-knowledge is praised thus: in that Yājñavalkya, even while rising up out of the path of saṃsāra, declared it to his beloved wife purely for her sake — as is indicated by the words "You speak what is dear; come and sit" (Bṛ. U. 2.4.4).
BR_C02_S05_V16: This indeed is that madhu which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa declared to the two Aśvins. Beholding it the seer spoke: "O Heroes, I make manifest for you that fierce deed of yours done for gain, like the thunder that reveals the rain — that madhu which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa declared to you both through the head of a horse."
BR_C02_S05_V16::block-0:
There we have said that this narrative is by way of praise. Now what is that narrative? It is now told. "Idam" — "this" — points to what has just been mentioned, since it is present in the intellect. The word "vai" is for recollection. "Tat" — that which was accomplished as a narrative and was uttered in another section, being remote, is here pointed out by means of the recollective "vai." What was indicated in the pravargya-section but not made manifest as the madhu, that very madhu has been pointed out here just now in the section beginning "This earth" (Bṛ. U. 2.5.11).

How was it indicated there in the other section? Thus: "Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa declared to these two the Brāhmaṇa called Madhu. That is their dear abode; by this very thing he reaches it. He said: 'I have been told by Indra: if you declare this to anyone else, on that very account I shall sever your head.' Therefore I am afraid that he might cut off my head; on this account I cannot teach you. They said: 'We will protect you from him.' 'How will you protect me?' 'When you receive us as pupils, we shall first cut off your head and place it elsewhere; then we shall fetch a horse's head and fix it on you. Through that you will teach us. When you teach us, then Indra will sever that head of yours; and then we shall fetch your own head and fix it on you again.' 'So be it,' he said, and accepted them as pupils. Having accepted them, they cut off his head and placed it elsewhere; they fetched a horse's head and fixed it on him. Through that he taught them. While he was teaching them, Indra severed his head; then they fetched his own head and fixed it on him." Only so much of the madhu as is a limb of the pravargya-rite was spoken of there, not that called Self-knowledge which is the secret. The narrative spoken of there is here exhibited as praise.

"This indeed is that madhu which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa, in this fashion, declared to the two Aśvins. Beholding this, the seer" — that is, beholding this very deed, the seer-mantra — "declared." How? "That deed (daṃsa)" — to be construed with what follows — "daṃsa" being the name of an action; what kind of deed? "Fierce, cruel, that of you both, O Heroes" — for the Aśvins are man-formed; for what purpose? "For gain (sanaye), for profit" — even in the world a person greedy of profit performs a cruel deed, and so they are seen to act as in the world. "That do I make manifest, do I disclose" — what was done by you both in secret. Like what? "Like the thunder, the cloud" — "na," upper-positioned, is here a particle of comparison in the Veda, not of negation, just as "aśvaṃ na" means "like a horse" (Ṛ.S. 1.6.24.1); "like the thunder reveals the rain through thunder-claps and the like" — even so do I make manifest your fierce deed.

Objection: How can these two mantras be praises of the Aśvins, since they are words of censure? Reply: This is no defect; this is itself praise, not censure. Since you both, even doing such an exceeding cruel deed, do not lose so much as a hair — that is, lose nothing — these two are praises. The worldly remember censure as praise; thus a censure shaped as praise is well known in the world. "Dadhyañc by name, an Ātharvaṇa" — "ha" is a meaningless particle.
BR_C02_S05_V17: This indeed is that madhu which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa declared to the two Aśvins. Beholding it the seer spoke: "O Aśvins, you set upon Dadhyañc the Ātharvaṇa a horse's head; faithful to truth he declared to you both that madhu of Tvaṣṭṛ, and likewise the secret one, O destroyers."
BR_C02_S05_V17::block-0:
"This indeed is that madhu" and so on, as before, is for displaying another mantra. Likewise this other mantra follows the same narrative. "The Ātharvaṇa Dadhyañc by name" — since there are other Ātharvaṇas, Śaṅkara distinguishes him: "Dadhyañc by name, an Ātharvaṇa." "To him, to Dadhyañc the Ātharvaṇa, O Aśvins" — these are the words of the mantra-seer. "A horse's (aśvya) — belonging to a horse — head, having severed the Brāhmaṇa's head and severed the horse's head, having performed such an exceedingly cruel deed, you two set on him the horse's head — directed it toward the Brāhmaṇa." And that Ātharvaṇa "declared (pra-vocat) to you both that madhu" — what he had earlier promised: "I shall declare it."

Why did he declare thus, even raising the doubt of his life? It is now told: "Faithful to truth (ṛtāyan)" — desiring to safeguard the truth that had earlier been promised; for the safeguarding of the dharma of truth is heavier even than life — this is its mark. What is the madhu that he declared? It is now stated: "Tvāṣṭra (of Tvaṣṭṛ)," Tvaṣṭṛ being the Sun, that which is connected with him; the head of the sacrifice, severed, became Tvaṣṭṛ; for the rejoining of that, the pravargya rite was instituted, and the knowledge that is the limb of the pravargya rite is the Tvāṣṭra madhu — that vision concerning the severing and rejoining of his head, that is the Tvāṣṭra madhu. "O destroyers (dasrau)" — destroyers of enemies' forces, slayers of foes.

Moreover, not only the Tvāṣṭra madhu connected with the rite did he declare to you; he further declared the secret (kakṣya), the hidden, the esoteric, the knowledge connected with the supreme Self, the madhu that is set forth in the Madhu-brāhmaṇa, the madhu illumined by these two adhyāyas — that too "he declared to you both," the verb being supplied.
BR_C02_S05_V18: This indeed is that madhu which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa declared to the two Aśvins. Beholding it the seer spoke: "He fashioned bodies of two-footed creatures, he fashioned bodies of four-footed creatures. Becoming first a bird, the Puruṣa entered into the bodies." Verily this Puruṣa, dwelling in all the cities, lies couched in the city; by him is nothing uncovered, by him is nothing unenclosed.
BR_C02_S05_V18::block-0:
"This indeed is that madhu" and so on, as before. The two mantras spoken so far conclude the narrative connected with the pravargya. The purport of the two adhyāyas dealing with the pravargya rite has been illumined by the two mantras taking the form of a narrative. The purport of the two adhyāyas concerning Brahman-knowledge has now to be illumined by the following two ṛks — therefore the text proceeds.

It was said that the Ātharvaṇa declared the secret madhu to you both. What is that madhu? It is now told: "He fashioned the cities (puraḥ-cakre)" — bodies as cities. From this beginning is the procedure of the differentiation of the undifferentiated: that very Parameśvara, while differentiating name and form which were unmanifest, having first created the worlds bhūḥ and the rest, fashioned (cakre) the bodies of two-footed creatures, those marked by two feet — human and bird bodies; likewise he fashioned the bodies of four-footed creatures, those marked by four feet, the bodies of cattle. "Puraḥ-purastāt" — first, before, that Īśvara, becoming a bird (the subtle body, liṅga-śarīra), entered into the bodies. The śruti explains the meaning of "the Puruṣa entered" thus: "Verily this Puruṣa is in all the cities, in all bodies, the puriśaya — the one who lies (śayanaṃ) in the city (puri) is called puruṣa. Nothing whatsoever is uncovered (anāvṛta) by him; likewise nothing whatsoever is unenclosed (asaṃvṛta) by him" — not entered into within. By an outer being and by an inner being it is not uncovered.

Thus he himself, in the form of name and form, with the inside-outside aspect, in the form of body-and-organ, abides established. The mantra beginning "He fashioned the cities" briefly states the oneness of the Self — that is the meaning.
BR_C02_S05_V19: This indeed is that madhu which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa declared to the two Aśvins. Beholding it the seer spoke: "For each form he became its counterpart; that of his is the form for being recognised. Indra, by his māyās, goes about as multi-formed, for his bays are yoked, ten times a hundred." Verily he is the bays, he is the ten and the thousands, the many and the infinite. This is that Brahman without an antecedent, without a subsequent, without an interior, without an exterior. This Self is Brahman, the all-experiencing — such is the teaching.
BR_C02_S05_V19::block-0:
"This indeed is that madhu" and so on, as before. "For each form he became its counterpart" — for each form, he became the counterpart, that is, he became another form. The counterpart (pratirūpa) is conformable: of whatever shape mother and father are, of that very shape, conformable to them, the son is born; for one with four feet is not born from one with two feet, nor one with two feet from one with four. He himself, the supreme Lord, while differentiating name and form, became the counterpart of each form. Why this assuming of counterpart-form on his part? It is now told: "That, of this Self, is the form for the sake of recognition (pratickṣaṇa) — for being made known." If name and form were not differentiated, then the form of this Self, devoid of upādhi and called the entire mass of cognition, would not be recognised; but when name and form become differentiated as body and organ, then his form is recognised.

"Indra (the supreme Īśvara) by māyās" — by cognitions, by the false notions wrought by name, form, and elements, but not in truth — "is multi-formed, is gone after as many-formed," though he is one in form, the very mass of cognition, by reason of avidyā-cognitions. From what cause?
