"Yoked, like horses to a chariot, for the manifestation of their respective objects, indeed, are his bays (harayaḥ) — those that carry off, namely the senses; ten hundreds, that is a thousand — and ten — by reason of the manifoldness of creatures' divisions, they are ten hundreds and ten." Therefore, by reason of the manifoldness of senses-and-objects, they are yoked only for the manifestation of those objects, not for the manifestation of the Self; for the Kāṭhaka says: "The Self-existent pierced the openings outward" (Ka. U. 2.1.1). Therefore by these very forms of objects he is moved after, not by the form of his own self-rasa as the entire mass of cognition.

Thus, then, the supreme Īśvara is one and the bays another — to one who concludes thus, the answer is given: "Verily he is the bays, he is the ten and the thousands, the many and the infinite," because of the infinitude of creatures' divisions. What more? "This is that Brahman who is the Self, apūrva — there is no cause prior to him, hence apūrva; anapara — there is no effect later than him, hence anapara; anantara — there is no kind in the interval between, hence anantara; likewise abāhya — there is nothing outside him, hence abāhya." What again is that uninterrupted Brahman? "This Self." Who is that? "He who is the inmost Self — the seer, hearer, thinker, cogniser, knower, sarvānubhū — by being the Self of all he experiences all, hence sarvānubhū" — such is the teaching, the instruction of all the Vedānta. This is the consummated meaning of all the Vedāntas; this is the immortal, the fearless; the meaning of the śāstra is concluded.
BR_C02_S06_V01: Now the line: Pautimāṣya from Gaupavana, Gaupavana from Pautimāṣya, Pautimāṣya from Gaupavana, Gaupavana from Kauśika, Kauśika from Kauṇḍinya, Kauṇḍinya from Śāṇḍilya, Śāṇḍilya from Kauśika and Gautama, Gautama —
BR_C02_S06_V02: From Āgniveśya, Āgniveśya from Śāṇḍilya and from Ānabhimlāta; Ānabhimlāta from Ānabhimlāta, Ānabhimlāta from Ānabhimlāta, Ānabhimlāta from Gautama, Gautama from Saitava and Prācīnayogya, Saitava and Prācīnayogya from Pārāśarya, Pārāśarya from Bhāradvāja, Bhāradvāja from Bhāradvāja and from Gautama, Gautama from Bhāradvāja, Bhāradvāja from Pārāśarya, Pārāśarya from Baijavāpāyana, Baijavāpāyana from Kauśikāyani, Kauśikāyani —
BR_C02_S06_V03: From Ghṛtakauśika, Ghṛtakauśika from Pārāśaryāyaṇa, Pārāśaryāyaṇa from Pārāśarya, Pārāśarya from Jātūkarṇya, Jātūkarṇya from Āsurāyaṇa and Yāska, Āsurāyaṇa from Traivaṇi, Traivaṇi from Aupajandhani, Aupajandhani from Āsuri, Āsuri from Bhāradvāja, Bhāradvāja from Ātreya, Ātreya from Māṇṭi, Māṇṭi from Gautama, Gautama from Gautama, Gautama from Vātsya, Vātsya from Śāṇḍilya, Śāṇḍilya from Kaiśorya Kāpya, Kaiśorya Kāpya from Kumārahārita, Kumārahārita from Gālava, Gālava from Vidarbhīkauṇḍinya, Vidarbhīkauṇḍinya from Vatsanapāt Bābhrava, Vatsanapāt Bābhrava from Pathin Saubhara, Pathin Saubhara from Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, Ayāsya Āṅgirasa from Ābhūti Tvāṣṭra, Ābhūti Tvāṣṭra from Viśvarūpa Tvāṣṭra, Viśvarūpa Tvāṣṭra from the two Aśvins, the two Aśvins from Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa, Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa from Atharvan Daiva, Atharvan Daiva from Mṛtyu Prādhvaṃsana, Mṛtyu Prādhvaṃsana from Pradhvaṃsana, Pradhvaṃsana from Ekarṣi, Ekarṣi from Vipracitti, Vipracitti from Vyaṣṭi, Vyaṣṭi from Sanāru, Sanāru from Sanātana, Sanātana from Sanaga, Sanaga from Parameṣṭhin, Parameṣṭhin from Brahman. Brahman is self-born. Salutation to Brahman!
BR_C02_S06_V03::block-0: Now, in this place, the line of teachers (vaṃśa) of the Madhu-kāṇḍa, which has Brahman-knowledge as its theme, is given by way of praise of that very Brahman-knowledge. This mantra, moreover, serves the purpose of self-study (svādhyāya) and of repetition (japa). Therein "vaṃśa" — "line" — is so called by analogy with a bamboo-stem: as the bamboo (vaṃśa) is jointed knot by knot, even so this line, from the top down to the reaching of the root. The line is the order of the succession of teachers of the four adhyāyas. Therein the one who stands in the nominative (prathamānta) is the disciple, the one in the ablative (pañcamyanta) is the teacher. Parameṣṭhin is Virāṭ; he is from Brahman, that is, from Hiraṇyagarbha; beyond that there is no further line of teachers. As for Brahman itself, that is eternal, self-born; to that Brahman, the self-born, salutation!
BR_C03_S01_INTRO1::block-0:
The Yājñavalkīya-kāṇḍa beginning with "Janako ha Vaideha" is now commenced. Although it shares its purport with the preceding Madhu-kāṇḍa, since the present section is predominantly devoted to reasoning (upapatti-pradhāna), there is no fault of repetition. The Madhu-kāṇḍa, after all, is predominantly āgamic (āgama-pradhāna). Āgama and upapatti, when joined and engaged in revealing the oneness of the Ātman, are able to display it like a bilva-fruit placed in the palm. For it has been said, "He is to be heard about, to be reflected upon" (Bṛ. Up. 2.4.5). Therefore, for ascertaining the very meaning of āgama after subjecting it to examination, this Yājñavalkīya-kāṇḍa, predominantly upapatti-based, is begun.

The narrative (ākhyāyikā), however, is either intended to praise the knowledge or to enjoin a means thereto. For dāna is a means well-known to the wise and seen in the śāstras: through gifts living beings are won over. Here also great wealth and the gift of a thousand cows are noted. Hence, by a śāstra whose principal purport lies elsewhere, the narrative has been undertaken in order to display dāna as a means to the attainment of vidyā. Furthermore, association with the knowers thereof and engaging them in dialogue is, as seen in nyāya-vidyā, a means to attaining knowledge; and that is shown forcefully in this adhyāya. The growth of insight upon association with the wise is also directly perceptible. Therefore, the narrative is solely for the purpose of displaying the means to the attainment of vidyā.
BR_C03_S01_V01: Oṁ. Janaka of Videha performed a sacrifice with abundant gifts. There the brāhmaṇas of the Kurus and Pañcālas had assembled. Janaka of Videha had a desire to know: "Who among these brāhmaṇas is the most learned?" He penned in a thousand cows; ten pādas of gold were tied to the horns of each, five on each horn.
BR_C03_S01_V01::block-0:
Janaka by name was a sovereign king of the Videhas; one born among them is Vaideha. He performed a yajña with abundant gifts (bahu-dakṣiṇa) — either a yajña called bahu-dakṣiṇa, well-known in another śākhā, or the aśvamedha, here called bahu-dakṣiṇa because of the abundance of its dakṣiṇās. By that he sacrificed (īje, ayajat). At that yajña the brāhmaṇas of the Kuru and Pañcāla countries — among whom an abundance of the learned is well-known — having been invited or desirous of witnessing, came together (abhi-sametāḥ).

Seeing such a great gathering of the learned, the yajamāna Janaka of Videha had a desire to know in particular, "Who, indeed, here is the most knowing of Brahman (brahmiṣṭha)?" — this was his vijijñāsā. How? "Who, pray, of these brāhmaṇas is the most anūcāna? All these are anūcānas, but who, pray, of these is anūcāna in the fullest measure?" He, having had this curiosity arise concerning the most anūcāna, in order to ascertain it penned in a thousand cows in their first prime (prathama-vayas), causing them to be confined in the cow-pen. Of what description were these confined cows? It is said: a pāda is a quarter-pala of gold; ten pādas were tied to the horns of each cow, five each on each horn.
BR_C03_S01_V02: He said to them, "Honoured brāhmaṇas, whoever among you is the most knowing of Brahman, let him drive away these cows." Those brāhmaṇas did not dare. Then Yājñavalkya said to his own brahmacārin, "Sāmaśrava, drive these away, dear one." He drove them away. The brāhmaṇas grew angry: "How can he say of us that he is the most knowing of Brahman?" Now Aśvala, the hotṛ of Janaka of Videha, was there. He asked him, "Are you, Yājñavalkya, the most knowing of Brahman among us?" He replied, "We bow to him who is most knowing of Brahman; we are simply desirous of cows." Then the hotṛ Aśvala resolved to question him on that very score.
BR_C03_S01_V02::block-0:
Having thus penned the cows, he addressed those brāhmaṇas: "O honoured brāhmaṇas" — invoking them — "whoever of you is the most knowing of Brahman (brahmiṣṭha) — all of you are brāhmaṇas, but who among you is brāhmaṇa in the fullest measure — let him drive these cows away (udajatām), let him take them off toward his own house." The brāhmaṇas did not dare (na dadhṛṣuḥ): being addressed thus, those brāhmaṇas were not bold to declare their own brahmiṣṭha-hood, were not forward (na pragalbhāḥ).

When the brāhmaṇas had become non-forward, then Yājñavalkya said to his own — that is, his own — brahmacārin, his disciple (antevāsin): "Drive (udaja) these cows toward our house, O dear one (somya), O Sāmaśrava" — for he listens to the rules of the Sāman; thus by implication Yājñavalkya is one who knows all four Vedas. He drove (udācakāra) the cows toward the ācārya's house. Since by accepting the wager of the brahmiṣṭha Yājñavalkya had implicitly declared his brahmiṣṭha-hood, the brāhmaṇas grew angry (cukrudhuḥ).

The purport of their anger is stated: "How can he say of us — each of whom is preeminent — that he is brahmiṣṭha?" Now, with the brāhmaṇas thus enraged, the hotṛ — the ṛtvik — of the yajamāna Janaka, Aśvala by name, was there (babhūva, āsīt). He, prideful of his being brahmiṣṭha and emboldened by the king's patronage, questioned (papraccha) Yājñavalkya. How? "Are you, indeed, O Yājñavalkya, brahmiṣṭha among us?" The pluti (lengthening of the vowel) is for reproach.

Yājñavalkya replied: "We bow to him who is brahmiṣṭha; for the moment we are merely desirous of cows." Aśvala, the hotṛ, then having his mind set on questioning him, since by his very acceptance of the wager of brahmiṣṭha he had taken on the claim, resolved (dadhre, dhṛtavān manaḥ) to question him on that very ground.
BR_C03_S01_V03: He said, "Yājñavalkya, since all this is enveloped by death, all this is overpowered by death — by what means does the yajamāna become wholly liberated from the grasp of death?" "By the hotṛ priest, by fire, by speech. For verily speech is the hotṛ of the yajña; that which is this speech is yonder fire — that is the hotṛ; that is liberation, that is full liberation."
BR_C03_S01_V03::block-0:
"Yājñavalkya," said he. There, in the Madhu-kāṇḍa, the yajamāna's escape from death by the five-membered karma joined with darśana (jñāna) was concisely explained in the Udgītha-prakaraṇa. The present extensive treatment is begun for the sake of particularizing the darśana included therein, this being the very subject of investigation. "This entire body of means belonging to the karma — the ṛtvik, fire, etc. — is enveloped (āptam, vyāptam) by death in the form of karma along with the inherent attachment, and not merely enveloped but overpowered (abhipannam) — brought into death's sway. By what means in the form of darśana does the yajamāna become wholly liberated from the grasp of death (mṛtyor āptim atimucyate) — that is, going beyond the range of death, becomes free, no longer subject to death?"

Objection: But it has been said in the Udgītha itself that one is wholly liberated by the contemplation of mukhya-prāṇa as Ātman. Reply: True — that has been said. But there is a particular not stated there; the present commencement is for that purpose, hence no fault. Yājñavalkya replies, "By the hotṛ ṛtvik, by Agni, by Speech." He explains the meaning: Who is the hotṛ by which one transcends death? "Speech, indeed, is the hotṛ of the yajña" — i.e., of the yajamāna, since the śruti says, "the yajña, verily, is the yajamāna" (Śat. Br. 14.2.2.24). The speech of the yajamāna is itself the hotṛ at the adhiyajña level.

How? That very speech of the yajamāna which is here — that is the well-known Agni at the adhidaivata level. This has been explained in the Tryanna-prakaraṇa. And that Agni is the hotṛ, since the śruti says, "Agni, verily, is the hotṛ" (Śat. Br. 4.2.6). These two means of the yajña — the hotṛ ṛtvik on the adhiyajña side and Speech on the adhyātma side — both, being limited (paricchinna), are enveloped by death, that is, by karma joined with the inherent attachment grounded in ignorance, suffering modification at every moment, brought into sway. When this pair is seen in the form of the Agni who is the adhidaivata, that vision becomes the means to the wholly-liberated state of death's transcendence for the yajamāna and the yajña.

Hence he says, "That is the liberation" (sa muktiḥ): that hotṛ, Agni, is liberation; the very seeing of the form of Agni is liberation. For at the very moment when one sees the pair of means in the form of Agni, then itself one is freed from death, namely from the inherent attachment, both adhyātmika and limited, and from the adhibhautika. Therefore that hotṛ, seen in the form of Agni, is the means to liberation for the yajamāna. "That is full liberation" (sā atimuktiḥ): that very liberation is the means to atimukti. The vision of the limited pair of means in the unlimited form of Agni at the adhidaivata level is muktiḥ; that mukti, the adhidaivata-vision, itself, by transcending death which has its locus in the limitation that is adhyātma-and-adhibhūta, becomes the attainment of the divine state of being-Agni — that fruit is called atimuktiḥ. Since mukti itself is the means to atimukti, he calls it sā atimuktiḥ. For the yajamāna's atimukti is precisely speech-and-the-rest becoming Agni-and-the-rest, as explained in the Udgītha-prakaraṇa. There, generally, only the contemplation of mukhya-prāṇa was said to be the means of mukti, not its particulars; here the particular contemplation of speech-etc. as Agni-etc. is described. The fruit, viz. transcendence over the grasp of death, is the same as that explained in the Udgītha-brāhmaṇa: "Having transcended death, he shines" (Bṛ. Up. 1.3.12–16) and the rest.
BR_C03_S01_V04: He said, "Yājñavalkya, since all this is enveloped by day-and-night, all this is overpowered by day-and-night — by what means does the yajamāna become wholly liberated from the grasp of day-and-night?" "By the adhvaryu priest, by the eye, by the sun. For verily the eye is the adhvaryu of the yajña; that which is this eye is yonder sun — that is the adhvaryu; that is liberation, that is full liberation."
BR_C03_S01_V04::block-0:
"Yājñavalkya," said he. The wholly-liberated state from death in the form of karma — born of the inherent ignorance and attachment — has been explained. Now must be stated the wholly-liberated state apart from kāla, since kāla is the cause of the modification of the means like darśapūrṇamāsa-etc., which are the locus of the karma joined with attachment, which is death. For even apart from the performance of the kriyā — both before and after the kriyā — kāla is observed to act as the cause of modification of the means. Therefore the wholly-liberated state apart from kāla is to be stated.

Hence he says, "Since all this is enveloped by day-and-night." Kāla is of two forms: of the form of day-and-night-etc., and of the form of tithi-etc. First, of the form of day-and-night, the atimukti is stated. By day-and-night everything is born, grows, and perishes; so too the means of yajña — the eye and the adhvaryu of the yajña, of the yajamāna. The remaining syllables should be construed as before.

The yajamāna's eye-and-adhvaryu — this pair of means, abandoning their adhyātma-and-adhibhūta limitation, is seen in the form of the adhidaivata-self: that is mukti — that adhvaryu, seen as the Sun, is mukti; and that very mukti is atimukti, as before. For one who has attained the state of being the Ātman of the Sun, day-and-night do not arise.
BR_C03_S01_V05: He said, "Yājñavalkya, since all this is enveloped by the bright and dark fortnights, all this is overpowered by them — by what means does the yajamāna become wholly liberated from the grasp of the bright and dark fortnights?" "By the udgātṛ priest, by the wind, by prāṇa. For verily prāṇa is the udgātṛ of the yajña; that which is this prāṇa is the wind — that is the udgātṛ; that is liberation, that is full liberation."
BR_C03_S01_V05::block-0:
Now the wholly-liberated state from kāla in the form of tithi-etc. is stated. "All this" — over day-and-night, which are non-particularized, the Sun is the agent, but not over the tithis like pratipad-etc. Of those tithis like pratipad-etc., the moon is the agent through their waxing and waning. Hence by attaining the moon, transcendence of the bright-and-dark fortnights occurs, just as transcendence of day-and-night occurs by attaining the Sun.

There, the prāṇa of the yajamāna is wind, and that very wind is the udgātṛ — as ascertained in the Udgītha-brāhmaṇa: "With speech, indeed, and with prāṇa did he sing" (Bṛ. Up. 1.3.24); and "the body of this prāṇa is water; its luminous form is yonder moon." Since prāṇa, wind, and the moon are essentially one, in the conclusion via the moon or via the wind there is no difference. Considering thus, this śruti concludes via the wind in the adhidaivata form. Moreover, the waxing and waning of the moon are caused by the wind. Hence the wind is also the cause of even the agent of the kāla called tithi-etc. So that one who has attained the form of wind has transcended the kāla in the form of tithi-etc. — this is even more thoroughly established. By this, in another śruti, the vision in the form of the moon is mukti and atimukti; here, in the Kāṇva recension, the vision of the pair of means in their causal form, the wind-Ātman, is mukti and atimukti — there is no contradiction between the two śrutis.
BR_C03_S01_V06: He said, "Yājñavalkya, since this antarikṣa appears, as it were, without support — by what step (ākrama) does the yajamāna ascend to the heavenly world?" "By the brahman priest, by the mind, by the moon. For verily the mind is the brahman of the yajña; that which is this mind is yonder moon — that is the brahman; that is liberation, that is full liberation." These are the wholly-liberated states. Now the sampads.
BR_C03_S01_V06::block-0:
The wholly-liberated state of the yajamāna from the death that is kāla has been explained. By what support (avaṣṭambha) does the one being wholly liberated, having transcended death which is the limitation, attain the fruit and become wholly liberated? This is now stated. "This well-known antarikṣa, ākāśa, is, as it were, without support (anārambaṇam iva)" — by the word "as it were" (iva), there is indeed a support there, but it is not known: this is the intent. That unknown support is asked about by the pronoun "by what" (kena), since otherwise the attainment of the fruit would be impossible. "By what support and ascent the yajamāna, attaining the fruit of karma, is wholly liberated — what is that?" — this is the subject of inquiry. "By what step (ākrama) does the yajamāna ascend to the heavenly world?" — that is, attains the heavenly world as fruit, is wholly liberated.

"By the brahman ṛtvik, by the mind, by the moon" — the syllabic arrangement is as before. There, on the adhyātma side, the well-known mind of the yajña, of the yajamāna; on the adhidaivata side, that yonder moon. For mind on the adhyātma side and the moon on the adhidaivata side are well-known. That very moon is the brahman ṛtvik — by it, the limited form of the brahman as adhibhūta and the mind on the adhyātma side, this pair, is seen in the unlimited form of the moon. By that moon-mind as support, one attains the heavenly world as fruit of karma, is wholly liberated — this is the purport.

"Iti" is for conclusion: "such are the wholly-liberated states from death." Since all the modes of contemplation pertaining to the limbs of the yajña on this occasion have been stated, there is the conclusion: "such are the atimokṣas" — i.e., wholly-liberated states of such description. "Now the sampads": now the sampads are stated. Sampad means the bringing about (sampādana) of the fruit of fruit-yielding karmas like agnihotra-etc. by some commonality, for the sake of that fruit; or it is the sampādana of the fruit alone. For those who, exerting themselves with full effort in the performance of the means to fruit, find such performance impossible due to some defect — for them now, having installed the fires, taking up some karma, agnihotra-etc., as is feasible, making it the support, when there is knowledge of the fruit of karma, whichever fruit they desire — that very fruit they bring about (sampādayati). Otherwise, even for those of the three varṇas qualified for them, karmas like rājasūya, aśvamedha, puruṣamedha, sarvamedha would be impossible — their study would be merely for self-study, if there were no means to attaining their fruit. Therefore for them the attainment of fruit is by sampad alone; hence the fruitfulness of even sampads. So sampads are commenced.
BR_C03_S01_V07: He said, "Yājñavalkya, with how many ṛc-verses will the hotṛ perform today in this yajña?" "With three." "Which are those three?" "The puroruk, the yājyā, and the śasyā as the third." "What does he conquer by them?" "Whatever there is here that bears prāṇa."
BR_C03_S01_V07::block-0:
"Yājñavalkya," he said, by way of address. "With how many ṛc-verses will the hotṛ here today in this yajña" — by how many in number, by which classes of ṛc, this hotṛ ṛtvik, in this yajña, will recite the śastra? The other replies: "With three classes of ṛc." To the one who said this, the other says: "Which three?" — this question concerns what is to be enumerated; the previous one concerned the number itself.

"The puroruk": those ṛcs which are recited prior to the time of the offering — that class of ṛc is called puroruk; those recited for the sake of the offering — that class is yājyā; those recited for the sake of the śastra — that class is śasyā. All ṛcs whatsoever, whether stotriyā or others, all are subsumed within these three classes. "What does he conquer by them?" — "Whatever bears prāṇa here": by the commonality of number, whatever class bears prāṇa, all that he conquers — all that fruit-class he brings about by the commonality of number-and-the-rest.
BR_C03_S01_V08: "Yājñavalkya," he said, "how many oblations will the adhvaryu offer in this yajña today?" "Three." "Which are those three?" "Those that, when offered, blaze up; those that, when offered, make a great noise; and those that, when offered, sink down." "What does he conquer by them?" "By those that blaze up when offered he conquers the world of the gods, for the world of the gods shines, as it were. By those that make a great noise when offered he conquers the world of the manes, for the world of the manes is exceedingly noisy. By those that sink down when offered he conquers the world of men, for the world of men is, as it were, below."
BR_C03_S01_V08::block-0:
"Yājñavalkya," — and so on, as before. "How many oblations will the adhvaryu offer in this yajña today?" — that is, how many classes of oblations are there? The reply is "Three." "Which are those three?" — as before. The other replies: those which, when offered, blaze up — namely the oblations of fuel-sticks and clarified butter (samidājyāhutayaḥ); those which, when offered, make a great noise — atinedante, that is, produce loud sound — namely the oblations of flesh and the like (māṃsādyāhutayaḥ); those which, when offered, lie down — adhi, going downward, lying upon the ground — namely the oblations of milk and Soma (payaḥsomāhutayaḥ).

"What does he conquer by them?" — by the oblations thus accomplished, what does he win? The oblations that blaze up when offered are characterised by blazing; and the fruit, called the world of the gods (devaloka), is itself blazing. By that common feature he meditates: "These very blazing oblations being accomplished by me are themselves directly the form of the world of the gods, the fruit of action; the fruit known as devaloka is being effected by me." Thus he brings about (sampādayati) this identification.

The oblations that, when offered, make a great noise (atinedante) — by them he conquers the world of the manes, on the strength of the common feature of producing harsh sound. For in connection with the world of the manes, in the city Saṃyaminī of Vaivasvata, those who are being led there cry out "Alas! we are slain! release, release!" — such is the sound that arises there. Likewise the oblations of cut portions (avadānāhutayaḥ) make a similar sound. Hence by this commonality with the world of the manes he meditates: "The world of the manes itself is being effected by me."

The oblations that, when offered, lie down (adhiśerate) — by them he conquers the world of men, by the common feature of being connected with the surface of the earth. For "as it were below" (adha iva) — that is, the world of men is itself below in relation to the higher worlds of the Sādhyas; or else with reference to its downward going. Therefore he meditates: "The world of men itself is being effected by me" — at the time of accomplishing the oblations of milk and Soma.
BR_C03_S01_V09: "Yājñavalkya," he said, "with how many deities does this brahman-priest protect the yajña on the south side today?" "With one." "Which is that one?" "The mind itself; for the mind is verily infinite, and the Viśvedevas are infinite — by it he wins an infinite world."
BR_C03_S01_V09::block-0:
"Yājñavalkya," — as before. This ṛtvik called brahman, seated on the brahman's seat to the south, protects the yajña. "With how many deities does he protect it?" — the use of the plural here is incidental (prāsaṅgika); for he protects it really with one deity alone. When this is known, the question with the plural would be inappropriate for one who himself knows; therefore, having seen in the previous two sections the plural in question and answer — "with how many?" "with how many?" "with three" "with three" — here too the question is begun in the plural just by analogy. Or else the plural is used to confound the opponent (prativādivyāmoha).

The other replies: "With one." That is the one deity by means of which the brahman, seated on the seat to the south, protects the yajña. "Which is that one?" "The mind itself" — mind is that deity; for the brahman engages himself only by mind, by meditation alone, as another śruti declares: "Of that yajña, mind and speech are the two paths; the brahman with his mind perfects one of them" (Chānd. Up. 4.16.1; 4.16.2). Hence mind alone is the deity; and by that mind the brahman protects the yajña.

And that mind, on account of its diversity of modifications (vṛttibheda), is anantam, infinite. The word "vai" indicates well-known fact (prasiddhāvadyotanārtha); the infinitude of the mind is well known. The deities who identify themselves with this infinitude — anantā vai viśvedevāḥ — "the Viśvedevas are infinite," as another śruti has: "All the gods become one there" — and so on. Therefore, by the commonality of infinitude (ānantyasāmānya), "by that he wins an infinite world."
BR_C03_S01_V10: "Yājñavalkya," he said, "how many stotriyās will this udgātṛ chant in this yajña today?" "Three." "Which are those three?" "The puronuvākyā, the yājyā, and the śasyā as the third." "Which of them are those that pertain to the body (adhyātmam)?" "Prāṇa is verily the puronuvākyā, apāna the yājyā, vyāna the śasyā." "What does he conquer by them?" "By the puronuvākyā he conquers the world of earth, by the yājyā the world of the mid-region, by the śasyā the world of heaven." Then the hotṛ Aśvala fell silent.
BR_C03_S01_V10::block-0:
"Yājñavalkya," — as before. "How many stotriyās will this udgātṛ chant?" A stotriyā is a ṛk-sāman aggregate of a certain number of ṛks. Whether stotriyā or śasyā, whatever ṛks there are, all of them are reckoned to be just three — so he says. And these are explained as: the puronuvākyā, the yājyā, and the śasyā as the third.

Now it was said earlier (V07): "Whatever there is here that breathes, all that he sacrifices." By what common feature is this the case? The reply is given here. "Which of those three ṛks are the ones pertaining to the body (adhyātmam)?" Prāṇa itself is the puronuvākyā, by the commonality of the syllable "pa" (pa-śabdasāmānya); apāna is the yājyā, on account of immediate sequence (ānantarya) — for through apāna the deities devour the oblation that is offered, and the yāga is verily an offering; vyāna is the śasyā, as another śruti declares: "Without inhaling, without exhaling, he utters the ṛk" (Chānd. Up. 1.3.4).

"What does he conquer by them?" — this has already been explained. There the particular relationship-commonality (viśeṣasambandhasāmānya) was not stated; that is now stated here, while everything else has already been explained. By the commonality of relation to a world (lokasambandhasāmānya), "by the puronuvākyā he conquers the world of earth"; "by the yājyā the world of the mid-region," by the commonality of being in the middle (madhyamatvasāmānya); "by the śasyā the world of heaven," by the commonality of being above (ūrdhvatvasāmānya). "Thereupon" — that is, on account of his own questions being settled — "the hotṛ Aśvala fell silent" (uparirāma) — "this one is not within our scope," thinking thus.
BR_C03_S02_INTRO1::block-0:
The connection of the narrative is well known. Liberation from death (mṛtyor atimuktiḥ) has been explained both from the standpoint of time (kāla-lakṣaṇāt) and from that of action (karma-lakṣaṇāt). But what then is this death from which liberation has been explained? It is that death which is the locus of natural ignorance and attachment (svābhāvika-ajñāna-saṅgāspada), bounded by the spheres of the body (adhyātma) and the elements (adhibhūta), characterised as the graspers and over-graspers (grahātigraha-lakṣaṇa). The forms — Agni, Āditya, and so forth — of one liberated from this death of bounded form have already been explained in the section on Udgītha; and certain particulars regarding it appeared in the question of Aśvala. And this is the fruit of rites accompanied by knowledge (jñāna-sahitānāṃ karmaṇām).

From this transmigratory state, characterised by the form of ends and means (sādhya-sādhana-rūpa), liberation must be effected; therefore the very nature of bondage-form death is now stated, for it is the bound one for whom liberation is to be effected. Even where the form of one liberated has been spoken of, even there he is not entirely freed from the death-forms graha and atigraha. Thus it is said: "Verily hunger is death" (Bṛ. Up. 1.2.1), "This indeed is death" (Śat. Brā. 10.5.2.3) — speaking with reference to the puruṣa within the sun; and "Death is one, but he is many" (Śat. Brā. 10.5.2.16). For one who has attained identity with that, it is said that he attains and goes beyond death; nor are graha and atigraha of the nature of death absent there. As will be said: "Now of this mind, heaven is the body, the form of light is yonder Āditya" (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.12), and "Mind is the graha, it is grasped by desire as the over-grasper" (Bṛ. Up. 3.2.7); and "Prāṇa indeed is the graha, it is grasped by apāna as the over-grasper" (Bṛ. Up. 3.2.2); and "Speech indeed is the graha, it is grasped by name as the over-grasper" (Bṛ. Up. 3.2.3). The same has been explained by us in the section on the threefold food (tryannavibhāga). And this has been carefully considered: that which is the cause of pravṛtti (engagement) cannot itself be the cause of nivṛtti (cessation).

Some, however, hold that everything is the cause of nivṛtti (cessation). On this view: "From every preceding death one is released, attaining each successive higher state — and one attains it only for the sake of withdrawal (vyāvṛtty-arthameva), not as an end in itself (na tu tādarthyam) — and so until the destruction of duality, all is death; only when duality is destroyed does one truly attain and transcend death. Therefore the intermediate liberation is relative and figurative (āpekṣikī gauṇī)." — All this is so, but it is not what the Bṛhadāraṇyaka teaches.

Objection (pūrvapakṣa): But oneness with the All is mokṣa, as the śruti has "Therefore he became all that" (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.10).

Reply: Granted, this too is true. But it is not the purport (tādarthya) of texts like "He who desires a village should sacrifice" (Tai. Ār. 12.10.4), "He who desires cattle should sacrifice" (Tai. Ār. 16.12.8). For if these had non-duality alone as their purport, with no purpose of village, cattle, heaven, etc., then village, cattle, heaven and the rest would not be apprehended; yet what are apprehended are the very specific varieties of the fruits of action (karma-phala-vaicitrya-viśeṣāḥ). And if the purport of Vedic actions were non-duality alone, then there would be no transmigration (saṃsāra) at all.

Objection: Even when non-duality is the purport, transmigration is a by-product (anuniṣpādita) — just as light meant for the perception of form illumines everything that happens to be there.

Reply: No, for there is no pramāṇa for it. If the purport of Vedic actions accompanied by knowledge were non-duality alone, while everything else were a by-product, there would be no pramāṇa for the latter — neither perception, nor inference, nor therefore āgama. 

Objection: Both can be shown by a single sentence — like the sentences regarding the leading of channels and the kindling of light.

Reply: Not so, for this contradicts the very nature of a sentence. It is not possible that a single meaning of one sentence should be the means both of pravṛtti and of nivṛtti. In the case of "leading channels" and "kindling light," the matter is direct perception (pratyakṣa), so there is no fault. As for the further argument that mantras are seen in this sense — this very sense is itself unestablished by pramāṇa; whether the mantras refer to this sense or to some other sense is itself a matter to be sought. Therefore death of the form graha-atigraha is bondage; from it liberation must be taught — hence this section is begun. And we know of no "half-old-woman" cleverness (ardhajaratīya-kauśala) of taking up an intermediate position, like the half-relations to objects.

As for the objection that "After saying 'one transcends death,' graha and atigraha are spoken of" — that is by association of meaning (artha-sambandha). All this bondage of the form ends-and-means is from non-release from graha and atigraha; for only when the fetter is fully known does one begin the effort to free the fettered one. Therefore the section is begun for that very purpose.
BR_C03_S02_INTRO1::block-1:
Some, however, hold that everything is a cause of nivṛtti (cessation). On their view, from one death after another one is released, attaining successively higher states — and one attains them only for the purpose of withdrawal (vyāvṛtty-artha), not as ends in themselves (na tādarthyam). Hence until the destruction of duality everything is death; only on the destruction of duality is one truly liberated from death. Hence in the interim, the liberation is relative and secondary (āpekṣikī gauṇī muktiḥ). All this is so — but it is not what the Bṛhadāraṇyaka teaches.

If it be said: oneness with the All is mokṣa, by the śruti "Therefore he became all that" (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.10) — granted; this too holds. But the purport (tādarthya) of texts like "He who desires a village should sacrifice" (Tai. Ār. 12.10.4), "He who desires cattle should sacrifice" (Tai. Ār. 16.12.8) is not that. For if their meaning were non-duality alone, with no village, cattle, svarga, etc. as their object, then village, cattle, svarga would not be apprehended; yet the special varieties of karma-phala (karma-phala-vaicitrya-viśeṣāḥ) are apprehended. If the Vedic actions had only non-duality as purport, saṃsāra itself would never have arisen.

If you say: even on the non-duality view, the by-products in the form of objects naturally come about (anuniṣpādita) — just as in the case of light meant for seeing form, everything else there is also illumined — that is not so, on account of the failure of pramāṇa. If the Vedic acts coupled with knowledge have non-duality as their purport, and the rest is incidental, there is no pramāṇa for the rest — neither pratyakṣa, nor anumāna, nor therefore āgama.

If it be said: both are shown by a single sentence — like "leading of channels" and "kindling of light" — that too is not so, on account of failing the property of a sentence. It is not possible to apprehend the meaning of a single sentence as the means both of pravṛtti and of nivṛtti. In the case of "leading channels" and "light," the matter is itself directly perceived, so there is no fault.

What is further said — that mantras are seen in this sense — that very sense is unattainable by pramāṇa; whether the mantras refer to this sense or to some other is itself to be sought. Therefore death of the form graha-atigraha is bondage; from that bondage mokṣa must be taught — for this purpose this section is begun. We do not understand any half-and-half kauśala (ardhajaratīya-kauśala) of an intermediate position, as in the relations to sense-objects. As for it being said "one transcends death" and then graha-atigraha being spoken of — that is by association of meaning (artha-sambandha). All this bondage of ends-and-means form arises from non-release from graha-atigraha; for the fetter being known, the effort for the fettered one's liberation can be undertaken. Therefore the section is begun with this very aim.
BR_C03_S02_V01: Then Jāratkārava Ārtabhāga questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," he said, "how many grahas are there, and how many atigrahas?" "Eight grahas and eight atigrahas." "Those eight grahas and eight atigrahas — which are they?"
BR_C03_S02_V01::block-0:
"Atha hainam" — the word "ha" carries the sense of tradition (aitihya). "Then," that is, after Aśvala had ceased, Jāratkārava — of the lineage of Jaratkāru — Ārtabhāga, son of Ṛtabhāga, questioned the said Yājñavalkya. "Yājñavalkya," he said — for purposes of address (abhimukhīkaraṇa). The question is as before: "How many grahas, how many atigrahas?" The word "iti" marks the close of the sentence.

Now, would the question be regarding ones already known, or ones not known? If the grahas and atigrahas are already known, then since the attribute of number pertaining to them too would be known, the question "how many grahas, how many atigrahas?" — a question about number — would be inappropriate. If, on the other hand, they are not known, then the question would be about the things to be numbered, namely "which are the grahas, which are the atigrahas?" — and not "how many grahas, how many atigrahas?" Moreover, when the general nature is known and only the specific is sought, a question is asked — as in "Which here are the Kaṭhas, which the Kalāpas?" But here there are no things called grahas and atigrahas well known to people in the world, that the question should be about a particular among them.

Objection: But it has been said "one transcends" (Bṛ. Up. 3.1.3, 4, 5); for there is liberation only of one held by a graha; "That is mukti, that is atimukti" (Bṛ. Up. 3.1.3, 4, 5, 6) — twice. Therefore grahas and atigrahas are presupposed.

Reply: Granted; but there only four grahas and atigrahas were known — speech, eye, prāṇa, and mind — and even there the question "how many?" would be inappropriate, since the number is known.

Answer: Not so; for that was not for the purpose of definite ascertainment (anavadhāraṇārthatva) — the fourfoldness was not what was intended there. Here, however, in the seeing of grahas and atigrahas, with the intention of expressing the attribute of being eightfold (aṣṭatva-guṇa), the question "how many?" is indeed appropriate. Therefore by the twofold expression "that is mukti, that is atimukti," mukti and atimukti are stated; the grahas and atigrahas too are established. Hence the question: "Of how many in number are the grahas, of how many the atigrahas?"

The other replies: "Eight grahas, eight atigrahas." "Those eight grahas that have been mentioned — which are they that must definitively be grasped?" — this is the further question.
BR_C03_S02_V02: "Prāṇa is verily the graha; it is grasped by apāna as the over-grasper; for through apāna one smells odours."
BR_C03_S02_V02::block-0: There he replies: "Prāṇa is verily the graha" — here "prāṇa" denotes the organ of smell (ghrāṇa), from the context (prakaraṇāt); it is together with air (vāyu-sahita). "By apāna" — that is, by odour (gandha); apāna being its associate (apānasacivatvāt), apāna here designates odour. For all the world smells the odour conveyed by apāna through the organ of smell. This is what is said: "For through apāna one smells odours."
BR_C03_S02_V03: "Speech is verily the graha; it is grasped by name as the over-grasper; for through speech one utters names."
BR_C03_S02_V04: "The tongue is verily the graha; it is grasped by taste as the over-grasper; for through the tongue one knows tastes."
BR_C03_S02_V05: Verily the eye is a graha (grasper); it is seized by form as the atigraha (over-grasper), for through the eye one sees forms.
BR_C03_S02_V06: Verily the ear is a graha; it is seized by sound as the atigraha, for through the ear one hears sounds.
BR_C03_S02_V07: Verily the mind is a graha; it is seized by desire as the atigraha, for through the mind one desires desires.
BR_C03_S02_V08: Verily the two hands are a graha; they are seized by action (karman) as the atigraha, for through the two hands one performs action.
BR_C03_S02_V09: Verily the skin is a graha; it is seized by touch as the atigraha, for through the skin one experiences touches. Thus these are the eight grahas and the eight atigrahas.
BR_C03_S02_V09::block-0:
"Verily speech is a graha" — for by speech, restricted to the bodily-self (adhyātma-paricchinnā), serving as the seat of attachment to objects, employed in utterances such as untruth, falsehood, the unseemly, the disgusting, and the like, the world is seized — that is, carried off; therefore speech is a graha (grasper). "It is seized by name as the atigraha" — that very graha called speech is seized by name, that is, by the object that is to be uttered, as the atigraha (over-grasper). The lengthening in atigraheṇa is a Vedic peculiarity (chāndasa). For speech has the utterable as its purpose; speech, when applied for the sake of that utterable object, becomes mastered by it; and there is no release for speech without performing that function for it; therefore it is said that speech is seized by name as the atigraha. Engaged through attachment to what is to be uttered, it becomes yoked to all calamities.

The rest is similar. Thus these eight, ending with the skin, are the grahas, and these eight, ending with touch, are the atigrahas.
BR_C03_S02_V10: "Yājñavalkya," he said, "this whole world is the food of Death; what then is that deity whose food is Death itself?" "Fire indeed is Death; it is the food of the waters. He who knows this conquers further death (punarmṛtyu)."
BR_C03_S02_V10::block-0:
When the grahas and atigrahas have been concluded, he speaks again — "Yājñavalkya," he said. "This whole world is the food of Death" — that is, this whole manifested universe (vyākṛtam) is the food of Death; everything is born and perishes, all of it being seized by Death in the form of grahas and atigrahas. "What then is that deity whose food is even Death?" — as is established by another śruti: "He of whom Death is the seasoning" (Kaṭha Up. 1.2.25).

The questioner's intent is this: if he says there is a Death of Death, there will be infinite regress (anavasthā); but if he does not say so, then liberation (mokṣa) from this Death whose mark is the grahas and atigrahas does not stand, since liberation can only come about by the destruction of the grahas, atigrahas, and Death. Should there be a Death even of Death, then the Death whose mark is the graha–atigraha could be destroyed. Hence, regarding the question as one difficult to answer, he asks, "What then is that deity?"

Now, there is indeed a Death of Death. Pūrvapakṣa: but then there would be infinite regress — for that one too there would be yet another Death. Siddhānta: not so, there is no infinite regress, for of the Death of all there cannot be another, further Death. How then is it known that there is a Death of Death? Because it is observed (dṛṣṭatvāt). Fire is seen to be the death of all, since it destroys; that fire in turn is consumed by water; therefore that fire is the food of the waters. Take it, then, that there is a Death of Death.

By that, the whole class of grahas and atigrahas is consumed by the Death of Death; and when that bondage is destroyed and consumed by Death, liberation from saṁsāra becomes intelligible. For the bondage was stated to consist of the grahas and atigrahas; and from that, liberation is established. Hence the human endeavour for the sake of bondage's release becomes fruitful — therefore he conquers further death (punarmṛtyu).
BR_C03_S02_V11: "Yājñavalkya," he said, "when this person dies, do the prāṇas depart out from him, or not?" "No," said Yājñavalkya, "they are gathered together right there itself; he swells, he is inflated; inflated, the dead one lies."
BR_C03_S02_V11::block-0:
When the higher Death has been consumed by Death and one has become liberated through the vision of the supreme Self (paramātma-darśana) — that purusha who is thus liberated and a knower (vidvān) — when (yatra) at the time he dies, do the prāṇas, namely the grahas such as speech and the atigrahas such as name, which abide within as impressions (vāsanā-rūpāḥ) and serve as their prompters (prayojakāḥ), depart upwards (ut-krāmanti) out from him, the dying knower of Brahman, or not? "No," said Yājñavalkya — they do not depart upwards. Right there itself (atra eva), in this very supreme Self, they go to non-difference (avibhāgam) — that is, in the knower the actions and instruments are gathered together (samavanīyante) in their own source (svayoni), in the very essence of the supreme Brahman; they are merged into oneness, they dissolve — like waves into the ocean.

And thus another śruti shows the dissolution of the prāṇas, designated by the word kalā, in the supreme Self: "Just so, of this seer, these sixteen kalās, which have the Person as their goal, on reaching the Person, go to their setting" (Praśna Up. 6.5) — it is shown that they go to non-difference with the supreme Self.

Is he then not dead? Indeed not — and yet this one is dead. Since he swells (ucchvayati), reaches the state of being puffed up; he is inflated (ādhmāyati), filled with external air, like a wineskin (dṛti); inflated thus, dead, he lies motionless. The purport of the sentence is that for the liberated one, when bondage has been destroyed, there is no going anywhere whatsoever.
BR_C03_S02_V12: "Yājñavalkya," he said, "when this person dies, what is it that does not leave him?" "Name; verily, name is endless; endless are the Viśve Devas; thereby he conquers an endless world indeed."
BR_C03_S02_V12::block-0:
Of the liberated one, are it the prāṇas alone that are gathered together, or also everything that prompts them? If only the prāṇas, and not everything that prompts them, then since the prompter persists, the prāṇas would arise again; if, however, the whole — desire, action, and the rest (kāma-karma-ādi) — is dissolved, then liberation (mokṣa) stands. With this purport comes the next question. "Yājñavalkya," he said, "when this person dies, what is it that does not leave him?"

The other answers — "Name." The meaning is that everything is gathered together (samavanīyate); but name alone is not dissolved, on account of its connection with form (ākṛti-sambandhāt). For name is eternal (nityaṁ hi nāma); "verily name is endless" — the very eternality is the endlessness (ānantya) of name.

The Viśve Devas, all the gods, are without end, presiding over that endlessness; "thereby he conquers an endless world indeed" — having attained as one's own Self those infinite Viśve Devas who preside over the endlessness of name, by that vision of endlessness he conquers an endless world itself.
BR_C03_S02_V13: "Yājñavalkya," he said, "when this person dies, his speech enters into fire, his prāṇa into the wind, his eye into the sun, his mind into the moon, his ear into the directions, his body into the earth, his self into ākāśa, the hairs of his body into the herbs, the hairs of his head into the trees, and his blood and seed are deposited in the waters — where then does this person remain?" "Take my hand, dear Ārtabhāga; we two alone shall know of this; this matter of ours is not for a public assembly." Then the two went apart and deliberated; and what they spoke of was karma alone, and what they extolled was karma alone — that one becomes virtuous indeed by virtuous action, and evil by evil action. Thereupon Jāratkārava Ārtabhāga ceased questioning.
BR_C03_S02_V13::block-0:
The bondage in the form of graha and atigraha was declared, having the nature of mortality (mṛtyu). And since there exists a death of that very mṛtyu, mokṣa is rendered intelligible. That mokṣa is the dissolution, here itself, of the very things called graha and atigraha — like the extinguishing of a lamp. The bondage of the form of graha and atigraha, of the nature of death — what is the cause that prompts it? With the desire to ascertain the very nature of that cause, this passage is begun: "Yājñavalkya," he said.

It is the prayojaka — the impelling cause — of bondage that the mantra investigates, since unless that cause is known, no genuine release can be conceived; for liberation is precisely the cessation of that which sustains bondage.
BR_C03_S02_V13::block-1:
Here some commentators expound thus: even when the prompting cause of graha and atigraha is destroyed, one is forsooth not yet liberated; reduced to a name only, separated from the Supreme Self by avidyā — which is like a saline patch sprung from one's own self — turned away from the world that is to be enjoyed, with desires and works cut off, one abides in an intermediate state. For such a one the perception of duality must be removed by the perception of unity with the Supreme Self — therefore from this point onwards the contemplation of the Supreme Self is to be undertaken. Thus, having imagined an intermediate state called "liberation," they connect the subsequent text accordingly.

Such is the pūrvapakṣa to be examined and refuted, since it posits a halfway condition between bondage and true mokṣa, which the śruti does not warrant.
BR_C03_S02_V13::block-2:
Against that it must be said: when the karaṇas are dispersed, how can there be śravaṇa, manana and nididhyāsana of the Supreme Self for one who is bodiless? — for they themselves say that the prāṇa has been completely withdrawn and a mere name remains; and it has been said "he lies dead" (Bṛ. U. 3.2.11); even by mere fancy this cannot be made out. If, alternatively, it be imagined that while still living, with avidyā alone remaining, one has turned away from what is to be enjoyed, what then is the cause of this? It must be stated. If it be said that the cause is the attainment of the Self that is the unity of the entire duality, that has already been refuted. The wise one endowed with the perception of the Self as the unity of duality together with karma, having died and his prāṇa having been completely withdrawn, would attain world-Selfhood, that is, the form of Hiraṇyagarbha; or while still living, with prāṇa unwithdrawn, having turned away from objects of enjoyment, dispassionate, he might face the Supreme Self. But both cannot be obtained by a means accomplished by a single effort. If it be a means for attaining Hiraṇyagarbha, it is not a means for turning away from him; if it be the means of turning the seeker towards the Supreme Self, that is, of withdrawal from objects of enjoyment, it is not the means for attaining Hiraṇyagarbha; for that which is the means of going is not also the means of ceasing to go.

If, again, having died and attained Hiraṇyagarbha, then with prāṇa withdrawn and a mere name remaining, one becomes qualified for the knowledge of the Supreme Self, then the instruction of Self-knowledge for the sake of beings such as ourselves becomes purposeless; for it is for the puruṣārtha (the highest end of man) of all that the knowledge of Brahman is taught — by the śruti "Whichever of the gods…" (Bṛ. U. 1.4.10) and so on. Therefore this fancy is utterly low and quite outside the śāstra. We shall now resume the topic at hand.
BR_C03_S02_V13::block-3:
Now, with the desire to ascertain by what cause the bondage characterised as graha and atigraha is impelled, the text says: "yatrāsya puruṣasya" — when this puruṣa, who is one not endowed with right vision, possessed of head, hands and the rest, has died — "vāk" his speech enters into fire, the wind his prāṇa enters, the sun his eye enters — and the construction is to be carried throughout: the moon his mind, the directions his ear, the earth his body, into ākāśa his ātman — here "ātman" denotes the seat, namely the heart's ākāśa; that enters ākāśa; into the herbs go the hairs of the body; into the trees go the hairs of the head; into the waters his blood and seed are "deposited" — "are deposited" is a mark of subsequent reassumption; for everywhere by the words "speech" and the rest are taken up the deities, not the karaṇas alone, which do not depart before liberation. There the karaṇas, unsuperintended by their deities, are like sickles and other tools laid aside; and the bodiless agent, the puruṣa, who is not independent — what does he resort to? That is asked: "kvāyaṃ tadā puruṣo bhavati" — resorting to what does the puruṣa become at that time? Resorting to which support, does he reassume the aggregate of body and senses afresh? By what is the bondage characterised as graha and atigraha set in motion? — that is the question.

To this it is answered: svabhāva (intrinsic nature), yadṛcchā (chance), kāla (time), karma, daiva, vijñāna alone, and śūnya (the void) — these have been imagined by the disputants; therefore, since this is a topic of many divergent doctrines, no settlement of the matter is possible by the procedure of mere disputation (jalpa-nyāya). If you wish here to settle the matter, "ahara somya hastam" — bring your hand, dear Ārtabhāga: we two alone shall know what is to be known of this concerning what you have asked, that we shall ascertain. Why? Because this matter cannot be settled by the two of us in the public assembly, in the gathering of people; therefore we shall go to a solitary place for deliberation. "Tau ha" and so on is the speech of the śruti. Yājñavalkya and Ārtabhāga, having gone to a solitary place, what did they do? — that is told: "tau ha utkramya" — having gone forth from the place of crowds, they deliberated; first, taking up one by one the views of the worldly disputants, they considered them. Having considered, what they finally said, casting aside all the pūrvapakṣas — hear that: it is karma alone, the cause of repeated re-assumption of the body-and-senses aggregate, that they declared there. Not only that — when the supposed causes — time, karma, daiva (destiny / Lord) — are admitted, what they extolled was karma alone. Since it has been ascertained that the re-assumption of body and senses, that is, the effect graha-atigraha and so on, is impelled by karma alone, therefore one becomes puṇya, righteous, by śāstra-enjoined puṇya-karma; by the opposite, evil; "pāpaḥ pāpena" — sinful by sin. Thus when the questions had been settled by Yājñavalkya, since Yājñavalkya could not be shaken, Jāratkārava Ārtabhāga ceased.
BR_C03_S03_INTRO1::block-0:
Then Bhujyu Lāhyāyani questioned him. The bondage characterised as graha and atigraha has been declared; that from which, together with its impelling cause, one is liberated when liberated, or that bound by which one transmigrates — that is mṛtyu; and from that mṛtyu mokṣa is intelligible, since there exists a death of mṛtyu. And the liberated one has no going anywhere — there is total cessation, with a mere name remaining, like the extinguishing of a lamp; this has been ascertained.

Now as regards those that transmigrate and those that are being liberated, the contact of body-and-senses with their own causes being equal in both, in the case of the liberated there is absolute non-reassumption, but in the case of the transmigrating there is repeated reassumption; that by which it is impelled is karma — this has been ascertained by deliberation. And on its destruction, with only the name remaining, the total cessation, namely mokṣa, occurs. And that karma is called puṇya and pāpa, on the strength of "puṇyo vai puṇyena karmaṇā bhavati pāpaḥ pāpena" (Bṛ. U. 3.2.13); the saṃsāra is brought about by these. Therein, by demerit one experiences sorrow in the immobile and mobile beings, in hells, in beasts, in pretas and so forth, where pain is intrinsically abundant, being born and dying again and again — this is well known to all the world like the king's highway.

But the puṇya that is according to śāstra — "by puṇya-karma alone one becomes puṇya" — that very thing the śruti emphasises here. And puṇya-karma alone is the means to all puruṣārthas — such is the import of all the śruti and smṛti pronouncements. Since mokṣa too is a puruṣārtha, it would seem to be accomplishable by that. As puṇya is more excellent, the fruit attained is more excellent — therefore by the highest excellence of puṇya, mokṣa would arise — such a doubt may arise; that must be removed. The action of utmost excellence accompanied by knowledge has only this much extent of effect, since karma and its fruit have for their sphere only that which is the locus of differentiated name and form; but karma has no operation in regard to that which is uneffected, eternal, of undifferentiated dharmin, of nature non-name-and-form, free from the nature of action, instrument and fruit; and where there is operation, that itself is saṃsāra. To declare this purport this brāhmaṇa is begun.
BR_C03_S03_INTRO1::block-1:
What some say — that karma joined with vidyā produces a different effect, like poison, curd and the like — that is not so, since mokṣa is not a thing to be produced; the destruction of bondage alone is mokṣa, not something effected; and we have said that the bondage is avidyā; and avidyā is not destructible by karma, since the sphere of karma's potency is the seen domain. The spheres of karma's potency are utpatti (production), āpti (reaching), vikāra (modification), and saṃskāra (purification); the potency of karma is to produce, to cause to attain, to modify, and to purify; there is no other sphere for the potency of karma, since none is known in the world. And mokṣa is not any one of these padārthas; we have said it is veiled by avidyā alone.

Well — let it be that mere karma has only this nature; but karma joined with vidyā, free from sankalpa, may have a different nature. For things known to have one power, like poison and curd, when joined with vidyā, mantra, sugar and the like, are seen to have potency in another domain. So let it be with karma — if so we say: no. Because there is no pramāṇa. There is in regard to karma's having potency in a different sphere, beyond the spheres mentioned, neither pratyakṣa, nor anumāna, nor upamāna, nor arthāpatti, nor śabda as pramāṇa.

Is it not that, in the absence of any other fruit, codanānyathānupapatti (the otherwise impossibility of the injunction) is the pramāṇa? For of the nitya-karmas no fruit is to be hypothesised by the Viśvajit-nyāya; nor is any heard fruit; yet they are enjoined; therefore by elimination mokṣa is understood as their fruit; otherwise men would not engage in them. — Is it not the very Viśvajit-nyāya that has come about, since mokṣa as fruit has been hypothesised? — That if mokṣa or any other fruit be not hypothesised, men would not engage in them; therefore mokṣa is hypothesised as fruit by śrutārthāpatti, just as in the Viśvajit. Then how is it said that this is not the Viśvajit-nyāya? — A fruit is hypothesised, and yet it is not the Viśvajit-nyāya — that is a contradictory statement. — If you say that mokṣa is not at all a fruit, no — for there would be the abandonment of the proposition; for it was proposed that karma produces an effect different, like poison, curd and the like; if that mokṣa be not at all the karma's effect or fruit, that proposition is given up.

If mokṣa be karma's effect, the difference from the fruits of svarga and so on must be stated. If it is not karma's effect, what then is the meaning of the very statement that mokṣa is the fruit of nitya-karmas? It must be told. Mere difference in the words "effect" and "fruit" cannot be the basis for assuming a distinction. And mokṣa is fruitless, and yet it is performed by nitya-karmas — that is, of nitya-karmas there is no fruit, but there is an effect — this purport is contradictory, like saying "fire is cold". If it be said: like in the case of jñāna — as mokṣa, the effect of jñāna, is spoken of even though not produced by jñāna, so karma's effect — no; for jñāna has the function of removing ajñāna; mokṣa is metaphorically called the effect of jñāna because jñāna removes the obstruction of ajñāna. But ajñāna is not to be removed by karma; nor can any obstruction other than ajñāna be hypothesised for mokṣa, since mokṣa is eternal and not separate from the very nature of the seeker — to be removed by karma. If it be said: it removes ajñāna only — no, because of dissimilarity — ajñāna is non-manifestation, contrary to jñāna which is of the nature of manifestation… (truncated)
BR_C03_S03_V01: Then Bhujyu Lāhyāyani questioned him: "Yājñavalkya," he said, "we were wandering as caraka students in the country of the Madras and came to the house of Patañjala Kāpya. He had a daughter possessed by a gandharva. We asked him, 'Who are you?' He said, 'Sudhanvan, of the line of Aṅgiras.' When we questioned him about the ends of the worlds, we then asked him, 'Where have the Pārikṣitas gone?' — Where have the Pārikṣitas gone? — That I ask you, Yājñavalkya: where have the Pārikṣitas gone?"
BR_C03_S03_V01::block-0:
"Atha" — thereafter; when Jāratkārava had ceased, Bhujyu by name, Lāhyāyani — Lāhya is the descendant of Lahya, his descendant is Lāhyāyani — questioned him; "Yājñavalkya," he said. At the outset, the contemplation of the aśvamedha was declared; the aśvamedha sacrifice yields the fruit of both the collective (samaṣṭi) and the individual (vyaṣṭi); whether combined with knowledge or accomplished by mere knowledge, it is the supreme limit of all karmas; for they remember that there is nothing higher than aśvamedha among puṇya nor higher than the slaying of an embryo among pāpa; by it one attains the samaṣṭi and the vyaṣṭis. Therein the vyaṣṭis, located within the cosmic egg, the fruits of the aśvamedha sacrifice, have been ascertained; "mṛtyur asyātmā bhavaty etāsāṃ devatānām eko bhavati" (Bṛ. U. 1.2.7) was said; and Mṛtyu, characterised by hunger, the buddhi-Self, the samaṣṭi, the firstborn, vāyu, sūtra, satya, Hiraṇyagarbha — his sphere is differentiated: he whose nature is everything that has the unity of duality, the inner Self of all beings, the liṅga, of formless rasa, on whom all the karmas of all beings depend, who is the supreme goal and supreme fruit of karmas and of the vijñānas connected with karma.

His range — how great, his pervasion how extensive, made spherical on all sides — that should be told; that being told, the entire saṃsāra, the sphere of bondage, becomes told. And to display the trans-worldly nature of that contemplation of the Self as samaṣṭi-vyaṣṭi, the upaniṣad makes a story (ākhyāyikā) about its own past; "and by this I shall confound the intellect of the disputant" — so he thinks.
BR_C03_S03_V01::block-1: "Madreṣu" — among the Madras, a certain country; "carakāḥ" — those who go about for vows for the sake of study, or adhvaryu priests called "carakas"; "paryavrajāma" — we wandered around. "Patañjalasya" — we, while wandering, came to the houses of one named Patañjala, of the kapi gotra (Kāpya). "His daughter was possessed by a gandharva" — possessed by some superhuman being, a gandharva, who had entered her; or the gandharva is the dhiṣṇya-fire, the ṛtvik-deity, who is determined to have such jñāna; for to a mere being, such knowledge is not possible. Surrounding her on all sides, we all asked, "Who are you?" — what is your name, what is your essence? He, the gandharva, said: "Sudhanvan" by name, of the Āṅgirasa gotra. When we asked him about the ends of the worlds, we then said to him — having begun to find out the dimensions of the cosmos and praising ourselves — namely, "where did the Pārikṣitas go?" And the gandharva told us everything. "Thus knowledge has been obtained by me from divine beings; that you do not have; therefore you are vanquished" — such is his import. "I, then, endowed with that vidyā, having received that āgama from the gandharva, ask you, Yājñavalkya: where did the Pārikṣitas go? — what do you know of that? Yājñavalkya, tell me — I ask: where did the Pārikṣitas go?"
BR_C03_S03_V02: He said: "He told you, surely, that they went where the performers of the aśvamedha go." "Where do the aśvamedha-performers go?" "Thirty-two times the chariot-day of the gods is this world; the earth, twice as great, surrounds it on all sides; the ocean, twice as great, surrounds the earth on all sides; then there is the space between them, as the edge of a razor or the wing of a mosquito. Indra, becoming Suparṇa, gave them to Vāyu; Vāyu, having placed them in himself, conducted them where the previous performers of aśvamedha had gone." Thus did he extol Vāyu indeed. Therefore Vāyu alone is vyaṣṭi, Vāyu is samaṣṭi. He who knows this conquers re-death. Thereupon Bhujyu Lāhyāyani ceased.
BR_C03_S03_V02::block-0:
"Sa hovāca" — Yājñavalkya said; "uvāca vai saḥ" — the word "vai" indicates recollection — that gandharva did indeed tell you. "Agacchan vai te" — the Pārikṣitas went "tat" — there. Where? — "yatra," where the aśvamedha-performers go. The question being thus settled, he asks: "kva nu aśvamedhayājino gacchanti" — where do the aśvamedha-performers go? With the desire to indicate their destination, he describes the dimensions of the cosmic shell. "Dvātriṃśataṃ vai" — "two more than thirty" — thirty-two; "devarathāhnyāni" — "deva" the sun; his rathaḥ, the deva-ratha; that which is measured by the going of that chariot in a day, that is the deva-rathāhnya; multiplied thirty-two times — these are devarathāhnyāni; the size of this world is so much, encircled by the lokāloka mountain — where the Vairāja body resides, and where the experiencing of the fruits of karma takes place for living beings; this is the loka, beyond which is aloka. The earth, twice as broad as the loka, surrounds it on all sides. Twice that, the samudra surrounds the earth — what the Paurāṇikas call "ghanoda."

There the dimension of the gap between the two halves of the cosmic shell is told, by which gap, going outwards, the aśvamedha-performers spread. There, the dimension is as great as the edge of a razor or the wing of a mosquito due to its subtlety; that is the size of the ākāśa, the opening, between the two cosmic shells; through that ākāśa, the Pārikṣitas, the aśvamedha-performers, having attained this, were given by Indra, the supreme Lord — He who, being the agni-cit in the aśvamedha, having become Suparṇa, the bird with wings and tail, of whom the contemplation has been declared by "tasya prācī dik śiraḥ" (Bṛ. U. 1.2.4) etc. — gave them to Vāyu, since being mūrta (corporeal) the self has no motion there. Vāyu, having placed them in himself — established as his own self — led them there where formerly the aśvamedha-performers had gone. "Evam iva vai" — thus indeed that gandharva extolled Vāyu alone, the destination of the Pārikṣitas. The story is concluded; the meaning derived from the story, however, the śruti, withdrawing from the story, declares to us in its own form. Since Vāyu is the inner Self of immobile and mobile beings and is also the outer Self, therefore the manifold pervasion as adhyātma, adhibhūta, and adhidaiva — that is Vāyu alone; likewise the samaṣṭi, by mere sūtra-Self, is Vāyu alone. Thus, he who comprehends Vāyu as Self in the form of samaṣṭi and vyaṣṭi — what is his fruit? — "apa punarmṛtyuṃ jayati" — having died once, he does not die again. Then, the question concerning the Self being settled, Bhujyu Lāhyāyani ceased.
BR_C03_S03_V02::block-1: Thus the third brāhmaṇa of the third adhyāya.
BR_C03_S04_INTRO1::block-0: Then Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa questioned him. "Bound by graha and atigraha impelled by puṇya and pāpa, repeatedly casting off graha and atigraha and reassuming them, one transmigrates" — so it was said. The supreme excellence of puṇya was explained — its sphere of differentiated being, the form of samaṣṭi-vyaṣṭi, the attainment of the unity of duality as Self. But that one who, seized by graha and atigraha, transmigrates — does he exist or not? And if he exists, of what nature is he? — In order to discern just the Self, the question of Uṣasta is begun. By the very ascertainment of his nirupādhi essence — free from the nature of action, instrument and fruit — one is liberated from the said bondage together with its impelling cause. The connection with the story is well known.
BR_C03_S04_V01: Then Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa questioned him: "Yājñavalkya," he said, "That which is Brahman direct and immediate, the Ātman who is innermost in all — explain that to me." "This is your Ātman who is innermost in all." "Which one, Yājñavalkya, is innermost in all?" "He who breathes through the prāṇa is your Ātman who is innermost in all; he who exhales through the apāna is your Ātman who is innermost in all; he who diffuses through the vyāna is your Ātman who is innermost in all; he who ascends through the udāna is your Ātman who is innermost in all. This is your Ātman who is innermost in all."
BR_C03_S04_V01::block-0:
Then Uṣasta, named so, son of Cakra, Cākrāyaṇa, questioned the Yājñavalkya at hand. "Yat" the Brahman that is "sākṣāt" — direct, unobstructed by anything for the seer; "aparokṣāt" — non-figurative, not in the figurative sense as in "the ear is Brahman," etc. Which is that? — "ya ātmā" — by the word "ātman" the inmost Self is denoted, since the word "ātman" is well-known in this sense; that which is the innermost of all is sarvāntara. If by the words "yat" and "yaḥ" the well-known Ātman is meant as Brahman, that very Ātman explain to me, mahyam, vyācakṣva — clearly, as one shows a cow having grasped it by the horn, so explain — say "this is that" thus.

Being so addressed, Yājñavalkya replied: "This is your Ātman who is innermost in all"; "sarvāntara" is taken to designate all qualifications. The Brahman which is sākṣāt — unobstructed — aparokṣāt — non-figurative — bṛhattamam — the largest — Ātman — who is the innermost of all — endowed with all these qualities is this. Which is that Ātman of yours? — that which is the aggregate of body and senses (kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta), that is yours; the Self by virtue of which one is endowed with self — that is your Ātman, that is, of yours, the aggregate of body and senses. Therein the body, within it the liṅgātman, the senses' aggregate, and the third about which there is doubt — among these which is my Ātman, sarvāntara, that you intend? When asked thus, the other replies: "He who breathes by means of the prāṇa moving in the mouth and nostrils" — who performs prāṇa-activity, by whom prāṇa is led — that is your Ātman, the vijñāna-maya; the rest is to be supplied similarly. "Yo'pānena apāniti yo vyānena vyāniti" — there is Vedic lengthening. All the activities of prāṇana etc. in the body-and-senses aggregate are accomplished by the one by whom they are accomplished, like a wooden machine; for in a wooden machine not superintended by something conscious, prāṇa-activities and the like do not occur. Therefore, governed by the vijñāna-maya, distinct from it like a wooden machine, the body undertakes prāṇa-activity etc.; therefore He who causes activity is distinct from the body-and-senses aggregate.
BR_C03_S04_V02: Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa said: "As one might say, 'this is a cow, this is a horse,' just so this Brahman is being merely indicated by you. That very Brahman which is direct and immediate, the Ātman who is innermost in all — explain that to me." "This is your Ātman who is innermost in all." "Which one, Yājñavalkya, is innermost in all?" "You cannot see the seer of seeing; you cannot hear the hearer of hearing; you cannot think the thinker of thinking; you cannot know the knower of knowing. This is your Ātman who is innermost in all; everything other than this is afflicted (ārta)." Thereupon Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa ceased.
BR_C03_S04_V02::block-0:
Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa said: As someone, having promised one thing earlier, may then in a contradicted state speak otherwise — "that is a cow, that is a horse, which moves or runs" — having promised at first "I shall show it as pratyakṣa," subsequently designates by the marks of motion and so on — just so this Brahman is designated by you by the marks of prāṇa-activity and the rest. Why prolong? Setting aside the deceit prompted by the thirst for cow-mongering, that very Brahman which is direct, immediate, the Ātman, the innermost of all — explain that to me. The other says: As I first declared, your Ātman is of such nature — I abide by that very pratijñā; that is just so as has been said by me. As to what you stated again, namely that I should make that Ātman an object like a pot — that cannot be done because of impossibility. Why is this impossible? — On account of the very nature of the entity (vastu-svābhāvyāt). What is that nature? — That He is the seer of seeing, etc.; for the Ātman is the dṛṣṭer-draṣṭā. Dṛṣṭi is of two kinds — laukikī and pāramārthikī. The laukikī is the inner-organ-modification connected with the eye; that, being effected, is born and perishes. But the dṛṣṭi which is of the Ātman, like the heat and light of fire, since it is the very nature of the seer, neither is born nor perishes. That, conjoined with the upādhi (the produced laukikī), is as it were superimposed; thus is it designated as "draṣṭā," and as if endowed with difference — "draṣṭā, dṛṣṭi." That laukikī dṛṣṭi which is in the form of an action through the eye, coloured by form, being produced, is as it were conjoined with the eternal Ātma-dṛṣṭi; suffused by its reflection, it arises and likewise perishes; hence the Ātman is figuratively spoken of as "draṣṭā" though seeing always — "he sees" or "does not see." But of the seer's dṛṣṭi there is never any other-becoming; thus he will say in the sixth chapter — "as it were he meditates, as it were he moves" (Bṛ. U. 4.3.7), and "there is no cessation of the seer's seeing" (Bṛ. U. 4.3.23).

This very meaning he conveys: of the laukikī dṛṣṭi as karman, the draṣṭā as pervader by his own eternal dṛṣṭi — you cannot see; that laukikī dṛṣṭi as object, being coloured by form, manifesting the form, does not pervade the Ātman, the pratyañc, who pervades it; therefore that pratyag-ātman, the seer of seeing, you cannot see. Likewise, the hearer of hearing you cannot hear; the thinker of mati, that is, of the mere mental modification, the pervader, you cannot think; likewise the knower of mere intellect-modification, vijñāti, you cannot know. This is the very nature of the entity; therefore it cannot be shown like a cow.
BR_C03_S04_V02::block-1:
In "na dṛṣṭer draṣṭāram," some explain the words otherwise — "do not see the doer of dṛṣṭi, the agent of dṛṣṭi, without distinguishing dṛṣṭi-types, the doer of dṛṣṭi merely"; "dṛṣṭeḥ" is karmaṇi-ṣaṣṭhī (objective genitive); that dṛṣṭi, being effected, becomes karman like a pot; "draṣṭāram" with tṛc-affix expresses agency of dṛṣṭi for the draṣṭā; thus "the seer of seeing" means "the agent of seeing" — such is the intent of those expositors. There the use of the word "dṛṣṭeḥ" with ṣaṣṭhī becomes useless — that dosha they do not see; or seeing it, they do not care, dismissing it as a tautology, a worthless or careless reading. How is the redundancy? — Because by the tṛc-affix the agency of dṛṣṭi is established, the use of "dṛṣṭeḥ" is useless; then "draṣṭāram na paśyeḥ" alone should be said. The tṛc-affix that comes after a verbal root is laid down for the agent of that very verb's meaning; the form actually used is just "gantāram, bhettāraṃ vā nayati" — not "gater gantāraṃ bhider bhettāram" without there being any special meaning. Nor is the doubled use to be jettisoned as arthavāda when there is a real meaning available; nor is it a faulty reading, since none of the recensions disagree; therefore the weakness lies in those expositors' intellect, not in the readers' carelessness.

As we have explained, distinguishing the laukikī dṛṣṭi, the Ātman is to be shown as endowed with the eternal dṛṣṭi — for that purpose the dṛṣṭi-word is used twice, as qualifying agent and object, to determine the Ātman's nature; and "na hi draṣṭur dṛṣṭeḥ" of another passage tallies as a single statement; thus also one-statement-ness with another śruti — "he sees the eyes" (Kena 1.7), "this hearing is heard" (Kena 1.8) — is established. By logic too: only thus is the Ātman's eternality intelligible, in the absence of modification (vikriyā); the eternal being modificatory is contradictory. "As it were he meditates" (Bṛ. U. 4.3.7), "there is no cessation of the seer's seeing" (Bṛ. U. 4.3.23), "this is the eternal greatness of the Brahman-knower" (Bṛ. U. 4.4.23) — these śruti-words do not go any other way.

Is it not that words like "draṣṭā," "śrotā," "mantā," "vijñātā," do not go without admitting the Ātman's vikriyā? — No, since they are anuvāda of ordinary expressions as they happen to occur; they are not for the determination of the Self's truth; from the impossibility of any other purport for "na dṛṣṭer draṣṭāram" and the like, we understand the qualification of "dṛṣṭi" was abandoned only out of misunderstanding. "This is your Ātman," qualified by all the said qualifications; therefore other than this Ātman, everything is ārta — afflicted; whether the effect, the body, or the liṅga of the form of the senses; this alone is the one anārta, indestructible, kūṭastha. Then Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa ceased.
BR_C03_S05_INTRO1::block-0: Bondage with its impelling cause has been declared. And of him who is bound, his existence has been ascertained, and his distinctness too. Now the means of bondage and liberation, namely Self-knowledge accompanied by sannyāsa, ought to be set forth — therefore the question of Kahola is begun.
BR_C03_S05_V01: Then Kahola Kauṣītakeya questioned him. He said: "Yājñavalkya, explain to me that very Brahman which is immediate and direct, the Self which is within all." "This is your Self which is within all." "Which one, Yājñavalkya, is the Self within all?" "That which transcends hunger and thirst, sorrow, delusion, old age, and death. Having known this very Self, Brāhmaṇas renounce the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, and live the life of mendicants. For the desire for sons is the desire for wealth, and the desire for wealth is the desire for worlds — both these are mere desires. Therefore let the Brāhmaṇa, having become disgusted with learning, desire to abide in the state of a child. Having become disgusted with both childhood and learning, he becomes a muni; and having become disgusted with both non-silence and silence, he becomes a Brāhmaṇa. By what means would he be a Brāhmaṇa? By that means by which he is. Anything other than this is afflicted." Thereupon Kahola Kauṣītakeya held his peace.
BR_C03_S05_V01::block-0:
