Then Kahola by name, the son of Kuṣītaka, hence Kauṣītakeya, questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," he said, as before — "Explain to me that very Brahman which is immediate and direct, the Self which is within all" — knowing which one is released from bondage. Yājñavalkya replied: "This is your Self."

A doubt arises: was a single Self questioned about by both Uṣasta and Kahola, or were two distinct selves possessing similar characteristics being asked about? Some explain thus: it is fitting that they are distinct, since otherwise the two questions would be redundant; for if a single Self were intended in both questions, the second question — already answered by the first — would be purposeless. The text cannot be reduced to mere arthavāda. Hence, they say, these are two distinct selves named the kṣetrajña and the Paramātman. This view is wrong, for the pratijñā in the answer "This is your Self" precludes it. Moreover, two selves cannot belong to one body-organ aggregate; one body-organ aggregate is endowed with self by one Self alone. Nor can the Self of Uṣasta and the Self of Kahola be different in kind, since the qualities of being non-figurative, of being Self, and of being innermost cannot apply to two equally — for if Brahman in the primary sense be the Self of one, then for the other it must be in a secondary sense. The same applies to selfhood and innermost-ness, since these notions are mutually contradictory between the two. Therefore the same Self is heard of twice for the sake of expressing a particular distinction. Whatever in the second question is repeated from the first is mere anuvāda — that some unstated particular concerning the same Self has yet to be told. What is that distinction? In the previous question, the question was whether a Self exists distinct from the body, having that bondage and its purpose declared. In the second question, that very Self's transcendence of saṃsāra-dharmas like hunger and the rest is being taught — by knowing which distinction, together with renunciation, one is freed from the bondage previously spoken of. Hence in both question and answer ending with "This is your Self," the import is identical. But how can transcendence of hunger and the like, and possession of those very qualities, be predicated of the very same Self — a coexistence of contradictory attributes? This has already been resolved: saṃsāra-hood is mere illusion arising from contact with the limiting adjuncts of body, organs, and the aggregate, which are modifications of name and form — as we have repeatedly stated, when explaining apparently contradictory śrutis. Just as rope, mother-of-pearl, and sky appear stained with snake, silver, and dirt — qualified by attributes superimposed by another — while in themselves rope, mother-of-pearl, and sky are pure, so there is no contradiction in the coexistence of contradictory attributes in entities.

If it is objected that, were name-and-form upādhis to truly exist, śrutis like "One only, without a second" (Chā. Up. 6.2.1) and "There is no manyness here whatsoever" (Br. Up. 4.4.19) would be contradicted — no; this is resolved by the analogy of water and foam, and by the analogies of clay and the like. When, by the highest insight, name and form, examined separately from the supreme Self in accordance with śruti, do not in truth exist as distinct entities — like the modifications of clay etc., or like the modifications of water, foam, jar etc. — then with reference to that, the Self becomes the object of supreme insight as expressed in "One only, without a second" and "There is no manyness here whatsoever." Like one possessing a form, abiding in one's own form, untouched in nature by anything yet not discriminated from the body-organ upādhis fashioned of name and form — when the perception of the upādhis of name and form alone becomes natural — then the entire usage "a different entity exists" arises.
BR_C03_S05_V01::block-1:
There, with reference to the supreme nature of the Self, the question is again raised: "Which, Yājñavalkya, is the innermost?" The other replies: "That which transcends hunger and thirst." The desire to eat is aśanāyā; the desire to drink is pipāsā. These — "who transcends them" — connects with what follows. Just as space, traversed though it be by the unwise as having floor and dust like a floor, in truth transcends the floor and dust because its nature is unaffected by them — so Brahman, though apprehended by the deluded as having hunger and thirst, with notions "I am hungry, I am thirsty," in truth transcends them, since by nature it is untouched by them. As the śruti says, "The outer one is not affected by the world's sorrows" (Kaṭha Up. 2.2.11) — meaning by sorrows superimposed by the unenlightened. Hunger and thirst are compounded together because they share prāṇa as their single substratum. Sorrow and delusion: śoka means desire — for, considering some desired object, that uneasiness one feels when overpowered by craving is the seed of desire, by which desire is kindled; moha is the discrimination-less confusion arising from contrary cognition, which is avidyā, the seed of every misfortune. Since śoka and moha have different effects, they are not compounded. Both reside in the manas. Likewise, residing in the body, He transcends old age and death. Jarā is the transformation of the body-organ aggregate, marked by wrinkles, gray hair, and the like; mṛtyu is its rupture, the conclusion of that transformation; both these abide in the body and are transcended.

Those hungers and the like which reside in prāṇa, manas, and body, ever recurring among living beings like day-and-night and like ocean waves, are spoken of as saṃsāra. That Self characterized as "the seer of seeing" and so on, immediate, unbroken, direct, non-figurative, and innermost — that Self is never touched by saṃsāra-dharmas of hunger, thirst, etc. — like space untouched by clouds and other defilements — among beings from Brahmā down to a tuft of grass. Knowing this very Self as one's own essence — "I am this supreme Brahman, ever liberated from all saṃsāra, ever satisfied" — Brāhmaṇas (Brāhmaṇas alone are entitled to vyutthāna, hence the word "Brāhmaṇas") arising in opposition, that is having performed an arising in the contrary direction. From what? Putraiṣaṇā: the desire for a son is the desire to win this world through a son — "by a son let me conquer this world" — the means of conquering the world being a son, hence the taking of a wife. Without taking a wife is the meaning. And vittaiṣaṇā: the acquisition of cows etc. as means of karma — "By performing rituals with this I shall conquer the world of the fathers," or, joined with vidyā, the world of the gods, or by hiraṇyagarbha-vidyā alone, the world of the gods through divine wealth. Some say there is no rising above divine wealth, since vyutthāna is supposed to depend on its strength. This is wrong, for "This much is desire" (Br. Up. 1.4.17) is read as including divine wealth among the eṣaṇās. The vidyā concerning Hiraṇyagarbha and other deities is called vitta because it is a means to the world of the gods; but Brahmavidyā, whose object is the unconditioned dense mass of consciousness, is not a cause of the world of the gods, by the śruti "Therefore he became all that" (Br. Up. 1.4.10) and "Their Self he becomes" (Br. Up. 1.4.1). And it is by the strength of that knowledge that vyutthāna takes place, by the special saying "having known this very Self" (Br. Up. 3.5.1). Therefore, from all three of these — means leading to non-self worlds.
BR_C03_S05_V01::block-2: Pūrvapakṣa: "Vyutthāyātha bhikṣācaryaṃ caranti" — the present-tense usage shows it to be merely arthavāda; no injunctive — neither liṅ, nor loṭ, nor tavya — is heard. Hence by mere arthavāda one cannot be made to renounce means like the sacred thread enjoined by śruti and smṛti: "He should study only as one wearing the sacred thread, and let him cause others to perform sacrifice or sacrifice himself" (Tai. Ār. 2.1.1). For the wandering ascetic, study is enjoined: "By renouncing the Veda one becomes a Śūdra, therefore one should not renounce the Veda"; and "By svādhyāya itself one renounces speech" (Āp. Dh. 2.21.10), says Āpastamba. "Forsaking Brahman, reviling the Veda, false witness, slaying a friend, and the eating of forbidden food and drink — drinking liquor is equal to all six" (Manu 11.56) — such defects are heard of in renouncing the Veda. "At the worship of teachers, elders, guests, at homa, japa, eating, ācamana, and svādhyāya — let him wear the sacred thread" (Āp. Dh. 1.15.1). Since duties such as guru-worship, svādhyāya, eating, and ācamana are enjoined as obligatory in śruti and smṛti even for the parivrājaka, and since the sacred thread is enjoined as a limb of guru-worship etc., its abandonment cannot be conceded. Even if vyutthāna from desires is enjoined, it is only from the three desires for son etc., not from all karma and its means. Total renunciation would be doing the unenjoined and abandoning what is enjoined — like the sacred thread. Thus a great trespass would be incurred from non-performance of the enjoined and performance of the prohibited. Hence the abandonment of marks like the sacred thread is mere blind tradition.
BR_C03_S05_V01::block-3: Siddhānta: No, by the śruti "The yati should give up the sacred thread, the Vedas, all that" (Kaṇṭhaśruti 2). Moreover, since all of the Upaniṣad is concerned with knowledge of the Self — "the Self is to be seen, heard, reflected upon" being the topic introduced — that very Self is to be known as immediate, direct, innermost, free of saṃsāra-dharmas like hunger; this is well-known. Since this entire Upaniṣad is devoted to that, it is not subordinate to some other injunction; hence it is not arthavāda, since the knowledge of the Self is to be performed. The Self must be known as different from a sādhana with a phala, untouched by hunger and the like. Hence non-discrimination between the Self and the not-Self is avidyā: "He thinks 'this one is other, I am other'" (Br. Up. 1.4.10), "He does not know"; "He goes from death to death who sees diversity here" (Br. Up. 4.4.19); "It is to be seen as one alone" (Chā. Up. 6.2.1); "One only without a second"; "That thou art" (Chā. Up. 6.8.7) — by these śrutis. Means, fruit, and action belong to a domain other than the Self that transcends saṃsāra-dharmas like hunger — within the realm of avidyā: "For where there is duality as it were" (Br. Up. 2.4.14); "He thinks 'this one is other, I am other'" (Br. Up. 1.4.10); "He does not know"; "But those who know otherwise than this" (Chā. Up. 7.25.2) — by these hundreds of texts. Vidyā and avidyā cannot coexist in one person, being mutually opposed like darkness and light. Therefore for the knower of the Self, the realm of avidyā — the diversity of action, agent, instrument, and fruit — should not be retained, since it is condemned as in "He goes from death to death," and since all means and fruits within the realm of avidyā are to be relinquished by the Self-knowledge contrary to it; and means like the sacred thread belong to that realm. Hence, distinct from the Self whose nature is non-means and non-fruit, eṣaṇā having different objects is heterogeneous. "Both these are mere eṣaṇās" — these means and fruits, the sacred thread etc. and the karmas accomplished by them, being themselves means, by the determinative reasoning "Both these are mere eṣaṇās." Vyutthāna from means like the sacred thread and from the rituals accomplished by them is precisely what is intended for injunction, since they belong to the realm of avidyā, are of the nature of eṣaṇā, and are to be abandoned. If it be objected: since the Upaniṣad is devoted to Self-knowledge, the śruti about vyutthāna is for praising it, not an injunction — no, since it is heard with the same agent as the knowledge intended to be enjoined; what is not to be done is never heard with the same agent as what is to be done. As the offerings, oblations, and partaking — "Having pressed, having offered, they partake" — are heard with the same agent because all are obligatory, so Self-knowledge, eṣaṇā-vyutthāna, and bhikṣācarya are heard with the same agent because all are obligatory. If it be argued that, since renunciation of the sacred thread and the rest is gained by implication from the very injunction of Self-knowledge — being objects of avidyā and of the form of eṣaṇā — it need not be enjoined separately — no; it is all the more well-grounded by the injunction of Self-knowledge itself, by the same-agent hearing being a strengthener; likewise for bhikṣācarya. The previous objection — that the present-tense usage makes it mere arthavāda — is no fault, since it is parallel to injunctions about the udumbara-yūpa.
BR_C03_S05_V01::block-4: By "Vyutthāya bhikṣācaryaṃ caranti," the parivrājaka order is enjoined; and in the parivrājaka āśrama, means like the sacred thread are enjoined together with their distinguishing marks by śruti and smṛti. Hence vyutthāna is from other things, even though they too are eṣaṇā. No: another parivrājya — characterized as eṣaṇā-vyutthāna and having the same agent as Self-knowledge — is established. That parivrājya which is characterized as vyutthāna from eṣaṇās is a limb of Self-knowledge, since it is of the nature of relinquishing the eṣaṇās opposed to Self-knowledge, and since eṣaṇā is within the realm of avidyā. Distinct from this, there is also an āśrama-form parivrājya, a means to attain fruits like the world of Brahman, in connection with which the sacred thread and other means with their marks are enjoined. The taking up of means in the form of eṣaṇā, while possible in another parivrājya as a mere āśrama-dharma, must not be allowed to set aside the Self-knowledge enjoined in all the Upaniṣads — for, by entertaining a wish to take up means in the form of eṣaṇā, objects of avidyā like the sacred thread, the cognition "I am Brahman, free of saṃsāra-dharmas like hunger, of the nature of non-means and non-fruit" is necessarily set aside; and that setting aside is improper, since all the Upaniṣads have it as their import. If it be argued that the very śruti "They live the bhikṣā life" enforces an eṣaṇā and so itself sets aside Self-knowledge — even granting that, having enjoined vyutthāna from eṣaṇās, the śruti enforcing bhikṣācarya as one part of eṣaṇā might enforce other connected items also — no; bhikṣācarya is not an end-producer, like partaking after offering. It is the action of disposing of the remainder, hence not productive. It is also not a saṃskāra. Eating is at best a saṃskāra of the person; bhikṣācarya is not. The unseen result of niyama is undesired for the Brahmavid. If the unseen result of niyama is undesired, what use is bhikṣācarya? No, vyutthāna by another means is enjoined. What use then is bhikṣācarya? If there were any, granted, we accept it. The texts pertaining to the parivrājaka — "Let him study while wearing the sacred thread" (Tai. Ār. 2.1.1) etc. — are explained as relating to the parivrājya of one not yet a knower; otherwise Self-knowledge would be set aside, as already said. "Without expectation, without undertaking, without salutation or praise; undecaying, with karmas exhausted — him the gods know as a Brāhmaṇa" (Mokṣadharma 263.34) — smṛti shows the absence of all karma in the knower; "The wise one is devoid of marks," "Therefore the knower of dharma is markless" (Aśva. 46.51). Hence the Self-knower attains only the parivrājya of the paramahaṃsa, characterized as vyutthāna and consisting in the relinquishment of all means of action.
BR_C03_S05_V01::block-5: Since the ancient Brāhmaṇas, having known this Self whose nature is neither means nor fruit, and rising up out of every form of means-and-fruit characterized as eṣaṇā, lived the bhikṣā life — having abandoned action aimed at the seen and unseen, and its means — therefore even today the Brāhmaṇa, the knower of Brahman, having become disgusted with paṇḍita-bhāva, this Self-knowledge being paṇḍita-bhāva, having fully comprehended it, that is, having made Self-knowledge complete by way of teacher and scripture, having risen up from the eṣaṇās — for that paṇḍitya culminates in eṣaṇā-vyutthāna, since it arises by overthrowing eṣaṇā and is opposed to eṣaṇā; without overthrowing eṣaṇā, paṇḍitya regarding the Self does not arise — hence eṣaṇā-vyutthāna is enjoined by Self-knowledge itself, strengthened by the liṅga-śruti of taking up the same-agent indicator. Hence, having risen up from the eṣaṇās, let him desire to abide in bālya — childlikeness consisting in jñāna-bala. The strength of others, the non-knowers of the Self, is the dependence on means and fruits; abandoning that strength, the wise one should rest in that strength alone which is Self-knowledge whose nature is non-means and non-fruit. When that is sought as refuge, the senses cannot drag him to the realm of eṣaṇā and place him there. The senses install the deluded one — devoid of the strength of knowledge — only in eṣaṇā, in the realm of seen and unseen. Bala here means the casting aside of all object-perceptions by Self-vidyā. Hence let him desire to abide in that bālya, that childlike state — as another śruti says, "By the Self one obtains vigor" (Kena Up. 2.4) and "This Self is not gained by one without strength" (Muṇḍ. Up. 3.2.4). Having become disgusted with both bālya and pāṇḍitya, fully exhausting them, then by reflection he becomes a muni, a yogī. This much alone has the Brāhmaṇa to do — namely, the casting aside of every notion of the not-Self. Having done this, the yogī is one whose duty is fulfilled. Having become disgusted with amauna and mauna — both of which, the casting aside of Self-knowledge and the casting aside of the notion of not-Self, are designated pāṇḍitya and bālya — the term mauna means the culminating fruit of the casting aside of the notion of not-Self. Disgusted with that too, then he becomes the Brāhmaṇa whose duty is fulfilled — the cognition "Brahman alone is all" arises. He is the Brāhmaṇa whose duty is fulfilled, hence the Brāhmaṇa; for then his Brāhmaṇa-hood is non-figurative, attained. Hence: "By what means would he be a Brāhmaṇa?" — by what conduct would he be one? By that by which he is — by whatever conduct one is — by that he is just such a Brāhmaṇa as has been described. "By whatever conduct" is for praise — this state of Brāhmaṇa-hood is being praised, not disregarding conduct. Hence apart from this state of Brāhmaṇa-hood, this Self-nature transcending hunger etc., ever satisfied — anything else, in the realm of avidyā, characterized as eṣaṇā, another entity — is afflicted, perishable, gripped by suffering, like dream, illusion, mirage-water, sapless. The Self alone is one, only, ever liberated. Thereupon Kahola Kauṣītakeya held his peace.
BR_C03_S06_V01: Then Gārgī Vācaknavī questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," she said, "since all this is woven, warp and woof, on water, on what then is water woven, warp and woof?" "On air, Gārgī." "On what, then, is air woven, warp and woof?" "On the worlds of the antarikṣa, Gārgī." "On what, then, are the worlds of the antarikṣa woven, warp and woof?" "On the worlds of the gandharvas, Gārgī." "On what, then, are the worlds of the gandharvas woven, warp and woof?" "On the worlds of the sun, Gārgī." "On what, then, are the worlds of the sun woven, warp and woof?" "On the worlds of the moon, Gārgī." "On what, then, are the worlds of the moon woven, warp and woof?" "On the worlds of the nakṣatras, Gārgī." "On what, then, are the worlds of the nakṣatras woven, warp and woof?" "On the worlds of the gods, Gārgī." "On what, then, are the worlds of the gods woven, warp and woof?" "On the worlds of Indra, Gārgī." "On what, then, are the worlds of Indra woven, warp and woof?" "On the worlds of Prajāpati, Gārgī." "On what, then, are the worlds of Prajāpati woven, warp and woof?" "On the worlds of Brahman, Gārgī." "On what, then, are the worlds of Brahman woven, warp and woof?" He said: "Gārgī, do not question too much, lest your head fall off. You are questioning beyond a deity that is not to be questioned. Gārgī, do not question too much." Thereupon Gārgī Vācaknavī held her peace.
BR_C03_S06_V01::block-0:
What was stated as the Brahman that is immediate, direct, the Self within all — for the sake of grasping the very nature of that innermost one, the section continues up to the Śākalya brāhmaṇa. The five elements from earth up to ākāśa are arranged within and without each other; refuting each outer one as one ascends inward, the seer's immediate, non-figurative, innermost Self, free of all saṃsāra-dharmas, is to be shown — hence this beginning.

Then Gārgī by name, daughter of Vacaknu, hence Vācaknavī, questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," she said: "all this earthen substance — woven warp and woof on water — ota is like the lengthwise warp threads, prota like the crosswise woof threads, or vice versa — meaning, pervaded inside and out by water; otherwise it would crumble like a fistful of barley flour." Thus far an inference is set forth: a coarse, limited effect is observed pervaded by an unlimited, subtle cause — like earth by water; thus each preceding one must be pervaded by each succeeding one — this is the import of the question, which proceeds up to the Self within all. There the five elements, conjoined, abide as the cause-form, the next ever subtler and more pervasive; and prior to the Paramātman there exists no other entity apart from these, by the śruti "the Truth of truth" (Br. Up. 2.3.6). The five elements are the truth, and the supreme Self is the truth of truth.

"On what is water woven warp and woof?" — since water too, being an effect, gross, and limited, must be in the warp-woof relation somewhere; where is its warp-woof relation? In this manner the chain of successive questions is to be construed.

"On air, Gārgī." Why not "on fire," one might ask — no fault: fire, without resorting to an earthly or watery substance, has no independent attainment of self like the other elements, hence no warp-woof relation is taught in it. "On what is air woven warp and woof?" "On the worlds of antarikṣa, Gārgī." Those very same elements conjoined are the worlds of antarikṣa; and they too — on the gandharva-worlds, on the āditya-worlds, on the candra-worlds, on the nakṣatra-worlds, on the deva-worlds, on the indra-worlds, on the elements that constitute the body of Virāṭ — the prajāpati-worlds, on the prajāpati-worlds — the brahma-worlds, the elements that constitute the cosmic egg. Everywhere it is the same five elements, but in successive degrees of subtlety, transformed into the abode-forms of beings' enjoyment, hence used in the plural. "On what are the brahma-worlds woven warp and woof?" — Yājñavalkya replied: "Gārgī, do not question too much, beyond the proper method, regarding a deity to be questioned by āgama, do not question by inference; otherwise your head, while questioning, would surely fall off — split apart." The deity's own question is one of the realm of āgama; Gārgī's question, being inferential, has overstepped the realm of that question. The deity whose question is hers is atipraśnya (over-questionable); the not-overquestionable is anatipraśnyā — i.e., the realm of her own question, accessible only by āgama. Thereupon Gārgī Vācaknavī held her peace.
BR_C03_S07_V01: Then Uddālaka Āruṇi questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," he said, "we lived among the Madras in the house of Patañjala Kāpya, studying yajña. He had a wife possessed by a gandharva. We asked him: 'Who are you?' He said: 'I am Kabandha Ātharvaṇa.' He said to Patañjala Kāpya and the yājñikas: 'Kāpya, do you know that thread by which this world and the next world and all beings are bound together?' Patañjala Kāpya said: 'I do not know it, sir.' He said to Patañjala Kāpya and the yājñikas: 'Kāpya, do you know that Inner Controller who controls this world and the next and all beings from within?' Patañjala Kāpya said: 'I do not know him, sir.' He said to Patañjala Kāpya and the yājñikas: 'Whoever, Kāpya, knows that thread and that Inner Controller — he is a knower of Brahman, of the worlds, of the gods, of the Vedas, of beings, of the Self; he is the all-knower.' To them he told it. I know it. If you, Yājñavalkya, while not knowing the thread and the Inner Controller, drive away the cows of Brahman-knowers, your head will fall off." "O Gautama, I do indeed know that thread and that Inner Controller." "Anyone may say 'I know, I know'; but tell as you know."
BR_C03_S07_V01::block-0:
Now the Sūtra, innermost to the brahma-worlds, must be taught — for which the section begins. It is to be questioned only by āgama, hence the introduction of āgama through an itihāsa. Then Uddālaka by name, son of Aruṇa, hence Āruṇi, questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," he said: "In the Madra country we dwelt — in the house of Patañjala Kāpya by name, of the Kapi gotra — studying yajña, that is, undertaking the study of yajña-śāstra. His wife was possessed by a gandharva; we asked him: 'Who are you?' He said: 'I am Kabandha by name, son of Atharvan, hence Ātharvaṇa.'

The gandharva said to Patañjala Kāpya and to the yājñikas, his disciples: 'Kāpya, do you know that thread? — that thread by which this world, this birth, and the other world, the birth that is to come, and all beings, from Brahmā down to a tuft of grass, are bound together — strung as on a thread, like a garland, supported. Do you know that thread?' Thus questioned, Kāpya replied: 'I do not know it, sir' — saying 'sir' in honor.

The gandharva again addressed our teacher and us: 'Kāpya, do you know that Inner Controller — qualified by the term antaryāmin — who, abiding within this world and the next world and all beings, controls them, makes them rotate as a wooden mechanism, causing each to perform its own appointed task?' Thus questioned, Patañjala Kāpya replied: 'I do not know him, sir' — saying 'sir' in honor.

Again the gandharva spoke; the knowledge of the Sūtra and the Antaryāmin within it is now praised: 'Whoever, Kāpya, knows that Sūtra and that Antaryāmin within the Sūtra, the controller of that very Sūtra — knows him as described — he is the knower of Brahman, the supreme Self; he knows the worlds, bhūr and the rest, controlled by the antaryāmin; he knows the gods like Agni who possess those worlds; he knows the Vedas, all proofs; he knows the beings, from Brahmā downward, supported by the Sūtra and controlled by the Antaryāmin within it; he knows the Self — endowed with agency and enjoyment, controlled by that very Antaryāmin; and he knows all the world likewise — thus.' Hearing this praise of the knowledge of the Sūtra and Antaryāmin, Kāpya was drawn to it, and so were we.

To us, drawn to it, the gandharva spoke of the Sūtra and the Antaryāmin. That knowledge of the Sūtra and Antaryāmin I know, having received it from the gandharva. If you, Yājñavalkya, are not the knower of that Sūtra and that Antaryāmin, not the knower of Brahman, and yet are wrongly driving away the cows that belong to the knowers of Brahman, then, scorched by my curse, your head — your skull — will surely fall off.

Thus addressed, Yājñavalkya said: "Gautama by gotra, I do know it — that Sūtra which the gandharva told you, and the Antaryāmin whom you came to know from the gandharva — I know him." Gautama replied: "Anyone might say 'I know, I know'; tell as you know."
BR_C03_S07_V02: He said: "Air, O Gautama, is that thread. Indeed, by air as the thread, this world and the next world and all beings are bound together. Therefore, O Gautama, of one who has departed they say: 'His limbs have come unstrung,' for indeed by air as the thread they are bound together." "Just so, Yājñavalkya. Now tell us of the Inner Controller."
BR_C03_S07_V02::block-0: Yājñavalkya said: that on which the brahma-worlds are at present woven warp and woof — like earth on water — that Sūtra, accessible only by āgama, is to be told. For its determination he speaks: "Air, O Gautama, is that Sūtra," not anything else. Air — the subtle pillar like ākāśa, supporter of earth and the rest, the seventeenfold liṅga consisting of the residual karma-impressions of beings, both samaṣṭi and vyaṣṭi — whose external divisions are the seven and seven Marut hosts, like waves of the ocean — that vāyavya tattva is called the Sūtra. "By air, O Gautama, as the Sūtra, this world and the next world and all beings are bound together, woven" — this is well-known. There is also a popular saying establishing it: how? — since air is the Sūtra, all is upheld by air; therefore, O Gautama, they say of the deceased: "His limbs have come unstrung," "his limbs have fallen apart" — for upon the Sūtra's withdrawal, the bead-like limbs strung upon it would naturally fall apart. Thus air is the Sūtra; if his limbs were strung upon it like beads, then their unstringing on the withdrawal of air is just so. Hence "By air, O Gautama, as the Sūtra they are bound together" — this is the conclusion. Gautama said: "Just so, Yājñavalkya — the Sūtra has been correctly stated. Now tell of the Antaryāmin within that very Sūtra, the controller of the Sūtra itself." Thus addressed, he speaks.
BR_C03_S07_V03: He who, dwelling in the earth, is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who controls the earth from within — He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.
BR_C03_S07_V03::block-0: He who, dwelling in the earth, is the antaryāmin. Lest the contingency arise everywhere — "all dwell in the earth" — He is qualified: He is within the earth, abhyantara. Here it might be supposed that the earth-deity herself is the antaryāmin; therefore He says: whom the antaryāmin, the earth-deity, does not know — "some other dwells in me." Whose body is the earth — whose body is none other than the earth — that very body which is the body of the earth-deity is His body; and the term "body" is upalakṣaṇa for instruments as well — and the instruments of the earth as well as Hers. The action and instruments of the earth-deity are conditioned by her own karma; that, in His case — the antaryāmin, ever liberated, having no karma of his own, of the nature of acting only for another — whatever action and instruments belong to that other, those are His, but not by his own constitution. Hence: "whose body is the earth." Only by the bare proximity of the Lord as witness do the regulated activity and abstention of the deity-effected body and instruments occur. Such a Lord, named Nārāyaṇa, controls the earth — the earth-deity — in her own activity, dwelling within: He is your Self, of you, of me, of all beings — this is upalakṣaṇa — the antaryāmin about whom you asked, the Immortal — devoid of all saṃsāra-dharmas.
BR_C03_S07_V04: He who, dwelling in the waters, is within the waters, whom the waters do not know, whose body is the waters, who controls the waters from within — He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.
BR_C03_S07_V05: He who, dwelling in fire, is within fire, whom fire does not know, whose body is fire, who controls fire from within — He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.
BR_C03_S07_V06: He who, dwelling in the antarikṣa, is within the antarikṣa, whom the antarikṣa does not know, whose body is the antarikṣa, who controls the antarikṣa from within — He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.
BR_C03_S07_V07: He who, dwelling in air, is within air, whom air does not know, whose body is air, who controls air from within — He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
BR_C03_S07_V08: He who, dwelling in heaven, is within heaven, whom heaven does not know, whose body is heaven, who controls heaven from within — He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
BR_C03_S07_V09: He who, dwelling in the sun, is within the sun, whom the sun does not know, whose body is the sun, who controls the sun from within — He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
BR_C03_S07_V10: He who, dwelling in the directions, is within the directions, whom the directions do not know, whose body is the directions, who controls the directions from within — He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
BR_C03_S07_V11: He who, dwelling in the moon and stars, is within the moon and stars, whom the moon and stars do not know, whose body is the moon and stars, who controls the moon and stars from within — He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
BR_C03_S07_V12: He who, dwelling in space (ākāśa), is within space, whom space does not know, whose body is space, who controls space from within — He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
BR_C03_S07_V13: He who, dwelling in darkness, is within darkness, whom darkness does not know, whose body is darkness, who controls darkness from within — He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
BR_C03_S07_V14: He who, dwelling in light (tejas), is within light, whom light does not know, whose body is light, who controls light from within — He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal. Thus the adhidaivata exposition; now the adhibhūta.
BR_C03_S07_V14::block-0:
The remainder is uniform with what was earlier expounded (samānam anyat); the same construction — "yaḥ ... tiṣṭhan, ... antaraḥ, yam ... na veda, yasya ... śarīram, yaḥ ... antaraḥ yamayati, eṣa ta ātmā antaryāmī amṛtaḥ" — is to be applied in turn to each locus. He who dwells in the waters (apsu), in fire (agnau), in the intermediate region (antarikṣe), in air (vāyau), in heaven (divi), in the sun (āditye), in the directions (dikṣu), in the moon-and-stars (candratārake), in space (ākāśe); and he who dwells in tamas — that is, in outer darkness which is of the nature of veiling (āvaraṇātmake bāhye tamasi) — and in tejas, which is its opposite, the common form of luminosity (tadviparīte prakāśasāmānye): in this way the vision (darśanam) of the inner controller (antaryāmī) is presented as residing in the deities (devatāsu); this is the adhidaivata exposition.

Now the adhibhūta is to be set forth. The vision of the antaryāmī as residing in the bhūtas — that is, in beings ranging from Brahmā down to a clump of grass (brahmādistambaparyanteṣu) — is what is termed adhibhūta. Thus the same one Self, the inner controller, immortal, is to be contemplated under three heads: as pervading the deities (adhidaivata), as pervading the elements and beings (adhibhūta), and (as will be set forth next) as pervading the body-and-organs (adhyātma); the diversity of loci does not split the unity of the antaryāmī, since the very purport (tātparya) of the section is the establishment of one Brahman as the inner ruler of all.
BR_C03_S07_V15: He who, abiding in all beings, is yet other than (interior to) all beings, whom no being knows, of whom all beings are the body, who controls all beings from within—He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal. Thus the teaching with reference to beings (adhibhūta); now with reference to the self (adhyātma).
BR_C03_S07_V16: He who, abiding in the prāṇa, is yet other than (interior to) prāṇa, whom prāṇa does not know, of whom prāṇa is the body, who controls prāṇa from within—He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
BR_C03_S07_V17: He who, abiding in speech, is yet other than (interior to) speech, whom speech does not know, of whom speech is the body, who controls speech from within—He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
BR_C03_S07_V18: He who, abiding in the eye, is yet other than (interior to) the eye, whom the eye does not know, of whom the eye is the body, who controls the eye from within—He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
BR_C03_S07_V19: He who, abiding in the ear, is yet other than (interior to) the ear, whom the ear does not know, of whom the ear is the body, who controls the ear from within—He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
BR_C03_S07_V20: He who, abiding in the mind (manas), is yet other than (interior to) the mind, whom the mind does not know, of whom the mind is the body, who controls the mind from within—He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
BR_C03_S07_V21: He who, abiding in the skin, is yet other than (interior to) the skin, whom the skin does not know, of whom the skin is the body, who controls the skin from within—He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
BR_C03_S07_V22: He who, abiding in vijñāna (the cognising intellect), is yet other than (interior to) vijñāna, whom vijñāna does not know, of whom vijñāna is the body, who controls vijñāna from within—He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
BR_C03_S07_V23: ‘He who, abiding in the seed, is within the seed, whom the seed does not know, whose body is the seed, who controls the seed from within — He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal. Unseen, He is the seer; unheard, He is the hearer; unthought, He is the thinker; uncognised, He is the cogniser. There is no other seer than He, no other hearer than He, no other thinker than He, no other cogniser than He. He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal. All else than He is wretched.’ Thereupon Uddālaka Āruṇi held his peace.
BR_C03_S07_V23::block-0: Now the adhyātma (in relation to the body): ‘Who, abiding in the prāṇa’ — that is, in the organ of smell together with the vital air; ‘who, in speech, in the eye, in the ear, in the manas, in the skin, in vijñāna, in the buddhi, in the seed (reta) — i.e. in the organ of generation.’ For what reason, then, do the deities Earth and the rest, who are great and real, fail to know — like men and the like — Him who abides in them as their inner controller (antaryāmin)? To this it is replied: ‘Unseen’ (adṛṣṭa) — He is not seen, not made an object of the visual perception of anyone; yet, being intimately present in the eye and being of the very nature of seeing (dṛśi-svarūpa), He is Himself the seer. Likewise ‘unheard’ — not having become an object of the hearing of anyone; yet, since His power of hearing is never dimmed and He is intimately present in all ears, He is the hearer. So too ‘unthought’ — not having become an object of the manas’ resolve (saṅkalpa), for everyone forms saṅkalpa only about what has been seen or heard; precisely because He is unseen and unheard He is unthought; yet, since His power of manana is never dimmed and He is intimately present in all minds, He is the thinker. Likewise ‘uncognised’ — not having become an object of definite ascertainment, as colour and the rest, or pleasure and the rest, are; yet, since His power of vijñāna is never dimmed and since He is present therein, He is the cogniser. Now there might arise the apprehension: ‘Whom the earth does not know’ and ‘whom all beings do not know’ — these knowers are themselves to be controlled, and another, distinct from them, is the controller, the antaryāmin. To remove this suspicion of His being other (than the very seer-hearer-thinker-cogniser), it is said: ‘There is no other than He’ — there is no seer other than this antaryāmin; likewise no other hearer than He, no other thinker than He, no other cogniser than He. Since beyond Him there is no seer, hearer, thinker or cogniser — He who, Himself unseen, is the seer; unheard, the hearer; unthought, the thinker; uncognised, the cogniser; immortal (amṛta), free from all the dharmas of saṃsāra, the apportioner of the fruits of action to all transmigratory beings — ‘He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal’; whatever is other than this Lord-Self is ārta (wretched, afflicted). Thereupon Uddālaka Āruṇi held his peace.
BR_C03_S08_INTRO1::block-0: Hereafter, Brahman — free from hunger and the rest (aśanāyādi-vinirmukta), without upādhis (nirupādhika), directly known (sākṣād-aparokṣāt), the innermost of all (sarvāntara) — has to be expounded; hence the present commencement —
BR_C03_S08_V01: Then Vācaknavī (Gārgī) said: ‘Venerable brāhmaṇas, well — let me ask this man two questions. If he answers them for me, none among you will ever vanquish him in any discussion of Brahman.’ ‘Ask, Gārgī,’ they replied.
BR_C03_S08_V01::block-0: ‘Then Vācaknavī said.’ Earlier she had been silenced by Yājñavalkya through fear of her head falling off, and had desisted; now, wishing to question again, she seeks the consent of the brāhmaṇas: ‘O brāhmaṇas, venerable (bhagavantaḥ — worthy of honour), please listen to my words; well, I shall ask this Yājñavalkya two more questions, if you grant your permission. If he answers those two questions for me — somehow — then never (jātu = at any time) shall any one among you be a vanquisher of this Yājñavalkya in brahmodya, i.e. in discourse upon Brahman; none whatsoever shall be such.’ Thus addressed, the brāhmaṇas gave their consent: ‘Ask, Gārgī.’
BR_C03_S08_V02: She said: ‘Yājñavalkya, just as a hero’s son of Kāśi or of Videha, having strung an unstrung bow, taking in his hand two foe-piercing arrows, would rise up against (his enemy) — even so have I risen against you with two questions. Answer them for me.’ ‘Ask, Gārgī,’ said he.
BR_C03_S08_V02::block-0: Having received permission, she said to Yājñavalkya: ‘I shall ask you two questions’ — this is supplied by anuṣaṅga. To his curiosity ‘What are those two?’, in order to bring out their hard-to-answer character, she states them with an illustration: ‘O Yājñavalkya, just as in the world a Kāśya — one born among the Kāśis (in Kāśi-vigraha: kāśiṣu bhavaḥ kāśyaḥ); valour is well-known in a Kāśya — or a Vaideha, the king of the Videhas, an ugraputra — that is, of fierce (warrior) lineage — having taken an unstrung (avatārita-jyāka) bow and, after that, again strung (āropita-jyāka) it, holding two bāṇavantau — by the word bāṇa is meant the bamboo-segment fitted to the tip of the arrow; since arrows can exist even without that, she specifies bāṇavantau (‘equipped with bāṇas’) — two such arrows. Their further qualification: ‘sapatnāti-vyādhinau’ — exceedingly piercing/tormenting to the foe (sapatna). ‘Taking them in his hand, would rise up’ (upa-uttiṣṭhet) — i.e. would present himself in proximity. ‘Even so I have risen up against you’ (upodasthām, perfect, ‘I have stood up close’) with two questions that are like arrows. ‘Answer them for me’ — if you are a knower of Brahman. The other replies: ‘Ask, Gārgī.’
BR_C03_S08_V03: She said: ‘Yājñavalkya, that which is above the heaven, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two — heaven and earth — that which they call past, present, and future, in what is that woven, warp and woof?’
BR_C03_S08_V03::block-0: ‘She said.’ ‘That which is above’ — above the upper hemisphere of the cosmic egg, which is dyaus; ‘that which is below the earth’ — below the lower hemisphere of the egg; ‘that which is between’ — in the middle of the upper and lower hemispheres, dyaus and pṛthivī; ‘and these two, heaven and earth themselves’; ‘that which is past, that which is present’ — engaged in its own activity now; ‘and that which is future’ — what will come to be after the present, knowable through inferential signs (liṅga-gamya); ‘all that they declare’ — speak of, on the authority of the āgama. The meaning is: in what does this whole multitude of duality become one? In what is that — the previously mentioned (entity) called sūtra — woven and inwoven (otaṃ ca protaṃ ca), as the substance ‘earth’ is in waters?
BR_C03_S08_V04: He said: ‘Gārgī, that which is above the heaven, that which is below the earth, that which is between heaven and earth, these two themselves, that which they call past, present, and future — that is woven, warp and woof, in ākāśa.’
BR_C03_S08_V04::block-0: The other (Yājñavalkya) said: ‘O Gārgī, all that you have spoken of — “above the heaven,” etc. — what they call sūtra, that sūtra is woven and inwoven (otaṃ ca protaṃ ca) in ākāśa.’ This manifested universe of the form of sūtra abides in the unmanifested ākāśa — as the substance ‘earth’ in waters — in all three times, at origination, persistence, and dissolution.
BR_C03_S08_V05: She said: ‘Salutation to you, Yājñavalkya, that you have answered me this. Now brace yourself for the other.’ ‘Ask, Gārgī,’ (he said).
BR_C03_S08_V05::block-0: Again she said ‘Salutation to you’ etc., to show how hard the question (just answered) is to answer: ‘You who have specifically resolved this question of mine.’ The reason for its being hard to answer: even the sūtra itself is, to begin with, beyond the reach of others, hard to express; how much more so That in which the sūtra itself is woven and inwoven? Therefore ‘salutation to you’ (namo’stu te). ‘For the other (aparasmai), the second question, dhārayasva — make yourself firm,’ that is, brace yourself. The other says: ‘Ask, Gārgī.’
BR_C03_S08_V06: She said: ‘Yājñavalkya, that which is above the heaven, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two — heaven and earth — that which they call past, present, and future, in what is that woven, warp and woof?’
BR_C03_S08_V06::block-0: What is else has been explained. ‘She said: “Yājñavalkya, that which is above the heaven,” etc. — the question and the answer are restated for the sake of firmly fixing the same meaning already expounded; nothing fresh, no new meaning, is being introduced.
BR_C03_S08_V07: He said: ‘That, O Gārgī, which is above the heaven, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, that which they speak of as the past, the present, and the future — all that is woven, warp and woof, on space alone.’ ‘And in what, pray, is space itself woven, warp and woof?’
BR_C03_S08_V07::block-0: Yājñavalkya, having repeated all that Gārgī had said, settled upon the very same purport already stated, namely, ‘in space alone.’ Gārgī asks: ‘And in what, pray, is space itself woven, warp and woof?’ Space itself, being beyond the three times, is hard to describe; harder still than that is the Imperishable (akṣara), in which space is woven warp and woof — hence it is unspeakable. So thinking, if she were not to take it up at all, that would be the fault called apratipatti (failure to grasp the topic), a niggrahasthāna (ground of defeat) in the system of the logicians; on the other hand, were she to speak even of what is unspeakable, that would be the fault called vipratipatti (contradictory grasp), another niggrahasthāna — for to declare what is by nature unspeakable is itself a contradiction. Hence Gārgī conceives this question as one hard to answer.
BR_C03_S08_V08: He said: ‘That, O Gārgī, the knowers of Brahman call the Imperishable (akṣara) — neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long, not red, not viscous, without shadow, without darkness, without air, without space, unattached, without taste, without smell, without eyes, without ears, without speech, without mind, without lustre, without breath, without mouth, without measure, having neither inside nor outside. It eats nothing whatever, and nothing eats it.’
BR_C03_S08_V08::block-0: Wishing to remove both these faults, the text says: ‘He said,’ i.e., Yājñavalkya said. ‘This is verily that’ about which you asked, ‘In what is space woven, warp and woof?’ What is it? It is the Imperishable — that which does not perish (na kṣīyate) or wear away (na kṣarati), hence akṣara (the nirvacana etymology). ‘That, O Gārgī, the brāhmaṇas — the knowers of Brahman — declare.’ By saying ‘the brāhmaṇas declare,’ he avoids both faults: ‘I am not myself speaking the unspeakable, nor am I failing to take up the question.’ When the question has thus been disposed of, Gārgī’s further request is to be supplied: ‘Tell me — what is that Imperishable which the brāhmaṇas declare?’ To this he replies: ‘It is not gross’ — it is other than the gross. ‘Then let it be subtle (aṇu)’ — ‘not subtle.’ ‘Then let it be short’ — ‘not short.’ ‘Then let it be long’ — ‘not long either.’ Thus by these four denials of magnitude, the property of substance is denied: that Imperishable is not a substance. ‘Then let redness (a quality) belong to it’ — ‘not red’; redness is a quality of fire. ‘Then let it have the unctuousness of water’ — ‘not unctuous.’ ‘Then let it have shadow’ — since the shadow itself is wholly indescribable, it is other than even shadow: ‘without shadow.’ ‘Then let it be darkness’ — ‘not darkness.’ ‘Then let it be air’ — ‘not air.’ ‘Then let it be space’ — ‘not space.’ ‘Then let it be of the nature of contact, like lac’ — ‘unattached.’ ‘Then let it have taste’ — ‘tasteless.’ ‘Likewise smell’ — ‘smell-less.’ ‘Then let it have eyes’ — ‘without eyes,’ for it has no instrument such as the eye, hence ‘without eyes,’ on the strength of the mantra ‘He sees without eyes’ (Śvet. 3.19). Likewise ‘without ears’ — ‘He hears without ears’ (Śvet. 3.19). ‘Then let it have speech’ — ‘without speech.’ Likewise ‘without mind,’ and ‘without lustre’ — that which has no lustre is atejaska; for in it there is no lustre such as the light of fire and the like. ‘Without breath (aprāṇam)’ — here the inner vital air (ādhyātmika vāyu) is denied as ‘without prāṇa.’ ‘Then mouth, the door’ — ‘without mouth.’ ‘Without measure (amātram)’ — that by which something is measured is mātrā; ‘without measure’ means it is not of the form of any measure, nor is anything measured by it. ‘Then let it be like a hollow’ — ‘without inside’: it has no inside. ‘Then let an outside be possible for it’ — ‘without outside.’ ‘Then let it be the eater’ — ‘it eats nothing.’ ‘Then let it be the food of someone’ — ‘nothing eats it.’ The meaning is: it is wholly free from every distinction. For it is one only, without a second — by what could what be distinguished?
BR_C03_S08_V09: ‘Verily, O Gārgī, by the rule of this Imperishable, the sun and the moon are held in their places. Verily, O Gārgī, by the rule of this Imperishable, heaven and earth are held in their places. Verily, O Gārgī, by the rule of this Imperishable, moments, hours, days and nights, fortnights, months, seasons, and years are held in their places. Verily, O Gārgī, by the rule of this Imperishable, some rivers flow eastward from the white (snowy) mountains, and others westward, each in whatever direction. Verily, O Gārgī, by the rule of this Imperishable, men praise those who give, the gods are dependent on the sacrificer, and the fathers on the spoon-offering.’
BR_C03_S08_V09::block-0: By the strenuous denial of many attributes, the existence of the Imperishable has been brought home by Śruti. Yet, in deference to ordinary understanding, doubt may still arise; therefore, in order to establish its existence, an inferential proof is now adduced — ‘Verily, of this Imperishable…’ The Imperishable already established as the innermost of all, the immediate and direct Brahman, the Self transcending hunger and the like — by its rule, just as the kingdom proceeds unbroken and regulated under the rule of the king, so likewise under the rule of this Imperishable: ‘O Gārgī, the sun and moon’ — the two lamps of day and night — stand fashioned for that purpose, made by the Ruler who knows the purposes of beings to be lit by them; like ordinary lamps that benefit the illumination of all creatures alike. Hence That exists by which these two, which would have been independent rulers, are made and held — they proceed with rising, setting, waxing, and waning fixed in time, place, and occasion. Therefore the Imperishable, the ruler of these two, exists, just like the maker and supporter of a lamp. ‘By the rule of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, heaven and earth’ — the sky and the earth, though by their having parts apt to break apart, by their heaviness apt to fall, and by their being conjoined apt to be sundered, and though they appear self-dependent because presided over by sentient deities — yet they remain held in their places by the rule of this Imperishable. For this Imperishable is the bridge of all order, the upholder of every limit; therefore heaven and earth do not transgress its rule. Hence the existence of this Imperishable is established. The fact that heaven and earth abide regulated is an unfailing mark; without a sentient Ruler beyond saṃsāra, this would not be intelligible — as the mantra says: ‘by whom heaven is fierce and the earth firm’ (Ṛg-Saṃhitā 10.121.5). ‘By the rule of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, moments and hours’ and the rest, the divisions of time, are reckoners of all things, past, future, and present, that are subject to birth — just as in the world a master’s appointed accountant heedfully reckons all income and expenditure, so this Imperishable, like the master, is the controller of these divisions of time. Likewise, the rivers flowing eastward — the Ganges and the like — flow forth from the white mountains such as the Himavat; and they flow on as set, regulated, even though they have the power to flow otherwise. This is the mark of the Ruler. Other rivers — Sindhu and the rest — flow westward; and others, in whatever direction they have been started, they do not deviate from. This too is the mark. Further, men, even those who know the standards of right judgment, praise those who give gold and the like, even causing pain to themselves; here the gift, the giver, and the receiver — their meeting and parting are seen at once visibly, but a further future meeting (with fruit) is unseen; nevertheless, men of discernment praise the givers seeing for themselves the connection of the gift with its fruit. And this — the connection of the doer with the fruit of his deed — would not be possible without a Ruler who knows the apportionment of fruits to deeds, since the act of giving perishes immediately on being seen. Therefore there exists One who joins the doers of charity with the fruit. (Pūrvapakṣa: ‘It is by an unseen [apūrva] potency.’) Reply: No — for in establishing apūrva itself…
BR_C03_S08_V10: ‘He, O Gārgī, who, without knowing this Imperishable, in this world offers oblations, performs sacrifices, and practises austerities for many thousands of years — for him such (fruit) becomes finite indeed. He, O Gārgī, who departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable, is a wretch (kṛpaṇa). But he who departs from this world having known this Imperishable, O Gārgī, he is a brāhmaṇa.’
BR_C03_S08_V10::block-0: Hence too the Imperishable exists, since the arising of saṃsāra is invariably linked to ignorance of It; and there must be That, by the knowledge of which there is the cutting-off of saṃsāra, since this is borne out by reasoning. (Objection:) ‘Cutting-off may come from action alone’? Not so — ‘He, O Gārgī, who, without knowing — without truly cognizing — this Imperishable, in this world offers oblations, sacrifices, performs austerities’ even for many thousands of years, his fruit becomes finite indeed: at the exhaustion of the enjoyment of that fruit his works are themselves spent. Moreover, that by the knowledge of which there is removal of wretchedness, the cutting-off of saṃsāra, and from the absence of the knowledge of which the doer of works, being a kṛpaṇa, partakes only of the fruits of what he has done and remains harnessed to the round of birth and death — that ruling Imperishable exists. This is what is said: ‘He who, O Gārgī, departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable, is a kṛpaṇa,’ like a slave bought for hire. ‘But he who, O Gārgī, departs from this world knowing this Imperishable, he is a brāhmaṇa.’
BR_C03_S08_V11: ‘That very Imperishable, O Gārgī, is unseen but is the Seer; unheard but is the Hearer; unthought of but is the Thinker; uncognized but is the Cognizer. There is no other seer than This; no other hearer than This; no other thinker than This; no other cognizer than This. In this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, is space woven, warp and woof.’
BR_C03_S08_V11::block-0: (Objection:) Just as in fire the burning and illumining are natural, so the rulership of this Imperishable is natural — even though it itself is non-sentient. To meet this, the text says —
BR_C03_S08_V11::block-1: ‘That very Imperishable, O Gārgī, is unseen’ — not seen by anyone, since it is not an object; but itself the Seer, since it is of the very nature of seeing. So too unheard — not an object of hearing — but itself the Hearer, being of the nature of hearing. So unthought, since not an object of mind, but itself the Thinker, being of the nature of mentation. So uncognized, since not an object of intellect, but itself the Cognizer, being of the nature of cognition. Further, ‘there is no other than this’ Imperishable that is the Seer, the agent of the act of seeing — this very Imperishable is the agent of seeing everywhere. Likewise no other than this is the Hearer; that very Imperishable is the Hearer everywhere. No other than this is the Thinker; that very Imperishable is the Thinker everywhere through every mind. No other than this is the Cognizer, the agent of the act of cognition; that very Imperishable, through every intellect, is the agent of cognition — not insentient pradhāna (refuting Sāṅkhya) or anything else. ‘In this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, is space woven, warp and woof.’ That which is direct, immediate Brahman, the innermost Self of all, transcending hunger and other dharmas of saṃsāra, in which space is woven warp and woof — this is the supreme summit, the supreme goal, this is the highest Brahman, this is the Truth of the truth (satyasya satyam) — namely, of all that is real from earth up to space.
BR_C03_S08_V12: She said: ‘Venerable brāhmaṇas, you may esteem yourselves greatly fortunate if you escape this man with mere salutation. Verily, none among you shall ever vanquish him in a debate on Brahman.’ Thereupon Vācaknavī (Gārgī) fell silent.
BR_C03_S08_V12::block-0: She said: ‘O venerable brāhmaṇas, hear my word: esteem this greatly’ — what? — ‘that you may escape from this Yājñavalkya with mere salutation,’ that is, having merely saluted him, hold that to be the great gain. As for victory over him, do not even hope it in mind, much less by deed; for, ‘never indeed among you’ at any time ‘shall anyone vanquish this Yājñavalkya in a debate on Brahman.’ ‘Should he answer my two questions, none shall vanquish him’ — so I had pledged earlier; even now this is my conviction — that in the matter of the Brahman-debate there is none equal to him. ‘Thereupon Vācaknavī fell silent.’
BR_C03_S08_V12::block-1: Here, in the Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa, this was said — ‘He whom the earth knows not, whom all beings know not,’ and ‘they who know not the Inner Controller and they who do know not’ — and that very Imperishable was declared as the Cognitive Element (cetanādhātu) of all, being the agent of the acts of seeing and the rest. Now what is the difference between these (Antaryāmin, Akṣara, Kṣetrajña), or what is common to them? Some say: of the supreme Brahman, the great-ocean-like Akṣara whose nature is wholly unmoved, the slightly-moved condition is the Antaryāmin; the highly-moved condition is the Kṣetrajña, who knows not the Antaryāmin; thus they posit five other conditions, and so claim eight conditions of Brahman. Others say these are powers of the Akṣara — and that the Akṣara has infinite powers. Yet others say they are modifications (vikāras) of the Akṣara. (Refutation:) The doctrines of conditions and of powers do not stand, for Śruti declares the Akṣara to be transcendent of hunger and the other dharmas of saṃsāra; for one and the same thing cannot at the same time be both transcendent of hunger and the rest, and possessed of conditions characterized by hunger and the rest, nor likewise possessed of powers. As for being modifications or having parts, the faults have been shown in the fourth (chapter). Therefore all these constructions are unreal. (Objector:) Then what is the distinction among these? (Reply:) We say it is due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi-kṛta); intrinsically there is neither difference nor non-difference among them, since their very nature is one homogeneous mass of Cognition, like a lump of salt — by the Śruti ‘without prior, without later, without inside, without outside’ (Bṛ. 2.5.19), ‘this Self is Brahman’ (Bṛ. 2.5.19), and in the Atharvan: ‘unborn, with outside and inside’ (Muṇḍ. 2.1.2). Hence the unconditioned Self, being indescribable, attribute-less, and one, is designated by ‘not this, not this’ (neti neti, Bṛ. 2.3.6). The Self, with the limiting adjuncts of body-and-organs qualified by ignorance, desire, and karma, is called the transmigrating jīva. The Self, with the adjunct of eternal, unsurpassed knowledge and power, is called the Antaryāmin, the Īśvara. He alone, free of adjuncts, alone, pure, in His own nature, is called the supreme Akṣara. And again, qualified by the body-and-organ adjuncts of Hiraṇyagarbha, the Unmanifest, deities, classes, individuals, men, beasts, ghosts, and so on, He bears their respective names and forms. Thus too has been explained ‘That moves, That moves not’ (Īśā 5). Likewise the Śrutis ‘This is your Self’ (Bṛ. 3.4.1; 3.5.1), ‘This is the Inner Self of all beings’ (Muṇḍ. 2.1.4), ‘He is hidden in all beings’ (Kaṭha 1.3.12), ‘That thou art’ (Chānd. 6.8.7), ‘I alone am all this’ (Chānd. 7.25.1), ‘The Self alone is all this,’ ‘There is no other seer than This’ (Bṛ. 3.7.23), and the like — none of these are mutually contradictory. Under any other construction these Śrutis cannot stand. Therefore the difference of these is due solely to the difference of upādhis, not otherwise — for in all the Upaniṣads it is firmly determined ‘One only, without a second.’
BR_C03_S09_INTRO1::block-0: Now Vidagdha Śākalya questioned him. By means of the gradation of subtlety from earth onwards, declaring how each preceding element is woven, warp and woof, in the next, he had revealed the all-innermost Brahman; and the rulership of that Brahman over the differentiated thread-distinctions in the manifest realm was set forth — for the mark is more clearly perceptible in the manifest realm. The same Brahman is now to be reached as direct and immediate, by way of the contraction and expansion of the deities to be ruled. For this purpose the Śākalya-brāhmaṇa is now begun —
BR_C03_S09_V01: Then Vidagdha Śākalya questioned him: ‘How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya?’ He answered, by this very nivid: ‘As many as are mentioned in the nivid of the Vaiśvadeva — three and three hundred, three and three thousand.’ ‘Yes,’ he said, ‘but how many gods exactly are there, Yājñavalkya?’ ‘Thirty-three.’ ‘Yes,’ he said, ‘but how many gods exactly are there, Yājñavalkya?’ ‘Six.’ ‘Yes,’ he said, ‘but how many gods exactly are there, Yājñavalkya?’ ‘Three.’ ‘Yes,’ he said, ‘but how many gods exactly are there, Yājñavalkya?’ ‘Two.’ ‘Yes,’ he said, ‘but how many gods exactly are there, Yājñavalkya?’ ‘One and a half.’ ‘Yes,’ he said, ‘but how many gods exactly are there, Yājñavalkya?’ ‘One.’ ‘Yes,’ he said, ‘but which are these three and three hundred, three and three thousand?’
BR_C03_S09_V01::block-0: ‘Then Vidagdha,’ so by name, ‘Śākalya,’ son of Śakala, ‘questioned him: how many in number are the gods, O Yājñavalkya?’ Yājñavalkya, indeed, ‘by this very nivid’ — to be uttered presently — ‘arrived at’ the very number which Śākalya had asked. ‘As many as are the gods’ in the ‘nivid’ of the Vaiśvadeva-recitation — nivids being certain mantra-formulas that name the deities, recited in the Vaiśvadeva-stotra and called nivids — as many gods as are heard in that nivid, so many gods. What, then, is that nivid? These nivid-pādas are now displayed: ‘three and three hundred,’ that is, three and three hundred gods; ‘three and three thousand’ — three and three thousand more — so many gods. Śākalya likewise replied: ‘Om.’ Thus their middle-grade number was rightly understood. He next asks the contracted number of those very gods: ‘How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya?’ ‘Thirty-three; six; three; two; one and a half; one.’ Having asked the number under contraction and expansion, he then asks the very nature (svarūpa) of what is being numbered: ‘Which are these three and three hundred, three and three thousand?’
BR_C03_S09_V02: He (Yājñavalkya) said: ‘These (three thousand and so on) are but the manifestations (mahimānaḥ) of these very gods; in truth there are only thirty-three gods.’ ‘Which are those thirty-three?’ ‘The eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras and the twelve Ādityas — these are thirty-one; together with Indra and Prajāpati, they make thirty-three.’
BR_C03_S09_V02::block-0: He (the other, i.e. Yājñavalkya) said: the ‘three and three hundred’ (trayaśca trī ca śatā) etc. are the mahimānaḥ — the glories, the manifestations (vibhūtayaḥ) — of these thirty-three gods; but in the highest sense (paramārthataḥ) there are only thirty-three gods. ‘Which are those thirty-three?’ — to this it is answered: the eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, the twelve Ādityas — these make thirty-one; Indra and Prajāpati are the two that complete the thirty-three (trayastriṁśataḥ pūraṇau).
BR_C03_S09_V03: ‘Which are the Vasus?’ ‘Fire, the earth, the air, the mid-region, the sun, the heaven, the moon and the stars — these are the Vasus; for in them all this (universe) is settled (hitam). Hence they are called Vasus.’
BR_C03_S09_V03::block-0: ‘Which are the Vasus?’ — herein the very nature (svarūpa) of each is asked. ‘Fire, the earth’ etc. — these, beginning with Agni and ending with the stars, are the Vasus; for, by transforming (vipariṇamantaḥ) themselves into the support of beings’ karma-fruits, into the aggregate of body and senses (kāryakaraṇasaṅghātarūpeṇa), and into the abodes of those (aggregates), they cause this whole world to dwell (vāsayanti) and themselves dwell (vasanti). Since they cause (all) to dwell, they are therefore called Vasus — this is the nirvacana (etymology).
BR_C03_S09_V04: ‘Which are the Rudras?’ ‘These ten prāṇas in the person, with the ātman (mind) as the eleventh; when these depart from this mortal body, they cause (the kinsfolk) to weep (rodayanti). Because they make them weep, therefore they are called Rudras.’
BR_C03_S09_V04::block-0: ‘Which are the Rudras?’ — These ten in the person, namely the karmendriyas and buddhīndriyas (organs of action and of knowledge), are the prāṇas; the ātman, that is, the mind, is the eleventh — the completer of the eleven (ekādaśānāṁ pūraṇaḥ). When these prāṇas, on the exhaustion of the enjoyment of karma-fruits of beings, depart from this mortal body — then (atha tadā) they cause those connected with (the deceased) to weep. There — because they make their kinsfolk weep — therefore they are called Rudras (rodayanti iti rudrāḥ — the nirvacana).
BR_C03_S09_V05: ‘Which are the Ādityas?’ ‘The twelve months of the year — these are the Ādityas; for they go on taking away (ādadānāḥ yanti) all this. Because they go taking all this away, therefore they are called Ādityas.’
BR_C03_S09_V05::block-0: ‘Which are the Ādityas?’ — The twelve months are well known as the limbs (avayavāḥ) of the year, that is, of time; these are the Ādityas. How? Because, revolving again and again, they go (yanti) taking up (ādadānāḥ — gṛhṇantaḥ, upādadataḥ) the lifespans and karma-fruits of beings. Since they go thus taking away all this — therefore Ādityas (nirvacana: ādadānāḥ yanti iti ādityāḥ).
BR_C03_S09_V06: ‘Which is Indra and which is Prajāpati?’ ‘Indra is verily the thunder (stanayitnu); Prajāpati is the sacrifice (yajña).’ ‘Which is the thunder?’ ‘The thunderbolt (aśani).’ ‘Which is the sacrifice?’ ‘The (sacrificial) animals.’
BR_C03_S09_V06::block-0: ‘Which is Indra, which is Prajāpati?’ — ‘Stanayitnu (thunder) verily is Indra; the sacrifice is Prajāpati.’ ‘Which is the stanayitnu?’ — ‘The aśani.’ Aśani is the thunderbolt (vajram), strength, valour (vīryam balam), that which strikes down beings — that is Indra; for that is Indra’s deed (karma). ‘Which is the sacrifice?’ — ‘The animals (paśavaḥ).’ For the animals are the means (sādhanāni) of the sacrifice; since the sacrifice is itself formless (arūpatvāt) and rests on the animals as its means (paśusādhanāśrayatvāt), the animals are spoken of as the sacrifice.
BR_C03_S09_V07: ‘Which are the six?’ ‘Fire, the earth, the air, the mid-region, the sun, and the heaven — these are the six; for these are all this (universe), the six.’
BR_C03_S09_V07::block-0: ‘Which are the six?’ — The very same beginning with Agni that were enumerated as Vasus, leaving out the moon and the stars, become six — distinguished by the count of six (ṣaṭsaṅkhyā-viśiṣṭāḥ). For these — since whatever has been said as the thirty-three, etc., all this — these very six become; that is, the entire expanse of Vasus and the rest is included (antarbhavati) within these six. This is the meaning.
BR_C03_S09_V08: ‘Which are those three gods?’ ‘These very three worlds, for in them all these gods are (contained).’ ‘Which are the two gods?’ ‘Food and prāṇa.’ ‘Which is the one and a half (adhyardha)?’ ‘He who blows (the wind that purifies — yo’yaṁ pavate).’
BR_C03_S09_V08::block-0: ‘Which are those three gods?’ — ‘These very three worlds.’ Combining the earth with fire there is one god; combining the mid-region with air, the second; combining heaven with the sun, the third — these are the three gods. For in these three gods all the gods are included; therefore these very three are the gods. This is the view of certain Nairuktas (etymologists). ‘Which are the two gods?’ — ‘Food and prāṇa, these two are the gods.’ In these two all the (gods) named are included. ‘Which is the adhyardha (one and a half)?’ — ‘This wind that blows (yo’yaṁ pavate vāyuḥ).’
BR_C03_S09_V09: ‘To this they say: since this (wind) blows as if it were one only, how is it adhyardha (one and a half)?’ ‘Because in him this all attained pre-eminent prosperity (adhyārdhnot) — therefore he is adhyardha.’ ‘Which is the one god?’ ‘Prāṇa. He is brahman; they call him tyat (That).’
BR_C03_S09_V09::block-0: There they raise (the objection — codayanti): ‘since this wind blows as one only (eka iva eva, eka eva pavate), how then is he adhyardha (one and a half)?’ — ‘Because in him this all attained adhi-ṛddhi (pre-eminent prosperity, adhyārdhnot) — when this wind exists, this all attains pre-eminence (adhi-ṛddhiṁ prāpnoti) — therefore he is adhyardha.’ ‘Which is the one god?’ — ‘Prāṇa.’ That prāṇa is brahman — being the self of all the gods, he is the great brahman (mahad-brahma); therefore they call him ‘tyat’ (That), designating brahman by the indirect (parokṣa) word ‘tyat’. Such is the unity (ekatvam) and multiplicity (nānātvam) of the gods — the inclusion (antarbhāvaḥ) of the infinite gods within the determined (nivit) numerical groups; and of those (groups) again, in the successively higher (counts of) thirty-three and so on, until (all are included) in the one prāṇa; and the entire infinite expansion is of that very one prāṇa. Thus the prāṇa alone is one, and is infinite, and is qualified by intermediate numbers (avāntara-saṅkhyā-viśiṣṭa). And there, in (this) one god, the distinction of name, form, action, quality and power is by reason of difference of office (adhikāra-bhedāt).
BR_C03_S09_V10: ‘He whose abode is verily the earth, whose world is fire, whose light is the mind — whoever knows that Person, the supreme resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower. O Yājñavalkya!’ ‘I do indeed know that Person, the supreme resort of every self, of whom you speak — he is verily this very person who is corporeal. Go on then and ask, O Śākalya: what is his deity?’ ‘The Immortal,’ said he.
BR_C03_S09_V10::block-0: Now an eightfold further differentiation of that same Prāṇa-Brahman is being taught —
BR_C03_S09_V10::block-1: ‘Pṛthivyeva yasya’ — of which deity the earth itself is the āyatana, the support; ‘agnirloko yasya’ — of whom the world is fire — by the nirvacana ‘lokayaty anena iti lokaḥ,’ that is, ‘he sees by it’; the meaning is ‘he sees by means of fire’; ‘mano-jyotiḥ’ — by separating the compound: ‘he by whom, with the mind as light, the activity of resolution and counter-resolution and the like is performed — he is mano-jyotiḥ’. The meaning is: he is a deity having the earth as body, having fire as his organ of sight, having the mind as his resolver, identifying himself with earth, possessed of the aggregate of body and organs. Whoever should thus know that Person of such specific marks — ‘sarvasyātmanaḥ parāyaṇam,’ the supreme resort of every adhyātmika self, that is, of the aggregate of body and organs constituting the inner self — supreme resort being its highest support: namely, of the seed-portion derived from the father, in the form of bone, marrow and semen, [resting] upon the mother-derived field-portion in the form of skin, flesh and blood, and likewise the supreme resort of the self-as-organs — ‘sa vai veditā syāt’; he who knows this thus is indeed a true knower, a paṇḍita: this is the import. The implied taunt is: ‘O Yājñavalkya, you, without knowing him, fancy yourself a paṇḍita!’ [Siddhānta-reply of Yājñavalkya:] If paṇḍitya is to be obtained by knowing him, then ‘veda vā ahaṁ taṁ puruṣam’ — the Person of whom you speak as the supreme resort of every self, him I do know. Here Śākalya’s [implied] words must be supplied: ‘If you know that Person, then state by what specifying mark he is.’ [Yājñavalkya answers:] Listen, with what specifying mark he is — ‘ya evāyaṁ śārīraḥ,’ that is, the one resident in the body, in the earth-portion of the body — ‘śārīra’ meaning the threefold mother-derived sheath; this is that very deity whom you, O Śākalya, have asked about; yet there remains another specifying mark to be stated; ‘tad vadaiva’ — the meaning is: just ask, O Śākalya. Thus provoked, overcome by impatience, like an elephant goaded by the ankuśa, he says: of that deity, the corporeal, what is the deity — that from which he is produced — that which is intended in this section by the rule ‘sā tasya devatā,’ ‘that is his deity’; ‘amṛtam iti hovāca’ — ‘amṛtam’ means the sap of the food consumed, which is the cause of the production of the mother-derived blood; for from that food-sap, blood, lodged in the woman, is produced; and from that blood arises the body which is the receptacle of the seed. The rest is the same.
BR_C03_S09_V11: ‘He whose abode is verily desire, whose world is the heart, whose light is the mind — whoever knows that Person, the supreme resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower. O Yājñavalkya!’ ‘I do know that Person, the supreme resort of every self, of whom you speak — he is verily this very person made of desire. Go on then and ask, O Śākalya: what is his deity?’ ‘Women,’ said he.
BR_C03_S09_V11::block-0: ‘Kāma eva yasyāyatanam’ — ‘kāma’ is the desire for union with woman; ‘kāma-śarīra’ is the meaning, i.e. one whose body is desire. ‘Hṛdayaṁ lokaḥ’ — by the heart, the buddhi, he sees. ‘Ya evāyaṁ kāmamayaḥ puruṣaḥ’ — even on the adhyātmika side he is verily made of desire; ‘what is his deity?’ — ‘Striyaḥ,’ ‘women,’ said he; for from woman the kindling of desire arises.
BR_C03_S09_V12: ‘He whose abode is verily forms, whose world is the eye, whose light is the mind — whoever knows that Person, the supreme resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower. O Yājñavalkya!’ ‘I do know that Person, the supreme resort of every self, of whom you speak — he is verily that Person who is in the sun. Go on then and ask, O Śākalya: what is his deity?’ ‘Truth,’ said he.
BR_C03_S09_V12::block-0: ‘Rūpāṇy eva yasyāyatanam’ — ‘rūpāṇi’ are white, black and the rest. ‘Ya evāsāv āditye puruṣaḥ’ — for the specific manifest effect of all forms is the Person in the sun; ‘what is his deity?’ — ‘Satyam iti hovāca’; ‘satyam’ here designates the eye; for the adhidaivata sun is produced from the adhyātmika eye.
BR_C03_S09_V13: ‘He whose abode is verily ākāśa, whose world is the ear, whose light is the mind — whoever knows that Person, the supreme resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower. O Yājñavalkya!’ ‘I do know that Person, the supreme resort of every self, of whom you speak — he is verily this Person who is in the ear, who is in the echo. Go on then and ask, O Śākalya: what is his deity?’ ‘The quarters,’ said he.
BR_C03_S09_V13::block-0: ‘Ākāśa eva yasyāyatanam.’ ‘Ya evāyaṁ śrotre bhavaḥ śrautraḥ’ — by nirvacana ‘he who is born in the ear is śrautra’; and there too, since he occurs especially at the time of the echo, he is ‘prātiśrutkaḥ’; ‘what is his deity?’ — ‘Diśaḥ,’ ‘the quarters,’ said he; for from the quarters this adhyātmika [hearer] is produced.
BR_C03_S09_V14: ‘He whose abode is verily darkness, whose world is the heart, whose light is the mind — whoever knows that Person, the supreme resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower. O Yājñavalkya!’ ‘I do know that Person, the supreme resort of every self, of whom you speak — he is verily this Person made of shadow. Go on then and ask, O Śākalya: what is his deity?’ ‘Death,’ said he.
BR_C03_S09_V14::block-0: ‘Tama eva yasyāyatanam.’ By ‘tamas’ here is taken the night-darkness and the like. ‘Adhyātmaṁ chāyāmayaḥ’ is the Person made of ignorance; ‘what is his deity?’ — ‘Mṛtyur iti hovāca’; death, on the adhidaivata side, is the cause of his production.
BR_C03_S09_V15: ‘He whose abode is verily forms, whose world is the eye, whose light is the mind — whoever knows that Person, the supreme resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower. O Yājñavalkya!’ ‘I do know that Person, the supreme resort of every self, of whom you speak — he is verily this Person in the mirror. Go on then and ask, O Śākalya: what is his deity?’ ‘The vital breath (asu),’ said he.
BR_C03_S09_V15::block-0: ‘Rūpāṇy eva yasyāyatanam.’ Earlier, the common forms were spoken of; here, however, the specific reflective forms are taken. The specific abode of the deity whose abode is form is that which holds the reflection — the mirror and the like; ‘what is his deity?’ — ‘Asur iti hovāca’; the production of that Person called the reflection is from ‘asu,’ the vital breath.
BR_C03_S09_V16: ‘He whose abode is verily the waters, whose world is the heart, whose light is the mind — whoever knows that Person, the supreme resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower. O Yājñavalkya!’ ‘I do know that Person, the supreme resort of every self, of whom you speak — he is verily this Person in the waters. Go on then and ask, O Śākalya: what is his deity?’ ‘Varuṇa,’ said he.
BR_C03_S09_V16::block-0: ‘Āpa eva yasya āyatanam.’ All waters in general are the abode; the specific abiding is in the waters that are sheltered in tanks, wells, ponds and the like; ‘what is his deity?’ — ‘Varuṇa,’ said he; for from Varuṇa proceed the rains that bring waters together; on the adhyātmika side, the very waters [of the body] are the cause of the production of the waters of tanks and so forth.
BR_C03_S09_V17: ‘He whose abode is verily semen, whose world is the heart, whose light is the mind — whoever knows that Person, the supreme resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower. O Yājñavalkya!’ ‘I do know that Person, the supreme resort of every self, of whom you speak — he is verily this Person made of the son. Go on then and ask, O Śākalya: what is his deity?’ ‘Prajāpati,’ said he.
BR_C03_S09_V17::block-0: ‘Reta eva yasyāyatanam’; ‘ya evāyaṁ putramayaḥ’ is the specific abode of the deity whose abode is semen — and ‘putramaya’ means the bone, marrow and semen produced from the father; ‘what is his deity?’ — ‘Prajāpatir iti hovāca’ — Prajāpati here denotes the father, for the production of the son is from the father.
BR_C03_S09_V18: "Śākalya," said Yājñavalkya, "have these brāhmaṇas indeed made you their charcoal-remover?"
BR_C03_S09_V18::block-0:
Having divided the Self eightfold by the distinction of devas, worlds and persons—each one threefold and threefold—each single deity has been declared, for the sake of upāsanā, as merely a particular form of prāṇa. Now, in order to bring back into the Ātman that which has been distributed fivefold by the division of the directions, the text proceeds.
