When Śākalya stood silent, Yājñavalkya, as though seizing him by a graha (the soma-cup that grasps and holds), addressed him: "Śākalya," said Yājñavalkya. The particle svit conveys conjecture: "Surely these brāhmaṇas"—aṅgārāvakṣayaṇam, that wherein burning coals are extinguished, namely the tongs and similar implements; have these brāhmaṇas certainly made you their aṅgārāvakṣayaṇa? "You, however, do not realize this—that you, your very self, are being burnt up by me"—such is the import.
BR_C03_S09_V19: "Yājñavalkya," said Śākalya, "in that you have thus over-spoken the brāhmaṇas of the Kurus and Pañcālas, what Brahman do you know?" "I know the directions, together with their devas and supports." "If you know the directions with their devas and supports—"
BR_C03_S09_V19::block-0:
Śākalya said, "Yājñavalkya, in that you have thus spoken excessively (atyavādīḥ, ati-uktavān asi) against the brāhmaṇas of the Kurus and Pañcālas—they themselves being afraid kept silent, and you have made them your charcoal-tongs—what Brahman do you know that you so abuse the brāhmaṇas?"

Yājñavalkya answers: "This much, indeed, is my knowledge of Brahman. What is that? I know the directions—that is, the cognition whose object is the quarters; and that not the quarters alone, but sa-devāḥ, together with the devas, the presiding deities of the directions, and further sa-pratiṣṭhāḥ, together with their supports." The other rejoins: "If you do know the directions with their devas and their supports—then your declared knowledge will bear fruit."
BR_C03_S09_V20: "Which deity are you in this eastern direction?" "The deity Āditya." "In what is that Āditya established?" "In the eye." "In what is the eye established?" "In forms; for by the eye one sees forms." "In what are the forms established?" "In the heart," he said, "for by the heart one knows forms; in the heart alone are forms established." "Even so it is, Yājñavalkya."
BR_C03_S09_V20::block-0:
Kindevataḥ—what deity belongs to you who have become a direction? Yājñavalkya, having mentally divided his hṛdaya-Ātman fivefold by the directions and made it the very self of the directions, and through that having taken up the entire universe as his Self, stands declaring "I am the Self of the directions," facing east—because of the words sa-pratiṣṭhāḥ. As is Yājñavalkya's pratijñā, so does Śākalya question: "Which deity are you in this direction?"

For everywhere in the Veda, whichever deity one worships, one becomes that very deity here, and so attains it. As will be said hereafter, "Having become a god, he attains the gods" (Bṛ. Up. 4.1.2). "In this eastern direction what is the deity that presides over you, the Self of the direction—by which deity are you endowed with the form of the eastern direction?"

The other answers: "The deity Āditya. In the eastern direction, Āditya is my deity; therefore I am ādityadeva." The clause sa-devāḥ has been provided for; sa-pratiṣṭhāḥ now needs to be elucidated, hence: "In what is that Āditya established?" "In the eye"—for in the adhyātma sphere Āditya has emerged from the eye, as declared by mantra and brāhmaṇa-vāda: "From the eye was the sun born" (Ṛ. Saṁ. 10.90.13), "From the eye, Āditya" (Ai. Up. 1.1.4), and the like; for the effect (kārya) is established in the cause (kāraṇa).

"In what is the eye established?" "In forms"—for the eye, itself of the nature of form, has been engaged by form for the apprehension of forms; the eye has been originated to grasp itself by those very forms by which it is engaged. Therefore the eye, with Āditya, with the eastern direction, with all that abides in it, is established in forms. The eastern direction, together with the eye, is wholly of the nature of form.

"In what are those forms established?" "In the heart," he said—the forms originate from the heart; the heart has indeed been transformed in the shape of forms; for it is by the heart that all the world cognizes forms. By "hṛdaya" the buddhi and manas, taken as one, are intended. Therefore in the heart alone are forms established; for it is by the heart that the recollection of forms in the form of vāsanās occurs. Hence forms are established in the heart. "Even so it is, Yājñavalkya."
BR_C03_S09_V21: "Which deity are you in this southern direction?" "The deity Yama." "In what is that Yama established?" "In the yajña." "In what is the yajña established?" "In the dakṣiṇā." "In what is the dakṣiṇā established?" "In śraddhā; for only when one has śraddhā does one give the dakṣiṇā; in śraddhā alone is the dakṣiṇā established." "In what is śraddhā established?" "In the heart," he said, "for by the heart one knows śraddhā; in the heart alone is śraddhā established." "Even so it is, Yājñavalkya."
BR_C03_S09_V21::block-0:
"Which deity are you in this southern direction?"—as before: which deity is yours in the southern direction? "The deity Yama"—Yama is my deity, since I am the Self of the southern direction. "In what is that Yama established?" "In the yajña"—Yama, together with the direction, is established in the yajña as cause. How then is Yama spoken of as the effect of the yajña? The yajña is accomplished by the ṛtvijs; the yajamāna, by means of the dakṣiṇā, purchases that yajña from them, and by that yajña he, together with Yama, attains the southern direction. Hence Yama, being kārya, is established in the yajña, together with the southern direction.

"In what is the yajña established?" "In the dakṣiṇā"—it is by means of the dakṣiṇā that the yajña is purchased; therefore the yajña is the effect of the dakṣiṇā. "In what is the dakṣiṇā established?" "In śraddhā"—śraddhā here means the willingness to give, the conviction of the existence (āstikya-buddhi) joined with bhakti. How is the dakṣiṇā established in it? Because only when one has śraddhā does one give the dakṣiṇā; one who lacks śraddhā does not give the dakṣiṇā. Therefore in śraddhā alone is the dakṣiṇā established.

"In what is śraddhā established?" "In the heart," he said—since śraddhā is a vṛtti of the heart; for by the heart one knows śraddhā, and a vṛtti is established in that which possesses the vṛtti. Therefore in the heart alone is śraddhā established. "Even so it is, Yājñavalkya."
BR_C03_S09_V22: "Which deity are you in this western direction?" "The deity Varuṇa." "In what is that Varuṇa established?" "In the waters." "In what are the waters established?" "In the seed." "In what is the seed established?" "In the heart; therefore, of one resembling the father, people say: 'He has, as it were, slipped out of the father's heart, he has been fashioned, as it were, out of the heart;' for in the heart alone is the seed established." "Even so it is, Yājñavalkya."
BR_C03_S09_V22::block-0:
"Which deity are you in this western direction?" In that direction Varuṇa is my presiding deity. "In what is that Varuṇa established?" "In the waters"—for Varuṇa is the effect of the waters, as the śruti says: "Verily, śraddhā is the waters" (Tai. Saṁ. 1.6.8.1) and "From śraddhā he created Varuṇa" (?).

"In what are the waters established?" "In the seed"—as the śruti declares, "From seed indeed were the waters created" (?). "In what is the seed established?" "In the heart"—because the seed is the effect of the heart; desire (kāma) is the vṛtti of the heart; for from the heart of the desirous one the seed leaps forth.

Therefore also, of a son born resembling (pratirūpa, anurūpa) the father, ordinary people say: "This son has, as it were, slipped out (sṛpta, viniḥsṛta) from the heart of his father, and has been fashioned, as it were, out of the heart"—just as a kuṇḍala is fashioned out of gold. Therefore in the heart alone is the seed established. "Even so it is, Yājñavalkya."
BR_C03_S09_V23: "Which deity are you in this northern direction?" "The deity Soma." "In what is that Soma established?" "In the dīkṣā." "In what is the dīkṣā established?" "In truth; therefore they say to one who has been initiated, 'Speak the truth;' in truth alone is the dīkṣā established." "In what is truth established?" "In the heart," he said, "for by the heart one knows truth; in the heart alone is truth established." "Even so it is, Yājñavalkya."
BR_C03_S09_V23::block-0:
"Which deity are you in this northern direction?" "The deity Soma"—the word "soma" is used by combining the soma-creeper and the deity Soma into one designation. "In what is that Soma established?" "In the dīkṣā"—for it is the dīkṣita yajamāna who buys the soma; having sacrificed with the purchased soma, the man of knowledge attains the northern direction, presided over by the deity Soma and full of soma.

"In what is the dīkṣā established?" "In truth"—how? Because the dīkṣā is established in truth, therefore they say to one who has taken the dīkṣā, "Speak the truth"—lest, the cause failing, the effect should also fail. Hence in truth alone is the dīkṣā established.

"In what is truth established?" "In the heart," he said—for by the heart one knows truth; therefore in the heart alone is truth established. "Even so it is, Yājñavalkya."
BR_C03_S09_V24: "Which deity are you in this fixed direction (the zenith)?" "The deity Agni." "In what is that Agni established?" "In speech." "In what is speech established?" "In the heart." "In what is the heart established?"
BR_C03_S09_V24::block-0:
"Which deity are you in this fixed direction?" Because for those who dwell on every side around Meru it does not deviate, the upward direction is called "dhruvā," the fixed one. "The deity Agni"—for in the upward region there is a great preponderance of light, and light is Agni. "In what is that Agni established?" "In speech." "In what is speech established?" "In the heart."

There Yājñavalkya, by means of his heart spread out into all the directions, has attained all the directions as his very Self. The directions, together with their devas and supports, have become the Self of him, Yājñavalkya, whose self consists of name, form and karma. Whatever is form has, together with the eastern direction, become the heart of Yājñavalkya; whatever is mere karma—of the nature of begetting a son and accompanied by knowledge, with its fruit and the presiding deities—has become his very heart in the southern, western and northern directions, as the self of the fruit of action; and whatever is name, together with the fixed (upward) direction, has, through the door of speech, become his very heart.

For only this much is all this: whatever is form, or karma, or name—all that is the heart alone. Hence the heart, which is the Self of all, is now asked about: "In what is the heart established?"
BR_C03_S09_V25: "O dullard!" said Yājñavalkya, "that you should think this could be elsewhere than in us! For if this were elsewhere than in us, dogs would devour it, or birds would tear it to pieces."
BR_C03_S09_V25::block-0:
"O Ahallika!" said Yājñavalkya—he addressed him by another name. Yatra, at whatever time, etat, this heart, the Self of this body, anyatra, in some other place, asmat, than ourselves—were it to subsist there, manyāsai, dost thou suppose? For yad—if indeed this heart were elsewhere than in us, then śvānaḥ, dogs, vā enat, this body, ad-yuḥ, would devour, or vayāṁsi, birds, vā enat, this very body, vimathnīran, would tear apart, would drag away.

Therefore the meaning is: it is in me, in this body, that the heart is established. And since the body itself is of the nature of name, form and karma, it too has its establishment in the heart.
BR_C03_S09_V26: "In what, then, are you and the Self established?" "In prāṇa." "In what is prāṇa established?" "In apāna." "In what is apāna established?" "In vyāna." "In what is vyāna established?" "In udāna." "In what is udāna established?" "In samāna." That Self is described as "not this, not this" (neti-neti). It is ungraspable, for It is not grasped; undecaying, for It does not decay; unattached, for It does not attach Itself; unfettered—It does not suffer, It does not perish. These are the eight abodes, the eight worlds, the eight gods, the eight puruṣas. He who, having drawn together and pulled back those puruṣas, transcended them—of that upaniṣadic Puruṣa I ask you. If you do not declare Him to me, your head will fall off. Śākalya did not know Him, and his head did indeed fall off; and robbers carried away his bones, taking them for something else.
BR_C03_S09_V26::block-0:
Thus the mutual support of the heart and the body has been stated, that of the effect (kārya) and the instruments (karaṇa). Hence I ask you: "In what are you and the Self established?"—you, the body, and your Self, the heart. The answer is: "In prāṇa"—the body and its Self would be established in prāṇa, in the function (vṛtti) of prāṇa. "In what is prāṇa established?" "In apāna"—for that prāṇa-function would itself rush forward, were it not held back by the apāna-function. "In what is apāna established?" "In vyāna"—for that apāna-function would go downward, and the prāṇa-function forward, were they not held in check by the intermediate vyāna-function. "In what is vyāna established?" "In udāna"—for all the three functions, were they not bound to udāna which stands like a pivot, would scatter in every direction. "In what is udāna established?" "In samāna"—for all these functions are indeed grounded in samāna. The purport is that the body, the heart, and the airs (vāyus) mutually support one another, and act as a collective bound together, set in motion for the purpose of the conscious (vijñānamaya) one.

That by which all this is regulated, in which all this is established, woven and interwoven up to ākāśa—of that unconditioned (nirupādhika) Brahman, immediate and not indirect (sākṣād aparokṣa), the indication must now be made: such is the present undertaking. "That very one"—he who was indicated in the Madhukāṇḍa as "not this, not this" (Bṛ. Up. 2.3.6), this same one is the Self. He is ungraspable (agṛhya), not graspable. How? Because He is beyond all the properties of the effect (kārya-dharma); therefore ungraspable. Why? "For He is not grasped"—whatever is a manifest (vyākṛta) object lying within the range of the instruments is within the range of grasping; but this Self-reality is the contrary of that. So too undecaying (aśīrya)—whatever is gross and compact, like the body, decays; but this is its contrary, hence "It does not decay." So too unattached (asaṅga)—a gross thing, when joined with another gross thing, becomes attached; but this is its contrary, hence "It does not attach." So too unfettered (asita), unbound—whatever is gross is bound; but this, being its contrary, is unbound; being unbound, It does not suffer; therefore It does not perish—being free from the properties of grasping, decaying, attaching, and binding, It does not perish, that is, does not undergo injury, does not come to destruction.

Breaking the order, leaving aside the narrative (ākhyāyikā), the Śruti, by way of haste, has indicated the upaniṣadic Puruṣa in His own form. Then, returning once more to the narrative, He says: "these eight abodes" which were spoken of, beginning with "He whose abode is the earth alone"; the eight worlds, beginning with the world of fire; the eight gods, beginning with "'The immortal,' He said" (Bṛ. Up. 3.9.10); the eight puruṣas, beginning with "the bodily Puruṣa". "He who, having drawn those puruṣas together (niruhya)"—having ascertained them with certainty—"and led them forth," having explained the world's structure through the division of eight tetrads, and again, by way of the eastern direction and so on, having drawn them back (pratyuhya), gathered them up into His own Self, the heart—"transcended"—has gone beyond the upādhi-properties of identification with the heart and the rest. He who, established in His own Self, is the upaniṣadic Puruṣa, free from hunger and the rest, to be known only in the Upaniṣads, not accessible through any other pramāṇa—of Him I ask you, who pride yourself on knowledge. "If you do not declare" Him clearly to me, "your head will fall off," so said Yājñavalkya. Śākalya did not know that upaniṣadic Puruṣa. His head did indeed fall off; and robbers carried away his bones, taking them for something else.
BR_C03_S09_V27: Then he said: "Revered Brāhmaṇas, let whoever among you wishes ask me, or all of you ask me; or whoever among you wishes, him I shall ask, or I shall ask all of you." Those Brāhmaṇas, however, did not dare to speak.
BR_C03_S09_V27::block-0: He whose Brahman has been indicated by the way of negating other things (anya-pratiṣedha) as "not this, not this"—how is His indication to be made by the way of positive statement (vidhi-mukha)? Resorting once more to the narrative, He says, "and the root of the world must be declared." The connection with the narrative is this: the cattle-wealth was to be carried off, having vanquished the Brāhmaṇas who do not know Brahman. Considering this to be the just course (nyāya), He says—
BR_C03_S09_V27::block-1: "Then he said." Then, when the Brāhmaṇas had become silent, he said, addressing them thus: "O revered Brāhmaṇas, whoever among you wishes—wishes, that is, 'I shall ask Yājñavalkya'—let him come to me and ask; or all of you ask me—let all of you ask me. Or whichever of you I wish—'let Yājñavalkya ask me'—him I shall ask; or I shall ask all of you." The Brāhmaṇas, even when so addressed, did not dare—they did not become bold enough to utter even a single word in reply.
BR_C03_S09_V28a:
He questioned them with these verses—
As is a tree, lord of the forest, even so verily is the puruṣa: his hairs are its leaves, his skin its outer bark.
BR_C03_S09_V28a::block-0: When those Brāhmaṇas had become irresolute, he questioned them with these verses to be stated. "As in the world a tree (vṛkṣa), lord of the forest (vanaspati)"—"vanaspati" is a qualifier of "vṛkṣa"—"even so is the puruṣa, not falsely (amṛṣā)"—amṛṣā means this is true. "His hairs"—the hairs of that puruṣa correspond to the leaves of the other, the tree. "His skin is its outer bark"—the skin of this puruṣa corresponds to the outer bark (utpāṭikā) of the other, the tree.
BR_C03_S09_V28b: From his skin flows blood, from the tree's skin flows sap (utpaṭa). Therefore, when wounded, blood flows from him, even as sap from a stricken tree.
BR_C03_S09_V28b::block-0: From the very skin of this puruṣa flows blood; from the skin of the tree there springs up the sap (utpaṭa)—from the skin itself it bursts forth. Thus everything is alike between the tree and the puruṣa. Therefore, from him when wounded (ātṛṇṇa)—when injured—that blood comes forth, even as the sap from a tree when struck (āhata), when cut.
BR_C03_S09_V28c: His muscles are its splinters, his sinew is its inner bark—it is firm. His bones are the wood within, his marrow is made like marrow.
BR_C03_S09_V28c::block-0: Likewise the flesh (māṃsa) of this puruṣa corresponds to the splinters (śakarāṇi)—that is, śakalas, fragments—of the tree. "Kināṭa"—the kināṭa of the tree, named so, is the bark-like layer attached to the wood, inner to the splinters; that corresponds to the sinew (snāva) of the puruṣa. "It is firm"—that kināṭa is, like the sinew, firm. The bones of the puruṣa: inside the sinew lie the bones; so too inside the kināṭa lies the wood (dāru). The marrow (majjā)—the marrow of the tree and of the puruṣa—is made alike (majjopamā): the term majjopamā means an analogue of marrow; there is no other distinction. As is the marrow of a tree, so of a puruṣa; as is the puruṣa's, so the tree's.
BR_C03_S09_V28d: If a tree is cut down, it grows up again from its root, anew. But the mortal man, when cut down by death, from what root does he grow forth?
BR_C03_S09_V28d::block-0: If a tree, having been cut (vṛkṇa, chinna), grows again—sprouts again, comes forth—from its root, newer (navatara) than before, fresher than the previous; up to this distinction, all between the tree and the puruṣa was understood as common. But this distinction is seen in the tree—that there is sprouting after being cut; whereas in the puruṣa, when cut down by death, there is no such sprouting seen; yet there must be sprouting from somewhere. Therefore I ask you—"the mortal (martya), the man, when cut down by death, from what root does he sprout forth?"—from where does the sprouting of the dead puruṣa come about, is the meaning.
BR_C03_S09_V28e: Do not say "From the seed (retas)"—for it is from one living that this is born. The tree, indeed, springs from a seed too; but verily there is birth after death—directly.
BR_C03_S09_V28e::block-0: If you should say thus—"It sprouts from the seed (retas)"—do not say so; you ought not to speak in this manner. Why? Because that seed is born from a living puruṣa, not from a dead one. Moreover, the tree is also dhānā-ruh—dhānā meaning seed; it is also seed-grown, not only stalk-grown (kāṇḍa-ruh). The word iva is meaningless here. Indeed, a tree, directly (añjasā), after dying, has rebirth (sambhava)—it would have rebirth from the seed, even after death—directly, again, the tree (vanaspati).
BR_C03_S09_V28f: If they were to pluck out a tree along with its root, it would not come into being again. But the mortal, when cut down by death, from what root does he grow forth?
BR_C03_S09_V28f::block-0: If they were to pluck out (āvṛheyuḥ)—were to lift up, were to uproot—the tree along with its root or its seed, it would not come into being again—it would not return into being. Hence I ask you: of the entire universe, what is the root? "From what root does the mortal, cut down by death, sprout forth?"
BR_C03_S09_V28g: ‘Once born, he is not born again; for who would beget him afresh? Brahman is consciousness and bliss, the supreme goal of the giver who bestows wealth and of him who, having stood firm, knows It.’ (7)
BR_C03_S09_V28g::block-0:
‘jāta eva’ — if you say, what is there here to be asked? for the possibility of birth is to be asked of one yet to be born, not of one already born; this man is already born, hence regarding him no question can arise — not so. How then? The dead is born again indeed; otherwise there would follow the consequence of the receiving of what was not done (akṛtābhyāgama) and the loss of what was done (kṛta-nāśa). Therefore I ask you — ‘who indeed would beget this dead one again?’ That the brāhmaṇas did not know — the root of the world from which the dead one sprouts again was not known by the brāhmaṇas. Hence, on account of his being most deeply versed in Brahman (brahmiṣṭhatva), the cows have been led away; the brāhmaṇas have been vanquished by Yājñavalkya. The narrative is concluded.

That which is the root of the world, and that by which word Brahman is directly designated, that about which Yājñavalkya questioned the brāhmaṇas — that, in its own form, the śruti now declares to us. ‘Vijñāna’ — vijñapti, knowing, is vijñāna; and that is ānanda — not, like the cognition of objects, interwoven with sorrow; but rather serene, auspicious, incomparable, effortless, ever-content, of one taste — such is the meaning. What is that Brahman, qualified by both these epithets? ‘rāti’ — here the nominative stands for the genitive sense of rāti (the giving); the meaning is ‘of wealth.’ Of the giver of wealth, of the sacrificer who performs karma, It is the parāyaṇa — the supreme goal, the bestower of the fruit of karma. Furthermore, having risen up beyond the eṣaṇās (the cravings for sons, wealth and worlds), one who, not being a doer of karma, abides in that very Brahman — he knows that Brahman, hence ‘tad-vit’; for him too, ‘of him standing firm and knowing It,’ that is, of the knower of Brahman, It is the parāyaṇa — such is the meaning.
BR_C03_S09_V28g::block-1: Here this is to be considered. The word ānanda is well known in the world as denoting pleasure (sukha); and here the word ānanda is heard as a qualification of Brahman — ‘ānandaṁ brahma.’ In other śrutis also: ‘He knew bliss as Brahman’ (Tai. U. 3.6.9), ‘the knower of the bliss of Brahman’ (Tai. U. 2.9.1), ‘if this bliss were not in the ākāśa’ (Tai. U. 2.7.1), ‘that which is plenitude is happiness’ (Chā. U. 7.23.1), ‘this is His supreme bliss,’ and so forth. The word ānanda is well known with reference to a pleasure that is an object of cognition (saṁvedya); and if the bliss of Brahman were also an object of cognition, then these words ānanda applied to Brahman would be fitting. But — by the authority of śruti, Brahman is precisely of the nature of cognized bliss; what is to be considered here? — Not so, because contradictory śruti-sentences are seen. True, the word ānanda is heard with respect to Brahman; but cognition is also denied where there is oneness — ‘when, for him, all has become the very Self, then by what should one see whom? then by what should one know what?’ (Bṛ. U. 4.5.15), ‘where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, knows nothing else, that is plenitude’ (Chā. U. 7.24.1), ‘embraced by the prājña-Self he knows nothing external’ (Bṛ. U. 4.3.21), and so on. Because contradictory śruti-sentences are seen, hence the inquiry must be made. Therefore it is fitting to investigate, in order to determine the meaning of the Vedic sentence. And on account of the disagreement among those who teach mokṣa: the Sāṅkhyas and the Vaiśeṣikas, who are upholders of mokṣa, are at variance, holding that there is no cognized happiness in mokṣa; others hold that there is unsurpassable happiness, self-cognized.
BR_C03_S09_V28g::block-2: (pūrvapakṣa.) Now, what is fitting? From the hearing of ‘ānanda’ and the rest — ‘eating, sporting, taking pleasure’ (Chā. U. 8.12.3), ‘if he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers’ (Chā. U. 8.2.1), ‘who is omniscient, all-knowing’ (Mu. U. 1.1.9), ‘he attains all desires’ (Tai. U. 2.5.1), and similar śrutis — happiness is cognized in mokṣa. (Objection.) But on account of the absence of distinction of factors of action (kāraka-vibhāga) in the state of oneness, cognition (vijñāna) is impossible; for an action is accomplished by many factors and cognition is an action. (Reply.) That is no fault: by the authority of the word, there can be cognition with bliss as its object; ‘vijñānam ānandam’ and the rest are utterances which would be unintelligible if the very nature of bliss were not cognizable — so we have said. (Objection.) But even by an utterance the coldness of fire and the heat of water are not produced, because utterances are informative (jñāpaka); nor can it be informed that fire is cold in some other place, or that water is hot in some unreachable region. (Reply.) Not so, because in the inner Self (pratyag-ātman) the cognition of bliss is seen. The utterances ‘vijñānam ānandam’ and the like are not, like sentences such as ‘fire is cold,’ propounding what contradicts perception and the rest. On the contrary, what they convey is experienced as not contradicted; ‘I am happy’ — thus one knows the Self of the very nature of happiness, by oneself; therefore there is, all the more, no contradiction with perception. Hence Brahman, which is bliss and of the nature of cognition, knows itself by itself. So the śrutis that propound bliss — ‘eating, sporting, taking pleasure,’ and the rest cited above — would be coherent.
BR_C03_S09_V28g::block-3: (siddhānta.) Not so; because in the absence of body and sense-organs (kārya-karaṇa), cognition is impossible. For mokṣa is the absolute disjunction from the body; and in the absence of the body the sense-organs are impossible, since they have no support; thence cognition is impossible, on account of the non-existence of body and sense-organs. And if cognition were to arise in the absence of body and the rest, then it would follow that all undertaking of body and sense-organs is purposeless. And on account of contradiction with oneness — if the supreme Brahman, of the nature of bliss, on account of being of the nature of eternal cognition, were to know the Self always, that cannot be; (then) the saṁsārin too, free from saṁsāra, would attain its very nature; like a handful of water cast into a reservoir, it would not stand apart for the cognition of the bliss-natured Brahman. Then ‘the released one knows the bliss-natured Self’ — this sentence becomes purposeless. Or, if the released one, being other (than Brahman), knows the bliss of Brahman, and (knows) the inner Self ‘I am of the nature of bliss’ — then there is contradiction with oneness; and being so, contradiction with all śrutis. A third alternative does not stand. Furthermore, in the case of the uninterrupted self-bliss-cognition of Brahman, the imagining of cognition and non-cognition is purposeless; if the cognition of Brahman concerning self-bliss is uninterrupted, that very cognition being its own nature, the imagining ‘he knows the self-bliss’ is unwarranted; for the imagining has meaning only when there is the contingency of (its being) the cognition of something other (than itself), as in ‘he knows the Self and another’; nor for one whose mind is fixed on an arrow and so forth uninterruptedly is there meaning in the imagining of cognition or non-cognition of the arrow. Or if it knows the self-bliss intermittently — then in the gap of the cognition of the Self there would follow that the cognition has another object; and the Self would be subject to modification, hence the consequence of impermanence. Therefore the śruti ‘vijñānam ānandam’ has only the purport of declaring the very nature (svarūpa-anvākhyāna), not the purport of the self-bliss being an object of cognition. (Objection.) If (bliss) is not an object of cognition, there is contradiction with the śrutis ‘eating, sporting’ (Chā. U. 8.12.3) and the like. (Reply.) Not so; because in the oneness of all-as-Self, those (śrutis) merely restate what is already obtained — for the released one, in the state of being all-as-Self, wherever, among yogins or gods, eating and the rest are obtained, that very thing as obtained is restated; for that very thing belongs to him on account of the all-as-Self state — for the praise of the liberation that is the all-as-Self state. (Objection.) If it is the restating of what is obtained, then sorrow too (would belong to him) — as eating and the like are obtained as occurring among yogins and the rest, so among the immobile and so on, sorrow as obtained (would also be ascribed to him). (Reply.) Not so; for the distinctions of being happy, being sorrowful and the like are superimposed by the delusion produced through contact with the limiting adjuncts of body and sense-organs fashioned out of name and form — by this all this has been disposed of. And the scope of the contradictory śrutis we have stated. Therefore, like ‘this is his supreme bliss’ (Bṛ. U. 4.3.32), all the bliss-sentences are to be so viewed.
BR_C04_S01_INTRO1::block-0:
‘Janako ha vaideha āsāñcakre.’ Its connection (with what precedes) is this. Having drawn out the eight puruṣas beginning with the bodily one (śārīra and the rest), and having reabsorbed them once more in the heart, and having again arrayed them five-fold by the divisions of the directions, and having reabsorbed them in the heart, and having gathered up both the heart and the body — which are mutually supports of each other — into the jagad-ātman called ‘samāna,’ the sūtra of the form of the fivefold function beginning with prāṇa, and having gone beyond that very jagad-ātman which abides as body, heart and sūtra — the Aupaniṣada Puruṣa, designated by ‘neti, neti,’ has been pointed out both directly and through the form of the material cause as ‘vijñānam ānandam.’

Of that very (Puruṣa), an apprehension is to be made anew through the door of the deities of speech and the rest. Hence this commencement of the two brāhmaṇas is for the purpose of (presenting) another means of apprehension. The narrative, however, is for the purpose of displaying conduct (ācāra) —
BR_C04_S01_V01: Oṁ. Janaka of Videha was seated (in his hall of audience). Then Yājñavalkya came up. To him he said, ‘Yājñavalkya, for what purpose have you come — desiring cattle, or desiring questions whose end is in the subtle?’ ‘Both indeed, O sovereign,’ said he. (1)
BR_C04_S01_V01::block-0: ‘Janako ha vaideha āsāñcakre’ — he made the seat, that is, gave audience (āsthāyikā) to those who came desiring to see the king. ‘Atha ha’ — at that very juncture, Yājñavalkya came up — having come for the sake of his own yoga-kṣema (welfare), or having seen the king’s desire to know, for the sake of favouring (him). Having paid him due reverence on his arrival, Janaka said: ‘O Yājñavalkya, for what purpose have you come? Desiring cattle once more, or desiring to hear from me questions ending in the subtle, that is, ending in the determinations of subtle realities?’ ‘Both indeed — cattle and questions, O sovereign’ — sam-rāj is the mark of one who has performed the vājapeya sacrifice; or, he who governs the kingdom by his own command — he is sam-rāj; the mode of address ‘O sam-rāj.’ Or it means the king of the entire Bhārata-varṣa.
BR_C04_S01_V02: ‘Whatever anyone has told you, that let us hear.’ ‘Jitvan Śailini told me: Speech indeed is Brahman.’ ‘As one who has a mother, a father and a teacher would speak, so did the Śailini speak: Speech indeed is Brahman; for what would a speechless man be? But did he tell you its abode and support?’ ‘He did not tell me.’ ‘In that case, this is one-footed, O sovereign.’ ‘Then do you, Yājñavalkya, tell us.’ ‘Speech itself is the abode, ākāśa is the support; one should worship It as prajñā (intelligence).’ ‘What is the prajñā-character, O Yājñavalkya?’ ‘Speech itself, O sovereign,’ he said. ‘Surely by speech, O sovereign, a friend is recognized; the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvāṅgirasas, itihāsa, purāṇa, vidyā, the Upaniṣads, ślokas, sūtras, anuvyākhyānas, vyākhyānas, what is sacrificed, what is offered in fire, what is fed, what is given to drink, this world, the world beyond, and all beings — by speech alone, O sovereign, are these recognized. Speech, O sovereign, is verily the supreme Brahman. Speech does not abandon him; all beings flow to him; having become a god, he goes to the gods, who, knowing thus, worships It.’ ‘I give you a thousand cows with a bull as huge as an elephant,’ said Janaka of Videha. Said Yājñavalkya, ‘My father held that one should not take (the gift) without having instructed.’ (2)
BR_C04_S01_V02::block-0:
‘But what someone has told you’ — for you have served many teachers — ‘that let us hear.’ The other says: ‘He told me — Jitvan by name, the offspring of Śilina, the Śailini — speech indeed is Brahman, that is, the deity Speech is Brahman.’ The other replies: ‘Just as one ‘who has a mother’ — i.e., one whose mother is the right instructress for her son, who is mātṛmān; and beyond that, one whose father is his instructor, pitṛmān; and from the upanayana up to the samāvartana, one whose teacher is the instructor, ācāryavān; thus one possessed of the threefold cause of purity is the very ācārya himself, and never in any way deviates from authority — as such a one would speak to his pupil, just so did the Śailini speak: Speech indeed is Brahman; for what would a speechless man be? — for a mute has nothing to do here or hereafter. But did he tell you its abode and support? — abode means body; support is what is the basis at all three times.’ The other says: ‘He did not tell me.’ The other replies: ‘If so, this is one-footed indeed — that Brahman of which only one foot is given, this Brahman of one foot, void of three feet, when worshipped does not yield fruit, that is the meaning. If so, you, being a knower, tell us, O Yājñavalkya.’

And he says: ‘Speech itself is the abode’ — speech itself is the instrument and the body of the deity Speech-Brahman; ākāśa, named the unmanifest (avyākṛta), is the pratiṣṭhā at the times of origination, abiding and dissolution. ‘One should worship It as prajñā’ — ‘prajñā’ is the upaniṣad, the fourth foot of Brahman; one should worship that Brahman taking it as prajñā. ‘What is the prajñā-character, Yājñavalkya — is prajñā itself, or what is occasioned by prajñā — like the abode and the support, distinct from Brahman, is it like that?’ — No. How then? ‘Speech itself, sovereign,’ he said — speech itself is prajñā, he said; not a prajñā distinct (from speech). How then is speech itself called prajñā? ‘By speech, sovereign, a friend (bandhu) is recognized’ — when one says ‘our friend,’ the friend is recognized; thus too the Ṛgveda and the rest; iṣṭa, the dharma occasioned by sacrifice; huta, by oblation; āśita, by giving food; pāyita, by giving drink; this world, this birth; the other world, the birth to be attained; and all beings — by speech alone, sovereign, are they recognized. Hence ‘speech, sovereign, is the supreme Brahman.’ Speech does not abandon the knower of Brahman as described; all beings flow to him with offerings and the like; having become a god here, after the falling of the body he goes to the gods — he who, knowing thus, worships It.

As the price of the vidyā, ‘a thousand cows with a bull like an elephant in their midst — the bull, an elephant-like one (hasti-ṛṣabha) — I give,’ said Janaka of Videha. Said Yājñavalkya: ‘Without having instructed the disciple — without making him fulfilled — one should not take wealth from the disciple — so my father held; this is my view too.’
BR_C04_S01_V03: ‘Whatever anyone has told you, that let us hear.’ ‘Udaṅka the Śaulbāyana told me: Prāṇa indeed is Brahman.’ ‘As one who has a mother, a father and a teacher would speak, so did the Śaulbāyana speak: Prāṇa indeed is Brahman; for what would a breathless man be? But did he tell you its abode and support?’ ‘He did not tell me.’ ‘In that case this is one-footed, O sovereign.’ ‘Then do you, Yājñavalkya, tell us.’ ‘Prāṇa itself is the abode, ākāśa is the support; one should worship It as priya (the dear).’ ‘What is the priya-character, Yājñavalkya?’ ‘Prāṇa itself, O sovereign,’ he said. ‘Surely, O sovereign, for the sake of prāṇa one performs sacrifices for the unworthy and accepts gifts from the unfit; even there, in whatever direction one goes, there is fear of being slain — for the sake of prāṇa alone, O sovereign. Prāṇa, O sovereign, is verily the supreme Brahman; prāṇa does not abandon him; all beings flow to him; having become a god, he goes to the gods, who, knowing thus, worships It.’ ‘I give you a thousand cows with a bull as huge as an elephant,’ said Janaka of Videha. Said Yājñavalkya, ‘My father held that one should not take (the gift) without having instructed.’ (3)
BR_C04_S01_V03::block-0: ‘Whatever anyone has told you’ — Udaṅka by name, the offspring of Śulba, the Śaulbāyana, told (me): ‘Prāṇa is Brahman’ — prāṇa, the Vāyu-deity, as before. Prāṇa itself is the abode; ākāśa is the support; the upaniṣad — ‘one should worship it as priya.’ How is the priya-ness? — ‘For the sake of prāṇa, O sovereign, for prāṇa’s sake, one performs sacrifices even for those who are unfit (the fallen and the like); one accepts even from one whose gift is not to be accepted, like the savage; there, in that direction, there is fear of being slain’ — vadhāśaṅkā is the meaning — ‘in whatever direction one goes, beset by robbers and the like, in that direction there is fear of slaying’; and all this comes about because of the dearness of prāṇa, for the sake of prāṇa alone, O sovereign. Therefore prāṇa, O sovereign, is the supreme Brahman; prāṇa does not abandon him; the rest is the same.
BR_C04_S01_V04: ‘Whatever anyone has told you, that let us hear.’ ‘Barku the Vārṣṇa told me: The eye indeed is Brahman.’ ‘As one who has a mother, a father and a teacher would speak, so did the Vārṣṇa speak: The eye indeed is Brahman; for what would a sightless man be? But did he tell you its abode and support?’ ‘He did not tell me.’ ‘This is one-footed, O sovereign.’ ‘Then do you, Yājñavalkya, tell us.’ ‘The eye itself is the abode, ākāśa is the support; one should worship It as satya (truth).’ ‘What is the satya-character, Yājñavalkya?’ ‘The eye itself, O sovereign,’ he said. ‘Surely, O sovereign, when one says to a man who has seen with the eye, ‘Did you see?’ — and he replies, ‘I saw,’ that is true. The eye, O sovereign, is the supreme Brahman; the eye does not abandon him; all beings flow to him; having become a god, he goes to the gods, who, knowing thus, worships It.’ ‘I give you a thousand cows with a bull as huge as an elephant,’ said Janaka of Videha. Said Yājñavalkya, ‘My father held that one should not take (the gift) without having instructed.’ (4)
BR_C04_S01_V04::block-0: ‘Whatever anyone’ — Barku by name, the offspring of Vṛṣṇa, the Vārṣṇa, (told): ‘The eye is Brahman’ — Āditya is the deity in the eye. The upaniṣad — satya (truth); for, what is heard by the ear may be untrue, but not what is seen by the eye; therefore, sovereign, when one sees, people say to him, ‘Did you see the elephant?’ — and if he says, ‘I saw,’ that is just true; if another says, ‘I heard’ — that may deviate (from fact); but what is seen by the eye, on account of its non-deviating, is just true.
BR_C04_S01_V05: ‘Whatever anyone has told you, that let us hear.’ ‘Gardabhīvipīta the Bhāradvāja told me: The ear indeed is Brahman.’ ‘As one who has a mother, a father and a teacher would speak, so did the Bhāradvāja speak: The ear indeed is Brahman; for what would a deaf man be? But did he tell you its abode and support?’ ‘He did not tell me.’ ‘This is one-footed, O sovereign.’ ‘Then do you, Yājñavalkya, tell us.’ ‘The ear itself is the abode, ākāśa is the support; one should worship It as ananta (the infinite).’ ‘What is the ananta-character, Yājñavalkya?’ ‘The directions themselves, O sovereign,’ he said. ‘Therefore, O sovereign, in whatever direction one goes, one does not reach its end; for the directions are infinite. The directions, O sovereign, are the ear; the ear, O sovereign, is the supreme Brahman; the ear does not abandon him; all beings flow to him; having become a god, he goes to the gods, who, knowing thus, worships It.’ ‘I give you a thousand cows with a bull as huge as an elephant,’ said Janaka of Videha. Said Yājñavalkya, ‘My father held that one should not take (the gift) without having instructed.’ (5)
BR_C04_S01_V05::block-0: ‘Whatever anyone’ — Gardabhīvipīta by name, by gotra a Bhāradvāja, (told): ‘The ear is Brahman’ — the direction (dik) is the deity in the ear. ‘One should worship It as ananta (the infinite).’ What is the infinity of the ear? — Since the directions themselves are the ear’s infinity — ‘therefore, sovereign, going in whichever direction, the eastern or the northern or any other, no one ever reaches its end; hence the directions are infinite; and the directions, sovereign, are the ear.’ Hence the very infinity of the directions is the ear’s infinity.
BR_C04_S01_V06: ‘Whatever anyone has told you, that let us hear.’ ‘Satyakāma the Jābāla told me: Manas indeed is Brahman.’ ‘As one who has a mother, a father and a teacher would speak, so did the Jābāla speak: Manas indeed is Brahman; for what would a mindless man be? But did he tell you its abode and support?’ ‘He did not tell me.’ ‘This is one-footed, O sovereign.’ ‘Then do you, Yājñavalkya, tell us.’ ‘Manas itself is the abode, ākāśa is the support; one should worship It as ānanda (bliss).’ ‘What is the ānanda-character, Yājñavalkya?’ ‘Manas itself, O sovereign,’ he said. ‘Surely, O sovereign, by manas one is drawn towards a woman; in her a like-formed son is born; he is the bliss. Manas, O sovereign, is the supreme Brahman; manas does not abandon him; all beings flow to him; having become a god, he goes to the gods, who, knowing thus, worships It.’ ‘I give you a thousand cows with a bull as huge as an elephant,’ said Janaka of Videha. Said Yājñavalkya, ‘My father held that one should not take (the gift) without having instructed.’ (6)
BR_C04_S01_V06::block-0: Satyakāma by name, the offspring of Jabālā, the Jābāla. Candramas (the moon) is the deity in manas. The upaniṣad — ‘ānanda’; since manas itself is bliss, therefore by manas, sovereign, one who desires a woman is drawn to (her) — abhihārya is prayed for, the meaning is. Hence, in whatever woman, being desirous of her, one is drawn, in her a like-formed (pratirūpa), conformable, son is born; that son is the cause of bliss; the manas by which he is brought about — that manas itself is bliss.
BR_C04_S01_V07: "Whatever someone has told you, let me hear it." "Vidagdha Śākalya told me, 'The heart, indeed, is Brahman.'" "Just as one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher would speak, so did Śākalya speak — 'The heart, indeed, is Brahman'; for what would there be for one without a heart? But did he tell you its abode and support?" "He did not tell me." "Then this, O emperor, is one-footed." "Then do you, indeed, tell us, Yājñavalkya." "The heart itself is its abode, ākāśa is its support; one should meditate on it as steadiness." "What is the nature of steadiness, Yājñavalkya?" "The heart itself, O emperor," he said. "The heart, O emperor, is the abode of all beings; the heart, O emperor, is the support of all beings; for in the heart alone, O emperor, all beings are established. The heart, O emperor, is the supreme Brahman. The heart does not abandon him; all beings flow towards him. Becoming a god, he reaches the gods — he who, knowing thus, meditates upon this." "I give you a thousand bull-elephants," said Janaka of Videha. Yājñavalkya said: "My father thought one ought not to take without instructing fully."
BR_C04_S01_V07::block-0: Vidagdha Śākalya — "the heart, indeed, is Brahman." "The heart, indeed, O emperor, is the abode of all beings." For beings, having the form of name, form and karma (nāma-rūpa-karmātmaka), have their resort in the heart, as we have stated in the Śākalya-brāhmaṇa, and they have the heart as their support (hṛdaya-pratiṣṭha). Therefore, "in the heart alone, O emperor, all beings stand established." Hence one should meditate on the heart as steadiness (sthiti); and the deity in the heart is Prajāpati.
BR_C04_S02_V01: Janaka of Videha, descending from his cushion, said: "Salutations to you, Yājñavalkya — instruct me." He replied: "Just as, O emperor, one about to undertake a long journey would procure a chariot or a boat, even so, with these upaniṣads you have made your mind composed (samāhita-ātman). Being thus eminent, wealthy, learned in the Vedas, and instructed in the upaniṣads — when released from this body, where will you go?" "That, sir, I do not know — where I shall go." "Then I shall tell you that — where you will go." "Let the venerable one speak."
BR_C04_S02_V01::block-0:
"Janaka of Videha" — since Yājñavalkya knows all the Brahmans (the various brahman-doctrines) together with their qualifications, therefore, abandoning his role of teacher, Janaka, rising from the kūrca (a special seat), drew near (upa) and slid down (avasarpan) — that is, fell at his feet — and said: "Salutations to you, Yājñavalkya — anu mā śādhi, that is, instruct me." The word iti is for completing the sentence.

Yājñavalkya said: "Just as in the world, O emperor, one about to go (eṣyan, gamiṣyan) on a long, extensive road, going by land would procure a chariot, or going by water would procure a boat — even so, conjoined (yukta) with these upaniṣads, meditating upon them, you are samāhita-ātman, that is, your self has been thoroughly composed and conjoined with these upaniṣads. Not merely composed by the upaniṣads — being also vṛndāraka (worthy of honour), āḍhya (wealthy), Īśvara (lord), not poor; adhīta-veda — one by whom the Veda has been studied; ukta-upaniṣatka — one to whom the upaniṣads have been declared by the teachers. Yet, even being thus endowed with all glories, you are still in the midst of fear (bhaya-madhyastha), unfulfilled (akṛta-artha), so long as you do not know the supreme Brahman. When released (vimucyamāna) from this body, by these substitutes for boat and chariot, that is, being thus composed — where (kva) will you go? What thing will you reach?" "That thing, O bhagavan (revered one), I do not know — where I shall go." "Then if you do not know that, going whither one becomes fulfilled, I shall tell you that — where you will go." "Let the venerable one speak, if he is gracious towards me."
BR_C04_S02_V02: "Indha by name, indeed, is this puruṣa who is in the right eye. Him, who is Indha, they call 'Indra' indirectly (parokṣeṇa) — for the gods, as it were, love the indirect and dislike the direct."
BR_C04_S02_V02::block-1: "Indha is his name, indeed." Of the name Indha — that puruṣa who is in the sun, who was previously declared to be Brahman as the eye (cakṣur vai brahma), namely the puruṣa established within the sun — He is this very one (saḥ eṣaḥ); the one who, in the right (dakṣiṇa) akṣan, that is, eye, is specifically established. He has the true name (satya-nāma); Him, this puruṣa — because of the quality of brilliance (dīpti-guṇatva), 'Indha' is His direct name; but Him, being Indha, they call 'Indra' indirectly (parokṣeṇa). For 'the gods, as it were, love the indirect (parokṣa-priyāḥ), and dislike the direct (pratyakṣa-dviṣaḥ)' — they hate the use of the direct name. Hence you have attained your Self as Vaiśvānara.
BR_C04_S02_V03: "Now this form which is in the left eye is His wife, Virāṭ. Of the two, the meeting-place (saṃstāva) is that ākāśa which is within the heart. Their food is that lump of blood (lohita-piṇḍa) within the heart. Their covering is that net-like thing within the heart. Their path which they traverse is the nāḍī that goes upwards from the heart. Like a hair split a thousandfold, just so subtle are the nāḍīs called Hitā, established within the heart; through them indeed the food flows on. Hence this (subtle body) has, as it were, more refined food than this bodily Self."
BR_C04_S02_V03::block-0:
"Now this puruṣa-form in the left eye" — She is His wife. He whom you have attained as the Vaiśvānara-Self — of that Indra, the enjoyer (bhoktṛ), this enjoyable one (bhogyā) is the wife, Virāṭ — being food (anna), being something to be enjoyed. Thus this very pair — the food and the eater (anna and attṛ) — form one couple (mithuna) in dream (svapna). How? "Of those two, this is the saṃstāva" — the meeting-place of Indrāṇī and Indra, where they together (sambhūya) make their congress (saṃstava) with each other. Which is that? "That ākāśa which is within the heart" (antarhṛdaye ākāśaḥ) — within the heart, that is, in the middle of the lump of flesh (māṃsa-piṇḍa) which is the heart.

"Now of these two, this is the food" about to be stated — that which is to be eaten, the cause of subsistence. What is it? "That lump of blood (lohita-piṇḍa) within the heart" — "lohita-piṇḍa" means the blood itself reduced to the form of a lump. The food eaten is digested in two ways: what is gross goes downward; the rest, again, being cooked by fire, is divided in two — the middle juice (madhyama-rasa), through the order of blood and so on, builds up the body which is the lump made of the five elements (pāñca-bhautika); the most subtle juice (aṇiṣṭha-rasa) is this lohita-piṇḍa, established in the heart of Indra in the form of the liṅga-ātman, when conjoined as a couple — that which they call taijasa. That, in the heart of Indra and Indrāṇī thus joined as a couple, having entered into the subtle nāḍīs, becomes the cause of subsistence.

This is what is said by "now of these two, this is the food," and so on. Furthermore: "Now of these two, this is the covering" — for one who has eaten and one who is sleeping there is in the world a covering, and the śruti imagines this commonality. What is the covering here? "That which within the heart is, as it were, a net (jālakam iva)" — being thickly perforated with many nāḍī-openings, it is like a net.

"Now of these two, this is the path (sṛti)" — the path; saṃcaraṇī, the means by which they two move (saṃcarataḥ anayā), the path of going from svapna (dream) to the place of jāgarita (waking). What is that path? "The nāḍī which goes upward from the heart, that is, with its face directed upwards rises (uccarati)." Its measure is now stated: "Just as in the world a hair split a thousandfold becomes exceedingly subtle, just so subtle are the nāḍīs of this body which are called Hitā" — well known by that name. They are established within the heart (antarhṛdaye), the lump of flesh; spreading out from the heart, they go everywhere, like the filaments of the kadamba-flower (kadamba-kesara-vat).

"Through these exceedingly subtle nāḍīs this food flows (āsravat) on (āsravati)" — that is, goes. This deity-body (devatā-śarīra), being built up by this food in the form of a rope (dāma-bhūta), endures. Therefore — since a body is built up by gross food, but this deity-body, the liṅga (the subtle body), endures built up by subtle food, even the food that builds up the gross body is itself "refined" (pravivikta) in comparison with the gross like urine, faeces and the rest; the food that sustains the liṅga is more subtle than even that — therefore, a refined-food (pravivikta-āhāra) being the gross body, more refined than even that refined-food this liṅga-ātman is, as it were (iva eva), "prajviktāhāratara" — more refined-fooded — than this body. From this body (śārīra), that is, from the bodily Self (Vaiśvānara-Self) — the taijasa is built up by subtle food.
BR_C04_S02_V04: "Of him, the eastern direction is the prāṇas going east; the southern direction is the prāṇas going south; the western direction is the prāṇas going west; the northern direction is the prāṇas going north; the upward direction is the upward prāṇas; the downward direction is the downward prāṇas; all directions are all prāṇas. That very Self is described as 'not this, not this' (neti neti); ungraspable, for He is not grasped; indestructible, for He is not destroyed; unattached, for He is not attached; unbound, He does not suffer; He is not injured. O Janaka, you have indeed attained the fearless," said Yājñavalkya. Janaka of Videha said: "Let the fearless come to you, Yājñavalkya, who, sir, declare to us the fearless. Salutations to you. These Videhas are yours; here am I."
BR_C04_S02_V04::block-0:
He, this Self in the heart, the taijasa, sustained by the subtle prāṇa, becomes the prāṇa Himself. For this knower (vidvān), having reached, in due order, from the Vaiśvānara to the taijasa, and from the taijasa to the heart-Self, and from the heart-Self to the prāṇa-Self — for him, the eastern direction is the eastward-going prāṇas (prāñco prāṇāḥ); likewise the southern direction is the southward prāṇas; the western direction is the westward prāṇas; the northern direction is the northward prāṇas; the upward direction is the upward prāṇas; the downward direction is the downward prāṇas; all directions are all the prāṇas.

Thus the knower, by stages, attains the prāṇa, which is the Self of all (sarva-ātmaka), as his own Self. Withdrawing that all-Self into the inner Self (pratyag-ātman), in the seer's seer-hood (draṣṭuḥ draṣṭṛ-bhāva), through neti neti, he reaches the fourth (turīya) Self. The Self whom this knower attains by this sequence — that very Self, described as 'neti neti', up to 'na riṣyati' — has been already explained.

"O Janaka, you have indeed attained the fearless" (abhayam) — that which is empty of all fear caused by birth, death and the rest. "Iti ha" — thus indeed Yājñavalkya is reported to have said. This is what was said earlier: "I shall now tell you that — where you will go."

Janaka of Videha said: "Let the fearless itself come even to you (tvā = tvām), the fearless Brahman, you who, O bhagavan (revered one), to us — to me — declare and bring me to it, by the removal of the obscuration of the upādhi-caused ajñāna. What more do I give as fee for this knowledge — to one who has given me the very Self directly! Therefore salutations to you. Let these Videhas be enjoyed by you as you please; and here am I, established in the state of a servant. Take, as you please, both me and the kingdom" — this is the meaning.
BR_C04_S03_INTRO1::block-0:
The connection (with what follows) is: "Yājñavalkya went to Janaka of Videha." The Self consisting of consciousness (vijñāna-maya ātman) is itself directly, immediately (sākṣād aparokṣāt), Brahman, the inmost of all, the supreme — from such śrutis as 'There is no other seer than this; there is no other seen than this' (Bṛ. U. 3.7.23) and the rest. That very Self, having entered here as marked by the signs of speaking and the rest, exists as something distinct (vyatirikta) — this was already established in the Madhu-kāṇḍa, in the Ajātaśatru-saṃvāda, by negating the agency and enjoyership belonging to the prāṇa and the rest. Yet, again, in the Auṣasta-praśna, having put forth the liṅga (probans) of prāṇana (breathing) and so on, by 'he breathes by prāṇa' and so on, and by 'the seer of seeing' (dṛṣṭer draṣṭā) and the like, He was apprehended in general as having an undiminished power-nature (alupta-śakti-svabhāva).

And His saṃsāra is due to extraneous upādhis — just as in a rope, salt-flat, mother-of-pearl, the sky and the like, the appearance of serpent, water, silver, dirtiness and the rest is due solely to the superimposition (āropaṇa) of an extraneous upādhi, not natural — even so. The unconditioned (nirupādhika), inexpressible (nirupākhya), to be designated only as 'neti neti' — direct, immediate, the inmost of all — is the Self, Brahman, the Imperishable (akṣara), the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), the Ruler (praśāsta), the puruṣa of the Upaniṣads, vijñāna, ānanda, Brahman — thus already established.
BR_C04_S03_INTRO1::block-1:
That very same is again named Indha; the more refined-fooded (pravivikta-āhāratara) is the liṅga-ātman in the inner heart; further beyond is the world-Self (jagad-ātman), having prāṇa as upādhi; and beyond even that, by knowledge (vidyā), dissolving the world-Self which is but an upādhi — like the serpent and the rest in the rope and the like — by 'sa eṣa neti neti', the Brahman, direct, the inmost of all, has been ascertained.

Thus, summarily, by āgama, Janaka has been brought to the fearless by Yājñavalkya. And here, by way of treating other matters, the waking, dream, deep-sleep and turīya (states) have been touched upon — Indha, pravivikta-āhāratara, all the prāṇas, 'sa eṣa neti neti'. Now, by way of the waking and dream states themselves, by extensive reasoning (mahatā tarkeṇa) the same is to be ascertained at length; the fearless is to be brought; and the existence of the Self, by removing the doubts of disputants — its distinctness (vyatiriktatva), purity (śuddhatva), self-luminosity (svayam-jyotiṣṭva), undiminished power-essence (alupta-śakti-svarūpatva), unsurpassed-bliss-nature (niratiśaya-ānanda-svābhāvya), and non-duality (advaitatva) — is to be ascertained: hence this is begun.

The story (ākhyāyikā) is for revealing the manner of giving and receiving the vidyā in the sampradāya, and especially for the praise of the vidyā — as is hinted by the granting of boons and so forth.
BR_C04_S03_V01: Yājñavalkya went to Janaka of Videha. He thought, "I shall not speak." Now once Janaka of Videha and Yājñavalkya had had a conversation about the agnihotra. Yājñavalkya granted him a boon. He chose as his boon the privilege of asking any question he pleased. Yājñavalkya granted it to him. The emperor questioned him first.
BR_C04_S03_V01::block-0:
"Yājñavalkya went to Janaka of Videha." While going, he thus thought (mene = cintitavān): "I shall not speak even a single thing to the king; the purpose of going is only for the sake of yoga-kṣema (livelihood and welfare)." Yet, even with the resolve "I shall not speak," Yājñavalkya answered every question that Janaka asked. What is the cause of his acting otherwise than what he resolved? — Here the śruti narrates the story (ākhyāyikā).

Formerly, indeed, there had been a conversation between Janaka and Yājñavalkya on the occasion of the agnihotra. There, perceiving Janaka's knowledge regarding the agnihotra and being satisfied, Yājñavalkya granted Janaka a boon. And Janaka chose as his boon the privilege of asking whatever he pleased (kāma-praśna). That boon Yājñavalkya granted him. By the strength of that boon-grant, even though Yājñavalkya did not wish to speak (avyācikhyāsu), and was sitting silent, the emperor (samrāṭ), Janaka, questioned him first.

The non-speaking (anukti) at the very moment of arrival was because brahma-vidyā is opposed (viruddha) to action, and because vidyā is independent (svatantra). For brahma-vidyā is independent, requiring no other co-operating means (sahakāri-sādhana-antara-nirapekṣā), and is the means to the puruṣārtha — thus too is established.
BR_C04_S03_V02: "Yājñavalkya, what serves as the light for this puruṣa?" "The light of the sun, O emperor," he said; "by the sun as light alone, he sits, moves about, performs work, and returns." "It is just so, Yājñavalkya."
BR_C04_S03_V02::block-0:
Addressing him as "Yājñavalkya" with a view to drawing his attention (abhimukhīkaraṇa): "What is the light of this puruṣa — by which light does he engage in activities? Whose-light is this one?" The puruṣa here is the ordinary (prākṛta) one, having the form of the aggregate of body and senses (kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta-rūpa), with head, hands and the rest. The question is: does this puruṣa engage in activity by some other light (jyotis) external to his own aggregate of limbs, or by a light included within his own aggregate of limbs? Does he, by such a light, accomplish the function of light (jyotiṣ-kārya)?

What follows from this — whether by a distinct or non-distinct light he accomplishes the function of light? Hear the reason: if it is established as his nature that he is the accomplisher of the function of light only by a distinct light, then in the case of an unseen action of light too, we shall infer it as having a distinct light alone for its cause. If, on the contrary, he engages by a non-distinct light, namely his own Self, then, even when no light is perceptible, on seeing the function of light a non-distinct light alone is to be inferred. If there be no rule (aniyama) — that is, if either a distinct or a non-distinct light is the cause of the puruṣa's activity — then there is nothing but indecision (anadhyavasāya) in regard to the question of light. Thinking thus, Janaka asks Yājñavalkya: "What is the light of this puruṣa?"

Objection: When such skill in inference (anumāna-kauśala) belongs to Janaka, what is the use of his asking? Why does he himself not arrive at the conclusion?

Reply: True; yet, owing to the extreme subtlety of the special relations between liṅga (probans) and liṅgin (probandum), even for many paṇḍitas it is held to be hard to ascertain — what to speak of one alone? Hence, indeed, in deciding subtle points of dharma, the deliberation (vyāpāra) of an assembly (pariṣad) is enjoined, and a particular kind of person is required: "a pariṣad of at least ten, or three, or even one" (Manu 12.111-112) — and so on. Therefore, although the king has the skill in inference, it is fitting that he should question Yājñavalkya, for there is gradation (tāratamya) in the skill of cognition among persons. Or else the śruti itself, by way of the story, presents the path of inference and instructs us, following the human-mind (puruṣa-mati).

Yājñavalkya too, knowing Janaka's intent, intending to teach him the distinct light of the Self, presented to Janaka first a liṅga which establishes a distinct (light): the well-known sun-light is the light, O emperor — thus he said. How? By the sun, which is the light distinct from his own aggregate of limbs and is the helper of the eye, this ordinary puruṣa sits down (āste = upaviśati); palyayate, moves around, going to a field or forest; and there, having gone, kuru kurute, performs action; vipalyeti, returns the way he came. The multiple qualifying expressions are for the purpose of showing the well-known fact of the sun's being a quite distinct light. The display of many external lights is for showing that the liṅga (sun-light) is unfailing (avyabhicārin). "It is just so, Yājñavalkya."
BR_C04_S03_V03: "When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, what indeed serves as the light of this puruṣa?" "The moon alone becomes his light; by the moon as light he sits, moves about, performs action, returns." "Even so it is, Yājñavalkya."
BR_C04_S03_V03::block-0: Likewise, when the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, what is the light of this puruṣa? The answer: the moon alone is his light. When the external aid of the sun ceases, the moon, by its own illumination, supports the activity of the cognitive senses; thus by the moon as light this puruṣa sits, moves about, performs action, and returns. Janaka assents: "Even so it is, Yājñavalkya."
BR_C04_S03_V04: "When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, and the moon has set, what is the light of this puruṣa?" "Fire alone becomes his light; by fire as light he sits, moves about, performs action, returns." "Even so it is, Yājñavalkya."
BR_C04_S03_V04::block-0: When the sun has set and the moon too has set, fire is the light. In the absence of both the celestial luminaries, the household fire and the like, by its own brightness, makes the senses operative upon their objects; hence by fire as light this puruṣa sits, moves about, performs action, and returns. Janaka again concurs.
BR_C04_S03_V05: "When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, and the moon has set, and the fire is gone out, what is the light of this puruṣa?" "Speech alone becomes his light; by speech as light he sits, moves about, performs action, returns. Therefore, your majesty, where one's own hand is not clearly discerned, when speech sounds forth, one goes there." "Even so it is, Yājñavalkya."
BR_C04_S03_V05::block-0: When the fire has gone out, speech is the light; by "vāk" sound (śabda) is here understood. By śabda as object the ear-organ is illumined; the ear-organ being illumined, discrimination arises in the manas; through that manas one engages in outward activity—"By manas alone one sees, by manas one hears" (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.3) is the brāhmaṇa. But how is speech a light, since the property of being a jyotis is not familiar with respect to speech? Anticipating this doubt the text says: "Therefore, your majesty (samrāṭ)." Since this puruṣa, aided by speech as light, conducts his transactions, the property of being a jyotis is established in respect of speech. How? "Even where"—at the time of the rains, when in the cloud-darkness all the lights are set, when one's own pāṇi (hand) is not clearly discerned—then, when all activity is checked because external lights are absent, where speech sounds forth, or a dog barks, or an ass brays, one goes (upa-ni-eti) up to that place: through that śabda as light contiguity arises between the ear and the manas; thereby speech assumes the office of jyotis; thereby, by speech as light, one approaches and is present there—this is the meaning. There he both performs action and returns. The mention here of speech as light is upalakṣaṇa for smell and the other objects too: when ghrāṇa and the rest are aided by gandha and the rest, pravṛtti and nivṛtti likewise follow; thus by these too the kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta receives anugraha. Even so it is, Yājñavalkya.
BR_C04_S03_V06: "When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, and the moon has set, the fire gone out, and speech stilled, what is the light of this puruṣa?" "The Self alone becomes his light; by the Self as light he sits, moves about, performs action, returns."
BR_C04_S03_V06::block-0: When speech too is stilled, and the external aids—gandha and the rest—are likewise stilled, all activity (sarva-pravṛtti) of this puruṣa would seem to come to a halt. The meaning is this: in the waking state the outward-turned senses—eye and the rest—when aided by external lights such as the sun, conduct manifest transaction for this puruṣa; thus in waking the operation of light is seen to be wrought through a light other than the aggregate of one's own limbs. Therefore we infer that even when all the external lights have set, in the state of svapna and suṣupti, and even in waking under such conditions, the operation of light belongs to a light other than the aggregate of one's own limbs. And in dream the operation of light is indeed seen—seeing the meeting and parting of friends, going to other regions, and so on; and from suṣupti the rising: "I slept happily, I knew nothing." Therefore there exists some other jyotis distinct (vyatirikta). What then is that light when speech has ceased? It is said: "the Self (Ātman) alone becomes his light." Ātman here means a jyotis distinct from the aggregate of effects, instruments, and limbs, that illumines the kārya-karaṇa, like the sun and other external lights, itself unilluminated by another, and inwardly placed by elimination (pāriśeṣya). It is established that there is a light distinct from the kārya-karaṇa. The light distinct from kārya-karaṇa, and yet anugrāhaka of the kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta, is seen apprehended by the external organs such as the eye; but this Ātma-jyotis is not so apprehended by the eye and the rest when the sun and the like have ceased. Yet, since the effect of light is seen, by the Self as light alone does he sit, move about, perform action, and return; hence we know that there exists, surely, an inner light. Further, this light is unlike the sun and the rest, and is non-elemental (abhautika); the very ground for this is its non-graspability by the eye and the rest, just as in the case of the sun and the rest.
BR_C04_S03_V06::block-1: Pūrvapakṣa (the Cārvāka-leaning naturalist, svabhāva-vāda): "No—because anugraha is seen only by what is of the same class. The thesis that there is established an inner light, distinct in class from the sun and the rest, is wrong. Why? Because anugraha is seen done to the bodily kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta by the sun and the like, which is of the same elemental class as the upakriyamāṇa. What is anumeya should follow what is dṛṣṭa. Even granting that the upakāraka light is something other than the kārya-karaṇa, like the sun, it must still be inferred to be of the same class as the saṅghāta, since it does anugraha to the saṅghāta, just like the sun. The vailakṣaṇya you allege based on inwardness and non-perceptibility falters by the anaikāntika of eye-lights and the like, which are themselves inward and unperceived yet bhautika. Hence the distinct Ātma-jyotis is mere wishful thinking on your part. Further, since the light follows the existence of the kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta, the light is to be inferred as a property of the saṅghāta. And inference resting on sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa is unreliable, since it is fallible; for by the strength of mere general observation alone you would establish a distinct light, like the sun, apart from the kārya-karaṇa. And what is given pratyakṣa cannot be set aside by anumāna. This kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta itself, in pratyakṣa, sees, hears, thinks, and knows. Even granting another upakāraka light like the sun, that light would itself not be the Ātman, but another light of the sun-type. The very kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta that performs perceiving and the rest must be the Ātman, none other; for an inference contradicting pratyakṣa is invalid." If it be asked: "How then, of an undamaged saṅghāta, can the agency of seeing etc. exist sometimes and sometimes not?"—we say: this is no fault, because such is dṛṣṭa; for what is observed cannot be branded inconsistent. We do not seek another cause for the firefly, in which we observe both prakāśa and aprakāśa. If even there one were to infer a hidden cause, then on some general resemblance everything would be inferable everywhere, which is unwelcome. Nor is it that things have no svabhāva: the heat of fire is not due to another cause, nor the coldness of water. If you say it depends on the dharma-adharma of beings, then you incur the same predicament for dharma-adharma itself, requiring yet another cause; and if granted, anavasthā ensues, which is unwelcome.
BR_C04_S03_V06::block-2: Siddhānta-refutation: "No—because in svapna and smṛti the seeing of what was seen alone is found." The svabhāva-vādin's claim that the act of seeing belongs to the deha alone, and not to anything distinct, is wrong. If perceiving were the deha's, in svapna only what was previously seen would be seen; an andha (one born blind), seeing a dream, sees only what was seen before, not unseen forms in Śākadvīpa and the like. Hence this is established: he who in dream sees a previously seen object is the very one who, when the eye was earlier intact, saw it—not the deha. If the deha were the seer, then with the eye by which it saw being removed, in dream the very thing previously seen would not be seen. There is in the world the well-known utterance, "Earlier I saw the peak of Himavat; today I saw it in dream," even from those whose eyes are removed and from the andha. Hence even when the eye is not removed, the dṛk in dream is the very dṛṣṭṛ, not the deha. Likewise, in smṛti, since the seer and the rememberer are one—he who is the dṛṣṭṛ is the smartṛ. When this is so, even with the eyes shut, while remembering, one sees a previously seen form just as if seeing it; therefore what is shut is not the dṛṣṭṛ; what, with closed eye, while remembering, sees the form, that itself was the dṛṣṭṛ even when the eyes were open. Moreover, the dead body, though anatomically intact, has no seeing of forms—if the deha alone were the dṛṣṭṛ, even in death the act of seeing should occur. Therefore that on whose departure seeing fails and on whose presence it occurs is the doer of seeing and the rest—not the deha. If it be said that the eye and the rest themselves are the doers of seeing—no, in the case of "What I saw, I touch," since with diverse agents pratisandhāna would not be possible. If you say the manas does it—no, since manas too is a viṣaya like rūpa, the property of being dṛṣṭṛ does not fit it. Therefore the inner one, distinct, is established—as the sun is distinct (vyatirikta) from what it lights. The objection, "the inner light must be of the same class as the saṅghāta, since the upakāraka is of the same class as that which is helped, like the sun and the rest," is wrong, since the rule of upakārya-upakāraka in same-class is not invariable. How? Anugraha by ignition done to fire by earthly fuel—grass, oil-cakes, and the like—is of the same earthly class. Yet by that alone, ignition's anugraha is not to be inferred everywhere as belonging only to the same class, since by water—of a different class—anugraha by ignition is seen done to the lightning-fire and the digestive fire (jaṭhara). Hence in upakārya-upakāraka there is no rule of same-class or different-class. Sometimes humans are aided by humans of the same class; sometimes by sthāvara, paśu, and the rest of different class. Hence the reason "because aided only by lights of the same class as the saṅghāta" is no reason at all. As to the objection that the reason "non-graspable by the eye etc." does not establish inwardness and vailakṣaṇya of the further light, being anaikāntika by eye-lights—this is wrong: by the qualification "distinct from the karaṇas such as the eye," the reason is rendered viśiṣṭa. As to the claim that the light is a property of the kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta—no, since this contradicts the inference made: that the light, like the sun, is something other than the kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta.
BR_C04_S03_V06::block-3: Reply to the Vijñāna-vādin (Yogācāra) and Mādhyamika: All these constructions—of momentary vijñāna self-luminous and self-cognized, of vijñāna with grāhya-grāhaka aspects later purified into pure vijñāna, and the further dissolution into śūnya as held by the Mādhyamikas—are pratipakṣa of this Vaidika śreyo-mārga, since they reject the distinct Ātma-jyotis that illumines buddhi-vijñāna. To those who admit external objects, we reply: ghaṭa and the rest do not light themselves; placed in tamas, ghaṭa is never lit by itself; only with conjunction of light from a lamp is sa-āloka ghaṭa seen. Even when ghaṭa and light are conjoined they remain other than each other, since at repeated conjunction and disjunction a difference is seen, like rajju and ghaṭa. Hence the avabhāsaka is vyatirikta. Nor does it light itself by itself. Objection: "the lamp lights itself." Reply: no—because the property of being avabhāsya is the same. Though the lamp lights another, being itself avabhāsātmaka, it does not transgress being avabhāsya by a distinct caitanya, just like ghaṭa. As to the difference that the lamp does not require another light—no: there is no genuine distinction, neither from itself nor from another. The lamp's being grasped by caitanya is no different from ghaṭa's being grasped by caitanya. The claim "the lamp lights itself and ghaṭa" is mithyā, for if it did not light itself one could ask what it would then be like; but no svataḥ-parataḥ difference of the lamp is found in such a state—since one's self-presence and self-absence cannot be conceived. Hence no kādācitka difference; thus "the lamp prakāśayati its own self" is mere falsehood. As regards the alleged self-grāhya-grāhakatā of vijñāna, the lamp is no dṛṣṭānta. Vijñāna's caitanya-grāhyatā is no different from external objects'; whether it be grāhya-vijñāna-grāhyatā or grāhaka-vijñāna-grāhyatā, on a doubtful matter the nyāya seen elsewhere is to be applied, not its contrary. Just as external lamps are grāhya by a distinct grāhaka, so vijñāna, being grāhya by caitanya, even while prakāśaka, is rightly to be grāhya by a vyatirikta caitanya, like a lamp—not ananya-grāhya. And he who is the further grāhṛ of vijñāna is the Ātman, the inner jyotis other than vijñāna. "This leads to anavasthā." No: grāhyatva alone is the liṅga of the grāhaka being a separate vastu, as established by nyāya; but it is no liṅga at all of either being only a grāhaka, or of the existence of a further grāhaka of that. Hence anavasthā does not follow. "If vijñāna's vyatirikta-grāhyatā require another karaṇa, anavasthā follows." No: there is no rule (nor restriction).
BR_C04_S03_V06::block-4: Refutation of momentariness (kṣaṇika-vāda): As to the claim that the sa-āloka ghaṭa arises again and again as different ghaṭas—this is wrong, because of pratyabhijñā at the next moment, "this is the very same ghaṭa." Objection: "pratyabhijñā arises by sādṛśya, as in cut and regrown hair and nails." No: even there kṣaṇikatva is not established, and besides, the unity is jāti-unity. Among severed and regrown hair and nails, the cognition of "hair-ness, nail-ness" rests on jāti-unity and is not abhrānta. In severed-and-regrown hair and nails one does not have the cognition based on individuality, "this is the very same one." In hair and nails of equal length seen after a long interval, one has the cognition "these are like the hair of that earlier time," not "these are the very same." In ghaṭa one has the cognition "this is the very same." Hence the dṛṣṭānta is not parallel. When pratyakṣa apprehends the object as "this very thing," it is not right to infer otherness; for inference contradicting pratyakṣa is mere ābhāsa. Further, sādṛśya-pratyaya is not possible if jñāna is kṣaṇika: only one who has seen one vastu can have the cognition of similarity on seeing another; but a vastu-seer does not abide for another moment to see the second vastu, since on the kṣaṇika-vāda jñāna is exhausted by a single seeing. The cognition "this is similar to that" requires "that"—the smaraṇa of dṛṣṭa—and "this"—the cognition of the present; if having remembered "that," one abides till the present-moment cognition "this," the kṣaṇika-vāda fails. If "that" cognition is exhausted in smaraṇa and "this" is a different fresh cognition that perishes, then sādṛśya-pratyaya "this is similar to that" is not possible, since there is no single cognizer of both.
