The use of "I see this, I saw that" likewise fails: if jñāna is exhausted by perceiving, the use "I saw" cannot stand for one who has seen, since the moment of utterance does not coexist; if it does, kṣaṇika-vāda fails. If the utterance and sādṛśya-pratyaya belong to one who has not seen, then like the inborn-blind speaking of distinctions of form, all this is a chain of the blind, and the composition of the omniscient śāstra and so forth would have to be admitted, which is not desired. Akṛtābhyāgama and kṛtavipraṇāśa are too well known on the kṣaṇa-vāda. Objection: "the cognition is one, like a chain (śṛṅkhalā) joining prior and posterior, and so 'this is similar to that'." No, since vartamāna and atīta are at different times. There the present-cognition is one śṛṅkhalā-link, the past another; the two are at different times. If the chain-cognition reaches both, then a single jñāna spans two moments and kṣaṇa-vāda fails again. Further, the distinctions of mama, tava, and so on become impossible, with collapse of all transactions.
BR_C04_S03_V06::block-5: Refutation of Vijñāna-mātra and Śūnya-vāda: If everything is mere sva-saṃvedya vijñāna, and vijñāna is admitted as having only the nature of svaccha-avabodha-avabhāsa, and there is no other dṛṣṭṛ for it, then the many constructions of anitya, duḥkha, śūnya, anātma do not fit. Vijñāna does not, like a dāḍima, have many contrary aspects, since its svabhāva is svaccha-avabhāsa. If anitya, duḥkha, and the rest were aspects of vijñāna, they would, being anubhūyamāna, become viṣayas vyatirikta (objects distinct from vijñāna). If anitya-duḥkha are the very identity of vijñāna, then their separation, and hence the construction of viśuddhi, is not possible: viśuddhi is from separation of mala that is in samyoga, as in mirrors and the like; one is never seen separated from one's own svabhāva—agni is not seen separated from prakāśa or auṣṇya, its svābhāvika dharmas. Even where the redness of flowers is removed by combination with another substance, conjunction is inferred prior, since by bīja-bhāvana the rise of further qualities in flowers and fruits is seen. Hence the construction of vijñāna's viśuddhi is unfounded. The mala constructed as vijñāna's viṣaya-viṣayy-ābhāsatva is also unsound, because there is no other to conjoin. Conjunction does not occur between an existent and a non-existent; and absent any other conjunction, a dharma seen of a thing, being its svabhāva, cannot be separated from it—as auṣṇya from agni or prabhā from savitṛ. Hence the doctrine that vijñāna is malina by anitya-saṃsarga and viśuddha by its removal is recognized as a chain of the blind, devoid of pramāṇa. As to the puruṣārtha of nirvāṇa for vijñāna, the locus of fruit fails: for one pricked by a thorn the cessation of the pain born of the prick is the fruit; but if the pricked one die, the locus for the fruit of cessation does not stand. So in total nirvāṇa: in the absence of the locus of fruit, the puruṣārtha-construction is futile. For him for whom the puruṣa-word denotes a sattva—Ātman or vijñāna—when the puruṣa himself nirvāṇa-s, who is left to whom puruṣārtha can pertain? But for him who admits an Ātman distinct from vijñāna, the seer of many objects, all this—dṛṣṭa, smaraṇa, conjunction with sukha-duḥkha, separation, kāluṣya from another's saṃyoga, viśuddhi from its removal—stands well. The śūnya-vādin's view contradicts every pramāṇa; hence we do not pause to refute it.
BR_C04_S03_V07: "Which is the Self?" "This puruṣa, made of cognition (vijñānamaya), among the prāṇas, the inner light within the heart—he, being uniform (samāna), wanders between the two worlds; he seems to think, seems to flicker; for becoming a dream, he transcends this world, the forms of mortality."
BR_C04_S03_V07::block-0: Although vyatiriktatva and the rest are established, yet through the bhrānti born of seeing the Self being aided by what seems of the same class, one fails to discriminate whether the Ātman is one of the karaṇas or distinct; hence Janaka asks: "katama Ātmā"—which is the Self?—since the subtlety of nyāya makes such a doubt natural. Or again: even the distinct one being established beyond the body, all the karaṇas appear as if vijñānavat, since the Ātman is not severally apprehended; hence the question. Or katama is asked among deha, indriya, prāṇa, and manas: which is the Self by whom you said "by the Self as light he sits"? Or "this puruṣa whom you call vijñānamaya, all these prāṇas seem vijñānamaya; in these prāṇas which one?"—as among assembled brāhmaṇas "all these are tejasvin; which is the knower of the six aṅgas?" In the first interpretation, only "katama Ātmā" is the question; the rest is the answer. In the second, "katama Ātmā prāṇeṣu" is the question. Or yet again, the entire "vijñānamayaḥ hṛdy-antar-jyotiḥ puruṣaḥ katamaḥ" is the question. The phrase "yo'yaṃ vijñānamayaḥ" is determinately referential; the iti of "katama Ātmā iti" closes the question; assuming no remote connection, "katama Ātmā iti" is the question, and "yo'yam" onward is the entire answer.
BR_C04_S03_V07::block-1: "Yo'yam"—the deixis is by the Self's pratyakṣatva. Vijñānamayaḥ—vijñāna-prāyaḥ; through the conjunction with the buddhi-vijñāna-upādhi, by lack of discrimination, he is called vijñānamaya, since he is apprehended only as conjoined with buddhi-vijñāna, like Rāhu conjoined with the Moon and Sun; for the buddhi is the instrument for all artha, like a lamp set in front in darkness; "By manas alone one sees, by manas one hears" (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.3) it has been said. Every viṣaya-jāta is apprehended only as qualified by buddhi-vijñāna's āloka, as in tamas qualified by the lamp's light; the other karaṇas are mere doors of the buddhi; therefore he is qualified by it as vijñānamaya. Those who explain "vijñānamaya" as a vikāra of the parama-Ātma-vijñapti are mistaken: in "vijñānamayaḥ," "vāṅmanomayaḥ" (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.5) and the like, the suffix-mayaḥ has the established Vedic meaning of "abundance," not their forced sense; a doubtful padārtha may be settled, where prayoga is determinate elsewhere, by the rest of the vākya or by the strength of nyāya; below the text reads "sa-dhīḥ." By the words "hṛdy antaḥ" the meaning vijñāna-prāyatva is justified. "Prāṇeṣu" is a saptamī indicating vyatireka—as in "on trees there is a stone," where sāmīpya is meant; for in respect of prāṇa the doubt of vyatirekāvyatirekatā exists; "prāṇeṣu" means "distinct from prāṇas"; that which is among them is distinct from them—as the tree from stones. "Hṛdi"—lest one think that in prāṇa even the buddhi might be of prāṇa-jāti, the text adds "antar." By "hṛd" the lotus-shaped piṇḍa of flesh is meant; by tātsthya the buddhi is hṛd; in that hṛd, in the buddhi. "Antar" indicates vyatireka from the buddhi-vṛtti. Jyotiḥ—since he is of the nature of avabhāsana, the Ātman is called jyotiḥ. By that avabhāsaka Ātman as jyotiḥ he sits, moves about, performs action; this kārya-karaṇa-piṇḍa appears as if cetanavān, like a ghaṭa placed in sunlight, or like an emerald gem placed in milk for testing—it makes the milk show its own colour. Likewise this Ātma-jyotiḥ, being subtler than the buddhi and even than the heart, though hṛdy-antaḥsthita, identifies with hṛdaya-and-the-rest, the kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta, and so casts the chāyā of Ātma-jyotiḥ, by sūkṣma-sthūla-tāratamya through paramparā, since it is the inmost of all. The buddhi being svaccha and most contiguous becomes the pratichāyā of Ātma-caitanya-jyotiḥ; hence even the discriminating first have the cognition "Ātmā in buddhi." Next, by saṃsarga with buddhi, manas appears as cetana; then in the indriyas, by manas-saṃyoga; then in the body, by indriya-saṃsarga. Thus by paramparā the entire kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta is illumined by the Ātman by his self-luminous caitanya-jyotiḥ. Hence in the kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta and its vṛttis, all the world has the Ātmābhimāna-buddhi at random, according to viveka. Bhagavat says in the Gītā: "As one sun lights this whole loka, so the kṣetrin lights the entire kṣetra" (Bh. Gī. 13.33); "That tejas which is in the sun…" (Bh. Gī. 15.12) and the rest. "The eternal among non-eternals, the conscious among the conscious…"
BR_C04_S03_V07::block-2: Of the bāhya-jyotis—aiding all karaṇas—on their setting, by way of antaḥkaraṇa the hṛdy-antar-jyotiḥ-puruṣa, the Ātman, is the anugrāhaka of the karaṇas, it has been said. Even when the bāhya-karaṇa-anugrāhakas sun and the rest are present, since the sun and the rest are para-artha, since for an acetana kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta sva-artha does not stand, in the absence of the Ātman's anugraha the kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta does not become fit for vyavahāra. Always, all saṃvyavahāra is by the Ātma-jyotiḥ-anugraha, by the other śruti "This heart and this manas, this saṃjñāna…" (Ai. Up. 3.1.2); all prāṇi-saṃvyavahāra is sa-abhimāna; and the cause of abhimāna we have explained by the marakata-maṇi-dṛṣṭānta. Yet, in the jāgrad-viṣaya, since Ātma-jyotiḥ is non-cognized by all karaṇas, since the buddhy-ādi-bāhya-ābhyantara-kārya-karaṇa-vyavahāra is in saṃnipāta, the Ātma-jyotiḥ cannot be drawn out and shown like the muñja-iṣīkā; hence, wishing to show it, the text begins with svapna: "sa samānaḥ sann ubhau lokāv anusañcarati." The puruṣa, the very svayaṃ-jyotis Ātman, being samāna, sadṛśa—with what? By prakṛtatva and saṃnihitatva, with the heart; by "hṛdi" the buddhi denoted by the word hṛd is prakṛtā and saṃnihitā; hence sāmānya is with it. What sāmānya? Failure of viveka, as between aśva and mahiṣa; the buddhi is avabhāsya, the Ātma-jyotiḥ avabhāsaka, like āloka; non-discrimination of avabhāsya and avabhāsaka is well known. By viśuddhatva the āloka becomes sadṛśa with what is avabhāsya; lighting rakta it becomes rakta-sadṛśa, rakta-ākāra; lighting harita, nīla, lohita, the āloka becomes their samāna; thus lighting buddhi, through buddhi the entire kṣetra is illumined—as said with the marakata-maṇi-nidarśana. Therefore samāna with all by way of buddhi-sāmānya; "sarva-mayaḥ" (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.5) the text will say for this very reason. Therefore he cannot be split off and shown by his own jyotiḥ-rūpa, like the muñja-iṣīkā; superimposing all transactions of nāma-rūpa upon the Ātman, and the dharma of jyotiḥ upon nāma-rūpa, and nāma-rūpa upon the Ātma-jyotiḥ, the entire world is bewildered—"this is the Ātman, this is not; possessed of these dharmas, not these; agent, non-agent; pure, impure; bound, free; standing, gone, come; existent, non-existent"—and so on by such vikalpas. Hence, being samāna, he wanders, in succession, through hundreds of saṃnipātas of receiving and discarding the bodily and sensory aggregates, the two lokas attained and to be attained, this loka and the para-loka. The dhī-sādṛśya alone, not svataḥ, is the cause of his wandering through both lokas: the sādṛśya born of the nāma-rūpa-upādhi-bhrānti is the cause, not svataḥ—therefore samāna, he wanders. To show this is pratyakṣa, the text says: "dhyāyatī'va"—as if he engages in dhyāna, as if he cintayati; he illumines, by his cit-svabhāva-jyoti residing in the buddhi engaged in the act of dhyāna, becoming sadṛśa with it, as if he dhyāyati—just like āloka. Hence the world's bhrānti "he thinks"; not paramārthataḥ does he think. Likewise "lelāyatī'va"—he excessively flickers as it were.
BR_C04_S03_V07::block-3: Pūrvapakṣa (Yogācāra-vijñāna-vādin): "There is no other illumining Ātma-jyotiḥ apart from dhī, since neither pratyakṣa nor anumāna apprehends anything beyond dhī—as another dhī at the same moment is also not apprehended. As to your sādṛśya of avabhāsya and avabhāsaka, the example of ghaṭa and āloka—let it be: there it is between two distinctly apprehended things; here we do not apprehend an illumining jyotis distinct from dhī by pratyakṣa or anumāna. Dhī itself, by being cit-svabhāva-avabhāsaka, has its own ākāra and viṣaya-ākāra. Hence neither anumāna nor pratyakṣa can establish a distinct illumining jyotis. As to your dṛṣṭānta of ghaṭa and āloka being distinct yet conjoined and showing sādṛśya—this is granted by us only as a concession; in truth, ghaṭa-avabhāsya-and-avabhāsaka are not different; the ghaṭa itself is sa-āloka, of avabhāsa-ātmaka nature; ghaṭa rises as different and different again; vijñāna alone shines forth as having sa-āloka-ghaṭādi-viṣaya-ākāra. If so, no external dṛṣṭānta exists, since all is mere vijñāna-svalakṣaṇa." Thus, having abundantly imagined of vijñāna itself the grāhya-grāhaka-ākāratā, they imagine its viśuddhi: "that vijñāna, freed of grāhya-grāhaka, becomes svacchī-bhūta, kṣaṇika and abides"—so some hold. The Mādhyamikas hold even its śānti: "that vijñāna too, being saṃvṛta, freed from grāhya-grāhaka-aṃśas, is śūnya alone—like external entities such as ghaṭa."
BR_C04_S03_V07::block-4: Siddhānta-refutation: All these constructions are pratipakṣa of this Vaidika-śreyo-mārga, since they reject the distinct Ātma-jyotiḥ-illuminer of buddhi-vijñāna. To those who admit external objects: ghaṭa is not svātmāvabhāsaka; placed in tamas, ghaṭa is never lit by itself; only with the dīpa-āloka-saṃyoga is sa-āloka ghaṭa seen; even when ghaṭa and āloka are conjoined, they are anya, since on repeated saṃśleṣa and viśleṣa a viśeṣa is seen, like rajju and ghaṭa; with anyatva there is vyatirikta-avabhāsakatva, not svātmā-avabhāsana. Objection: "a dīpa lights itself; lokika folk do not seek another light to see a lamp, as they do for a ghaṭa; therefore the lamp lights itself." No—because avabhāsyatva is the same. Though a lamp lights another, being itself avabhāsātmaka, it does not transgress being avabhāsya by a vyatirikta-caitanya, like a ghaṭa. So vyatirikta-avabhāsyatva is necessary. Objection: "ghaṭa, while caitanya-avabhāsya, requires another āloka; not so the lamp." No—neither svataḥ nor parataḥ is there a viśeṣa: the ghaṭa's caitanya-avabhāsyatva and the lamp's are alike. "The lamp lights itself and ghaṭa" is asat. How? When it does not light itself, of what nature would it then be? No svataḥ-parataḥ viśeṣa of the lamp is found; that is avabhāsya in respect of which a viśeṣa appears in saṃnidhi or asaṃnidhi of an avabhāsaka; svātma-saṃnidhi or asaṃnidhi cannot be conceived for the lamp; hence with no kādācitka viśeṣa, "the lamp lights itself" is mere mṛṣā. Caitanya-grāhyatva of a lamp is non-different from that of ghaṭas. Hence the lamp is no dṛṣṭānta for vijñāna's self-grāhya-grāhakatā. Vijñāna's caitanya-grāhyatva is non-different from external viṣayas; on the doubtful question whether it be grāhya-vijñāna-grāhya or grāhaka-vijñāna-grāhya, the nyāya seen elsewhere is to be applied; just as external lamps are grāhya by a distinct grāhaka, so vijñāna, being caitanya-grāhya, even while prakāśaka, is rightly to be vyatirikta-caitanya-grāhya, like a lamp—not ananya-grāhya. He who is the further grāhṛ of vijñāna is the Ātman, the inner jyotis other than vijñāna. Anavasthā does not follow, since grāhyatva alone is the liṅga of grāhakam being a different vastu, not of the existence of further grāhakas of that grāhaka.
BR_C04_S03_V07::block-5: Refutation of momentariness, vijñāna-mātra and śūnya-vāda: "Sa-āloka ghaṭa rises again as another ghaṭa"—asat, due to pratyabhijñā at the next moment, "this is the same ghaṭa." Objection: "sādṛśya gives pratyabhijñā, like cut and regrown hair and nails." No: kṣaṇikatva is unproved there too, and there is jāty-ekatva; in cut-and-regrown hair and nails the cognition "keśa-tva, nakha-tva" rests on jāty-ekatva, abhrānta; one does not have the vyakti-cognition "this very one," but in ghaṭa one does. Hence the dṛṣṭānta is not parallel. When pratyakṣa apprehends the object as "this very thing," otherness cannot be inferred; for inference contradicting pratyakṣa is mere ābhāsa. Sādṛśya-pratyaya is impossible if jñāna is kṣaṇika: only an ekavastu-darśin abiding for another moment can have sādṛśya-pratyaya; but the kṣaṇika does not abide. Vyapadeśa "I see this, I saw that" likewise fails: if jñāna is exhausted by perceiving, the moment of utterance does not coexist with the perceived; if it does, kṣaṇika-vāda fails. Akṛtābhyāgama and kṛta-vipraṇāśa are notorious on the kṣaṇa-vāda. As to a śṛṅkhalā-pratyaya joining prior and posterior: vartamāna and atīta are at different times; if a single jñāna spans both, kṣaṇika-vāda fails. With sa-svabhāva-anyasaṃyogābhāva, vijñāna's mala-construction is unfounded; with no saṃyogi-mala, viśuddhi-construction fails too. As to the puruṣārtha of nirvāṇa: in absence of phala-āśraya, puruṣārtha-construction is futile; for him who admits an Ātman vyatirikta from vijñāna, dṛṣṭa, smaraṇa, conjunction with sukha-duḥkha, vyatireka, kāluṣya, and viśuddhi all fit. The śūnya-vāda contradicts every pramāṇa; we do not pause to refute it.
BR_C04_S03_V08: This very puruṣa, while being born and assuming a body, becomes joined with evils; and while departing and dying, he abandons evils.
BR_C04_S03_V08::block-0: Just as in this single body, becoming a dream, he transcends the forms of mortality—the kārya-karaṇa—and abides in his own Ātma-jyotis in svapna, so this same prakṛta puruṣa, jāyamānaḥ—being born—how being born? abhisampadyamānaḥ śarīram, attaining the deha-indriya-saṅghāta, that is, attaining Ātma-bhāva in the body—pāpmabhiḥ, by the kārya-karaṇa that is the locus of dharma-adharma in which pāpman inheres, becomes saṃsṛjyate, conjoined. He, mriyamāṇaḥ—departing, going aloft to another body—is glossed by utkrāman; those very pāpman-formed kārya-karaṇa to which he was joined, vijahāti, separates from them, abandons them. As here, in svapna and jāgrat-vṛtti, in one and the same body he ceaselessly wanders by upādāna and parityāga of the pāpman-formed kārya-karaṇa, samāna with dhī—so this puruṣa, in the two ihaloka and paraloka, by janma and maraṇa, ceaselessly attains upādāna and parityāga of the kārya-karaṇa, and wanders till saṃsāra-mokṣa. Thus is established the otherness of this Ātma-jyotis from the kārya-karaṇa-rūpa pāpman, by saṃyoga and viyoga; if it were a property of them, neither saṃyoga nor viyoga with them would be possible.
BR_C04_S03_V09: Of this puruṣa there are only two abodes—this and the world beyond; the third is the abode of dream, the junction. Standing in that junction-abode, he sees both abodes—this and the world beyond. Now, what serves him as the means to the abode beyond, with that means he, on attaining it, sees both evils and bliss-states. When he falls asleep, taking a portion of this all-encompassing world, having torn it down himself and built it up himself, by his own splendour, by his own light, he sleeps. Here this puruṣa becomes self-luminous (svayaṃ-jyotis).
BR_C04_S03_V09::block-0: Pūrvapakṣa: "This puruṣa has no two lokas through which by janma-maraṇa he successively wanders, like svapna and jāgrat. Svapna and jāgrat are pratyakṣa; ihaloka and paraloka are not so by any pramāṇa. Hence svapna and jāgrat alone are ihaloka and paraloka." To this it is said:
BR_C04_S03_V09::block-1: Of this puruṣa there are only two sthānas—not three or four. Which two? "This"—the present jāgrat-janma, the abode qualified by śarīra, indriya, viṣaya, vedanā, pratyakṣataḥ experienced; and "paraloka-sthāna"—the abode that is the paraloka, to be experienced after separation from body and the rest. Objection: "is svapna not also paraloka? then dvayam avadhāraṇa is wrong." Reply: how then? "Sandhyam," the saṃdhi between ihaloka and paraloka—what arises in the saṃdhi is sāndhya, that is the third svapna-sthāna. Hence the dvitva-avadhāraṇa of sthāna stands; the saṃdhi between two villages does not deserve to be counted as a third on a par with the two villages. How is the existence of paraloka-sthāna inferred, in relation to which the svapna-sthāna would be saṃdhya? Because, abiding in that saṃdhya svapna-sthāna, he sees both sthānas—"this and paraloka." Hence beyond svapna and jāgrat there exist two lokas through which the puruṣa, samāna with dhī, wanders by janma-maraṇa-saṃtāna-prabandha. How, then, abiding in svapna, does he see the two lokas? With what āśraya, by what method? It is said: "yathākramaḥ"—ākrama is that by which one āśrayates—the support, the avaṣṭambha; whatever ākrama he has, that is yathākrama. This puruṣa, in respect of the paraloka-sthāna to be attained, becomes yathākrama, that is, endowed with the means of attaining paraloka—vidyā, karma, pūrva-prajñā. That ākrama, becoming forth-tending toward the paraloka-sthāna, like a seed sprouting, ākramya—taking it as support—"sees the both"—the bahuvacana on account of the multiplicity of the fruits of dharma and adharma; "both" means "of both kinds." Which? "Pāpman"—the fruits of pāpa; not the direct seeing of pāpman themselves; hence pāpa-phala-duḥkha. "Ānanda"—dharma-phala-sukha. He sees both, formed of vāsanās of what was seen in earlier births, and the petty fruits of dharma-adharma pertaining to the next janma, prompted by dharma-adharma or by deva-anugraha. How is it known that paraloka-sthāna-bhāvī seeing of pāpman and ānanda occurs in svapna? Because in this very janma, what cannot be experienced is also seen abundantly; svapna is not unprecedented seeing; svapna is mostly remembrance of what was previously seen. Hence beyond svapna and jāgrat exist two lokas. As to the saying that the kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta puruṣa, in the absence of the bāhya-jyotis sun and the rest, conducts vyavahāra by a vyatirikta Ātman as jyotis—the very absence of the sun and the rest does not happen, where this distinct svayaṃ-jyotis would be apprehended; for ever this kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta is apprehended only as conjoined; hence it is, by its own distinct svabhāva-jyotī-rūpa, asat-sama or asat. To show that somewhere indeed the distinct one is apprehended in his own jyotī-rūpa, free of the saṃsarga of bāhya-ādhyātmika-bhūta-bhautika, the text says: he, the prakṛta Ātman, "yatra prasvapiti"—when he sleeps deeply.
BR_C04_S03_V10: There are no chariots, no chariot-yokings, no roads; but he creates chariots, chariot-yokings, and roads. There are no joys, gladnesses, delights; but he creates joys, gladnesses, delights. There are no pools, lotus-tanks, flowing streams; but he creates pools, lotus-tanks, flowing streams—for he is the maker (kartṛ).
BR_C04_S03_V10::block-0: Pūrvapakṣa: "How is the puruṣa svayaṃ-jyotis here, since, just as in jāgrat, all transactions of grāhya-grāhaka are seen, and the cakṣur-ādi-anugrāhaka sun-lights and the rest are seen as in jāgrat? Where, then, is the viśeṣa-avadhāraṇa, 'here this puruṣa becomes svayaṃ-jyotis'?" Reply: by the vailakṣaṇya of svapna-darśana. In jāgrat, Ātma-jyotiḥ is mixed up with the operations of indriya, buddhi, manas, āloka and the rest. But here, in svapna, by absence of the indriyas and the absence of the sun-and-the-rest as their anugrāhakas, it is viviktam, kevalam—hence vilakṣaṇa. Pūrvapakṣa: "But objects are apprehended in svapna just as in jāgrat; how then is vailakṣaṇya stated by absence of the indriyas?" Hear:
BR_C04_S03_V10::block-1: There—in svapna—are not the viṣayas in the form of rathas; likewise no ratha-yogas, the horses and the rest yoked to chariots; nor pathāḥ, paths for chariots. Yet ratha, ratha-yoga, and paths he creates by himself. How, in the absence of the very materials of ratha—wood and the rest? It has indeed been said: "Taking a portion of this all-encompassing world, having torn it down himself, having built it up himself." The mātrā is the antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti, the vāsanā of this loka; taking that, the antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti of ratha-and-the-rest-vāsanā-rūpa, prompted by the karma whose nimitta is the apprehension of those objects, stands forth as dṛśya. That is said by "having built it up himself"; that itself is said by "creates ratha and the rest." Yet there exist neither karaṇas, nor karaṇa-anugrāhaka sun-lights, nor objects illumined by them; only their vāsanā-mātra, alone, taking the form of the antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti prompted by the upalabdhi-karma-nimitta, is seen as dṛśya. The jyotiḥ in which it is seen, of unbroken sight—that is the Ātma-jyotis, here viviktam, like a sword from its sheath. Likewise, no ānandas—the special joys—no muds, harṣas due to lābha of son and the rest, no pra-mudāḥ, those very with prakarṣa; yet he creates ānanda and the rest. So no veśāntas, ponds; no puṣkariṇīs, lakes; no sravantyaḥ, rivers; yet he creates veśānta and the rest of vāsanā-mātra-rūpa. Why? "He himself is kartṛ." His being kartṛ is in respect of being the cause of the karma which is the cause of the rise of the citta-vṛtti that is the locus of the vāsanā—we have explained. But not pratyakṣa-kartṛtva there—since the sādhanas are absent; without kāraka there is no kriyā; nor are there hands, feet and the rest, kriyā-kārakas; where they are present, namely in jāgrat, by the kārya-karaṇa illumined by the Ātma-jyotis the karma is wrought, the antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti's rise becomes the cause of which the ratha-vāsanā-āśraya is the locus. Hence "he is kartṛ"; thus also "by the Ātman alone, by jyotis, he sits, moves about, performs action" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.6). And there too, the cit-jyotis is not paramārthataḥ kartṛ, beyond avabhāsakatva—what by the cit-Ātma-jyotis, by way of the antaḥkaraṇa, illumines the kārya-karaṇa, those, illumined, are engaged in karmas; in respect of those, the kartṛtva is figuratively (upacāreṇa) ascribed to the Ātman. As to the previous "dhyāyatī'va lelāyatī'va" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.7), this is repeated as the hetv-artha here in "sa hi kartṛ."
BR_C04_S03_V11: On this very theme there occur these verses (ślokas). Having struck down the body, as it were, by means of dream, the unsleeping one looks upon the sleeping ones; having taken the luminous (śukra) impressions, he comes back to his (waking) station — the golden Person, the lone Swan.
BR_C04_S03_V11::block-0: tat ete — on this teaching just declared, these ślokas, that is, mantras, occur. svapnena, by the state of dream; śārīram, the body; abhiprahatya, having reduced to inactivity; asuptaḥ, himself unsleeping, since by his very nature his power of seeing and the rest are never lost; suptān, the externally and inwardly directed states which have arisen as the contents of mental modifications, taking shape as latent impressions (vāsanā), all of them now sunk back into their causal form — these sleepers; abhicākaśīti, illumines them, that is, sees them by his unwithdrawn ātma-dṛṣṭi, makes them manifest. śukram, the pure, lustrous form which is the bare essence of the indriyas; ādāya, having taken up; punaḥ, again, for the sake of action, returns to the waking station; hiraṇmayaḥ, golden as it were, having for its nature the light of consciousness; puruṣaḥ — ekahaṁsaḥ — eka eva hanti iti ekahaṁsaḥ: that one alone moves through waking, dream, this world, the next world, and so on; therefore he is called the lone Swan. The vigraha is thus: hanti gacchati iti haṁsaḥ; ekaḥ ca asau haṁsaḥ ca iti ekahaṁsaḥ — pravṛtti through the states is established, while his own self-luminosity (svayaṁjyotiṣṭva) is not lost.
BR_C04_S03_V12: Guarding the lower nest by the prāṇa, immortal himself, he wanders outside the nest; the immortal goes wherever he wishes — the golden Person, the lone Swan.
BR_C04_S03_V12::block-0: Likewise, prāṇena, by the breath of fivefold function (prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna); rakṣan, guarding, fully protecting it — for otherwise the false impression of being dead would arise; avaram, the lower, despicable on account of being a conglomerate of many impurities and therefore extremely loathsome; kulāyam, the nest, that is, the body; he himself, on the other hand, bahis tasmāt kulāyāt, outside that nest; caritvā — although strictly speaking, even when seeing dream he abides in the body itself, yet because at that time there is no functional connection (sambandha-abhāva) with the body, he is said, like ākāśa abiding in a pot, to wander outside it: such is the figure (upacāra). amṛtaḥ, by his very dharma free from dying; īyate, moves; yatra kāmam — to whatever object the kāma, the desire-modification, has arisen, to that very kāma, arisen in the form of vāsanā, he proceeds. The pravṛtti is towards the dream-objects; the nivṛtti, that is the withdrawal from death-fear, is shown by the word amṛtaḥ. The pūrvapakṣin, who imagines that the Self truly dies in deep sleep or dream, is here set aside; the siddhānta is that the Ātman is by nature deathless, as the śruti itself states by amṛtaḥ.
BR_C04_S03_V13: In the dream-state, moving up and down, the deva fashions many forms — now as if delighting with women, now as if laughing, and now as if seeing fearful sights.
BR_C04_S03_V13::block-0: Further: svapna-ante, in the dream-station; uccāvacam — uccam, the high, namely the deva-status and the like; avacam, the low, namely the tiryak (animal) state and the like, despicable; that uccāvacam (samāhāra-dvandva); īyamānaḥ, attaining; rūpāṇi, forms; devaḥ, the luminous one (dyotanāvān); kurute, fashions, brings into being many vāsanā-forms beyond counting. uta api, and also, as if delighting with women — like one who laughs (jakṣat) with companions; uta iva api bhayāni — that of which one is afraid, hence ‘bhayāni’: lions, tigers and the like — paśyann iva, as if seeing them. The repeated ‘iva’ (uta-iva, jakṣad-uta-iva) is load-bearing: it indicates that the apparent agency is upādhi-kṛta, not ātma-svābhāvika. The pravṛtti into pleasure and fear belongs to the vāsanā-rūpa fashioned by the deva; the nivṛtti, the freedom of the witness, is preserved in the very word ‘iva’.
BR_C04_S03_V14: ‘They see his sport, but no one sees him.’ ‘One should not awaken him suddenly,’ they say; ‘hard-to-cure does it become for him whom he does not recover.’ Some, however, say: ‘this very dream of his is the very waking-place; for whatever he sees in waking, that very he sees in sleep.’ Therefore here this Person is svayaṁ-jyotiḥ. ‘So I, being such, give to you, Bhagavān, a thousand; speak further for the sake of liberation,’ said Janaka.
BR_C04_S03_V14::block-0: ārāmam, the playground (ākrīḍā), the field of sport, fashioned by him out of vāsanās, of this — of the Ātman; people see — village, city, woman, food and the like, all fashioned out of vāsanās, taking the form of his ākrīḍana; tam na paśyati kaścana, none whatsoever sees him. Alas! He abides utterly distinct (atyanta-viviktaḥ), within reach of seeing, yet — what misfortune of the world! — although capable of being seen, the world does not see the Ātman. Thus the śruti shows compassion (anukrośa) towards the world. The intent: the supremely distinct, self-luminous Ātman is in dream. ‘taṁ na āyataṁ bodhayet ity āhuḥ’ — even loka-prasiddhi establishes that in dream the ātma-jyotis is distinct from the body and indriyas. What is that prasiddhi? ‘One should not awaken him suddenly’ — thus say physicians and others. Surely they perceive that he, having withdrawn through the gates of the indriyas from the waking body, abides outside, alone; that is why they say so. They also point to the fault: when violently awakened, he does not, those gates of the senses being suddenly invoked, return — and that is what is meant by ‘durbhiṣajyaṁ hāsmai bhavati yam eṣa na pratipadyate.’ ‘yam’ means: that very station of the indriya-gates from which, having taken the śukra (the lustrous indriya-essence), he withdrew; if this Self does not re-enter that indriya-station, but sometimes re-enters indriyamātrāḥ in transposition, then, due to the resultant defects of blindness, deafness and the like, ‘durbhiṣajyam, ha asmai, bhavati’ — by the dative, ‘to this body,’ becomes ‘hard-to-cure’; the body becomes painfully treatable. Therefore even by prasiddhi the svayaṁjyotiṣṭvam in dream is established. ‘svapno bhūtvā atikrāmati mṛtyo rūpāṇi’ — therefore in dream the Ātman is svayaṁjyotiḥ. atho api khalu — others, however, say: ‘this very (dream) is his waking-place’; not a separate sandhya-sthāna distinct from this world and the next; rather it is precisely this very world, the waking-place. ‘If so, what then?’ Hear what follows: if dream is the very waking-place, then this Ātman is not separated from the kārya-karaṇas (effects and instruments — body and senses), but mixed with them; therefore the Ātman is not svayaṁ-jyotiḥ — to bādh (refute) the svayaṁjyotiṣṭvam, others (the pūrvapakṣin) say: ‘jāgarita-deśa eva asya eṣa.’ Their hetu: as the ‘elephant’ and other padārthas which the worldly man sees in jāgarita, those very things he sees even in sleep. That is asat (false), because of indriya-uparama (cessation of the senses); only when the indriyas have ceased does he see dreams; therefore there is no possibility of any other jyotis there. As stated, ‘na tatra rathā na ratha-yogāḥ’ (Bṛhad. Up. 4.3.10). Therefore here this Person verily is svayaṁ-jyotiḥ. By the dṛṣṭānta of dream, that the svayaṁ-jyotiḥ Ātman exists is shown; ‘atikrāmati mṛtyo rūpāṇi’ also; coursing successively through this world, the next world and so on, he is distinct from this world, the next world and so on, and likewise distinct from the two nests, jāgrat and svapna; and from the kramasaṁcāra (sequential coursing) his nityatva (eternality) too — all this is established by Yājñavalkya. Therefore as vidyā-niṣkraya (price for the teaching of vidyā) Janaka offers a thousand: ‘being thus enlightened by you, Bhagavān, I give you a thousand; speak further for the sake of complete vimokṣa from the bondage of kāma.’ Here pravṛtti and nivṛtti are conjoined: pravṛtti through dream-objects (kāmas) and nivṛtti through the discriminative knowledge of asaṅgatva. Schools: against the Bhāṭṭa/Mīmāṁsaka and Vaiśeṣika who hold that the Ātman is intrinsically a kartṛ, the Vedāntin establishes that all kartṛtva is upādhi-kṛta; against the Cārvāka who denies any sentience apart from the body, the very dream-experience is the dṛṣṭānta of an ātma-jyotis distinct from kārya-karaṇa; the siddhānta is that of advaita: svayaṁ-jyotiḥ ātmā.
BR_C04_S03_V15: Verily, this Self, having sported, having coursed, having merely seen good and evil in the saṁprasāda (deep sleep), comes back again the way he went, to his own station, just for dream. Whatever he sees there, with that he is unconnected; for unattached (asaṅga) is this Person. ‘Just so it is, Yājñavalkya. So I, being such, give to you, Bhagavān, a thousand; speak further for the sake of liberation alone.’
BR_C04_S03_V15::block-0: leading bhāṣya — That which was prastuta — that this Ātman abides as the very jyotis itself — has been pratyakṣatas demonstrated by ‘atrāyaṁ puruṣaḥ svayaṁ-jyotir-bhavati’ in dream. But as for what was said — ‘svapno bhūtvemaṁ lokam atikrāmati mṛtyo rūpāṇi’ (Bṛhad. Up. 4.3.7) — here this is doubted: he transgresses only the rūpas of mṛtyu, not mṛtyu itself; for the seeing of joy, terror and the like in dream, even when separated from the kārya-karaṇa, is pratyakṣa; therefore surely he does not transgress mṛtyu; for the kārya of mṛtyu, namely karman, is seen in the form of joy and terror; and if he is by his very svabhāva bound by mṛtyu, then no vimokṣa is possible — for none is freed from his svabhāva. But if mṛtyu is not his svabhāva, then mokṣa from it is possible. To show that mṛtyu is not the Ātman’s own dharma, when prompted by Janaka with ‘ata ūrdhvaṁ vimokṣāya brūhi,’ Yājñavalkya, with the desire to show this, proceeded thus —
BR_C04_S03_V15::block-1: saḥ vai — that prakṛta (under-discussion) svayaṁ-jyotiḥ Puruṣa, this very one shown in dream; etasmin saṁprasāde — samyak prasīdati asmin iti saṁprasādaḥ; in jāgarita, having abandoned the cloudiness born of the impact of hundreds of activities of body and indriyas, freed from them, he becomes slightly clear in dream; here in suṣupta, however, he becomes thoroughly clear — therefore suṣupti is called saṁprasāda; ‘tīrṇo hi tadā sarvāñ chokān’ (4.3.22), ‘salila eko draṣṭā’ (4.3.31) — thus will the suṣupta-stha Ātman be described. Saḥ vai eṣaḥ etasmin saṁprasāde, gradually saṁprasanna, abiding in suṣupti; how saṁprasanna? — desiring to enter suṣupti from svapna, in the very svapna-avasthā ratvā (having sported), having enjoyed delight through seeing friend, kin and the like; caritvā, having coursed in many ways, that is, having experienced the fatigue (śrama) which is the fruit of his coursing — this is the meaning; dṛṣṭvā eva, only by seeing, na kṛtvā (not by doing); puṇyaṁ ca, the fruit of merit; pāpaṁ ca, the fruit of demerit; for there is no direct dṛṣṭi of puṇya-pāpa themselves, as we have said; therefore he is not bound (anubaddha) by puṇya-pāpa; he who does puṇya-pāpa is bound by them; one is not bound by mere seeing. Therefore, having become svapna, he transgresses mṛtyu itself, not merely mṛtyu-rūpāṇi alone. Hence there is no āśaṅkā that mṛtyu is the ātma-svabhāva. If mṛtyu were his svabhāva, he would do (puṇya-pāpa) even in svapna; but he does not; if it were svabhāva, kriyā would persist; there would be anirmokṣatā; but it is not svabhāva, since it is absent in svapna; therefore vimokṣa from mṛtyu, that is, from puṇya-pāpa, is possible for him. Objection: but in jāgarita his svabhāva is just so. Reply: no — that is buddhy-ādy-upādhi-kṛta, brought about by the upādhis like buddhi; that has been pratipādita through the simile ‘dhyāyatīva lelāyatīva’ (4.3.7). Therefore, since in svapna alone there is the absolute atikramaṇa (transgression) of mṛtyu-rūpa, there is neither the āśaṅkā of svābhāvikatva nor the anirmokṣatā. There ‘caritvā’ — the meaning is, having experienced the fatigue which is the fruit of coursing; thereafter, after the experience of saṁprasāda, again ‘pratinyāyam’ — yathānyāyam, yathāgatam: niścita āyaḥ nyāyaḥ, ayanam āyaḥ nirgamanam (departure); pratinyāyaḥ is that āgamana which is the reverse of the previous gamana — ‘yathāgataṁ punar āgacchati,’ such is the meaning. pratiyoni, yathāsthāna; for from the svapna-sthāna having attained suṣupti, he comes back again to his very station — pratiyoni ādravati, svapnāyaiva, just for the sake of svapna-sthāna. Objection: how is it ascertained that in svapna he does not perform puṇya-pāpa but only sees their fruit? — for as in jāgarita, so in svapna he performs them, the dṛśya being equally direct. Reply: saḥ ātmā, yat kiñcit tatra svapne paśyati, the puṇya-pāpa-phala; anvāgataḥ, unconnected, unbound by that-which-is-seen, he becomes; he is not anubaddha; for if it were truly done by him in svapna, he would be bound by it; even on rising from svapna he would be samanvāgata; but that is not so in loka — there is no prasiddhi of being followed-up by deeds done in svapna; for none considers himself an offender (āgaskārin) for an offense done in svapna; nor does the world censure or shun one upon hearing of an offense seen in svapna; hence he is just unconnected by it; therefore in svapna he is upalabhyate as if doing, but in paramārtha there is no kriyā at all. Citation: ‘uteva strībhiḥ saha modamānaḥ.’ The pūrvapakṣa is that the kartṛtva belongs to the Ātman intrinsically; the siddhānta of Vedānta is that asaṅgatā is the cause of akartṛtva (asaṅgatvāt akartṛtvam), as the śruti itself declares, ‘asaṅgo hyayaṁ puruṣaḥ.’
BR_C04_S03_V16: Verily, this very Self, having sported, having coursed, having merely seen good and evil in this dream, comes back again the way he went, to his own station, just for the waking-state. Whatever he sees there, with that he is unconnected; for unattached is this Person. ‘Just so it is, Yājñavalkya. So I, being such, give to you, Bhagavān, a thousand; speak further for the sake of liberation alone.’
BR_C04_S03_V16::block-0: There, by ‘asaṅgo hyayaṁ puruṣaḥ’ (Bṛhad. Up. 4.3.15), asaṅgatā has been declared as the hetu for akartṛtva. And earlier it has been said: ‘karma-vaśāt sa īyate yatra kāmam’ — and kāma is precisely saṅga; therefore the hetu uttered, ‘asaṅgo hyayaṁ puruṣaḥ,’ would seem asiddha (unestablished). But this objection (of the pūrvapakṣin) is not so. How, then? — it is just to teach that ‘he is asaṅga only,’ that this declaration is made: saḥ vai eṣaḥ etasmin svapne, this very Person, returned from saṁprasāda into svapna, ratvā, having sported as he wishes, caritvā yathākāmam, having coursed; dṛṣṭvā eva puṇyaṁ ca pāpaṁ ca — all as before; buddhāntāya eva, just for the jāgarita-sthāna. Therefore this Puruṣa is asaṅga eva. Were he saṅga-vān, kāmin (afflicted with desire), in svapna, then by the doṣas born of that saṅga he would be lipta (smeared) when he came back to buddhānta. The śabdārtha and vigraha: ‘a-saṅga’ — saṅgaḥ saṅjate iti saṅgaḥ; na vidyate saṅgaḥ asya iti asaṅgaḥ — asambandhaḥ, that whose nature is non-conjunction with anything. The schools: against the Sāṁkhya who admits a separate puruṣa but still requires bondage to be sambandha-ja, the Vedāntin states that the Ātman is asaṅga in his very nature; against the Naiyāyika who imputes kartṛtva by samavāya, the bhāṣya replies that absence of saṅga rules out any samavāya-relation with kāma. The pravṛtti through dream-objects is real only at the level of upādhi; the nivṛtti, the absence of being smeared upon return, is the very proof of asaṅgatā.
BR_C04_S03_V17: Verily, this very Self, having sported, having coursed, having merely seen good and evil in this waking-state, comes back again the way he went, to his own station, just for the dream-state.
BR_C04_S03_V17::block-0: leading bhāṣya — Just as in svapna, due to asaṅgatva, by the doṣas born of svapna-prasaṅga he is not lipta when he returns to jāgarita, in the same way by the doṣas born of jāgarita-saṅga he is not lipta even in buddhānta — that is now stated —
BR_C04_S03_V17::block-1: Saḥ vai eṣaḥ etasmin buddhānte, in jāgarita; ratvā, caritvā — and so on as before. saḥ yat tatra buddhānte kiñcit paśyati, anvāgataḥ tena bhavati — asaṅgo hyayaṁ puruṣaḥ. Objection: how is ‘dṛṣṭvā eva’ to be ascertained? In jāgarita he certainly does perform puṇya-pāpa and sees their fruit. Reply: no — because of kāraka-avabhāsakatva: by the kartṛtva-upapatti, by his being merely the illuminator of the kārakas. By ‘ātmanaivāyaṁ jyotiṣāste’ (Bṛhad. Up. 4.3.6), illumined by the ātma-jyotis, the kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta transacts; by that, kartṛtva is upacarita (figuratively imputed) to him, not svataḥ kartṛtva. Thus too has been said: ‘dhyāyatīva lelāyatīva’ (4.3.7) — buddhy-ādy-upādhi-kṛta only, not svataḥ. But here, in the perspective of paramārtha, irrespective of upādhi, it is said: ‘dṛṣṭvā eva puṇyaṁ ca pāpaṁ ca, na kṛtvā.’ Hence there is no āśaṅkā of pūrva-apara-vyāghāta (contradiction between earlier and later), since the nirupādhika Self in paramārtha does not act, is not lipta by kriyā-phala. So too says Bhagavān: ‘anāditvān nirguṇatvāt paramātmāyam avyayaḥ | śarīrastho’pi kaunteya na karoti na lipyate’ (Bhagavad-gītā 13.31). The thousand-gift, by the way, is precisely the dṛṣṭānta of kāma-praviveka — the disjunction from kāma — already shown. Likewise, by the two paragraphs ‘sa vai eṣa etasmin svapne’ and ‘sa vai eṣa etasmin buddhānte,’ asaṅgatā alone is taught: since one whom going to svapnānta, who is saṁprasanna, is asambaddha (unconnected) with what was done in buddhānta — for no theft and other kārya is observed — therefore in all three sthānas (states) he is svataḥ asaṅga; therefore amṛta, distinct from the three sthāna-dharmas. ‘pratiyoni ādravati svapnāntāyaiva’ — that is, for saṁprasāda; for ‘svapna’ here designates the dṛśya-vṛtti (perceptive functioning), and the suffix ‘anta’ admits the special qualification, since ‘etasmā antāya dhāvati’ (4.3.19) will describe suṣupta. Even should one say that, given ‘svapnānte ratvā caritvā’ (4.3.34) and ‘etāv ubhāv antāv anusañcarati svapnāntaṁ ca buddhāntaṁ ca’ (4.3.18), the word ‘svapna’ here refers to ordinary dream as dṛśya-vṛtti — even so, no harm is done; the asaṅgatā which is the siṣādhayiṣitā (intended to be established) is established all the same; for, having merely seen puṇya and pāpa, having ratvā and caritvā in jāgarita, he comes to svapnānta unfollowed by the jāgarita-doṣa. Schools: against the Yogācāra who reduces all to vijñāna-pariṇāma and thus would deny a witness distinct from the changing states, the bhāṣya posits an asaṅga sākṣin distinct from the three sthānas; against the Bhāṭṭa whose karman-doctrine ties the Self by samavāya, asaṅgatā is the very śabda of śruti.
BR_C04_S03_V18: Just as a great fish swims along both banks of a river, the eastern and the western, even so this Person courses along these two extremes — the dream-end and the waking-end.
BR_C04_S03_V18::block-0: leading bhāṣya — Thus this Puruṣa-Ātman is svayaṁ-jyotiḥ, vilakṣaṇa from the kārya-karaṇa, and likewise vilakṣaṇa from kāma and karman, the two prayojakas (instigators) of those — for ‘asaṅgo hyayaṁ puruṣaḥ,’ from the asaṅgatva — this artha (purport) has been pratipādita through the three kaṇḍikās beginning with ‘sa vai eṣa etasmin saṁprasāde’ (4.3.15). There the asaṅgatā of the Ātman — whence? — for from jāgarita to svapna, from svapna to saṁprasāda, from saṁprasāda again to svapna, in sequence to buddhānta jāgarita, and from buddhānta back to svapnānta — by such anukrama-saṁcāra is the vyatireka (separateness) of the three sthānas sādhitaḥ (established). Earlier too this artha has been upanyasta: ‘svapno bhūtvemaṁ lokam atikrāmati mṛtyo rūpāṇi’ (4.3.7); having pratipādita that in detail, only the dṛṣṭānta-mātra (the bare illustration) remains; that I shall now state — thus he begins —
BR_C04_S03_V18::block-1: tat tatra etasmin, yathā — in the artha thus shown, this dṛṣṭānta is taken up: yathā loke mahā-matsyaḥ — mahān ca asau matsyaḥ ca: not removable by the river’s current — that is, who even obstructs the current, the svacchanda-cārī (one who moves at will); ubhe kūle nadyāḥ pūrvaṁ ca aparaṁ ca anukrameṇa sañcarati; though so coursing, by the velocity of the udaka-srotas (water-current) flowing between the two banks, he is not paravaśī-kṛta (made dependent) — evam eva ayaṁ puruṣaḥ etau ubhau antau anusañcarati. Which two? — svapnāntaṁ ca buddhāntaṁ ca. The fruit (phala) of showing the dṛṣṭānta is: the kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta which is mṛtyu-rūpa, together with its prayojakas kāma and karman, is anātma-dharma; this Ātman is vilakṣaṇa from this — thus has been vyākhyātam (explained) in detail. Thus the pravṛtti among the three states belongs to the upādhi; the nivṛtti — the asaṅgatva of the witness — belongs to the svayaṁ-jyotiḥ Puruṣa. Schools: the Sāṁkhya, by his prakṛti-puruṣa-viveka, also reaches a vilakṣaṇa puruṣa, but admits two ultimate principles; the Advaita-siddhānta is that the very mahā-matsya is not within the river but is its draṣṭā, asaṅga, and one without a second.
BR_C04_S03_V19: Just as in this space a falcon (śyena) or an eagle (suparṇa), having flown about and become weary, folds its wings and resorts to its nest for repose, even so this puruṣa hastens to that state in which, fallen asleep, he desires no desire whatsoever, sees no dream whatsoever.
BR_C04_S03_V19::block-0: Here, by the traversal of the three states (sthāna-traya-anusañcāra), the distinction of the self-luminous Ātman from the aggregate of body and organs, and his being free from desire and karma, has been declared; intrinsically this Self is not endowed with the attributes of saṃsāra — his saṃsāritva is solely due to upādhi and is superimposed by avidyā (adhyāropita). This is the comprehensive purport that has been stated. Yet therein the threefold form of waking, dream and deep sleep has been shown only as scattered, not gathered together and exhibited in one place — for in the waking state he is observed, through avidyā, as being conjoined with attachment (saṅga), with mortality (mṛtyu), and with the body-organ aggregate; in the dream state he is observed as conjoined only with desires (kāma) but freed from the form of mortality; in deep sleep, again, he becomes serene (samprasanna) and unattached (asaṅga), and thus even his unattachedness (asaṅgatā) is seen. The fruit, however, summed up by way of unitary purport (eka-vākyatā) — namely his innate nature as ever-free, ever-awake, ever-pure (nitya-mukta-buddha-śuddha-svabhāva) — has not been displayed in one place gathered together; therefore, in order to display that, this section is begun. For in deep sleep his nature, about to be declared, is such — "That, verily, is this his form, transcending all longing, free from evil, fearless" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.21); since such, exceedingly distinct, is this state, the śruti wishes to enter into deep sleep. How that is so it answers — by an illustration this meaning becomes manifest; therefore an example is taken up here.
BR_C04_S03_V19::block-1: "Tat — yathā" — just as in this elemental ākāśa a śyena (falcon) or a suparṇa — by the word suparṇa a swift falcon is meant — having sported and flown about (vihṛtya viparipatya) in this space, becomes weary (śrānta), exhausted by the action characterised by manifold flying about; "saṃhṛtya pakṣau" — having drawn together its wings and folded them well; "saṃlaya" — that into which one fully reposes (samyak līyate asmin), the nest (nīḍa); "nīḍāyaiva" — for the nest alone; "dhriyate" — is held up by its own self, supports itself by itself. As is this dṛṣṭānta, even so this puruṣa hastens "etasmai antāya" — "unto this end." The qualification of what is denoted by the word "anta" follows: "yatra" — in which end, having fallen asleep, he desires no desire whatsoever (na kañcana kāmaṃ kāmayate), and likewise sees no dream whatsoever (na kañcana svapnam paśyati). By "na kañcana kāmam" every desire whatsoever, both of dream and of waking, is negated without distinction, since the word "kañcana" is uttered without qualification. Likewise by "na kañcana svapnam" — even the seeing in the waking state the śruti regards as "svapna," and therefore declares: he sees no dream whatsoever. So another śruti says: "His are three abodes, three dreams" (Ait. Up. 1.3.12). As in the dṛṣṭānta the bird's resort to its own nest is for the dispelling of the fatigue born of flying, so when the puruṣa, in waking and dream, gets conjoined with the actions and their fruits born of the conjunction of body and organs, fatigue arises in him as in the bird from flying; for the dispelling of that fatigue he enters his own nest, his own abode — his own Ātman, distinct from all the dharmas of saṃsāra and devoid of the toil of all action, agency and fruit.
BR_C04_S03_V20: These nāḍīs of his, called "Hitā," are as fine as a hair split a thousandfold, and stand of that very fineness, filled with white, blue, yellow, green, and red. When they (as it were) slay him, (as it were) overpower him, an elephant (as it were) chases him, he (as it were) falls into a pit — whatever fear he sees in waking, that very thing he, in this state, supposes through avidyā. But when he supposes himself, as it were, a god, as it were a king — "I myself am all this" — that is his highest world.
BR_C04_S03_V20::block-0: If this is his nature — being void of all the dharmas of saṃsāra — and if his being endowed with saṃsāric attributes is solely due to extraneous upādhis, and if avidyā is the cause of that upādhi-conditioned saṃsāra-dharmitva — then is that avidyā svābhāvika (intrinsic) to the Self, or is it āgantuka (adventitious) like desire and karma? If it be adventitious, mokṣa is feasible. What proof is there of its adventitiousness? And how is avidyā not a property of the Self? In order to ascertain the true nature of avidyā, the seed of all evils, the next section is begun.
BR_C04_S03_V20::block-1: "Tāḥ vai" — those, indeed, of this puruṣa characterised by head, hands, etc., "etāḥ hitā nāma nāḍyaḥ" — are these nāḍīs called Hitā; like a hair split a thousandfold ("keśaḥ sahasradhā bhinnaḥ"), they stand of that very dimension in fineness ("aṇimnā"). They are filled with the rasas (humours) — white, blue, yellow, green and red; that is, they are full of these specific colours of humours. These specific colours of humours arise from the various proportions of mutual conjunction of vāta, pitta and śleṣma, and so are diverse and many. In these subtle nāḍīs — of dimension equal to the thousandth division of a hair-tip, filled with the rasas of white etc., pervading the whole body — there abides the seventeenfold subtle body (saptadaśakaṃ liṅgam, the liṅga-śarīra). Resting in it are all the vāsanās generated by the experience of the high and low dharmas of saṃsāra; that liṅga, the receptacle of the vāsanās, on account of its subtlety transparent like a sphaṭika gem (sphaṭika-maṇi-kalpam), through contact with the upādhi of the rasas in the nāḍīs, with its specific functions arisen by the impulsion of dharma and adharma, presents itself through the vāsanās in the form of women, chariots, elephants, and other figures. Now this being so — "yatra" — at whatever time, the cognition arises (false, generated by vāsanā, called avidyā): "some enemies or thieves come to me and slay me"; this is what is said: "They (as it were) slay him" — the dreamer; likewise "jinanti iva" — overpower him as it were, subjugate him as it were; none in fact slay or subjugate, it is merely a delusion arising from the manifestation of the vāsanās of avidyā. Likewise "hastīva enaṃ vicchāyayati" — an elephant as it were drives him, scares him away, makes him flee. "gartam iva patati" — he sees himself as falling into a pit, an old well or the like; such a wretched vāsanā arises in him, exceedingly low, having for its substratum a function of the antaḥkaraṇa illumined by adharma, since it is of the nature of pain. What more? "yad eva jāgrad bhayaṃ paśyati" — whatever fear he sees in waking, characterised by elephants and the like, that very fear, even without the actual elephant etc. being present, in this dream he imagines through the vāsanā of avidyā, falsely arisen.
BR_C04_S03_V20::block-2: Now, again, "yatra" — when avidyā is being attenuated and vidyā is rising — what is its viṣaya, what is its lakṣaṇa, is being told — when, at whatever time, he himself becomes "deva iva," as a god: when knowledge regarding deities (devatā-viṣayā vidyā) has arisen in the waking state, then through that vāsanā so risen he imagines himself as a god in dream too. So it is said: "deva iva, rāja iva" — like a king consecrated upon his throne; even in dream the king-vāsanā-vāsita imagines "I am king." Thus, when avidyā is being utterly diminished, and vidyā having all-Self for its viṣaya (sarvātma-viṣayā vidyā) has arisen, then in dream too, being filled with that bhāva, he imagines: "I myself am verily all this" — "aham eva idaṃ sarvo'smi." That sarvātma-bhāva is for this Self the supreme world (paramo lokaḥ), the natural and supreme state of selfhood. But that which, even by the breadth of a hair-tip, is seen as other than the sarvātma-bhāva — "this is not myself" — that very state is avidyā. The non-Self worlds (anātma-bhāvāḥ lokāḥ) which are presented by that avidyā — ranging down to the immobile — are aparama (non-supreme). With reference to these worlds of empirical transaction, this sarvātma-bhāva, integral, without inside or outside, is supreme — that is his paramo lokaḥ. Therefore, when avidyā is being attenuated and vidyā has reached its consummation (kāṣṭhāṃ gatāyām), the sarvātma-bhāva is mokṣa: just as the self-luminosity is directly perceived in dream, even so the fruit of vidyā is realised — this is the meaning. Likewise when avidyā is waxing and vidyā is fading, of avidyā...
BR_C04_S03_V21: That, verily, is this his form, transcending all longing, free from evil, fearless. Just as a man embraced by a beloved wife knows nothing without or within, even so this puruṣa, embraced by the prājña Ātman, knows nothing without or within. That, verily, is this his form — wherein desire is fulfilled, in which the Self alone is desired, in which there is no desire — the form beyond sorrow.
BR_C04_S03_V21::block-0: Now that sarvātma-bhāva which is mokṣa, the fruit of vidyā, devoid of action-agency-fruit (kriyā-kāraka-phala-śūnyam), is now directly indicated, wherein avidyā, kāma and karma are not. That very thing has been brought up: "yatra supto na kañcana kāmaṃ kāmayate na kañcana svapnaṃ paśyati" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.19); that very form is being declared. Of him who is the sarvātma-bhāva, declared as "sa asya paramo lokaḥ" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.20) — that. "Aticchandāḥ" — meaning aticchandam (the visarga-ending being read on account of its being applied to rūpa); chandas means kāma, that rūpa from which all longing has departed (atigataḥ chandaḥ yasmād rūpāt) is aticchandam. There is another word "chandas," ending in a halant, which denotes Vedic metres (gāyatrī etc.); but here the word denotes desire, hence it ends in a vowel; even so the reading "aticchandāḥ" is to be regarded as a peculiarity of the recension (svādhyāya-dharma). In ordinary usage too the word "chanda" is used in the sense of desire — "svacchandaḥ," "paracchandaḥ," etc. Therefore one should construe it as aticchandam — "this is the rūpa which is destitute of desire." "Apahatapāpma" — by the word pāpman, dharma and adharma are denoted, since it has been said "is conjoined with pāpmans" and "sheds his pāpmans" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.8); "apahatapāpma" means free of dharma and adharma. Further, "abhayam" — fear is the kārya (effect) of avidyā, as has been said "through avidyā he supposes fear" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.20); this is a negation of the cause through the effect (kārya-dvāreṇa kāraṇa-pratiṣedha); "abhayam rūpam" means the form devoid of avidyā. This sarvātma-bhāva which is the fruit of vidyā — that very thing is the rūpa that is aticchanda, apahatapāpman and abhaya — devoid of all dharmas of saṃsāra, and hence "abhayaṃ rūpam." This very thing was already adumbrated, by the way of āgama, at the close of the previous brāhmaṇa: "Janaka, you have attained fearlessness" (Bṛ. Up. 4.2.4); but here it is amplified through tarka (reasoning) for the firming of the conviction in the sense of the āgama already shown.
BR_C04_S03_V21::block-1: This Ātman is by his very nature self-luminous, the light of caitanya (caitanya-jyotiḥ-svabhāva); by his own caitanya-jyotis he illumines all — "that whatever there he sees, sports, moves, knows" — has been said. And it has been established by reasoning that the eternal nature of the Self is its self-luminous caitanyatva. If this Ātman remains here in deep sleep undestroyed in his own form, why does he not know himself as "I am," nor know the externals as "these bhūtas," as in waking and dream? To this it is replied: hear the cause of non-knowing here; oneness alone is the cause of non-knowing (ekatvam eva ajñāna-hetuḥ). How that is, is being said. By an example the intended sense becomes pratyakṣī — perceptible — therefore: "tat" — there, as in the world, by a beloved (priyā) wife who is desiring him, the lover when fully embraced (samparisvaktaḥ samyak parisvaktaḥ) knows nothing external apart from himself — "there is some other object distinct from me" — nor anything internal — "I am here, happy or unhappy"; but when not embraced by her and separated from her, he knows everything — both external and internal; after the embrace, however, on account of attaining oneness (ekatva-āpatti), he does not know. Even so, as is the dṛṣṭānta — this puruṣa, the kṣetrajña, who, due to contact with elemental aggregates, like a salt-lump (saindhava-khilya-vat) appears as separated, and like the reflection of the moon etc. in water has entered into the body-organ — that very puruṣa, by the prājña — by the supreme, natural, his own Self, the higher Light (pareṇa jyotiṣā) — when fully embraced, becomes unitary, without interval, the All-Self, knowing nothing within or without; this is the import.
BR_C04_S03_V22: Here a father is no father, a mother no mother, the worlds no worlds, the gods no gods, the Vedas no Vedas. Here a thief is no thief, a slayer of an embryo no slayer, a Caṇḍāla no Caṇḍāla, a Paulkasa no Paulkasa, a śramaṇa no śramaṇa, a tāpasa no tāpasa; he is unfollowed by puṇya, unfollowed by pāpa — for then he has crossed over all the sorrows of the heart.
BR_C04_S03_V22::block-0: It has been declared that the prakṛta self-luminous Ātman is free from avidyā, kāma and karma, since the Self is asaṅga and these are āgantuka (adventitious). Therein this doubt arises: even though caitanya is the svabhāva, on account of becoming one (ekī-bhāva), he does not know — like the man and woman embraced — has been said; and there it has been said by way of digression: like kāma and karma, even self-luminosity (svayañjyotiṣṭva) is not the svabhāva of the Self, since it is not apprehended in samprasāda (deep sleep). To remove this objection, by adducing the example of man and woman, it was incidentally stated that the non-grasping in sleep of the existing self-luminosity is due to oneness (ekī-bhāva-hetu) and not adventitious like kāma-karma. Having stated this incidentally, the prakṛta (the matter at hand) is now resumed. The prakṛta here is this: the form which is grasped directly in sleep of the Self is verily free from avidyā, kāma and karma. That very thing is now declared as it is (yathābhūtam) — beyond all relations is this rūpa. Since here in this sleep-state "this is his form, transcending all longing, free from evil, fearless," therefore here a father — janayitṛ — and his fatherhood (pitṛtva) towards his son, which is karma-nimittam, is set aside; from that karma he is here unconnected; therefore even a father becomes "apitā," being free from the karma that is the cause of the father-son relation. Likewise the son too becomes "aputraḥ" of the father — this follows by sāmarthya. The cause of the relation in both is karma, which here he transcends. "Apahatapāpma" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.21) has been said. Likewise "mātā amātā."
BR_C04_S03_V22::block-1: Lokas — to be conquered by karma and conquered — by the absence of relation with that karma the lokas become alokāḥ. Likewise devas, who are part of karma — by the cessation of relation with that karma, devas become adevāḥ. Likewise Vedas — declarative of sādhya-sādhana relation, having mantra-lakṣaṇa, ancillary to karma by way of denotation, studied and to be studied — these are connected with the puruṣa only on account of karma; by the transcendence of that karma, even the Vedas at this time become "avedāḥ." Not only is he beyond connection with auspicious karma, but with most ghoraja (terrible) inauspicious karmas too he is unconnected — to declare this it is said: "atra stenaḥ" — a thief, a stealer of brahman's gold, is here understood by way of being read along with bhrūṇa-han; by that ghora karma at this time he is freed, by which karma he is called the great pātakin (sinner) and stenaḥ. Likewise bhrūṇahā abhrūṇahā. "Caṇḍāla" — not merely is he free from karma generated in the present, but even from sahaja (innate, inherited) karma — that which produces an exceedingly low birth — he is here free; the Caṇḍāla, namely, is one born of a śūdra in a brāhmaṇī, the very Caṇḍāla; he, by being unconnected with the karma that is the cause of his jāti, becomes an acaṇḍāla. Paulkasa — Pulkasa himself is Paulkasa, born of a śūdra in a kṣatriyā; he too becomes apulkasa. Likewise he is unconnected with the karmas characterised by āśrama: śramaṇa — the parivrāṭ — by being free from the karma that is its cause, becomes aśramaṇa; tāpasa — the vānaprastha — atāpasa. The mention of both is by way of upalakṣaṇa (illustrative reference) for all varṇas and āśramas. What more? "Ananvāgatam" — not followed by puṇya, not followed by pāpa — "tīrṇo hi tadā sarvāñ chokān hṛdayasya bhavati" — for then he has crossed over all the śokas (sorrows) of the heart, since he has utterly transcended the cause of saṃsāra.
BR_C04_S03_V22::block-2: Now those vādins who say: "the kāmas and vāsanās lodged in the heart, having approached the Self related to the heart, get attached, and even on the dissolution of the heart they remain in the Self, like the fragrance of flowers etc. lodged in saturated oil (puṭa-taila)" — to such, the texts "kāmaḥ saṅkalpaḥ" (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.3), "hṛdaye hyeva rūpāṇi" (Bṛ. Up. 3.9.20), "hṛdayasya śokāḥ" and the like would be utterly purposeless. If they should say: "because they are produced by the heart-instrument" — no; on account of the qualification "hṛdi śritāḥ" (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.7); for if the heart be a mere karaṇa (instrument), the statement "hṛdi śritāḥ" is not coherent, nor is "hṛdaye hyeva rūpāṇi pratiṣṭhitāni" (Bṛ. Up. 3.9.20). And since the purity of the Self (ātma-viśuddhi) is intended to be expressed, the use of the word "resting in the heart" is fitting in its literal sense. From the śruti "dhyāyatīva lelāyatīva" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.7), no other meaning is possible. If you say, on account of the qualification "kāmā ye'sya hṛdi śritāḥ" (which) shows that some kāmas reside in the Self too — no, since the qualification is with reference to those not so resting. The qualification "ye hṛdi" is not made with reference to another āśraya being expected; rather it is with reference to those kāmas not lodged in the heart. Those kāmas which are not yet aroused, future, or which were and have been removed by their counter-active (pratipakṣa) — they are not lodged in the heart; and they too are conceivable. Therefore the qualification with reference to them is fitting — "those that are arisen and operating in their viṣaya, all those are released." If even so the qualification be useless — no; because of the greater effort to be applied to those, since they are heya (to be discarded). Otherwise, the residing of kāmas in the Self would be assumed contrary to śruti and contrary to what is desired. If you say, on the strength of "na kañcana kāmaṃ kāmayate" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.19), the prāpti-pratiṣedha (negation of what would be obtained), kāmas resting in the Self is heard — no, because of "sadhīḥ svapno bhūtvā" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.7), the kāma-relation is on account of par-nimitta (extraneous cause); and from the asaṅga-vacana (declaration of unattachedness); for if there be kāma-āśrayatva, asaṅga-vacana would not be tenable, and we have said that saṅga is itself kāma. If you say, on the strength of the śruti "ātmakāmaḥ" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.21), that his kāma is ātma-viṣaya — no, since that is meant to deny kāma other than the Self.
BR_C04_S03_V22::block-3: If you say it is established by the nyāya of the Vaiśeṣika and other tantras (schools) that the Self is the substratum of kāma etc. — no, since these Vaiśeṣika etc. tantra-upapattis are to be set aside as conflicting with the special śruti "hṛdi śritāḥ" (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.7) etc.; for in conflict with śruti they are admitted as nyāya-ābhāsa (semblance of reasoning). And since it would contradict self-luminosity: kāmas etc., being in dream a mere viṣaya of consciousness alone (kevala-dṛśi-mātra-viṣaya), establish self-luminosity, which would be set aside if kāma-āśrayatva were imagined. The samavāya (inherence) of the Self in kāmas etc. would not be tenable from their being seen; like a feature in the eye, the dṛśya is something distinct from the draṣṭā — therefore the draṣṭā's self-luminosity is established. That would be sublated if kāma-āśrayatva were imagined. And it would be in conflict with the entire purport of all śāstras: in imagining a portion in the Highest, and kāma-āśrayatva, the entire purport of all śāstras would be at odds; we have spoken of this at length in the fourth (chapter). For with great effort the imaginations of kāma-āśrayatva have to be refuted, in order to establish the śāstrārtha of the oneness of the Self with the para; and if such imaginations be made, the very śāstrārtha would be set aside. So too the imagination by some (the Naiyāyikas etc.) that icchā etc. are properties of the Self...
BR_C04_S03_V23: When (it is said) that he sees not, he is verily seeing though he sees not; for there is no cessation of the seeing of the seer, since it is imperishable. But there is no second thing other than him, separate, that he might see.
BR_C04_S03_V23::block-0: On account of being one — like the man and woman — he does not see, has been said; and self-luminous (svayañjyotis), too. Self-luminosity (svayañjyotiṣṭva) means caitanya-ātma-svabhāvatā (the nature of being the conscious-light Self). If, like the heat of fire (agni-uṣṇatva), the Ātman is by nature caitanya-ātma-svabhāva, how is it that even in oneness he should give up his svabhāva and not know? If he does not give it up, how here in sleep does he not see? This is contradictory — caitanya is the ātma-svabhāva and yet he does not know. We reply: there is no contradiction, both are possible. How?
BR_C04_S03_V23::block-1: "Yad vai" — what in deep sleep "tat na paśyati," that, even seeing ("paśyan vai tat na paśyati"), he is verily seeing yet does not see. What you understand as "there he sees not in sleep," that you should not so understand. Why? Because "paśyan vai bhavati" — he is verily seeing there. But, you ask, we know thus that he does not see in sleep, since the eye or the manas — the karaṇa for seeing — is not engaged; for in actions of seeing, hearing etc., the karaṇas being engaged we have the vyavahāra "he sees," "he hears"; and we do not see the karaṇas to be engaged; therefore he sees not. — Not so; rather he is verily paśyan. How? "Na hi" — for, of the draṣṭā, the doer of seeing, that dṛṣṭi (seeing) — its viparilopa (cessation) is not. As the heat of fire, so long as the fire exists, even so this Ātman, the draṣṭā, is avināśin (imperishable); and on account of the imperishability of the Ātman, his dṛṣṭi too is imperishable, since it endures as long as the draṣṭā. But, you object, this is contradictory: "his dṛṣṭi does not cease," and yet "the dṛṣṭi is performed by the draṣṭā"; for it is on account of being the doer of dṛṣṭi that he is called draṣṭā; if the dṛṣṭi is being performed by the draṣṭā, it cannot be said "it does not cease." If on the strength of the statement "it does not cease" you say it is imperishable — no, the statement is jñāpaka (informative); for the destruction of what is kṛtaka (made), being established by reasoning, cannot be averted by hundreds of statements; the statement merely indicates the matter as it stands. — This is no defect, since dṛṣṭi can be tenable in the manner of the illumining by the sun etc.: just as the sun etc., being themselves of nitya-prakāśa-svabhāva, illumine by their natural eternal prakāśa; for it is not said that they, being of aprakāśātmā, illumine by producing prakāśa, but rather they illumine by their own eternal natural prakāśa. So this Ātman, by his unceasing eternal dṛṣṭi, is called draṣṭā.
BR_C04_S03_V23::block-2: If you say it is therefore gauṇa (figurative) draṣṭṛtva — no, since this very form establishes its mukhyatva (primary character). For if there were observed any other manner of draṣṭṛtva of the Self, then this draṣṭṛtva would be gauṇa; but the Ātman has no other manner of darśana. Therefore in this very manner the mukhya draṣṭṛtva is tenable, and not otherwise — just as in the case of the sun etc. the prakāśayitṛtva is by their natural eternal unmade prakāśa, and that very prakāśayitṛtva is mukhya, as no other prakāśayitṛtva is possible. Therefore the dṛṣṭi of the draṣṭā does not cease — and there is not even a smell of contradiction. — But, you say, the use of the word with the tṛc-pratyaya-anta (suffix tṛ — agent) is observed only of the doer of an anitya kriyā, as in chettā, bhettā, gantā; so also draṣṭā. — No, since prakāśayitṛ is also so used. — Let it be so in prakāśakas, where there is no other possibility, but not in the Ātman. — No, on the strength of the śruti of the non-cessation of dṛṣṭi ("dṛṣṭi-aviparilopa-śruteḥ"). "I see — I do not see" — from the experience, you say, no. — No, since this depends on a particular activity of the karaṇa; and in those whose eye is removed (uddhṛta-cakṣus), in dream the non-cessation of ātma-dṛṣṭi is observed. Therefore the dṛṣṭi of the Ātman is by its very nature non-ceasing; and hence by that non-ceasing dṛṣṭi of self-luminous nature, he is verily paśyan in deep sleep.
BR_C04_S03_V23::block-3: How then is it said "he does not see"? — "Na tu tad asti" — there is not that. What that? — A second viṣaya. Of what specification? — "Tato'nyat" — other than the draṣṭā, separate (vibhaktam) by way of otherness — "yat paśyet" — that he might apprehend. For that which is the cause of viśeṣa-darśana (perception of particulars) — antaḥkaraṇa, the eye, the rūpa — that was set up as separate by avidyā; that, at this time, has become one, because of the embrace of the Ātman by his higher Self (parā-pariṣvaṅga). For of the parichinna (limited) draṣṭā, the karaṇa stands as separate for the sake of viśeṣa-darśana. But this one, fully embraced by his own all-Self — by his own higher prājña Ātman, like the puruṣa by his beloved (priyayā) — there is no separate standing of karaṇas and viṣayas; and from the absence of these there is no viśeṣa-darśana. For that is performed by the karaṇas, not by the Ātman; it merely appears as if performed by the Ātman. Therefore this delusion is karaṇa-kṛta (effected by karaṇas) — that the Ātman's dṛṣṭi ceases.
BR_C04_S03_V24: When (it is said) that he smells not, he is verily smelling though he smells not; for there is no cessation of the smelling of the smeller, since it is imperishable. But there is no second thing other than him, separate, that he might smell.
BR_C04_S03_V25: When (it is said) that he tastes not, he is verily tasting though he tastes not; for there is no cessation of the tasting of the taster, since it is imperishable. But there is no second thing other than him, separate, that he might taste.
BR_C04_S03_V26: When (it is said) that he speaks not, he is verily speaking though he speaks not; for there is no cessation of the speaking of the speaker, since it is imperishable. But there is no second thing other than him, separate, that he might speak.
BR_C04_S03_V27: Verily, when It does not hear, even then It is hearing, though It hears not; for there is no possible cessation of the hearing on the part of the hearer, because of his imperishability; but there is not that second thing, separate from It, which It could hear.
BR_C04_S03_V28: Verily, when It does not think, even then It is thinking, though It thinks not; for there is no possible cessation of the thinking on the part of the thinker, because of his imperishability; but there is not that second thing, separate from It, which It could think of.
BR_C04_S03_V29: Verily, when It does not touch, even then It is touching, though It touches not; for there is no possible cessation of the touching on the part of the toucher, because of his imperishability; but there is not that second thing, separate from It, which It could touch.
BR_C04_S03_V30: Verily, when It does not know, even then It is knowing, though It knows not; for there is no possible cessation of the knowing on the part of the knower, because of his imperishability; but there is not that second thing, separate from It, which It could know.
BR_C04_S03_V30::block-0: The same construction applies to the rest — "that which It does not smell," "that which It does not taste," "that which It does not speak," "that which It does not hear," "that which It does not think," "that which It does not touch," "that which It does not know." Although thinking (manana) and knowing (vijñāna) co-operate with seeing and the rest, yet because there exists a function of theirs which is independent of the eye and other organs, ranging over past, future, and present objects, they are mentioned separately.
BR_C04_S03_V30::block-1: Now is there really a difference of attributes among seeing and the rest, like the heat, illumination, and burning of fire? Or is the apparent difference in attributes of one and the same undivided property due merely to extraneous adjuncts (upādhi)? Some explain here as follows: the substance which is the Self has, of its own nature, both unity and plurality — just as a cow has unity as the substance "cow" and a mutual difference among the attributes such as the dewlap; just as in gross objects there is unity and plurality, so in partless, formless entities unity and plurality may be inferred, since this is universally seen without exception; thus in the Self too, in the same manner, there is mutual difference among seeing and the rest, while there is unity with the Self. This is not so, for the passage has another purport — this text "Verily, when It," etc., is not intended to set forth a difference of attributes such as seeing and the rest. What then? When the doubt arises — "If the Self is the light of consciousness (caitanya-ātma-jyotis), why does It not know in deep sleep? Surely, then, It must not be the light of consciousness" — to refute this, the text "Verily, when It," etc., is begun. That intrinsic nature of being the light of consciousness which, in waking and dream, is indicated through the manifold adjuncts beginning with the eye, becoming the basis of usage spoken of by the words "sight" and the rest, in deep sleep, when the operation of the differentiating adjuncts ceases, is not manifested and so its nature is not noticed; and although it appears as if differentiated through the difference of adjuncts, by mere restatement of what is found, its existence is asserted. To suppose there a difference of attributes such as seeing is born of ignorance of the intended meaning; it conflicts with the śruti which says (the Self) is a single homogeneous mass of consciousness like a lump of salt; and with śrutis such as "Knowledge, bliss" (Bṛ. Up. 3.9.28), "Truth, knowledge" (Tai. Up. 2.1.1), "Brahman is consciousness" (Ait. Up. 3.1.3). Also from the usage of words — and worldly usage shows "He knows form by the eye," "He knows sound by the ear," "He knows the taste of food by the tongue," — thus everywhere it shows that what is denoted by words like seeing is itself denoted by the word "knowledge"; and the usage of words is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). And from the fitness of the illustration — just as in the world a crystal endowed with the natural property of transparency, solely by reason of contact with the difference of adjuncts such as green, blue, red, takes on those forms, and properties such as green, blue, red distinct from its natural transparency cannot be imagined of the crystal — so by reason of contact with the difference of adjuncts such as the eye, the difference of powers like seeing is indicated of the Self-light whose nature is a homogeneous mass of consciousness, this being due to the natural transparency of the consciousness-mass, like the natural transparency of crystal. And from being self-luminous (svayañjyotiṣṭva) — just as the light of the sun, when conjoined with diverse objects illumined, becomes inseparable from the differences of green, blue, yellow, red, and assumes their forms in appearance, so this Self illumines the entire world and the eye and the rest assume its form; and accordingly it is said "By the Self alone, this light, he sits" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.6) and so on. Nor can plurality of selves be imagined in the case of partless entities, there being no example. Even what is supposed about ākāśa — that all-pervadingness and similar properties differ — and about the atoms — that they have multiple qualities such as smell, taste, etc. — when investigated, that too turns out to be due to extraneous adjuncts. As for ākāśa, all-pervadingness is not its own attribute; rather, by virtue of being the substratum of all adjuncts, the usage of all-pervadingness arises with reference to its existence in its own form everywhere; ākāśa is not by itself gone or not gone anywhere.
BR_C04_S03_V31: When there is, as it were, another, then one can see another, one can smell another, one can taste another, one can speak to another, one can hear another, one can think of another, one can touch another, one can know another.
