BR_C04_S03_V31::block-0: It has been said that there is no second thing, separate as something other, which It might know as in waking and dream; therefore in deep sleep It does not cognise any particular. Now if such be Its very nature, what is the cause of Its having particular cognition by abandoning Its own nature? Or, if particular cognition itself is Its very nature, why does It not cognise any particular here? It is replied — listen: in waking or dream, where (yatra) something other than the Self, like another thing, is set up by avidyā, there, treating the thing set up by avidyā as different and conceiving the Self as if other, while in truth there is neither a thing distinct from the Self nor a Self distinct from it — one as if other sees, that is, perceives, another; this is shown in dream as immediate experience — "as if killing, as if conquering" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.20). Likewise, one as if other smells, tastes, speaks, hears, thinks, touches, and knows another.
BR_C04_S03_V32: An ocean, a single seer without duality, becomes He; this, O Emperor, is the world (state) of Brahman — thus did Yājñavalkya teach him. This is his highest goal, this his highest treasure, this his highest world, this his highest bliss; on a particle of this very bliss other beings live.
BR_C04_S03_V32::block-0: But where in deep sleep that avidyā which sets up another thing has subsided, since there is then no thing differentiated by otherness from avidyā, with what should It see what, or smell, or know? Therefore, embraced by Its own intelligent (prājña) Self, whose nature is self-luminous, whole, perfectly serene, with desires fulfilled, having the Self as its sole desire, become transparent like water — like water (salila), so this is salila — one (eka), there being no second; for it is by avidyā that a second is set apart; that is calmed here, hence "one"; seer (draṣṭā), since the seeing of the Self-light by nature is never lost; non-dual (advaita), since there is no second thing to be seen. This is the immortal, the fearless; this is the brahmaloka — Brahman itself is the loka, hence brahmaloka; for at this time the very Supreme, with the difference of body and organs withdrawn, abides in His own Self-light with all relations stilled, O Emperor — thus indeed did Yājñavalkya teach (anuśaśāsa) Janaka — this is the śruti's statement. How did he instruct? This is the highest goal of this consciousness-self (vijñānamaya); other goals, characterized by the assumption of a body, ranging from Brahmā down to a clump of grass, being conjured up by avidyā, those goals are inferior to this, since they fall within the sphere of avidyā; this, however, is the highest, the supreme, of the goals such as godhood that are to be achieved by works and meditations — that which is the state of being all-Self, where one sees naught else, hears naught else, knows naught else. And this is the highest treasure (paramā sampat) — of all treasures and superhuman powers, this is the highest, because it is natural; other treasures are made. So too this is His highest world; the other worlds depending on the fruit of works are inferior to this; but this is not measured by any work, since it is natural; this is His highest world. So too this is His highest bliss (ānanda); other classes of joy that arise from the contact of object and sense organ, in comparison with these, this is His highest bliss, because it is eternal; from another śruti, "That which is the Infinite (bhūmā), that is bliss" (Chā. Up. 7.23.1); where one sees another, knows another, that is small, mortal, not the primary joy; this, on the contrary, is the opposite; therefore this is His highest bliss. On a particle, a fragment, of this very bliss — set forth by avidyā and grasped only at the time of the contact of objects and sense organs — other beings live; what beings? Their nature divided up by avidyā out of that very bliss, conceived as other than Brahman, those other beings live, drawing on the bliss made manifest through the contact of object and sense organ.
BR_C04_S03_V33: Whoever among men is prosperous, succeeded, the lord of others, perfectly endowed with all human enjoyments — that is the highest bliss of men. A hundredfold of these human blisses make one bliss of the manes who have won their world; a hundredfold of these blisses of the manes make one bliss in the world of the gandharvas; a hundredfold of these gandharva-blisses make one bliss of the karma-devas who have attained godhood by works; a hundredfold of these karma-deva blisses make one bliss of the ājāna-devas, and (this same is the bliss of) the śrotriya who is sinless and unsmitten by desire; a hundredfold of these ājāna-deva blisses make one bliss in the world of Prajāpati, and (this same is the bliss of) the śrotriya who is sinless and unsmitten by desire; a hundredfold of these blisses in the world of Prajāpati make one bliss in the world of Brahman, and (this same is the bliss of) the śrotriya who is sinless and unsmitten by desire — and this very is the highest bliss; this, O Emperor, is the world of Brahman — so said Yājñavalkya. "I give Your Holiness a thousand cows. Beyond this, instruct me for liberation alone" — Then Yājñavalkya was afraid, thinking, "This wise king has driven me to my last shelters."
BR_C04_S03_V33::block-0: Wishing to bring near to him the Bliss-possessor whose particles, the limbs of that highest bliss, are subsisted upon by all beings from Brahmā down to man, by way of the particles of that bliss, He speaks — as one teaches the salt-mountain by particles of rock-salt. He, whatsoever man among men, is prosperous (rāddha), accomplished, undeprived, that is, complete in all limbs; succeeded (samṛddha), endowed with the materials of enjoyment; furthermore, the lord (adhipati) over others of the same class, an independent lord, not a feudatory; with all (sarvaiḥ) — by "human" (mānuṣyaka) is excluded the materials of divine enjoyment, only the materials of human enjoyment — even though endowed, he who is most abundantly endowed (sampannatama), is the highest bliss of men. Here, by indicating bliss and the blissful by the same identity, it is shown that they are not different in essence; for it has already been said in such passages as "When there is, as it were, another" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.31) that this is only a particle of the highest bliss spread out as object and subject; therefore this designation, "the highest bliss," by way of identity, is fitting. A king like Yudhiṣṭhira is the example here. Beginning from this seen human bliss, multiplying by a hundredfold each time, one is led upward to the highest bliss, where difference ceases and which is sought to be conveyed; here, this bliss, increasing by hundredfold steps, where it experiences the limit of growth, where the calculable difference ceases, due to the absence of seeing, hearing, and thinking of another — that highest bliss the text seeks to expound, saying: a hundred such blisses of men, that is one bliss of the manes; their qualifying epithet is "those who have won their world" (jitalokānām); having pleased the manes by the rite of śrāddha and the like, they whose world (loka) has been won (jita) by that work are the manes who have won their world; their bliss, in measure a hundredfold the human bliss, is one. That too, multiplied a hundredfold, is one bliss in the gandharva-loka. That, multiplied a hundredfold, is one bliss of the karma-devas; those who attain godhood by Vedic works such as the Agnihotra are karma-devas. So too one bliss of the ājāna-devas; ājānataḥ, by very birth, those gods who are gods are ājāna-devas; and the śrotriya, one who has studied the Veda, sinless (avṛjina), free from the sin called vṛjina, that is, performing as enjoined, unsmitten by desire (akāmahata), free of thirst, with regard to all the objects up to those of the ājāna-devas — for one such, the bliss is equal to that of the ājāna-devas; and this is brought along by the word "and." That, multiplied a hundredfold in measure, is one bliss in the Prajāpati-loka, in the Virāj body; so too one possessed of that knowledge, a śrotriya who has studied the Veda, sinless and so on, as before. That, multiplied a hundredfold in measure, is one bliss in the brahmaloka, in the body of Hiraṇyagarbha; "and one who is" etc., as before. Beyond this, calculation ceases; this is what has been called the highest bliss, of which highest bliss the blisses of brahmaloka and the rest are particles, like droplets of the ocean. Thus the blisses, increasing in growth a hundredfold each step, where they all become one, and which is directly perceptible to the śrotriya — this very same is the highest bliss whose mark is supreme tranquillity (samprasāda); for there, one sees naught else and hears naught else; therefore it is bhūmā, immortal because it is bhūmā; the others are the opposite. Here being a śrotriya and being sinless are equal; the difference made by being unsmitten by desire causes the hundredfold growth in the blisses; here these means — being a śrotriya, sinless, unsmitten by desire — are the resources for it.
BR_C04_S03_V34: He, having sported and rejoiced in this dream-state, having seen good and evil, again reverts according to his original course back to his waking state.
BR_C04_S03_V34::block-0: Here the consciousness-self (vijñānamaya), self-luminous Self has been shown in dream; by the transit between dream-state and waking-state has been shown its distinctness from body and organs, and the discrimination of desires and works through the example of the great fish, on the basis of non-attachment (asaṅgatā); again the effect of avidyā has been shown in dream itself by such passages as "as if killing" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.20); thereby the very nature of avidyā has been ascertained — as the superimposition (adhyāsa) of attributes that do not belong to It and as the (mistaken) ascription of attributes of the non-Self; so too the effect of vidyā (true knowledge) has been shown — the state of being all-Self, in dream itself as immediately experienced — "He thinks, I am all; this is his highest world" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.20); and there the state of being all-Self is His nature, thus the form of His which transcends the relation with all the dharmas of saṃsāra such as avidyā, desire, and works is grasped directly in deep sleep — this has been made known; this self-luminous Self is the highest bliss; this is the object of vidyā; this very is the supreme tranquillity (samprasāda) and the very limit of joy — all this has been expounded by the text up to this point. And all this is meant as an illustration (dṛṣṭānta) for the topic of liberation (vimokṣa) and of bondage; and these — bondage and liberation, with their causes and details, have been pointed out as the effects of avidyā and vidyā, that whole is just the illustration; whereas the corresponding actual bondage and liberation with their causes — the subjects of the question on desire — must be expounded by you, thus Janaka questions again — "Beyond this, instruct me for liberation alone." There it has been said that the one Self, self-luminous, like a great fish, transits the dream-state and waking-state unattached; just as that one, abandoning the death-formed body and organs and assuming them, transits the dream-state and waking-state like a great fish, so when being born and dying, He is conjoined with and disjoined from these very death-formed entities — "He transits both worlds" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.7), there the transit through dream-state and waking-state was hinted at as the illustration. So now in detail with its cause, the transit must be described; for that purpose this section is begun. There from the waking-state He has been led into the dream-state; therefore the state of supreme tranquillity (samprasāda) is the illustration of liberation; from there, having returned, the empirical usage of saṃsāra in the waking-state must be shown, and so this is connected with that. He, having attained tranquillity in due succession from waking to dream, having abided in this tranquillity, again slightly fallen — having sported and roamed in the dream-state, etc., as before — runs back to the waking-state alone.
BR_C04_S03_V35: Just as a heavily-laden cart goes along creaking, so too this embodied Self, mounted (an-vārūḍha) by the prājña Ātman, goes forth groaning when one becomes such a one whose breath is upward.
BR_C04_S03_V35::block-0: From here onward saṃsāra is being described. Just as this Ātman, having come from the dream-state (svapnānta) to the waking-state (buddhānta), even so will it pass from this body to another body — thus the śruti gives an illustration here. Tat — there, in the world; yathā — as; anaḥ — a cart; susamāhitam — well-laden, or thoroughly loaded — the vigraha is su-samyak āhitam, packed densely with household-vessels (bhāṇḍa-upaskaraṇa) such as mortar (ulūkhala), pestle (musala), winnow (śūrpa), pot (piṭhara) and the rest, and with food and the like, that is, oppressed by its load (sambhāra-ākrāntam); thus burdened by load, utsarjat — making a creaking sound, yāyāt — would proceed, when driven by a cart-driver (śākaṭika); evam eva — even so, as in the cited illustration; ayam — this; śārīraḥ — born within the body; ātmā — Self, namely the liṅga-upādhi (the subtle-body conditioning), which, like the dream- and waking-states, wanders through this world and the other world by the marks of association with and dissociation from sin through birth and death — that one whose departure the prāṇa and the rest follow in departing — that Self is an-vārūḍha — mounted upon, presided over, and illumined by the para Ātman (the supreme Self), the prājña, whose intrinsic nature is self-luminous (svayam-jyotiḥ-svabhāva). And so it has been said, ‘this one sits illumined by the Self alone as light’ (Br. Up. 4.3.6) — utsarjan yāti, goes forth crying out. There, when the liṅga (the subtle body), in which prāṇa is the chief, moves illumined by the Light that is the cit-Ātman, the Ātman conditioned by it also seems to move; thus too another śruti, ‘On whom going forth shall I depart’ (Praśna 6.3) and the rest, and ‘it as it were thinks’ (Br. Up. 4.3.7); for this very reason it has been said — prājñena ātmanā an-vārūḍhaḥ; otherwise, having become one with the prājña, how could it, like the cart, go forth crying out? Therefore the liṅga-upādhi-Self, with the vital marma-points (mortal junctures) being severed, afflicted by the sensation of pain, going crying out, proceeds. At what time? It is said: yatra etat bhavati — etat being adverbial to the action — ūrdhva-ucchvāsī, that is, when its breath becomes upward. The reiteration of what is plainly observed is for the sake of vairāgya: such, indeed, is this painful saṃsāra, in which, at the time of departure, when the marma-points are being torn through, there is loss of memory in one afflicted with the sensation of pain, and, in him whose mind is rendered helpless by another, an inability in undertaking the means to puruṣārtha (the human ends); therefore, until this state arrives, just so long should one be free from negligence (apramatta) in the duty of pursuing the means to puruṣārtha — thus does the śruti, out of compassion (kāruṇyāt), speak.
BR_C04_S03_V36: Whenever this body falls into thinness — whether through old age (jarā) or through being struck by sickness (upatapanam) — it falls into thinness; just as a mango or a fig or a pippala-fruit is loosed from its stalk (bandhana), even so this puruṣa, having been wholly loosed from these limbs (aṅgas), runs back again, in the reverse course (pratinyāyam), to its appropriate matrix (pratiyoni), only for the sake of prāṇa (the regathering of the vital array).
BR_C04_S03_V36::block-0: Now this his upward-breathing — at what time, from what cause, in what manner, and for what purpose may it occur? — this is being explained. This natural body (prākṛta-piṇḍa), endowed with head, hands, and the rest, yatra — at what time; aṇimānam — atomic-state, the bhāva of the aṇu, that is, aṇutva — meaning emaciation (kārśya); ni-eti — falls into. From what cause? jarayā vā — by old age, having ripened of itself like a fruit ripened by time (kāla-pakva-phala-vat), it grows lean. Or upatapatā — by upatapan, fever and other illness; for one being afflicted by disease, owing to disordered digestive fire (viṣamāgnitā), does not digest the food eaten; thence the body, not nourished by the essence of food, falls into emaciation — that is what is said by upatapatā vā. It enters atomic-state. When it has reached extreme emaciation through old age and the like, then it becomes upward-breathing; when upward-breathing, then, like a heavily laden cart, it goes forth groaning. Subjugation by old age, distress through illness, and falling into emaciation — these inevitable misfortunes for one possessed of a body — are stated for the sake of vairāgya. When this one goes forth groaning, in what manner does it release the body? — an illustration is given: tat — there; yathā — as; āmram vā — a mango fruit; udumbaram vā — a fig fruit; pippalam vā — a pippala-fruit. The presenting of various and dissimilar illustrations is for the sake of declaring that the cause of death is not fixed (anīyata-nimittatva); for the causes of death are unfixed and innumerable; this too is for vairāgya — since this one has many possible causes of death, therefore he ever stands in the mouth of Mṛtyu. Bandhanāt — that by which it is bound, namely the stalk (vṛnta) — that is, the sap which is the cause of binding, or that on which it is bound, namely the stalk itself, is called bandhana — from that sap or stalk, the bandhana, it is loosed by manifold causes such as wind and the rest. Evam eva — even so; ayaṃ puruṣaḥ — this puruṣa, the liṅga-ātman, that is, the liṅga-upādhi; from these limbs, the eye and other limbs of the body, having been sam-pra-mucya — wholly and without remainder loosed — not as in the going to suṣupti, where one is preserved by prāṇa; but rather, having gathered up the breath together with the wind, again pratinyāyam — by the word ‘again’ it is shown that earlier too this one has many times gone from body to body, just as one repeatedly passes between dream and waking — pratinyāyam, that is, the return-going as one came (yathāgatam); pratiyoni — toward each womb, by force of karma and śruta and the rest, it runs (ādravati). For what purpose? Prāṇāya eva — that is, only for the array of the prāṇas (prāṇa-vyūha). Since one goes only with prāṇa, the qualification ‘only for prāṇa’ would be useless; for the going from body to another body is for the sake of the prāṇa-vyūha; for thereby the accomplishment of the purpose of experiencing the fruits of karma is brought about, not by the mere existence of prāṇa. Therefore the qualification ‘for the sake of the prāṇa-vyūha’ is fitting on account of purposiveness.
BR_C04_S03_V37: Just as the Ugras, the executors of penalty, the heralds (sūtas) and the village-headmen (grāmaṇīs), make ready (prati-kalpante) for an arriving king with food, drink and lodgings, saying ‘He comes! He arrives!’ — even so do all beings make ready for one who knows thus, saying ‘This Brahman comes! This one arrives!’
BR_C04_S03_V37::block-0: Pūrvapakṣa: Now, when this one is going forth, having abandoned this body, there is no capacity to take up another distinct body, for the body and senses are gone; nor are there others, like servants belonging to him, awaiting him with another body prepared, as a house is prepared for a king. If so, how can the taking up of another body occur? Siddhānta: It is replied — the whole world has been received as a means for the experiencing of the fruits of one’s own karma; and this one is engaged in the experiencing of the fruits of his karma, desiring to pass from body to body; therefore, the whole world, set in motion by his karma, having made ready that very means fit for the experiencing of the fruits of his karma, indeed waits — by the śruti, ‘the puruṣa is born into the world he has fashioned’ (Śat. Br. 6.2.2.27), as for one desiring to attain waking from dream. How? An illustration well-known in the world is given:
BR_C04_S03_V37::block-1: Tat — there; yathā — as; rājānam — a king consecrated for sovereignty (rājyābhiṣikta); āyāntam — coming into his own realm; ugrāḥ — particular castes, or those of cruel office; pratyenasaḥ — pratyenasaḥ are those appointed in respect of each crime (eṇas = sin), namely those engaged in the chastisement of thieves and the like — the vigraha is prati-prati enasi pāpakarmaṇi niyuktāḥ; sūta-grāmaṇyaḥ — sūtas and grāmaṇīs together: sūtas are particular varṇa-saṅkara castes, grāmaṇīs are leaders of the village; they, having beforehand discerned the king’s arrival, with foods — varieties such as bhojya, bhakṣya and the like; with drinks — wine and the rest; with lodgings — palaces and the rest, prati-kalpante — wait with everything made ready, saying, ‘This king comes! This one arrives!’ Just as this illustration, even so, evam-vidam — for the knower of the fruit of karma, that is, the saṃsārin; for the fruit of karma is what was being treated of, and that is referred to by the word ‘evam’; sarvāṇi bhūtāni — all beings, the makers of bodies and the favourers of the senses, namely Āditya and the rest, set in motion by his karma, with the readied means for the experience of the fruit of karma, wait, saying, ‘This Brahman, the experiencer and the doer, comes to us, this one arrives’ — that is, even so they wait, having indeed prepared everything.
BR_C04_S03_V38: Just as the Ugras, the executors of penalty, the heralds and the village-headmen come together (abhi-sam-āyanti) towards a king who is about to set out, even so all the prāṇas come together towards this Self at the time of death, when one becomes such whose breath is upward.
BR_C04_S03_V38::block-0: Pūrvapakṣa: With this one thus desiring to depart, who go along with him? And those who go — do they go pushed by his action, or do they themselves go by force of his karma? — that is, the beings which fashion the body for the next world. Siddhānta: Here an illustration is given. Tat — there; yathā — as; rājānam — a king; prayiyāsantam — desiring intensely to set out; ugrāḥ pratyenasaḥ sūtagrāmaṇyaḥ — these likewise abhi-sam-āyanti — come towards him in attendance, that is, with one accord they come facing him, even though uncommanded by the king, merely from cognizance of his desire to set out. Evam eva — even so; imam ātmānam — this Self, the experiencer; antakāle — at the time of death; sarve prāṇāḥ — all the prāṇas, namely speech and the rest; abhi-sam-āyanti — come together towards him. ‘Yatra etat ūrdhva-ucchvāsī bhavati’ — this has already been explained.
BR_C04_S04_INTRO1::block-0: ‘Sa yatrāyamātmā’ — the description of saṃsāra was being treated of; it has been said, ‘There this puruṣa, having been wholly loosed from these limbs’ (Br. Up. 4.3.36). At what time and in what manner does that complete loosing occur? Saṃsaraṇa is to be described in detail, and so the next section is begun —
BR_C04_S04_V01: When this Self falls into weakness (abalya) and falls, as it were, into a stupor (sammoha), then these prāṇas come together towards him; he, gathering up these tejomātras, descends into the heart alone; and when this person of the eye (cākṣuṣa puruṣa) turns away, then he becomes one who does not cognize forms.
BR_C04_S04_V01::block-0: This Ātman that is being treated of, yatra — at what time; abalyam — the state of want of strength; ni etya — having gone into. The body’s weakness is figuratively spoken of as the Ātman’s weakness — ‘abalyaṃ ni-etya’; for the Self is not, of itself, possessed of weakness, since it is incorporeal (amūrtatva). Likewise sammoham iva — ‘sammoha’ is the state of being deluded, the absence of discrimination — like delusion he goes (ni-eti). For there is, of itself, neither delusion nor non-delusion in the Ātman, since its nature is the eternal light of caitanya (nitya-caitanya-jyotiḥ-svabhāvatva); hence the word ‘iva’ — ‘sammoham iva ni eti.’ For at the time of departure, the agitation due to the withdrawal of the karaṇas is, as it were, observed in the Self by ordinary people; and so they say, ‘He is bewildered, he is bewildered.’ Or, the use of the word ‘iva’ may be applied to both: ‘abalyam iva ni etya, sammoham iva ni eti’ — since both are equally caused by external upādhis and have the same agent referred to. Then at this time these prāṇas, speech and the rest, abhi-sam-āyanti — come together towards this Ātman; this is the loosing of the embodied Self from its limbs. How again is this loosing? In what way do they come together towards the Ātman? It is said: that Ātman, etāḥ tejomātrāḥ — these portions (mātrās) of tejas, that is, the components of light, since they illumine forms and the rest, namely the karaṇas (organs) such as the eye and the rest; he, samabhyādadānaḥ — wholly without remainder gathering them up, taking them up facing-forward, withdrawing them. ‘Sam’ is a qualifier as compared with the dream-state; for in svapna there is no entire and unblemished gathering — only some gathering exists, by the texts ‘speech is grasped, the eye is grasped’ (Br. Up. 2.1.17), ‘taking a portion of all that pertains to this world’ (Br. Up. 4.3.9), ‘taking the seed (śukra)’ (Br. Up. 4.3.11), and the like. Hṛdayam eva — the puṇḍarīka-ākāśa, the lotus-space of the heart; an-vavakrāmati — descends, that is, vijñāna becomes manifest in the heart, when the dispersion of the buddhi and the rest is withdrawn. For there is no motion or modification of withdrawal of dispersion in the Self of itself, since it is said ‘it as it were thinks, it as it were trembles’ (Br. Up. 4.3.2); all modification is super-imposed (adhyāropita) upon It only through the upādhi of buddhi and the rest. When then is the gathering up of the tejomātras? It is said: saḥ yatra eṣaḥ — that one which is in the eye, the cākṣuṣa puruṣa, the portion of Āditya, set in motion by the karma of the experiencer, dwells favouring the eye so long as the body is sustained; but at the time of death he leaves off favouring the eye, and attains his own ādityātman; this very thing has been said — ‘when of this dead puruṣa speech goes to fire, prāṇa to wind, the eye to the sun’ (Br. Up. 3.2.13) and so on; again at the time of taking on a body they will come into association; likewise for one falling asleep and waking up. This is what is being said: cākṣuṣaḥ puruṣaḥ — at what time? — parāṅ paryāvartate — completely turns aside, that is, turns away on every side. Now at this time he becomes arūpajña — the one about to die does not cognize form; then this Ātman becomes the gatherer-up of the tejomātras of the eye and the rest, as in the dream-time.
BR_C04_S04_V02: ‘He becomes one — they say he does not see; he becomes one — they say he does not smell; he becomes one — they say he does not taste; he becomes one — they say he does not speak; he becomes one — they say he does not hear; he becomes one — they say he does not think; he becomes one — they say he does not touch; he becomes one — they say he does not cognize.’ The tip of his heart begins to glow (pradyotate); by that glow this Self goes forth, either through the eye, or through the head, or through other parts of the body. As he departs, prāṇa departs after him; as prāṇa departs, all the prāṇas depart after it. He becomes endowed with vijñāna (sa-vijñāna); he descends following that very vijñāna. Vidyā (true knowledge) and karma take hold of him together, as does pūrva-prajñā (former cognition).
BR_C04_S04_V02::block-0: He becomes one — that is, the body of karaṇas (organs) becomes one with its own liṅga-ātman; then those standing nearby say of him, ‘He sees!’ (in negation: he does not see). Likewise on the cessation of the deity of smell, the organ of smell becomes one with the liṅga-ātman; then they say, ‘He does not smell.’ The same is to be understood of the rest. The deity of the tongue is Soma or Varuṇa; on cessation of that deity they say, ‘He does not taste.’ Likewise ‘he does not speak, hear, think, touch, cognize.’ Then is observed the cessation of the deities and the unification of the karaṇas in the heart. There, when the karaṇas are withdrawn into the heart, the inner vyāpāra (activity) is described: tasya ha etasya — of this prakṛta hṛdaya, that is, of the cavity of the heart; agram — the mouth of the nāḍī, the door of departure; pradyotate — glows, as in dream, by its own splendour produced by the gathering up of the tejomātras, by its own jyotis, that is, by the Ātman alone. Thus by the heart’s tip glowing with that ātma-jyotis, this Ātman, the vijñāna-maya liṅga-upādhi, niṣkrāmati — goes forth. So in the Atharvan: ‘On whom going forth shall I depart, on whose remaining shall I remain?’ — he created the prāṇa (Praśna 6.3). And there the ātma-caitanya-jyotis is always more manifest; for through that upādhi all the modifications of birth, death, going, coming, and the rest are super-imposed on the Ātman. The twelvefold karaṇa, beginning with buddhi, is constituted of that very thing; that is the sūtra, that is the jīvana, that is the inner-Self of the world (jagatas tasthuṣaś ca antarātmā). By that pradyota — that splendour at the tip of the heart — going forth, by which path does he go forth? It is said: cakṣuṣṭo vā — through the eye, if there be jñāna or karma productive of the attainment of āditya-loka; mūrdhno vā — through the head, if it be productive of the attainment of brahma-loka; anyebhyo vā śarīra-deśebhyaḥ — through other limbs of the body, according to karma, according to śruta. Tam — that vijñāna-ātman; utkrāmantam — going forth for the next world, that is, with intent set toward the next world; prāṇaḥ — like a person of all-inclusive office in relation to a king, an-utkrāmati — departs after him; and that prāṇa departing, vāgādayaḥ sarve prāṇāḥ — all the prāṇas, speech and the rest, depart after it. This is the desire to mention them in the order of importance; not that successive movement in some meaningful sequence is here intended. Now this Ātman is sa-vijñāna, that is, possessed of distinct vijñāna as in dream, by force of karma, not independently; for if he were sa-vijñāna by independence, all would be kṛta-kṛtya (have done what was to be done); but that is not attained; therefore Vyāsa said: ‘ever permeated with the bhāva of That’ (B.G. 8.6). Through karma being roused, by the distinct vijñāna of vāsanā that is lodged in particular antaḥkaraṇa-vṛttis, the whole world becomes sa-vijñāna at this time; and only with vijñāna is the going-forth — anvavakrāmati follows it, that is, illumined by particular vijñāna alone. Therefore for the sake of independence at that time, the cultivation of yoga-dharmas, the practice of parisaṅkhyāna (discriminative reflection), and the accumulation of distinguished puṇya should be undertaken by śraddhāvants who desire the next world, by the ever-watchful (apramatta). The matter of all śāstras is to be put into effect with effort — also abstention from misdeed (duścarita). For at that time nothing can be accomplished, since for one being led by karma there is no independence. ‘He becomes puṇya by puṇya karma, pāpa by pāpa karma’ (Br. Up. 3.2.13) — this has been said. For establishing the means of the cessation of this very calamity, the upaniṣads of all śākhās have been engaged.
BR_C04_S04_V02::block-1: It has been said that he goes forth like a cart heaped with its load. What, then, of one who has set forth for the next world, is the pathyadana — the wayfarer’s provision — corresponding to the load of the cart-driver, by which he subsists having reached the next world, and by which the next body is initiated? Thus it is said: tam — him, this Self going to the next world; vidyākarmaṇī — vidyā and karma together: vidyā of every kind, both enjoined and forbidden, and what is neither enjoined nor forbidden; likewise karma, enjoined and forbidden, and that which is neither enjoined nor forbidden; samanvārabhete — they wholly take hold of him, hold him fast, follow him; and pūrva-prajñā ca — pūrva-prajñā is the prajñā whose object was experienced earlier, that is, the vāsanā left by the experience of the fruits of past karma; and that vāsanā becomes a contributing factor (aṅga) in the initiation of new karma and in the ripening of karma; thereby it too holds him. For without that vāsanā there is no possibility either of doing karma or of experiencing its fruit. There is no skill of the indriyas in an unrehearsed object; whereas of indriyas already set in motion by the vāsanā of past experience, skill arises here even without practice; we observe in some, in respect of certain actions characterized as painting and the like, skill from birth itself even without practice here, and in some non-skill in others though endowed with extreme aptitude; likewise in the experiencing of objects, in some by their very nature skill or non-skill is observed; and all this depends on the rising or non-rising of pūrva-prajñā; therefore without pūrva-prajñā there is no possibility of any one’s engagement either in karma or in the experiencing of fruits. Therefore these three — vidyā, karma, and pūrva-prajñā — are the wayfarer’s provision for the next world, like the load of the cart-driver. Since vidyā and karma together with pūrva-prajñā are the means for the obtaining and experiencing of the next body, therefore one should practice only auspicious vidyā and karma and the rest, so that there may be conjunction with and experience of the desired body — this is the purport of the section.
BR_C04_S04_V03: Just as a tṛṇa-jalāyukā (a leech upon a blade of grass), having reached the end of one blade, takes up another foothold (ākrama) and draws itself together (ātmānam upasaṃharati), even so this Self, having struck down this body and rendered it insensate (avidyām gamayitvā), takes up another foothold and draws itself together.
BR_C04_S04_V03::block-0: Pūrvapakṣa: Thus he, his sambhāra of vidyā and the rest gathered, attaining another body, having released the prior body, like a bird going to another tree, attains another body? Or, by an ātivāhika (vehicular) intermediate body, is he conducted to the place of the karma-fruit-birth? Further, when he is here, do the all-pervading karaṇas obtain their functioning? Or, do the karaṇas, contracted while in the body, of the dead one, like the light of a lamp from a broken pot, pervade everywhere and again contract at the initiating of the next body? Further, does only the manas go, as in the Vaiśeṣika system, toward the place of the initiating of the next body? Or is there yet another supposition in the Vedānta system? Siddhānta: It is said: ‘these all are equal, all are infinite’ (Br. Up. 1.5.13) — śruti has it that the karaṇas are sarvātmaka (all-comprising), since they reside in the sarvātmaka prāṇa; their adhyātmika and adhibhautika circumscription is brought about by prāṇi-karma, jñāna, and bhāvanā; and from that, although by their nature the prāṇas are all-pervading and infinite, by force of the initiating of the next body in conformity with karma, jñāna, and vāsanā, the functioning of the prāṇas contracts and expands; and so it has been said: ‘equal with a midge, equal with a mosquito, equal with an elephant, equal with these three worlds, equal with this all’ (Br. Up. 1.3.22); and so this very statement is in keeping — ‘he who worships these as infinite’ (Br. Up. 1.5.13) and the like, and ‘as one worships him, so’ etc. There the vāsanā called pūrva-prajñā, dependent upon vidyā and karma, like a leech, continuous, just as in the dream-time, initiates another body from this body, dwelling in the heart only. Again at the initiating of the next body, the prior abode-body is released — to this purport an illustration is taken up:
BR_C04_S04_V03::block-1: Tat — there, in the transit (saṃcāra) to another body, this is the example: yathā — by which manner; tṛṇa-jalāyukā — the tṛṇa-jalūkā, the grass-leech; tṛṇasya antam — the end of the blade of grass, having gone to and reached; anyam — another blade of grass; ākramam — the vigraha is ākramyate iti ākramaḥ — that foothold; ākramya — having taken hold of, having relied upon; ātmānam — its own prior limb; upasaṃharati — into the place of the last limb. Even so this Ātman — the saṃsārin already treated of — idam śarīram — this previously taken-up body; ni-hatya — like one desiring to take up dream, having caused it to fall; avidyām gamayitvā — having rendered it acetana, by drawing it into himself; anyam — another; ākramam — like the grass-leech taking another blade — śarīrāntaram — another body, having taken hold of, by the extended vāsanā; ātmānam upasaṃharati — there he initiates ātmabhāva — as in dream, while still standing in the body in another place — when the body is being initiated, jaṅgama or sthāvara. There, by force of karma, the karaṇas which have obtained their functioning combine; and the outer body, made of the kuśa-mṛttikā-equivalent (gross matter), is initiated; and there, awaiting the array of karaṇas, for the favouring of speech and the rest, the agni-and-other deities take their seats. This is the procedure of the initiating of another body.
BR_C04_S04_V04: Just as a goldsmith, taking a portion of gold, fashions another newer and more beautiful form, so too this Self, having struck down this body and reduced it to avidyā, fashions another newer and more beautiful form — pertaining to the Fathers, or to the Gandharvas, or to the gods, or to Prajāpati, or to Brahman, or to other beings.
BR_C04_S04_V04::block-0: Here a doubt arises regarding the commencement of another body: does the Self, in undertaking another body, repeatedly take up that very same eternally appropriated material as its upādāna and crush it again and again to start the new body, or does it take up wholly fresh material each time afresh? With reference to this question a dṛṣṭānta is now stated.
BR_C04_S04_V04::block-1: The word tat means 'in this matter, with reference to this point.' Just as the peśaskārī — peśas means gold, he who works it (peśaḥ karoti iti peśaskārī) is the goldsmith — taking a portion (mātrām) of gold, that is, cutting off and grasping (apacchidya gṛhītvā) a piece, fashions (tanute, nirminoti) another form newer than the previous configuration (racanāviśeṣāt navataram abhinavataram) and more beautiful than the previous beauty (kalyāṇāt kalyāṇataram) — so too this Self, and the rest as before. The very same five bhūtas, beginning with earth and ending with ākāśa, that are eternally appropriated, which were explained in the fourth chapter as 'the two forms of Brahman' (Bṛ. Up. 2.3.1) — these stand in the place of the gold (peśaḥsthānīyāni). Crushing these again and again (upamṛdya upamṛdya), the Self makes another and another body, a newer and more beautiful form, that is, a particular configuration (saṃsthānaviśeṣam), meaning another body. It makes a body pertaining to the Fathers (pitryam) — that is, suitable for the enjoyment of the Pitṛloka; or pertaining to the Gandharvas, suitable for the enjoyment of the Gandharvas; similarly daivam, that of the gods; prājāpatyam, that of Prajāpati; or brāhmam, that of Brahmā — each according to action and according to scripture (yathākarma yathāśrutam); or the body of any other beings — and the verb 'makes another body' must be construed accordingly throughout.
BR_C04_S04_V05: Verily, this Self is Brahman — consisting of vijñāna, of mind, of prāṇa, of eye, of ear, of earth, of water, of air, of ākāśa, of fire and of non-fire, of desire and of non-desire, of anger and of non-anger, of dharma and of adharma, of all things; this is what is meant by saying 'consisting of this' and 'consisting of that.' As a man acts, as he conducts himself, so he becomes: doing good he becomes good, doing evil he becomes evil; one becomes meritorious by good action, evil by evil. But others say: this puruṣa indeed consists of desire alone — as is his desire, such is his resolve; as is his resolve, such is the action he performs; as is the action he performs, such does he become.
BR_C04_S04_V05::block-0: Those things that are termed 'bonds,' which exist as upādhis of this Self, by being conjoined with which it is imagined as 'consisting of that' — these are gathered together and indicated here in one place.
BR_C04_S04_V05::block-1: He, verily, this Self that thus transmigrates, is Brahman alone, the supreme — that very one which is beyond hunger and the rest. Vijñānamayaḥ — vijñāna means buddhi, characterized by it, having that as its predominant feature; for it has been said: 'Which is the Self? — He who is this vijñānamaya among the prāṇas' (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.7); vijñānamayaḥ means 'mostly vijñāna,' since the property of buddhi is imagined to belong to him — 'as if he meditates, as if he flutters' (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.7). So too manomayaḥ, on account of association with manas; prāṇamayaḥ, since prāṇa with its fivefold function is that with which he is identified, by which the conscious one appears as if moving. Cakṣurmayaḥ at the time of seeing form; śrotramayaḥ at the time of hearing sound. Thus, when each particular indriya operates, he becomes identified with that. Thus, being permeated through buddhi and prāṇa with the cakṣus and other karaṇas, he becomes identified with the elements, beginning with earth, that initiate the body. When a body of earth is begun, he is pṛthivīmayaḥ; in the worlds of Varuṇa and others, when an aqueous body is begun, he is āpomayaḥ; for an aerial body vāyumayaḥ, for an ākāśa body ākāśamayaḥ. Thus the divine bodies are tejomaya; identifying with them at their commencement he becomes tejomayaḥ. The bodies of beasts, hells and pretas, distinct from these, are atejomaya; with reference to those it is said 'atejomayaḥ.' Thus, being identified with the aggregate of effect-and-organ (kāryakaraṇa-saṅghāta), the Self, perceiving another object yet to be obtained — 'this has been obtained by me, that is yet to be obtained by me' — through such a perverted notion (viparītapratyaya) and the longing for it, becomes kāmamayaḥ. When one perceives the defect in that desire and the longing for its object subsides, the citta becomes serene, unsoiled, peaceful — identified with that he is akāmamayaḥ. When such desire is thwarted by something, the kāma transforms as anger, and being identified therewith he is krodhamayaḥ; when by some means that anger is removed, the citta is serene and unagitated, said to be akrodha — identified with that he is akrodhamayaḥ. Thus, having been identified with desire and anger and with their absence, he becomes dharmamayaḥ and adharmamayaḥ; for without kāma and krodha and the like, the pravṛtti towards dharma and the rest does not occur — as remembered by the Smṛti: 'Whatever action he performs, all that is the activity of desire' (Manu 2.4). Becoming dharmamaya and adharmamaya he becomes sarvamayaḥ — every effect of dharma and adharma, all the manifest universe (yāvat kiñcid vyākṛtam), is the fruit of dharma and adharma; obtaining each, he becomes identified with it. In short, this is established for him: that he is idammayaḥ, identified with the perceived object and the like; therefore he is also adomayaḥ. The word adaḥ refers indirectly (parokṣaṃ) by means of an effect that is being perceived; for the bhāvanāviśeṣas in the antaḥkaraṇa are infinite and cannot be specified individually, but in this and that moment they are inferred from their effect — 'this is in his heart, that is in his heart.' Thus by the perceived effect, the indirect inner activity is designated as 'idammaya' — 'this one is now adomaya.' In brief, as is the manner in which he is wont to act (yathākārī) and to conduct himself (yathācārī), so he becomes; karaṇa is fixed action governed by injunction and prohibition (vidhi-pratiṣedha-gamyā), caraṇa is non-fixed conduct — that is the difference. 'Sādhukārī sādhur bhavati' qualifies yathākārī; 'pāpakārī pāpo bhavati' qualifies yathācārī. By the use of the suffix indicating habituality (tācchīlya-pratyaya), the absolute purport is the very identification with that.
BR_C04_S04_V05::block-2: Now others, skilled in bondage and liberation, indeed say (atha apy anye bandha-mokṣa-kuśalāḥ khalu āhuḥ): true, with kāma and the rest as their antecedent, puṇya and apuṇya are the cause of taking on a body; nevertheless, it is the puruṣa, prompted by kāma, who accumulates the actions of merit and demerit; when kāma is abandoned, action, even though present, does not become productive of further merit and demerit; even when puṇya and apuṇya are accumulated, they are not, in one devoid of kāma, originators of fruit. Therefore kāma alone is the root of saṃsāra. So too has it been declared in the Ātharvaṇa: 'He who, thinking of objects, longs for them — by reason of those longings he is born here and there' (Muṇḍ. Up. 3.2.2). Therefore this puruṣa is kāmamaya alone; the being identified with anything else is, even when present, not a cause — hence it is determined: 'kāmamaya eva.' Since he is kāmamaya, with whatever desire he is yathākāmaḥ, such is his kratu — that desire, manifest at first as a mere slight longing in respect of some object, when unimpeded becomes clearer and attains the state of kratu. Kratu means adhyavasāya, niścaya, after which action sets in (yad-anantarā kriyā pravartate). Yatkratuḥ means: of such a form is his resolution as is the desired effect; tatkarma kurute — he performs that action which is fitting for the realization of the fruit envisaged by his resolve. Whatever action he performs, that he attains — its fruit he attains. Therefore, in his being sarvamaya and being a saṃsārī, kāma alone is the cause.
BR_C04_S04_V06: Concerning this there is the verse: 'Attached, he goes along with the action, to the place where the liṅga, the mind, is firmly fixed; having reached the end of the action — of whatever he does here — he comes back from that world to this world for fresh action.' Thus indeed for one who desires. Now of him who does not desire — who is without desire, free from desire, whose desires are fulfilled, who desires only the Self — his prāṇas do not depart; being Brahman alone, he attains Brahman.
BR_C04_S04_V06::block-0: Tat — in that very matter, there is also this śloka, a mantra. Tad eva eti — to that very thing he goes, sakta — attached, that is, with arisen longing for it. How does he go? Saha karmaṇā — accompanied by that very action: by the action which, attached to its fruit, he performed, with that action itself he goes there, attains its fruit. What is that to which he goes? Liṅgaṃ manaḥ — since the predominant member of the liṅga is the mind, the liṅga is called manas; or, that by which one infers, comprehends, is the liṅga, that is the mind — wherein the mind of this saṃsārī is niṣakta, fixed with niścaya, with arisen longing; for it was through that longing that he performed that action; therefore, by the very strength of the attachment of that mind, the obtaining of that fruit through that action befalls him. By this is established that kāma is the root of saṃsāra. Therefore, for one whose desires are uprooted, the brahmavid, even existing actions become barren of progeny — as the Śruti declares: 'For him whose desires are fulfilled and whose Self is realized, all desires here itself dissolve' (Muṇḍ. Up. 3.2.2). Further: prāpyāntaṃ karmaṇaḥ — having reached, that is, having enjoyed the end, the consummation of the karman, that is, having brought the fruit of the action to its termination; whose karman? — of that, of whatever karma he performs in this world; having enjoyed the fruit of that action and reached its end, he comes back (punar aiti) from that world, to this world for action — for this world is karma-pradhāna, hence 'karmaṇe'; for performing further action; having again performed action, by reason of attachment to its fruit, he again goes to that world — thus. Iti nu — thus indeed, the desiring one transmigrates. Since only the desiring one transmigrates thus, atha — therefore, the non-desiring one nowhere transmigrates. The course (gati) was stated for one attached to fruit; for one without kāma, since action does not arise, the non-desiring one is liberated as such. How is one non-desiring? He who is akāma is non-desiring (akāmayamāna). How is one akāma? — he is niṣkāma from whom desires have departed. How do desires depart? Because he is āptakāma, one whose desires have been obtained. How are desires obtained? Through being ātmakāma — for him the Self alone, and not anything else as a separate object, is the thing to be desired; the Self alone — without inner or outer, whole, prajñānaghana, of one taste, with nothing above, beside, or below — there being no other object to be desired apart from the Self. 'For him to whom all has become the Self, what would he see, hear, think, know — and through what?' Knowing thus, what would he desire? An object becomes desirable only when known as other; and there is no such other for the brahmavid, the āptakāma. He who, by being ātmakāma, is āptakāma, that very one is niṣkāma, akāma, akāmayamāna — and is liberated. For one to whom the Self alone is everything, there is no anātman to be desired. To say there is an anātman, an other, to be desired, while at the same time saying that all has become the Self alone — is contradictory. For the seer of the Self as all, since there is nothing to be desired, there can be no karman. Those who, even for the brahmavid, postulate karman for the sake of avoiding pratyavāya — for them, the Self is not all, since the pratyavāya to be averted, distinct from the Self, is admitted as an object of intent. He by whom the Self is known as that which is ever beyond hunger and the like and never connected with pratyavāya — him we call brahmavid; he sees the Self as ever transcending hunger and the rest.
BR_C04_S04_V06::block-1: For such a non-desiring one, since action is absent and the cause of departure is absent, the prāṇas — speech and the rest — do not depart, do not ascend out of the body. And the wise one, āptakāma through ātmakāmatā, is right here itself Brahman. By way of dṛṣṭānta, the form of all-self Brahman has been displayed: 'This indeed is His āptakāma, akāma form' (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.21); to him this is now applied as the dārṣṭāntika object, by 'atha akāmayamānaḥ' and the rest. How is such a one liberated? Is now stated: He who beholds the Self as in suṣupti, undifferenced, advaita, of unbroken cit-light by nature — for that very non-desiring one, since action is absent and the cause of departure is absent, the prāṇas, speech and the rest, do not depart. Rather, that wise one is here itself Brahman, even though he appears to possess a body; being Brahman alone, he attains Brahman. Since for him the kāmas — the determinants of his being non-Brahman — do not exist, therefore here itself, being Brahman alone, he attains Brahman, and not in some time after the falling of the body. For there is no obtaining of a different state for the wise one when dead, distinct from his state when living; only by the absence of joining a further body is it said 'he attains Brahman.' If liberation were the obtaining of a different state, the meaning intended by all the Upaniṣads — namely the oneness of the Self — would be set aside; mokṣa would become the effect of action and not of jñāna, which is undesired; and the anityatva of mokṣa would follow, for no thing produced by kriyā is seen to be eternal; and mokṣa is admitted to be eternal — 'eṣa nityo mahimā' (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.23). Nothing eternal can be conceived as different from the natural svabhāva. If the svabhāva of the Self be natural like the heat of fire, it cannot be said to be the consequent of human effort (puruṣavyāpārānubhāvī); for fire's heat or light is not the consequent of fire's activity. To say a thing is consequent on fire's activity and yet svābhāvika is contradictory. If it be said that heat and light are consequent on the activity of burning — no, because they depend on the removal of the obstruction of another's perception for their manifestation. Fire is manifested by its qualities of heat and light upon kindling; that is not relative to the fire itself, but, rather, the heat and light of fire — qualities obstructed from another's perception, not connected with anyone's seeing — become manifest, on removal of obstruction relative to kindling, to the seer; relative to that there arises the bhrānti that 'these heat and light came into being subsequent to kindling.' If it be said that heat and light too are not svābhāvika — then we should have to give an example of a svābhāvika dharma of fire; and it cannot be said that things have no svābhāvika dharma at all.
BR_C04_S04_V06::block-2: Nor is mokṣa, like the breaking of a fetter (nigaḍa-bhaṅga), the abhāva-bhūta cessation of bondage — since the oneness of the paramātman is admitted, on the strength of the Śruti 'ekam evādvitīyam' (Chānd. Up. 6.2.1); nor is there another bound, of whom liberation would be the cessation of fetters as in the case of breaking shackles; we have at length declared the absence of any other distinct from the Paramātman. Therefore the usage 'mokṣa' applies merely to the cessation of avidyā — and so we have said — just as upon the cessation of nescience of a serpent in a rope, the cessation of the serpent and so on follows.
BR_C04_S04_V06::block-3: Those who maintain that in mokṣa another vijñāna and another ānanda become manifest — they should state the meaning of the word 'manifestation' (abhivyakti). If it be just the worldly meaning, the pervasion of the upalabdhi by its object — then it must be told whether what is manifested is something existent or non-existent. If existent: for the one liberated, that which is manifested would be of the very nature of his Self; the obstruction of upalabdhi cannot be supposed, since it is ever-manifest, and the special statement that 'it is manifested for the liberated one' becomes meaningless. If, on the contrary, it is manifested only at some time, by reason of some obstruction of upalabdhi — that thing would not be of the Self; thence follows manifestation through something else, and thus dependence on a means of manifestation. If they share the same locus as upalabdhi, no postulating of obstruction can stand, and so manifestation is either always or never; for postulating an interim there is no pramāṇa. Nor is it possible that, for things sharing the same locus as one — being of the very nature of him — they should bear to one another the relation of object and subject. He for whom there is saṃsāritva prior to manifestation of vijñāna and sukha, and muktatva after manifestation — he must be other than the eternal-manifest jñāna-svarūpa Paramātman, by the extreme heterogeneity, like coldness from heat; and by such postulation of difference from Paramātman, the Vedic conclusion is abandoned. If it is objected: if mokṣa be without distinction (nirviśeṣa) just as in the present, no greater effort is warranted for it, and the śāstra would be in vain — no, because its purpose is the dispelling of the avidyā-bhrama; in reality there is no distinction of muktāmuktatva, since the Self is ever of one form; but the avidyā concerning the Self is dispelled by the vijñāna born of śāstropadeśa; therefore prior to the obtaining of that upadeśa, effort is appropriate. If it be said that there is in the Self the distinction of removal and non-removal of avidyā in the avidyāvat — no, since avidyā is admitted to be the object of imagination only, like the serpent-water-silver-impurity in rope-saline-shell-sky; we have already said that this is a non-defect. If it be said that, like timira and atimira sights, the Self has the distinction of being agent and non-agent of avidyā — no, because the Self's being agent of avidyā has been negated by 'as if it meditates, as if it flutters' (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.7); since the avidyā-bhrama is produced by the convergence of many activities; and since it admits of being an object — and he by whom the avidyā-bhrama is grasped as distinct, like a pot, is not himself avidyābhramavān. From the cognition 'I do not know, I am stupefied,' if it be said that avidyābhramavattvam itself is so — no, because the discrimination of that very thing is grasped; for he who grasps a thing in distinction is not himself called deluded with respect to that thing; and his discriminative grasping and his delusion both being there is contradictory. You say 'it is seen that I do not know, I am stupefied' — and that the seer of that, as ajñāna and stupefaction, is the seer; thus it becomes the object of his sight, attaining the state of object. How then can these — which are objects — be qualifications of the seer who is the agent? If they qualify the dṛśi, how can they be objects pervaded by the dṛśi? For an object is something pervaded by the agent's action; and the pervaded is one thing, the pervader another; the pervader is not pervaded by itself. Tell, then, how, in such a case, ajñāna and stupefaction can qualify the dṛśi? Nor is the discriminating seer of ajñāna himself ajñāna.
BR_C04_S04_V07: Concerning that there is the verse: 'When all the desires that are lodged in his heart are released, then the mortal becomes immortal; here itself he attains Brahman.' Just as the slough of a snake lies dead and cast off on an anthill, so does this body lie. Then this disembodied, immortal one is prāṇa, Brahman alone, the very tejas. 'I, sir, give to you a thousand,' so said Janaka of Videha.
BR_C04_S04_V07::block-0: The dārṣṭāntika of the dṛṣṭānta of going to svapna and buddhānta, namely saṃsāra, has been described. The cause of saṃsāra has been declared to be vidyā, karman, and pūrva-prajñā. The upādhis in the form of body-and-organ (kāryakaraṇa-lakṣaṇa-bhūta) by which, when surrounded, he experiences saṃsāritva — these too have been mentioned. With respect to them, having raised the pūrvapakṣa that dharma and adharma are the immediate prompters, it has been determined: 'kāma alone.' Just as this artha was determined by the Brāhmaṇa, so by the mantra also; thus, having stated bandha and the cause of bandha, the prakaraṇa has been concluded: 'iti nu kāmayamānaḥ' (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.6). Beginning with 'atha akāmayamānaḥ' (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.6) the dārṣṭāntika of the dṛṣṭānta of suṣupta — namely the sarvātmabhāva-mokṣa — has been declared. As the cause of mokṣa, the āptakāmatva through ātmakāmatā has been stated; and that, by implication, is not to be obtained without ātmajñāna; therefore by sāmarthya brahmavidyā alone has been stated as the cause of mokṣa. Hence, although kāma was said to be the root, by the inverse of the cause of mokṣa, avidyā as the cause of bandha has also been stated. Here too, mokṣa and the means of mokṣa have been declared by the Brāhmaṇa; for the firming up of that very point, the mantra denoted by the word śloka is now cited.
BR_C04_S04_V07::block-1: Tat — in that very matter, this śloka, this mantra, occurs. Yadā — at the time when sarve, all the kāmas, the diverse forms of tṛṣṇā that are well-known in the world as the eṣaṇās for son, wealth, and worlds, of this well-known puruṣa, lodged in his heart, in the buddhi — are pramucyante, are released, dissolved together with their root for the brahmavid who is ātmakāma — atha, then, the mortal, marana-dharmā, by being severed from kāma at its very root, becomes immortal. By implication, the desires whose objects are non-Self, marked by avidyā, are themselves the mṛtyus; thus, on severance of mṛtyu, the wise one, even while living, becomes immortal. Atra — in this very body, while existent — brahma samaśnute, attains the brahma-bhāva, mokṣa. Therefore mokṣa requires no going to another place. Hence for the wise one the prāṇas do not depart; in their established form they are dissolved into their cause, the puruṣa; the mere name remains — so it has been declared. How, when the prāṇas are absorbed and the body too dissolves into its cause, the wise one — liberated, all-self, abiding right here — does not, as before, again attain dehitva, the saṃsāritva? In this regard the dṛṣṭānta is now stated. As in the world, the slough of a serpent is called ahi-nirlvayanī; in an anthill — vālmīka, that is, the ahi's resort, the anthill and the like — being prati-asta, cast off, abandoned by the snake who has gone forth (anātmabhāvena), it lies (śayīta). Even so — as in the dṛṣṭānta — this body, like the body of a snake, abandoned by the liberated one with anātmabhāva, lies as if dead. The other, the snake-stationed liberated one, having become sarvātma-bhūta, abiding in the very same place like the serpent, is yet bodiless (aśarīraḥ); not, as before, sa-śarīra. For previously, by the bhāva of being one with the body driven by kāma and karma, he was sa-śarīra and martya; on departing from that, now he is aśarīra, hence amṛta. Prāṇa — he who lives, prāṇiti iti prāṇaḥ — for in the upcoming śloka 'prāṇasya prāṇam' (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.18) and in another Śruti 'prāṇa-bandhanaṃ hi somya manaḥ' (Chānd. Up. 6.8.2); and by the strength of the prakaraṇa-vākya, the supreme Self alone is here designated by the word prāṇa. Brahmaiva, the Paramātman alone. What further? Tejas eva — vijñāna, light: by which ātmajyotis the world, illumined, having vijñāna-light, exists with prajñānetra, undimmed. The kāmapraśna — the boon for vimokṣa given by Yājñavalkya to Janaka, with cause and effect, in the form of dṛṣṭānta and dārṣṭāntika of bandha and mokṣa — has been determined here at length by the Śruti taking the form of the Janaka-Yājñavalkya ākhyāyikā; the means of vimokṣa from saṃsāra has been stated for living beings. Now the Śruti itself says: by Janaka thus was uttered, in payment for the vidyā. How? 'I, thus liberated by you, give to you, the bhagavān, a thousand for the sake of the vidyā-niṣkraya' — so said Janaka of Videha. Here, when the matter of vimokṣa was so determined, why does he not, like the half-statement, dedicate his Videha kingdom and the very Self, but rather give only a thousand? What is the abhiprāya there? Some explain: Janaka was an aficionado (rasika) of adhyātmavidyā; though already heard, he wishes to hear the very same artha again through mantras; hence he does not surrender all.
BR_C04_S04_V08: Concerning that there are these verses: 'The path is subtle, far-extended, ancient; it has touched me, by me alone has it been realized. By it the wise, the brahmavids, depart hence, after the body's fall, upward, liberated, to the heavenly world.'
BR_C04_S04_V08::block-0: On the artha — the mokṣa of the brahmavid who is ātmakāma — declared by mantra and brāhmaṇa, these ślokas are vistarapratipādakas. Aṇuḥ — sūkṣma, on account of being difficult to know; vitataḥ — extended, far-spread, or by the alternative reading 'vitaraḥ,' meaning 'the cause of crossing across very clearly'; the mokṣasādhana jñānamārga is purāṇaḥ, ancient, since manifested by the eternal Śruti — not, like the path of the kudṛṣṭi born of tārkika-buddhi, of recent date. Māṃ spṛṣṭaḥ — by me obtained; for he who attains a thing, that thing as it were touches him, gets joined to him; thus this brahmavidyā-mokṣamārga, by reason of having been obtained by me, is termed 'mām spṛṣṭaḥ.' Not merely 'obtained' by me, but also anuvitto mayaiva — anuvedana means the consummation in fruit, in completion, of vidyā after its ripening, like the satiation that ends the act of eating; previously there was only the mere relation to the obtaining of jñāna — that is the difference. Is this mantradṛk alone the only one to obtain the fruit of brahmavidyā, that no other has obtained it, that he says 'anuvitto mayaiva'? — Not so a defect, since this is praise of brahmavidyā as that whose fruit is uttama and self-witnessed; thus, the ātmajñāna, witnessed by self-cognition, brings the conviction 'I am fulfilled' — what greater than this could there be? — by such words brahmavidyā is praised; not that any other brahmavid does not obtain its fruit, by the all-comprehending Śruti 'tad yo yo devānām' (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.10). That very thing he says — tena, by that very brahmavidyā-path, dhīrāḥ — those endowed with prajñā, others too who are brahmavids, apiyanti — go, attain the fruit of brahmavidyā, mokṣa, the svargaṃ lokam. The word 'svargaloka,' though it can denote tri-viṣṭapa, here, by virtue of context, denotes mokṣa. Itaḥ — from this fall of the body, ūrdhvam — upward, having become viumukta even while living.
BR_C04_S04_V09: In that path they say there is white, blue, yellow, green, and red. This is the path realized by Brahman; by it the brahmavid, who has done meritorious deeds and is luminous, goes.
BR_C04_S04_V09::block-0: Concerning that path of mokṣa-sādhana there is divergence among mumukṣus. How? Some mumukṣus say it is in that — śuklam, śuddham, vimalam — pure; others nīlam, others piṅgalam, haritam, lohitam — as each has seen. The nāḍīs, suṣumnā and the rest, are filled with the rasas of phlegm and the like — since they are spoken of as 'of white,' 'of blue,' 'of piṅgala' and so on. Or they consider Āditya as the mokṣamārga of such a kind — by another Śruti, 'eṣa śuklaḥ eṣa nīlaḥ' (Chānd. Up. 8.6.1). Since the darśanamārga cannot have the white and the rest as its colours. In every way, however, these śuklādis are other than the brahmavidyā-mārga that is the topic. Is not 'śuklaḥ' the śuddha advaita-mārga? — No, since it is associated, in continuous flow, with words denoting colours such as nīla and pīta; the śuklas etc. that yogins hold to be mokṣa-paths are not mokṣa-mārgas; they are saṃsāra-viṣayas only — 'cakṣuṣṭo vā mūrdhno vā anyebhyo vā śarīradeśebhyaḥ' (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.2) — by reason of association with departure from the body's regions; they conduct only to brahma-loka and the rest. Therefore this very is the mokṣa-mārga: he who, through ātmakāmatva, by reason of being āptakāma in the dwindling of all kāmas, has cakṣur and the other kārya-karaṇas absorbed right here, like the extinction of a lamp without further movement — this is that jñāna-mārga, the path; brahmaṇā — by the very form of the Paramātman, by him who has abandoned all eṣaṇās — anuvittaḥ. Tena — by that brahmavidyā-mārga, the brahmavid, others also, eti. Of what kind is the brahmavid who goes by it? It is said: previously having been puṇyakṛt, then after again abandoning the eṣaṇās of son and the rest, joining the Self with the paramātma-tejas, having become well-attained therein, tejasaśca — having become Self-natured, here itself. Such a brahmavid goes by that path. There is no taking of one who combines puṇya etc. — by reason of contradiction, as we have said: 'apuṇya-puṇya-uparame yaṃ punarbhava-nirbhayāḥ. śāntāḥ saṃnyāsino yānti tasmai mokṣātmane namaḥ' (MBh., Rāj. Dh. 47.55); 'tyaja dharmam adharmaṃ ca' (Mokṣa Dh. 329.40) — and by other Smṛti passages teaching the abandoning of puṇyāpuṇya; 'nirāśiṣam anārambhaṃ nirnamaskāram astutim. akṣīṇaṃ kṣīṇa-karmāṇaṃ taṃ devā brāhmaṇaṃ viduḥ' (Mokṣa Dh. 263.34); 'naitādṛśaṃ brāhmaṇasyāsti vittaṃ yathaikatā samatā satyatā ca. śīlaṃ sthitir daṇḍa-nidhānam ārjavaṃ tatas tataś ca uparamaḥ kriyābhyaḥ' (Mokṣa Dh. 175.37) and so on. And He will teach here itself — 'eṣa nityo mahimā brāhmaṇasya na vardhate karmaṇā no kanīyān' (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.23) — having stated the cause for there being no purpose of action; with 'tasmād evaṃ-vic chānto dāntaḥ' (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.23) and the rest, the cessation of all kriyā. Therefore, puṇyakṛttva is just as expounded. Or else: he who, being a brahmavid, goes by that — he is puṇyakṛt and tejasvī. This is the praise of the brahmavid; in the world, mahābhāgya is famous in the puṇyakṛt and the tejasvī yogin; therefore, by the analogy with these two, the brahmavid is here being praised, on account of his renowned mahābhāgya in the world.
BR_C04_S04_V10: Into blind darkness enter those who worship avidyā; into a darkness greater than that, as it were, those who delight in vidyā.
BR_C04_S04_V10::block-0: Andham — adarśanātmaka, the saṃsāra-niyāmaka tamas — they enter, attain. Who? Those who worship avidyā — that which is other than vidyā, of the form of sādhya-sādhana, that is, follow karman. Tataḥ — than that, bhūya iva — far more darkness, as it were, do they enter. Who? Ye u — those who, in vidyā that is the propounder of avidyā-vastu, in the karma-purpose Trayī-vidyā alone, ratāḥ, are intent: holding 'the Veda is exclusively concerned with vidhi-pratiṣedha, there is no other,' that is, those who do not regard the meaning of the Upaniṣads.
BR_C04_S04_V11: Joyless, indeed, are those worlds, covered with blind darkness; into them, after death, go those who are unwise, who do not know.
BR_C04_S04_V11::block-0: If they enter the darkness of the form of non-vision, what is the dosa? Is now stated: ananda — anānanda, asukha — joyless, by name, are those lokas, covered, pervaded, with that blind, adarśana-lakṣaṇa tamas — they are the gocara of that ajñāna-tamas; those, ye, after dying, go to. Who? Those who are avidvāṃsaḥ. Is it by mere not-being-learned, in general? It is said: no — abudhaḥ, the form ending in the kvip-pratyaya of the dhātu budh in the sense of cognition, that is, those devoid of ātmāvagama; janāḥ — common, prākṛta, or simply 'those who follow the dharma of birth.'
BR_C04_S04_V12: If a man should know the Self, saying "I am this" — what could he wish for, for the sake of whom could he afflict the body in following its course? (12)
BR_C04_S04_V12::block-0:
If (cet) a person should thoroughly know (vijānīyāt) the Self (ātmānam) — that Self which is one's own (svam), the supreme (param), the knower of all that is desired by every living being (sarva-prāṇi-manīṣita-jña), seated in the heart (hṛt-stham), transcending the dharmas of hunger and so forth (aśanāyādi-dharma-atīta) — perchance some one among thousands. The word cet ("if") indicates the rare attainability (durlabhatva) of the knowledge of the Self (ātma-vidyā). How? Saying, "I am (asmi, bhavāmi) this very supreme Ātman, the witness of the cognitions of all living beings (sarva-prāṇi-pratyaya-sākṣī), He who has been declared by 'neti neti' and the rest, beyond whom there is no other seer, hearer, thinker, or knower (na anyo'sti draṣṭā śrotā mantā vijñātā), the same in all (samaḥ), abiding in all beings, whose nature is eternally pure, awake and free (nitya-śuddha-buddha-mukta-svabhāvaḥ)." Then such a puruṣa — wishing what (kim icchan)? Wishing what other thing (anyad vastu) as fruit, distinct from his own essential nature (tat-svarūpa-vyatirikta) — and for whose sake (kasya kāmāya), for the purpose of which other Self distinct from his own (ātmano vyatiriktasya), would he act? For there is no fruit to be sought for that Self, nor is there any other besides the Self for whose sake he might desire — since all is of the nature of the Self (sarvasya ātma-bhūtatvāt). Therefore, wishing what, for whose sake, would he afflict (anusañjvaret) the body, fall away (bhraṃśeta), become miserable in following the misery imposed by the body-adjunct (śarīra-upādhi-kṛta-duḥkham anu duḥkhī syāt), and burn in the wake of the body's burning (śarīra-tāpam anutapyeta)?

For only one who sees the not-Self (anātma-darśin), longing after another thing distinct from It, thinking "this should be mine, this for the son, this for the wife," striving thus and thus, becomes ensconced in the unbroken sequence of births and deaths (punaḥ-punar-janana-maraṇa-prabandha-rūḍha) and is afflicted by bodily disease in their wake. But for the seer of the universal Self (sarva-ātma-darśin), no such thing is possible — this is what is here declared.
BR_C04_S04_V13: He by whom the Self has been found and awakened — entered into this perilous, impenetrable thicket — he is the maker of the universe, for he is the maker of all; the world is his, indeed he himself is the world. (13)
BR_C04_S04_V13::block-0:
Further: he by whom — by which Brāhmaṇa — the Self (ātmā) has been found out (anuvittaḥ = anulabdhaḥ), awakened (pratibuddhaḥ = sākṣātkṛtaḥ). How? Realised in the form of the inmost Self (pratyak-ātmatvena avagataḥ) thus: "I am the supreme Brahman." That Self entered into this saṃdehya — i.e., into the saṃdeha (perilous predicament), the heaped-up host of many calamities (aneka-anartha-saṅkaṭa-upacaye), the gahana (impenetrable thicket), the rugged ground beset with hundreds and thousands of contrary discriminations (aneka-śata-sahasra-viveka-vijñāna-pratipakṣe). "He by whom" — that is, by way of awakened realisation (pratibodhena anuvittaḥ).

He is viśva-kṛt — the maker of the universe. How is this universe-makership? Is the name "viśva-kṛt" his merely as an appellation? Anticipating this doubt, the text continues: "For he, indeed (saḥ hi), since he is the maker of all (sarvasya kartā) — not in name only." Not only is he viśva-kṛt employed by another (para-prayuktaḥ); rather, his is the entire world (tasya lokaḥ sarvaḥ). And lest one ask, "Is the world some other thing of his?" — the text says: "sa u loka eva" — he himself is the world. By the word loka the Self is meant: all is his Self, and he is the Self of all (sa ca sarvasya ātmā) — this is the meaning.

This inmost Self (pratyak-ātmā), found out by the Brāhmaṇa through awakening, that has "entered" into the impenetrable thicket of calamity — he is no transmigrator (saṃsārī), but the very Supreme. Since he is the maker of the universe, the Self of all, and all is his Self, the conclusion to be settled is: "I am one only, without a second (eka eva advitīyaḥ), the Supreme alone." This is the purport of the verse.
BR_C04_S04_V14: Even while in this very world, we have come to know That; if we had not known It, great would be the destruction. Those who know It become immortal; the others go only to sorrow. (14)
BR_C04_S04_V14::block-0:
Further: "In this very place" (iha eva), in this dense thicket of innumerable evils, "being so" (santaḥ), being indeed deluded by the long sleep of ajñāna (ajñāna-dīrgha-nidrā-mohitāḥ santaḥ), yet somehow we have come to know That — even "this Brahman" — under the form of the Self (ātmatvena); the meaning is, "Aha! we are blessed, our purpose accomplished (kṛtārthāḥ)." If we had not known this Brahman — for vedanam is the act of knowing (vedaḥ), one possessing this is a vedī, a knower; the very vedī is here vedi, the not-vedi is avedi — if I were avedi, what fault would arise? Mahatī — boundless in measure, of the form of birth, death, and the rest — vinaṣṭiḥ, destruction. "Aha, we are released from this great destruction (mahato vināśāt nirmuktāḥ), since we have known the non-dual Brahman (advayaṃ brahma)" — that is the sense.

As we, having known Brahman, are released from this destruction, so those who know That become immortal (amṛtāḥ). But those who do not so know Brahman — "the others (itare)," namely, those distinct from the knowers of Brahman, the not-knowers of Brahman (a-brahma-vidaḥ) — go (apiyanti = pratipadyante) to sorrow alone, namely, sorrow of the form of birth and death; for those who do not know there is never any cessation from it (na kadācid api aviduṣāṃ tato vinivṛttiḥ). For verily they take up sorrow itself as the Self.
BR_C04_S04_V15: When one directly perceives this resplendent Self, the Lord of what has been and what is to be — then one no longer wishes to shield oneself from It. (15)
BR_C04_S04_V15::block-0:
But when, having somehow attained some supremely compassionate teacher (parama-kāruṇika ācārya) and obtained his grace, one comes to see (paśyati) — directly perceives (sākṣātkaroti) — afterwards (anu = paścāt), this very Self of his own, the deva — the resplendent (dyotanavantam) one, or the giver (dātāram) of the fruits of action to all living beings according to their respective karmas (yathā-karma-anurūpam) — directly (añjasā = sākṣāt), the īśāna, the Lord (svāmin) of bhūta-bhavya, of the three times (kāla-traya) — then he does not (na) seek to shield (gopāyitum icchati) himself in any special way from that resplendent Lord.

All people seek concealment (guptim) from the Lord because of their seeing difference (bheda-darśin); but this man, the seer of oneness (ekatva-darśin), does not fear from any quarter (na bibheti kutaścana). Therefore he does not seek to shield himself when he sees the īśāna deva directly, as the very Self (ātmatvena). At that time he does not blame anyone either, for he sees all as his own Self; seeing thus, whom would he blame?
BR_C04_S04_V16: On this side of which the year revolves with its days — this Light of lights the gods worship as life and immortality. (16)
BR_C04_S04_V16::block-0: Further: "on this side of (arvāk) which Lord (īśānāt)" — meaning, in any other range than His — the saṃvatsara, the year, the soul of time (kāla-ātmā), the limiter of every born thing (sarvasya janimataḥ paricchettā), itself unable to delimit Him (yam aparicchindan), revolves on the hither side only (arvāk eva vartate); ahobhiḥ — by its own limbs, that is, by days and nights (svāvayavaiḥ ahorātraiḥ). That is the jyotiṣāṃ jyotiḥ, the Light of lights, since it is the illuminator even of the lights such as the sun (āditya-ādi-jyotiṣām api avabhāsakatvāt). The gods worship It as āyus, life, as the immortal Light. Whatever is other than It dies; that is no light. For It is the Light, the life, of all (sarvasya hi etat jyotiḥ āyuḥ). Since the gods worship that Light through the attribute of life (āyur-guṇena), they themselves become endowed with long life (āyuṣmantaḥ). Hence by one desirous of life, Brahman should be worshipped through the attribute of life — this is the meaning.
BR_C04_S04_V17: In whom the five fivefold-folk, and the ākāśa, are established — that I deem to be the Self; knowing It, I, the immortal, am Brahman, the immortal. (17)
BR_C04_S04_V17::block-0: Further: "in whom" (yasmin), in which Brahman, the five fivefold-folk (pañca pañca-janāḥ) — namely, the gandharvas and the rest, just five in number: gandharvas, pitṛs, devas, asuras, rakṣas; or the four varṇas with the niṣāda as fifth — and the ākāśa, that called the Unmanifest (avyākṛta-ākhya) — in which the sūtra is woven warp and woof (otaṃ ca protaṃ ca), as said: "In this verily Imperishable, O Gārgī, is the ākāśa" (Bṛ. Up. 3.8.11) — in whom these are established (pratiṣṭhitaḥ) — that very Ātman, the immortal Brahman, I deem (manye); I do not know the Self as anything other than That. Then what? "Being a knower (vidvān), I am the immortal Brahman." Through ajñāna alone was I a mortal (martyaḥ); on the going of that, I, the wise one, am verily the immortal.
BR_C04_S04_V18: They who know It as the Prāṇa of prāṇa, the Eye of the eye, the Ear of the ear, the Mind of the mind — they have realised the ancient, primeval Brahman. (18)
BR_C04_S04_V18::block-0: Further: illumined by that very caitanya-ātma-jyotis (the light that is the conscious Self), the prāṇa breathes through it as Self; thus He is the Prāṇa even of prāṇa — the prāṇasya prāṇa. Likewise He is the Eye even of the eye, the Ear even of the ear; for it is by the power of Brahman, presiding over them (brahma-śakti-adhiṣṭhita), that the eye and the rest possess their capacity for seeing and so on (darśana-ādi-sāmarthya). By themselves, when devoid of the light that is the conscious Self (caitanya-ātma-jyotiḥ-śūnyāni), they are no different from a log of wood or a clod of earth (kāṣṭha-loṣṭa-samāni). And the Mind even of the mind. Those who know thus — those who know the inmost Self (pratyak-ātmā) whose existence is inferred from the activities of the eye and the rest (cakṣur-ādi-vyāpāra-anumita-astitvam), and not as something objective (na viṣaya-bhūtam) — they have, with certainty (niścayena), known (jñātavantaḥ) Brahman, the puruāṇa (ancient, chiraṃtana), the agrya (born first, agre bhavam). For so it is in the Atharvan: "That which the knowers of the Self know" (Mu. Up. 2.2.10).
