BR_C04_S04_V19: Through the mind alone is It to be perceived; here there is no plurality whatsoever. From death to death he goes who sees here as if there were plurality. (19)
BR_C04_S04_V19::block-0: The means of seeing that Brahman is now declared. By the mind alone (manasā eva) — by the mind purified by knowledge of the highest reality (paramārtha-jñāna-saṃskṛtena) and preceded by the instruction of the teacher (ācārya-upadeśa-pūrvakam) — It is to be intuited continuously (anudraṣṭavyam). And in that range of vision — in Brahman — there is here no nānā, no plurality (kiñcana, anything at all). When plurality does not really exist, one superimposes plurality (nānātvam adhyāropayati) upon It through avidyā. He goes from death (mṛtyoḥ) to death (mṛtyum āpnoti) — from one dying to another. Who? "He who sees here as if (iva) there were plurality." Apart from the superimposition (adhyāropaṇa) due to avidyā, there is, in the highest sense, no duality (na asti paramārthato dvaitam) — that is the meaning.
BR_C04_S04_V20: It is to be perceived in one form alone — this immeasurable, eternal, free from impurity, beyond ākāśa, unborn, the great enduring Ātman. (20)
BR_C04_S04_V20::block-0: Since it is thus, therefore, ekadhā eva — in one form alone, by the single mode of being a homogeneous mass of pure consciousness (vijñāna-ghana-eka-rasa), continuous like ākāśa — it is to be perceived (anudraṣṭavyam). For this Brahman is apramayam, that is, apramēyam — beyond measurement — because of the oneness of all (sarva-ekatvāt). One thing is measured by another distinct thing; but this is one only — hence apramēya. Dhruvam means nityam, kūṭastham, immovable — that is the meaning. Pūrvapakṣa: But this is contradictory — to say it is apramēya and also that it is known; for 'is known' means is measured by pramāṇas, and 'apramēya' is the negation of that. Siddhānta: This is no fault, for the negation is meant to deny pramēyatva by pramāṇas independent of āgama, as in the case of other objects. Just as other objects are made the content of pramāṇas not requiring scripture, so this Self-reality cannot be made the content of any other pramāṇa. When everything is the Self, by what could one see or know what? Even the āgama makes it known only by negating the operation of pramātṛ, pramāṇa and the rest, not by accepting the relation of designating word and designated object. Therefore, it is not communicated even by āgama in the manner of svarga, Meru and the like; for it is the very Self of the communicator. Communicating and the communicator pertain to a content distinct from oneself — the relation arises only when there is bheda. And jñāna in regard to it is simply the cessation of the notion of non-Self (parātma-bhāva-nivṛtti); no direct apprehension of Self-being is to be performed in it, because the Self-being is already existent. The Self-being is eternal in everyone — only it appears as if pertaining to non-Self. Hence apart from the cessation of that false appearance of non-Self, no Self-being is enjoined therein. Upon the cessation of the notion of non-Self as Self, the natural Self-being in one's own Ātman remains alone — and this is what is called 'the Ātman is known.' By itself, being apramēya, it is not made the content of any other pramāṇa. Thus both statements are non-contradictory. Virajaḥ — vigata-rajas — rajas is the impurity of dharma, adharma and the rest; free from that. Paraḥ — beyond, distinct, subtle, all-pervading, beyond even the ākāśa called avyākṛta. Ajaḥ — does not take birth; by negating birth, the subsequent transformations of being (bhāva-vikāras) are also negated, since all of them have birth as their starting point. Ātmā mahān — vast in measure, greater than all. Dhruvaḥ — imperishable.
BR_C04_S04_V21: Knowing that very Self, let the wise brāhmaṇa cultivate insight (prajñā). Let him not meditate upon many words, for that is the wearying of speech. (21)
BR_C04_S04_V21::block-0: That very Ātman, of such a nature, the dhīraḥ — the wise one — having known by upadeśa and by śāstra, let the brāhmaṇa cultivate prajñā — that insight which has the content taught by śāstra and ācārya, and which brings the desire to know to its consummation. The meaning is that he should adopt the means leading to such prajñā — saṃnyāsa, śama, dama, uparama, titikṣā and samādhāna. Let him not anudhyāyāt — not contemplate — bahūn many śabdān words. Since plurality is here negated, the few words conveying solely the oneness of Ātman are permitted; thus 'Meditate on the Ātman with Om' (Muṇḍ. Up. 2.2.6), and 'Release other words' (Muṇḍ. Up. 2.2.5) in the Ātharvaṇa. Vāco viglāpanam — that which especially produces glāni, weariness, śrama, fatigue of speech — hi, because, that meditation on many words is so.
BR_C04_S04_V22: Verily, this great unborn Ātman is he who is the vijñānamaya among the prāṇas, who is this ākāśa within the heart — therein he reposes. He is the controller of all, the lord of all, the sovereign of all. He grows not greater by good action, nor lesser by evil. He is the supreme lord of all, the lord of beings, the protector of beings, the bridge that holds these worlds asunder. Him the brāhmaṇas seek to know by recitation of the Veda, by yajña, by dāna, by tapas without self-mortification of starvation. Knowing this very one, one becomes a muni. Desiring this very one as their world, the wandering renouncers go forth. Knowing this, the ancient knowers desired no progeny, saying: 'What shall we do with offspring, we whose world is this Ātman?' Rising above the desire for sons, for wealth, and for worlds, they wander as mendicants; for the desire for sons is the desire for wealth, and the desire for wealth is the desire for worlds — both indeed are mere desires. This Ātman is 'not this, not this' (neti neti) — ungraspable, for it is not grasped; indestructible, for it is not destroyed; unattached, for it does not attach; unbound, it does not suffer; it is not injured. Two thoughts do not cross over him: 'thus I have done evil,' and 'thus I have done good.' He crosses over both. Neither what is done nor what is undone afflicts him. (22)
BR_C04_S04_V22::block-0: Bandha and mokṣa, with their causes, have been declared by mantra and brāhmaṇa, and by the verses (ślokas) the very nature of mokṣa has been set forth in detail. Now, regarding this Self, this section is begun in order to show how the entire Veda finds its appropriate use. The phrase 'Sa vā eṣaḥ' and what follows is a recapitulation of what has been said in this prapāṭhaka, together with its purpose, in order to indicate that here is found the application of the entire Veda apart from the kāmya portion. 'Saḥ' refers to one previously mentioned. Who is the one referred to? He is identified — 'yaḥ eṣa vijñānamayaḥ' — lest the reference be misconstrued as relating to the immediately preceding sentence. Which 'eṣaḥ' is meant? The one specified as 'vijñānamayaḥ prāṇeṣu.' This identification by the earlier phrasing removes doubt; for it was said earlier at the start of Janaka's question: 'Which is the Ātman? — Yo'yaṃ vijñānamayaḥ prāṇeṣu' (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.7). The meaning is: this self-luminous Ātman, who has been established by the statement 'vijñānamayaḥ prāṇeṣu,' has been freed by demonstrating that desire, action and avidyā are not properties of the Self, and has been brought to identity with the Paramātman — 'this very one is the Supreme; there is no other.' This Ātman is now declared the great unborn Ātman directly. 'Yo'yaṃ vijñānamayaḥ prāṇeṣu' has the meaning already explained. 'Yaḥ eṣaḥ antarhṛdaye' — within the lotus of the heart — is this ākāśa which is the locus of buddhi-vijñāna; in that ākāśa, together with the buddhi-vijñāna, he reposes. Or, at the time of saṃprasāda (deep sleep), the ākāśa within the heart is the unconditioned Paramātman alone, the very nature of vijñānamaya; in that own nature called ākāśa, the Paramātman, he reposes. This was explained in the fourth chapter as the answer to 'Where was he then?' (Bṛ. Up. 2.1.16). And he is the controller (vaśī) of all — Brahmā, Indra and the rest; for everyone moves under his sway. So it has been said: 'Under the rule of this Imperishable...' (Bṛ. Up. 3.8.9). Not merely controller, but Īśāna — ruler of all, of Brahmā, Indra and so forth. And lest his lordship be thought due merely to birth, like a prince's lordship over more powerful servants, the text says: sarvasyādhipatiḥ — sovereign, the protector who oversees, hence svatantra — independent — not, like a prince, dependent on ministers and servants. These three — vaśitva, īśānatva, ādhipatya — are in cause-effect relation: because he is sovereign of all, hence he is the lord of all; for whoever oversees and protects another, he is undoubtedly his lord; and because he is lord of all, therefore controller of all. Further, that very being, the inner light in the heart — the puruṣa, the vijñānamaya — does not become greater by good action, śāstra-ordained karman; he does not increase from his prior state by any quality. Nor does he become lesser by śāstra-prohibited evil action; he does not decline from his prior state. This is the meaning. Furthermore, anyone exercising oversight, protection and the rest is bound by the dharma and adharma born of favour and harm to others; how then is he free from these? Because he is the supreme lord (sarveśvaraḥ), it is in his very nature to rule even over karman; therefore karman cannot bind him. Further, he is bhūtādhipati — the lord of all beings, from Brahmā down to a tuft of grass; this is the meaning of the term as already explained.
BR_C04_S04_V22::block-1: But those who explain that one desires to know him as illumined by the recitation of the Veda — comprising both mantra and brāhmaṇa portions — for them, only the Āraṇyaka portion would qualify as 'recitation of the Veda'; for the karma-kāṇḍa does not illumine the Supreme Ātman, as the special śruti says: 'taṃ tvaupaniṣadam' (Bṛ. Up. 3.9.26). 'By recitation of the Veda' is unqualified and hence comprehends the whole; nor is it proper to set aside any portion. Pūrvapakṣa: But on your view also, except for the Upaniṣads, only one portion is taken — would not that too involve such partiality? Siddhānta: No, on the first interpretation there is no contradiction, hence on our view this defect does not arise. When by 'vedānuvacana' the daily svādhyāya is enjoined, the Upaniṣad too is included, and so no portion of what 'vedānuvacana' denotes is set aside. And from being mentioned alongside yajña and the rest — the text uses 'vedānuvacana' while it goes on to enumerate yajña and other karmans; therefore karman alone is meant by 'vedānuvacana,' for the daily svādhyāya is itself karman.
BR_C04_S04_V22::block-2: Pūrvapakṣa: How then is the Self desired to be known by karmans such as daily svādhyāya? They do not illumine the Self, as the Upaniṣads do. Siddhānta: This is no defect; karmans serve the purpose of purification (viśuddhi-hetutva). Those purified by karmans, having become viśuddhātmā, are able to know the Self — illumined by the Upaniṣad — without obstruction. Thus the Ātharvaṇa: 'One of pure sattva, meditating, beholds him niṣkalam' (Muṇḍ. Up. 3.1.8). And smṛti: 'Knowledge arises in men by the destruction of pāpa-karman' (Mokṣa-dharma 204.8) and so on. Pūrvapakṣa: How is it understood that nitya karmans serve the purpose of saṃskāra? Siddhānta: From the śruti: 'He is verily the ātma-yājī who knows: by this such-and-such limb is purified for me, by this such-and-such limb is upheld' (Śat. Br. 11.2.6.13), and the like. And in all the smṛti-śāstras, karmans are said to be saṃskāra-artha — 'forty-eight saṃskāras' (Gau. Dh. 1.8.8 ff.) and so on. In the Gītā: 'Yajña, dāna and tapas are purifying for the wise' (Bh. G. 18.5); 'All these knowers of yajña have their faults consumed by yajña' (Bh. G. 4.30). Yajñena — both dravya-yajñas and jñāna-yajñas serve saṃskāra; in one purified, of viśuddha-sattva, the arising of jñāna will occur unobstructed; hence by yajña they desire to know. Dānena — dāna also, for it destroys pāpa and increases dharma. Tapasā — since tapas is undifferentiated and might apply to kṛcchra, cāndrāyaṇa and the like, it is qualified by 'anāśakena.' 'Anāśaka' means abstention from desires (kāmān-aśanam), not abstention from food; for by abstention from food one merely dies — there is no Ātman-knowing. By the words 'vedānuvacana,' 'yajña,' 'dāna,' 'tapas,' all nitya-karman is indicated. Thus all nitya-karman, set apart from kāmya, becomes a means to mokṣa through the rise of Ātman-knowledge; thus there is consistency of teaching with the karma-kāṇḍa. Knowing this very Ātman as illumined, by the reasoning declared, one becomes a muni — from manana, the muni; that is, a yogin. 'Knowing this very one, he becomes a muni' — none other. Pūrvapakṣa: But muni-hood would arise from knowing other things too; how is 'this very one' insisted upon? Siddhānta: Indeed, by knowing other things one might become a muni; but in such a case one would not be a muni only — he would also be a karmin. Knowing this auponiṣada-puruṣa, however, one is a muni only, not a karmin; hence the unique muni-hood is intended for him, and so 'this very one' is emphasized. When this is known, since 'who shall see whom?' arises and action is impossible, manana alone remains. Further, desiring this very Ātman as their own world, the pravrājins, those whose conduct is renunciation, pravrajanti — go forth; that is, they renounce all karmans. From the emphasis 'desiring this very world,' it is gathered that those desiring the three external worlds have no adhikāra in pārivrājya; one residing in Kāśī who wishes to reach Gaṅgādvāra does not set out facing east. Therefore, for those desiring the three external worlds, the means are sons, karman, and the lower brahma-vidyā: 'this world is to be conquered by a son, not by any other karman' (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.16). Hence those desiring those means renounce putra and the rest, and there is no pārivrājya for them.
BR_C04_S04_V22::block-3: Therefore, 'desiring the Ātman as their world, they go forth' — this is a vidhi confirmed by arthavāda; for if it were merely a sārthavāda, there would be no proper congruence with the praise of the world. The subsequent text 'etad dha sma' and so on is an arthavāda in respect of 'pravrajanti.' If it were itself an arthavāda, it would not require another arthavāda; but 'pravrajanti' here does require 'etad dha sma' as its arthavāda. Because the ancient knowers, having ceased from progeny and karmans, indeed renounced, therefore present-day persons too renounce — pravrajeyuḥ, should renounce. So construed, it cannot face the praise of the world. We have shown this through the teaching of co-agency with vijñāna and the like. From being recited together with vedānuvacana etc., the conclusion follows. Just as vedānuvacana and the rest, ordained as means of Ātman-knowing, are taken in their literal sense and not as arthavāda, so pārivrājya, recited with them, cannot be taken as arthavāda for attainment of the Ātman-loka. From the teaching of distinction of fruit (phala-vibhāga): 'knowing this very Ātman as the world' distinguishes the Ātman from the external world as another fruit, just as 'this world is to be conquered by a son alone, not by any other karman; the pitṛ-loka by karman.' Nor is 'pravrajanti' meant in the sense of an established practice serving to praise the world, requiring an arthavāda as a principal text would; if so, it would be heard but once. Therefore the view that this is praise of the world is mere bhrānti. Nor is praise made by means of an action that is itself to be performed; for if pārivrājya, while being something to be performed, were for the sake of praising something else, then darśapūrṇamāsa and the rest, which are also to be performed, would be for praise. And no enjoinedness of pārivrājya is established elsewhere from which it could here be a mere praise. Even if a vidhi for pārivrājya were posited somewhere, here itself it is principal, not possible elsewhere. And if pārivrājya is posited for those without adhikāra in karman, then climbing trees and the like would be similarly enjoined, since they too are without established kartavyatā. Therefore not a trace of stuti-character is possible here.
BR_C04_S04_V22::block-4: Pūrvapakṣa: If this Ātman is desired as a world, why should not karmans be undertaken as the means to its attainment, rather than pārivrājya? Siddhānta: Here is the answer — because of the non-relation of this Ātman-loka with karman. The Ātman whom one renounces desiring it cannot be related to karman as means, fruit, or as something to be produced or modified. Therefore, the nature of this Ātman is: 'sa eṣa neti neti, agrāhyaḥ — for he is not grasped' and so forth. Since the Ātman thus characterized is unconnected with the means and fruit of karman, distinct from all the dharmas of saṃsāra, beyond hunger and the rest, possessed of dharmas like 'asthūla' and so on, unborn, undecaying, immortal, undying, fearless, of the nature of a homogeneous mass of vijñāna like a piece of salt-rock, self-luminous, one only without a second, without prior, without subsequent, without inner, without outer — this is established by āgama and reasoning, and especially here in this Janaka-Yājñavalkya dialogue. Therefore, when the Ātman of such characteristics is known as Self, no undertaking of karman is fitting. Hence the Ātman is without distinctions. A man with eyes, walking on a path in daytime, does not fall into a well or onto a thorn. Since the entire fruit of karman is included within the fruit of vidyā, and a knower does not strive after what is attainable without effort: 'If honey were obtained from the arka, why would one go to the mountain? Once the desired object is attained, what wise person would make further effort?' 'All karman in its entirety, O Pārtha, ends in jñāna' (Bh. G. 4.33), as in the Gītā. Here too it has been said that other beings live on a fragment of this very supreme bliss attained by the brahmavid. Hence for the brahmavids there is no undertaking of karman.
BR_C04_S04_V22::block-5: Since one thus turned away from all eṣaṇās, having approached this 'neti neti' Ātman as the Self, abides in that very form, therefore — the two states about to be mentioned do not cross over (na tarataḥ), do not reach, this knower of the 'neti neti' Self. Which two? 'I have done evil (pāpaṃ akaravam) — alas, my conduct is wretched; by this evil deed I shall reach hell' — this remorse occurring after a pāpa-karman thus done does not cross over the one who is neti-neti-Self. Likewise, 'I have done kalyāṇa — yajña, dāna and so on, śubhaṃ karman, on account of desire for fruit; therefore I shall enjoy its fruit, sukha, in another body' — this joy too does not cross over him. Both these — puṇya and pāpa — this brahmavid crosses over. Thus, for the brahmavid saṃnyāsin, both karmans are exhausted: those done in former births, and those done in this birth; and apūrva-karmans are not begun. Further: nor do kṛta-akṛte afflict him — kṛta is the performance of nitya-karman, akṛta is its non-performance; both kṛta and akṛta also do not afflict (na tapataḥ) him. To the non-knower, the kṛta afflicts by giving its fruit, and the akṛta by producing pratyavāya; but this brahmavid burns up all karmans by the fire of Ātman-vidyā: 'as kindled fire reduces wood to ashes' (Bh. G. 4.37) and similar smṛti. Of those karmans that have begun the body, the destruction is only by enjoyment. Hence the brahmavid is unconnected with karman.
BR_C04_S04_V23: This very thing has been declared by a verse: 'This is the eternal greatness of the brāhmaṇa — it does not increase by karman, nor become less. Of that very one let one be the knower of the path; knowing it, one is not stained by evil action.' Therefore, knowing thus, having become śānta, dānta, uparata, titikṣu, samāhita, one beholds the Self in the Self alone, beholds all as the Self. Evil does not cross over him; he crosses over all evil. Evil afflicts him not; he afflicts all evil. Free from evil, free from passion, free from doubt, he becomes a true brāhmaṇa. This is the brahmaloka, O sovereign. To this you have been led, said Yājñavalkya. 'Such am I; to the venerable I give Videha, and myself together with it for service,' said Janaka. (23)
BR_C04_S04_V23::block-0: That same matter declared by the brāhmaṇa is illumined (abhyuktam) by the ṛk-mantra. This — characterized by 'neti neti' — is the nityo mahimā, eternal greatness. Other greatnesses, being made by karman, are non-eternal; this, being distinct from them, is svābhāvika and hence eternal — the greatness of the brahmavid brāhmaṇa who has renounced all eṣaṇās. Why is it eternal? — the cause is given: 'na vardhate karmaṇā' — by śubha-karman performed it does not undergo the transformation of growth; 'no kanīyān' — by aśubha-karman it does not undergo the transformation of decline. All vikriyās have only growth and decline as cause; both are negated. Hence, being avikriya, this greatness is eternal. Therefore let one become the knower of the path (padavid) of that very greatness — pada being padyate, that which is reached, known: the very svarūpa of the greatness is the path; the knower of that. What is gained by knowing the pada? — knowing him, the greatness, one is not stained (na lipyate) by pāpa karman of the nature of dharma and adharma; both, indeed, are pāpa for the knower. Because thus this brāhmaṇa-greatness, of the nature of 'neti neti,' is unconnected with karman, therefore one knowing thus — śāntaḥ — withdrawn from external sense-functioning; dāntaḥ — withdrawn from inner thirst; uparataḥ — released from all eṣaṇās, a saṃnyāsin; titikṣuḥ — enduring of dvandvas; samāhitaḥ — having become one-pointed by withdrawing from the agitation of senses and inner organ; this was previously stated as 'having known childlikeness and learnedness' (Bṛ. Up. 3.5.1). In the Self alone — in his own kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta — he beholds the Ātman, the inward conscious one. Is it then perceived as something limited to that? It is said: no — he beholds all (sarvam) as Ātman; nothing apart from the Ātman, even the size of a hair-tip, exists — thus he beholds. From manana, he becomes a muni, having abandoned the threefold state called jāgrat, svapna, suṣupti. Such a beholding brāhmaṇa — pāpa, of the nature of puṇya-pāpa, does not cross over him, does not reach him. The brahmavid crosses over all pāpa — pervading and transcending it by Self-being. Pāpa of the nature of kṛta-akṛta does not afflict him through producing iṣṭa-fruit and pratyavāya. He, the brahmavid, afflicts all pāpa — burns it to ash by the fire of all-Self-vision. He of such knowledge is vipāpaḥ — free from dharma and adharma; virajaḥ — free from rajas, where rajas is kāma; thus free from kāma; avicikitsaḥ — with cut doubts, with mind firm in 'I am — Sarvātman, the Supreme Brahman.' He becomes a brāhmaṇa — at this stage, he is the principal, primary brāhmaṇa; before this state of abiding in brahma-svarūpa, his brāhmaṇa-hood was secondary. This is the brahma-loka — Brahman itself is the loka, the brahmaloka, principal, unfigured, characterized by all-Self-being, O sovereign. To this brahmaloka, the fearless, of the nature 'neti neti,' you have been led — thus said Yājñavalkya. Thus brought to the brahma-bhāva by Yājñavalkya, Janaka, having become Brahman, replies: 'Being brought by you to the brahma-bhāva, to the venerable, I give the Videha country, my entire kingdom, and myself together with the Videhas, for the work of a servant — dāsya-karma.' By the connecting word 'ca' the giving is so connected. Thus the brahma-vidyā together with saṃnyāsa is concluded.
BR_C04_S04_V24: Verily, this great unborn Ātman is the eater of food and the bestower of wealth. He who knows thus obtains wealth. (24)
BR_C04_S04_V24::block-0: He who has been explained in the Janaka-Yājñavalkya dialogue — that very Ātman is this great, unborn Ātman, annādaḥ — abiding in all bhūtas as the eater of all annas; vasudānaḥ — vasu being dhana, all the karma-fruit of beings, and he the giver thereof, the one who joins beings to their fruit according to their karman. He who knows this Ātman — the unborn, the eater of food, the bestower of wealth — together with the qualities of being annāda and vasudāna, becomes the Self in all bhūtas, eats anna, and obtains vasu, the entire karma-fruit, by his Sarvātman-hood. Thus he who knows as said. Or alternatively, even by those desirous of seen fruits, he is to be worshipped of such qualities; thereby one becomes annāda and the obtainer of vasu — by seen fruits, by the relation of being eater of food, of cows, horses and the like.
BR_C04_S04_V25: Verily, this great unborn Ātman is undecaying, undying, immortal, fearless, Brahman. Brahman indeed is fearless. He who knows thus becomes verily Brahman, the fearless. (25)
BR_C04_S04_V25::block-0: Now the meaning of the entire Āraṇyaka that has been declared is here gathered up and indicated in this kaṇḍikā — 'this is the entire Āraṇyaka-meaning.' Sa vā eṣa mahānaja ātmā ajaraḥ — does not decay, does not undergo modification; amaraḥ — and since undecaying, hence undying; he who is born and decays, he perishes or dies; this one, by virtue of ajatva and ajaratva, is avināśī — and hence amṛtaḥ. Since he is excluded from the three bhāva-vikāras beginning with birth (jani-prabhṛti), he is also excluded from the other three transformations and from the kāma, karma, moha and the like — of the form of mṛtyu — that they bring about. Abhayaḥ on this very ground; for since he is endowed with such qualifications, hence free from fear; bhayam is indeed an effect of avidyā; by the negation of its effect and of bhāva-vikāras, the negation of avidyā itself is to be known as established. The fearless Ātman, qualified by such qualities — what is he? Brahman — pari-vṛḍha, niratiśaya, mahat — that is the meaning. Abhayaṃ vai Brahma — this is well-known in the world: 'Brahman is fearless.' Hence it is fitting that the Ātman of such qualifications is called Brahman. He who knows the Ātman thus described as the fearless Brahman, becomes verily the fearless Brahman. This is the brief meaning of the entire Upaniṣad as stated. For the proper realization of this very meaning, the imagination of utpatti, sthiti, pralaya and the rest, and the superimposition of kriyā-kāraka-phala on the Ātman, has been made; and by removing those, the truth has been re-conveyed by the device of removing the superimposed distinctions through 'neti neti.' Just as for the comprehension of the nature of numbers from one up to the highest, one superimposes lines — saying 'this line is one, this is ten, this is a hundred, this is a thousand' — and conveys the nature of pure number, not the line-being of number; just as one wishing to teach the akṣaras a, etc., adopts the device of joining paper, ink, line and the like, and conveys the true nature of the varṇas, not the paper-and-ink-being of the akṣaras — so here too, by adopting the many devices of utpatti and so on, the one Brahman-truth has been conveyed; and again, for purifying the distinctions generated by these imagined devices, the upasaṃhāra of the truth has been made by 'neti neti.' That so concluded, purified, alone, with its fruit, jñāna alone is at the end in this kaṇḍikā.
BR_C04_S05_INTRO1::block-0: By the Madhu-kāṇḍa, predominantly āgama-based, the Brahma-tattva was determined. Then, by the Yājñavalkīya-kāṇḍa, predominantly upapatti-based, by adopting the standpoints of pakṣa and pratipakṣa, it was investigated by way of vigṛhya-vāda (combative reasoning). And in the sixth (chapter), by the relation of disciple and ācārya, by the method of question and answer, it was investigated in detail and concluded. Now, the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa, occupying the place of nigamana (conclusion), is begun. This is the method accepted by experts in vākya: 'By referring to the hetu, the re-statement of the pratijñā is nigamana' (Nyāya-sūtra 1.1.39). Or alternatively: by the Madhu-kāṇḍa, predominantly āgama-based, the Ātman-knowledge with saṃnyāsa as the means of immortality has been declared; that very same Ātman-knowledge with saṃnyāsa as the means of immortality is reached also by tarka — for the Yājñavalkīya-kāṇḍa is predominantly tarka-based. Therefore by śāstra and tarka this is established: this Ātman-knowledge with saṃnyāsa is the means of amṛtatva. Hence those endowed with śāstra-śraddhā, desiring to attain amṛtatva, must accept this; for an artha settled by both āgama and upapatti is worthy of śraddhā, on account of its being avyabhicārī — uncontradicted. The meanings of the akṣaras as explained in the fourth (adhyāya) are to be understood here too; whichever akṣaras are unexplained, those we shall explain.
BR_C04_S05_V01: Then, indeed, Yājñavalkya had two wives, Maitreyī and Kātyāyanī. Of the two, Maitreyī was a discourser on Brahman; Kātyāyanī then had only the intelligence of a woman. Then Yājñavalkya was about to take up another mode of life. (1)
BR_C04_S05_V01::block-0: 'Atha' is for showing the immediate sequence after the teaching by hetu. The preceding portions are predominantly hetu-based. Immediately following that, the artha pratijñāted (declared as the proposition) is gathered up by āgama-prominence in the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa. The 'ha' is an indicator of past narrative. Of the ṛṣi Yājñavalkya, indeed, two wives — bhāryās — there were: Maitreyī by name, one; the other, Kātyāyanī by name. Of these two wives, Maitreyī, ha kila — was a brahmavādinī, of the nature of speaking on Brahman. Strī-prajñā — that prajñā which is appropriate to a strī, that very prajñā being hers, of the nature of seeking household needs — such was Kātyāyanī then, at that time. Atha — being so, ha kila Yājñavalkya — was about to take up another vṛtta, distinct from the prior gārhasthya-vṛtta — namely, the pārivrājya-vṛtta — being desirous of taking it up (upākariṣyan, upācikīrṣuḥ).
BR_C04_S05_V02::block-0: "O Maitreyī!" — thus did Yājñavalkya address his elder wife. Having addressed her, he said: "Going forth (pravrajiṣyan) — about to take to the life of pārivrājya (the wandering renunciate) — verily, O Maitreyī (vai are), I am about to depart from this station, namely the householder's life (gārhasthya). Maitreyī, grant me leave! Well then (hanta) — if you so wish, with this Kātyāyanī let me make a settlement (antaṃ karavāṇi)." The rest has already been explained earlier.
BR_C04_S05_V03::block-0: Maitreyī said: "My lord (bhagoḥ), if this entire earth, filled with wealth, were to become mine — would I become immortal thereby, or not?" "No," said Yājñavalkya, "as is the life of those endowed with provisions, even so would your life be; but of immortality (amṛtatva) there is no hope through wealth."
BR_C04_S05_V04::block-0: She, having been thus addressed, Maitreyī spoke: "If this whole earth were filled with wealth, would I become immortal — that is, would I, by means of action (karman) accomplished through wealth, be immortal, or would I not?" "No," said Yājñavalkya, and so on — the rest is the same as before.
BR_C04_S05_V05::block-0: He said: "Verily, you, being beloved (priyā) to us from the very beginning, have now caused our affection to grow (priyam avṛdhat) — you have confirmed and strengthened it. Therefore I am pleased. Well then (hanta) — if you wish to know the means to immortality (amṛtatva-sādhana), O lady (bhavati), I shall expound that means of immortality to you."
BR_C04_S05_V06::block-0: "Verily, O Maitreyī, when the Ātman is seen" — and how is it seen? — that is now stated. First, through the teacher and scripture (ācārya-āgama), it is heard (śruta); next, through reasoning, by means of upapatti (logical congruence), it is reflected upon (mata) — that is, examined (vicārita); for śravaṇa proceeds through scripture alone, while manana proceeds through upapatti; thereafter it is fully known (vijñāta) — ascertained as "thus it is, and not otherwise." What ensues thereby? It is said: "this all becomes known." "This all" — that is, whatever is other than the Ātman; for apart from the Ātman nothing whatsoever exists (ātma-vyatirekeṇa abhāvāt). Thus the threefold discipline of śravaṇa, manana, and nididhyāsana culminates in vijñāna, wherein, the Ātman alone being the substratum, the entire manifold stands disclosed.
BR_C04_S05_V10::block-0: Bhāṣya: "Tam (him)"—the one who sees otherwise than the truth—"parādāt" means he would push him away, render him unrelated to the state of absolute oneness (kaivalya). The implication is: through this transgression—namely, that this one views Me through the form of the non-Self (anātman)—he becomes estranged from the Self.
BR_C04_S05_V12::block-0: Bhāṣya: In the fourth (mantra), by the very mention of the out-breathing of words (śabda-niḥśvāsa), the out-breathing of the worlds and other objects was implicitly conveyed by entailment (sāmarthyāt), and hence was not stated separately. But here, since this is the conclusion of the entire teaching of the śāstra (sarva-śāstrārtha-upasaṃhāra), the meaning—though already obtained by implication (artha-prāpta)—must yet be made explicit; therefore it is stated separately.
BR_C04_S05_V13::block-0: Bhāṣya: At the dissolution of all effects effected by true knowledge (vidyā-nimitte sarva-kārya-pralaye), the one Ātman alone abides—like a lump of salt (saindhava-ghana-vat)—without anything inside or outside (anantaraḥ abāhyaḥ), entire, a single mass of pure consciousness (prajñāna-ghana). Previously, however, owing to the special association with the elemental modifications (bhūta-mātrā-saṃsarga-viśeṣāt), He had appeared as one possessing particular cognitions (labdha-viśeṣa-vijñānaḥ). When that particular cognition is dissolved by vidyā, and likewise the elemental association which is its cause, then there is no consciousness after departure (na pretya saṃjñā asti). Thus has it been declared by Yājñavalkya.
BR_C04_S05_V14::block-0: Bhāṣya: She (Maitreyī) said—"O Bhagavān, you have plunged me right here (atraiva), in this very matter, namely 'It is verily prajñāna-ghana, there is no consciousness after departure,' into the midst of delusion (moha-antam = moha-madhyam)—you have caused me to become deluded (āpīpipat = āpīpadat = avagamitavān asi, sammohitavān asi); hence I do not at all comprehend (vijānāmi) this Ātman of the stated character through discrimination (vivekataḥ)." He (Yājñavalkya) replied—"I do not speak delusion. For this Ātman is imperishable (avināśī). Vinanaṃ śīlam asya iti vināśī—that whose nature is destruction is vināśī; not that is avināśī. By 'vināśa' is meant change (vikriyā); thus avināśī means the changeless Ātman (avikriyaḥ ātmā). O Maitreyī, this Ātman in question is anucchitti-dharmā (whose nature is non-dissolution). Ucchitti = ucchedaḥ = end, destruction; he whose dharma is ucchitti is ucchitti-dharmā; not he is anucchitti-dharmā. Hence the Ātman has neither change-marked nor dissolution-marked destruction."
BR_C04_S05_V15::block-0: Bhāṣya: In all four chapters (prapāṭhakas), the one Ātman has been determined as the supreme Brahman (paraṃ brahma) in equal measure. The means of attaining It (upāya-viśeṣa) differ in different places, but the goal attained (upeya) is that very Ātman which was declared in the fourth chapter by 'athāta ādeśo neti neti' (BU 2.3.6). The same is determined in the fifth, in the dialogue between Śākalya and Yājñavalkya by the staking of prāṇa, again at the close of the fifth, again in the Janaka–Yājñavalkya dialogue, and again here at the close of the Upaniṣad. To show that the steady abiding (niṣṭhā) in this Ātman is the import of all four chapters and that no other meaning is intended in the interval, the conclusion is given at the end—'sa eṣa neti neti,' etc. Since, even when the Reality (tattva) is investigated through a hundred modes, the only firm ground that is found, by reasoning or by scripture, is the 'neti neti' Ātman and no other—therefore this very thing alone is the means to immortality (amṛtatva-sādhana), namely this knowledge of the 'neti neti' Ātman together with complete renunciation (sarva-saṃnyāsa). Wishing to summarise this, he says: "Etāvat"—just this much, namely this vision of the non-dual Ātman by 'neti neti'—this alone, independent of any other auxiliary cause, O Maitreyī, is the means to immortality. What you asked—'Whatever you, Bhagavān, know, that alone tell me as the means to immortality' (BU 4.5.4)—you should know it as just this much. Thus, having declared the knowledge of the Self, the means to immortality, to his beloved wife, what did Yājñavalkya do? What he had earlier resolved—'I shall go forth (pravrajiṣyan asmi)' (BU 4.5.2)—he carried out: "vijahāra" means he went forth into the homeless life (pravrajitavān). The teaching of Brahman (brahma-vidyā) is now concluded, culminating in saṃnyāsa. This much is the entire teaching, this is the Vedic instruction (vedānuśāsana), this is the supreme niṣṭhā, this is the end of all that ought to be done for the puruṣārtha.
BR_C04_S05_V15::block-1: Bhāṣya: Now, for clear understanding of the meaning of the śāstra, an inquiry is undertaken. For the texts appear conflicting. There are passages indicating a single āśrama (ekāśramya) such as: 'One should offer the agnihotra throughout life' (yāvajjīvam agnihotraṃ juhuyāt); 'One should sacrifice with the darśapūrṇamāsa throughout life' (yāvajjīvaṃ darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ yajeta); 'Performing works here, one should desire to live a hundred years' (Īśā 2); 'This indeed is the lifelong session that is the agnihotra' (Śat. Br. 12.4.1.1). And there are other passages establishing other āśramas: 'Having known, having risen up, they go forth' (BU 3.5.1); 'Having completed studentship one should become a householder; from the household, having become a forest-dweller, one should go forth, or otherwise, from studentship itself one should go forth, or from the household, or from the forest' (Jābāla 4); 'There are two paths going further forth—the path of action and saṃnyāsa; of these, saṃnyāsa surpasses'; 'Not by works, not by progeny, not by wealth, but by renunciation alone did some attain immortality' (Tai. Nār. 10.5). Similarly there are smṛtis: 'The lifelong celibate goes forth' (Āp. Dh. 2.21.8.10); 'One whose celibacy is unbroken—whatever he wishes, that he may enter' (Vas. 8.2); 'Some hold an option among the āśramas' (Gau. Dh. 3.1); and 'Having studied the Vedas in studentship, having sought sons and grandsons for purifying the manes, having installed the fires and performed sacrifices according to rule, having entered the forest, he should then aspire to become a muni' (Mokṣa-Dharma 175.6); 'Having performed the prājāpatya offering with all his wealth as dakṣiṇā, having taken the fires into himself, the brāhmaṇa should go forth from the home' (Manu 6.38)—and so forth. Thus the texts of śruti and smṛti, mutually contradictory, are found by the hundreds, teaching either the rising up (vyutthāna), or the option, or the sequence, or freely chosen passage among the āśramas. So too the conduct of those who know them. There is also disagreement among the learned exegetes. Hence the meaning of the śāstra cannot be discriminated by dull intellects. Only those whose intellect is fully matured in the principles of the śāstra can determine the proper scope of these passages. Therefore we shall, according to the capacity of our understanding, deliberate so as to make known the proper scope of these texts.
BR_C04_S05_V15::block-2: Bhāṣya: (Pūrvapakṣa:) Since no other meaning is possible for passages like 'yāvajjīvam,' the import of the Veda terminates in action (kriyāvasāna eva vedārthaḥ). For the funeral rite is mentioned ('They burn him with the sacrificial vessels'); and the lifelong sessions (jarāmarya) are heard of; and there is the indication 'The body ends in ashes' (Īśā 17)—on the renunciate option, the body would not end in ashes. The smṛti also says: 'The one whose rule from impregnation to cremation is laid down with mantras—he alone is qualified for this śāstra, no other' (Manu 2.16). What rite is enjoined here in the Veda accompanied by mantras—of that the smṛti shows the cremation as its end. By showing the absence of qualification (for the renunciate), the absolute non-qualification of the non-actor in the śruti is understood. There is also the censure of dispensing with the fires: 'He is a hero-slayer of the gods who lays down the fire' (Tai. Saṃ. 1.5.2.1). (Objection:) Owing to the prescription of vyutthāna and the rest, terminating in action is only optional in the Vedic import. (Reply:) No—because the texts of vyutthāna serve another purpose. Since passages like 'One offers agnihotra throughout life' have life itself as their occasion (jīvana-mātra-nimittatvāt), and other meanings cannot be devised, the texts on vyutthāna may apply to those not qualified for action; from the mantra 'Performing works here, one should desire to live a hundred years' (Īśā 2), and from the absence of any gap in the agent's connection with works other than at decrepitude or death, the agent's body must end in cremation, not as an option. The blind, the lame, and the like, who are not qualified for works, are to be befriended by the śruti—hence the prescription of other āśramas like vyutthāna is not unfounded. (Objection:) Then the text prescribing the sequence of pārivrājya would be without scope. (Reply:) No—because of the exception in the viśvajit and sarvamedha rites: the lifelong agnihotra rule is overridden in the case of viśvajit and sarvamedha, and there the sequence applies—'Having completed studentship one should become a householder; from the household, having become a forest-dweller, one should go forth' (Jābāla 4). Since there is no contradiction on this scope of the text on the sequence of pārivrājya. If one were to assign it to another scope, the lifelong rule would be confined within itself; but in interpreting the sequence as referring to viśvajit and sarvamedha, no obstacle arises.
BR_C04_S05_V15::block-3: Bhāṣya: (Siddhānta:) No—because the knowledge of the Self (ātma-jñāna) is admitted to be the cause of immortality. From 'ātmety evopāsīta' (BU 1.4.7) up to 'sa eṣa neti neti,' the knowledge of the Ātman summed up in this body of the text is conceded by you yourself to be the means to immortality. Yet the assertion that this alone, independent of all else, is the means to immortality, you do not concede. I therefore ask: why does your honour not concede the knowledge of the Self? Hear the reason. Just as for one desirous of heaven, ignorant of the means of attaining heaven, the agnihotra and the rest are made known as means; so here too, for one desirous of immortality, ignorant of the means thereto, the questioned 'whatever you, Bhagavān, know, that tell me' (BU 4.5.4)—the means of immortality is made known by the Veda in 'etāvad are' (BU 4.5.15). Then, just as the agnihotra and the rest are accepted as means to heaven exactly as made known, so here too the knowledge of the Self ought to be accepted as means to immortality precisely as made known—for the authority is equal in both. If so, what would follow? Since knowledge of the Self uproots the cause of all action (sarva-karma-hetu-upamardakatvāt), upon the rise of vidyā there would be cessation of works (karma-nivṛtti). For karmas like the agnihotra, conjoined with wife and fire, are accomplished by the recipient-factor (sampradāna-kāraka) which is the object of the discriminative cognition of difference (bheda-buddhi-viṣaya). Without the recipient deity—Indra and the rest—delimited by another cognition, the rite cannot be accomplished. The cognition of the recipient-factor by which the recipient is taught as instrument of the rite—that cognition is dissolved here by vidyā, as in: 'He who reveres a divinity as other thinking 'I am one, that is another' does not know' (BU 1.4.10); 'The gods reject him who, apart from the Self, regards the gods as other' (BU 4.5.12); 'From death to death does he go who sees here as if many' (BU 4.4.19); 'Verily one should behold the entire Ātman as one' (BU 4.4.20). Nor does Self-knowledge depend on place, time, occasion, etc., since it has the firmly-established Self for its object (vyavasthita-ātma-vastu-viṣayatvāt). Action, on the other hand, depends on the agent, and so requires place, time, etc.; but knowledge, being object-dependent (vastu-tantratva), does not require place, time, occasion. Just as fire is hot and ākāśa is formless, so is Self-knowledge. (Objection:) Then the binding force of the karma-vidhi—itself a valid pramāṇa—would be cancelled, and obstruction between two equally-valid pramāṇas is improper. (Reply:) No—since it merely cancels the cognition of innate difference (svābhāvika-bheda-buddhi-mātra-nirodhakatvāt). Self-knowledge does not cancel another vidhi; it merely uproots the natural cognition of difference. (Objection:) Even so, by removing the cause, the karma cannot stand, and so the vidhi itself is cancelled. (Reply:) No—just as the prohibition of desire blocks engagement in the optional rite, so this is no fault. Just as one engaged in sacrifice as means to heaven from 'svarga-kāmo yajeta' (BU 4.4.23) is, when desire is uprooted by the prohibition of desire, prevented from undertaking the optional sacrifice, the optional vidhi itself is not abolished thereby. (Objection:) Through the cognition of the futility of the optional vidhi by the prohibition of desire, since engagement is impossible, it is in effect cancelled. (Reply:) Be it so—let the karma-vidhi too be similarly cancelled. (Objection:) But then, as in the case of the optional vidhi under the prohibition of desire, the very pramāṇa-status would fail. (Reply:) Where there is nothing to be performed…
BR_C04_S06_V03::block-0: Now, after this, the lineage (vaṃśa) of the Yājñavalkīya-kāṇḍa is begun, just as was the lineage of the Madhu-kāṇḍa. The explanation, however, is as before. Brahman is self-existent (svayambhū); salutation to Brahman, Oṃ.
BR_C05_S01_V01::block-0: The supplementary section (khila-kāṇḍa) beginning with pūrṇam adaḥ is now commenced. Throughout the four preceding chapters, that very Brahman which is direct and immediate, the Self that is innermost to all, free from all upādhis, transcending hunger and the rest, designated by neti-neti, has been ascertained — the knowledge of which alone is the means to immortality. Now, the upāsanās of that same Self when conditioned by upādhis, brought within the range of word-meaning and similar transactional dealings, which were not previously stated and which are not in conflict with karma, productive of high prosperity (abhyudaya) and conducive to liberation by stages (krama-mukti), are to be set forth — such is the connection of what follows. As ancillary to all upāsanās, the Oṃkāra together with dama, dāna, and dayā are intended to be enjoined. Pūrṇam adaḥ — “pūrṇa” means that which is not separated off from anything, i.e., all-pervading; the suffix is to be construed in the sense of the agent (kartṛ). “Adaḥ” is a pronoun denoting what is remote, and refers to the supreme Brahman. That is full, all-pervading like ākāśa, undivided, and free from upādhis. That very same is this conditioned (sopādhika) Brahman, located in name-and-form, brought within transactional dealings, full only by its own essence as the supreme Self, by which it pervades — not by the limited particularised form arising from the upādhi. From that full causal Brahman, this effected (kāryātmaka) Brahman that has assumed particularity “rises forth” (udricyate), i.e., goes forth, comes out. Even though it rises forth as effect, it does not abandon that fullness which is its own essence — its being the supreme Self; only that which is full rises forth. From this full effected Brahman, having taken (ādāya) the fullness, that is, having brought it back to the unitary essence of the Self by means of true knowledge (vidyā), having dispelled the appearance of otherness — born of association with upādhis in the form of the elements and produced by avidyā — Brahman alone, full, with nothing within or beyond, having the single essence of compacted consciousness, remains. What was said previously — “Brahman alone was this in the beginning; it knew only itself; therefore it became all that” (Bṛ. U. 1.4.10) — that is the meaning of this mantra. There the word “Brahman” corresponds to “pūrṇam adaḥ”; “this is full” corresponds to “Brahman alone was this in the beginning”; and so a different śruti says, “What is here, that is there; what is there, that is here” (Ka. U. 2.1.10). Hence the “pūrṇa” denoted by the word “adaḥ” is Brahman, and that very same is the “pūrṇa” here, established in effect, conjoined with the upādhis of name-and-form, made to rise forth by avidyā, appearing as if other than that absolute essence. That — having known the Self alone as the supreme, full Brahman with the conviction “I am that full Brahman, adaḥ” — having taken the fullness, having dispelled the non-fullness produced by avidyā and arising from contact with the upādhis of name-and-form, by this brahmavidyā Brahman alone, full, remains. Thus too has it been said: “Therefore it became all that.” That Brahman which is the meaning of all the upaniṣads is here re-stated by this mantra for the sake of connection with what follows. For the means about to be stated — known as Oṃkāra, dama, dāna, and dayā — are intended as means to brahmavidyā, and from the connection with the supplementary chapter (khila-prakaraṇa) they are also limbs of every upāsanā.
BR_C05_S01_V01::block-1: Here some [pūrvapakṣins] explain thus: From the full cause, the full effect rises forth; the effect, having risen forth, is itself, even at present, full, an actually existing reality in the form of duality. Again at the time of dissolution, having taken the fullness of the full effect into itself, only the full causal form remains. Thus, in all three times — origination, continuance, and dissolution — both effect and cause are full; and that one fullness is designated diversely by reference to the distinction of effect and cause. So Brahman is one, of the nature of duality-and-non-duality (dvaitādvaita). Just as the ocean is itself of the nature of water, waves, foam, bubbles, and the like, and just as water is real and the waves, foam, and bubbles arising from it, having the property of appearing and disappearing, are real as identical with the ocean — so all this duality is in truth real, like the waves and the rest in the place of water, while the supreme Brahman is in the place of the ocean-water itself. Thus, since duality is real, the validity of the karma-kāṇḍa is established. But if duality were like a mirage, untrue, fashioned by avidyā, and the non-dual alone were real in the highest sense, then the karma-kāṇḍa would, owing to absence of object, become invalid; and so there would be contradiction. The upaniṣad, being a part of the Veda, would be authoritative as expounding the supreme non-dual reality, while the karma-kāṇḍa would be unauthoritative, having unreal duality as its sphere. Wishing to remove this contradiction, the śruti has stated this reality of effect and cause, like the ocean, by the words pūrṇam adaḥ etc. — [thus the pūrvapakṣa]. Siddhānta: That is not so. For neither restrictive exception of a particular case (apavāda) nor option (vikalpa) is possible here. This conjecture has not been well thought out. Why? In the case of action one may indeed make an exception to a general rule (utsarga) for one particular case — as where harm to all beings is forbidden by general rule, “not injuring any beings except at the tīrthas” (Cha. U. 8.15.1), permission for himsā is granted at the “tīrtha,” the special case of the jyotiṣṭoma and the like; but not so in the case of an existent reality (vastu): here, having taught non-dual Brahman as a general rule, it cannot be excepted in respect of one part of itself, since, given that Brahman is non-dual, “a part of it” cannot be made out. So too option is not possible. Just as in “At the atirātra he takes up the ṣoḍaśin” and “At the atirātra he does not take up the ṣoḍaśin,” since taking and not taking depend on the human agent (puruṣa-tantra), an option is admissible — but not so here in the case of a reality, where the option “let it be dual or non-dual” cannot be made, since the Self-substance (ātma-vastu) is not subject to human discretion (apuruṣa-tantra), and since the simultaneous dual-and-non-dual nature of one entity is itself contradictory. Therefore this conjecture has not been well thought out. There is, moreover, conflict with śruti and reasoning. Such śrutis as: like a mass of salt, a homogeneous mass with a single essence of consciousness, undivided, free from distinctions of front, back, outer, inner, both within and without, unborn, neti-neti, neither gross nor minute, neither short nor long, free from old age, fearless, immortal — these śrutis, with their settled meaning, free from doubt, error, and suspicion, would all be cast into the ocean as having no effect. So too there is conflict with reasoning, since for what has parts, is multifold, and has activity, eternality is not made out; and the eternality of the Self is inferred from the observation of memory and the like, which would be contradicted by non-eternality. Your imagined view itself becomes pointless; and on this view the futility of the karma-kāṇḍa is patent, since it would entail the doctrine of the un-done arriving and the done perishing (akṛtābhyāgama-kṛta-vipraṇāśa). [Pūrvapakṣa:] Surely there are illustrations like the ocean for Brahman’s being dual-and-non-dual; how, then, is it said by you …
BR_C05_S01_V01::block-2: Oṃ kham brahma is the mantra. This mantra, not employed elsewhere, is here employed by the brāhmaṇa for an act of meditation (dhyāna-karman). Here, “brahma” is the substantive (viśeṣya), and “kham” is the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa). The mention of qualifier and substantive is by way of co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), as in “blue lotus” — kham brahma. The word “brahman” is by itself unqualified, denoting only the great-thing (bṛhad-vastu); hence it is qualified — kham brahma. That very Brahman which is kham is denoted by the word Oṃ, or rather is itself of the very form of the word Oṃ; either way, the co-referentiality is unobjectionable. Here the word Oṃ is used as a means for the upāsanā of Brahman, just as another śruti says: “This is the best support; this is the supreme support” (Ka. U. 1.2.17), “One should yoke the self with Oṃ” (Tai. Nā. 24.1), “One should meditate on the supreme Puruṣa with this very syllable Oṃ” (Pra. U. 5.5), “Meditate thus on the Self with Oṃ” (Mu. U. 2.2.6), and so on. The teaching admits of no other purport. Just as elsewhere — “He recites with Oṃ; he chants with Oṃ” (Cha. U. 1.1.9) and so on — the application (viniyoga) of the Oṃkāra at the beginning and end of svādhyāya is understood from the prescribed use, no other purport is so understood here; therefore, here the syllable Oṃ is taught only as a means of dhyāna. Although the words Brahman, Ātman, and the like are denotative of Brahman, yet by the authority of śruti, the Oṃkāra is the closest designation of Brahman. Hence this is the supreme means in the apprehension of Brahman. And that in two ways — as symbol (pratīka) and as designation (abhidhāna). As pratīka — just as the image of Viṣṇu and the like is taken as identical with him, so the Oṃkāra is to be apprehended as Brahman. For Brahman becomes gracious to one who takes the Oṃkāra as support: “This is the best support; this is the supreme support; knowing this support, one is exalted in the Brahma-loka” (Ka. U. 1.2.17), so says the śruti.
BR_C05_S01_V01::block-3: Now, lest there be the apprehension that “kham” means the elemental sky, he says — “the ancient kham,” the ākāśa of the supreme Self; that is the meaning. That ancient kham, the supreme-Self ākāśa, since it is not the object of the eye and the rest, is supportless and impossible to grasp; therefore one places it on the Oṃkāra by śraddhā and bhakti, by a special bhāva — just as the world places Viṣṇu on a stone image marked with the limbs of Viṣṇu. “Vāyuram kham” — vāyu is in this; therefore vāyuram, the [elemental] kham, mere kham — that is what is called kham, not the ancient kham; thus did he say. Who is he? The son of Kauravyāyaṇī. For the principal usage of the word “kha” is in the kha permeated by air; hence it is fitting that the conviction (saṃpratyaya) be in the principal sense — so he thinks. There, whether the ancient kham is Brahman in its non-conditioned essence, or the vāyuram kham is conditioned Brahman, in either case the Oṃkāra serves as means by way of pratīka, like an image, as another śruti says: “This indeed, O Satyakāma, is both the higher and the lower Brahman, namely Oṃkāra” (Pra. U. 5.2). Only with regard to the meaning of the word “kha” is there difference. “Veda is this Oṃkāra” — “Veda” means: by which one knows what is to be known; therefore Veda is the Oṃkāra, the designator, the abhidhāna; by that designation, the Brahman that is to be known is illumined and uttered, the seeker (sādhaka) knows it, perceives it; therefore the brāhmaṇas know this as Veda. Hence to the brāhmaṇas the Oṃkāra’s being a means is intended in the sense of designation. Or: “Veda is this” etc. is arthavāda; how? The Oṃkāra has been enjoined as the pratīka of Brahman; by the co-referentiality of “Oṃ kham brahma” there is praise of it now in the form of being Veda. For all this Veda is verily the Oṃkāra; this entire Veda differentiated as Ṛk, Yajus, Sāman, etc., has its source in this and consists of this — so another śruti says: “Just as all leaves are [held together] by a peg” (Cha. U. 2.23.3), and so on. Further, this Veda is Oṃkāra in this respect: whatever is to be known, all that is known by the Oṃkāra alone — by it the brāhmaṇa knows. Therefore this Oṃkāra is Veda; the Veda-hood of the other Veda also is for that very reason. Hence this distinguished Oṃkāra is to be apprehended as a means. Or else: “Veda is that.” What is that? That Oṃkāra which the brāhmaṇas know. For to the brāhmaṇas it is to be known under various forms — praṇava, udgītha, and the rest. When that is employed as means, the entire Veda becomes employed as means.
BR_C05_S02_V01::block-0: Now this beginning is for the purpose of enjoining the threefold means — dama and the rest. “Trayāḥ” means three in number; “prājāpatyāḥ” means children of Prajāpati. What did they do? They “dwelt in brahmacarya” with their father Prajāpati — being disciples; for the principal characteristic of discipleship is brahmacarya — that is the meaning. Who are they? Specifically, the gods (devas), human beings (manuṣyas), and the asuras. Having dwelt in brahmacarya, what did they do? Among them the gods spoke to their father, Prajāpati. Saying what? “May your honour speak to us” — that is, “let your instruction be uttered.” To them, thus seeking, he uttered this single syllable — “da.” Having uttered, the father asked them: “Did you understand?” — that is, “did you understand the meaning of the syllable I uttered for instruction, or not?” The gods said: “We have understood.” “If so, say what was uttered by me.” The gods said: “Dāmyata — ‘restrain yourselves’: by nature you are unrestrained, therefore become restrained — that is what your honour says to us.” The other replied: “Oṃ — yes, you have understood rightly.”
BR_C05_S02_V02::block-0: The rest is similar. “By nature you are greedy; therefore distribute according to your capacity — ‘datta’ — that is what your honour says to us; what else would he say to us as our good?” — thus the human beings.
BR_C05_S02_V03::block-0: Likewise, the asuras: “Dayadhvam” — “you are cruel, given to himsā and the like; therefore, show compassion (dayā) to creatures.” This very instruction of Prajāpati continues even today. He who as Prajāpati of yore instructed the gods and the rest, even now instructs through the divine speech in the form of thunder. How is this divine speech heard? What is that thundering? “Da, da, da” — namely, “restrain (dāmyata), give (datta), be compassionate (dayadhvam)” — for the indication of these sentences the syllable “da” is thrice uttered, by way of imitation. The thundering is not literally three-fold in count, since there is no fixed number-restriction known in the world. Since even now Prajāpati instructs “restrain, give, be compassionate,” for that reason this triad — what triad? — “dama, dāna, dayā” — is to be learned (śikṣet), is to be taken up: one should resolve, “Prajāpati’s instruction is to be carried out by us.” So too the smṛti: “The threefold gate of hell, destructive of the self — desire, anger, and greed; therefore one should abandon these three” (Bh. Gītā 16.21). For this very vidhi the previous portion is the auxiliary. Even so, why did Prajāpati, in addressing the gods and the rest, utter just the three “da”s for them severally seeking instruction? And how, hearing the same single syllable “da,” did they understand his intent distinctly? — knowers of another’s intent, [the commentators] propose alternatives. Here some say: aware of their own faultiness due to being unrestrained, greedy, and lacking compassion, they dwelt with Prajāpati already apprehensive — “What will he say to us?” To them, on merely hearing the syllable “da,” the apprehension of its meaning arose by reason of self-suspicion (ātma-śaṅkā). For in the world too it is well known: sons and disciples, when being instructed, are to be turned away from their faults. Therefore the utterance of just “da” by Prajāpati is fitting; from the connection of the syllable “da” in dama and the rest, the gods and the others, in accordance with their own respective fault, understood distinctly. The fruit, however, is this: when one’s own fault is known, one can be turned away even by a brief teaching, as the gods and the others were by the mere syllable “da.” [Pūrvapakṣa:] Surely this instruction of the three — gods and the others — should be taken up severally by gods and others, each one only one of them; even today not all three are to be learned by men. — To this it is said: this triad was practised by superior beings, by gods and the others of yore; therefore it is to be learned by men alone. Then would not compassion be unfit for practice — how? — being practised by the asuras, who are unworthy? — No, since the three are equal. Hence here a different intent: gods and the rest are the three sons of Prajāpati; what is good is what should be taught by a father to his sons; and Prajāpati, knowing the good, does not teach otherwise. Therefore the instruction of his sons by Prajāpati is the supreme good. Hence this triad is to be learned by men alone. Or else: there are no other gods or asuras besides men; among men themselves, those who are unrestrained though endowed with other excellent qualities are gods; men in whom greed predominates are men; those who are cruel and given to himsā are asuras. These are themselves men; with reference to the threefold defects of being unrestrained, etc., they receive the names “gods,” “men,” and “asuras”; with reference to the other qualities — sattva, rajas, and tamas — likewise. Therefore this triad is to be learned by men alone, since the instruction by Prajāpati was given with reference to them …
BR_C05_S03_INTRO1::block-0: The triad of means — dama and the rest — has been enjoined as ancillary to all upāsanā; one who is restrained, free from greed, and compassionate is qualified for all upāsanās. The vision (darśana) of the unconditioned (nirupādhika) Brahman is past; now, the fruits in the form of abhyudaya of that very Self when sopādhika are to be told. To that purpose is this beginning.
BR_C05_S03_V01::block-0: “Eṣa prajāpatir yad-dhṛdayam” — that Prajāpati instructs has just been said. Who, then, is that instructor Prajāpati? It is said: this Prajāpati. Who? “Yad hṛdayam” — by “hṛdaya” is meant the buddhi located in the heart; that very heart, in which, at the close of the Śākalya-brāhmaṇa, the gathering up of names, forms, and actions was stated by way of the divisions of the directions, that very heart, the support of all beings, the inner Self of all beings, is Prajāpati, the creator of creatures. This is Brahman — by reason of greatness (bṛhattva) and of being all-Self, it is Brahman. “This is everything” — in the fifth chapter the all-ness of the heart was declared. Since that is everything, therefore the heart is Brahman to be meditated upon (upāsya). Here first the upāsanā concerning the very syllables of the name “hṛdaya” is stated; this name “hṛdaya” has three syllables — three syllables are in this; what then are these three syllables? “Hṛ” is one syllable; “they bring” — from the root √hṛ in the sense of bringing, “hṛ” is its form; he who knows that, since for the heart, for Brahman, his own [organs] — the indriyas — and others, the objects, sound and the rest, bring (abhiharanti) their respective work, and the heart brings [things] for the sake of the experiencer — therefore that the “hṛ” syllable belongs to the name “hṛdaya” — to such a knower his own kinsmen and others unconnected bring tribute (bali); “tribute” is supplied as the elliptical word. The fruit corresponds to the level of vijñāna. Likewise “da” is also one syllable; this too — the syllable “da” is the form of √dā in the sense of giving, fastened in the syllables of the name “hṛdaya.” Here also: for the heart, for Brahman, his own organs and the other objects give their respective vīrya, and the heart gives its own vīrya to the experiencer; therefore the syllable “da” — he who knows thus, to him his own and others give. Likewise “ya” is also one syllable; from √i in the sense of going, “ya” is its form, fastened in this name; he who knows thus, he attains (eti) the heavenly world (svarga-loka). Thus, even from the syllables of the name such a distinguished fruit is obtained — what need to say of upāsanā of the heart’s own essence? — hence the laying down of the syllables of the name is by way of praise of the heart.
BR_C05_S04_V01::block-0: Wishing to enjoin the upāsanā of that very Brahman called “heart” as “satya,” he says — “tat”: by “tat” the heart-Brahman is referred to; “vai” is for recollection; “tat” which is the heart-Brahman is recollected — this is the first “tat.” “Tat etat” is said in another mode — this is the second “tat.” What now is that other mode? “Etadeva tat” — by the word “etat” a third “tat” is connected; “etat,” keeping in mind what is to be said, is uttered. “Āsa” means “became.” What was that very thing? What was said as “heart Brahman” — “tat” — the third “tat” is so applied. He specifies what that is: “satyam eva.” Sat (the manifested) and tyat (the unmanifested), the formed and the formless, [together] are satya, Brahman, consisting of the five elements — that is the meaning. Whoever knows this Brahman as the Self of satya — “mahat” because of greatness, “yakṣa” because worshipful, “prathamajaṃ” first-born, born first of all from saṃsāra; that very Brahman first-born; he who knows it as “satyam brahma” — this is the fruit declared: just as by the satya-Brahman these worlds were brought under one’s sway, conquered, so he who knows the great Yakṣa, the first-born, satya-Brahman, conquers these worlds; further: “jita in nu” — “let it be so,” “the enemy is conquered, like Brahman”; the supplement is “the enemy.” “Asat” — he becomes non-existent — that enemy becomes conquered and non-existent — that is the meaning. Whose is this fruit, he again concludes: “he who knows this great Yakṣa, the first-born, as ‘satya-Brahman.’” Hence the fruit corresponding to the vidyā is fitting, since indeed Brahman is satya.
BR_C05_S05_V01::block-0:
Mantra: In the beginning there were only the waters; those waters created Truth, Truth created Brahman, Brahman created Prajāpati, Prajāpati created the gods. Those gods worship Truth alone. That Truth is of three syllables: "sa", "tī", "yam". The first and last syllables are truth; in the middle is untruth. That untruth is encompassed on both sides by truth, and so becomes preponderantly truth. Untruth never injures one who knows thus.

Bhāṣya: This is said for the praise of Truth, which is Brahman. It was earlier stated, "The great yakṣa, the first-born"; how is its first-born status established? Therefore it is said: "In the beginning there were only the waters" (āpa eveda agra āsuḥ). "Waters" here means the oblations such as agnihotra and the rest, which inhere in ritual action; because the oblation of agnihotra and so forth is of liquid nature, water-hood is ascribed to them. Those waters, after the conclusion of the rites of agnihotra and the like, do not relinquish their inherence in ritual action by means of some unseen subtle self, and remain accompanied by the other elements, not alone; but on account of inhering in ritual action, the primacy belongs to the waters. Thus all the elements, prior to manifestation, in their unmanifest state together with their agents, are designated as "waters". Those waters, becoming the seed of the world, abode in unmanifest form. Those alone, in the beginning, were this entire world transformed into name and form; nothing else of the modified order existed. Those waters then created Truth; therefore Truth, Brahman, is the first-born. This is the birth of Hiraṇyagarbha, the Sūtrātman, namely the manifestation of the unmanifest world. Why is that Brahman called "Truth"? On account of greatness. How greatness? Because it is the creator of all. How? That which is Truth, Brahman, created Prajāpati, the lord of creatures, the Virāj, the instrumental cause of the sun and the rest – "created" must be supplied. Prajāpati then created the gods; that Virāj Prajāpati created the gods. Since everything is thus born in sequence from Truth, Brahman, therefore Truth is great Brahman. But how is it called yakṣa? It is said: those gods, when thus created, surpassing even their father Virāj, worship that very Truth, Brahman; therefore this first-born is the great yakṣa. Hence it is to be worshipped wholeheartedly. The name of that Truth, Brahman, is also "satya". This consists of three syllables. What are those syllables? It is said: "sa" is one syllable; "tī" is one syllable – "tī" with the long ī affix is for indicative purposes; "yam" is one syllable. Among these the first and last syllables, "sa" and "yam", are truth, because they are devoid of the form of death. In the middle is untruth, for death is untruth, and there is the common feature of "ta" between death (mṛtyu) and untruth (anṛta). That untruth, the syllable "ta", which is of the form of death, is on both sides encompassed, pervaded, included by truth in the form of "sa" and "yam"; hence it is rendered ineffective. It becomes preponderantly truth, an abundance of truth. One who knows in this way the abundance of truth and the ineffectiveness of all death-bound untruth – such a knower untruth never injures, even if at some time uttered through inadvertence.
BR_C05_S05_V02::block-0:
Mantra: That which is Truth is yonder sun, the puruṣa in that orb, and this puruṣa in the right eye. These two stand established in each other: the former in the latter through rays, the latter in the former through prāṇas. When one is about to depart, he sees that orb pure, and these rays no longer return to him.

Bhāṣya: Now upāsanā of Truth, Brahman, in a particular configuration is being explained. "That which" – what is that? Truth, Brahman, the first-born. What is it? "Yonder, that one". Who is that? The sun. But who is yonder sun? "He who is". Who is he? He who is the puruṣa identifying with that solar orb – he is that Truth, Brahman. "And this one" – in the body, the puruṣa in the right eye; by the word "and" the connection "he too is Truth, Brahman" is implied. Since these two puruṣas, abiding in the sun and the eye, are particular configurations of one and the same Truth, Brahman, therefore they are established in each other – the solar in the ocular and the ocular in the solar – because the adhyātma and the adhidaivata are mutually helpers and helped. How established? It is said: this sun is established in the ocular adhyātma puruṣa by means of rays, favouring it through illumination; and this ocular puruṣa is established in yonder solar adhidaiva by means of prāṇas, favouring the sun. When this experiencer in the body, who is consciousness (vijñānamaya), is about to depart – at that time, that ocular solar puruṣa, withdrawing his rays, stands forth in pure form alone with indifference. Then this conscious one beholds this orb wholly pure, devoid of rays, like the lunar orb. This omen-vision is shown incidentally, with the intent: how indeed should a person become diligent in what is to be done? Or rather: thus, having previously approached the ocular puruṣa for the sake of favouring him by his lord's duty, these rays, as if conforming to the exhaustion of his karma, no longer come, no longer return to him. Hence it is to be understood that, on account of this mutual relation of helper and helped, these two are portions of one and the same Truth, the Self.
BR_C05_S05_V03::block-0:
Mantra: For the puruṣa in yonder orb, "bhūḥ" is the head – one head, one syllable; "bhuvaḥ" is the two arms – two arms, two syllables; "svaḥ" is the foundation – two feet, two syllables. His upaniṣad is "ahar". He destroys (hanti) and abandons (jahāti) sin who knows thus.

Bhāṣya: Among them, who is that one? He who is the puruṣa in this solar orb, named "satya". His limbs are the vyāhṛtis. How? "Bhūḥ" – this vyāhṛti is his head, on account of primacy; here the śruti itself states the commonality – "one", endowed with the number one, is the head; likewise "bhūḥ" is one syllable. "Bhuvaḥ" is the two arms, on account of the commonality of duality; two arms, these two syllables. Likewise "svaḥ" is the foundation; two feet – these two syllables. "Pratiṣṭhe" means feet, because by them one stands firm. Of this puruṣa whose limbs are the vyāhṛtis, of this Brahman who is Truth, the upaniṣad is the secret name; by which name, when uttered, that Brahman becomes facing one as in worldly usage. What is that? It is said: "ahar". And this form "ahar" is from the roots han (to destroy) and hā (to abandon), which one knows; he who knows thus destroys and abandons sin.
BR_C05_S05_V04::block-0:
Mantra: For this puruṣa in the right eye, "bhūḥ" is the head – one head, one syllable; "bhuvaḥ" is the two arms – two arms, two syllables; "svaḥ" is the foundation – two feet, two syllables. His upaniṣad is "aham". He destroys and abandons sin who knows thus.

Bhāṣya: Likewise, for this puruṣa in the right eye, all the rest – "bhūḥ" is the head and so on – is the same. His upaniṣad is "aham", because he is the inner Self (pratyagātman). As before, from the roots han and hā.
BR_C05_S06_INTRO1::block-0: Bhāṣya (Introduction): Because of the multiplicity of upādhis and the multiplicity of qualifying attributes, intending to enjoin the upāsanā of that very Brahman now under discussion, qualified by the upādhi of mind, he says –
BR_C05_S06_V01::block-0:
Mantra: This puruṣa, made of mind, of the nature of light, abides within the heart, like a grain of rice or barley. He is the lord of all, the master of all; he rules all this, whatsoever exists.

Bhāṣya: "Manomaya" means consisting predominantly of mind, because he is apprehended in the mind, and is apprehended through the mind – hence this puruṣa is "manomaya". "Bhāḥsatya" – light alone is the truth, the very being, the essential nature of him; thus he is "bhāḥsatya", that is, luminous; because the mind illumines all objects and because he is made of mind, he is luminous. "Within the heart" means inside the heart, that is to say, there. "Like a grain of rice or barley" – in measure, of such size; he is seen in that inner heart by yogins, this is the meaning. "He, this one, is the lord of all" – the master of all entities differentiated from himself; even when one is master, sometimes he is dependent on ministers and the like, but this one is not so. Then what? He is "adhipati", standing over and protecting. "He rules all this, whatsoever" – whatever world there is, he rules all of it. Thus by upāsanā of the manomaya the fruit is the very attainment of that form. The Brāhmaṇa text declares: "As one worships him, so one becomes" (Śat. Br. 10.5.2.20).
BR_C05_S07_V01::block-0:
Mantra: They say lightning is Brahman; lightning (vidyut) is so called from "vidāna" (cleaving). Lightning cleaves him from sin who knows thus – "lightning is Brahman". For verily lightning is Brahman.

Bhāṣya: Likewise another upāsanā with a special fruit of Truth, Brahman, is begun – "They say lightning is Brahman". The etymology of "vidyut", lightning, is being explained: from "vidāna", cleaving, it splits asunder the dense darkness of clouds and shines forth; hence "vidyut". One who knows lightning of such a quality as Brahman – he cleaves, splits, destroys his sins; whatever sins are inimical to this Self of his, all of them he splits asunder – this is the meaning. He who knows thus – "lightning is Brahman" – obtains a corresponding fruit, since lightning indeed is Brahman.
BR_C05_S08_V01::block-0:
Mantra: One should worship Speech as a milch-cow. She has four udders – svāhā-kāra, vaṣaṭ-kāra, hanta-kāra, svadhā-kāra. The gods live on two of her udders, svāhā-kāra and vaṣaṭ-kāra; men on hanta-kāra; the Fathers on svadhā-kāra. Her bull is prāṇa, her calf the mind.

Bhāṣya: Again another upāsanā, of that very Brahman: "Speech indeed is Brahman". "Vāc" is the threefold Veda (trayī) – the word. That Speech as a milch-cow – like a milch-cow, a milch-cow; just as a cow yields milk through her four udders for the calf, so the cow that is Speech yields food, like milk, through the udders to be mentioned, for the gods and others. What, then, are those udders? And which are those for whom she yields? Of that Speech, the milch-cow, the gods drink upon two udders, occupying the place of calves. Which two? Svāhā-kāra and vaṣaṭ-kāra; for through these the oblation is given to the gods. Men drink hanta-kāra; for with "hanta" they offer food to men. The Fathers drink svadhā-kāra; for with svadhā-kāra they offer the svadhā oblation to the Fathers. Of that cow Speech, prāṇa is the bull, for through prāṇa Speech is brought forth. Mind is the calf, for by mind Speech is made to flow; for when an object has been deliberated upon by mind, then Speech proceeds; therefore mind has the place of the calf. Thus the worshipper of Speech as a cow attains identity with that very form.
BR_C05_S09_V01::block-0: This Vaiśvānara fire which is here within the person, by which this food is digested, of it this is the sound which one hears upon stopping the ears. When one is about to depart, one no longer hears this sound.
BR_C05_S09_V01::block-1: Bhāṣya: ‘ayam agnir vaiśvānaraḥ’—as before, another upāsanā is being introduced. This fire is Vaiśvānara. Which fire is meant? It is replied: ‘yo’yam antaḥ puruṣe’—the one which is here within the person. Is it the fire that constructs the body? No; it is said: ‘yenedam annaṁ pacyate’—that fire, named Vaiśvānara, by which this food is cooked. What food? ‘yad idam adyate’—that which is eaten and consumed by living beings as food; the meaning is the gastric fire (jāṭhara). To indicate it directly through perception, this is said: of that fire, which is the gastric fire cooking food, this is the sound. Which? ‘yam etat’—‘etat’ here is an adverb qualifying the action—‘karṇāv apidhāya’—stopping the ears by closing them with the fingers, one hears this sound.
