One should meditate upon Prajāpati, the Vaiśvānara fire, in this manner. Here too the fruit is identification with that (tādbhāvya). Incidentally, this characteristic of the omen of imminent death is stated: when this experiencer in the body is about to depart, he does not hear this sound.
BR_C05_S10_V01::block-0: When the person departs from this world he reaches the wind. The wind opens out for him there an aperture as wide as the hub of a chariot wheel; through that he ascends upward. He reaches the sun; the sun opens out for him an aperture as wide as the hole of a lambara; through that he ascends. He reaches the moon, which opens an aperture as wide as a drum; through that he ascends. He attains a world free from grief, free from cold, and there he dwells for endless years.
BR_C05_S10_V01::block-1: Bhāṣya: For all the upāsanās in this section the path and fruit are now declared. ‘yadā vai puruṣaḥ’—when the knower departs from this world, that is, abandons the body, he then reaches the wind. In the intermediate region the wind stands spread crosswise, dense and impenetrable. That wind, on his arriving there, opens itself out, separating its own parts, that is, makes itself perforated—this is the meaning. Of what dimension is the aperture? It is said: like the well-known dimension of the hub-hole of a chariot wheel; through that aperture the knower ascends upward. He reaches the sun. The sun stands blocking the path of one wishing to go to Brahmaloka; that too gives passage to such a knowing upāsaka—it opens out for him there. Like the aperture of a lambara, a particular musical instrument; through that he ascends. He reaches the moon; that too opens out for him there, like the well-known aperture of a drum; through that he ascends. He reaches the world of Prajāpati. Of what description? ‘aśokam’—free from mental sorrow; ‘ahimam’—free from cold, that is, free from bodily suffering, this is the meaning. Having attained that, he dwells in it for ‘śāśvatīḥ samāḥ’—eternal years; the meaning is, he dwells for many kalpas of Brahmā.
BR_C05_S11_V01::block-0: This indeed is the supreme tapas—that one suffers when smitten with disease; he wins the supreme world who knows thus. This indeed is the supreme tapas—that one departed is borne to the forest; he wins the supreme world who knows thus. This indeed is the supreme tapas—that one departed is laid upon the fire; he wins the supreme world who knows thus.
BR_C05_S11_V01::block-1: Bhāṣya: ‘etad vai paramaṁ tapaḥ’—what is that? ‘yad vyāhitaḥ’—being afflicted, that is, gripped by fever and the like, what one suffers, that—‘this is supreme tapas’—one should so reflect, on account of the common feature of suffering. For the knower who reflects thus, that very suffering becomes tapas, the cause of the destruction of karma, provided he does not blame and does not despair. He alone, his sins burnt by that vijñāna-tapas, wins the supreme world—he who knows thus. Likewise the one about to die forms this resolve at the very outset. What? ‘etad vai paramaṁ tapaḥ’—that I, when departed, shall be borne by the ṛtviks from the village to the forest for the final rite; on account of the common feature of going from village to forest, that shall be supreme tapas for me; for going from village to forest is well known as supreme tapas. He wins the supreme world, who knows thus. Likewise: ‘etad vai paramaṁ tapaḥ’—that one departed is placed upon the fire, on account of the common feature of entering fire. He wins the supreme world, who knows thus.
BR_C05_S12_V01::block-0: Some say food is Brahman; that is not so, for food rots without prāṇa. Some say prāṇa is Brahman; that is not so, for prāṇa dries up without food. These two divinities, having become unified, attain supremacy. Hence Prātṛda once said to his father: ‘What good can I do for one who knows thus, what evil can I do?’ The father said, holding him back with his hand: ‘Not so, Prātṛda; who indeed attains supremacy by becoming the unity of these two?’ He then said this to him: ‘vi’—food is vi, for in food are all these beings established (viṣṭāni); ‘ram’—prāṇa is ram, for in prāṇa all these beings rejoice (ramante). All beings indeed enter into him, and all beings rejoice in him, who knows thus.
BR_C05_S12_V01::block-1: Bhāṣya: ‘annaṁ brahma’—wishing to enjoin yet another upāsanā, he says: food is Brahman—‘that which is eaten is Brahman’—so some teachers say; but it should not be taken thus that food is Brahman. Others say: prāṇa is Brahman; that too should not be so taken. Why then should ‘food is Brahman’ not be accepted? Because food rots, gets soaked, comes to a putrid condition, in the absence of prāṇa; how can it then deserve to be Brahman? For Brahman is that which is imperishable. Then let prāṇa be Brahman; not so; because prāṇa indeed dries up, undergoes desiccation, without food; for prāṇa is the eater, hence it cannot sustain itself without food, the eatable; therefore prāṇa indeed dries up without food. Hence Brahmanhood does not stand for either separately; therefore these two divinities, food and prāṇa, having attained ekadhābhāva—the state of unity—reach supremacy, that is, attain Brahmanhood. Determining thus, Prātṛda by name once said to his own father: ‘kiṁsvit’—‘svit’ is in the sense of conjecture; ‘as I have conceived Brahman, what good service might I render to one who knows thus, what worship—what worship indeed could I offer him?’—this is the import; ‘what evil could I render to such a knower?’—he is one whose duty is fully accomplished, this is the implication. The knower of food and prāṇa as conjoined Brahman is neither cut down by ill-treatment nor magnified by good treatment. To him speaking thus the father said, restraining him with his hand: ‘mā prātṛda—do not say so. Who indeed attains supremacy by becoming the unity of these two, food and prāṇa? No knower whatsoever attains supremacy by this view of Brahman; therefore you must not say that he is one whose duty is accomplished. If so, may your honour please tell how one attains supremacy.’ To him he said this teaching about to be uttered. What? ‘vi iti’; what is that ‘vi’? It is said—‘food indeed is vi’; for in food, since these all beings are viṣṭāni, taken refuge, hence food is called vi. And ‘ram iti’; the father also uttered ‘ram’; what again is that ‘ram’? Prāṇa indeed is ram; whence? It is said: in prāṇa, since when there is the support of strength, all beings rejoice (ramante), hence prāṇa is ram. Food has the property of being the refuge of all beings, and prāṇa has the property of being the delight of all beings. For no one who is without abode and without refuge rejoices; nor, even when there is an abode, does one without prāṇa, the weak one, rejoice; but when one is provided with abode and is endowed with prāṇa and strength, then, considering himself fulfilled, the world rejoices—as per the śruti ‘yuvā syāt sādhuyuvādhyāyakaḥ’ (Tai. U. 2.8.3) and the like. Now he states the fruit for one who knows thus: all beings indeed enter into him, by the knowledge of the property of food; all beings rejoice in him, by the knowledge of the property of prāṇa—he who knows thus.
BR_C05_S13_V01::block-0: ‘Uktha—prāṇa indeed is the uktha; for prāṇa raises up all this. From him the knower of the uktha gets a hero who rises up. He wins union and co-residence with the uktha—he who knows thus.’
BR_C05_S13_V01::block-1: Bhāṣya: ‘ukthaṁ’—similarly another upāsanā. The uktha is the śastra (chant); for it is the principal element in the mahāvrata sacrifice. What again is that uktha? ‘prāṇo vai uktham’—prāṇa is the uktha; and prāṇa is the chief among the senses, and the uktha is the chief among the śastras—therefore one should meditate ‘uktha’ on prāṇa. How is prāṇa the uktha? It is said: because prāṇa raises up all this; from raising up (utthāpana), prāṇa is uktha; for nothing without prāṇa rises up. He states the fruit of this upāsanā: ‘ut’—from him, this knower, there rises a knower of the uktha, that is, a knower of prāṇa, a hero, namely a son—this seen fruit is meant. The unseen fruit is sāyujya and salokatā with the uktha—this he wins, who knows thus.
BR_C05_S13_V02::block-0: ‘Yajus—prāṇa indeed is the yajus; for in prāṇa all these beings are joined together. All beings are joined to him for supremacy. He wins union and co-residence with the yajus—he who knows thus.’
BR_C05_S13_V02::block-1: Bhāṣya: One should meditate on prāṇa as ‘yajus’; prāṇa indeed is the yajus. How is prāṇa the yajus? Because in prāṇa all beings are joined together; for in the absence of prāṇa there is no power of conjunction in anyone with anything; hence, since it joins (yunakti), prāṇa is yajus. He states the fruit of one who knows thus: ‘yujyante’—they exert themselves, this is the meaning; for him, the knower; all beings; for śraiṣṭhya, supremacy—‘may this one be our chief’; sāyujya with the yajus, that is prāṇa, and the rest is all the same as before.
BR_C05_S13_V03::block-0: ‘Sāman—prāṇa indeed is the sāman; for in prāṇa all these beings come together harmoniously. All beings indeed come together harmoniously for him for supremacy. He wins union and co-residence with the sāman—he who knows thus.’
BR_C05_S13_V03::block-1: Bhāṣya: One should meditate on prāṇa as ‘sāman’. ‘prāṇo vai sāma’; how is prāṇa the sāman? Because in prāṇa all beings ‘samyañci saṅgacchante’—come together harmoniously; through being the cause of saṅgamana (coming together) and the attainment of equality (sāmya), prāṇa is sāman. ‘samyañci saṅgacchante ha asmai’—come together harmoniously for him, for the knower, all beings; not only do they come together, but for śraiṣṭhya also, the state of supremacy, they become competent for him. ‘sāmnaḥ sāyujyam’ etc., as before.
BR_C05_S13_V04::block-0: ‘Kṣatra—prāṇa indeed is the kṣatra; for prāṇa is verily the kṣatra. Prāṇa protects this body from being injured. He attains the kṣatra that has no other protector; he wins union and co-residence with the kṣatra—he who knows thus.’
BR_C05_S13_V04::block-1: Bhāṣya: One should meditate on that prāṇa as ‘kṣatra’. ‘prāṇo vai kṣatram’; this is well known—‘prāṇo hi vai kṣatram’. How is it well known? It is said: prāṇa protects, that is, guards this piṇḍa, the body; ‘kṣaṇitoḥ’—from being wounded by weapons and the like, since it again fills it up with flesh; therefore by the protection from injury (kṣata-trāṇa) the kṣatra-hood of prāṇa is well known. He states the fruit for the knower: ‘pra kṣatram atram’—‘atram’ means that which is not protected by anything else; the kṣatra is prāṇa; he attains that ‘atra’ kṣatra, prāṇa—this is the meaning. Or, by the reading in another recension, ‘kṣatra-mātra’—he attains the very state of kṣatra, that is, becomes prāṇa, this is the meaning. ‘kṣatrasya sāyujyaṁ salokatāṁ jayati, ya evaṁ veda’—he wins union and co-residence with the kṣatra, he who knows thus.
BR_C05_S14_V01::block-0: The upāsanā of Brahman as conditioned by the heart and other manifold upādhis has been taught; now, accordingly, the upāsanā of Brahman as conditioned by the upādhi of the gāyatrī is to be set forth, and so the section is begun. Among all the metres, indeed, the gāyatrī-metre is principal; the very text will say further on that it is called gāyatrī because it protects (trāṇa) the prāṇas of the gayas, that is, of the singers who employ it; and no other metre has this capacity to protect the prāṇas of the singers. Moreover, she is of the very nature of prāṇa, and prāṇa is the Self of all the metres; and prāṇa, as it has been said, is kṣatra, since it protects from injury (kṣatatrāṇa); and prāṇa is gāyatrī. Therefore the upāsanā of just this is intended to be enjoined. Furthermore, since she is the cause of the second birth of the foremost of the twice-born — for the text 'By the gāyatrī he created the brāhmaṇa, by the triṣṭubh the rājanya, by the jagatī the vaiśya' (?) shows that the second birth of the foremost twice-born is occasioned by the gāyatrī — therefore the gāyatrī is principal. The śruti shows the connection of the brāhmaṇa with the highest puruṣārtha in such passages as 'Having transcended through Brahman, the brāhmaṇas speak; that brāhmaṇa becomes free from sin, free from rajas, free from doubt' (Bṛ. U. 3.5.1; 3.8.8; 3.8.10; 4.4.23); and that brāhmaṇa-hood is rooted in the birth from the gāyatrī. Hence the true nature (sva-tattva) of the gāyatrī must be expounded. For he who is born of the gāyatrī, the foremost of the twice-born, is, without restriction, qualified for the means to the highest puruṣārtha; therefore the connection with the supreme puruṣārtha is rooted in her. So, in order to enjoin her upāsanā, the text says: 'bhūmi, antarikṣa, dyau' — these are eight syllables; that of which the syllables are eight, that is aṣṭākṣaram, this collection of eight syllables. The particles 'ha vai' indicate something well-known. 'Ekam' means 'the first'; 'gāyatryai' means 'of the gāyatrī'; 'padam' means 'foot'. The eight is filled out simply by the consonant 'y'. 'Etadu ha eva' — this very thing is the first foot of this gāyatrī, of the form of bhūmi etc., having the three worlds as its self, on account of the common feature of being eight-syllabled. Thus, of him who knows this triple-world-formed first foot of the gāyatrī, this is the fruit: that knower conquers all that is to be conquered in these three worlds — he who knows this foot of hers in this manner.
BR_C05_S14_V02::block-0: Likewise, 'ṛcaḥ, yajūṃṣi, sāmāni' — the syllables of these names of the trayī-vidyā too are just eight; in the same way, eight syllables, indeed, constitute a single second foot of the gāyatrī. 'Etadu ha eva asya' — this very second foot of hers, characterised by ṛk, yajus and sāman, is constituted by them, simply on the strength of the common feature of being eight-syllabled. He, the worshipper, conquers as much as is the fruit-aggregate that is attained through the trayī-vidyā — that much he conquers, who knows this foot of hers, characterised by the three Vedas, in this manner.
BR_C05_S14_V03::block-0: Likewise, 'prāṇa, apāna, vyāna' — these too, the syllables of the names prāṇa and the rest, are eight; and that is the third foot of the gāyatrī. As much as is this aggregate of breathing creatures, that much he conquers — he who knows this third foot of the gāyatrī in this manner. Now, after that, the fourth foot of the three-footed gāyatrī, which is of the nature of word (śabdātmikā), is spoken of as that which is the meaning denoted (abhidheya): of this gāyatrī under discussion, this very thing — about to be stated — is the turīya, the visible foot, parorajas, the one yonder who shines; that is, the puruṣa within the solar disk. The śruti herself glosses the meaning of the words 'turīya' and the rest: 'yat vai caturtham' — what is well-known in the world as the fourth, that is here designated by the word turīya. As to what is meant by 'darśata padam' it says — 'dadṛśe iva' — for this puruṣa within the disk is, as it were, seen; hence he is called the visible foot. As to the meaning of the word 'parorajas' it says — 'sarvam' — the whole — 'u hi eva eṣa' — verily this puruṣa stationed in the disk — 'rajaḥ' — the entire mass that has arisen as rajas, the entire world, that is — he heats up from above and above (uparyupari), in the manner of overlordship — he heats the whole world, the entire dust-realm. The repetition 'uparyupari' is for the purpose of declaring overlordship over all the worlds; if it be objected that, since the word 'sarva' alone suffices, the repetition is purposeless — this is no defect; for the word 'sarva' might apply only to the worlds above which the savitṛ is seen, and the repetition is meant to remove that doubt, on the strength of the other śruti, 'and over those worlds yonder beyond him he has lordship, and over the desires of the gods' (Chā. U. 1.6.8); therefore the repetition is meant to comprehend all without exception. Just as that savitṛ heats with śrī characterised by overlordship over all and with yaśas — fame — even so does he heat with śrī and yaśas, who knows in this manner this turīya, this darśata foot of hers.
BR_C05_S14_V04::block-0: 'Saiṣā' — that very three-footed gāyatrī which has been described, characterised by the three worlds, the trayī-vidyā and prāṇa, is established in this fourth, the turīya, in the visible foot beyond rajas, since this is the rasa, the essence, of the embodied (mūrta) and the unembodied (amūrta), of the savitṛ. For when the rasa departs, a thing becomes sapless and unestablished — like a piece of wood whose pith has been burnt; just so the world consisting of mūrta and amūrta, which is the three-footed gāyatrī, is established in the savitṛ, since he is its rasa, together with all three feet. That fourth foot is established in satya. What is that satya? — 'cakṣur vai satyam'. How is the eye satya? — this is well-known: 'cakṣur hi vai satyam'. How well-known? — 'tasmāt': because if right now two persons came forward in dispute, speaking against each other, one saying 'I saw it' and the other saying 'I heard it — the thing is not as you saw it' — of these two, him who says 'I saw it' should we believe; not him who says 'I heard it'. For false hearing is possible for the hearer; but false seeing is not possible for the eye; therefore we should not give credence to the one who says 'I heard'. Hence, since the eye is the cause of the apprehension of truth, the eye is satya. In that satya, the eye, the turīya foot is established together with the three other feet — that is the meaning. And it has been said elsewhere: 'In what is that āditya established? — In the eye' (Bṛ. U. 3.9.20). That satya, which is the support of the turīya foot, is established in bala — strength. What is that bala? — 'prāṇo vai balam'; in that bala, prāṇa, satya is established. So too it has been said: 'In the sūtra all that is woven warp and woof' (Bṛ. U. 3.7.2). Since satya is established in bala, therefore they say: 'bala is more potent (ojīyas) than satya' — that is, more vigorous; in the world too it is well-known that whatever has another for its support, the support is stronger than what is supported on it; for nowhere is the weak seen to be the support of the strong. By this very reasoning, this gāyatrī is established adhyātmam — within the body, in the prāṇa within. This very gāyatrī is prāṇa; hence in the gāyatrī the world is established, since in prāṇa all the gods, all the Vedas, the karmas and their fruit become one. This very gāyatrī, being of the nature of prāṇa, is the Self of the world. 'Sā ha eṣā gayāṃs tatre' — she protected the gayas. Who, then, are the gayas? The prāṇas, vāk and the rest, are gayas, since they produce sound (śabda-karaṇāt); these she — this gāyatrī — protected. Because she protected the gayas, therefore she is named gāyatrī; she is renowned as gāyatrī because of the protection (trāṇa) of the gayas. The ācārya, in the upanayana of the eight-year-old boy, recites unto him this very gāyatrī known as the sāvitrī, whose deity is the savitṛ — foot by foot, half-verse by half-verse, and entire; this very direct prāṇa, the Self of the world, has been delivered to the boy and explained here and now, no other. That ācārya, to whichever boy he recites — anuvakti — protects (trāyate) the gayas, the prāṇas, of that boy from falling into hells and so forth.
BR_C05_S14_V05::block-0: 'Tāmetām' — that very sāvitrī, certain śākhins recite (anvāhuḥ) to the initiate as anuṣṭubh — having anuṣṭubh as its source, in the anuṣṭubh metre. Their intention the text states: vāk is anuṣṭubh, and vāk in the body is sarasvatī; we recite that very vāk, sarasvatī, to the boy — saying thus. 'Na tathā kuryāt' — one should not act so, one should not so understand; what they say is merely false. What then? — one should recite the gāyatrī alone as sāvitrī. Why? Because it has been said that prāṇa is the gāyatrī; when prāṇa is taught, vāk and sarasvatī and the other prāṇas — all become offered to the boy. Now, having said this incidentally, the text praises the knower of the gāyatrī: even if such a knower receives, as it were, much in pratigraha — for, of him whose Self is everything, there is in truth nothing called 'much', because the knower has the nature of all — even so, that aggregate of pratigraha is not equal even to one foot of the gāyatrī.
BR_C05_S14_V06::block-0: 'Sa ya imāṃs trīn' — he who, knowing the gāyatrī, should accept these three worlds — bhūr and the rest — full of the wealth of cows, horses and so on — that pratigraha would gain only this, the first foot of the gāyatrī as expounded; that is, the fruit of the knowledge of the first foot would be enjoyed thereby; that pratigraha would not be a producer of further evil. Then again, he who would accept as much as is this trayī-vidyā, would gain this second foot of hers; the fruit of the knowledge of the second foot would be enjoyed thereby. Likewise, he who would accept as much as is this aggregate of breathing creatures, would gain this third foot of hers; the fruit of the knowledge of the third foot would be enjoyed thereby. This is said by way of supposition (kalpanā): if anyone were to receive even an amount equal to all three feet, that would only suffice to wear out the fruit of the knowledge of those three feet, and would not be capable of producing any further fault; but no such giver or receiver actually exists — this is set up only for the praise of the knowledge of gāyatrī. Even if such a giver and receiver were imagined possible, that pratigraha would not be free from offence. Why? Because there yet remains, beyond all that, the supreme puruṣārtha — knowledge — which has the fourth foot of the gāyatrī as its object. The text shows this — 'atha asyāḥ etadeva turīyaṃ darśataṃ padaṃ parorajāḥ ya eṣa tapati'; this is in no way attainable by any receiving — that is, just as the previous three feet were attainable by their corresponding pratigrahas, so this fourth is not attainable by any pratigraha at all. Even that statement was made by way of supposition; in truth (paramārthataḥ), how could one receive such an amount, equal to the three worlds and the rest? Therefore the gāyatrī is to be worshipped in this manner — that is the import.
BR_C05_S14_V07::block-0: 'Tasyā upasthānam' — the upasthāna, the approach with reverence, the act of bowing (namaskaraṇa) to that gāyatrī, by means of this mantra. What, then, is that mantra? — 'O gāyatrī, thou art ekapadī by the foot consisting of the three worlds, dvipadī by the second consisting of the trayī-vidyā, tripadī by the third consisting of prāṇa and the rest, and catuṣpadī by the fourth, the turīya. Thus by the four feet thou art known (padyase) by the upāsakas; but beyond that, in thy own supreme self that is unconditioned (nirupādhika), thou art apad — thou whose foot, by which thou couldst be reached, does not exist; thou art that footless one, since thou art not reached, on account of having the nature of the Self that is neti-neti. Therefore, for the sphere of vyavahāra, salutation to thee, the turīya, the visible (darśata) foot, parorajas! That enemy of mine, the sin yonder, the obstructor of the attainment of thee — let that yonder, that act of his, the obstruction of the attainment of thee, never reach me — let it not reach (mā prāpat). The word iti is for the conclusion of the mantra. Whomsoever the knower himself should hate, towards him the upasthāna is performed thus — naming that enemy as 'so-and-so'. 'Asmai' — to this Yajñadatta, may the desire he has fixed upon never become accomplished — thus does he stand in upāsana; and that desire of his, of Devadatta, will not become accomplished. To whom? — to him for whom he so stands. Or 'I will gain that' — what Devadatta has set his mind on — thus he stands. 'Asau ado mā prāpat' and the like three mantra-portions are to be optionally chosen according to one's desire.
BR_C05_S14_V08::block-0: An arthavāda is now spoken to enjoin the mukha — the mouth — of the gāyatrī. 'Etat ha vai' — this is, indeed, recounted in the tradition: in that matter of the knowledge of gāyatrī, Janaka the Vaideha said to one Buḍila by name, the son of Aśvatarāśva, hence Āśvatarāśvi. 'Yat nu' — 'nu' indicates conjecture, 'ho' means 'aho!' — 'that which thou saidst, 'I am a knower of the gāyatrī' — how unbecoming of such an utterance is this!' Then how? If thou art a knower of the gāyatrī, why dost thou go about, by the fault of pratigraha, in the form of an elephant, bearing burdens? He, reminded by the king, replies — 'Mukhaṃ hi asyāḥ' — 'Because of her, the gāyatrī, O Samrāṭ, I did not know the mukha — I have not understood the mouth — thus he said'; due to the want of one limb, my knowledge of the gāyatrī has become fruitless.
BR_C05_S14_V08::block-1: Hear, then. Of that gāyatrī, agni alone is the mukha. Just as, even when ordinary people, the laukikas, place much fuel as it were upon the fire, the fire burns up all that fuel — even so the knower of this — that is, one who knows that agni is the mukha of the gāyatrī, becoming himself of the very nature of gāyatrī with agni for mouth — even though he commits, as it were, much sin, that of pratigraha and the like, having consumed (sampsāya — having eaten up) all that aggregate of sin, he becomes pure (śuddha) like agni, purified (pūta) from that fault of pratigraha, of the very nature of gāyatrī, ageless (ajara) and immortal (amṛta).
BR_C05_S15_V01::block-0: He who practises the combination of knowledge and action (jñāna-karma-samuccaya) prays to Āditya at the time of death; and there is a reason for this; for that very deity is the fourth foot of the Gāyatrī, the upāsanā of which has been the running topic; therefore that very Lord is here invoked. 'By a hiraṇmaya — that is, luminous — vessel': just as some desired object is covered by a vessel, so this Brahman, called Satya, appears as though concealed by the luminous orb, since it is invisible to those whose minds are not collected (asamāhita-cetas). And this is what the mantra states — 'satyasya apihitaṃ mukham', the principal (mukhya) form of Satya is veiled; that veiling, like the lid of a vessel, is the cause obstructing vision. 'That do thou', O Pūṣan — who, because of nourishing the world, is Pūṣā, namely Savitṛ — 'apāvṛṇu', uncover; that is, remove the cause obstructing vision. 'Satyadharmāya' — for one whose dharma is satya, that is, for me whose nature is truth, meaning for him who is none other than thy very Self; 'dṛṣṭaye', for the sake of seeing. The names beginning with 'Pūṣan' are vocatives addressed to Savitṛ. 'Ekarṣe' — he is the one (eka) and the seer (ṛṣi), hence Ekarṣi; called ṛṣi because of seeing; for he, being the Self and the eye of the entire world, sees everything; or, because he alone (eka) goes, he is Ekarṣi, as the mantra-word declares: 'Sūrya alone moves' (Tai. Saṁ. 8.4.18). 'Yama' — for all controlling (saṁyamana) of the world is wrought by thee. 'Sūrya' — because thou rightly impellest (su-īrayate) the juices, the rays, the vital airs (prāṇa) and the intellects of the world. 'Prājāpatya' — son of Prajāpati, the Lord, or of Hiraṇyagarbha; O Prājāpatya. 'Vyūha', disperse, scatter the rays; 'samūha', withdraw and contract thine own tejas, by which I may be able to behold thee; for, with vision overpowered by tejas, I should be unable to see thy true form clearly, as one is unable to see forms in the presence of dazzling lightning; therefore withdraw thy tejas. 'That form of thine which is the most auspicious (kalyāṇatama) of all auspicious things — that of thine I behold' — 'paśyāmi' is used for 'paśyāmaḥ' by interchange of person.
BR_C05_S15_V01::block-1: 'That puruṣa who dwells there' — namely the puruṣa who is the constituent of the Vyāhṛti bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ, called puruṣa because of his puruṣa-form — 'that very one I am, I become'; and since the Upaniṣad has declared 'I am he' (aham aham) as referring to the puruṣa in the eye and the puruṣa in the sun, that very identity is here recalled. 'So'haṃ asmi' is to be construed with 'amṛtam' — 'I am he, the immortal'. The connection is: when the body of me, the immortal, the truthful, falls, may the prāṇa, the vāyu, that is in the body return to anila, the outer wind itself; likewise let the other deities go each to its own source (prakṛti); and let this body, ending in ashes, return to the earth. Now, at this very moment, he prays to the deity Agni, who is established in the mind as the saṅkalpa-form of the Self — 'Oṃ krato'. 'Oṃ' and 'krato' are both vocatives; 'Oṃ' because Agni is symbolised by the praṇava (oṅkāra-pratīka); 'kratu' because he is mind-formed (manomaya). 'O Oṃ, O Krato, smara — remember what is to be remembered'; for at the time of death the desired course is attained through remembrance of thee; therefore the prayer — 'remember what has been done by me'. The repetition is for the sake of emphasis (ādara). Further, 'O Agni, lead us, conduct us, by the auspicious path (supatha) — to wealth (rāye), that is, for attaining the fruit of action; not by the southern, dark path which entails return (punarāvṛtti), but rather by the bright (śukla) supatha. 'Knowing all the cognitions, all the activities of all beings, O deva' — viśvāni vayunāni vidvān. Further, 'yuyodhi' — drive away, dissociate from us, the crooked (juhurāṇa) sin, all the mass of pāpa; freed from that pāpa, by thy grace we shall pass on by the northern path; but we are unable to render service to thee — therefore 'most abundant (bhūyiṣṭha)…' [The text continues.]
BR_C06_S01_V01::block-0: Oṃ. It has been said that prāṇa is the Gāyatrī. For what reason, then, is prāṇa the form of Gāyatrī, and not vāk and the other organs? — because prāṇa is the eldest (jyeṣṭha) and the best (śreṣṭha), while vāk and the rest do not possess the qualities of seniority and excellence. The present section is begun in the wish to ascertain how prāṇa is jyeṣṭha and śreṣṭha. Or else: under the forms of uktha, yajus, sāman, kṣatra, etc., the upāsanā of prāṇa alone has been previously enjoined, even though there are also cakṣus and other organs; here only the reason for that is connected by way of sequence (ānantarya); it is not a continuation of what was said before. The intention is — since this kāṇḍa is supplementary (khila), whatever distinct fruit-yielding upāsanā regarding prāṇa was not stated earlier must be stated here.
BR_C06_S01_V01::block-1: 'Yaḥ' — whoever; 'ha vai' — these two are for emphasis (avadhāraṇa); whoever knows prāṇa as endowed with the qualities of jyeṣṭha and śreṣṭha that are about to be expounded — he indeed becomes jyeṣṭha and śreṣṭha. Thus enticed by the fruit, he becomes ready to question. To him the text replies — 'prāṇo vai jyeṣṭhaś ca śreṣṭhaś ca'. But how is it known that prāṇa is the eldest and the best, when at the time of impregnation (niṣeka-kāla) the seminal–menstrual conjunction is undifferentiated as regards the whole group of prāṇa and the rest? Even so, since the semen does not develop without prāṇa, prāṇa is the first to obtain functioning, before cakṣus and the others; therefore prāṇa is jyeṣṭha — the eldest in age (vayasā). From the time of impregnation prāṇa nourishes the embryo; only after prāṇa has obtained its functioning do cakṣus and the rest obtain theirs; therefore it is fitting that prāṇa be senior to cakṣus and the others. There is sometimes one who is the eldest in a family but, being deficient in qualities, is not the best; while a middle or youngest one, rich in qualities, may be the best though not the eldest; but it is not so here, the text declares — prāṇa alone is both jyeṣṭha and śreṣṭha. How then is the excellence (śraiṣṭhya) of prāṇa known? — that we shall show here through the dialogue (saṃvāda) that follows.
BR_C06_S01_V01::block-2: In every way, then, he who knows, that is, meditates upon, prāṇa as endowed with the qualities of jyeṣṭha and śreṣṭha, becomes the eldest and the best among his own kin (jñāti), through the power of the upāsanā of jyeṣṭha-śreṣṭha qualities. Even apart from his own kin, among those amid whom he wishes to become jyeṣṭha and śreṣṭha — 'bubhūṣati', desires to become — among them too the meditator on prāṇa as jyeṣṭha and śreṣṭha becomes jyeṣṭha and śreṣṭha. Objection (pūrvapakṣa): seniority is occasioned by age (vayas); how can it accrue from mere wish? Reply (siddhānta): no fault here, for what is intended by jyeṣṭhatva is the priority in obtaining functioning (vṛtti-lābha), as in the case of prāṇa itself.
BR_C06_S01_V02::block-0: 'He who knows vasiṣṭhā becomes vasiṣṭha among his own.' The fruit corresponds to the upāsanā. And among those, apart from his kin, amid whom he desires to become vasiṣṭha, he too becomes vasiṣṭha. Let it be said, then, who is this vasiṣṭhā? Vāk indeed is vasiṣṭhā. She is called vasiṣṭhā either because she causes one to dwell most abundantly (vāsayati atiśayena) or because she dwells most abundantly (vaste atiśayena); for those skilled in speech (vāgmin), being wealthy, dwell with abundance. Or, taking the root vas in the sense of covering (ācchādana), vasiṣṭhā is so called because the eloquent overpower (abhibhavanti) others by speech. Hence, by knowing vāk as endowed with the quality of vasiṣṭhā, one becomes endowed with the quality of vasiṣṭha — the fruit corresponding to the upāsanā.
BR_C06_S01_V03::block-0: 'He who knows pratiṣṭhā' — 'pratitiṣṭhati anayā' — that by which one stands firm is pratiṣṭhā; he who knows that pratiṣṭhā as endowed with the quality of pratiṣṭhā, his fruit is this — he stands firm in even (sama) place and time, and also in difficult (durga) terrain or hard times like famine. If so, let it be told who is this pratiṣṭhā: 'cakṣur vai pratiṣṭhā', the eye indeed is pratiṣṭhā. How is the eye pratiṣṭhā? — 'cakṣuṣā hi same ca durge ca' — having seen with the eye, one stands firm in the even and in the rough. Hence the corresponding fruit — 'he stands firm on level ground, he stands firm in rough places, he who knows thus.'
BR_C06_S01_V04::block-0: 'He who knows sampad' — he who knows that which is endowed with the quality of sampad; his fruit is this — to such a knower it is fully attained (sampadyate); what? — whatever desire (kāma) he longs for. But what is endowed with the quality of sampad? 'Śrotraṃ vai sampat' — the ear indeed is sampad. How is the ear endowed with the quality of sampad? — because, when the ear exists, all the Vedas are fully obtained (abhisampanna), since one who possesses the organ of hearing is qualified for adhyayana; and the kāmas are dependent on the actions enjoined by the Vedas; therefore the ear is sampad. Hence the fruit corresponds to the knowledge — to him is fully attained whatever desire he longs for, who knows thus.
BR_C06_S01_V05::block-0: 'He who knows āyatana' — 'āyatana' means support (āśraya); he who knows that becomes the support of his own kin, and the support of other people too. But what then is that āyatana? 'Mano vai āyatana' — the mind is the āyatana, the support of the senses (indriya) and of objects (viṣaya); for, taking refuge in the mind, objects come to be the bhogya of the Self; and the indriyas, depending on the saṅkalpa of the mind, engage (pravṛtti) and disengage (nivṛtti); hence the mind is the āyatana of the indriyas. Therefore the fruit corresponds to the upāsanā — he becomes the āyatana of his own and of other people, who knows thus.
BR_C06_S01_V06::block-0: 'He who knows prajāti' — he is born forth (prajāyate), is endowed with progeny (prajā) and cattle (paśu). 'Reto vai prajātiḥ' — semen indeed is prajāti; by 'retas' the prajanana-organ is indicated by lakṣaṇā. The fruit corresponds to that knowledge — he is born forth, with progeny and cattle, who knows thus.
BR_C06_S01_V07::block-0: 'These prāṇas' — vāk and the rest — quarrelling (vivadamānāḥ), that is, speaking contradictorily, for the sake of (deciding) 'I am the better' (ahaṃ-śreyas), went to Brahman — went to Prajāpati, who is denoted by the word 'brahman'; and having gone, they spoke to that Brahman: 'Who among us is vasiṣṭha — who among us dwells (vasati) and causes others to dwell (vāsayati)?' Being thus questioned, that Brahman replied — 'He, on whose departure (utkrānte) from the body this body is regarded as worse (pāpīyas) than before — he among you is vasiṣṭha.'
BR_C06_S01_V07::block-1: Indeed the body itself, being a conglomerate of many impurities (aśuci-saṅghāta), is itself pāpa even while alive; that, on whose departure, becomes still more grievous than that — this is said for the purpose of vairāgya, calling it 'pāpīyas'. He who is such — he among you shall be the vasiṣṭha. Though Prajāpati knew the vasiṣṭha, he did not say 'this one is the vasiṣṭha', in order to avoid causing displeasure to the others (apriya-parihāra).
BR_C06_S01_V08::block-0: Thus addressed by Brahman, the prāṇas (vital faculties), in order to test their own potency relative to the Self, departed in succession. Among them, speech (vāk) was the first to depart from this body. Having departed and dwelt away for a year, it returned and said: "How were you able to live without me?" To this question they replied: "As in the world the dumb who cannot speak with speech, yet performing the function of breathing with prāṇa, performing the function of seeing with the eye, similarly hearing with the ear, knowing with the mind objects such as what ought and ought not to be done, generating progeny with semen — even thus did we live." Speech, having received this answer from the prāṇas and having understood that the Self does not abide in itself alone, then re-entered.
BR_C06_S01_V09::block-0: The eye departed; having dwelt away for a year, it returned and said: "How were you able to live without me?" They replied: "As the blind, not seeing with the eye, yet breathing with prāṇa, speaking with speech, hearing with the ear, knowing with the mind, generating progeny with semen — even thus did we live." Then the eye re-entered.
BR_C06_S01_V10::block-0: The ear departed; having dwelt away for a year, it returned and said: "How were you able to live without me?" They replied: "As the deaf, not hearing with the ear, yet breathing with prāṇa, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, knowing with the mind, generating progeny with semen — even thus did we live." Then the ear re-entered.
BR_C06_S01_V11::block-0: The mind departed; having dwelt away for a year, it returned and said: "How were you able to live without me?" They replied: "As the witless, not knowing with the mind, yet breathing with prāṇa, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, generating progeny with semen — even thus did we live." Then the mind re-entered.
BR_C06_S01_V12::block-0: Likewise, "the eye departed" and the rest, as before. The ear, the mind, and the procreative power (prajāti) — these too are to be understood after the same pattern.
BR_C06_S01_V13::block-0: Now when prāṇa was about to depart — that is, was preparing to make its exit — at that very moment speech and the others were dislodged from their stations. To illustrate with what? The text says: as in the world a great and excellent steed (mahāsuhaya) — "great" by reason of stature, "excellent steed" being a horse endowed with the requisite signs of breed, "saindhava" because born in the Sindhu country and thus of noble pedigree — would, when its rider has mounted to test it, simultaneously uproot the tethering pegs (paḍvīśa-śaṅku, the stakes to which its feet are bound), wrenching them all out at once; even thus did prāṇa uproot these vital faculties beginning with speech and dislodge them from their stations.
BR_C06_S01_V13::block-1: These speech and the rest then said: "O Bhagavan, do not depart; for verily we shall not be able to live without you." The implication: if our preeminence has thus been recognized by you — "I am the foremost here" — then render unto me, that very one, your tribute (bali, tax). This dialogue of the prāṇas is contrived: it is an instruction in the method by which the wise man examines preeminence. For by this very method does the knowing one (vidvān) carry on the inquiry, "Who indeed here is foremost?" That mode of examination is set forth in the form of a dialogue. Otherwise, with these faculties acting in cooperation as a single aggregate (saṃhatya-kāriṇām), it could not literally be the case that each in turn departs for the duration of merely one year. Therefore it is the wise man alone who, desiring to know which among speech and the rest is principal (pradhāna) for the sake of upāsanā, conducts the inquiry by this method. The prāṇas, when thus solicited for tribute, gave their assent: "So be it."
BR_C06_S01_V14::block-0: Speech, being the first to come forward to render the tribute, said: "Whatever excellence (vasiṣṭhatva) is mine, that very excellence is yours; by virtue of that quality of being most excellent, you are vasiṣṭha." Likewise the eye said: "Whatever firm support (pratiṣṭhā) is mine, that you are." The ear surrendered the quality of being attainment (sampad). The mind surrendered the quality of being abode (āyatana). Semen surrendered the quality of being procreation (prajāti). Each in turn presented his characteristic excellence. Then prāṇa said: "If so, you have rendered the tribute well; now tell me — for me, possessed of these qualities, what is the food and what is the garment?" The others answered: "Whatever food there is in the world, down to that of dogs, worms, and insects and moths — namely the food of dogs, of worms, of insects and moths — together with all that is eaten by living beings whatsoever, all that is your food." The intent here is to enjoin the vision (dṛṣṭi) that all is the food of prāṇa.
BR_C06_S01_V14::block-1: Some, however — those who hold themselves to be knowers of prāṇa-as-food — assert that there is no fault in eating anything whatsoever. That is unsound, because such consumption stands prohibited by other scripture. If it be urged that there is here an option (vikalpa) on that account — no, because this passage is not enjoining (avidhāyaka). The clause "verily for him there is nothing eaten that is not food" is by way of eulogy (stuti) of the enjoined cognition that all is the food of prāṇa; for thereby the unity of import (ekavākyatā) is secured. It has no power to set aside what is enjoined by other scripture, since this is given over to a different purport (anyaparatva). What is here intended is the vision that everything is food for prāṇa as such, not the injunction "let one eat everything." The pretended cognition that there is no fault in indiscriminate eating is mere falsity (mithyā), there being no pramāṇa for it. — If it be argued: since the wise one has become prāṇa, by very capacity all-foodness is established and hence there is no fault — no, for total all-foodness is not established. True, the wise man is prāṇa; but the wisdom belongs to him as conditioned by a particular bodily-sensory aggregate (kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta), and through that aggregate the eating of every kind of food — that of worms, insects, gods, and so on — is not feasible. Hence to declare absence of fault in eating all foods there is meaningless, since the fault of eating all foods is not, in his case, even arising. — "But becoming prāṇa he does eat the food of worms and insects too." Granted; yet there is no prohibition having that as object. Hence — "the dyer painting the kiṁśuka by divine hand" (i.e., a needless explanation): there absence of fault holds; therefore the declaration "absence of fault" in that mode is meaningless, the fault of eating all foods being not even prima facie operative there. But where the prohibition operates by relation to the bodily-sensory aggregate, by that relation there is no countermand (pratiprasava) here. Therefore in transgressing such prohibitions there would be fault alone, since "verily for him" and the rest has a different purport. Nor is the vision of all-foodness here being enjoined for the body of a brāhmaṇa and the like, but only for prāṇa as such. As, even though prāṇa be food in general for all, some particular item of food is the cause of life only for some particular being — as poison for the poison-born worm — that very item, though it is food for prāṇa in another, is seen to produce a fault in the form of death and the like — even so, though prāṇa be food for all, in eating prohibited food there will arise fault precisely on account of the body-relation as a brāhmaṇa and so forth. Therefore the cognition that there is no fault in eating the unfit-to-be-eaten is mere mithyājñāna (false cognition).
BR_C06_S01_V14::block-2: "Water is the garment" — water, when drunk, stands as garment to you. Here too the vision is enjoined that for prāṇa water is the garment; water cannot be employed in the function of an actual garment. Hence in the act of drinking water as it naturally occurs, only this vision (darśanamātra) is to be performed. "Verily for him no non-food is eaten" — for him who knows thus, that all is the food of prāṇa, no non-food, nothing not-to-be-eaten, is eaten as it were; even though he should have eaten the inedible, it is to be deemed as having eaten only the edible, and he is not tainted by the fault arising therein — this we have said is praise of the vidyā (vidyā-stuti). Likewise, "nor non-food is accepted" — even though he should have accepted what is not to be accepted, such as an elephant, that too is to be deemed as if only what is acceptable were accepted; even there he is not tainted by the fault of accepting the unacceptable. This is again purely for the sake of eulogy. "He who knows thus the food of this prāṇa" — but the result (phala) is precisely the state of being prāṇātman; this is not stated with intent of result (phala-abhipreta) but with intent of eulogy (stuty-abhipreta). — "But why is this itself not the result?" — No; for the seer of the prāṇa-Self the very state of being prāṇātman is the result; and there, for the all-self that has become prāṇātman, even the inedible is edible, and the unacceptable is acceptable — taking just what is naturally available, the vidyā is praised. Therefore the passage has not the form of an injunction with a result. Since water is the garment of prāṇa, therefore the wise brāhmaṇas, śrotriyas — those who have studied the Veda — when about to eat (aśiṣyantaḥ), sip water (āchamana); and after eating they sip water again. What is their intent in this sipping? The text answers: they think "we are clothing this prāṇa, this ana, making it not naked." And so it is in the world: he who gives a garment to another thinks "I make him not naked"; and water has been said to be the garment of prāṇa. The cognition to be performed is: "the water that I drink — that I give as garment to prāṇa" — for this purpose is the present injunction. — "But the one about to eat and the one who has eaten sips water thinking 'I shall be ritually pure (prayata)'; if its purpose were also the clothing of prāṇa, sipping would have a twofold function, and one act cannot have two functions; if it is for ritual purity, then not for clothing; if for clothing, then not for purity; therefore let there be a second separate sipping for the clothing of prāṇa." — No, for two distinct kriyās are quite possible. There are indeed two acts: the sipping enjoined by smṛti for one about to eat and one who has eaten serves the purpose of ritual purity, being a mere kriyā, and there ritual purity does not require any vision and the like. There the cognition of water as the garment of prāṇa is enjoined as the itikartavyatā (mode of accomplishing) operating upon the waters that are the limb of the sipping; in that being performed, the sipping's purpose of ritual purity is not set aside, since the sipping qua kriyā is distinct. Hence in the sipping of one about to eat and of one who has eaten, only the vision "water is the garment of prāṇa" is enjoined as a darśanamātra, since it is not obtainable from any other source.
BR_C06_S02_INTRO1::block-0: The connection (sambandha) is with "Śvetaketu ha vā Āruṇeya" and the rest. This is the supplementary section (khilādhikāra); here whatever has been left unsaid is now stated. At the close of the seventh adhyāya, by the one who practises the combination of jñāna and karma (jñāna-karma-samuccaya-kārin) a request was made to Agni for the path: "Agne, naya supathā" — "O Agni, lead by the good path." There the existence of multiple paths was indicated by the mantra through implication, by force of the qualifying word "supathā" (good path); for the paths are routes for the receiving of the matured fruits of action (kṛta-vipāka-pratipatti-mārga). It will also be said: "yat kṛtvā" (Bṛ. Up. 6.2.2) and so forth. Here the question — how many are the paths for the receiving of the fruit of karma — is taken up; the present beginning is for the sake of summing up the entire course of saṃsāra: such is the extent of the course of saṃsāra, such the maturation of action both spontaneous (svābhāvika) and scriptural (śāstrīya) accompanied by knowledge (sa-vijñāna). Although in "dvayā ha prājāpatyāḥ" (Bṛ. Up. 1.3.1) the spontaneous evil (svābhāvika pāpman) was indicated, its maturation — "this is its effect" — was not exhibited; only the maturation of the scriptural was shown, ending with the realization of the threefold-food Self (try-anna-ātma-pratipatti), since at the commencement of brahmavidyā the kindling of detachment (vairāgya) towards them was intended.
BR_C06_S02_INTRO1::block-1: There too it was said that by karma alone is reached the world of the fathers (pitṛloka), and by vidyā together with karma joined to vidyā is reached the world of the gods (devaloka). But by which path the world of the fathers is reached, and by which the world of the gods, was not stated. That, in the present supplementary section, must be stated without remainder; hence the present beginning. And at the end the summing up of the entire śāstra is intended. Further, it was said "this much is amṛtatva" (immortality), and "there is no hope of amṛtatva from karma"; the reason for this was not stated; the present beginning is for that purpose. Since such is the course of karma — there is no operation in eternal amṛtatva — therefore by force of implication this much alone is the means of amṛtatva, and the role of reason (hetu) is established. Moreover, in the agnihotra section it was said: "But of these two thou knowest neither the going forth, nor the path, nor the establishing, nor the satiation, nor the return, nor the world that arises in opposition." In the answer to that, by the passage "verily these two oblations, when offered, ascend" (Śat. Br. 11.6.2.4) and so on, the effect of the oblation was stated; and that effect is of the agent's offering-act (āhuti-lakṣaṇa karma) as fruit (phala); for not without dependence on the agent (kartṛ) can the going-forth and the rest, as the effect of the oblation-action, be undertaken on its own, since action's undertaking of effect has the agent for its purpose, and karma rests on its instrument. There, by way of eulogy of the agnihotra, the sixfold effect was stated as belonging to the agnihotra itself; here, however, that very same is taught in its sixfold form as the result of the agent (kartuḥ phala), the cognition of the fruit of karma being intended.
BR_C06_S02_INTRO1::block-2: Through that very gateway, the meditation on the five fires (pañcāgni-darśana) is here intended to be enjoined as the means of attaining the northern path (uttara-mārga-pratipatti-sādhana). Thus, the summing up of the entire course of saṃsāra (this is the consummation of the karma-kāṇḍa) — desirous to display these two together, the upaniṣad sets forth the narrative.
BR_C06_S02_V01::block-0: Śvetaketu, son of Āruṇi (the descendant of Aruṇa), being instructed by his father, came to the assembly of the Pañcālas to spread his own fame. He approached Pravāhaṇa, son of Jīvala, the king of the Pañcālas, who was being attended upon by his servants. The king, having previously heard of Śvetaketu's pride in his learning and judging that he should be humbled, addressed him as soon as he came into view, calling out 'Boy!' — the prolongation of the vowel indicating rebuke. Thus addressed, Śvetaketu, angered, replied 'Sir!' — using a form of address unfit for a kṣatriya. The king then said: 'Have you been instructed by your father?' The other answered: 'Om, indeed I have been instructed; ask, if you have any doubt.'
BR_C06_S02_V02::block-0: If so, do you know in what manner these creatures, while departing (dying), branch off in different directions? The prolongation indicates inquiry. When beings travel along a common road, at a place where the road becomes twofold, some take one path and some another — that is the divergence. The question is: do you know how creatures thus diverge? 'No,' he said. 'Then do you know how they return again to this world?' 'No, indeed,' said Śvetaketu. 'Do you know how, although beings die again and again by the established law, the other world is not filled?' 'No, indeed,' he said. 'Do you know on the offering of which oblation by number the waters, becoming endowed with human voice — that is, having transformed into human shape — rise up and speak?' 'No, indeed,' he said. 'Do you know the means of entry (pratipad) into the path of the gods (devayāna) or the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) — the action which, when performed, leads beings to attain the path of the gods or the path of the fathers? Do you know this means by which the worlds of the gods and the fathers are reached? On this matter the word of the ṛṣi, the mantra, has also been heard by us, revealing this very meaning. What is that mantra? — I have heard of two paths: one belonging to the fathers, conducting to the world of the fathers; the other belonging to the gods, leading to the gods. Who go by these two? Mortals — for it is mortals who travel by them. By these two paths this whole moving universe proceeds, that which is between the father and the mother. Who are this father and mother? They are Heaven and Earth, the two halves of the cosmic shell, for the brāhmaṇa text declares: "This earth indeed is the mother, that yonder is the father" (Śata. Brā. 13.3.9.7). Within the two halves of the cosmic shell, that is, within the realm of saṃsāra alone, do these two paths exist; they do not lead to the absolute attainment of immortality (mokṣa).' The other replied: 'I do not know even one of these questions out of this whole set,' said Śvetaketu.
BR_C06_S02_V03::block-0: Then, having stripped him of the pride born of his self-conceit in learning, the king invited Śvetaketu to lodge with him, saying: 'Let your honour stay here; let water for the feet and arghya be brought.' Disregarding that lodging, the boy ran back to his father. Coming to him, he said: 'Indeed, sir, you formerly told us that you had instructed us fully — how then is it thus?' Hearing his son's reproachful words, the father said: 'Wise one (sumedhas — having a fine intellect), how has this distress come upon you? Listen to what happened to me. The kṣatriya (raja­nya-bandhu — the term is used here as a slight) asked me five questions, and out of them I do not know even one.' When asked by his father what those questions were, the son began to recite their leading words, saying: 'These are they.'
BR_C06_S02_V04::block-0: The father, soothing his angered son, said: 'Dear child, take it from us in this way: that whatever knowledge I knew, I have told you all of it. Who is dearer to me than you, for whose sake I should hold back anything? I too do not know that which the king has asked. Therefore come, let us go there and dwell as students in the king's house for the sake of this knowledge.' The son said: 'Let your honour go alone; I cannot bear to look upon his face.' So Gautama — Āruṇi, of the Gautama gotra — came to where the seat of Pravāhaṇa Jaivali was. The two genitives stand for the nominative. The king had a fitting seat brought for Gautama who had come, had water brought through his servants, and had the priest offer him the arghya with mantras and the madhuparka. Having thus paid him honour, he said to him: 'We grant a boon to the venerable Gautama' — that is, a gift of cattle, horses and the like.
BR_C06_S02_V05::block-0: Gautama said: 'This boon has been promised to me by you; stand firm in this promise. Hold to your pledge. The very speech that you uttered in the presence of the boy, my son — that speech in the form of questions — that alone tell me; that itself is our boon.'
BR_C06_S02_V06::block-0: The king said: 'O Gautama, that which you ask belongs to the boons of the gods (daiva); ask for some boon among those of men (mānuṣa).'
BR_C06_S02_V07::block-0: Gautama said: 'It is well known to your honour that I too possess these — there is no need of what you wish to give as a human boon, since I too have abundance of gold acquired, of cows and horses, of female servants, of attendants and apparel — the supplying being understood throughout. What is already mine should not be asked from you, nor given by you; and the boon has been promised by you. You yourself know what is fitting here; the promise must be upheld by you. My intent is this: let your honour not become un-generous (avadānya, niggardly) towards us alone, while being generous everywhere else, with respect to wealth that is abundant, of unending fruit (ananta), and unbounded — extending to sons and grandsons. Let it not be that you are a non-giver to me alone, while there is nothing you would withhold from others.' Thus addressed, the king said: 'You then, O Gautama, by the established way (tīrthena, the path enjoined by śāstra) wish to obtain the vidyā from me.' Thus addressed, Gautama said: 'I approach your honour as a pupil.' For in former times, brāhmaṇas seeking knowledge in distress used to approach kṣatriyas, or kṣatriyas vaiśyas, by the pupil's mode — by speech alone, not by formal entry-rituals (upāyana) and personal service. Hence Gautama dwelt there merely by the declaration of his approach (upāyana-kīrti), without performing the upāyana-rite.
BR_C06_S02_V08::block-0: When Gautama had thus spoken about being in straits, the king, considering him aggrieved and seeking to placate him, said: 'O Gautama, do not be offended with us — do not take offence; the offence on our side should not be held to mind. As your forefathers (pitāmahas) did not take offence at our forefathers in like circumstances, so the conduct of those forefathers should be preserved by your honour also towards us. Just as this vidyā that you have asked for has, before this transmission, never dwelt in any brāhmaṇa — so you yourself know; this vidyā has always come down through the kṣatriya lineage. That established custom should also have been preserved by me, were it possible — and so I said, "Among the boons of the gods, O Gautama, ask for boons among those of men." Not that there is any boon I would not give you. Beyond this it cannot be preserved. That very vidyā too I shall now speak to you. For who else, indeed, when you speak thus, is fit to refuse you, saying "I shall not tell"? How then shall I not tell you?'
BR_C06_S02_V09::block-0: Beginning with "asau vai loko'gnir gautama" — the fourth question is being settled first; the breaking of order is because the settling of the other questions depends on the settling of this one. "That world is the fire, O Gautama" — meaning the heavenly world (dyuloka). On the heavenly world the dṛṣṭi (contemplative regard) of fire is enjoined upon what is not literally fire, just as upon woman and man. Of that fire which is the heavenly world, the sun alone is the kindling-stick (samidh), because of igniting; for by the sun this world is kindled. The rays are the smoke, by the common feature of rising up from the kindling-stick; for from the sun rays go forth, and from the kindling-stick smoke rises up in the world. Day is the flame, by the common feature of luminosity. The directions are the live coals, by the common feature of subsidence. The intermediate directions are the sparks, by the common feature of being scattered like sparks. Into that fire which is the heavenly world, possessed of such qualities, the gods Indra and the rest offer faith (śraddhā), placing it in as a substitute for the oblation-substance. From that oblation King Soma comes into being — for the manes and the brāhmaṇas. Now, who are the gods, how do they offer, and what indeed is the oblation-substance called "faith"? — to make this clear it has been told by us in connection with the agnihotra: with regard to the determination of the six categories beginning with "the going up of these two — neither do you know" (Śat. Br. 11.6.2.4) and the rest. "These two agnihotra-oblations, when offered, going up are real" (Śat. Br. 11.6.2.6,7); "they enter the mid-region" (Śat. Br. 11.6.2.6); "they make the mid-region the āhavanīya, the wind the kindling-stick, the rays themselves the bright oblation"; "they nourish the mid-region" (Śat. Br. 11.6.2.6); "thence they go up" (Śat. Br. 11.6.2.6); "they enter the sky" (Śat. Br. 11.6.2.7); "they make the sky the āhavanīya, the sun the kindling-stick" (Śat. Br. 11.6.2.7) — and so on, all this has been said. There the agnihotra-oblations together with their accessories themselves go up. Just as here, by which means and as which they are known — by the āhavanīya-fire, kindling-stick, smoke, live coals, sparks, oblation-substance — even so they go up from this world to that world. There the fire as fire-ness, the kindling-stick as kindling-stick-ness, the smoke as smoke-ness, live coals as live-coal-ness, sparks as spark-ness, the oblation-substance as the oblation-substance of milk and the rest, abide even in the unmanifest condition at the beginning of creation by the supreme subtle Self. That very existing rite of agnihotra-form together with its means, abiding in the apūrva form, again at the time of manifestation undergoes transformation, making mid-region and the rest into āhavanīya and the like. Even so now too the rite called agnihotra. Thus the entire universe being of the nature of the transformation of the apūrva of the agnihotra-oblation — for the sake of praising the two oblations the six categories beginning with "going up" and ending with "rising again toward the world" have been settled below in the karma-prakaraṇa. But here, when the maturation of karma for the agent is to be expounded, the contemplation of the five fires beginning with the heavenly-world-fire, as the means of attaining the northern path for the enjoyment of the fruit of qualified karma, is what is being enjoined; therefore the contemplation of the heavenly-world-fire and the rest is being introduced. Of these, those who are the prāṇas in the adhyātma-aspect, who here are the offerers in the agnihotra, those very ones, when transformed into the ādhidaivika aspect, become Indra and the rest; they are the offerers there in the heavenly-world-fire; and they here...
BR_C06_S02_V10::block-0: "Parjanya is the fire, O Gautama" — the second receptacle of oblation, in the order of the cycling of the two oblations. Parjanya means the deity-self (devatātman) presiding over the means of rain. Of him the year alone is the kindling-stick; for by the year, turning round through its own limbs from autumn down to summer, the fire Parjanya is kindled. The clouds are the smoke, because they arise from smoke, or because they are recognised like smoke. Lightning is the flame, by the common feature of luminosity. The thunderbolt is the live coals, by the common feature of subsided hardness. "Hrādunayaḥ" — the rumbling thunder-sounds — are the sparks, by the common feature of dispersion in many directions. "In that very fire" — this is the indication of the substratum of the oblation. "The gods" — those very ones who are the offerers — "offer King Soma"; that very Soma which arose when faith was offered into the heavenly-world-fire is offered into the second fire, the Parjanya-fire; from that oblation of Soma rain arises.
BR_C06_S02_V11::block-0: "This world is the fire, O Gautama." "This world" means that which is the receptacle of the birth and enjoyment of beings, marked by action, agent, and fruit; that is the third fire. Of that fire the earth alone is the kindling-stick; for it is by the earth, replete with the enjoyment of many beings, that this world is kindled. Fire is the smoke, by the common feature of arising from the earth as substratum; for it is taking shelter in earthy fuel-substance that fire rises up, just as smoke rises supported by the kindling-stick. Night is the flame, by the common feature of arising through connection with the kindling-stick; for it is through connection with the kindling-stick that the flame of fire arises, and likewise night arises through connection with the earth as kindling-stick — for they call the nightly darkness "the shadow of the earth." The moon is the live coals, by the common feature of being produced from it; for from the flame the live coals arise, and likewise at night the moon; or by the common feature of subsidence. The constellations are the sparks, by the common feature of being scattered like sparks. "In that very fire" and so on as before. "They offer rain" — from that oblation food arises, since it is well-known that food, namely rice and barley and the rest, is produced from rain.
BR_C06_S02_V12::block-0: "Puruṣa is the fire, O Gautama" — the well-known person possessing head, hands and the rest is the fourth fire. Of him the open mouth (vyātta = vivṛta) is the kindling-stick; for it is by the open mouth that the puruṣa shines forth in speech, recitation and the like — just as fire by the kindling-stick. The prāṇa is the smoke, by the common feature of rising from it; for from the mouth the prāṇa rises up. Speech as sound is the flame, by the common feature of being a manifester; the flame is a manifester (of objects), and likewise speech as sound is the manifester of what is to be expressed (abhidheya). The eye is the live coals, by the common feature of subsidence, or because it is the substratum of light. The ear is the sparks, by the common feature of dispersion. Into that they offer food. — But surely, the gods are not seen here as offering food! No fault: for the prāṇas are fit to be regarded as gods (devatva). At the ādhidaiva level Indra and the rest are gods; those very ones at the adhyātma level are the prāṇas; and they are the casters of food into the puruṣa; from that oblation semen (retas) arises; for semen is the transformation of food.
BR_C06_S02_V13::block-0: "Woman is the fire, O Gautama." Yoṣā means woman, the fifth substratum-fire of the oblation; her organ of generation alone is the kindling-stick; for by it she is kindled. The hairs are the smoke, by the common feature of arising from it. The yoni is the flame, by the common feature of colour. "What he does within (yad antaḥ karoti) — those are the live coals" — antaḥkaraṇa here means the act of intercourse; those are the live coals, by the common feature of being the cause of subsiding — intercourse is the cause of the subsidence of vigour and the like, and likewise the live-coal-condition is the cause of fire's subsidence. The pleasures (abhinandāḥ) — the small bits of pleasure — are the sparks, by the common feature of being minute. Into that they offer semen. From that oblation the puruṣa arises. Thus, being offered in succession into the five fires — heaven, parjanya, this world, puruṣa, woman — the waters under the names faith, soma, rain, food, semen, attaining a graded series of grossening, having been called by the word "faith," begin to bear the name puruṣa. The fourth question that was asked — "Do you know in what number of oblations being offered the waters become possessed of human voice and rising up speak?" (Bṛ. Up. 6.2.2) — that very one is settled: in the fifth oblation, when offered in the fire of the woman, the waters in the form of semen become possessed of human voice. That puruṣa, being thus born in succession, lives. For how long? — "as long as he lives," that is, as long as the karma which is the cause of his abiding in this body persists. Then, on its exhaustion, when he dies.
BR_C06_S02_V14::block-0: "Then" — at that time — they (the ṛtvik priests) carry him, the dead one, to the fire (agnaye) — that is, for the fire's purpose itself, for the final oblation. For him in the form of an oblation, the well-known fire alone is the substratum of the homa, not some imagined fire; the well-known is the kindling-stick as kindling-stick; smoke as smoke; flame as flame; live coals as live coals; sparks as sparks — that is, all is just as is well-known. Into that they offer the puruṣa as the final oblation. From that oblation, the puruṣa, of brilliant colour (bhāsvara-varṇa), of surpassing radiance, comes into being — having been refined by the rites beginning with insemination (niṣeka) and ending with the final oblation.
BR_C06_S02_V15::block-0: Now, in order to dispose of the first question he says — "Those"; who? — those who know thus this five-fire-contemplation as stated; by the word "thus" the five fires possessed of fire, kindling-stick, smoke, flame, live coals, sparks, faith and the rest are indicated; "those who know these five fires thus" is the meaning.
BR_C06_S02_V15::block-1:
Pūrvapakṣa: But surely this contemplation has the agnihotra-oblation-contemplation as its scope; for there, in the determination of the six categories beginning with "going up," it has been said, "They make heaven the āhavanīya" (Śat. Br. 11.6.2.7) and so on; here too there is much similarity — that yonder world is fire, that the sun is the kindling-stick, etc. Therefore this contemplation is a supplement of that.
Siddhānta: No; from the inclusion of question and answer regarding "in how many." Just as much as is comprehended by the question and the answer "in how many," so much is fit to be referred to by the word "thus"; otherwise the question would be useless. And, since the number is well-known (in agnihotra), the fires alone need be stated. If it be said that what is well-known is being merely restated, then it is fitting to restate just as it is presented (already), and not as "that world is the fire." If it is for indication, even so indication by the first and the last alone would be fitting. And from another śruti — for in the same context, in the Chāndogya śruti, "Knows the five fires" (Chā. Up. 5.10.10), since precisely the number five is taken up, this five-fire-contemplation is not a supplement of agnihotra. As for the similarity of fire, kindling-stick and the rest, that is for the praise of the agnihotra, as we have said. Therefore the apprehension of the path beginning with the flame is not from the cognition of the six categories beginning with "going up"; rather, by "thus" it is taking up of the topic that the path beginning with the flame is enjoined.
BR_C06_S02_V15::block-2: Now who are these "those who thus know"? — householders alone. — But surely for them the apprehension of the path beginning with smoke through the means of yajña and the like is what is intended. — No, since the means of yajña and the like obtain even for householders who do not thus know, and since the bhikṣu (renunciate) and the vānaprastha are taken up by the connection with "forest," and since the five-fire-contemplation is connected with householder-karma. Hence brahmacārins too are not included by "those who thus know"; their entry into the northern path is on the strength of smṛti — "Of the eighty-eight thousand ṛṣis of upward-flowing seed, the path is to the north of Aryaman; they obtained immortality" (?). Therefore those householders who know thus — "I am born of fire, the offspring of fire," thus, born in succession from the fires, fire-formed — those who know, and those who in the forest, the vānaprasthas and parivrājakas dwelling permanently in the forest, being endowed with faith, worship satya — Brahman in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha — and not faith itself, all these reach the flame. As long as the householders do not know the five-fire-vidyā or satya-Brahman, so long, by the cycle of the oblation of faith and the rest, when the fifth oblation is offered, born from the woman-fire, again rising up to this world they perform agnihotra and other karma; by that karma, by the smoke-path, again to the world of the manes; again by the parjanya-path, they return to this world. Then again born from the woman-fire, again performing karma — thus, like a water-wheel (ghaṭīyantra), they revolve again and again by going and coming. But when they thus know, then, released from the revolving of the water-wheel, they reach the flame. "Flame" here is not merely the blaze of fire, but the deity presiding over the flame, expressed by the word "flame," definitely established as the characteristic of the northern path; that they reach. For the parivrājakas have no direct connection with the flame of fire itself; therefore the deity alone designated by the word "flame" is taken. Hence the deity "day"; since the restriction of time of death is not established, the word "day" too is the deity; for death takes place at the exhaustion of life-span; for it cannot be restricted that one who knows thus must die only on a day, the time of death; nor do they, having departed by night, await day, since from another śruti — "As quickly as one might apply the mind, that long he goes to the sun" (Chā. Up. 8.6.5). "From day, the waxing fortnight" — conducted by the deity "day," they reach the deity of the waxing fortnight, that is, the deity of the bright fortnight. "From the waxing fortnight, the six months in which the sun goes northward" — they reach those months, conducted by the bright-fortnight deity; from "months" being plural, the six uttarāyaṇa-deities move as a group; from those months, conducted by the six-month deities, they reach the deity presiding over the deva-loka. From deva-loka, the sun; from the sun, the lightning-deity (vaidyuta) — they reach the deity presiding over lightning. To those who have reached the lightning-deity, a person dwelling in Brahmaloka, mind-born (mānasa), created by Brahman through the mind, comes and conducts them to the worlds of Brahman; "Brahmalokas" in the plural — these are understood as differentiated by lower and higher levels, both because of the use of the plural and because of the gradation of upāsana. Conducted there by that puruṣa, in those worlds of Brahman they dwell, supreme...
BR_C06_S02_V16::block-0: Now again those who do not know thus, the mere ritualists who know only the six categories connected with the agnihotra-oblation beginning with "going up" — they who win the worlds by yajña (agnihotra and the rest), by dāna (giving to those who beg outside the sacrificial enclosure, the gift of substance), by tapas (austerity outside the enclosure other than dīkṣā etc., such as kṛcchra, cāndrāyaṇa and the like) — by "worlds" being plural, gradation of the fruit there too is intended. They reach the smoke. As in the northern path, so here too the deities alone are designated by the words "smoke" and the rest — that is, they reach the smoke-deity; the carrying-forward (ātivāhika) function of the deities is just as before. From smoke they reach night, the night-deity; from her, the waning fortnight, the waning-fortnight deity; from her, the six months in which the sun goes south — they reach the specific month-deities. From the months, the world of the manes; from the world of the manes, the moon. Reaching the moon they become food; them, having become food there — just as here in the yajña the ṛtviks consume King Soma, saying "Wax! Wane!" — even so the gods consume them having reached the moon, like servants by their masters; "āpyāyasva apakṣīyasva" is not a mantra; rather, having repeatedly augmented (the soma) in the cup, having effected its diminishing by drinking, they drink again and again — that is the meaning. So too the gods, those who have obtained bodies in the soma-loka, the ritualists like serving instruments, repeatedly resting them and giving them fruit according to karma, consume them — for this is their nourishment, like the nourishment of the soma — gods consume those who have become their instruments. When for those ritualists that yajña-dāna-and-the-rest karma which led them to the soma-loka exhausts itself (paryavaiti), then they come into being into this very well-known ākāśa; those waters expressed by the word "faith," offered into the heavenly-world-fire, transformed into the soma-form, by which the body, made of water, was constructed in the soma-loka for the enjoyment of the ritualists — those, on the exhaustion of karma, like a snowball at the touch of sun, dissolve away; dissolved, they become subtle, as it were ākāśa-natured; that itself is said: "They come into being into this very ākāśa." Those ritualists again, with that body, are blown here and there by easterly and other winds, traversing the mid-region; therefore he says — "From ākāśa, wind." From wind they reach rain; this has been said — "into the parjanya-fire they offer King Soma." Then, having become rain, they fall onto this earth. Reaching the earth they become food, viz., rice, barley and the like; this has been said — "into the fire which is this world they offer rain; from that oblation food arises." Again they are offered into the puruṣa-fire, having become food, in the seed-cast (retaḥ-sic); from there, having become semen, they are offered into the woman-fire; from there they are born; rising up to the world, they perform agnihotra and other karma. Then by smoke and the rest again to the soma-loka, again to this world — thus these ritualists revolve like a water-wheel, having become a circle, they whirl about repeatedly until they know Brahman either for the northern path or for sadyo-mukti (immediate liberation); "Thus, desiring, one transmigrates" (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.6) has been said. Now again those who do not know these two paths — neither the northern nor the southern — for the apprehension of the northern or southern path...
BR_C06_S03_V01::block-0: He who desires, "May I attain greatness," should — during the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day — having observed the upasad-vow for twelve days, having gathered all herbs and fruits in a vessel or cup of udumbara wood, having swept around and smeared the place, having installed the fire and strewn the kuśa-grass, having consecrated the clarified butter according to the standard rite, having mixed the mantha (gruel) under a male nakṣatra, offer it as oblation. The mantra is: "Whatever gods, O Jātavedas (Agni), being adverse, frustrate the desires of a man — to them I offer their share; may they, satisfied, satisfy me with all desires, svāhā. She who, lying athwart, distributes (the desires) — to thee, with this stream of ghee, I sacrifice; the propitiating one am I, svāhā."
BR_C06_S03_V01::block-1:
"He who desires" — the courses of knowledge (jñāna) and karma have been declared. Among them, knowledge is independent (svatantra); karma, however, depends on the twofold means of divine and human wealth. Therefore wealth is to be acquired for the sake of karma; and that wealth must be earned by a means that incurs no transgression. For this purpose the karma called mantha is now begun, for the attainment of greatness; and once greatness is attained, wealth follows as a matter of course.

This is now stated: "He who desires" — he who, being a seeker of wealth and qualified for karma, desires; what? "May I attain mahat" — i.e., may I become great. The proper time for the prescribed mantha-karma is now stated: "in the northern course (udagayana) of the sun."
